text:
1. Title
The Hebrew title of Genesis is its first word, "Bereshith" (In the beginning), following the Hebrew tradition of taking the first word of a book as its title. Origen, the Church Father of Alexandria, also used this title when translating the Hebrew Bible into Greek.
However, the later Septuagint, reflecting the contents of Genesis, used the title "Genesis Kosmou" (the origin of the universe) or "Genesis" (origin).
This Greek title was subsequently adopted as it stands in many Bible translations, and the English title "Genesis," as well as the title "Changsegi" ("Record of the Creation of the World") in the Korean Revised Version, also follows this tradition.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The author of the Pentateuch of Moses, including Genesis, is Moses. Genesis contains a wide variety of material about the creation and the age of the patriarchs, so it would have been impossible to write it without God's inspiration. Moses received direct revelation from God, and since he was an educated man who had studied in the palace of Egypt (Acts 7:22), he was the right person to write Genesis. Jesus also said that Moses wrote these books.
(2 Peter 1:20-21) Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
(Mark 12:26) But concerning the dead rising, have you not read about the burning bush in the Book of Moses, how God told him, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?
(John 5:46-47) If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me. But since you do not believe what he wrote, how will you believe what I say?”
Date of Writing
It would be some time in the period between the exodus and the death of Moses, that is, between 1446 and 1407 B.C. This is inferred because, while Moses was with the people of Israel, he could handle the records and documents of Israel.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Motive for Writing
Genesis is the first book of the Bible and the first book of the Pentateuch of Moses. The Pentateuch was written by Moses (1527-1407 B.C.), the leader of the exodus era, as he was bringing his life to a close, and it contains the eternal standard by which the people of Israel must believe and live. It is a comprehensive summary of God's history of salvation and the Law, from the beginning through the exodus and the wilderness life.
At the time Moses wrote this book, Israel, as the descendants of Abraham, had been slaves in Egypt for about 400 years, had come out in the exodus, and, after making the covenant with God at Mount Sinai, was in the early stage of being formed in earnest as the chosen people. It was also a time of upheaval, just before the conquest of Canaan after forty years of wilderness life.
Yet their future was uncertain. In this situation Moses, receiving God's revelation, wrote Genesis in order to make clear who God is, how Israel became a chosen nation, and why Canaan became the Promised Land. Genesis was written to help the people of Israel in the wilderness understand the redemptive history of the past and to give them assurance and hope for the future.
Genesis also reveals to believers of later generations the origin and principles of redemptive history, and shows the plan of the creation of the universe, the salvation of humankind, and the salvation of all peoples through Israel.
Background
In that age, polytheism and belief in regional gods were widespread throughout the world. This was true of Mesopotamia, Egypt, Canaan, and all the other regions connected with the patriarchs. Yet even against this background, Genesis stresses the absolute monotheism of the LORD. Human beings are bound to be influenced by their age and circumstances, but Genesis transcended these. This means that the whole Bible, including Genesis, transcends the limits of its time and records the revelation and truth of God.
4. The Structure of Genesis
The History of Humankind Viewed as a Whole (chapters 1–11)
A. The Creation of Heaven and Earth (chapters 1–2)
God's sovereignty displayed in the creation of the material world
B. Adam and His Family (chapters 3–5)
The fall of man - God's sovereignty in the testing of man
C. Noah and His Family (chapters 6–11)
The flood - God's sovereignty in judgment within history
The tower of Babel - God's sovereignty in the scattering of humankind
The History of Israel Viewed in Detail (chapters 12–50)
A. Abraham (12:1–25:18)
Supernatural call - the call from his native land, his relatives, and his father's house toward the Promised Land
B. Isaac (25:19–26:35)
Supernatural birth - birth through the power of God
C. Jacob (27:1–36:43)
Supernatural protection - protecting Jacob, a man of imperfect character, through many circumstances, and bringing him back to his homeland with great wealth, wives, and children
D. Joseph (37:1–50:26)
Supernatural control - governing circumstances so that in every situation all things work together for good, and leading him to the glory of prime minister of Egypt

1. Title
It is a free rendering of "Exodus," the title in the Septuagint (LXX), the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which carries the meaning of departure or going out.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The author of the Pentateuch of Moses, including Exodus, is Moses. Not only various passages of the Old Testament (15:1, 17:24, Joshua 8:12, Isaiah 19:8) but also Jewish tradition repeatedly identify Moses, the leader of the exodus, as the author of this book.
Date of Writing
It would be some time in the period between the exodus and the death of Moses, that is, between 1446 and 1407 B.C.
It is a book written at about the time when Moses (1527-1407 B.C.), the leader of the people, was about to cross the Jordan River into the land of Canaan, so that the exodus era was gradually drawing to a close and the era of the conquest of Canaan was about to begin.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Motive for Writing
The historical records of the Pentateuch record actual historical facts as they were, but they record them from the viewpoint of redemptive history. That is, each historical event is interpreted in connection with the decisive event of Christ's redemption and the salvation of humankind. It was also written to show what meaning the major events have in the process of human salvation, which is God's ultimate purpose.
Background
Exodus is the second book of the Pentateuch of Moses. Whereas Genesis was, for Moses and his contemporaries, a retrospective record of the past history before the exodus and the wilderness life, from Exodus onward the books are experiential records, written to leave to later generations events that they had experienced directly in their own generation.
4. The Structure of Exodus
A. The Exodus and the Power of God (chapters 1-18)
1. God's plan through Moses (chapters 1-4)
1) The increase and oppression of Israel (chapter 1)
2) Moses in Egypt and Moses in Midian (chapter 2)
3) God who called Moses (chapter 3)
4) Moses, who received a new mission (chapter 4)
2. Obstruction by Pharaoh (chapters 5-11)
1) Eight demands and eight refusals
2) The ten plagues
3. The fulfillment of the exodus (chapters 12-18)
1) From Goshen to the Red Sea: the Passover and the leading of Israel (chapters 12, 13)
2) The crossing of the Red Sea: the judgment of the pursuing Egyptian army and the deliverance of Israel (chapter 14)
3) From the Red Sea to Sinai: the song of praise for the exodus and the tent before Mount Sinai (chapters 15-18)
B. The Law and the Holiness of God (chapters 19-24)
1. Preparation for the Law (the Sinai covenant) (chapter 19)
2. The Law of the Ten Commandments (chapter 20)
3. The laws for social life (chapters 21-23)
4. The covenant of the Law with God (chapter 24)
C. The Tabernacle and the Wisdom of God (chapters 25-40)
1. The design of the tabernacle (chapters 25-31)
1) The ark of the covenant, the table, and the lampstand (chapter 25)
2) The tent, the frames, and the veil (chapter 26)
3) The altar of burnt offering, the court hangings, and the olive oil (chapter 27)
4) The holy garments of the priests (chapter 28)
5) The consecration of the priesthood (chapter 29)
6) The altar of incense, the bronze basin, the anointing oil, and the incense (chapter 30)
7) The craftsmen of the tabernacle, and the Sabbath (chapter 31)
2. The delay of the tabernacle (chapters 32-34)
1) The apostasy of Israel, judgment, and the intercession of Moses (chapter 32)
2) Moses, who saw the glory of God (chapter 33)
3) Forty days on Mount Sinai the second time (chapter 34)
3. The completion of the tabernacle (chapters 35-40)
1) The offering of materials for the tabernacle (chapter 35)
2) The framework and curtains of the tabernacle (chapter 36)
3) The sacred furnishings of the tabernacle (chapters 37-38)
4) The garments of the priests (chapter 39)
5) The completion of the tabernacle (chapters 39-40)
6) The glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle (chapter 40)
5. Lessons from Exodus
1) Lessons shown through "Moses," the man of God
Understanding Moses and learning from the events shown through Moses is important for understanding Jesus Christ and for examining ourselves.
1) Moses, growing up as a man of God
Moses was saved from death through the compassion of Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:6) and grew up under parents of faith (Exodus 2:9-10, Hebrews 11:23-24). From childhood he was raised with instruction in his Hebrew identity.
2) Moses in Egypt
As the son of Pharaoh's daughter, he learned the learning of Egypt and was a man mighty in words and deeds (Acts 7:22-23). But he relied on his own strength and acted in the heat of his temper, and he made the mistake of killing an Egyptian (Exodus 2:12). In the end he had to flee to the wilderness of Midian (Exodus 2:14-15).
3) The heart needed to become a man of God
Moses did not turn away from the suffering of his people, and he chose to abandon the wealth of Egypt and to be with the people of God (Hebrews 11:25-26). Moses was a man with a right heart. He refused to be called the son of the princess, refused the pleasures of Egypt, refused the treasures, chose to suffer with the people of God, and had a good heart to deliver the people of God; it was because of these things that God trained him.
4) Forty years of training in the wilderness
For forty years in Midian, tending sheep, he was changed into a humble and meek man (Numbers 12:3). Through deep fellowship with God he laid down his own righteousness and learned to rely on the power of God.
5) God's call and ministry
After being tempered in the wilderness, Moses received the call of God (Exodus 3:4, 10). But he still felt his own inadequacy and hesitated (Exodus 4:1, 10, 13). In the end he was established as the leader who would lead Israel out of Egypt.
6) The imperfect Moses
Moses also made mistakes. Because he did not circumcise his son, God sought to kill Moses (Exodus 4:24), and in the wilderness he heard the word "speak to the rock to bring out water," but he struck the rock and brought out the water, thus disobeying the command; and as though he himself were giving the water, he came to commit the sin of obscuring the glory of God (Numbers 20:7-12). When we see that even a man as meek and as well-tempered as Moses sinned, we ourselves should also take heed to the word of God and rely on it.
7) Moses, a man of faith
Moses was exalted as the one who wrote the Pentateuch (Luke 24:27, 44), he was a man who spoke with God as with a friend (Exodus 33:11, Numbers 12:8), and he received the holy Law of God. He became the man who protected the people of Israel by instituting the Passover and the sprinkling of blood. He was raised to the ranks of faith in Hebrews chapter 11 (Hebrews 11:24-29).
He was faithful as a mediator for Israel (Hebrews 3:1-2, 5-6), and he appears as a prophet who prefigures Jesus Christ (Deuteronomy 18:15, Acts 7:37). Also, he became a great man of God who appeared in glory on the Mount of Transfiguration (Matthew 17:3).

2) We should examine the events revealed through the event of the Passover (the blood of the lamb).
3) The crossing of the Red Sea has great meaning not only for the people of Israel but also for ourselves.
4) The giving of the Law and the sin of Israel enable those who have been saved to understand clearly the holy will of God.
5) The design and completion of the tabernacle, and the presence and fullness of the LORD, give wisdom for knowing Jesus Christ.
The structure of the tabernacle:
Exodus 25-31 records the design of the tabernacle, chapters 32-34 the wickedness of man who broke the Law, and chapters 35-41 the construction of the tabernacle.
The meaning of the tabernacle:
It is the place where sinful man meets God, God's answer to the broken Law, and a wondrous providence that saves sinners.
The main elements of the tabernacle:
The gate: The Law is not the way that leads sinners to God. Instead, one must approach through the gate of grace.
The altar: A picture of the cross (conversion); it represents the cross of Christ, who became the atoning sacrifice. "The wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23), and redemption is accomplished through a substitutionary death.
The basin: A life set apart from the world (cleansed by the word)
The white linen (the fence): It symbolizes the Law, which is the perfect righteousness of God, and sinners cannot approach through it.
The main elements of the Holy Place in the tabernacle:
The bread of the Presence: Fellowship with the Lord (the bread of life)
The lampstand: The work of the Holy Spirit (the light of the world, testimony)
The altar of incense: The highest of the furnishings of the Holy Place; the highest-level act in the life of a believer is the act of prayer and intercession
The veil: A symbol of the body of Jesus. The way into the Most Holy Place (a life of obedience to the word)
The mercy seat: Peace and victory enjoyed under the blood of Jesus
The bread: Being ground into flour and baked in the oven symbolizes the sacrifice and suffering of Jesus.
The oil: The Holy Spirit (the only source of light)
The golden lampstand: The Lord, who is the head
The six branches: The six branches on each side symbolize the members of the body, coming out through the wound in the side (the vine and the branches, John 15:5)
The sea otter skin that covered the Holy Place of the tabernacle:
Although it looks lacking, being yellowish-brown and gray, it has the characteristic of being waterproof and enduring the weather. This means that although the human appearance of Jesus seems unattractive on the outside (Isaiah 53:2), He is perfect within.
The symbolism of the materials used in the tabernacle:
Acacia wood: humanity
Gold: deity
Silver: the atoning blood
Bronze: holiness
The meaning of the colors seen in the tabernacle:
Purple: kingship
Scarlet: sacrifice and blood
White (fine linen): righteousness
Blue: holiness
The tabernacle prefigures the redemptive work of Jesus Christ, and through it we can enjoy complete victory and peace.

1. Title
This book came to be called Leviticus because of the Septuagint. Since its contents contain an unusually large amount of teaching about sacrificial rites, the translators of the Septuagint named this book in Greek "Leveitikon," meaning "concerning the Levites." This name was used as "Leviticus" in the Latin version, the Vulgate, and what translated it is the Korean title "Leviticus."
However, the original Hebrew name of Leviticus was "Vayikra." This means "And He called." This indicates that the story continues from Exodus. In Exodus, God spoke from a mountain which it was forbidden to approach; now in Leviticus God is present with them in the tent of meeting and speaks.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The author of the Pentateuch of Moses, including Exodus, is Moses. Not only various passages of the Old Testament (15:1, 17:24, Joshua 8:12, Isaiah 19:8) but also Jewish tradition repeatedly identify Moses, the leader of the exodus, as the author of this book.
Date of Writing
Leviticus was very likely written after Exodus was written. Since it was a revelation given during the fifty days from the first day of the first month of the second year after the exodus, when the tent of meeting was set up, until the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, when they left Mount Sinai (Numbers 10:11), the date of writing of this book can be said to be a time falling between the beginning of the second year after the exodus (1445 B.C.) and 1406 B.C.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Genesis deals with the creation and fall of man, / Exodus deals with redemption.
Leviticus deals with how a person redeemed by blood is united with the Lord and has fellowship with Him.
Leviticus clearly shows that "there is no way to approach the holy God except by blood." Leviticus may well be called "the book of blood."
1. Being cleansed of sin and made clean through sacrifice (Hebrews 9:22, Hebrews 10).  2. The cleansed people being sanctified and walking in the light (1 John 1:5-2:6, Ephesians 5:8-14, 2 Corinthians 6:14-18, 2 Timothy 3:15-17).
Background
Leviticus was written after the exodus, immediately after the covenant was made with God at Mount Sinai. It is the revelation that God gave to Moses (Leviticus 1:1) in the situation immediately after the tabernacle was completed, in the first year after the people of Israel escaped from Egypt, around 1446 B.C. (Exodus 40:17).
Moses received the Law directly from God in the wilderness of Sinai, that is, around Mount Sinai, and it was a time when the people of Israel lived encamped around the tabernacle. At that time the people of Israel, who had long been enslaved in Egypt, had come out in the exodus by the grace of God, but their faith and way of life were not yet established.
Therefore, before entering the land of Canaan, they needed to break away from the polytheistic culture and idolatry of Egypt, to establish the laws and ordinances by which to live as the holy people of God, and to learn how to serve God.
Motive for Writing
Leviticus concentrates on holiness and sacrifice among the laws that God gave to the people of Israel.
God said, "Because I am holy, you too must be holy" (Leviticus 19:2), and teaches the people of Israel how they must live a holy life. It presents ways of practicing holiness in everyday life (food, disease, the holiness code, and so on).
The sacrificial system and atonement
To restore the right relationship between God and the people of Israel, it stresses the importance of sacrifice and atonement.
It records the way of approaching God and the ordinances for receiving forgiveness of sin (the burnt offering, grain offering, peace offering, sin offering, guilt offering, and so on).
Establishing the duties and role of the priesthood
It entrusted the office of priest to Aaron and his descendants (the tribe of Levi), and prescribed the methods and duties of serving in the tabernacle.
It presented the standards (purity, dedication, and so on) for becoming a holy priest.
Ethics and morality as the people of God
It teaches not merely religious duties but also how to maintain holiness in moral and social life.
It makes clear the ethical ordinances for living a life set apart from the Gentile nations (for example, sexual purity, fair judgment, the law of helping the poor, and so on).
4. The Structure of Leviticus
The Way of Approaching the Holy God (chapters 1-16)
1) Offering sacrifices to God for atonement [the five offerings] (chapters 1-7) - prefiguring various parts of the work of Jesus Christ
Sacrifices with a pleasing aroma (voluntary)
Burnt offering - giving Himself voluntarily to God on the cross, complete devotion to God (John 10:18, 1 Peter 2:24)
Grain offering - the perfect life of Jesus as a human being during His public ministry (the offering of grain)
Peace offering - reconciliation with God, the fact of reconciliation made by His becoming the propitiation, the offering of reconciliation, a fragrant offering (1 John 4:9-10, 1 John 2:2, Ephesians 5:2, Romans 3:25)
Offerings without aroma (compulsory) - the figure of Christ who bore and carried our sins and transgressions (Isaiah 53:5-6)
Sin offering - an offering for sin
Guilt offering - an offering for guilt, an offering without aroma
The burnt offering + guilt offering + sin offering have no portion for man and belong only to Jesus. What we have a share in are the grain offering and the peace offering. The life of Jesus: through the life of the grain offering + peace offering -> He offered the guilt offering + sin offering.  Ourselves: settling sin through the guilt offering + sin offering -> a life of the grain offering and peace offering. (Psalms 50:5, 14)
2) Approaching through the priests (chapters 8-10)
3) Approaching through purity (chapters 11-15)
4) Approaching through the Day of Atonement (chapters 16-17)
The Way of Holy Living (chapters 17-27)
1) Holy living through the Law (chapter 17)
2) Holy living through ethical standards (chapters 18-22)
3) Holy living through the festivals (chapters 23-25)
Passover: the death of Christ (Exodus 12:13, 1 Corinthians 5:7).
Feast of Unleavened Bread: the holy life of the Christian (1 Corinthians 5:8). They ate unleavened bread (bread without leaven) for seven days. From the time of being saved through Jesus Christ until the Lord comes, a holy life is required.
Feast of Firstfruits: the resurrection of Christ; one sheaf of the first ears of grain was offered. It was offered on the day after the Sabbath so that it might be accepted. The day Jesus rose.
Pentecost: on the basis of the death and resurrection of Jesus, the Holy Spirit came down (Acts 1:3-5, Acts 2:1-4). Leaven was put into the bread and it was offered. The two loaves of bread refer to Jews and Gentiles, and that leaven was put in shows that sinners will be accepted (Ephesians 2:11-18).
Feast of Trumpets: a trumpet of assembly, meaning the gathering of the saints (1 Thessalonians 4:16-18, 1 Corinthians 15:51-52). At the same time it speaks of gathering into their own land the Jews who had been scattered throughout the world.
Day of Atonement: it speaks of the salvation of Israel through their repentance (Zechariah 12:10-14, Ezekiel 39:26-27, Romans 11:25-26).
Feast of Tabernacles (Ingathering, Booths): a type of the millennial kingdom. That they also gather for a solemn assembly on the eighth day is a type of the eternal heavenly kingdom.
4) Holy living through blessings and curses (chapter 26)
5) Holy living through vows (chapter 27)

1. Title
In the 3rd century B.C., in Alexandria, seventy Jews translated the Hebrew Bible into a Greek Bible. The Hebrew name of this book is "Bemidbar," which means "in the wilderness" and was taken from the first words of the book; meanwhile, the book title "Arithmoi" given by the Septuagint is the origin of the English word "arithmetic," and the English version's "NUMBERS" means numbers. The book was titled Numbers (Minsugi in Korean) because the title reflects the fact that the number of the children of Israel was counted twice, in the first half and the second half (chapters 1-4 and 26).
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
It has historical and stylistic consistency with the Pentateuch of Moses, and in the text the allusion to Mosaic authorship ("The LORD said to Moses") appears more than 80 times.
Date of Writing
The period between after the exodus and before the death of Moses, that is, between 1446 and 1407 B.C., in the latter part.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
At the time the Pentateuch was being written, the people of Israel were still a newly born community of God's chosen people. They were the descendants of Abraham, a people who had lived as slaves in Egypt for about 400 years and then, by the grace of God, experienced the glorious escape called the exodus. It was not long since they had made the covenant with God at Mount Sinai, and it was the early period of the history of the chosen people, when not even one generation had yet passed.
This point in time was also a time of upheaval, when, bringing to a close forty years of wilderness life, they were about to begin in earnest the war of conquest before Canaan, the "Promised Land," in accordance with the covenant that God had promised to their ancestors long ago, from the time of Abraham.
At this important point, Moses, the leader of the exodus era, looking at the end of one era and the beginning of a new one, wrote the Pentateuch, inspired by the Holy Spirit, for the people of his own day and also for all the descendants who would settle in the land of Canaan in the future. That is, it is the word of God for those who had to live out the rest of their lives in the midst of fierce war, and for all the generations who would live as the people of God even after settling.
Motive for Writing
The core content of the whole Pentateuch can be summarized in two main points. The first is the history in which Israel, the chosen people of God, was formed; the second is the Law that God gave.
First, from before the foundation of the world God set apart in a special way the people of Israel, whose origin lies in the twelve sons of Jacob, and had been leading them. In the whole course of how they came to go down to Egypt, the story of their living as slaves in Egypt for about 400 years, and their passage through the wilderness for forty years after the exodus, God's guidance and sovereignty are revealed. Throughout all this history, God established Israel as the chosen people at the center of redemptive history.
And now Israel, as the people of God, must fulfill its role as God's firstborn nation, revering God above and standing before all peoples below. For this, God gave them the Law, and each book of the Pentateuch conveys that Law in a variety of contexts.
The Pentateuch and Numbers
Genesis is the story of the ancestors of Israel, the chosen people, and covers the history from the creation of heaven and earth in the beginning to the migration of the twelve sons of Jacob to Egypt. So the remaining four books apart from Genesis, that is, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, are written centering on the events and the Law of the exodus era, and each book has a different emphasis:
Exodus and Numbers are records centered on events.
Leviticus, on the other hand, is a book that focuses on the various legal provisions concerning sacrifices, purification, festivals, and so on connected with the tabernacle, and Deuteronomy contains Moses, on the verge of death, telling the second generation of the exodus once more, in the form of a sermon, the history of the exodus and the Law.
Comparing Exodus and Numbers, Exodus centers on Israel's escape from Egypt, the events of the early wilderness period, and the journey up to the completion of the tabernacle (the first day of the first month of the second year of the exodus), and also deals with laws such as the Ten Commandments. Numbers covers the whole of the wilderness life from the first month of the second year of the exodus to the tenth month of the fortieth year, and some laws are inserted here and there in the form of narrative.
4. The Structure of Numbers
1) The old generation of the people of Israel preparing to set out for the conquest of Canaan (chapters 1-10)
2) The sins and failures of the old generation of the people of Israel (chapters 11-25)
3) The new generation of the people of Israel preparing for the conquest of Canaan (chapters 26-36)
※ The 16 major events of Numbers and their meaning

No.|Event|Meaning|Chapter and verse|
1|The first census of the army at Mount Sinai|Reorganization as an army for the effective carrying out of the work of conquering Canaan|1:1-46|
2|The appointment of the seventy elders|Reorganization of the command structure in order to lead the people more systematically|11:16-25|
3|The incident of Miriam's leprosy|Prohibition of private slander against a servant whom God has appointed|12:4-16|
4|The sending of spies into Canaan|A clear contrast between faith and unbelief regarding God's promise|13:1-33|
5|The great rebellion at Kadesh|The cause of the 38 years of wandering in the wilderness and a type of the final judgment|14:1-10|
6|The rebellion and judgment of Korah and his company|The perversity of trying to cancel, from human motives, authority entrusted by God|16:1-35|
7|Aaron's staff that budded|God's measure to end the problem of religious leadership|17:1-13|
8|Moses' mistake with the water at Meribah|The cause of Moses, the leader of the exodus, being refused entry into Canaan|20:2-13|
9|The death of Aaron|Retribution for sin and the finitude of the human priesthood|20:22-29|
10|The bronze serpent incident|A type of the cross of Jesus in the New Testament era|21:4-9|
11|The false prophet Balaam incident|The futility of human attempts to obstruct God's redemptive history|22:1-24:25|
12|The righteous indignation of Phinehas|An expression of zeal of faith seeking to restore the purity of Israel|25:1-9|
13|The second census of the army on the plains of Moab|Reorganizing the military organization and preparing the distribution of inheritance. Explicit change of generation|26:1-65|
14|The request of the daughters of Zelophehad for an inheritance|The occasion by which the daughters' right of inheritance was secured|27:1-11|
15|The designation of Joshua as the new leader|The unfolding of continuous redemptive history and God's sovereign choice|27:12-23|
16|The distribution of the land east of the Jordan|An exceptional event outside the principle of distributing the inheritance|32:1-42|

4. Characteristics of Numbers
Characteristics of the Contents
Scope of the record
Exodus records the journey from the escape from Egypt to Sinai, and Leviticus records the Law received during the stay at Sinai, whereas Numbers records the course from the departure from Sinai to the wilderness of Moab opposite Canaan.
Census
The two censuses carried out at God's command are recorded in detail.
Event-centered record
Numbers is not intended as a continuous historical record, but was written with events at its center, for the purpose of instruction and warning.
Characteristics of time
Most of the 40-year history is concentrated on events of the second year and the fortieth year after the exodus, and the 38 years in between are hardly recorded at all. This shows that the Bible is not mere history but a record of redemptive history that deals only with the parts important for human salvation.
Sinfulness and the character of God
Through various events and institutions it reveals human sinfulness and folly, and it shows God's justice and mercy in response to them, and everywhere prefigures Jesus Christ.
Spiritual meaning
Through the process by which Israel, freed from slavery in Egypt, enters the Promised Land as the chosen people, Numbers explains the process by which a human being who was a slave of the devil is saved by the grace of God and becomes a free child of God,
and through the 38 years of wilderness life it explains the life of faith by which a saved believer lives in the world until reaching heaven.
The God of Numbers
In Numbers, God appears as One who is both majestic and merciful. During the 38 years of wilderness life recorded in Numbers, the people of Israel rebelled against and defied God many times, and each time He called them to account for their sins and punished them, but on the other hand He did not destroy them utterly; again He showed mercy and forgave them, and in the end He leads them into the land of Canaan. Through Numbers God shows that He judges that sinful generation, but does not forsake the people He has once chosen.
(Numbers 14:18) ‘The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, forgiving iniquity and transgression. Yet He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished; He will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon their children to the third and fourth generation.’
Numbers and Christ
Numbers also contains prophecies and types concerning Jesus Christ.
1) Prophecy concerning Christ
The false prophet Balaam tried to curse Israel, but through God's compelling intervention he instead prophesied a blessing on Israel, and among these he prophesied concerning Jesus Christ.
(Numbers 24:17) I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel. He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth.
2) Types concerning Christ
① The bronze serpent in the wilderness, which prefigures the suffering of Jesus on the cross (Numbers 21:4-9)
② The rock that brings out water, which prefigures Christ, who quenches the thirst of our souls with the living water of the word (Numbers 20:11)
③ The manna, which explains Christ, who is the word, the food of the soul, and life (Numbers 11:7)
④ Aaron's budding staff, which explains Christ, who by His resurrection gives eternal new life (Numbers 17:8)
⑤ The cities of refuge, which explain Christ, who is the shelter for sinners to flee to (Numbers 35:15)
⑥ The water for cleansing impurity, which explains Christ, who cleanses sinners (Numbers 19)
Numbers and the Church
Numbers begins with the matter of "the numbering of the congregation" (Numbers 1:2).
Unlike the other books of the Pentateuch, Numbers mainly records the journey and events of the wilderness life of the congregation of Israel. As the sermon of Deacon Stephen of the early church referred to Israel in the wilderness as the "church in the wilderness" (Acts 7:38), the journey of the congregation of Israel in Numbers up to Canaan can be called a type of church life today.
Just as God led the congregation of Israel in the wilderness with the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, fed them with manna, and supplied them with water from the rock, so today also God leads the church by His word, supplies all that the church needs, protects it, and guides it.
Seeing how the people of Israel were punished for doing wrong during the wilderness life, believers and the church living today should receive instruction and take it as a warning so as not to commit the same errors.

1. Title
The Korean title Sinmyeonggi means a book that explains the commandments in detail. In Hebrew it derives from "Haddevarim" (Devarim), a word meaning "the words." The English title Deuteronomy is a compound of the Greek words "deuteros" and "nomos," and has the meaning "second law."
This is because the first law was given at Mount Sinai, and before the entry into Canaan that word was explained anew and in detail; for this reason Deuteronomy is called the "second law." In that sense, Deuteronomy means "the second law."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Considering that the contents or purpose of writing of Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell sermon for the second generation of the exodus, who stood just before taking the land of Canaan, it is certain that Deuteronomy was written by Moses (Deuteronomy 31:9, 24-26). Deuteronomy was written on the plains of Moab, toward the end of the journey, after the people of Israel had wandered in the wilderness for forty years.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
Deuteronomy was written when the new generation of Israel, who after the exodus, at Kadesh-barnea, facing the Promised Land, had been under twenty years of age or not yet born when the people turned back to the wilderness as a result of disobedience, had at last crossed the Brook of Zered and stood before the conquest of the land of Canaan. Because he himself could not enter the land of Canaan, Moses, facing death, left words like a testament for those among the people of Israel who had been born in the wilderness and had not experienced the exodus, and for those who had experienced it as children.
The old generation had died in the wilderness because of disobedience, the new generation stood before the great mission of conquering the land of Canaan, and Moses would die east of the Jordan and could not go with them into the land of Canaan; in this situation Moses repeated once more the lessons and ordinances that the people of Israel must surely remember, and was preparing the new generation.
Motive for Writing
① The purpose is to teach the words that must be kept at the point when the old generation had died in the wilderness because of disobedience and the new generation was entering Canaan.
② The purpose is to point out past errors so that they would never again follow in the footsteps of the old generation.
③ The purpose is to have them receive blessings in both body and spirit by obeying the word of God.
④ The purpose is to show the justice and love of God.
4. The Structure of Deuteronomy
Deuteronomy is a book composed of three sermons that Moses delivered to the people of Israel when they were encamped in the wilderness of Moab, just before entering the Promised Land. That is, the Law and all the ordinances of God that had been conveyed since the second year of the exodus were proclaimed again through Moses around the end of the fortieth year of the exodus.
(Deuteronomy 5:5) “At that time I was standing between the LORD and you to declare to you the word of the LORD, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. And He said:”
This was absolutely necessary for the new generation of the people, who had not directly experienced the crossing of the Red Sea or the receiving of the Law at Mount Sinai. When the old generation of the time of the exodus, who had cast away grace and rebelled, perished in the wilderness, and when Moses' own death drew near, it was necessary for him to renew the covenant for the new generation and to make their dedication to God explicit.
Moreover, Moses' three sermons have respectively a retrospective, a self-reflective, and a covenantal character.
1) Moses' first sermon - a retrospective on past history (the past) / Deuteronomy 1-4
In his first sermon, Moses recalls the events of the forty years since the exodus and stresses that God's salvation is not a mere theory or idea but an actual historical event. And by reminding them that there was blessing when they obeyed the word of God and judgment when they disobeyed, he seeks to urge the new generation to make a decision of faith. In a word, it is a sermon summarizing the journey from the time of receiving the Law to arriving at the Jordan River.
2) Moses' second sermon - a reinterpretation of the various laws (the present) / Deuteronomy 5-26
This sermon explains the concrete content of the obedience that God desires and the right way of serving God. Moses reinterprets the meaning of the various laws given to Israel, and deals broadly with the Ten Commandments first, then the ritual law, civil law, social law, and so on. Combining exhortation and warning, he stresses the importance of the Law.
① Israel's moral obligations centered on the Ten Commandments (Deuteronomy 5-11)
② Israel's ritual obligations concerning sacrifices, tithes, and festivals (Deuteronomy 12:1, 16:17)
③ Included are the ordinances for leaders for a just society (Deuteronomy 16:18, 18:22), mutual obligations among people (Deuteronomy 19:1, 26:19), religious law, criminal law, military law, property law, moral law, and so on.
3) Moses' third sermon - a view of future history (the future) / Deuteronomy 27-30
Moses' third sermon is the concluding sermon of Deuteronomy, and at the same time the conclusion of the whole Pentateuch. This sermon gives exhortation to keep the Law and warns of the blessings and curses that will be given according to obedience and disobedience (Deuteronomy 27-28). Among these, what is especially important is the fact that the Sinai covenant was renewed on the plains of Moab.
4) Moses' final appearance - the death of Moses and the appearance of Joshua / Deuteronomy 31-34
This part is the scene in which, as Moses, the author of the Pentateuch and the leader of Israel's history of salvation from Exodus to Deuteronomy, meets death, one era of redemptive history is brought to a close and a new era begins. It contains historical facts such as the appointment of Joshua as successor, Moses' farewell address, and his burial.

4. The Theme of Deuteronomy
The theme of Deuteronomy can be seen, in a word, as the principle of God's creation and providence in history, or it can be understood as the practical lessons of past history. Its core can be summarized in the truth that when one obeys God, blessing follows, and when one disobeys, only curse follows.
In the end, it can be expressed with the saying that life is a choice. Deuteronomy 28 describes well the results of obedience and disobedience, and when the amounts written are compared, the warnings against disobedience are greater than the content about obedience, by a ratio of about 1:4. This can be said to be because God, who knows human nature well, stressed the warnings against disobedience all the more. Likewise, it can be confirmed that throughout the whole Bible, there is far more mention of hell than of heaven.
(Deuteronomy 10:12-13) “And now, O Israel, what does the LORD your God ask of you but to fear the LORD your God by walking in all His ways, to love Him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments and statutes of the LORD that I am giving you this day for your own good?”
In these words there appear five verbs expressing action. Summed up in a word, this is "obedience." Those verbs are "fear," "walk," "love," "serve," and "keep." Then why does God demand obedience? It is for the reason "for your own good," that is, for our benefit.
Paul also reminds us that this book is not only for Israel but contains a lesson for all of us.
(1 Corinthians 9:10) “Isn’t He actually speaking on our behalf? Indeed, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest.”
(Deuteronomy 5:1) “Then Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: Hear, O Israel, the statutes and ordinances that I declare in your hearing this day. Learn them and observe them carefully.”
In this verse as well the verbs "listen," "learn," and "keep and do" are used, and this shows the core of the exhortation that is repeated throughout Deuteronomy. The great lesson that Deuteronomy stresses from beginning to end is precisely obedience. And not mere literal obedience, but obedience that wells up from affection toward God and a heart of reverence. This can be called the overall theme of Deuteronomy.
4. Characteristics of Deuteronomy
① If Genesis shows the fall of man, Exodus redemption and the power of God, Leviticus union through atonement, and Numbers God's guidance, testing, and training, then Deuteronomy is the book that shows the faithful God. It can be called a kind of abridged edition of the Pentateuch, summarizing and organizing the history of the exodus, which proceeded centered on Moses himself, and the various laws given through him.
② Deuteronomy is a sermon that, through a retrospective of past history and a reinterpretation of the Law, urges faith and dedication on the second generation of the exodus and on all the descendants.
③ It is a book in which, not only the period immediately after the era of the conquest of Canaan, but even the ordinances concerning the kings and prophets of the monarchy period that would come afterward are presented concretely from a prophetic perspective.
④ From Genesis to Numbers there is no concrete revelation of God's love, but in Deuteronomy the direct revelation of God's love appears repeatedly.
⑤ Of the books of the Pentateuch, Deuteronomy is the one Jesus quoted most. It is quoted in 21 of the 27 books of the New Testament, and appears to be quoted a total of 83 times (Matthew 4:4-10, Mark 7:10, 10:19, etc.).
⑥ It is a book in which the word "land" appears about 200 times, showing a strong emphasis on, and preoccupation with, the Promised Land.
Deuteronomy and Christ
1) Christ as Mediator
(Deuteronomy 5:5) “At that time I was standing between the LORD and you to declare to you the word of the LORD, because you were afraid of the fire and would not go up the mountain. And He said:”
(Galatians 3:20) “A mediator is unnecessary, however, for only one party; but God is one.”
(1 Timothy 2:5) “For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,”
After Adam and Eve sinned and were driven out of the garden of Eden, the relationship between God and man was broken. Of course, through prophets such as Moses, fellowship between God and man was possible to some extent, but it was temporary and partial, individual, and possible only in a limited place. But Jesus Christ came to this earth and became the eternal Mediator.
2) Christ as Prophet
(Deuteronomy 18:15-19) “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.…I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him. And I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name.”
Moses was not the perfect prophet. He prophesied the coming of Jesus Christ and said, "You shall listen to him." This word is connected with the word spoken to Peter, James, and John on the Mount of Transfiguration.
(Matthew 17:1-5) “After six days Jesus took with Him Peter, James, and John the brother of James, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. There He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light.…This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!”
(Deuteronomy 34:9-11) “Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him…Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses…”
By showing in advance, through events of the Old Testament era, as types, the things that would happen in the New Testament era, it is God's way to give assurance that the work of God is accomplished within His plan and providence. In that respect Moses can be called a type of Jesus Christ. He was the liberator of the nation, a prophet, and one who even carried out the roles of priest and king. All these offices prefigure the appearance of Jesus.
Also, by the inspiration of God, Moses realized the coming of a Savior like himself but far greater, that is, Jesus Christ.
(Acts 3:22) “Moses said, ‘The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers…’”
The aspects of Christ that Moses prefigures are very diverse. Besides the aspects of liberator of the nation, mediator, prophet, priest, and king, his birth background, the danger of his infancy, being rejected by his own people, and his dedication to the people to the end all prefigure Jesus as well.
3) Christ as Savior
(Deuteronomy 21:22-23) “If a man has committed a sin worthy of death, and he is executed, and you hang his body on a tree,…anyone who is hung on a tree is under God’s curse”
(Galatians 3:13-14) “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us…”
The reason the sinless Jesus died on the cross was to take the place of us sinners. No one has kept the Law perfectly, and the wages of sin is death. God cannot forgive anyone without satisfying the demands of the Law. Jesus was hung on the cross and satisfied the Law, and because of this, the way was opened to be made righteous not by the Law but by faith.

1. Title
The title of this book, "Joshua," was given after the name of Joshua son of Nun, who, as the successor of Moses, led the war of conquest of the land of Canaan with the help of God.
This book also agrees with the titles of the Septuagint, "Iesous Naus" (Joshua son of Nun), and of the Latin Bible (Vulgate), "Liber Josue" (the Book of Joshua).
2. Author and Date of Writing
The book of Joshua is a historical book covering from the death of Moses to after the death of Joshua, and it is hard to think that Joshua alone wrote all of it. However, it is quite possible that Joshua personally wrote a large part of it.
Author
(Joshua 24:26-27) Joshua recorded these things in the Book of the Law of God. Then he took a large stone and set it up there under the oak that was near the sanctuary of the LORD. And Joshua said to all the people, “You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us, and it will be a witness against you if you ever deny your God.”
Here it is recorded that Joshua personally wrote the word of God in the book of the Law.

(Joshua 18:4) Appoint three men from each tribe, and I will send them out to survey the land and map it out, according to the inheritance of each. Then they will return to me
(Joshua 18:9-10) So the men departed and went throughout the land, mapping it city by city into seven portions. Then they returned with the document to Joshua at the camp in Shiloh. And Joshua cast lots for them in the presence of the LORD at Shiloh, where he distributed the land to the Israelites according to their divisions.
It is recorded that men were sent out tribe by tribe to survey the land and record it on a map, and that Joshua then distributed it himself. This shows that much of the content of the book of Joshua was recorded in real time in the days of Joshua.
The events after Joshua's death (for example, Caleb's conquest, Othniel's victory, the migration of the tribe of Dan, Joshua's burial, and so on) are parts supplemented by later historians under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit (see 2 Peter 1:20-21).
Jewish tradition too holds that Joshua wrote most of the book of Joshua.
Just as Moses wrote Deuteronomy, which includes the content after his own death, it is generally considered that the book of Joshua was also written mainly by Joshua, with later historians adding a part.
Date of Writing
The date of writing of this book is around 1390 B.C., but the dates of the other added portions are presumed to be later than that.
From the fact that Sidon is mentioned as a great city (11:8, 19:28), we can tell that the added portion was written in the 12th century B.C. Also, the fact that the Phoenicians are called Sidonians, after the old name, likewise shows that it was added in the 12th century B.C. Accordingly, most scholars today regard its final date as the end of the period when Othniel was active as judge (1370-1330 B.C.).
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
Joshua was the person who, after the death of Moses, was set up as the leader of Israel and led the war of the conquest of Canaan. After forty years of wilderness life following the exodus, the people of Israel were staying on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan River, preparing for the conquest of Canaan.
In the land of Canaan, various peoples (the Canaanites, Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites, and so on) lived scattered as city-states, each king ruling independently, and a culture centered on strong city-states had taken root. In Canaan the polytheistic beliefs of Baal, Asherah, and others were widespread, and sexually corrupt religious rituals were at the center.
God commanded Israel not to make covenants with the foreign peoples, not to serve their gods, and to drive out the Canaanite peoples thoroughly. Israel was composed of twelve tribes, but they were not people who had received formal military training. Leading these people of Israel, Joshua, as the successor of Moses, had to fulfill at the same time the roles of spiritual leader and military leader.
Motive for Writing
The book of Joshua is not a mere record of war, but a book of the Bible that shows how the Promised Land given by God was conquered and distributed. The book of Joshua emphasizes the following.
God is the One who faithfully keeps His promises. Obedience brings victory, and disobedience produces defeat.  Israel must preserve its identity as the holy people of God.
Therefore the reasons why Joshua was written are as follows.
1. The fulfillment of God's promise
→ To make known the fact that God gave the people of Israel the land of Canaan that He had promised to Abraham (Joshua 24:2-13)
2. The emphasis on God's power
→ To show that the conquest of Canaan was achieved not by Israel's strength but by God's help (Joshua 23:9-10)
3. The testimony to God's faithfulness
→ To prove that God is the One who surely keeps the word He has promised (Joshua 23:14)
4. The teaching of God's sovereignty and grace
→ To show that the land of Canaan was given by the grace of God, and to cause Israel to serve God alone (Joshua 24:14)
5. The lesson: a type of the eternal inheritance
→ To show the eternal inheritance that will be given to believers through Jesus Christ
4. Characteristics of the Book of Joshua
① It is a historical book in which Joshua, who is the successor of Moses and the agent of God, fulfills God's promise through war, and at the same time a biography showing Joshua's personal faith and mission.
② The book of Joshua is the connection and completion of the Pentateuch of Moses.
The relationship between the Pentateuch of Moses and the book of Joshua shows the flow of Moses → Joshua / Jesus → the apostles, like the four Gospels and the book of Acts in the New Testament.
The Pentateuch of Moses records the deeds of Moses, who established Judaism, and the book of Joshua is a record about the one who followed after Moses. This is because the four Gospels likewise record the deeds of Jesus Christ, and the book of Acts is a record about the apostles who followed after Jesus Christ.
③ That Israel came to possess the Promised Land was due to God's active intervention and help, and through this it shows that God's promise is surely fulfilled, so that it causes us to praise God's faithfulness. It also has the characteristic of letting us know that Israel's victory and life of rest were achieved through faith in God and obedience.
④ In the Pentateuch of Moses God revealed His will in various ways, but the book of Joshua emphasizes that God's will must be known through the book of the Law written by Moses.
⑤ The fulfillment of God's covenant concerning the land of Canaan through Joshua is a type of the salvation to come through Jesus Christ. Therefore the book of Joshua is not only a book recording the history of Israel and the starting point of its life of faith, but also a book of the Bible that lets us know God's providence in redemptive history.
5. The Structure of the Book of Joshua
1) Entering Canaan (chapters 1-5)
It deals with the process of preparation until the people of Israel, having finished their wilderness life, enter the land of Canaan in earnest.
God sets up Joshua as the successor of Moses, gives him the authority of a leader, and repeatedly encourages him. As his first task as leader, Joshua orders the spying out of the city of Jericho, and this leads to the salvation of Rahab the prostitute.
In the scene of crossing the Jordan River, as soon as the priests first set their feet in the Jordan, the water is divided by a miracle of God, and Israel at last sets foot in the Promised Land. They set up twelve stones at Gilgal as a memorial, and perform circumcision again on the generation born in the wilderness, recovering their identity as the covenant people. They also keep the Passover, and eat the produce of Canaan for the first time in that land.
2) Conquering Canaan (chapters 6-12)
It is a record of the battles in which Joshua conquers the cities of various parts of Canaan according to God's command.
At Jericho, the first conquered place, the city is brought down by marching around it and shouting in the manner God commanded, showing a victory by the power of God. In the battle of the city of Ai that follows, they fail at first because of Achan's sin, but after removing the sin they win again.
Afterward, because of the covenant with Gibeon, a battle with the allied forces of southern Canaan takes place, and Joshua experiences the miracle of the sun and moon standing still and wins the victory. In the northern campaign that follows, he defeats the allied forces centered on Jabin, king of Hazor.
As a result, Israel conquers the central, southern, and northern parts of the whole of Canaan, secures military initiative, and begins actually to possess the land that God promised.
3) Distributing Canaan (chapters 13-21)
After the conquest is finished, God commands that the conquered land be distributed to each tribe through Joshua.
First, the land east of the Jordan (the region of Gilead and Bashan) had already been given in the time of Moses to Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and afterward the western region of Canaan is also divided among the tribes. Caleb requests Hebron, and it is granted to him according to his faith and loyalty.
The land is distributed to each tribe by casting lots, and the boundaries of the land and the cities are determined.
The tribe of Levi has no inheritance, but the cities of refuge and the Levitical cities are given, distributed evenly in each region, and God's justice and mercy are reflected. This distribution is an important climax that lets them actually experience the fulfillment of God's promise. Everything was accomplished just as the LORD had told them.
4) Settling in Canaan (chapters 22-24)
After the distribution was finished, the people of Israel settle in their respective lands, and an incident occurs in which the tribes east of the Jordan, on returning home, build an altar. This was a crisis that threatened to spread into internal strife, but as the misunderstanding was cleared up and they were reconciled, it became an occasion to confirm their union once more.
Afterward Joshua grew old, and on two occasions he left the people of Israel an exhortation like a last will. Remembering the grace and guidance of God, he strongly urges them to cast away foreign gods and idols and to serve the LORD alone.
The people renew the covenant before Joshua, and at Shechem a stone pillar is set up to engrave their promise with God. After faithfully fulfilling his mission as a servant of God throughout his life, Joshua departs from the world. With this, the history of the exodus generation comes to a close.
6. The Book of Joshua and Christ
1) Joshua son of Nun
① In his name, Joshua in Hebrew means "the LORD is salvation" (Matthew 1:21). As a Greek name it is "Jesus."
② In the way he leads the people of Israel to the Promised Land (Hebrews 2:10): just as Joshua led the people of Israel to the land of Canaan, Jesus leads sinners to heaven by His grace.
③ In the way he wins victory in the battle against the rebellious Canaanite peoples (1 Corinthians 15:57)
④ In the way he gives rest to Israel
(Hebrews 4:8) For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day.
-Eternal rest is given through Jesus.
(Matthew 11:28) Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
By believing in Jesus, the burden of our sins is lifted and we find rest for our hearts.
2) The scarlet cord
Rahab the prostitute, one of the Canaanite peoples who could not but be destroyed, believed in God and received a sign of salvation (Joshua 2:13-18)
-It symbolizes the grace of the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 9:12, 14) (Ephesians 1:7)
3) The commander of the LORD's army
The commander of the LORD's army who appeared to encourage Joshua (Joshua 5:15)
-It symbolizes Jesus Christ, our Captain (Revelation 19:11-14)

1. Title
The Korean title Sasagi ("Book of the Judges"), which means a record of the deeds of the judges who appeared as saviors and leaders of Israel in a difficult age when oppression by other peoples never ceased, is the same as the Hebrew title of the Bible, "Shophetim" (Shope-tim).
The title of this book in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, "Kritai" (kritai), and the title of the Latin Bible, "Liber Judicum" (Liber judicum - the Book of the Judges), also agree with the title of the Hebrew Bible. The judges were so named because, in an age without a king, they appeared as military leaders and, after gaining the trust of the people, served as internal arbiters of each tribe, chiefly in the role of judges; they were rulers who were non-hereditary and non-regular leaders.
2. Author and Date of Writing
From the content and style of the book of Judges, it appears to have been written by one person. This record is presumed to have been written by a religious leader, looking back on the period of the judges, soon after Israel entered the monarchy. Accordingly, the time of writing appears to be between the accession of King Saul (1051 B.C.) and before David conquered Jerusalem (1004 B.C.).
1) The repeated phrase "In those days there was no king in Israel" (17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25) is an expression looking back on the past from a point after kings had arisen.
2) The statement "The Jebusites have lived in Jerusalem to this day" (1:21) shows that it was written before David conquered Jerusalem (see 2 Samuel 5:6-7).
3) The mention that Canaanites were in Gezer (1:29) reflects the situation before the king of Egypt gave Gezer to Solomon through his daughter at her marriage (see 1 Kings 9:16).
Who the author of Judges is is not made certain within the Bible, but the Talmud regards Samuel as the author of Judges, Ruth, and the books of Samuel.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
At the end of the book of Joshua, Joshua strongly exhorts the people of Israel to serve God alone in the land they received as their inheritance. But in the book of Judges, although God's salvation continues, an atmosphere of oppression and defeat is strongly evident. The reason is that "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (21:25).
Yet the book of Judges is not a book containing only despair. Within it are God's grace and compassion, that is, the message of the gospel. Through this we can learn the deep spiritual truths that God wishes to teach.
Motive for Writing
The book of Judges is a book directly connected with the book of Joshua, and both books naturally continue by mentioning the death of Joshua.
Joshua conquered the main regions of Canaan and distributed the land to the twelve tribes. But the remaining regions each tribe had to conquer for itself, and in this process they came to coexist with the Canaanite peoples without driving them out completely.
As a result, the Canaanite peoples gradually grew strong, oppressed Israel, and plundered it, and at each moment of crisis God raised up judges to save Israel. In this way the period of the judges was a time when Israel repeatedly went through crises.
The time when this book was written is presumed to be the period when Israel had passed through the age of the judges and had just made the transition to the monarchy. Through this book, the author
•stresses that Israel's suffering was not only a problem of its political system but was because there was no wholehearted faith in God.
•conveys a warning to the people of Israel, who had entered the age of the monarchy, not to rely only on the political system and not to depart from God.
4. The Structure of Judges
1) Causes leading to the period of the judges (1:1-2:5)
(1) Political and military background - the partial conquest of Canaan by Israel (chapter 1)
① The victory of the tribes of Judah and Simeon in the conquest of southern Canaan (1:1-20)
② Benjamin, which failed to remove the Jebusites (1:21)
③ The tribe of Joseph, which partially succeeded in occupying central Canaan (1:22-29)

4. The Theme of Judges
The purpose of Judges is to show God's judgment on Israel's disobedience, and God's grace working ceaselessly even in the midst of it. Furthermore, this book explains the background by which Israel, having rejected the rule of God, came in the end to need a centralized and hereditary monarchy.
Israel, by serving the gods of the Canaanite peoples instead of God, lost the blessing and failed to conquer the enemies completely (3:1-6). Because of this, they fell into a state of moral and social disorder and in the end longed for the monarchy.

While Joshua was still alive, and for some years after his death, Israel served God well and lived in peace, enjoying blessings in the land where they had settled. But afterward the people of Israel departed from God and came to suffer, and Israel's spiritual condition and God's mercy are shown in the following repeating cyclical structure
	1.	Sin – As the years passed, the people departed from God and served idols.
	2.	Discipline – God withdrew His protection, and Israel suffered at the hands of enemies.
	3.	Supplication – In their affliction Israel cried out to God.
	4.	Deliverance – God raised up a judge and saved Israel.
	5.	Forgetfulness – As time passed they again forgot God and sinned.
This cycle is repeated throughout the book of Judges.
God as Seen in Judges
Through the book of Judges we can learn the following facts about God:
	1.	He is almighty, yet also merciful and gracious
	2.	He is righteous in anger and judgment
	3.	God's ways of working are varied, but to man He commands simply and clearly
	4.	He is the One who governs the history of all peoples
	5.	He is the One who is with sinful man and seeks to win their hearts
In the book of Judges the expression "Lord" appears 178 times and the expression "God" 62 times, so that God's presence and sovereignty are emphasized.
5. Characteristics of Judges
	1. An age of spiritual decline
Unlike the joy of victory and settlement in the time of Joshua, the book of Judges shows a dark picture of an age of defeat and corruption.
	2. The repetition of sin and grace
The contrast is clear between Israel, which forgot God's deliverance and sinned again and again, and the love of God, who forgave them ceaselessly.
	3. The absence of leaders and confusion
Without a unifying leader like Moses or Joshua, and without a king, within a tribal confederation Israel wanders, having lost its political and religious center.
	4. The tragedy of war among kinsmen
In the book of Judges is recorded the first war among kinsmen (fratricidal war) in the history of Israel.

1. Title
It derives from "Rut" in the Hebrew Bible's title and "Routh" in the Septuagint (LXX), the Greek Old Testament, and the book was named after Ruth, the "Moabite" woman who is the central figure of this book.
2. Author and Date of Writing
The Talmud says that "Samuel wrote Joshua, Judges, and Ruth," but this cannot be known precisely, and it is inferred that the author was either Samuel or a person of the time of David. It is reasonable to regard it as having been written by someone from among those who came out of Samuel's school of the prophets, who, out of the history of the then-established Davidic dynasty, introduced the quiet yet moving episode of Ruth, honoring Ruth and wishing to survey God's providence in establishing the family to which such a Ruth belonged as the royal dynasty of all Israel.
Accordingly, the date of writing too is regarded as being between 1010 and 970 B.C., the period of David's reign.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
It was written primarily to show that David's appointment as king came about through the providence of God, who had blessed the faith of his ancestors from long before.
Also, to us, it was meant to show that behind the birth of Jesus Christ, who came into the world through David's bloodline, there were such people of faith, even though they were Gentiles, and to make known that there is a wondrous providence of God's redemptive history.
The text of Ruth emphasizes several times that Ruth is a "Moabite woman" (Moabitess) (1:22, 2:2,21, 4:5,10). Ruth was a foreign woman and a widow, but she came to have faith in the LORD God, and through her loyalty to God and to her mother-in-law she was incorporated into the community of Israel.
Ruth devotedly cared for her mother-in-law "Naomi," a widow without any hope who had lost her husband and both sons, and was personally blessed and continued the family line of her dead husband, and furthermore she received the redemptive-historical blessing of becoming an ancestor of David and of Jesus Christ.
Similarly to Ruth, Rahab the prostitute too was a Gentile, but she was saved by faith and entered the ranks of the chosen people, and became an ancestor of Boaz, Ruth's husband. In this way it shows that God's salvation is a grace given not by bloodline but by faith. Rahab married Salmon of the tribe of Judah, and became the ancestor of Boaz, who married Ruth, and further obtained the blessing of becoming an ancestor of David and of Jesus Christ.
(Ruth 4:21-22) Salmon was the father of Boaz, Boaz was the father of Obed, Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.
(Matthew 1:5) Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab, Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth, Obed the father of Jesse,
This becomes a practical example that clearly testifies, already in the Old Testament era, to the truth of redemptive history that God's salvation does not depend on bloodline. God accomplishes redemptive history even through believing Gentiles. This agrees with the covenant made to Abraham, "all the peoples of the earth shall be blessed," and in the end opened the way of salvation for all peoples through Jesus Christ.
And that God caused David and Jesus to be born through the Gentiles "Rahab" and "Ruth" shows that later Gentiles, though they may not belong to the chosen community of Israel, can receive the grace of coming to belong to the chosen community of God through true faith in God and in Jesus Christ the Redeemer.
The Goel System
Meanwhile, in connection with the truth of redemption, what cannot be omitted from Ruth is the "Goel" system.
"Goel" is a word derived from the meaning "kinsman," and it is a system in which, when a brother or close relative died without offspring, or sold land or inheritance because of poverty, the kinsman, through levirate marriage, carries on that bloodline, and also buys back the inheritance on his behalf and returns it, so that the inheritance in Israel may not be cut off through death or poverty.  This was a kind of mutual-protection system by which the members belonging to the blood community protected one another's families and property.
In Ruth, the reason Naomi, who had lost husband, sons, and property and had reached a state of bankruptcy, could be restored was none other than "Boaz," the "kinsman (goel)," that is, the "kinsman redeemer."
This is a type showing that Jesus Christ in the New Testament has become our true Goel. Jesus Christ is the Goel who redeemed us from sin and death with His own blood, and whoever believes in Him can recover lost life and enjoy a full life.
(1 Peter 1:18) For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.
Thus, Ruth seems on the surface to be a story of the love and faith of a little woman, Ruth, but behind it there is truly the providence of the redemptive history of the great God.
Therefore, when we read Ruth, we should meditate deeply not merely on it as a personal story of a pitiable and sincere woman moving from unhappiness to happiness, but as a story in which, behind it, is contained God's wondrous providence and grace of redemptive history.
4. The Structure of Ruth
Chapter 1. [Introduction] Ruth's choice and decision: fall and repentance
Chapter 2. [Development] Ruth's devotion and a new opportunity: God's loving-kindness/grace
Chapter 3. [Climax] The response to Ruth's appeal: approaching by grace and the covenantal confirmation of redemption
Chapter 4. [Conclusion] The blessing and reward that came upon Ruth: the fulfillment of redemption, lawful marriage, and the eternal inheritance
5. Characteristics of Ruth
It is one of the two books in the whole Bible that bear a woman's name, Ruth and Esther.
Ruth is a young Gentile Moabite woman, but she came to live among the Hebrews and marries a Hebrew of the family line of King David.
Esther is a young Hebrew woman, but she came to live among Gentiles and marries King Xerxes of the great empire of Persia.
In particular, Ruth is unique in the Bible in that the whole book is a story about one woman. In particular, although most of the characters in this book are Jews, the fact that it praises Ruth's virtue shows all the more the nobility of her conduct.
And Ruth is one of the four women included in the genealogy of Christ and is a person of virtue. (Tamar, Rahab, Bathsheba)

1. Title
The books of 1 and 2 Samuel are named after the name of Samuel. In the early Hebrew original text these two books were not divided. The division into 1 and 2 first made in the Greek version, the Septuagint (translated from Hebrew into Greek around the 3rd century B.C.), became the tradition. It is now applied as it is in all versions, and it is also divided in the Hebrew Bible.
2. Author and Date of Writing
It is not known precisely who wrote the books of 1 and 2 Samuel. Since the death of Samuel is recorded in 1 Samuel 25:1, it is thought that the first half of 1 Samuel (chapters 1-24) was written by Samuel, but the rest of 1 Samuel and the book of 2 Samuel cannot be known precisely, and it is very likely that they were written by the prophets Nathan and Gad, or by an anonymous prophet in the early period of the divided kingdom of north and south. (1 Samuel 25:1, 1 Chronicles 29:29-30)
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The historical background of the beginning of 1 Samuel corresponds to the late period of the judges, and it is a record of about 100 years (some books say 115 years) from the birth of Samuel, who was the last judge, to the death of Saul, who was the first king.
In the process of transition from the age of the judges, the theocratic age, to the age of the monarchy at the demand of the people, it records the role of Samuel, the last judge, who also opened the age of the prophets, the failure of the first king Saul, the anointing of David as the next king, and the process of preparation (suffering and training) for becoming the next king.
Purpose of Writing
It is to remind Israel, which had entered the age of the monarchy, that although it had taken the form of a monarchy like the surrounding nations, this was the result of their wrong choice, and, through the process of transition, to make them realize that, unlike the surrounding nations, it is a theocratic monarchy in which God Himself rules and exercises providence.
 ("Theocratic kingdom" means that God rules through the king. That is, God exercises providence behind the scenes, and the king means a monarchy that rules according to God's will.)
Also, in the redemptive-historical sense, it shows how the authority to rule Israel was delegated to the house of David. This is the emergence of the Davidic dynasty, a type of Jesus Christ, the Messiah and King who would come later through the royal house of David.

2) Service as Saul's attendant (16:14-chapter 20)

-God's sovereignty in leading, in the process of transition from the age of the judges, the theocratic age, to the age of the monarchy, to a theocratic monarchy.
-The role of Samuel, the last judge, who also opened the age of the prophets; the appearance of the first king Saul and his wretched end through disobedience; and David's preparation and training process as the next king.
 -The effect of sin. Sin necessarily brings discipline with it. It has an enormously evil effect not only on the individual but also on the community (family, nation) to which he belongs. The sin of Eli's two sons, the people's mistake of choosing a human king, the disobedience of the first king Saul.
-The lesson through Saul's failure, David's training, and the qualities of faith and character suited to the heart of God.

1. Title
The books of 1 and 2 Samuel are named after the name of Samuel. In the early Hebrew original text these two books were not divided. The division into 1 and 2 first made in the Greek version, the Septuagint (translated from Hebrew into Greek around the 3rd century B.C.), became the tradition. It is now applied as it is in all versions, and it is also divided in the Hebrew Bible.
2. Author and Date of Writing
The author is not clear. What is thought most suitable is the view from ancient times that the first 24 chapters of 1 Samuel were written by Samuel himself, and that the rest, through 2 Samuel, was written by the two prophets Nathan and Gad (see Sidlow Baxter).
In light of the expression in 1 Samuel 27:6, "Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day," it is estimated to be around 930-900 B.C., the early period of the divided kingdom.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The era of 2 Samuel corresponds to the early monarchy period (about 1010-970 B.C.), when David ruled all Israel and established a united kingdom, but the time of writing appears to be after the northern and southern kingdoms were divided. This has the purpose of conveying to the people of the divided-kingdom period the truth that God's rule continues. At the same time, it has meaning for us today also, as a book showing the prototype of the kingdom of God.
Purpose of Writing
Emphasis on God's sovereignty
It shows that David's united kingdom was established and grew under the powerful providence of God. It makes us realize that the Lord of history is God.
The importance of obedience
Through David's personal successes and failures, it testifies that the destiny of both the nation and the individual depends on whether one obeys God.
The limits of human rule and the hope of the messianic kingdom
It reveals that even David's kingdom, the greatest in the history of Israel, was distorted and suffered because of human sinfulness. Through this it stresses that the perfect kingdom is accomplished only by the descendant of David, the Messiah Jesus Christ, and causes us to hold hope for the eternal messianic kingdom.
