5. The Themes of 2 Samuel
1) The right path of life
David's journey of success and failure, joy and sorrow presents the path of life that believers should walk. Keeping the purity of faith is the key to success, and it teaches that carelessness leads to the trap of sin.
2) The fulfillment of God's promise
After being anointed, David went through many hardships over about 20 years until he became king of Israel. But God's promise was in the end fulfilled without delay, and this applies equally to us.
3) God first
By moving the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, David began a rule that put the presence of God at the center. His God-centered life made him a man after God's heart.
4) The Davidic covenant
God was pleased with David's heart in wishing to build the temple and promised him an eternal kingship. This covenant will ultimately be fulfilled in the messianic kingdom through Jesus Christ.
5) The secret of victory in spiritual warfare
All of David's victories in war came because the LORD gave him the victory. In spiritual warfare also, likewise, victory is possible only by God's help.
6) The contagiousness and destructiveness of sin
David's sin did not end with himself but had an evil effect on his children and the whole nation. Sin surely spreads and brings serious destruction.
7) God's grace and sin
David committed a great sin, but when he sincerely repented, God forgave him. God bestows abundant grace on those who repent.
8) The sinfulness of all people
Even the great David was not free from sin. There is no perfectly righteous person, and a sinner obtains God's forgiveness and salvation by repenting.
9) Obedience to God's sovereignty
David accepted afflictions such as the death of his child, rebellion, and insults as God's discipline, and obeyed. This shows the attitude of true fear of God.
10) Perfect reconciliation and unity possible only in Christ
David strove for reconciliation, but by human strength alone he could not achieve perfect unity. True reconciliation is possible only within the gospel of Jesus Christ.

1. Title
In the Hebrew original, it was a single book, not divided into First and Second, and its original title was Melakim, meaning "Kings." It was divided into two parts because the length of a scroll was limited when the book was translated into Greek, a language whose text runs about one third longer than Hebrew.
Around the 2nd century B.C., the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) edited it into two books, First and Second, and the Korean Bible follows this division, editing it as 1 and 2 Kings, with the meaning "the record of the various kings."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Jewish tradition (the Talmud) names Jeremiah as the author, but this is uncertain. It is estimated to have been written between 587 and 586 B.C., after the leading people of southern Judah, which fell to Babylon in 586 B.C., had all been taken away to Babylon, and before the first return of the exiles took place.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
2 Kings is a book written around the time of the Babylonian exile, and it was written to explain why the people of Israel, though God's chosen people, lost their nation and became captives.
Beginning with King Saul, Israel enjoyed its golden age in the times of David and Solomon; in Solomon's time especially, the temple was built and the nation became powerful.
But after Solomon's death the nation was divided into north and south and gradually declined, and northern Israel was destroyed by Assyria and southern Judah by Babylon. The destruction of the temple and of Jerusalem brought great confusion of faith to the people. Along with the question, "Why must the LORD's chosen people lose their nation and live as captives in a foreign land?", it even caused doubt about their own identity.
In response, the author of the books of Kings explains from the standpoint of faith why God judged Israel, and seeks to convey the message that they should return to God through repentance and faith.

Purpose of Writing
It was written to recall the downfall of Israel, which, though it disliked God's direct rule and eagerly wanted a king to govern it, was divided into southern Judah and northern Israel before the third generation had passed, and to recall God's judgment on fallen humanity that had left God, the Lord of history and the source of love.
It is an expression of thanksgiving for God's boundless love and grace, which, despite the corruption of the kings and the people marked by unceasing evil deeds and disobedience, connected the history of the chosen people promised to Abraham and David even to their own generation.

5. Summary of the Content from 1 Samuel to 1 Kings
1 Samuel
Samuel, who was obtained through Hannah's prayer and vow, was a faithful judge of God, but Israel did not want the theocratic rule in which God governed them directly; wanting monarchic rule like the Gentiles, they asked for a king, and to that rebellious wish of Israel God granted Saul as king.
But unlike his beginning, Saul disobeyed out of fear of men, and was rejected, together with God's sorrowful regret: "I regret that I have made Saul king." Even so, God was preparing David, a man after His own heart, in place of the disobedient Saul. Man looks at outward appearance, knowledge, and refinement and longs for such a person, but God, who looks at the heart, took David from the sheepfold and refined him for a long time in order to use him preciously.
2 Samuel
It was only after a long fifteen years from his anointing as king that David became king of Judah, and only after another seven years that he became king of all Israel. When he came forth refined through suffering for so long, the Lord made him the greatest man of faith.
David's courtesy toward the Lord's anointed, shown when he mourned, wept, and fasted at the death of King Saul, who had so desperately tried to kill him, is enough to shock and instruct us. Yet even David committed the sins of adultery and murder through a moment of pride and idleness. Had it not been for God's mercy and forgiveness, he too would have been forsaken by God in his last years, but the Lord's mercy, which has compassion on one who repents thoroughly, raised David up once more and repaid him with greater blessing and grace.
1 Kings
Solomon, having become king, began with the humility of telling God of his own insufficiency and asking for wisdom, but once he had successfully built the temple and come to enjoy splendor, he did not rely on God's word; by taking foreign women as wives according to his own wisdom and thoughts, he fell into the sin of idolatry.
By disobeying the God who had given peace and blessing, he brought about not only the downfall of an individual but even the division of the nation. Moreover, even in the dark situation of the divided kingdom, God diligently sent prophets, rebuked sin, and earnestly urged the people to return to God.
6. Main Content of 2 Kings
1) Emphasis on obedience
God sent prophets to bring back to Himself the kings and people who did not acknowledge His sovereignty and disobeyed, and warned and exhorted them unceasingly, yet Israel did not turn back to the end and was destroyed. Through this, the book emphasizes to us who live today that only those who obey can enjoy blessing and peace.
2) Awakening vigilance against sin
Israel, thinking that the judgment of sin was not carried out immediately, let down its guard, kept doing evil, and was destroyed. This awakens great vigilance in us, who say with our lips that the day of the Lord's coming is near, yet compromise with the world and live for the things that are seen.
3) God's love that does not give up
Just as God inflicted the extreme discipline of the destruction of Israel and Judah but did not wipe out the nation itself, He promised salvation to the individual who repents, and the book confirms God's love: He judges sin most severely, but He never abandons in the end the one He has once chosen.

1. Title
The Hebrew name of 1 and 2 Chronicles is "Dibre Hayamim" (the words of the days, i.e., of each age). The book of Chronicles, which was originally a single book, was written more than 100 years after the books of Kings were written. The division into two books, First and Second, as in the present Bible, began with the Greek translation around 150 B.C. Originally, Chronicles was placed at the very end of the 39 books of the Old Testament.
2. Author and Date of Writing
According to Jewish tradition, Ezra wrote these Chronicles together with the book of Ezra.
Dr. W. F. Albright, a modern scholar, compared the frequent use of genealogies, the similar emphasis on ritual procedure, and the fidelity of both to the Law of Moses, and concluded that these two books share the same concerns and form.
The closing words of 2 Chronicles (2 Chronicles 36:22, 23) are repeated as the introduction to the book of Ezra (Ezra 1:1-3). Therefore, Chronicles and Ezra are connected histories, and it seems that Ezra wrote them around 450 B.C.
That 2 Chronicles ends abruptly in the middle of the content of Cyrus's decree suggests Ezra's intention, regarding Chronicles as the last canonical book of the Old Testament, to lead his readers back to the book of Ezra.
Later, the positions of Ezra and Chronicles, which had stood side by side in the Hebrew Bible, were separated by Nehemiah's autobiography, which mentions Darius II, who came to the throne in 423 B.C. (Nehemiah 12:22). Therefore we can see that Chronicles was incorporated as the last book of the Old Testament canon in 420 B.C.

3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
2 Kings closes leaving a strangely dark sorrow. The capital was laid waste, the palace was burned, the nation lay in ruins, and the people were driven out.
After losing their nation and finishing their life in captivity, the Jews returned to a devastated Judea, but in a reality where the former glory had vanished, they were in a situation in which they could easily lose their identity and hope. Above all, the greatest lack was the fact that there was no king. The throne of David was something special that God had covenanted, and the reality that this throne was now gone came to the Jews as a great sense of loss.

Purpose of Writing
1 Chronicles asks, "Why now, does it emphasize faith and the temple again?" The reason is clear. The restoration of the relationship with God, and especially of faith centered on the temple, is the very way by which the nation can live again. The one who wrote 1 Chronicles appears to have been a priest, and in order to set right the ruined faith, he retells history centered on the role of the temple and the importance of faith.
1 Chronicles emphasizes three important messages: that even in an age without a king, God is still with His people.
First, the lesson of the past.
The reason the kingdom of Judah was destroyed was that it abandoned the covenant with God and fell into idolatry.
Second, the promise of prophecy.
Although the throne is gone, the promise of the Savior through the descendant of David is still alive. The house of David remains, and it gives hope that from this house the Messiah who will rule the whole world will come.
Third, the presence now.
That Cyrus, king of Persia, permitted the Jews' return and the rebuilding of the temple was certain proof that God is still with His people. From this perspective, 1 Chronicles is not a mere historical record. It is a book that shows, from God's point of view, the past, the present, and the future, which a ruined nation and people must remember in order to rise again.
4. Structure of 1 Chronicles - (A Book on the Division of Israel and Judah)
First, chapters 1 through 9 show through genealogies who God's people are and how the covenant of David has been carried on. This is a very important starting point for the restoration of identity. After that, the death of Saul is mentioned briefly, and then the reign of David and the process of preparing for the temple are dealt with in detail. This too develops from a viewpoint centered on faith and the temple rather than on politics.

6. Main Content of 1 Chronicles
Above all, the temple is the most emphasized theme throughout 1 Chronicles. The temple is a sign that, in an age when the king has vanished, God is still with His people, and it is the center of the people's life and faith. The temple was the starting point from which Israel could live once more as a nation. The idea is that everything, looking back on past sins, rebuilding present faith, and looking to future hope, begins at the temple.
"A nation that has left God cannot exist. Only when God is placed at the center can the people and the nation come alive again." 1 Chronicles is a book that gives the belief that even in an age without a king, God is still the Sovereign, and that one can begin again centered on His temple. For the returned Jews, this book contains, beyond mere comfort, a powerful call to re-establish the foundation of faith and life.

1. Title
The Hebrew name of 1 and 2 Chronicles is "Dibre Hayamim" (the words of the days, i.e., of each age). The book of Chronicles, which was originally a single book, was written more than 100 years after the books of Kings were written. The division into two books, First and Second, as in the present Bible, began with the Greek translation around 150 B.C. Originally, Chronicles was placed at the very end of the 39 books of the Old Testament.
2. Author and Date of Writing
This book is regarded as the work of Ezra, the author of Ezra and Nehemiah, and the reason is clearly shown in the stylistic similarity between 2 Chronicles and the book of Ezra, and in the fact that the wording of (2 Chronicles 36:22) and (Ezra 1:1-3) is identical. The date of writing is regarded as about 450 B.C., just after the second return from Babylon (458 B.C.), the period of Ezra's main activity.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The time when Ezra wrote this book was about 450 B.C., just after the second return of the exiles, which took place in 458 B.C.
At that time, more than 70 years had passed since those who returned to Israel in the first return (516 B.C.) had rebuilt the temple of Zerubbabel, yet the glory of God promised to the chosen people had still not come, and they continued to be persecuted by the Gentile nations. Therefore, not only had the deep emotion they felt when the foundation of the temple was laid and when the temple was dedicated faded, but their faith in God centered on the temple had declined, and they were obscuring the glory of God with false offerings.
Jerusalem, where the temple stood, was in a state of having no wall even to hold off the attacks of enemies, and because of this the persecution by the surrounding peoples was very severe.
Besides this outward ruin, their spiritual condition was also greatly in decline. The priests did not properly carry out the mission entrusted to them, and instead associated with Gentiles for their own gain and took the lead in damaging the holiness of the chosen people. The people also neglected the tithe, so that the livelihood of the priests and Levites became difficult, and because of this they left their duties, and in the end a vicious cycle repeated in which not even the regular sacrifices could be offered (Nehemiah 3:10-14).
Observance of the Sabbath, clearly stated in the Law, was also almost ignored (Nehemiah 13:13), and, tainted by Gentile culture and religion, marriage with foreigners also became common.
Purpose of Writing
Written in such circumstances, 2 Chronicles emphasizes that once God has chosen a people, His promise does not change and His protection also continues. But it reminds us of the principle that God's salvation and protection are not unconditional: blessing when they obey, and discipline when they disobey.
Their forefathers disobeyed God and were judged, but God disciplined them in love and in the end restored them. Therefore, it teaches that the people who have now returned from captivity must not repeat the mistakes of the past, but must rebuild the glory of the history of the chosen people by obeying the word of God.
In this way, 2 Chronicles was written to give comfort and hope to the people of that time by assuring them of the history of the chosen people that has continued by God's grace. This gives the same lesson to Christians of the New Testament today. That is, it shows that a person once saved by God's love may be disciplined but will never perish, and that blessing in this world and the world to come depends on whether one obeys before God.
Through 2 Chronicles we can find God's unchanging love and His providence amid human sin. Also, by examining the strengths and weaknesses of the kings of southern Judah, we learn in what attitude we should live before God today.
1) God chose Israel as His chosen people
2) For the fulfillment of the Davidic covenant, it proves the fact that He preserved them (the generation of the returned exiles) even after the nation fell because of the sins of their forefathers, and restored them to the promised land
3) It emphasizes that prosperity and ruin are determined by whether or not one obeys God

6. Main Content of 2 Chronicles
1) Understanding redemptive history
In the history of Israel, frustration and glory coexist. In the whole Bible too, there is the figure of the sinner who despairs before judgment, and there is also the joy of salvation through the grace of Christ. There is creation, and there is the final end of history. In this way, we must broadly understand the flow of salvation that runs from creation to the end.
The books of Kings, which deal with the history of the same period, emphasize from the prophetic viewpoint the judgment on disobedience,
while 2 Chronicles emphasizes God's love and unconditional salvation.
Both of these perspectives are true, and we should not view the history of redemption narrowly but with balance.
2) The God who keeps His promises
Even though the kings of Judah repeatedly disobeyed, God kept to the end the covenant He made with David.
In 2 Samuel 7:14-17 God promised that He would discipline David's descendants but would not withdraw His favor, and that covenant was fulfilled through Jesus Christ. Human kings failed, but true salvation and victory were accomplished in Jesus Christ, the heir of the spiritual house of David.
3) God's unchanging love
Israel was destroyed through disobedience and corruption, but God restored them with unchanging love.
The return of the captive people was the fulfillment of prophecy, and this shows that God's love does not end even with human sin.
4) Faith first
Israel in the time of the united kingdom enjoyed great blessing centered on the temple in the time of Solomon. The restoration of faith in God was the secret of blessing.
This principle applies equally across the ages. Christians today too can enjoy God's blessing when they put God first in their lives, that is, when they first seek His kingdom and His righteousness.

1. Title
The book takes its name from Ezra, who was the leader of Israel's faith reform and also the author of this book. In the Hebrew original and the Septuagint, Ezra and Nehemiah form a single book, but the Latin Bible (the Vulgate) divided them into Ezra and Nehemiah according to their authors. In content, the two books alike deal with the history of the period of the return from exile, so they are related to each other and have a complementary character.
2. Author and Date of Writing
The author of Ezra is Ezra, a scribe and priest who led the second return from exile and the faith reform. Ezra also wrote 1 and 2 Chronicles. The second return from exile took place in 458 B.C. under Ezra, and the third return took place in 445 B.C. under Nehemiah. The writing of the book of Ezra is dated to about 444 B.C., when Nehemiah took up his post as governor of Judah.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
After Israel was destroyed in 586 B.C. by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and the temple was demolished, it came to live in captivity for 70 years, as God's word had said. And, as promised, after 70 years it returned to its homeland in three waves. Ezra, who led the second return, recorded in detail the rebuilding of the temple and the faith reform carried out by the people who returned in the first and second returns, intending to give lessons of faith, in the near term, to those of the third return, and then to people after them.

6. Main Content of Ezra
Ezra is a book of restoration. Although Israel's disobedience caused them to be taken away to a foreign land, the loving hand of God went after them. God allowed the Israelites the suffering called the exile. But the promise followed them that when the time was fulfilled they would return. It means that the God of Israel, God our Father, has boundless compassion.
God could never break a promise. God disciplined them, but He did not cast them off utterly. Rather, He prepared a way of restoration.
(Lamentations 3:32-33) Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion. For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.
As this word says, God allowed the suffering of the Babylonian captivity, but through it He led them to recover their faith and to be able to return to that land.
This is the same truth for us, saved Christians. Our faith too may fall back, and we may be tempted by worldly things. God may discipline us severely. But we will never fall from God's grace. However far faith may fall back, there is a way of restoration. Rather, He restores faith through the pain of discipline. This is the hand of God's rich grace.
It is a word given to teach us God's way of restoring His people to a place of fellowship and blessing.

The title of this book was given as "Nehemiah" after the name of the protagonist who led the third return, the project of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem, and the people's faith reform. 2. Author and Date of Writing
From the first-person narration that appears often in this book, we can tell that the protagonist Nehemiah is the author. And this book was written in Nehemiah's later years (421-400 B.C.).

3. Motive and Background of Writing

When Nehemiah heard this news, he came back to Jerusalem (third return, 445 B.C.), and the book deals with how he rebuilt the wall and took the lead in the people's faith reform movement.
Nehemiah's third return gives more concrete form to the restoration of the community of the chosen people, which had already begun with the two previous returns.

4. Structure of Nehemiah
Part 1 - The Rebuilding of the Wall of Jerusalem (chapters 1-7)
Nehemiah heard the news that the people of Israel were being insulted by the Gentiles, that the restoration of the theocratic state through the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem had been frustrated, and that the city was broken down and its gates burned. Although he was an official of the Persian kingdom at that time, as one of the LORD's people he could not turn away from the wretched reality of his homeland.
Therefore Nehemiah judged that to set up again the foundation of the nation as soon as possible, even a single day sooner, was more important than anything, and with the permission of Artaxerxes, king of Persia, he came back to Jerusalem.
After arriving in Jerusalem, he first inspected for himself the broken-down walls in order to rebuild them. Then he encouraged the discouraged people by stressing God's help and faith in the LORD. In this way the rebuilding of the wall began in earnest.
But Nehemiah's project of rebuilding the wall was by no means smooth. Externally there was interference from the Gentile peoples who were jealous of Israel's restoration, and internally fear, frustration, and conflict arising from the gap between rich and poor among the people became great obstacles.
Nevertheless, with burning faith and outstanding leadership Nehemiah overcame all these difficulties, and in the end he was able to complete the wall miraculously in only 52 days.
I. The Various Preparations for Rebuilding the Wall (1:1 - 2:20)
1. The sad news of the breaking down of the wall of Jerusalem (1:1-3)
2. Nehemiah's intercession for the rebuilding of the wall (1:4 - 2:8)
3. Nehemiah's return to Jerusalem (2:9-11)
4. Nehemiah's preparation for rebuilding the wall (2:12-20)
II. The Process and Completion of Rebuilding the Wall (3:1 - 7:73)
1. The list and duties of those who took part in rebuilding the wall (3:1-32)
2. The schemes of the opposing forces against the rebuilding of the wall (4:1 - 6:14)
3. The completion of the wall of Jerusalem (6:15-19)
4. The appointment of those who managed the city of Jerusalem (7:1-4)
5. The census of those of the first return from exile (7:5-73)

Part 2 - The Reform Movement of the People of Israel (chapters 8-13)
If Part 1 is the outward rebuilding of the wall for maintaining the community of the chosen people,
Part 2 is the inward faith reform movement that deals with the process by which they actually came to be equipped with the qualities of the chosen people.
At that time Israel had been harassed externally by Gentile powers, and because it lived together with the Gentiles it had also become Gentilized internally in many respects. Therefore, in order to make them a covenant people again, it was necessary to educate them thoroughly in the word of God and to stir up anew their consciousness of being the chosen people.
In Part 1, Nehemiah, who had outstanding administrative qualities, was used as God's instrument to lay the outward foundation of the theocratic state, whereas
in Part 2, Ezra the scribe and Nehemiah the governor were used together to cultivate the inner qualities of the people of the theocratic state.
I. The Spiritual Revival of Israel through the Renewal of the Covenant (8:1 - 10:39)
1. Ezra's interpretation of the Law (8:1-18)
2. Ezra's renewal of the covenant (9:1 - 10:39)
II. The Spiritual Revival of Israel through Obedience to the Covenant (11:1 - 13:31)
1. The resettlement of the people in Jerusalem (11:1-36)
2. The genealogical survey of the priests and Levites (12:1-26)
3. The dedication ceremony of the wall of Jerusalem (12:27-47)
4. The reform movement by Nehemiah (13:1-31)
 6. Main Content of Nehemiah
1) An attitude of self-denial
Nehemiah gave up the comfortable position of a high official of the Persian empire, shared in the suffering of his kinsmen, and helped the revival of faith. This prefigures the ministry of Jesus, who came to this earth as the Son of God and saved sinners, and shows the attitude of self-denial that God's servants should have.
2) God, the Sovereign of the world
God, the Sovereign of this world, moves even the hearts of the kings of Gentile empires and carries out His will. Therefore, when God's chosen people deeply trust God, the Sovereign of the world, and live according to His will, they become instruments for extending the kingdom of God. Moreover, for the individual as well, in the concrete events of this world, being led according to God's will, he enjoys spiritual blessing and finally reaches even the kingdom of heaven.
3) Rebuilding of faith
Just as in rebuilding the temple, there were all kinds of dangers and schemes of obstruction in rebuilding the wall. This is in line with the fact that when a believer who has wandered away from the Lord wishes to live a life of faith again, the forces of Satan fear this and obstruct it. But one who clearly realizes the need to rebuild faith will overcome these things steadfastly and set up his faith rightly before God.
4) A life worthy of the new covenant
The renewal of the covenant requires not merely reform in theory but even reform in actual life. Therefore a believer living under the new covenant must live a life that has actually changed in every area of life toward what is fitting to God's will.
5) A life of prayer
To know God's will, the first thing to do is pray. Continual prayer is necessary even in the process of carrying it out, and when one meets obstacles, still more prayer is necessary. By persevering to the end, the Lord's will is finally accomplished.

1. Title
"Esther" derives from "Ester," the Persian-style name of Esther, the protagonist of this book. Esther's Hebrew name is "Hadassah." It means the "myrtle tree," which is used as a material for perfume. But after she became the queen of Xerxes she changed her name to Esther, and it became the title of this book.
2. Author and Date of Writing
The author is regarded as an anonymous Jew who lived in Persia at that time. Some scholars even conjecture that it may have been Mordecai. The reason is that to write the book of Esther one has to be familiar with two things: one has to be well acquainted with affairs of the Persian court, and one has to be a person who knows well the circumstances of the Jews. For that reason it is regarded as Mordecai.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
It covers the third year through the twelfth year of the reign of Xerxes (483-474 B.C.). This was an event that occurred between the first return from exile under Zerubbabel (537 B.C.) and the second return from exile carried out under the leadership of Ezra (458 B.C.), and in terms of the book of Ezra, it is placed between Ezra 6, where the first return is completed, and Ezra 7, where the second return begins.
 In 538 B.C. Cyrus, the founder of the Persian empire, issued a decree permitting the captives to return to their homeland. But not all the descendants of Israel went back at that time. In the first return only 50,000 returned, and so a considerable number of Jews still remained in the former land of Babylon, including Susa, and among them were persons who had risen even to high office in Persia, such as Mordecai and Esther, the protagonists of this book, and Nehemiah of the book of Nehemiah.
The book of Esther is a record of an event in which, from the conflict between the descendants of Israel living in Susa, Persia, and the Amalekites, one of the foreign peoples also living in Susa, all the people of Israel within the Persian empire faced the crisis of being annihilated, but through the devotion of a woman named Esther and the sovereign providence of God working behind her they were saved and the Jews triumphed.
Motive of Writing
It was to awaken the faith of the Jews who were living in the foreign land of Susa.
The author wanted to let the Jews, his own people, know what kind of God God is. He wanted to emphasize the fact that God is not one who worked only in ancient times, but one who is still providing and working in the age in which they now live.
Although the Jews had been driven out of the promised land of Canaan and were living in a foreign land, he wrote this book to make them realize that they were still under God's protection and care, so that they might rely on God again.
Probably the book of Esther must have stirred up a faith awakening among the Jews who had returned to the promised land after the Babylonian captivity, and among the Jews who were still staying in foreign lands.
It was to let the Jewish descendants know about Purim.
Its purpose is to tell the origin of how Purim began, and to have this festival kept regularly so that they would realize that they are God's chosen people and His people. This festival is still observed by the Jews to this day.
4. Structure of Esther
 Part 1: Beginning - The deposition of Vashti and the enthronement of Esther (1:1 - 2:18)
 Part 2: Development - Haman's plot to annihilate the Jews (2:19-4:17)
 Part 3: Climax - The execution of Haman and the triumph of Mordecai (5:1- 8:2)
 Part 4: Conclusion - The victory of the Jews and the establishment of Purim (8:3- 10:3)

5. Main Content of Esther
The most important theme is God's wondrous and marvelous providence.
For the Christian who loves God and walks in the right way, He works all things together and finally gives blessing; and for the person who goes against God and walks in an evil way, even if he seems to prosper for the moment, we can clearly see the providence of God, who mobilizes everything to punish him.
7. Characteristics of the Book of Esther
1. It is one of the two books in the Old Testament named after a woman. (Ruth and Esther)
2. The name of God never appears. (Even the word "faith" never appears.)
Like the Song of Songs, this book does not contain the name of God. For that reason there was a time when people hesitated to recognize it as canonical, but it soon came to be recognized as canonical. This is because, although the name of God does not appear, God's providence is felt so strongly.
Paradoxical as it is, the reason there is no figure or name of God in the book of Esther is to make the unseen hand of God and God's providence in protecting His people be seen more vividly.
Of course, since everything disguises itself as coincidence, one might carelessly think it luck. But even if it looks like coincidence to human eyes, in God's eyes there is no coincidence, so by that very fact we can know it is God's providence.
Judging from these points, the book of Esther itself testifies that it has sufficient authority as canon.
Campbell Morgan: "We cannot go on reading even a single line of the book of Esther without being conscious of the existence of God."
Charles Swindoll: "Read the famous works of Shakespeare. We cannot find the name Shakespeare even once in those works. Yet in the footsteps of the characters in the works Shakespeare wrote, we can read Shakespeare's wit, Shakespeare's tenacity, and his dream. In the same way, although the word 'God' never appears in Esther, in all the events and characters that appear in the book of Esther we can read God's providence, God's will, and God's purpose."

1. Title
The name of this book was given after the name of its protagonist, Job. The setting of the book of Job is Uz in northern Arabia, and judging from the Arabic background, it is derived from the Arabic "Aba," which means "to repent" and "to return," so its meaning is "one who repents."
2. Author and Date of Writing
There are conjectures about the author, such as Job, Moses, and Jeremiah, but it cannot be stated precisely.
3. Background
The historical setting of the book of Job would be the patriarchal age.
1) There is no concrete mention of Israel's religious ceremonies or sacrificial system.
(the office of priest, the Law, the tabernacle, religious festivals, etc.)
2) The environmental references are similar to those of the patriarchal age in which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob lived.
For example, Job's wealth was reckoned in livestock. This is likewise the case with Abraham (Genesis 12:16, 13:2) and Jacob (Genesis 30:43, 32:5). Also, the Sabeans and the Chaldeans (1:15, :17) led a nomadic life in the time of Abraham, but in later times they settled down.
3) Similar to the patriarchs, Terah, who lived 205 years, and Abraham, who lived 175 years, Job lived another 140 years after he was healed of his illness.
4) The (Hebrew) qesitah (42:11), translated "a piece of gold," is used twice elsewhere in the Bible (Genesis 33:19, Joshua 24:32), and in both it is described as a unit of currency that Jacob paid to buy land.
5) The title for God, "the Almighty" (Hebrew Shaddai), appears 31 times in the book of Job, but is used only 17 times elsewhere in the Old Testament.
This title was a designation commonly used in the patriarchal age.
4. Structure of Job
By presenting in dialogue form the debate between Job and his three friends over Job's suffering, the book develops its content so as not only to make us think from many angles about the problem of why a righteous person suffers unexpected affliction, but also to enable us to discover for ourselves the principles and attitude of faith that resolve this problem of suffering and the problems of life as a whole.
 1. Introduction (chapters 1-2)
By introducing Job's righteous and blameless faith, it shows that Job's suffering was by no means because of sin. And by showing the scene of the heavenly council, it clarifies the fundamental cause of Job's suffering.
   1:1-5 _ Job's attitude of godliness even amid wealth
   1:6-19 _ Satan's accusation
   1:20-22 _ Job's attitude of godliness even amid adversity
   2:1-8 _ Satan's intensified accusation
   2:9-13 _ Job's attitude of godliness even amid the worst of circumstances

2. Main Body (3:1-42:6)
Through three rounds of dialogue with Job's three friends, the problems and limits of the various human viewpoints on suffering are revealed. In this process it shows that suffering has a clear good purpose and reason. But in these dialogues Job makes the mistake of asserting his own righteousness. Job, who had not complained even before the devil's testing, came instead to sin because of the accusations of his three friends. The three friends, so to speak, troubled Job even more than the devil did. And all this debate and conflict is finally settled by the word of God.
   1) Chapter 3: Job's lament
   2) The first dialogue
      Chapters 4-7: Eliphaz : Job
      Chapters 8-10: Bildad : Job
      Chapters 11-14: Zophar : Job
   3) The second dialogue
      Chapters 15-17: Eliphaz : Job
      Chapters 18-19: Bildad : Job
      Chapters 20-21: Zophar : Job
   4) The third dialogue
      Chapters 22-24: Eliphaz : Job
      Chapters 25-31: Bildad : Job
      Chapters 32-37: The words of Elihu
   5) God's intervention (chapters 38-41)

3. Conclusion (chapter 42)
Even if human reason cannot understand God's providence, it lets us know that God has faithfulness and justice, and the boundless love that desires to bless human beings.
     42:1-6 _ Job's repentance
     42:7-9 _ The rebuke of the three friends
     42:10-17 _ Job's blessing
5. Main Content of Job
1. The theme of the book of Job is the suffering that a righteous person receives.
Suffering is universal, belonging to all people. "To God there are children without sin, but there are no children without suffering."
Christians sometimes come to have questions.
	•	Why does calamity strike a person who serves God faithfully and is an example to others?
	•	Why do the wicked, who disregard God and look down on others, live in peace instead?
	•	If God is almighty and just, why does He leave things as they are, with the righteous suffering and the wicked prospering?
	•	Is God truly a just God?
	•	Is God truly almighty?
	•	Is God not one who cannot maintain justice and order even in this world?
The book of Job was written for the purpose of answering such questions.
2. God, who does not give the answer to the questions immediately
Job did not know the reason for his suffering, but through the whole book of Job we discover the noble purpose of God contained in suffering. The book of Job does not present the correct answer to the questions right away. Before God Himself answers, it first presents a new viewpoint for looking at suffering through the debate with the three friends and the appearance of Elihu.
Then why does God not answer our questions immediately, but make us go through such a long process? It is because, through the process of suffering, as we wrestle with the problem, we come to have a new perspective on God and on ourselves.
Through the process of suffering we obtain the "threefold crown" of praise, glory, and honor. Although we cannot know the cause of personal hardship and trial, as we strive to overcome it with faith and trust, we experience new understanding and maturity. This is the core theme that the book of Job wants to convey to us.
No Pains, No Gains! No Cross, No Crown!
3. Suffering, Another Name for Blessing
While suffering, Job knew nothing at all about the council that took place in heaven and its result. So he even made wrong expressions, such as telling God that he would rather die. Job was a godly man, but there were also parts of him that needed to be corrected before God. God records at the beginning of the book of Job the spiritual event that took place in heaven, and at the end clearly shows the blessing He gave to Job.
In this way, if we knew what took place in heaven and what blessing was prepared at the end of it, we would be able to trust God's providence and purpose even in the pain we are now going through. That is why many people who are going through unexplained pain are comforted through the book of Job.
By showing in advance the cause and the result of suffering, the book of Job gives us a basis for believing in God's providence and blessing even amid pain we cannot understand. It shows that pain does not end merely as pain, but that within it are God's will and purpose, and a prepared blessing.
"Behind a frowning providence He hides a smiling face." (William Cowper)
Even suffering and sorrow have benefit. Just as the sun is hidden behind the dark clouds...
The central message of the book of Job is the blessing, through suffering, given to the one who trusts and obeys God though he does not understand.

1. Title
The title Psalms comes from the Greek "psalmos." This word is a translation of the Hebrew "mizmor," which means "song," and it is found in the titles of many psalms and is simply translated "psalm" (e.g., Psalm 3). This Greek name for the Psalms was established in the New Testament period (Luke 20:42; Acts 1:20). The Hebrew name of the Psalms is "Tehillim" (songs of praise), a name which suggests that the typical use of these songs is in praise offered to God in public worship.
2. Author
Titles and Authors of the Psalms
1. The Meaning of the Psalm Titles
	•	Many psalms have titles (e.g., Psalms 3 and 4). The titles may include liturgical instructions, historical background, the name of the author (writer), and so on.
	•	The Hebrew "of …" is translated, depending on the context, as "belonging to …," "written by …," "concerning …," or "for …."
Example: "A Psalm of David" → generally means that David wrote it.
	•	As ancient Near Eastern literature has been discovered and understanding of Hebrew and literary conventions has deepened, many scholars now acknowledge that a considerable number of psalms were written before the Babylonian exile. Also, there was an ancient custom of recording the author in the title, and the New Testament writers likewise acknowledge David as the author of the psalms attributed to David (Mark 12:36, Acts 1:16, etc.)
2. David and the Other Authors
	•	David: 73 psalms appear with him as author in the title, and the New Testament mentions 2 more (Psalm 2 in Acts 4:25 and Psalm 95 in Hebrews 4:7).
	•	Other authors:
	•	Asaph (12 psalms), the sons of Korah (11 psalms), Asaph (12 psalms), Solomon (2 psalms, presumed to be Psalms 72 and 127), Moses (1 psalm, Psalm 90)
	•	The authorship of the remaining psalms is unclear.
	•	The name Asaph means "one who gathers and heaps up," and he was from the tribe of Levi. He was one of the three musicians of David's time (Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun), and in the time of David and Solomon he served as the head of the temple choir (1 Chronicles 15:16-19, 2 Chronicles 5:6, 12). Also, as recorded in 2 Chronicles 29:30, he was a man of such outstanding spirituality that he was called a "seer." Asaph set up not only his own ministry but also his descendants as those who give praise (1 Chronicles 25:1-9), and after returning from the Babylonian captivity, they also took charge of the praise when the foundation of the temple was laid (Ezra 3:10).
Historical Information in the Titles
1. Psalms Connected with Specific Events in David's Life
	•	14 psalms are related to concrete events in David's life.
	•	In some cases the title is written in the third person → this does not mean it was added later; the author himself may also use the third person.
	•	It does not mean that it was written right at the time of the event, but that the event served as its background.
2. The Interpretive Value of the Historical Information
It helps in understanding the meaning and application of the Psalms.

3. Background and Classification
• Psalms of Petition
They set forth a difficult situation before the LORD and ask for help. There are communal psalms of petition, dealing with the distress faced by the whole people of God, and individual psalms of petition, dealing with the distress faced by a particular individual among the people. They make up about one third of the whole Psalter.
• Psalms of Lament
An individual or a community appeals to God about the pain, hardship, sorrow, despair, and so on that they are going through, and asks for help. They give deep sympathy and comfort, and by showing faith that comes to God even in a moment of suffering, they exhort believers to the same attitude of faith. Like the psalms of petition, there are individual psalms of lament and communal psalms of lament.
• Psalms of Thanksgiving
These psalms give thanks to God for having answered a plea. Sometimes this plea can be identified with the plea of a psalm of petition. There are communal psalms of thanksgiving, like Psalm 9, and individual psalms of thanksgiving, like Psalm 30.
• Psalms of Praise
They call upon the people of God to praise God's great attributes and acts, and cause them to praise.
The praise may focus on particular attributes, as in the praise of God's mercy in Psalm 145,
or it may focus on praise of God's universal kingship over creation, as in Psalm 93, or praise of God's work of creation, as in Psalm 8.
• Psalms in Honor of God's Law
These psalms speak of the wonder of the Law of Moses, and, like Psalm 119, help believers to have a heart to obey the Word more fully.
• Wisdom Psalms
These psalms take up themes from the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs) and make these themes the content of the song (Psalms 1 and 37).
• Psalms of Trust
These psalms enable believers to deepen their trust in God despite all kinds of difficult circumstances (Psalm 23).
• Royal Psalms
These psalms are related to the Davidic monarchy as an instrument of blessing for the people of God.
Some are prayers, as in Psalm 20, and some are thanksgiving, as in Psalm 21.
Whether they set forth a model, as in Psalms 20 and 21, or describe the reign of a king that only the Messiah can fully fulfill, as in Psalms 2 and 72,
or focus mainly on a future aspect, as in Psalm 110, all the royal psalms are related to the Messiah, the ultimate heir of David.
• Historical Psalms
These psalms draw lessons from the history of how God dealt with His people. In general the focus is communal (Psalm 78).
• Zion Psalms
"Songs of Zion" refers to the psalms that sing of the glory of Zion, the city of God and the place of God's presence, which makes His people dwell securely. (Psalms 46, 48, 76, 84, 87, and 122).
• Prophetic Psalms
These psalms reflect themes found in the prophetic books, and especially urge the people to covenant faithfulness (e.g., Psalm 81).

Besides these, there are psalms expressing repentance (Psalms 6, 25, 32, 38, 51, 130, and 143), psalms asserting one's own innocence (e.g., Psalm 26), a psalm revealing a deep longing for God (Psalm 27), theocratic psalms praising God's sovereignty and reign and His righteousness (Psalms 93-100), and psalms containing imprecations. There are also psalms especially related to liturgical events, for example Psalm 24 and probably Psalms 68 and 118.
To these are added the psalms that the Jews recited as acts of praise and thanksgiving at the Jewish festivals (Psalms 113-118) and the psalms called songs of ascent to the temple (Psalms 120-134). Meanwhile, a psalm may fit a particular category well and at the same time have characteristics of another category. For example, Psalm 34 is a psalm of thanksgiving and at the same time has an element of wisdom.
4. Structure of the Psalms
The Psalms is a collection of 150 individual songs. The standard Hebrew text divides the Psalms into five "books," probably in imitation of the five books of the Pentateuch of Moses. The psalm that ends each book closes with a doxology (Psalms 41:13), and Psalm 150 as a whole is the conclusion of Book 5 and of the whole Psalter.
The Formation and Editing of the Psalms
1. Various Periods and Sources
	•	The result of collecting and editing from many sources, from the time of Moses (15th century B.C.) down to the post-exilic period (e.g., Psalm 137).
2. Features of the Composition
	•	Divided into 5 books.
	•	Similar psalms are grouped together (e.g., Psalms 113-118, which the Jews recite with praise and thanksgiving at the Jewish festivals; Psalms 120-134, songs of ascent to the temple; and the final Hallelujah psalms, Psalms 146-150).
	•	There are psalms with the same content (Psalms 14 and 53).
	•	Psalms 72:20 records "The prayers of David are ended," but there are David psalms after it as well.

The main content of Book 1 centers on prayers that cry out to God in pain, and confessions of trust that God alone is the only Savior often appear. It opens the door by proclaiming in Psalm 107 that God answers prayer, and ends majestically with five Hallelujah psalms (Psalms 146-150). Between them are included psalms confirming that the promise God gave to David is still valid (Psalms 110, 132, and 144), two collections of psalms of David (Psalms 108-110 and 138-145), Psalm 119, the longest psalm, which praises the value of the Law at length, and the fifteen "songs of ascent to the temple" (Psalms 120-134) that were sung on the pilgrim way toward Jerusalem.|

5. Main Content of the Psalms
The Psalms is fundamentally a hymnal used by the people of God. The Psalms takes the basic theological themes of the Old Testament and turns those themes into song.
Therefore the themes common to the whole Old Testament appear repeatedly in the Psalms as well, and the following themes are included.

1) God is the one true God
The one true God, who is the Creator of heaven and earth and who rules over all things, will fully reveal His lovingkindness and justice at the time He has appointed. All human beings must know and love this God, who has perfect moral purity, majestic power and wisdom, unchanging faithfulness, and endless love.

2) Creation and the Fall
God made human beings as beings with dignity and purpose, but since the Fall all human beings are in sin and weakness that can be healed only by God's grace.

3) Election and Covenant
The one true God chose Israel for Himself and binds His people to Himself with His covenant. This covenant contained God's will to save people and to shine light on the world through them.

4) Qualifications According to the Covenant
Through the covenant God gives grace to His people. The grace is threefold. First, He forgives their sins. Second, He shapes their lives so that they reveal God's glory in this world. Third, He entrusts them with the mission of leading the Gentiles to the light of God.
The people of God must take hold of this grace in their hearts. That is, they must believe the promises of the covenant, build up strength to obey God's commands, and live the rest of their lives in that way. A person who lives such a life is called faithful and is distinguished from the unfaithful. The faithful will deeply enjoy God's love and endlessly delight in the joy of knowing God.
All who are saved are members of the church, the people of God. They influence one another's lives. The spiritual and moral state of the church affects the state of each person, and each person's spiritual and moral life also contributes to the community. So they share one another's joys and sorrows.
However, people who are saved on this earth often suffer even within the same church, or are persecuted by people who are not the people of God. Before such suffering, the people of God must not take personal revenge, but must come in prayer, believing that God will set everything right in His time.

5) Eschatology
The story of the people of God is moving toward a glorious future. At that time everyone will know the LORD and take part in the people of God. One of the great glories given to the people of God is the fact that, by God's wonderful wisdom, their faithfulness contributes to this story of redemptive history advancing toward its goal.
The Messiah, the final descendant of David, will lead His people with the great mission of leading the Gentiles to the light.
7. Imprecations in the Psalms
Many psalms contain requests for God's help when people of faith are threatened by enemies. The enemies spoken of here are often people who persecute the godly, and sometimes Gentile oppressors. Contained in these requests for help are prayers that God would punish those enemies.
Christians who know the teaching and example of Jesus (see Matthew 5:38-48, Luke 23:34, 1 Peter 2:19-23; Acts 7:6) may be shocked at such prayers of imprecation. Then the question arises of how it is possible for the people of God to pray in this way. Some thought that this is evidence that the ethics of the New Testament are higher and superior to those of the Old. Others held that these imprecations apply only to the church's fight against the ultimate enemies, Satan and the devil. But these two views are insufficient. The reason is that the New Testament writers describe themselves as heirs of the ethics of the Old Testament (see Matthew 22:34-40), that there are expressions of imprecation within the New Testament as well (1 Corinthians 16:22, Galatians 1:8-9, Revelation 6:9-10), and that they even used the imprecations of some psalms as they stand (Acts 1:20 and Romans 11:9-10 quote Psalms 69 and 109).
The principles that help in understanding these psalms are as follows.

1) Those who are cursed are not people who became enemies over trivial matters.
They are those who hate the faithful because of their faith, and who use merciless and deceitful methods to mock God and oppress the godly (see Psalms 5:4-6, 9-10, 10:15, 42:3, 94:2-7).

2) These imprecations have the form of poetry, and they may use exaggerated and vivid expressions. Whether they are fulfilled is left to God.
3) These imprecations are expressions of moral indignation, not personal revenge.
One who knows God cannot bear that those who persecute the faithful and cause people to turn away from God go unpunished and instead prosper. Zion is the city that is the center of God's love (see Psalms 48 and 122). God cannot tolerate the cruel people who rejoice when this city is destroyed.
Such psalms are prayers that God would reveal His righteousness before the whole world (see Psalms 10:17-18). They are also prayers asking that God fulfill exactly the promises He has spoken. Psalms 35:5 recalls Psalms 1:4, and Psalms 137:9 also has Isaiah 13:16 as its background. In most cases it presupposes that the persecutor will not repent. But there are also cases, like Psalms 83:17, in which the hope is to lead to repentance through punishment.

4) The ethics of the Old Testament forbid personal revenge (Leviticus 19:17-18, Proverbs 24:17, 25:21-22).
The New Testament also follows this principle as it is (see Romans 12:19-21). When the New Testament writers quote or use these imprecatory psalms, they follow the guidance of the Old Testament as it is. The prayer longing for the Lord's swift coming means disaster for the unrepentant (2 Thessalonians 1:5-10). But Christians should most deeply desire that even those who harm the church come to believe in Christ and love the people of God (see Luke 23:34, Romans 9:1-3, 10:1, 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Peter 3:9). Therefore, when asking God for protection from persecutors, they must at the same time clearly ask that those persecutors repent.

1. Title
The common name of the book is "Proverbs," which was taken from the phrase "The proverbs of Solomon" in 1:1.
The word "proverb" is derived from mashal (Hebrew), a word with the root meaning "to be like" or "to represent."
In fact, most of the Proverbs is taught by means of comparison. The Proverbs is chiefly a collection of concise maxims concerning human conduct and character in the spiritual, moral, and social spheres. These were brought together to form a collection of wise sayings called Proverbs.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The seven headings in Proverbs that provide the author and date of writing are as follows.
[Proverbs 1:1] These are the proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel,
[Proverbs 10:1] The proverbs of Solomon: A wise son brings joy to his father, but a foolish son grief to his mother.
[Proverbs 22:17] Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise— apply your mind to my knowledge—
[Proverbs 24:23] These also are sayings of the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not good.
[Proverbs 25:1] These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah:
[Proverbs 30:1] These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh—the burden that this man declared to Ithiel: “I am weary, O God, and worn out.
[Proverbs 31:1] These are the words of King Lemuel—the burden that his mother taught him:
When Proverbs is divided into three parts, the first part of each (1:1, 10:1, 25:1) records that Solomon, the son of David, is the author of most of the proverbs. Solomon (971-931 B.C.), the third king of Israel after Saul and David, composed 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs. Of these, 800 are included in Proverbs.
[1 Kings 4:32] Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five.
The three books of the Bible written by Solomon, the Song of Songs, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes, were written at different periods of Solomon's life.
The Song of Songs was written in his youth, when he was in love,
Proverbs was written when he reached middle age and his intellectual powers were at their peak,
and Ecclesiastes was written when he was old and deeply disappointed and disillusioned about the dissipation that had occupied so much of his life.
Also, Hezekiah (729-686 B.C.) ordered that Solomon's second collection of writings (chapters 25-29) be gathered and recorded.
[Proverbs 25:1] These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah:
Hezekiah was not a direct author of proverbs as Solomon was, but he was interested in bringing spiritual benefit to his officials by means of the word of God.
Finally, Agur (chapter 30) is known as the son of Jakeh, and Lemuel (chapter 31) is introduced simply as a sage and is known as both a king and a wise man. They are also known as Gentile kings, yet they became authors of Proverbs.
However, a point to be noted about the authors of Proverbs is that, although it is important to identify the human authors or editors of Proverbs, whoever they were, the real author is God, who inspired them and caused His will to be conveyed without a single error or mistake. If this is overlooked, all the effort concerning authorship ends in theological and speculative debate.
Date of Writing
It is in fact unreasonable to state concretely the date at which Proverbs was completed as a single book.
However, many Old Testament scholars presume that Proverbs, which was partially written during Solomon's reign (970-931 B.C.), was completed as a single book around the 2nd century B.C., like the various wisdom writings written in the intertestamental period.
In particular, the fact that Proverbs in its present form was not completed before the time of King Hezekiah (728-697 B.C.) can be considered as internal evidence of the Bible. Furthermore, the fact that the teachings mentioned in various places in Proverbs were understood as including more universal teachings of faith or the teachings of the sages suggests the possibility that Proverbs had already been completed before about 400 B.C.
However, as already mentioned, most of Proverbs was written by Solomon, and this fact explains that the date of his authorship is approximately 950-700 B.C.
3. Motive and Purpose of Writing
[Proverbs 1:2-6] for gaining wisdom and discipline, for comprehending words of insight, and for receiving instruction in wise living and in righteousness, justice, and equity. To impart prudence to the simple and knowledge and discretion to the young, let the wise listen and gain instruction, and the discerning acquire wise counsel by understanding the proverbs and parables, the sayings and riddles of the wise.
It is to make us know wisdom and instruction, to make us understand words of insight, to make us live a complete life according to instruction, to make the simple prudent, and to make us understand proverbs and parables, the words of the wise and their riddles.
As Proverbs itself makes clear, Proverbs gives teaching and exhortation on how those who fear God should think and act, and is a book to help young people in particular to have the wisdom of God.
The "wisdom" of Proverbs takes the fear of God and obedience to God's Law as its foundation. Proverbs is chiefly about individual ethics, that is, not as a means for sinners to come to God, but as a way for the people of God to walk with God on this earth.
However, even though Proverbs does not give a detailed explanation of the way of salvation, the central verse of the whole of Proverbs, such as "the fear of the LORD" (1:7), fundamentally explains how a sinner restores fellowship with God.
The counsel of Proverbs is beneficial to everyone. Whether a person is saved or not, the counsel of Proverbs is beneficial to everyone, but one who is not saved has no right to claim salvation because he has done these good deeds.
4. Structure of Proverbs
It is difficult to classify the structure of Proverbs, in which theological ideas and theological teachings are not systematized, according to content. Therefore it is preferable to analyze the structure centering on the headings mentioned within Proverbs.
1) The first collection of Solomon's proverbs (1:1-9:18)
2) The second collection of Solomon's proverbs (10:1-22:16)
3) The collection of the teachings of the wise (22:17-24:34)
4) The collection of Solomon's proverbs edited by Hezekiah's officials (25:1-29:27)
5) The proverbs of Agur (30:1-33)
6) The teaching of King Lemuel (31:1-9)
7) Proverbs on the ideal wife (31:10-31)
5. Key Word, Key Verses, Key Chapter
Proverbs consists of 31 chapters, 915 verses, and 15,043 words (in English).
1) Key word: Wisdom
Not only is the word "wisdom" mentioned 122 times in Proverbs alone (searched with the Bethlehem concordance program), but the whole content of Proverbs can be summarized in the words "the essence and pursuit of wisdom." That is, various explanations of wisdom appear, which can be summarized as follows.

① Wisdom causes one to fear God and honor one's parents (1:7, 8).
② Wisdom rebukes sin and evil (1:10, 15, 32, 33).
③ One who pursues wisdom receives a moral reward (2:1, 4, 5, 9).
④ One who pursues wisdom receives a bodily reward (3:8-10).
⑤ Wisdom turns one back from evil (4:11, 12, 18).
⑥ Wisdom rejects fleshly desire (5:18, 19).
⑦ Wisdom awakens the lazy (6:6, 9-11).
⑧ Wisdom restrains lust (6:25, 27).
⑨ Wisdom overcomes temptation (7:22, 23).
⑩ Wisdom rejoices in God, its source (8:30).
⑪ Wisdom gladly accepts rebuke (9:8).
⑫ Wisdom is the righteousness of life (11:19).
⑬ Wisdom causes one to use right language (12:22).
⑭ Wisdom restrains the tongue (15:28).
⑮ Wisdom is following God's will (16:1).
⑯ Wisdom avoids strife (17:1).
⑰ Wisdom makes one diligent (20:13).
Moreover, in Proverbs, expressions such as instruction (1:2), prudence (1:4), learning (1:5), and discretion (22:3) appear as words similar to wisdom, showing the various aspects of wisdom.
However, the wisdom that appears in the text does not mean mere intellectual ability, speculative learning, or skillful worldly conduct. It has a character of faith and practice that arises from acknowledging and fearing the sovereignty of the LORD, who created heaven and earth and governs history (1:7). This wisdom also appears personified (8:1-5), and this is important in that it prefigures Christ, who would later become incarnate and fulfill wisdom.
2) Key verses: 1:7, 9:10
[Proverbs 1:7] The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline.
[Proverbs 9:10] The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.
The fear of God (in the Korean and Chinese-character term, "reverence" and "fear" are combined) can be called the central concept in Proverbs. Proverbs uses several special methods to emphasize this central concept.
The fear of God is written repeatedly at the beginning (1:7) and the end (9:10) of Part 1 of Proverbs (1:7-9:10).
This structure shows well that the fear of God is the central concept of Part 1 of Proverbs (chapters 1-9).
The fear of God is also written at the beginning (1:7) and the very end (31:30) of Proverbs.
[Proverbs 31:30] Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised.
This structure also shows that the fear of God is the central concept of the whole of Proverbs.
3) Key chapter: Chapter 31
Chapter 31, the last chapter of Proverbs, consists of the proverbs that King Lemuel's mother gave to her son. Its content, however, has the character of a conclusion as well as that of an appendix to the whole of Proverbs.
Chapter 31 first gives teaching on the attitude a ruler should have (31:1-9), and also teaching on the wisdom a virtuous woman should have (31:10-31). Among these, the teaching on the virtuous woman is the exact opposite of the figure of the adulteress who appears several times in Proverbs (5:1-23, 7:6-27), and shows a desirable image of a woman.
But if we look for a more positive meaning in this content, we can find the desirable attitude of life that believers, as the bride of Christ, should aim at. That is, chapter 31 defines the virtues of the virtuous woman as being diligent, doing good to her husband, caring for the poor neighbor, always speaking good words, taking good care of her household, and above all fearing the LORD. This teaching applies not merely to women; as a summary of the whole content of Proverbs, which stresses wisdom, it can be said to show well the attitude of life that everyone who pursues theocentric wisdom should aim at.

1. Title
The Korean title Jeondoseo, meaning "the book that conveys truth," is a translation of "Qoheleth," the Hebrew word meaning "one who lectures to the congregation with public authority," that is, "preacher," which is freely rendered "the Preacher" in Ecclesiastes 1:1 of this book. The Septuagint, the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, translated it as "Ekklesiastes," which became the origin of "Ecclesiastes" in English Bibles.
"Ecclesiastes" is not a Hebrew word but comes from the Greek "ekklesia," which is translated "church" or "assembly" in the New Testament. This conveys the idea of a preacher or debater who speaks to a congregation. (1:1-2/12:8-10)
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
In Ecclesiastes 1:1-2, 12 the name of Solomon is stated as the author. No king in the Old Testament had qualifications more suited to writing this book than Solomon.
Solomon was the king of Israel and also a great sage of all places and ages. His name <Shelomo> means "peace," and he also had as an additional name "Jedidiah," meaning "beloved of God."
Date of Writing
This book is presumed to have been written around 935 B.C., at the end of his life, as a discourse-sermon in which Solomon, having reached old age, looked toward death and reflected on his life according to the wisdom-literature tradition of the time.

3. Motive and Purpose of Writing
 The purpose of writing this book is to make people recognize that human beings cannot obtain the true value of life through physical pleasure alone, and that only when they serve God alone and abide in Him can they enjoy the true value of life. That is, when glory and blessing obtained only through a person's own experience or knowledge become the ultimate purpose of life, only frustration and emptiness exist.
The central words of Ecclesiastes are "under the sun" and "futile." Human happiness lies not in natural wisdom or knowledge, worldly wealth, honor and power, worldly pleasure, or a formal religious life, but in fearing God. That is, humans who have left God have no happiness.
In the end, the aged Preacher wishes that his readers might avoid the many pitfalls that come in life. And he wishes that they might have a true change in life before it is too late. In the end, Ecclesiastes has become a guide to life for many people.
Many people live in the world largely in a state lacking a personal encounter and relationship with God. People live with a philosophy of their own. But the value of life comes when one relies on God and lives in Him.
Life has a past, a present, and a future. If the present world becomes the ultimate purpose of life, everything is merely futile. Ecclesiastes tells us to live with a true hope for the future, that is, for the world to come, even if our life in the past or present is a meaningless one. And it reminds us that we should see all the creatures of this world as God's creation and use everything given to us in life for the glory of God.
① Even if one tries everything to satisfy the heart of man who has left God, it is merely futile.
② Only to fear God and keep His commandments is the happiness and duty of life.
- The words that form the core of Ecclesiastes are "man" (47 times), "toil" (36 times), "under the sun" (30 times), "futility" (38 times), "wisdom" or "wise" (52 times), "evil" (22 times), and so on.
