5. Analysis of the Five Books of Poetry
When we look at the five poetical books as a whole, there is a clear spiritual progress. It is clear that God also placed meaning in the arrangement of the Bible. The five books of poetry show the following spiritual progress.
In the end, the five books of poetry show a progress in which the old, self-centered life dies, and one begins a new life in God, learns the lessons of training and nurture in God's school and of being separated from worldly desires, and finally comes to experience fellowship with the Bridegroom in heaven. This shows in order the spiritual progress that believers go through.
* suffering → worship → wisdom → purpose in life & love in marriage
A Christian goes through the following process of growth.
First, he learns to have a heart that can give up not only his evil but even his good.
Second, like a child beginning to walk, he learns to walk by the strength of faith. Even when he sometimes falls, he shows progress.
Third, he experiences that he must submit his own will to Christ, the wisdom of God, and be subject to Christ.
Fourth, he learns that he must be freed from the spirit of the present age and live seeking the things above.
Fifth, he enters into intimate and united fellowship with Christ, full of joy.
Comparison of Proverbs and Ecclesiastes
Proverbs says that wise choices produce good results and foolish choices produce bad results. But Ecclesiastes says that life under the sun is often not so.
In Proverbs, it is made clear that Jesus is the foundation of everything, whereas Ecclesiastes says that Jesus is the goal of everything.
In Proverbs wisdom is for godliness, whereas in Ecclesiastes wisdom is for prudence and sagacity.
The common conclusion of the two books tells us that only wisdom in Christ gives true happiness to human life.

6. The Meaning of Ecclesiastes
A "futile" life: "under the sun" | A "blessed" life: "in the Lord"   -> Only life in the Lord has value, meaning, and purpose worth living. -> Human happiness lies not in natural wisdom or knowledge, worldly wealth, honor and power, worldly pleasure, or a formal religious life, but in fearing God. That is, humans who have left God have no happiness.
※ The chief end of man is to glorify God and to enjoy Him forever.
A life of vanity upon vanity, the absurdities of the world, suffering, illness, and so on... what cannot be understood can be overcome by what we already know, that is, the gospel. God's faithfulness and love toward us are clearly revealed through the gospel. Only through faith can we overcome a reality we cannot understand and live a right life.
Our life in this present world is like the Friday on which Jesus was nailed to the cross. Even if we are in a reality like "Why have You forsaken me?", let us look in faith toward the morning of the resurrection, that is, Sunday.

1. Title
The title in the Hebrew original, ‘Shir HaShirim,’ means ‘the song of songs’ or ‘the most beautiful song.’ Most English versions likewise use ‘Song of Songs’ as the title. The title of the Korean Revised Version, ‘Aga’ (a Sino-Korean title meaning ‘elegant and refined song’), is a rendering of the title of the Hebrew original.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
It was written through Solomon, the third king of Israel, who was so gifted in literature that he composed three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs.
Date of Writing
The queens and concubines still numbered only 140, and Solomon's love is utterly pure and passionate. From this it is estimated that the book was written within the early part of Solomon's reign (970–930 BC), between 970 and 960 BC.
3. Motive and Purpose of Writing
From Genesis to Revelation, the whole of Scripture unfolds the story of the Shepherd who left the high throne of glory in heaven and came down into this dark world in order to win His bride. When He died, rose again, and ascended, He promised, ‘I will come again and receive you to Myself.’ And the church has waited a long time for His coming. One day He will come again to fulfill His promise. To understand the Song of Songs, one must think of the relationship between Jesus the Bridegroom and the church and the believer as His bride.
It is said that the Jews did not allow young people under the age of thirty to read this book, in order to keep them from reading it merely as a matter of carnal interest or from carelessly using its beautiful expressions. In the same way, we may say that only mature Christians who have grown in the grace and knowledge of Christ can rightly understand this book and perceive the Lord's mystery in it.
The Jews compared Proverbs to the ‘temple,’ Ecclesiastes to the ‘Holy Place,’ and the Song of Songs to the ‘Most Holy Place.’ The Song of Songs was recognized by the Jews as Scripture from ancient times, and the early church also accepted it without hesitation.
Purpose
【It is only fitting that this book is called the song of songs. There is no other song like it. As you read it, a joy comes into the heart that cannot be compared with earthly pleasures, as heaven is higher than the earth. It is rightly said that this is a song that only grace can teach and only experience can learn.
Speaking of the union of the vine and its branches, Jesus went on to say, ‘I have told you these things so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete.’ (John 15:11)
The apostle John, who was loved by Jesus, also spoke of the One ‘who was from the beginning,’ the One ‘who was with the Father,’ who was revealed to us so that we might share in the fellowship that He enjoys, and he says, ‘We write these things so that our joy may be complete.’ (1 John 1:4)
Union with Christ, abiding in Christ—what is not guaranteed here? Peace, perfect peace; rest, perfect rest; the answer to every prayer; victory over every enemy; a holy life; overflowing fruitfulness—all of these are the joyful fruits obtained by abiding in Christ. The practical use of this precious book is to deepen this union and to keep us abiding in Him always.】 <Hudson Taylor>

Therefore believers who have been born again by the Spirit of God need a fuller experience in Christ, and should long to advance toward a deeper union and fellowship with the Lord and to the place of love. It is saying that what is required of the bride for such a union to be granted is higher devotion and obedience.
4. Structure of the Song of Songs
Part 1  1:2–2:7    A Dissatisfied Life and Its Cure
A woman who longs for true satisfaction because her life has none meets the king. The Bridegroom not only satisfied the deepest longing of the bride's soul but also found His own satisfaction in the bride.
Part 2  2:8–3:5    Broken Fellowship and Restoration
Because of her own fault, the bride returned to the world, and so the fellowship was broken. With a single-minded resolve to seek the Bridegroom with her whole heart, the bride sets out to look for Him. But when she was separated from the world, her fellowship with the Bridegroom was restored.
Part 3  3:6–5:1    Unbroken Fellowship
The bride marries the Bridegroom and comes to share in His security and glory. Captivated by the Bridegroom, she wants others to become the same. The Bridegroom delights in the bride and invites her to a place of service.
Part 4  5:2–6:10   Fellowship Broken Again and Restored
Once again the bride fails. This time it is not because of worldliness, as before, but because of spiritual pride and laziness. Restoration was far more difficult this time, but again the bride diligently sets out to seek the Bridegroom. When she confessed her love for the Bridegroom to the point that a desire arose in others to go out and seek Him with her, He met the bride, the fellowship was restored, and the communion is never interrupted again.
Part 5  6:11–8:4   The Fruit of an Acknowledged Union
The Bridegroom and the bride not only taste satisfaction and joy in one another, but the women of Jerusalem also acknowledge the bride's standing and beauty.
Part 6  8:5–14     Unrestrained Fellowship
Leaning on her beloved, the bride begs Him to bind her to Himself more firmly, and she serves in the Bridegroom's vineyard until the Bridegroom calls her out from her work in the world.
Comparison of Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs
It is interesting to contrast the Song of Songs with the book that precedes it. Ecclesiastes teaches emphatically, ‘Vanity of vanities, all is vanity,’ whereas the Song of Songs shows how true blessing and satisfaction can be possessed.

5. Explanatory Notes for Understanding the Song of Songs
A. Four Perspectives
In the Song of Songs, the ‘king’ refers to Solomon and at the same time prefigures Jesus Christ,
and the ‘woman’ refers to the Shulammite woman and at the same time prefigures the Christian.
The relationship between Jesus Christ and the believer is the relationship between bridegroom and bride.
	1)	The relationship of love between husband and wife
	2)	The relationship between the LORD God and Israel
	3)	The relationship between Christ and the church
	4)	The relationship between the Lord and the believer
B. The Wisdom of Distinguishing the Speakers
The speakers are the Bridegroom, the bride, and the women of Jerusalem.
The bride calls the Bridegroom ‘my beloved.’
The Bridegroom calls the bride ‘my darling.’
The title by which the women of Jerusalem address the bride is
‘the most beautiful of women’ in Parts 1 through 4,
but in Part 5 they call her ‘the Shulammite,’ ‘the king's bride,’ or ‘the noble one's daughter.’

1. Title
It is called ‘Isaiah’ after the name of its author. The original word for Isaiah, ‘Yeshayahu,’ is a compound of ‘yeshua,’ meaning ‘salvation,’ and ‘Yah,’ which refers to the LORD, and means ‘the LORD is salvation.’
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
Isaiah son of Amoz, who was active in the southern kingdom of Judah between the eighth and seventh centuries BC. Amoz is presumed to have been either a brother or a son of Amaziah, the ninth king of Judah.
His ministry began in the year King Uzziah died (Isa 6:1, about 740 BC).
He lived through the reigns of four kings: Uzziah and Jotham, who were on the whole good kings; Ahaz, who was an evil king; and Hezekiah, who was counted among the very good kings. Since he recorded the death of Sennacherib king of Assyria (681 BC), Isaiah must have ministered for a long period of at least sixty years.
His social standing was also high, because he was close to the kings Ahaz and Hezekiah. Because of his high standing, he would have recorded the reigns of successive kings. Isaiah's high social standing is related to the ministry God gave him. The talents and the social status and authority that God gave were connected with the task entrusted to him. Because he was a prophet who worked in a dark age, he was given learning and high rank for the sake of the ministry entrusted to him.
Date of Writing
Between about 739 BC, toward the end of Uzziah's reign, and about 680 BC, when Isaiah is said to have been martyred.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
Because of disobedience, the northern kingdom of Israel was destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC. Yet the southern kingdom of Judah, following the example of northern Israel, looked for protection and salvation not to God but to the Gentile powers of Assyria and Egypt. Isaiah wrote in order to rebuke them for this unbelief and lead them to repent. The Jews compared Proverbs to the ‘temple,’ Ecclesiastes to the ‘Holy Place,’ and the book of Isaiah to the ‘Most Holy Place.’ The book of Isaiah was recognized by the Jews as Scripture from ancient times, and the early church also accepted it without hesitation.
Motives for Writing
1) To proclaim God's judgment
Judah's society was outwardly prosperous, but inwardly injustice, corruption, and idolatry were rampant. Through Isaiah, God made known to such a southern Judah His holy judgment on sin.
2) To proclaim God's salvation
God's pronouncement of judgment did not have judgment as its aim; its aim was salvation. God promised to preserve a ‘remnant’ and to bring about a new salvation, and he testified that God Himself would save Jerusalem in its crisis of destruction (Isaiah 37).
Isaiah proclaimed the ultimate salvation by prophesying the coming Messiah (Immanuel, the Prince of Peace, the suffering Servant).
3) To urge true dependence on God
In this situation Judah did not rely on God but tried to secure its safety through visible great powers and political alliances (Egypt, Assyria). To the foolish people of southern Judah, Isaiah taught that trusting in God alone is the true way, as in the words, “By repentance and rest you would be saved” (Isa 30:15).
4) To reveal God's holiness and sovereignty
This foolishness of the people of southern Judah came from their ignorance of God.
God is high and holy (Isaiah 6), and He rules over the history of the nations. Great powers such as Assyria and Babylon are merely instruments of God, and in the end they come under judgment in the course of carrying out God's purpose. The book of Isaiah reveals that God is the sovereign of the whole world.
5) To set forth the hope of the glory to come
Isaiah intended to bring hope to the people of southern Judah. By making known that, despite the present judgment and suffering, God is the One who has promised a new heaven and a new earth, the salvation of the nations, and the restoration of Zion (Isaiah 60–66), he sought to give hope and comfort to a people fallen into despair.
4. Structure of Isaiah
Part 1 [Chapters 1–39] God's Judgment
▶ Chapters 1–6: Judah's Wickedness and Isaiah's Call
The people's sin is the result of God's people rebelling against the Lord's will, trusting the surrounding nations, and practicing idolatry; the people were left in ruins and the land became a wasteland and was isolated.
At such a time Isaiah saw the glory of God, repented of his own sin and the sin of the people, and received a holy calling. “The LORD says: ‘Come now, let us reason together…’”
▶ Chapters 7–12: Prophecy of the Messiah
These are prophecies about Immanuel and the work and salvation of the Messiah. God's grace appeared in the salvation of sinners, and the Savior is conceived by a virgin and brings it to completion.
“Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will conceive…”
▶ Chapters 13–23: Judgment on the Nations
There are extensive prophecies of judgment on the peoples around Israel—Babylon, Assyria, Persia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Aram, Sidon, Tyre, and others—and God's judgment was carried out in accordance with justice.
To those on whom He should have compassion, God judges with compassion; to those who harden their hearts, He judges with justice.
▶ Chapters 24–39: Judgment on Israel
The judgment on the nations around Israel signifies the salvation of Israel. At the same time, God's people have many enemies around them, but God judges them and saves His people. Blessed is the one who, though disciplined by God, is not cast aside, rather than the one who is used as God's instrument and then cast aside.
Part 2 [Chapters 40–66] God's Plan of Salvation and Restoration
Chapters 40–48: The Salvation of God's People
By using Cyrus king of Persia as His instrument to set the chosen people Israel free from captivity in Babylon, God shows His power as Savior, warns against all idolatry, and exhorts to faith in God.
In particular, through the words of the first ‘Servant of the LORD’ passage (Isa 42:1-9), it shows that because God loves His people, He sends the Messiah, His Servant. And the contrast between the words of the ‘prophecy of the restoration of the chosen people’ (Isaiah 40–45) and the ‘prophecy of the fall of the Babylonian empire’ (Isaiah 46–47), which serves idols, well shows the ultimate victory of faith in the LORD God.
Meanwhile, it also says that the chosen people Israel must be ‘God's witnesses,’ revealing the glory of God to all peoples.
Chapters 49–57: The Suffering and Victory of the Messiah, the Savior
Centering on the three ‘Servant of the LORD’ passages (Isa 49:1-7, 50:4-9, 52:13-53:12), it shows that the LORD will accomplish, through the Messiah, the work of redemption for the salvation of the people. It also records the LORD God's invitation to all peoples of the world to obtain eternal salvation through repentance and faith.
Chapters 58–66: The Ultimate Restoration to Be Realized and Completed
This is the concluding part of the whole book, and it prophesies the return of the people of Israel from Babylon. In the first place, it records the joy and delight of the chosen people arising from the rebuilding of Israel as a theocratic state, begun by the return from captivity, the restoration of the LORD's rule, and the restoration of the relationship between God and the people of Israel. Ultimately, it prophesies the glory and blessing that believers of every generation will enjoy through the coming of the Messianic kingdom.

5. Christ in the Book of Isaiah
The sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments each record the history of a different age in their content. The Bible truly contains a wide variety of content and form. Yet its fundamental theme and purpose are all the same: ‘salvation through the redemptive work of our Lord Jesus Christ, carried out through the history of all humanity.’
The book of Isaiah is the book that, among the Old Testament prophetic books, shows most clearly and vividly the fundamental theme of the whole Bible—the redemptive work of Jesus Christ and His appearance—and, in particular, the first coming of Jesus Christ and the salvation of believers through Him.
(1) Christ the King
[Isaiah 9:6] For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.
‘A child’ refers to Jesus Christ, the Messiah who is to come, the ‘Son’ whom God promised to give to His people.
It prophesies that Jesus Christ, unlike the other kings of the world, will bear every burden Himself and will reign with excellence and faithfulness. As One who transcends all the laws of nature, He is wonderful and miraculous, and He possesses honor and excellence. Jesus the Messiah came to this earth transcending the laws of nature, carried out the work of destroying the power of sin, and died, but rose again and accomplished the work that completed salvation.
(2) Christ Who Came from the Stump of Jesse
[Isaiah 11:1] Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit.
‘A shoot’ is the Messiah, and He will be born from the stump of Jesse, that is, from the house of David.
That the prophet used the name ‘Jesse’ instead of ‘David’ implies that the shoot that comes from him will be born in the status that preceded David, that is, the lowly status symbolized by his father Jesse, who was a farmer.
‘A Branch from his roots will bear fruit’—just as a tender branch sprouts from a root buried in the ground, the Messiah will come from the fallen house of David as a lowly and insignificant human being. For this reason He had to be called a despised and lowly Nazarene.
[Matthew 2:23] and he went and lived in a town called Nazareth. So was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophets: “He will be called a Nazarene.”
* ‘Nazareth’—a word derived from the Hebrew ‘netzer,’ meaning ‘shoot, young sprout.’ It was a town in Galilee located about 90 km north of Jerusalem, on infertile sandy ground, and economically a poor town because of the surrounding hills. It is a name that appears neither in the Old Testament, nor in the Apocrypha, nor in the Antiquities of Josephus, but is new in the New Testament. Nazareth was one of the towns held in contempt (John 1:46), and it was there, in Nazareth, that Jesus grew up, mocked as ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ When Christians were treated as ‘the sect of the Nazarenes’ (Acts 24:5), the word ‘Nazarene’ carried a nuance of slander and insult. Jesus came as the Messiah who was a branch from the royal line of David, of which only a stump remained, and a shoot that grew up in lowly circumstances amid mockery and contempt.
(3) Christ Who Came as the Servant of the LORD
[Isaiah 42:1] “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations.
In the book of Isaiah, chapters 42–53 are called ‘the Songs of the Servant of the LORD.’ These chapters may be called the most precious writing in Isaiah; they introduce the Messiah, that is, Christ, as a servant sent by the LORD God, who obeys and is faithful thoroughly to God's will to save the holy people whom God has chosen. The Songs of the Servant of the LORD are famous for being written in the most beautiful and elegant prose in all the prophetic books of Isaiah.
Through these, Isaiah introduces Christ as the Servant who will manifest the glory of the LORD (49:3), who teaches His word to the people and enlightens them (50:4), and who gladly accepts suffering like a lamb led to the slaughter, becoming a sacrifice of atonement for our sins (53:4-9). It also says that when Christ has finished the work of redemption through the suffering of God's Servant, God will greatly exalt Him.
[Isaiah 52:13] Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.
[Isaiah 53:12] Therefore I will allot Him a portion with the great, and He will divide the spoils with the strong, because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.
Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Servant of the LORD, came to this earth as the light of salvation, and as the mediator between God and man ministered as a servant who truly labors for both God and man.
For sinners He also came into the world weak and with no beauty of form, devoted Himself while being despised by men, and, although He was without sin, bore the suffering of the cross, which is truly unbearable for a human being. Our Lord Jesus Christ gave up His position as God the Father and silently took up and carried out the position of a servant who had to bear the lowly and agonizing ministry of the Lamb who carries the sin of the world.
It makes us give boundless thanks that I, who am not worthy of such pure love, have been saved by unconditional grace, and we learn the great grace and love of Christ.
(4) Christ the Mediator
[Isaiah 62:1-5] For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep still, until her righteousness shines like a bright light, her salvation like a blazing torch. Nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory. You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow. You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God. No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride. For as a young man marries a young woman, so your sons will marry you; and as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
Isaiah speaks of the restoration of the relationship between God and Israel. The Servant of the LORD, that is, the Messiah, who appears here as ‘I,’ is the mediator who establishes the relationship between the people of Israel and God.
The Messiah's work of mediation is to give the people of Israel righteousness, glory, and a new name so that they may have full standing before God, and to enable the LORD to take the inheritance of the people of Israel as a beautiful crown and royal diadem in the hand of the people of Zion, and to take them as a virgin and a bride, as Hephzibah and Beulah.
For us believers today, who have received the blessing of becoming children of God by believing the gospel of Christ, this makes us realize that this blessing was not given by chance but was given according to what was prepared from the beginning, and moves us to render endless thanks and praise to the LORD.
(5) Christ the Light and Comforter
[Isaiah 9:1-2] Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress. In the past He humbled the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but in the future He will honor the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.
The whole land of Israel will fall into great suffering because of God's discipline, but nevertheless, by God's grace, the days of that suffering will come to a complete end, and those who were in that suffering will be comforted.
This was prophesied looking toward the day when the Messiah, Jesus Christ, would come; it means that, with the coming of Jesus Christ, the true Light, the fear and suffering of all sinners who were under God's wrathful judgment will vanish like the morning dew.
Our Lord Jesus Christ is not One who judges lives wounded by sin, but One who embraces and restores them. Jesus Christ is the great light to those who suffer in darkness, and the Comforter who does not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick.
This prophecy that God would show His glory from the darkest and most painful land and restore His people and bring them glory was fulfilled through the early Galilean ministry of Jesus Christ, the only begotten God.
[Matthew 4:13-16] Leaving Nazareth, He went and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali, to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the Way of the Sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles— the people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.”
It prophesied that humankind, which was in sin, would receive the light of the gospel through the coming of Christ, the true Light, and be saved. And this prophecy was fulfilled just as it said.
[John 1:3-4] Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men.
We are people who have lived in the darkness of sin, who lived in sin that is gloomy and pitch-dark. From that dark state, the light of salvation shone upon us through Jesus Christ, and until now He has been leading us into the light of the Word so that we may live as children of light.

1. Title
It is called ‘Jeremiah’ after the name of its author. ‘Jeremiah’ means “the LORD establishes, the LORD exalts,” and it also carries the sense “the LORD hurls.” God's plan—to hurl away sinful Judah and afterward to raise up the remnant again—is contained in his name.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The book of Jeremiah records that Jeremiah is its author (Jer 1:1).
Jeremiah was the son of the priest Hilkiah and lived in Anathoth, north of Jerusalem.
As an object lesson for Judah, he was not permitted to marry (Jer 16:2), because of his message that God's judgment and destruction would come through the invasion of Babylon. He was threatened by his own people and family and was even imprisoned. Jeremiah survived when Babylon attacked Jerusalem, and it is said that he was later taken to Egypt and died there.
Date of Writing
About 626–580 BC.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background: 2 Chronicles 35:20∼36:21, 2 Kings 23:29∼25:21
The historical situation of Jeremiah's day was the closing period of the decline of southern Judah.
In the international situation at the beginning of Jeremiah's ministry, Chaldean Babylon and Assyria were contending for power and so took no interest in southern Judah, and Judah was therefore in a somewhat peaceful state. Internally, it was a period when Josiah <640∼609 BC> had ascended the throne and was pursuing religious reform and building up inner strength by purifying the temple and removing the high places, the Asherah poles, and the carved idols.
But in 609 BC Josiah was killed in battle with Neco king of Egypt at Megiddo. <2 Chronicles 35:20∼24> After that, the kings made Egypt and Assyria, not God, the objects of their trust, and by continuing in evil deeds and misrule they sent Judah rushing along the road of rapid decline.
During the reigns of the kings in the time of Jeremiah's ministry <Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah>, Judah was in a time of darkness. The nation's standing declined, and the people grew steadily weaker. Jehoahaz reigned only a short period of three months and was soon deposed. In the time of Jehoiakim, the wickedness spread and deepened still further.
Jehoiachin, after reigning three months, was taken captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. Zedekiah was a very weak man and a puppet of another nation. And so Judah was invaded for the first time by Babylon in 606 BC and subjugated, and after being invaded repeatedly in 597 BC and 586 BC, it was finally destroyed.
※ The Situation of the Great Powers at the Time
- The fall of Assyria began, and the struggle for power between Egypt and Babylon began, so the international situation was unsettled.
- Pharaoh Neco II of Egypt advanced to Carchemish in order to consolidate his influence in Palestine and Syria
- Josiah was killed in an engagement with the army of Pharaoh Neco (2 Kings 23:29-30)
- Jehoahaz, who succeeded him, was deposed by Neco after three months (2 Kings 23:31-34)
- Next, Josiah's son Jehoiakim (609–597 BC) ascended the throne
- In 606 BC sovereignty was lost (the reason this is regarded as the time of southern Judah's downfall)
- In 605 BC Babylon won the battle of Carchemish, ended Egypt's rule over Palestine, and firmly extended its own rule (rising as the strongest nation)
- Jehoiakim rebelled against Babylon in 601 BC, but because of this was invaded by Babylon in 598 BC
- Jehoiakim died and his son Jehoiachin ascended the throne, but after three months he bowed before Babylon's military might and was taken captive (2 Kings 24)
- With Jehoiachin's uncle, that is, Josiah's son Zedekiah (597–587 BC), it came to an end
- Ruled for 344 years by twenty kings, it was never able to recover from its rebellion and finally perished
- The people and leaders of Judah acted rebelliously against God, and in order to compromise with present sins and preserve comfort (to preserve their vested interests), they failed to discern the times, maintained a pro-Egypt policy, and perished

Motive for Writing
The key words of this book are decline and judgment. This period in which Jeremiah was active was one of extreme religious and moral corruption. Therefore Jeremiah's mission was not an easy one. For he had to toll the bell of death for his own people.
This people had turned their backs on the LORD and followed false prophets who led them into idolatry. Jeremiah delivered the call to repent, but the people of Judah did not repent. We read of Jeremiah weeping. Thus he felt very great grief over this fallen people.
Jeremiah prophesied captivity in Babylon and was persecuted by the people.
Had Judah repented and turned its heart to God, God would have delivered them from Babylon. Because they were stubborn in their sin they had to be punished, but God promised to restore them “for His own name's sake.”
So that his message might be well understood, Jeremiah used many illustrations expressed in dramatic actions: springs and cisterns (Jer 2:13), (Jer 8:22), the useless waistband (Jer 13:1~11), the pottery (Jeremiah 18–19), the yoke (chapter 27), and the book thrown into the river (Jer 51:59~64).
At that time southern Judah was full of sin, and its leaders were corrupt. Such people did not even have the possibility of conversion. So God says that praying for them is of no more use.
The message of Jeremiah that came out under these circumstances was “the proclamation and warning of disaster.” Its main content is the proclamation of God's solemn warning of judgment toward the people of Judah of that era and its fulfillment, and the message of restoration that gives hope of a new salvation.

1. Title
The first Hebrew word of chapters 1, 2, and 4, 'Ekah' (Ekah: how), is the formal title of the book in the Hebrew Bible. Instead of 'Ekah,' the rabbis used as the title the Hebrew word 'Ginoth' (Ginoth), meaning 'dirges' or 'laments,' because this word better reflects the content of the book. The 'Septuagint' (The Septuagint Version, the Greek Old Testament) followed the rabbis' position and gave it the title 'Threnoi' (Threnoi: tears or laments), and the title 'Lamentations of Jeremiah' originated in the Syriac and Vulgate versions.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
Who wrote Lamentations is not indicated in the book itself.
However, there is no great disagreement that the prophet Jeremiah, who wrote the book of Jeremiah, is the author. Judging from the fact that the fall of Jerusalem is witnessed vividly on the spot and that the content is poured out from the Lord's own heart, the author is a prophet who had the heart of the Lord.
Its style is almost identical to that of the book of Jeremiah, and 2 Chronicles 35:25 says, "Jeremiah composed laments for him."
The preface to these 'Lamentations' in the 'Septuagint' records: "After Israel was taken captive and Jerusalem was laid waste, Jeremiah sat down on the ground, weeping, and mourned, singing this lament over Jerusalem …"
Date of Writing
This book was written immediately after Jerusalem was destroyed, at the time when the deportation to Babylon was beginning.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon besieged the city of Jerusalem from January 588 BC until July 586 BC. Jerusalem was taken on July 19, and on August 15 the city and the temple were burned. Not long after Jerusalem fell, Jeremiah was forcibly taken to Egypt by those who opposed him (Jer 43:6-7). The 'Lamentations' appear to have been written after the fall of Jerusalem and before he was forcibly taken away.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The northern dynasty was captured and destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC, but Jerusalem was preserved for another 114 years. In spite of this mercy and grace of God, Judah did not understand, followed northern Israel, and still walked in the way of evil. As a result, it incurred the wrath of God and met the tragic fate of having Jerusalem, the symbol of the chosen people, utterly destroyed.
The international situation at that time was in turmoil over supremacy in the Middle East. The powers of Babylon and Egypt confronted each other, and Israel, caught between them, had its fate swayed by shifts in power.
Pharaoh Neco king of Egypt invaded Jerusalem, carried off to Egypt Jehoahaz, the king of Judah whom the people had set up at that time, and installed his brother Eliakim (Jehoiakim) as king (2 Chronicles 36:1-4).
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon invaded Jerusalem in 605 BC and made King Jehoiakim submit (2 Kings 24:1; the first Babylonian captivity).
King Nebuchadnezzar attacked Judah again in 597 BC and carried off to Babylon the eighteen-year-old King Jehoiachin and the people (2 Kings 24:10-17; the second Babylonian captivity). And in place of Jehoiachin he made his uncle Mattaniah king and changed his name to Zedekiah.
During Zedekiah's reign an anti-Babylonian movement arose in Jerusalem. Those who joined this movement urged King Zedekiah to resist Babylon and ask Egypt for help.
At this time Jeremiah strongly tried to dissuade them, delivering the completely opposite message given to him by God. For a while Zedekiah seemed to listen to the will of God, but in the end he turned to a pro-Egyptian policy. As a result, in 588 BC King Nebuchadnezzar invaded again and besieged Jerusalem, and the city of Jerusalem fell eighteen months later, in the eleventh year of Zedekiah.
Babylon made Judah a province of Babylon and appointed Gedaliah governor, but two months after he became governor he was murdered by Ishmael, a member of the royal family. Many of the people left in the land of Canaan, fearing Babylon's retaliation, fled to Egypt. Jerusalem was thus left utterly abandoned. The book of Lamentations was written precisely at this time.
Motive for Writing
After the king and the people were taken to Babylon, Jeremiah remained in Judah and continued his ministry for the remaining people (Jeremiah 40–42).
Although it was a situation of despair in which the nation had perished and the covenant with God seemed to have been annulled, Jeremiah did not abandon the people and did his best to the end in his ministry.
He explained to the people God's judgment on the consequences of their wickedness, and wrote the 'Lamentations' for the purpose of leading them to place a new hope in the unchanging covenant-keeping God as they sincerely repented.
"Jeremiah appealed to the people that in their desperate situation they must 'open the door of prayer to approach God and plead for God's mercy.'" (Calvin)

4. Structure of Lamentations
Chapter 1 – The Fall of Jerusalem
It consists of the lament of Jeremiah and the lament of personified Jerusalem. Jerusalem has been laid waste because of its heinous sins. It appeals for God to look upon this tragedy of Jerusalem.
Chapter 2 – The Wrath of God
Chapter 2 speaks of the cause. Although Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, they were merely used as an instrument of God. Under the thorough and severe judgment, Jeremiah keenly feels how heinous the chosen people's own sin against God was. Through Babylon, God abolished all the religious ceremonies, destroyed the priests, the prophets, and the kings, and tore down the temple and the palaces. Jeremiah pours out great sorrow before Israel's wickedness and the wrath of God that followed from it.
Chapter 3 – Prayer Seeking Compassion
Jeremiah first speaks of extreme suffering. This is a shadow of the suffering Christ would later undergo on the cross. Then, recalling God's passionate love and faithful character, he finds comfort and hope there. And he appeals to God for deliverance and implores Him to take vengeance on the enemies.
Chapter 4 – The Siege of Jerusalem
Jeremiah describes in detail the siege of Jerusalem and recalls the suffering and hunger of the poor and the rich. Looking back on the cause of the judgment, he also points out the sins of the prophets and priests and the folly of trusting in what is of the flesh. And he ends with hope for the restoration of Jerusalem.
Chapter 5 – Prayer for Restoration
It piteously describes the bitter condition of his people. God's punishment of them was thorough, but that punishment has now come to an end, and he asks God for help in repentance, so that they may believe this and return. He earnestly hopes for the restoration of Israel.

5. The Place of Lamentations
Its Position in the Arrangement of the Bible
① In the Hebrew Bible, 'Lamentations' is placed together with the Song of Songs, Ruth, Esther, and Ecclesiastes in the Megilloth (the five scrolls). In the Septuagint, however, it is placed after the book of Jeremiah, as in our present Korean Bible, which follows the English translations.
② If the book of Jeremiah is a book that mainly warns of the destruction of Jerusalem, Lamentations looks back and reflects on it after its fulfillment.

A Type of Christ Who Would Suffer for the Atonement of Our Sins
The wrath of God that fell on Israel is like a prelude to the judgment that will fall on all who have turned their backs on God and lived as His enemies. In place of us, who deserve God's judgment because of our own sins, Christ bore the cross of wrath and received the judgment of atonement. Thus God's wrath against us passed over.
The wretched situation of Lamentations is a model of the judgment that we should have received under God's judgment, and it is precisely the hardship that our Lord underwent in place of each person, in place of 'me.'

1. Title
It is called ‘Ezekiel (Hebrew: Yechezkel)’ after the name of the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel means ‘God is strong; God strengthens,’ and it fits well with the content of the book of Ezekiel, which records the figure of the almighty and strong God who, beyond human imagination, governs history according to His will, and the grace by which He purifies the people of Israel, who had come to ruin through sin, and makes them strong again.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
Ezekiel was born the son of Buzi, a priest of the line of Zadok, and he was of priestly descent, having spent his youth in Judah as a priest's son. From his childhood he would have heard of King Josiah's reform (621 BC), of Assyria's destruction by Babylon (612 BC), of Egypt's defeat by Babylon (605 BC, the battle of Carchemish), and of King Nebuchadnezzar's taking many leaders of Judah, including Daniel, into captivity (605 BC).
And he himself was taken captive to Babylon along with Jehoiachin, the nineteenth king of Judah, during Nebuchadnezzar's second invasion in 597 BC. Ezekiel lived at Tel-abib in the Nippur region by the River ‘Kebar’ in southern Babylon, where Jews mainly gathered and lived at that time, and in 593 BC, five years after the captivity, he received his call as a prophet. Ezekiel's age at this time is presumed to have been thirty, and he was active as a prophet for twenty-two years, until he was fifty-two.
※ The ‘Kebar’ River: A major branch of the Euphrates, located in the area where a canal connecting the Euphrates with the main cities of Babylon was being built; it is presumed that many Jewish captives were mobilized for the work. It is a place more than roughly 1,000 km away from Jerusalem.
The prophet Jeremiah was active in Jerusalem in southern Judah, but Ezekiel and Daniel were active in Babylon.
Ezekiel was active within the Jewish captive community in the southern region of the Babylonian Empire,
while Daniel was active in the capital of the Babylonian Empire as one of the high officials of the central government.
When Ezekiel began his activity as a prophet, seven years still remained until the fall of southern Judah in 586 BC. Ezekiel carried out his ministry as a prophet for seven years before the fall of Judah and for fifteen years after it.
Date of Writing
About twenty-two years, from the fifth day of the fourth month of 593 BC, the fifth year of Ezekiel's captivity, until the first day of the first month of 571 BC, before Egypt was conquered by Babylon.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
➀ The age in which Ezekiel was active was a time when the international situation was greatly shaken. In 612 BC, Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which had long been the strongest nation in the Middle East, was destroyed by the allied forces of Babylon and the Medes, and Egypt too was gradually weakening. In its place, Babylon rose rapidly to become a great power under the rule of Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar.
Jehoiakim king of Judah at first submitted to Babylon but rebelled after three years, and his son Jehoiachin, who succeeded him, was taken captive when Jerusalem fell to the Babylonian army after only three months. It appears that Ezekiel was also taken captive to Babylon at this time.
Zedekiah, the last king, also rebelled against Babylon and relied on Egypt, and in the end, in 586 BC, he met the tragedy of Jerusalem being completely destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's army and even the temple being demolished.
➁ There was a reason for such destruction. Manasseh, the fourteenth king of Judah, reigned fifty-five years, promoted idolatry, shed innocent blood, and committed grave sins. After that King Josiah carried out a sweeping reform, but when he was killed at the battle of Megiddo, the spark of that reform did not last long. Afterward Judah again leaned toward syncretism and idolatry, and Zedekiah, the last king, disregarded Jeremiah's warnings and showed the unbelief of relying on Egypt.
➂ Among the people of Judah at that time there was a mistaken belief that Jerusalem, where the temple, the symbol of God's presence, stood, would never be destroyed by the Gentiles. And with a mistaken spiritual superiority—thinking that they who remained in the land of Judah were under God's protection, while those taken captive to Babylon were being punished for their sins—there was also a conflict between the Babylonian captive group and the remaining group in Jerusalem over the question “Who is more righteous?”
Motive for Writing
Ezekiel first prophesied the complete destruction of Judah and Jerusalem. By thoroughly shattering the mistaken notion of the chosen people held by the people of Judah at that time, this shows the principle of God's righteous judgment: that everyone who sins and does not repent, without exception, is destroyed.
Therefore he said that the people of Judah who had been taken captive to Babylon at that time should humbly accept it as the natural result of their sins and ought to take this discipline as an opportunity for the restoration of faith.
And he proclaimed that God is the righteous One who thoroughly disciplines those who sin and, at the same time, that He will not forsake the chosen people forever but will care for them to the end, and He promised to restore them.
4. Structure of Ezekiel
Under the theme of the whole Bible, ‘salvation through the Messiah,’ the book of Ezekiel proclaims “God's judgment and salvation.” The declaration of God most frequently repeated in the book of Ezekiel, namely “you (they) will know that I am the LORD” (mentioned about 54 times directly, and more than 72 times if indirect expressions are included), is the theme of the book of Ezekiel. This word is a word of God's redemptive love, saying that they will come to know that the LORD is the God of judgment and at the same time the God of salvation.
God is the holy God who is wrathful against sin, but He is the loving God who has compassion on sinners. The book of Ezekiel teaches God's zeal, who judges sin yet saves the sinner. Through the book of Ezekiel we can know God's righteousness and love, which show love toward the sinner after judgment on sin has been given.
Part 1: Ezekiel's Call and Commission (chapters 1–3)
A call account like this is recorded in all the prophetic books, but this book has the distinction of describing it at the greatest length and in the greatest detail and glory. In the text, the scene in which Ezekiel witnesses the glory of God through a mysterious vision is described at length. By showing the omniscience and omnipotence of God, who is the subject giving the revelation, His omnipresence, and His glorious aspect, God intends to give trust in the revelations that are given afterward.
Part 2: Judgment on Judah (chapters 4–24)
Ezekiel's primary ministry is the declaration of God's stern judgment that will come upon Judah. To the people of Judah who had been taken captive to Babylon, Ezekiel prophesied the fact that Judah, because of its rebellion before God, could not but soon perish, so as to make it an occasion for them to repent and, at the same time, to make them realize that God is the Ruler of history.
1. Four symbolic acts prophesying the destruction of Jerusalem (chapters 4, 5)
2. Two messages prophesying the destruction of Judah (chapters 6, 7) – Judgment on Israel that serves idols and its end
3. Visions prophesying the judgment of Judah (chapters 8–11) – The defiled temple and the Spirit of God leaving the temple
4. Messages of symbols and parables prophesying the judgment of Judah (chapters 12–19)
	•	A symbolic act concerning going into captivity (chapter 12)
	•	Words of warning and judgment against false prophets (chapter 13)
	•	Words of warning and judgment against elders who serve idols (chapters 14–15)
	•	The parable of the adulterous woman (chapter 16)
	•	The parable of the two eagles and the vine (chapter 17)
	•	God's love toward sinners (chapter 18)
5. Messages of judgment related to the history of Judah's rebellion (chapters 20–24)
Part 3: Judgment on the Nations (chapters 25–32)
God's righteous judgment is not only for the people of Judah; judgment is also prophesied on the surrounding Gentile nations that had had a harmful influence on Israel at that time. The judgment of seven nations in all is prophesied.
1. Ammon: Because it despised and mocked when the sanctuary was defiled and the land of Israel became desolate, it is destroyed.
2. Moab: Because it despised the house of Judah, it becomes the possession of the people of the east.
3. Edom: Although it was a brother nation to Judah, it harbored a grudge, so it is judged and made desolate.
4. Philistia: Because historically it continually troubled the chosen people, it is judged and utterly destroyed.
5. Tyre: Although it had once enjoyed great glory and wealth, it was proud and violated the glory of God and did much harm to the history of the chosen people, so it is judged and destroyed.
6. Sidon: Because it despised God, it is judged and destroyed.
7. Egypt: Because it was proud and opposed God, it receives a great curse.
Part 4: The Restoration of Israel (chapters 33–39)
Although the earlier part continually prophesies the judgment that will come because of Judah's rebellion and God's stern judgment that will come upon the nations that opposed God and troubled the chosen people, from here on the restoration of Israel that will come after the judgment is recorded.
1. Ezekiel's recommissioning and the fall of the city of Jerusalem (chapter 33)
2. The LORD God, the Good Shepherd (chapter 34)
3. Words of judgment against Edom (chapter 35)
4. Words concerning the restoration of Israel (chapter 36)
5. The vision of the dry bones and God's everlasting promise (chapter 37)
6. Prophecy of the final war with ‘Gog’ (chapters 38–39)
Part 5: The New Temple and the New Israel (chapters 40–48)
These mysterious scenes that Ezekiel witnessed first give hope of restoration to the captive chosen people by showing them the form of the new temple, and show us the form of the church of the New Testament age. The detailed patterns of the new temple and the various ordinances concerning worship show the form of the holy church that God has established and show the character of the Messianic kingdom that will be brought about by the return of Christ.
1. The building of the new temple, showing the relationship between restored Israel and God (chapters 40–43)
2. The new worship to be offered in the new temple (chapters 44–46)
3. The distribution of the new land (chapters 47–48)
The Messianic kingdom in which believers will take part is a kingdom centered on the LORD that begins in the new temple, the symbol of the LORD's presence; it is to serve God with holy worship distinct from the worship offered until now, and to enjoy eternal life in the new heaven and new earth, where God's grace overflows.

Key Content
The book of Ezekiel records repeated declarations about idols and judgment to the point of tedium. This shows that God's judgment on Jerusalem was unavoidable, and it is also an expression of God's earnest heart that desires them to turn from sin. It makes known that the captive people must first return to God before returning to Jerusalem. Ezekiel's message, cried out while looking at the kingdom of Judah on the verge of destruction, can be summarized in two main points.
The first is that ‘today we are experiencing God's judgment because of our sins.’
The second is that ‘nevertheless the Lord will surely restore us again.’
He proclaims that the reality of suffering they are undergoing is ‘because of sin,’ and, looking to the word of promise that God will never give up on Israel but will ‘restore’ it again, has them endure their present pain. This is the heart of the message of the book of Ezekiel.
Through the book of Ezekiel, in the present hopeless dark age, we learn hope beyond despair through faith that looks to God. The words of restoration in the latter part show the event of the Messiah's cross and the restoration of redemption. The book of Ezekiel is quoted many times in the New Testament, and a great distinguishing feature is that it runs parallel with the words of the book of Revelation and prophesies the coming of the kingdom of God that will come upon this earth.

Comparison of the Books of Ezekiel and Jeremiah
Jeremiah and Ezekiel were the prophets who were active at the closest times, and they left the most numerous and most concrete prophecies concerning the destruction of southern Judah; when the prophecies concerning the destruction of southern Judah are compared, the characteristics of the two men's messages become plainly evident.
Jeremiah delivered the word of God in southern Judah, the scene where the terrible judgment of God was coming, and Ezekiel delivered the word of God in Babylon to the Babylonian captives who had to look on at the destruction of Jerusalem.

1. Title
The Hebrew Bible took the name of the book's protagonist and author, ‘Daniel,’ as the title of the book. Accordingly, the English Bibles and the Korean Revised Version also fixed ‘Daniel’ as the title. ‘Daniel’ means ‘God is my judge,’ which also agrees well with the content of the book, which shows that God, as the Ruler of human history, will exercise the rise and fall of the nations and the ultimate judgment.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The book itself gives internal testimony that Daniel is the author. That is, Daniel continually uses the autobiographical first person (“I, Daniel”) (8:1,15 9:2,20, 10:2, 12:11). Moreover, the overall unity of the book also proves that Daniel is the author, and the accurate depictions of the persons, events, and customs of the Babylonian Empire, the Medo-Persian transitional empire, and the early Persian Empire that appear in the content are things that no one but Daniel, who lived in that age, could have written. Not only that, but Jewish traditions such as the Talmud also testify that the author of this book is Daniel. Decisively, in Matthew 24:15 Jesus acknowledged that Daniel wrote this book by the words “spoken of by the prophet Daniel.”
Nevertheless, there has been the most controversy about the authorship and date of writing of the book of Daniel. Critics have claimed that an anonymous author who experienced the great persecution of Antiochus Epiphanes around the second century BC wrote this book, or else that the individual fragmentary records were revised by many people over a long period of transmission and were compiled and settled into the present form after the second century BC. They put forward many arguments on this basis, but in reality the greatest reason among them is that what the book of Daniel prophesies was fulfilled too perfectly and in too much detail to be called prophecy. This, on the contrary, is counter-evidence of how certain and detailed the prophecies of Daniel are, and at the same time confirms the historicity of the Bible.
Date of Writing
The last revelation Daniel received is the revelation by the bank of the Hiddekel River (Daniel 10–12), and since the time when this revelation was given is stated as 536 BC (in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia), the time of the writing of this book is presumed to be between 536 BC and 530 BC, the year of Daniel's death.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The first background is King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon's three invasions of Jerusalem.
It was also written against the background of the seventy years of captivity in Babylon, the era of Darius the Mede after Babylon was destroyed by the allied forces of the Medes and Persians,
and after that, up to the third year of Cyrus king of Persia, the early period of Israel's return (2 Chronicles 36:22-23, Daniel 6:1, Daniel 9:1, Daniel 10:1, Daniel 11:1).
Motive for Writing
Israel was a people who believed in the LORD God alone. The people of Judah at that time held the mistaken belief that Jerusalem, where the temple, the symbol of God's presence, stood, would never be destroyed by the Gentiles. But as a result of departing from God and sinning, Jerusalem was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and the temple was torn down. As many people died or were taken captive, the people of Judah fell into great shock.
They came to doubt: “Could it be that God lost to the gods of Babylon?” and “Does God really love us?” So some thought that God had abandoned Israel, and others mistakenly thought that God was not the only God but was no more than a god equal or inferior to the other gods of the Gentiles.
 cf) The doubts of the people seen in Malachi
	⁃	Is God still concerned about us?
	⁃	Even if He is concerned, does He really love us?
	⁃	If so, what is the reason for all this suffering we are facing?
	⁃	Is justice really carried out in this world?

In this age of confusion, God showed three important facts through Daniel.
1) All authority is given by God
Even the power of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon was permitted by God.
2) God still loves His people
Daniel was in danger of death several times for keeping his faith, but God helped him every time. Daniel's victory was evidence that God was still caring for His people.
3) God is the Lord of history
Through the revelation (prophecy) given to Daniel, God showed that He is the One who governs the rise and fall of nations. The rise and fall of nations is a process of development toward God's final victory (the kingdom of God) through the second coming of Jesus.
In that sense, it tells us that the fall of the two kingdoms of Israel was not because God no longer regarded Israel as His chosen people or because God was inferior to other gods, but was a temporary discipline toward themselves, who had been endlessly rebellious.
It was also necessary to give them a mature understanding of history: that God, until He gains complete victory by establishing the kingdom of God through the Son of Man, governs and watches over the history not only of Israel but even of the great empires.

In fact, the people of Israel came to know God deeply through their life in captivity.

After returning from Babylon, they did not serve idols again for about 500 years. There are two reasons they were able to change like this.
1) Because they saw that all of God's prophecies were fulfilled exactly
Destruction, captivity, return — they saw that every prophecy God had spoken was fulfilled exactly.
2) Thanks to the faith of Daniel and his three friends
As the stories of the miracles and protection God worked through them were handed down, the Jews became convinced that “God still loves us.”
 Also, the revelation conveyed through Daniel enabled the people of God to resolve to strengthen their faith in the LORD while hoping for the coming of the Messiah and the building of the kingdom of God through Him.

The revelation that appears in the book of Daniel is progressive revelation. As the words are added gradually, what was given at first is supplemented, completed, and expanded.

and chapters 7–12 are purely prophesied content.

6. Daniel and the New Testament
The book of Daniel is deeply connected with the New Testament and contains important prophecies about Jesus and the kingdom of God.
1) The book that became the foundation of the book of Revelation
The rise and fall of the nations and the prophecy of the final judgment in the book of Daniel connect with the content of the book of Revelation.
2) Jesus also quoted the book of Daniel
In Matthew 24:15 Jesus directly referred to the book of Daniel and said, “let the reader understand.”
3) A model of faith
Hebrews 11 praises the faith of Daniel and his three friends and introduces how they believed in God even in the lions' den and in the fire.
4) Gabriel and Michael
The names of the angel Gabriel (Luke) and Michael (Jude, Revelation) appear for the first time in the book of Daniel.
5) The meaning of the ‘stone cut out’
The ‘stone cut out’ in Daniel chapter 2 symbolizes Jesus Christ, who will bring down the kingdoms of the world and establish the eternal kingdom of God.
6) The prophecy of the ‘Son of Man’ and Jesus
Jesus: ‘from now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven’ (Matthew 26:64)
The vision Daniel saw: ‘One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence’ (Daniel 7:13) — corresponds.
7) Prophecy of the Messiah's suffering and salvation
The ‘Anointed One’ of Daniel chapter 9 (Daniel 9:24-26) prophesies Jesus Christ, who will put away the sins of the world and bring in everlasting righteousness. This shows both the first coming of Jesus (suffering and the cross) and His second coming (glory and judgment) (Luke 19:12-13).
8) The ‘Son of Man’ is the Old Testament appearance of Jesus Christ
The ‘Son of Man who is entrusted with the authority of the eternal kingdom’ (Daniel 7:13-14) and ‘the Son as the giver of revelation’ (Daniel 10:5-9) who appear in the book of Daniel point precisely to Jesus Christ.
The ‘Son of Man’ is Jesus, who, as God the Son, came in a human body and accomplished salvation, and His appearance is shown also in the Old Testament book of Daniel. This Son of Man is the One who, as the triune God, received the authority of the eternal kingdom, and who, as the giver of revelation, accomplishes the salvation of humankind, and His work will surely be completed.

1. Title
The Hebrew Bible took the name of the book's author, ‘Hosea,’ as the title of the book. Hosea carries the meaning ‘to save,’ that is, ‘savior.’ The ministry of Hosea, the prophet of love, is also a prefiguring of the saving ministry and the ministry of proclaiming the word of Jesus Christ, who likewise carries the meaning ‘Savior.’
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The author of this book is Hosea, whose name has the meaning [the LORD is salvation]. Hosea is a prophet of love who appealed for repentance. He was a prophet from northern Israel and the son of Beeri. He was active in northern Israel together with Amos, a prophet from southern Judah.
Date of Writing
The exact time when the book of Hosea was written cannot be known, but it is presumed, as verse 1 says, to have been written in the time of Jeroboam II.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
At that time northern Israel was very prosperous politically and economically, but spiritually it was seriously corrupted by widespread idolatry and moral decay.
Although their prosperity was a blessing God had bestowed on them, they mistook it as having been achieved entirely by their own efforts, and showed the pride of not relying on God, the source of life and blessing.
1) Political and social sins
The age when Jeroboam II ruled northern Israel enjoyed national prosperity and peace. This was the result of the fact that the kings of Assyria, who were then reigning as an empire, showed no intention of invading Israel, and of the fact that Israel maintained peaceful relations with Uzziah king of southern Judah.
But the political leaders who led the age of national prosperity and peace became even more proud and unrestrained, and did not fear being under God's law. Those in power spread rumors, plotted conspiracies, and even engaged in robbery and murder in order to keep their power.
Moreover, for nearly twenty years after Jeroboam died, bloody coups for the usurpation of the throne occurred in succession. And those who seized the throne by coup attempted to hold on to their kingship not by relying on God, the Sovereign of that nation, but by making alliances with neighboring nations or paying tribute.
Hosea regarded these confused political circumstances as acts of sin before God. And he proclaimed that God's severe judgment on such sin would appear as the destruction of the nation.
2) Religious sins
Despite the religious zeal of the religious leaders and the people within the temple or sanctuaries, it did not translate into practical actions of following God in social life. And there was no knowledge that comes from experiencing and knowing God. He proclaimed that religious zeal that does not change life is nothing more than formalism, and that God abhors it.
Moreover, the people committed the sin of regarding the various idols of Israel as their gods and relying on them. Besides the LORD God, they also served Baal at many local high places and tried the practice of divination under various trees.
The people of northern Israel thought of the LORD as the God of Mount Sinai and the wilderness, a God of the past. At the same time, they regarded Baal as the god who could actually help them in farming in the land of Canaan, where they now lived. So they served the LORD, the God of their ancestors and tradition, and also served Baal as the one with power who could solve the problems of present food, clothing, and shelter.
In addition, the priests' impurity and immorality and their lack of the knowledge of God were another main factor that disturbed the religious situation of Hosea's time.
Motive for Writing
Political and economic revival led the people of Israel into extreme religious and moral decay, marked by materialism and a worldly, this-world-oriented selfishness.
 When Israel's religious and moral decay reached its peak, northern Israel was completely destroyed as the neighboring Assyrian kings Pul (2 Kings 15:19), Tiglath-pileser III, Shalmaneser V, and Sargon II attacked. In the emergency, the people of Israel failed to face the fact that they were being judged for having sinned against God, and without a heart of repentance they tried to solve it by human means.
Rather than repent and rely on God, the political leaders went back and forth between the neighboring great powers Assyria and Egypt, trying to escape destruction by winning favor with bribes and tribute.
Hosea cried out that the only way Israel could live was to repent and return to God. Hosea made them know that, although Israel had sinned, if it repented God would accept them unconditionally with overflowing love. That is, he emphasized that God is love.
4. Structure of Hosea
(1) The Marriage Life of the Prophet Hosea (chapters 1–3)
God has the prophet Hosea marry the promiscuous Gomer. Through that married life, it symbolically expresses God's unconditional and absolute love for the chosen people. But it shows by contrast the rebellion of the people of northern Israel, who betrayed this love of God and committed every kind of sin.
(2) Israel's Unbelief and Its Judgment (chapters 4–13)
It directly points out and rebukes the wickedness of northern Israel from various aspects, appeals for repentance, and proclaims God's judgment and restoration. It consists of nine messages in all.
1) Introduction (4:1-3)
2) Main body (4:4-13:16)

5. Main Themes of Hosea
The book of Hosea is a book that makes us look back again on our life of faith.
The age in which Hosea lived was a time of great material abundance. Jeroboam II ruled the nation for forty-one years and brought about great revival, both politically and economically. But in the midst of that period of prosperity, the people of northern Israel gradually departed from God and walked the road of corruption.
Even so, the people of Israel did not realize their sins. But God did not leave their sins alone, and intended to judge Israel through Assyria. The prophet Hosea knew this, but the people did not know it at all. So Hosea cried out earnestly that the only way Israel could live was to repent and return to God.
Hosea also emphasized that however great the sin one has committed, God is still the God of love, and that whenever the people repent and return, He forgives and accepts them. God shows through Hosea's life that even if Israel's sin is great, He does not want them to perish.
God commanded Hosea to marry a promiscuous woman, Gomer. After marrying Hosea, Gomer returned to a life of sin and left her husband, but God told Hosea to pay a price and bring her back. Hosea obeyed the word of God, went to find Gomer, and took her again as his wife.
This story symbolizes the relationship between God and Israel. Hosea represents God, and Gomer represents Israel.
Gomer's promiscuity signifies the people of Israel having fallen into idolatry. But just as Gomer was received again, when a people fallen into sin truly repent, God forgives them and takes them in again at any time.
In this way the book of Hosea contains a message of sin and judgment, repentance and love, and restoration. Even if human beings stumble and fail because of sin, God does not utterly abandon them but always waits for them to return. It also shows that the restoration of Israel is completed through the redemption of Jesus Christ.
In the end, the book of Hosea is a book that shows God's deep heart and unchanging love through the life of the prophet Hosea.
It conveys the blessed truth that even though Israel had drifted far away through sin, because Jesus paid the price with His own blood, God will surely accept anyone who repents and returns.

1. Title
The Hebrew title ‘Joel,’ which uses the author's name as it is, means ‘the LORD is God.’ In the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament, the transliteration of the Hebrew title as it stands, ‘Joel,’ was likewise used as the title, and the English Bibles without exception use ‘Joel,’ and the Korean Bibles all use ‘Yoel.’ The meaning of this title also agrees well with the content of this book, which emphasizes God's strong providence as Judge in history.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author: Joel (son of Pethuel, a prophet; the name means ‘the LORD is God’)
Nothing specific is known about Joel's status. His father is Pethuel, and this name means ‘God is sincere.’ Since names were usually given by the father, judging from the meanings of the names of Joel and his father, it is highly probable that he was raised in a devout family.
Some scholars suggest the possibility that Joel came from a priestly family, on the basis of the fact that Joel often mentions the grain offering (the meal offering) and the drink offering (the wine offering), as well as priests, days of fasting, the proclamation of a solemn assembly, the house of the LORD, the portico (the court in front of the temple), and the altar.
Also, judging from the fact that Joel often mentions Zion, Jerusalem, vines, granaries, and so on, he is presumed to have lived near Jerusalem and to have been active mainly in Jerusalem.
Date of Writing
It is not known exactly in the time of which king the book of Joel was written. There are two views among scholars.
One is the early-date theory, the claim that the book of Joel was written during the reign of Joash, the eighth king of southern Judah (835~796 BC).
The other is the late-date theory, the claim that it was written after the religious reform of Nehemiah (about 432 BC).
These two views have long been sharply opposed.
Grounds for the early-date theory
1. In the early period of King Joash, the high priest Jehoiada ruled in the king's stead, so there could not but be few mentions of the king
2. The sound of the trumpet in Zion was to summon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and it can be presumed that at that time trumpets were also blown in each city in accordance with the ordinances of the law
3. The Greeks appear, but they are portrayed not as a mighty empire yet, but only as slave traders dealing with the merchants of Tyre and Sidon
4. The similar passages in other prophetic books may rather be cases of the other prophetic books quoting the book of Joel
5. Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt, Edom, and so on mentioned in the book of Joel coincide with Israel's actual enemies in the ninth century BC
6. The ‘Valley of Jehoshaphat’ that Joel mentions is the Valley of Beracah (2 Chronicles 20:20–28), where King Jehoshaphat (872~848 BC) defeated Ammon and Moab, showing that Joel was active at a time not far from that age
7. The prophecy against Philistia (3:4–8) was fulfilled in the time of King Uzziah (791~739 BC) (2 Chronicles 26:6–7)
Grounds for the late-date theory
1. There is no mention of a king at all in the text, and instead the priests lead the repentance of the whole people (1:13–14, 2:15–17)
2. There is a scene in which the trumpet is blown in Zion to summon the people, which appears to be a situation centered on a small area (2:1–15)
3. There is a mention of the Greeks, who became powerful from the fifth century BC (3:6)
4. There are many expressions that seem to quote passages of other prophetic books [1:19(Amos 7:4), 2:10,31(Isaiah 13:10, 13), 3:3(Obadiah 1:11)]
5. The vocabulary and style are similar to post-exilic writings
6. There is no rebuke of idolatry, which commonly appears in the prophetic books of the pre-exilic age

In fact, several commentaries, such as Explore the Book (H. Sidlow Baxter) and the Grand Commentary, also support the early-date theory.
Although the two views are opposed, whichever one is chosen, there is no great difference in understanding or interpreting the book of Joel.
However, there is also the opinion that the late-date theory is somewhat more persuasive, for the following reasons.
1. The prophetic books before the Babylonian captivity mainly prophesied destruction by foreign powers such as Assyria or Babylon, but the prophetic books after the captivity emphasize worldwide judgment. The book of Joel likewise prophesies that many nations will gather and take part in war and that in the end the final judgment on the whole world will come.
2. The expression in 3:1, ‘when I restore Judah and Jerusalem from captivity,’ refers to the event of returning from the Babylonian captivity, and seems to have been written at a time when they had already returned or were about to return (see Psalm 126).
3. The phrase ‘they have scattered Israel among the nations and divided up My land’ describes the destruction by Babylon and the captivity.
4. The words in 3:5, ‘For you took My silver and gold and carried off My finest treasures to your temples.’ refer to the incident in which Babylon plundered the vessels and treasures of the Jerusalem temple.
5. The statement ‘You sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks, to send them far from their homeland’ seems to have been written by someone who directly witnessed the existence of the Greeks, who were growing steadily stronger around the fifth century BC.
Therefore the view that the book of Joel was written at the time of the return from the Babylonian captivity or afterward is the more probable.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The high priest Jehoiada drove Athaliah, the daughter born between Ahab king of northern Israel and Jezebel, from the throne (2 Kings 11:4–16, 2 Chronicles 23:1–21) and restored the Davidic dynasty. As a result, Joash came to reign as king of southern Judah.
This period was before the Assyrian Empire had emerged as a powerful nation in the Near East. In the region of Palestine, southern Judah, northern Israel, Phoenicia, Philistia, and Edom were in opposition to one another, and to the south Egypt still exercised influence as a great power.
In the midst of this, a plague of locusts struck the land of southern Judah, and the whole land was laid waste. With severe drought and famine added to this, the situation became very serious. The people felt their survival threatened and were seized with anxiety and fear, and began to ask deeply what the reason and cause of such a disaster might be.
Purpose of Writing
Through the prophet Joel, God points out that the cause of such a disaster lies in the unbelief and wickedness of the people of southern Judah, urging them to repent, and also exhorts that the plague of locusts and the famine that followed are a forerunner of the judgment that will come in the greater and more fearful “day of the LORD” yet to come, and that they should turn back quickly before that day comes so as not to come to eternal destruction.
And it is in order that, by promising the blessing and hope of salvation to those who return, they may rely on God all the more and live in hope.
