5. Central Theme: God's Judgment and Grace
(Joel 2:13) “So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God. For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster.”
The plague of locusts and the drought mentioned in this book were the rod of God's discipline on the sinful people of Israel. At the same time, they were a type foreshadowing ‘the Day of the LORD,’ that is, the final judgment that God will carry out by intervening directly in human history.
Just as a plague of locusts has occurred in the present reality, so the ‘day of the LORD’ will surely come, and because that day is drawing near, the people must repent, and when they repent they will receive the blessing of eternal salvation that God has promised—this is the central theme of the book of Joel.
① Warning about the day of the LORD:
It has the two-sidedness of mentioning judgment and at the same time salvation. On this day, eternal blessing and salvation will be given to those who repent and return to God, but only resolute judgment will be given to unbelievers who oppose God.
② The purpose of discipline:
Even if they are the chosen people, God surely disciplines them when they sin. And the purpose of that discipline is not destruction but that they repent and arrive at ultimate salvation.
③ God is rich in grace and mercy:
Sinners can at any time obtain forgiveness of sins from Him and also obtain abundant blessing, if only they turn from their sin and repent.
④ True repentance:
True repentance does not consist of formal acts such as fasting and tearing one's clothes, but of tearing one's heart and truly being contrite.
⑤ The blessing God gives:
The salvation and blessing that God promises to His chosen people go beyond the earthly and material level to the spiritual and eternal level of the world to come.
⑥ The outpouring of the Holy Spirit:
By pouring out the Holy Spirit on all people without distinction, the grace of salvation will come through the work of the Holy Spirit.
⑦ The plague of locusts was limited to Judah or the region of Palestine, but the judgment of the day of the LORD is universal.
⑧ Because human beings were created as lords of all creation, the whole universe came to suffer because of human sin. Likewise, through human salvation the whole universe will be freed from suffering.
Key Term: "The Day of the LORD" ( = the Day of the Lord )
God sent a plague of locusts and a drought upon the sinful people of Israel. This was not the final judgment but a warning from God urging repentance. But those who, despite this warning, do not repent in the end and keep on sinning will surely receive the judgment of destruction on the day when God intervenes directly in human history. That day is precisely ‘the Day of the LORD.’
The book of Joel thus conveys a message, first to Israel, the people of God, and further to people of every generation, to repent and be saved rather than destroyed on the day of God's solemn judgment.
Therefore the key term of the book of Joel can be said to be ‘the Day of the LORD.’ In the New Testament, the expression ‘the Day of the Lord’ is used in this same sense.
6. Characteristics of the Book of Joel
This book is made up of just three chapters and only 73 verses, a very small prophetic book, yet its influence is so great that it is quoted in many parts of the Old and New Testaments by Isaiah, Jeremiah, Peter, John, Paul, and others.
Representative examples of quotation:    Joel 1:6 ➞ (Revelation 9:2-3)   Joel 2:28-32 ➞ (Acts 2:16-21)   Joel 2:28-29 ➞ (Romans 5:5)   Joel 3:13 ➞ (Isaiah 63:2-3, Revelation 14:18-20)
Through the prophecy of the locust plague, it shows more clearly than any other prophetic book how serious the consequences of sin are for human life and for creation.
It prophesies so clearly about the coming of the Holy Spirit that, compared with the book of Acts, it is called the Acts of the Holy Spirit of the Old Testament.

1. Title
The name of the author who wrote this book, ‘Amos,’ was used as its title. ‘Amos’ means ‘burden’ or ‘burden-bearer.’ The meaning of this title well reflects the fact that, as a man of southern Judah, the ministry of proclaiming God's judgment to the rebellious people of northern Israel must have been a heavy burden to him, yet he carried out that work faithfully with boldness and patience.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author: Amos
The writer of the book of Amos is clearly ‘Amos.’ This is made clear in the opening part of the book, and the frequent use of the first-person expression ‘I’ throughout the text shows that fact all the more surely.
Amos was from the southern kingdom of Judah, but he was a prophet who prophesied mainly to the northern kingdom of Israel. Among the Minor Prophets, Amos is the only one who was from southern Judah and prophesied to northern Israel.
He frequently prophesied the destruction and judgment of northern Israel, so much so that he is called ‘the prophet of disaster.’
Amos's hometown, ‘Tekoa’ (Amos 1:1), is a highland village at an elevation of 840 m, about 16 km south of Jerusalem and about 10 km south of Bethlehem. The land there was dry and sandy and not suited to farming, but it was a good environment for raising sheep and for herding. There Amos tended sheep and cultivated sycamore trees (Amos 7:14 ‘I am a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees’).
Date of Writing
According to Amos 1:1, Amos was active during the time when Uzziah king of southern Judah (791–739 BC) and Jeroboam II of northern Israel (793–753 BC) were reigning. It appears that he prophesied in northern Israel for a relatively short time at the period when the two nations were at their most prosperous politically and economically, and then returned to his hometown and wrote this book not long afterward.
Therefore the date of writing of the book of Amos is presumed to be about 760–755 BC, when the reigns of the two kings had reached their peak.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The age when Amos was active was a time when both southern Judah and northern Israel were greatly prospering politically, economically, and militarily. In particular, Jeroboam II (793–753 BC), king of northern Israel, took advantage of the weakening of Assyria, the rising power north of Palestine, through continued wars, to attack Aram (Syria) and conquer its capital Damascus. To the south, he also took Moab, securing territory from the entrance of Hamath (Numbers 34:8), the northern boundary of the land God had promised to Israel through Moses, to the Sea of the Arabah (the Dead Sea) in the south.
In the history of Israel, apart from David and Solomon in the era of the united kingdom, the reign of Jeroboam II was the only time when such a wide territory was ruled. He was also excellent in running the state, developing intermediary trade by making use of geographical advantages and greatly increasing wealth. As a result, northern Israel enjoyed its most splendid heyday, politically and economically, since David and Solomon.
But in every age, when a nation prospers outwardly, religious and moral decay always follows behind. When materialism, a worldly way of life, and self-centered selfishness spread, spiritual values collapse. Northern Israel was no exception. In the midst of economic stability and abundance, the people forgot God and sought only their own comfort. Luxury and dissipation were rampant (Amos 6:4-6), the tax laws were abused (Amos 5:11), the poor were exploited (Amos 2:6), and the righteous were oppressed (Amos 5:12).
Their religious life was nothing more than formal worship. They believed that if they merely kept the sacrifices and festivals, God would protect them (Amos 4:4-5, 5:21-24). Moreover, they were possessed by an exclusive sense of being the chosen people, thinking, ‘God is our God alone,’ and supposed that God would protect them and destroy the Gentile nations on ‘the day of the LORD’ (Amos 5:18-20). They even accepted and served foreign gods in order to obtain material blessings (Amos 5:25-27). In the end, in pursuit of wealth and glory, the people of northern Israel destroyed not only their relationship with God (the vertical relationship) but also their relationships with other people (the horizontal relationship), and did injustice.
Purpose of Writing
The purpose for which the prophet Amos wrote this book was to make the people of northern Israel realize that, even though they were God's chosen people, if they abandoned justice and righteousness and continued in a corrupt life, they could not escape God's judgment. He proclaimed that only by seeking God alone and restoring the righteousness that had collapsed could they be saved in the midst of destruction.
Amos also warned not only northern Israel but also the people of southern Judah. If southern Judah too continued to practice injustice, it would not escape the same judgment.
He left this message in writing, warning that not only the people of northern Israel at that time but anyone in any age who turns away from God and perverts justice cannot escape God's judgment. Therefore we too, who live in a world far more corrupt than the age of Amos, must humbly examine ourselves before this word.

5. Central Theme: God's Judgment and Grace
The book of Amos is not greatly different from the other Old Testament prophetic books in that it rebukes the sins of the people of northern Israel, who were in extreme religious and moral decay, and warns of God's judgment. But the distinctive theme of this book is that the decay of northern Israel was not mere moral corruption but lay in their not practicing righteousness by departing from God and not fearing Him. Amos makes clear that unless true faith toward God and a righteous life are restored, no matter how much they are God's chosen people, and no matter how much they offer sacrifices according to the law, they can never be saved from destruction.
If the book of Hosea is a book that sees northern Israel's decay as ‘a betrayal of God's love’ and urges them through repentance to restore a loving relationship with God, the book of Amos emphasizes God's righteous judgment all the more.
By Hosea revealing God's love and Amos revealing God's righteousness, the two books show that the love and righteousness of God spoken of by the whole Bible are in perfect harmony.
(1) The Basic Themes of the Book of Amos
1) God's judgment falls on all people impartially.
God's judgment is absolutely righteous, applied equally to Israel as well as to the Gentiles. But the people of northern Israel were arrogantly sure that, because they were God's chosen people by descent, they would never be judged. Yet even if they are God's people, if they have sinned, they cannot escape judgment for that sin before the righteous God.
2) A right relationship with God cannot be established by formal worship or offerings.
God desires not simply to receive sacrifices and offerings but those who sincerely seek Him and return. Only when the right relationship with God is restored is a righteous life restored, and true fellowship is achieved within it.
3) God's judgment is discipline for restoration, not destruction.
God's judgment on Israel is not a punishment of eternal destruction according to the wages of sin, as with the Gentiles, but a discipline of love that awakens them to return to God. The history of Israel is also a lesson for the life of faith of each individual. Therefore, when believers receive God's discipline, they should not take it lightly or be discouraged, but realize that it is the rod of love and draw even nearer to God.
6. Characteristics of the Book of Amos
(1) A Concise and Powerful Prophetic Book
The book of Amos is the writing of a prophet who had no professional education, but the content of its prophecy is concise and clear, and its theme is distinct. It conveys the word in a direct and intense tone rather than with ornate expressions or rhetoric, which is a part that well shows the simple and frank character of Amos, who had lived as a shepherd.
(2) A Book That Emphasizes Righteousness and Justice
The book of Amos emphasizes the importance of ‘righteousness’ and ‘social justice’ more strongly than other prophetic books. He saw ‘righteousness’ as the attitude of life that a believer ought to have before God, and taught that it must be manifested not only in the relationship with God (the vertical relationship) but also in the relationship with people (the horizontal relationship).
(3) A Prophet of Southern Judah Who Ministered in Northern Israel
Amos was a prophet from southern Judah who was active in northern Israel (Amos 1:1). So at Bethel, the religious center of northern Israel and the stronghold of idol worship, he was even slandered and persecuted by the priest Amaziah (Amos 7:10-13).
(4) A Prophet Who Was a Shepherd Yet Well Versed in the Word
Although Amos came from a shepherd's background (Amos 7:14), he had a deep understanding and knowledge of the law of the Pentateuch. The content of the Pentateuch is often quoted in his prophecy, which shows that he was not a mere farmer or shepherd but a man who had meditated deeply on the word and was prepared. He was a prophet endowed with both intellectual ability and spiritual insight.
(5) A Prophetic Book That Proclaims Both Judgment and Restoration
The book of Amos prophesies the destruction of northern Israel so strongly that its writer, Amos, is called ‘the prophet of disaster.’ Yet at the end of this book, it also contains a call to repentance and a promise of the restoration of Israel. This structure of proclaiming judgment and restoration together also connects with God's consistent message of salvation flowing through the prophetic books as a whole.
7. Christ in the Book of Amos
Compared with the other prophetic books, the book of Amos has almost no direct mention of Jesus Christ and His ministry. Indirectly, however, it shows the figure of Christ as Mediator, Christ as Judge, and Christ as Savior.
First, the figure of Christ as Mediator appears in the scene where the prophet Amos pleads for the judgment on the people of northern Israel to be postponed (Amos 7:2, 5). His figure interceding before God for the people calls to mind Jesus Christ, who would become the Mediator of humankind.
Next, the figure of Christ as Judge is revealed in the figure of the Lord standing beside the altar in the vision of the destruction of the temple (Amos 9:1). This symbolically shows the authority of Jesus Christ, who will judge the whole world in righteousness on the last day of the world (Revelation 5).
Finally, the figure of Christ as Savior appears as the One who rebuilds David's fallen tent, gathers the people of Israel scattered among the nations, and establishes the eternal Messianic kingdom (Amos 9:11-15). This prophecy prefigures Jesus Christ, who came as a descendant of David and accomplished the kingdom of salvation.

1. Title
‘Obadiah’ is a transliteration of the Old Testament Hebrew title ‘Ovadyah,’ and its meaning is ‘servant of the LORD’ or ‘worshipper of the LORD.’
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author: Obadiah
The author of this book is ‘Obadiah.’ Nothing at all is known about Obadiah's family line or his personal career, such as his activity as a prophet. However, judging from the fact that the book expresses that he directly witnessed the fall of Jerusalem, it seems clear that the author was a prophet from southern Judah.
Date of Writing
The date of writing of this book is presumed to be about 586 BC, immediately after the fall of Jerusalem and southern Judah.
① Among several hypotheses that the Edomites allied with other nations to attack and capture Jerusalem, the only one that is firmly proved is the fall of southern Judah in 586 BC. In particular, the content of Ezekiel 35, which declares judgment on the sin Edom committed at the fall of southern Judah, is similar to the book of Obadiah in many points.
② The calamities of verses 10-14 of this book well explain the situation at the time of the fall of southern Judah. ‘The day of the destruction of the people of Judah’ (verse 12) and ‘the day of their distress’ (verse 13), and so on, can be understood as referring to the fall of southern Judah, and the scene of those fleeing from the distress being captured by the Edomites at the crossroads (verse 14) and the expression ‘survivors in the day of distress’ (verse 14) likewise explain well the situation of the fall of southern Judah.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
Background
The conflict between ‘the people of Israel’ and ‘the Edomites’ is a history that has been repeated for so long that it began with Jacob and Esau struggling in the womb. Even so, God recognized the Edomites as a brother nation of the people of Israel.
So when the Israelites, during their hard journey after the exodus, were refused passage through Edom, although going through Edom was a shortcut, they did not fight because it was a brother nation, and went around by the rough road.
Also, when giving the law, He permitted the third-generation descendants of an Edomite who had been naturalized into Israel to take part in the assembly of the LORD, even opening a way by which they could in effect become the chosen people.
Despite God's special grace and consideration, the Edomites continued to oppose the people of Israel, beginning with deliberately obstructing the way of the Israelites who had come out of Egypt, and going on until in 586 BC they allied with Babylon and destroyed southern Judah.
The first prophecy given in the Bible about these Edomites was that they would become servants of the people of Israel, and because Edom continually opposed the people of Israel, many prophets prophesied Edom's destruction.
Purpose of Writing
The incident in which the Edomites entered Jerusalem with the Babylonian army, attacked southern Judah, tore down the temple, and handed over the people of southern Judah to Babylon to be slaughtered was a great shock to the people of southern Judah at that time.
Moreover, in the situation of being destroyed by the Babylonian Empire under God's discipline, the shame and humiliation suffered at the hands of Edom plunged the people into despair that they had been completely abandoned by God.
Therefore the prophet Obadiah wanted to teach the people of southern Judah this: even if they now, because of past sins, were disciplined by God, lost their country, and were mocked and shamed by a Gentile people like Edom, they must be made to realize that this did not mean they had been completely forsaken by God.
Furthermore, even during the time of discipline, when they repent and return to the LORD, God, though He disciplines sin, shows the boundless favor that He never forsakes the chosen people themselves. Through this he sought to help the people recover their faith in God and have a new hope even while living in Babylon as captives.
For this reason Obadiah needed to prophesy, in contrast to each other, the destruction of all Gentile nations hostile to God, including Edom, and the restoration of the chosen people Israel. So this prophecy was written concisely in one chapter.
This book also has important meaning for believers of the New Testament age. It is a precious book that clearly shows the redemptive-historical truth that God disciplines the sins of those who are saved, but never forsakes forever the saved person himself.
4. Structure of Obadiah
(1)  Part 1 _ Prophecy of Edom's Destruction (1:1-14)
1) Declaration of judgment on Edom (1:1-9)
2) The reasons for judgment on Edom (1:10-14)
(2) Part 2 _ Prophecy of the Coming of the Day of the LORD (1:15-21)
1) Prophecy of the judgment of the nations (1:15-16)
2) Prophecy of the restoration of the chosen people Israel (1:17-20)
3) Prophecy of the expansion and coming of the Messianic kingdom (1:21)
5. Themes of Obadiah
(1) God is the righteous Judge who repays according to deeds.
While prophesying Edom's destruction, Obadiah at the same time clearly states the specific causes by which they would suffer wretched destruction (Obadiah 1:10-14).
This is clear evidence of God's righteousness, who judges the wicked and punishes them according to their deeds.
This righteousness of God will appear most clearly at the final judgment at the end of the world.
(2) God is the all-knowing One who watches every move of human beings.
In fact, Edom's helping the Babylonian army and hastening the fall of southern Judah was indirect rather than direct. Even so, as this book clearly states, God rebuked even their secret sins (Obadiah 1:11-12).
Therefore believers must strive all the more for a godly life before the God who watches our conduct.
(3) For the saved there is discipline, but no destruction.
To the people He has once saved, God is the infinitely gracious One who, although He may discipline them for a time for their sins, ultimately brings them themselves to salvation.
Therefore, even if the people of God are in suffering at present, they must hold even more firmly to their faith in God within the hope of ultimate salvation, and overcome suffering with perseverance.
(4) Victory is given in the end to the saved.
In the present world there exist forces of evil that for a time persecute the people of God and oppose God, but at the final judgment at the end of the world all forces of evil will be destroyed, and only the saved believers from among all the nations of the world will gather and come before the LORD.
6. Characteristics of the Book of Obadiah
	•	It is the book with the smallest volume in the whole Old Testament.
	•	Together with the book of Nahum, which prophesied judgment on Assyria, it is a rare prophetic book whose main object is Gentiles rather than the people of Israel.
	•	It is a prophetic book that proclaims only stern judgment, with no content at all urging repentance toward those who are the objects of judgment.
	•	It prophesies an event that would be fulfilled after a long span of about 300 years, namely Edom's destruction, yet records it realistically and vividly, as though looking back on something that had already happened.
	•	While the description of the destruction Edom would suffer appears extremely dramatic and gruesome, no rebuke of the people of Israel appears at all. This seems to be in order to contrast dramatically God's ultimate protection of His own people with the destruction that will necessarily come upon those who oppose the people of God.
	•	It clearly shows the assurance of the coming of the kingdom of God, in which all the nations of the world will belong to the LORD at the end of the world.
7. Christ in the Book of Obadiah
(1) Christ as the Judge Who Holds Sovereignty over All Nations
The punishment of all the evil forces of this world that oppose God, represented by the Edomites, and the judgment of all nations to be carried out on the day of the LORD will be carried out only by Jesus Christ, who has been entrusted with all authority from God.
And the judgment of all nations, including Edom, prophesied in this book ultimately prefigures the final judgment on the forces of Satan that oppose the LORD God and the believers of the New Testament age, and this will be accomplished with the return of Christ.
(2) Christ as the Savior of His People
(Obadiah 1:21) The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
The ‘deliverers who ascend Mount Zion’ in this book ultimately refers to Christ, who will save humankind that was held captive by sin, and to the believers who will spread the gospel of Christ throughout the world.
This book testifies that through these deliverers all the nations of the world will belong to the LORD.
This is a prophecy of the expansion and completion of the Messianic kingdom that will be accomplished through Christ and the church.

1. Title
The Hebrew title of this book, "Jonah," reflects the name of its author, and its meaning is "dove."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author: Jonah
	⁃	Jonah was a prophet who actually ministered during the reign of Jeroboam II, the thirteenth king of the northern kingdom of Israel.
	⁃	Jesus acknowledged the real existence of Jonah and the historicity of the events recorded in this book.
	⁃	In the history of Assyria there was a period in which a religious tendency toward the worship of one God appeared, which bears on the content of this book.
	⁃	The book's statement that Nineveh was an exceedingly great city reflects the situation of the Assyrian Empire, which was at its strongest in the time of "Jeroboam II (794–752 B.C.)," the period of Jonah's ministry.
	⁃	This is because the content of the book is such a detailed and realistic account that it can only be viewed as the record of one who experienced the events firsthand.
Date of Writing
The period in which the prophet Jonah ministered came about one generation after "the death of the prophet Elisha (798 B.C.)," and it almost coincides with the reign of "Jeroboam II (794–752 B.C.)," the second political and economic golden age of the northern kingdom of Israel after the time of David and Solomon.
At that time Assyria was also somewhat weaker in national strength than under its earlier kings.
(This was the era governed by kings such as Shalmaneser III (Shalmaneser Ⅲ, 783–773 B.C.), Ashur-dan III (Assurdayan Ⅲ, 773–755 B.C.), and Ashur-nirari II (Assurninari Ⅱ, 755–745 B.C.).)
The war with Ararat, a rising state to the north, had dragged on, and a great plague had broken out around 765–759 B.C. and killed many people. On top of this, around June 15, 763 B.C., a total solar eclipse occurred, and the ominous sign of the land of Assyria being wrapped in pitch-black darkness greatly unsettled the people.
This became the background that enabled the entire population of Nineveh to repent even at the message of judgment that the prophet Jonah proclaimed for only a single day.
In other words, Nineveh had already become what is called a "field white for harvest" (John 4:35), ready to be reaped.
Taking these facts together, the date of writing of this book is estimated to be around 760 B.C., immediately after Jonah experienced the events recorded in the book and returned to the northern kingdom of Israel.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
The period in which Jonah, the author of this book and also its protagonist, ministered as a prophet was during the reign of Jeroboam II of the northern kingdom of Israel (794–752 B.C.). The international situation in the Near East at that time worked very favorably for the northern kingdom of Israel, and it enjoyed its political and economic peak since the time of David and Solomon.
Aram (Syria), the greatest enemy of the northern kingdom of Israel, was losing its power after being attacked by Assyria.
Assyria, too, was compelled to withdraw from Damascus, the capital of Aram, because of its war with Ararat, a rising state to the north.
Jeroboam II used this opportune moment to conquer Damascus, the capital of Aram (2 Kings 14:28), and was able to recover most of the territory of the northern region from the time of David and Solomon of old.
Assyria, for its part, was indeed temporarily weakened by various domestic circumstances, including its war with Ararat. Nevertheless, it was the most powerful potential threat to the northern kingdom of Israel, for no one knew when it would reorganize its national strength and invade the Palestinian region again.
For this reason the people of the northern kingdom of Israel not only did not relax in the least their hostility toward Assyria, but, because of their exclusive consciousness of being the chosen people, they heightened their unconditional contempt for the Gentiles all the more.
Their exclusive consciousness of being the chosen people was, in the end, completely at odds with the merciful character of God, who has an absolute love and a plan of salvation not only for Israel, the chosen people of the Old Testament, but for all peoples of the world.
Purpose of the Writing
God called the prophet Jonah, who, like all the people of Israel, held an exclusive consciousness of being the chosen people. And He had him proclaim a message of judgment in the city of Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian Empire, toward which the people of the northern kingdom of Israel felt the greatest hostility.
Thus He let the prophet Jonah see and experience for himself the work of salvation, in which the people of Nineveh, having heard the message of judgment, repented and were saved.
And He had him spread that experience to the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, so that he would rebuke the error of their exclusive consciousness of being the chosen people, and also so that they would know the absolute love that He has, as God the Creator, not only for Israel, the chosen people, but for all peoples of the world.
Moreover, He made them realize God's boundless lovingkindness, by which He grants forgiveness and salvation at any time to anyone who repents of his sin, regardless of bloodline or status.
Based on this personal experience of his own, the prophet Jonah was made to realize that God is not the God of the Israelite people alone, and that from the beginning, before He unfolded the Old Testament history of redemption centered on the people of Israel, He had a plan of salvation for all peoples of the world.
He also wrote this book in order that they might abandon their exclusive consciousness of being the chosen people and carry out the missionary calling as the chosen people toward all peoples of the world.

5. The Theme of Jonah
This book is a personal account of the prophet Jonah, who disobeyed God's calling to proclaim a message of judgment in the city of Nineveh so that the city would repent and come to salvation, was disciplined by God, and in the end became obedient.
And Jonah's account has as its great theme, first of all, the fact that God loves not only Israel, the chosen people, but all peoples of the world, and that from the beginning He had a plan to save them.
(1) God is the God of all peoples of the world.
Furthermore, God's dominion is not limited to the people of Israel and the territory they possess, but is universal and without limit, extending to all human beings, to all creatures of the natural world, and even to all the laws of nature.
(2) All of God's plans are perfectly fulfilled under any circumstances.
That God thwarted all of Jonah's attempts to evade his mission and consistently carried out the goal of the salvation of Nineveh is an excellent illustration of this fact.
(3) The saving grace of God is a universal principle given equally to everyone.
(4) Everyone who has been called to be God's people has been given the mission of evangelism.
The carrying out of this mission must not be frustrated or hindered by any other factor, such as personal prejudice or ethnic sentiment.
From the standpoint of the Jewish disciples who received the mission of early evangelism, Jerusalem and all Judea were their own kinsmen. Samaria was a land of enemies. The ends of the earth were people who had nothing to do with them.
(5) God's grace is boundless.
God forgave the disobedient Jonah, and He forgave at once the people of Nineveh, who had practiced wickedness for hundreds of years, when they repented. And even now God immediately grants forgiveness and salvation to any sinner who repents and turns back. We must all strive to spread the gospel so that all peoples of the world may meet this God of grace.
6. Characteristics of the Book of Jonah
The book of Jonah is unusual in showing, with concentration, God's concern for the Gentiles and His plan of salvation for them.
It shows the event in which the people of Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, which could be called the representative of the Gentiles of that time, heard the message of judgment through the prophet Jonah, repented, and were saved. Through this it shows that God fundamentally loves not only Israel, the chosen people of the Old Testament, but all peoples of the world, and that He has a plan of salvation for them.
Of course, it is not that there are no references to the salvation of the Gentiles in other books of the Old Testament, but this book alone testifies to it through a real event in which an entire city of a Gentile nation was saved.
For this reason this book has even come to be nicknamed "the New Testament in the Old Testament."
	•	In terms of content, this book should be regarded less as a prophetic book than as a historical book recording the repentance and salvation of the people of Nineveh, or as a biography recording Jonah's personal experience. Nevertheless, the reason it is classified as a prophetic book is that its author, Jonah, was a prophet. It is also because the content of this book has a prophetic character, showing in typological form the repentance and salvation of the Gentiles that would take place in the New Testament era.
	•	This book differs from the other prophetic books, which generally have Israel, the chosen people, mainly as the object of their prophetic proclamation. Together with the book of Nahum, by revealing that He is the God not only of Israel but of all peoples of the world, it posed a strong challenge to the people of Israel, who, because of their extremely exclusive and chauvinistic consciousness of being the chosen people, held an attitude of unconditional contempt toward the Gentiles.
	•	Unlike the other prophets, who generally obeyed God's calling absolutely, the prophet Jonah refused God's calling and was disciplined. Even so, it is a remarkable prophetic book that records the personal experience of the prophet Jonah, who reluctantly carried out the calling while complaining.
	•	Supernatural miracles appear in succession throughout the book, which lets one feel its liveliness and dynamism.
	•	While dealing with theological content of great depth concerning the salvation of the Gentiles, it uses a simple style and easy vocabulary overall, which broadens the range of understanding of its content.
	•	The prayer of Jonah in chapter 2 of Jonah has many points in common with the content of the Psalms (Psalms 18:6-8, 17, 30, 31:23, 42:8, 103:4, 142:4, 143:4).
	•	Through the event in which Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish, it prefigures the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ most vividly among the books of the Old Testament.
7. Christ in the Book of Jonah
1) Christ Who Rose on the Third Day
Jonah entered the belly of the fish and came out alive after three days, went to Nineveh, and proclaimed that Nineveh would be judged after forty days. Hearing Jonah's message, everyone in the city of Nineveh, beginning with the king, put on sackcloth and repented.
That the king and people of the city of Nineveh all repented was because Jonah had come out alive from the belly of the fish after three days. Since Jonah had been in the belly of the fish for three days, there must have been some marks on his skin. Also, the men who had sailed with Jonah on the ship may have testified that Jonah had been thrown into the sea. In any case, the fact that Jonah went into the belly of the fish and came out alive after three days must have been a sign to the people of Nineveh that they could believe Jonah's message of judgment.
This is a type of Jesus, who died, was buried in the tomb, and rose again on the third day.
The resurrection of Jesus is certain evidence that compels us to believe in the deity of Jesus and in what He has done.
2) Christ Proclaimed to the Gentiles
God sent the prophet Jonah to the city of Nineveh in Assyria, where Gentiles lived, and had him proclaim a message of judgment. And He caused them to repent and obtain salvation. This showed in advance that the gospel, brought to completion through Jesus Christ, would in the future be conveyed to the Gentiles, and that many Gentiles would repent and obtain salvation.
3) Christ Who Is the Lord of Judgment
The fact that the people of Nineveh, who had been so cruel, repented upon hearing Jonah's message of judgment gives, paradoxically, a solemn warning of how much greater a judgment will fall on unbelievers today who, though they hear the gospel of Jesus Christ, are hardened and do not repent.
Jesus is greater than Jonah. For those who do not accept the gospel that Jesus has completed, there is nothing but judgment.

1. Title
The title "Micah," which reflects the name of its author, derives from the Hebrew title "Mikah" and means "Who is like the LORD?" The words in Micah 7:18, "Who is a God like You?", are probably a confession connected with the name of the prophet Micah himself.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author: Micah
	•	The author of this book is "Micah." His name appears in the book, and the prophet Jeremiah also quotes the book and so testifies that its author is "Micah."
	•	The prophet "Micah" came from Moresheth, a small country village located about 40 km southwest of Jerusalem. Because this place was near Gath, one of the five great cities of the Philistines of old, it was called "Moresheth-Gath."
	•	Since there is no mention at all of the parents or ancestors of the prophet "Micah," it can be surmised that he came from a humble family. Also, since references to the habits of shepherds' lives appear frequently in the messages he proclaimed, he is presumed to have been of shepherd origin.
Date of Writing
"Micah" ministered as a prophet during the reigns of three kings of Judah in the south: Jotham (the 11th king, 747–731 B.C.), Ahaz (the 12th king, 731–716 B.C.), and Hezekiah (the 13th king, 715–687 B.C.), and that span is at most 60 years. In general, however, his period of activity is estimated at about 45 years, from around 735 B.C., the end of King Jotham's reign, to 690 B.C., the end of King Hezekiah's reign.
During his ministry Micah personally witnessed the destruction of the northern kingdom of Israel, which he had prophesied (722 B.C.), and through his strong rebuke of idolatry and immorality he must have had a direct influence on King Hezekiah's religious reform (Jeremiah 26:18-19), and, more distantly, on the reform of King Josiah.
The date of writing of this book is estimated at around 700 B.C., the latter half of the prophet Micah's prophetic activity.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
The kingdoms of Judah in the south and Israel in the north each enjoyed great political and economic prosperity during the reigns of Uzziah (the 10th king of Judah, 791–739 B.C.) and Jeroboam II (the 13th king of Israel in the north, 793–753 B.C.). The reason was that, with the powerful nation of Assyria rising anew to the north of Palestine, Aram, which had been troubling Israel all along, was weakened. As a result, the Palestinian region came to enjoy, for a short time, a period of peace without war.
But that peace did not last long. Around 735 B.C., when the prophet Micah began his ministry, Tiglath-pileser III (745~727 B.C.), king of Assyria, came to the throne and began to expand his power southward. Because of the threat of Assyrian invasion, Judah in the south and Israel in the north were enveloped in great anxiety. At this time the two nations ought to have united and strengthened their national power for the sake of their security, but the reality was entirely different.
Instead, the people and the political and religious leaders pursued their own comfort and wealth and were absorbed only in amassing property by every means. The poor and the weak groaned, suffering under the exploitation and oppression of the leaders. As a result, society as a whole showed the end-stage symptoms of moral decay and rampant injustice. Moreover, among the wealthy and the powerful there were many who flattered Assyria or Egypt and followed their foreign customs and idolatry. The two nations were also deeply corrupt religiously.
The prophet Micah came from Moresheth, a relatively wealthy agricultural region located near the border between the Philistines and Judah in the south. He could sense, more keenly than anyone, the Palestinian international situation, which was changing rapidly because of Assyria's southward policy. And this unsettled state of the times must have made him realize that God's judgment was imminent upon Israel, the people of God, who had fallen religiously and morally.
Purpose of the Writing
The prophet Micah sought to minimize the shock of the people of the kingdoms of Judah in the south and Israel in the north, who were being destroyed under God's judgment, and furthermore to build up their faith. He wished that, in the situation of destruction, the people would realize what its root cause was rather than be frustrated and despair. Thus he hoped that even after being taken away into captivity they would repent and return to God. He wrote this book to instill the hope that God will surely restore those who return to Him, and will let them enjoy eternal blessing not only on this earth but also in the eternal Messianic kingdom.
4. Structure of Micah
(1) Part 1 _ Declaration of Judgment and Promise of Restoration for Israel (Chapters 1-2)
1) Declaration of Judgment on Israel (Chapter 1)
2) The Reason for Judgment and Prophecy of Restoration (Chapter 2)
(2) Part 2 _ Prophecy of the Destruction of Jerusalem and the Coming of the Messianic Kingdom (Chapters 3-5)
1) Rebuke of the Leaders' Sins and Prophecy of the Destruction of Jerusalem (Chapter 3)
2) Prophecy of the Coming of the Messianic Kingdom (Chapter 4)
3) Prophecy of the Coming of the Messiah (Chapter 5)
(2) Part 3 _ Exhortation to Immediate Repentance and Promise of Salvation for Israel (Chapters 6-7)
1) God's Plea Concerning the Justice of the Judgment (Chapter 6)
2) Promise of Salvation and the Prophet's Thanksgiving (Chapter 7)
5. The Theme of Micah
The central content of the book of Micah is "present judgment and future blessing." The present judgment was brought upon the Israelites by their disobedience in breaking the conditional covenant of works, and the future blessing is the fulfillment of the unconditional covenant, given by God's unchanging grace and faithfulness.
Like the other prophetic books, this book rebukes the sins of Judah in the south and Israel in the north, which had fallen religiously and morally, and at the same time conveys God's judgment upon them and His promise of restoration. Yet while dealing with the same content, the prophet Micah presents a special perspective. In a situation where destruction had already been decided, he emphasizes in what attitude of faith the people of God should receive that discipline.
Micah testifies that God's judgment is both irreversible and righteous, and he teaches that the people should bear that discipline by repenting of their sins and enduring with patience, rather than meeting it with resentment. He also exhorts them to obey, hoping in the promise of restoration and salvation that will be given in the future. Basing himself on God's love and faithfulness to His covenant, he repeatedly confirms that the promise of restoration will surely be fulfilled.
	•	God not only governs the world He created by the laws of love and justice, but also requires the people of Israel whom He chose to practice that love and justice. Therefore the practice of love and justice is a duty that the saints on this earth ought to perform, and it is a character that they must have in order to become citizens of the coming Messianic kingdom.
	•	God surely disciplines even His chosen people when they sin. The destruction of Judah in the south and Israel in the north is historical evidence that God's judgment on wickedness is surely carried out.
	•	The saints must realize that God's discipline is the rod of love meant to cleanse them from sin and lead them on the right path. Therefore they must humbly receive that discipline with a heart of patience and obedience.
	•	In a nation or a church, the spiritual and moral corruption of its leaders endangers the existence of the whole community. In whatever sphere, political or religious, the authority of a leader is rightly recognized only when he practices justice in God's stead. If given power or authority is abused for personal gain, the result can lead not only to personal ruin but to the destruction of the nation.
	•	God's discipline for sin does not cancel His promise of salvation. God disciplines His people's sin with justice, but after the discipline He is faithful to the covenant and will surely save His people and let them enjoy the blessings of the Messianic kingdom.
	•	In the end, the blessing of eternal life is given to the saints who believe in the gospel of Christ, and the day of final judgment, when eternal punishment will fall on unbelievers who do not repent to the end and deny Christ, will surely come.
6. Characteristics of the Book of Micah
	•	In the book of Micah, expressions in the form of questions appear frequently. And these questions do not demand a particular answer; their answers are clear, and they are given with the intention that the one questioned realize his own wickedness.
	•	The three sermons recorded in the book of Micah all share a common structure. Each sermon begins with a declaration of judgment on the people of Israel and ends with a prophecy of restoration. This composition shows the formal unity of the book.
	•	The book of Micah resembles the book of Isaiah in many parts in terms of content. For that reason it is sometimes called "the little Isaiah."
	•	The prophet Micah deals together with the prophetic themes of prophets who were active in his own time, such as Amos, Hosea, and Isaiah. He is like Amos in warning against the injustice of the leaders of society and demanding justice, and similar to Hosea in emphasizing God's love within the prophecy of restoration. Also, the part that describes in detail the Messianic kingdom to come shows the same perspective as Isaiah.
	•	It contains many wordplays related to the names of the cities that are the objects of judgment.
	•	In the book of Micah, expressions related to the daily lives of ordinary people of that time, such as shepherds and farmers, appear frequently. This shows how closely Micah's prophecy, which cried out for the realization of justice on the side of the poor, was tied to reality.
	•	Compared with the other minor prophets, the book of Micah gives very great weight, relative to its total length, to prophecy about the Messianic kingdom.
7. Christ in the Book of Micah
Among the twelve minor prophets, this book gives the most direct and yet richest prophecies about Jesus Christ and His work.
(1) Prophecy of the Birth of Jesus Christ in Bethlehem
(Micah 5:2) But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel — One whose origins are of old, from the days of eternity.
(Matthew 2:4-6) And when he had assembled all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where the Christ was to be born. “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written: ‘But you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah, for out of you will come a ruler who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.’”
(2) The Passion of Christ and the Suffering to Come from the Rejection by Israel, the Chosen People

(3) Christ the Judge
(Micah 5:10-15) “In that day,” declares the LORD, “I will remove your horses from among you and wreck your chariots. I will remove the cities of your land and tear down all your strongholds. I will cut the sorceries from your hand, and you will have no fortune-tellers. I will also cut off the carved images and sacred pillars from among you, so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands. I will root out the Asherah poles from your midst and demolish your cities. I will take vengeance in anger and wrath upon the nations that have not obeyed Me.”
(4) Christ the Shepherd

(John 10:14) I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me,
(5) Christ the King

(6) Christ Who Existed from the Beginning

1. Title
The title of this book directly reflects "Nahum" in the Hebrew original, and, like the titles of the other prophetic books, it is taken from the name of the author.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
In this very verse the author of the book identifies himself as "Nahum the Elkoshite."
"Nahum" means "comfort" or "consolation," and it is a shortened form of "Nehemiah," which means "the LORD's comfort"; when applied to a person it carries the meaning of "comforter."
The meaning of a prophet's name sums up his ministry and message. This prophet's name and the title of the book show that the content of the book, which proclaims God's judgment on Assyria, a great threatening presence to Judah in the south, was a great consolation and comfort to the people of Judah in the south.
However, nothing is known about "Nahum" other than what is stated in this verse, that he was an "Elkoshite."
The region of Elkosh is presumed to be "Kessijeh," which lies in the southwest of Judah in the south, midway between Jerusalem and Gaza.
Date of Writing
The date of writing of this book is generally placed between 663 and 612 B.C. The reason is, first, that Nahum 3:8-10 already speaks of the fall of Thebes (No-amon) of Egypt, which occurred in 663 B.C., as a past event.
Also, the book itself was written in anticipation of the fall of Nineveh, which took place in 612 B.C.
Seen in this way, the prophet "Nahum" appears to have been active somewhat earlier than Zephaniah, Habakkuk, and Jeremiah, the prophets of the last days of Judah in the south, or else active at almost the same time as they.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
Like the book of Jonah, this book takes as its subject Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrian Empire. But whereas the book of Jonah records the repentance and salvation of the people of Nineveh, the book of Nahum prophesies the destruction of Nineveh, so the two books form a great contrast.
About a hundred years before the book of Nahum was written (around 760 B.C.), Nineveh was full of wickedness and was in a state in which it could not but receive God's judgment. But God sent Jonah to urge repentance, and when the people of Nineveh humbly repented, God withdrew the disaster He had intended to bring. This came entirely from God's mercy and love.
However, about a hundred years after that repentance, the people of Nineveh in Nahum's time had forgotten that grace and returned again to evil. They were even more proud and wicked than before, and they cruelly oppressed and tormented the surrounding nations.
The Assyrian Empire experienced great revival in the times of Tiglath-pileser III (745-727 B.C.) and his son Shalmaneser V (727-722 B.C.), and carried on wars of conquest without ceasing. This expansionist policy made the nation extremely warlike and cruel in disposition, and it was common to seize the property of other peoples and to abuse them.
According to ancient records, Assyria took pride in thoroughly destroying its enemies, and it is said to have inflicted cruel punishments on rebels, such as flaying them or mutilating their bodies. It also forcibly relocated conquered peoples and made them intermingle, trying thereby to destroy their ethnic identity, religion, and culture. This policy produced great confusion and suffering, and in the end Assyria became a cruel empire built upon the blood of other peoples.
A representative example of this Assyrian policy of assimilation is Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.
Motive of the Writing
God wished to make known how thorough is the judgment, based on God's justice, upon Nineveh, which had betrayed God's grace and love and acted rebelliously once again. At the same time, He had this book written in order to comfort the people of Judah in the south, who had been oppressed by Assyria, and to give them hope.
Furthermore, through the judgment and destruction of Nineveh, God, the Sovereign over all the nations and all peoples of the world, lets it be known through this book that He surely judges sin, and thereby comforts His children and also causes them to be established more rightly.
Meanwhile, the prophecy of Nineveh's destruction recorded in this book was fulfilled when Nineveh was destroyed in 612 B.C. by the allied forces of Nabopolassar of Babylon (Nabopolassar, 625-605 B.C.) and Cyaxares II of Media (Cyaxares II, 625-585 B.C.).
