It is divided into a preface (Nahum 1:1) and the main body (Nahum 1:2-3:19).
The main body is further divided into three parts.
	•	First part, verses 1:2-15: the message of God's judgment on Nineveh
	•	Middle part (chapter 2): the horror of the destruction of Nineveh, which received God's judgment
	•	Latter part (chapter 3): the cause and inevitability of Nineveh's destruction
(1) Preface (1:1) - The author of the book, its subject, and its divine origin
(2) Main Body (1:2-3:19)
1) Proclamation of the Prophecy of God's Judgment on Nineveh (Chapter 1)
2) Prophecy of the Circumstances and Horror at the Time of Nineveh's Destruction (Chapter 2)
3) The Cause and Inevitability of Nineveh's Destruction (Chapter 3)
5. The Theme of Nahum
Together with the book of Jonah, this book is a prophetic book recording the word of God concerning Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. Whereas the book of Jonah deals mainly with the repentance and salvation of Nineveh, the book of Nahum deals with the destruction of Nineveh through God's righteous judgment, so the two books contain opposing themes.
The people of Nineveh, who once repented because of the warning of God delivered by Jonah, were unable to pass that faith on to the next generation. In the end their descendants again lived rebellious lives, and God declared judgment upon them. This shows that God's sovereignty extends over the whole world, and that God's righteous judgment will surely come upon those who live in wickedness.
That is, whereas the book of Jonah, through the repentance of Nineveh, shows God's plan of salvation for all humanity, including the Gentile peoples, the book of Nahum reveals God's justice and absolute sovereignty through His judgment on Nineveh, which had fallen again.
Summarizing the main themes of this book from this perspective, they are as follows.
1) The LORD God is the only Ruler who governs the whole world and the history of humanity, and He is faithful.
Judah in the south was suffering under Assyrian oppression at that time, but God will in the end judge Assyria and save Judah in the south. In the same way, the saints of today also suffer because of evil powers, but those powers of evil too are under God's sovereignty. On the last day God will judge them and give all the saints true freedom, peace, and rest.
2) God's righteous judgment is gracious news to the saints.
The message of God's judgment on Nineveh was a warning of destruction to the Assyrians, but to the people of Judah in the south, who lived under the Assyrian threat, it was a word of great comfort and hope. In the same way, for the saints today who suffer at the hands of the wicked in an unjust world, God's final judgment becomes not a message of fear but a message of comfort and hope.
5. Characteristics of the Revelation of Nahum
	•	It conveys a message on a theme completely different from that of the book of Jonah, a prophetic book concerning the same object.
	•	If the book of Jonah is a prophetic book that proclaims repentance and salvation, Nahum proclaims destruction; and if the book of Jonah was based on a historical experience, the book of Nahum is prophecy throughout.
	•	It is composed of forceful sentences and a rhythmic tone, and gives the most vividness of all the prophetic books (Nahum 3:1-4).
	•	In style it is poetic, but in content it depicts terrible and fearful scenes.
	•	The destruction of the unrighteous who oppose the chosen people and God, and the salvation of the people of God, appear in sharp contrast.
	•	Nahum 1:2-9 is an acrostic passage in which the first sentences begin in the order of the Hebrew alphabet.
6. The Book of Nahum and Christ
The central theme that the whole Bible conveys is only one: the salvation of humanity through the redemptive work of Jesus Christ. That is, the Bible is a book that shows the history of that redemption and its various aspects, centering on one unified theme: the salvation of the saints accomplished by the redemptive work of Jesus Christ.
The truths related to Christ that the book of Nahum shows are as follows.
Nahum 1:2-8 describes God's righteous character in judging the wickedness of Assyria with the words "jealous," "vengeance," "wrath," "righteousness," "patience," "power," "goodness," and "holiness."
Such a character of God is also the essential character of Jesus Christ. This is because God the Father, Jesus Christ the Son, and God the Holy Spirit are essentially the same Triune God. Therefore, when Jesus Christ comes again and judges the nations, He will judge in accordance with this very holy and righteous character.
Moreover, the apostle Paul, in the New Testament, quoted the word of the book of Nahum and connected it with the gospel of Jesus Christ. Nahum 1:15, while prophesying the salvation of Judah in the south and the destruction of Nineveh, speaks of how beautiful are the feet of the one who proclaims peace and good news. Paul quoted this word, pointing to those who preach the gospel, and explained the gospel of salvation of Jesus Christ (Romans 10:15).
(Isaiah 52:7) How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation, who say to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
(Nahum 1:15) Look to the mountains— the feet of one who brings good news, who proclaims peace! Celebrate your feasts, O Judah; fulfill your vows. For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off.
(Romans 10:15) And how can they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
Thus Nahum 1:9-15 is first a word that prophesies the destruction of Nineveh and the salvation of Judah in the south. But at a deeper level it is a word that prophetically shows the completion of redemption, in which Jesus Christ will come again, completely destroy the power of Satan, and finally save the people of God from the power of sin and death.

1. Title
The title of this book, "Habakkuk," derives from the title of the Hebrew original, and means "one who embraces, one who clings." It uses the name of the prophet "Habakkuk," the writer, as the title.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The book itself identifies its author as the prophet Habakkuk. However, nothing at all is known about Habakkuk personally beyond the facts that appear in the content of the book. Only, because he had many religious doubts and questions, later people gave him the nickname "the Thomas of the Old Testament." Also, because of the poetic style of the book, he was praised as the author of a prophetic book in which the ability of Isaiah and the sensibility of Jeremiah are blended.
And based on chapter 3 of Habakkuk, he is presumed to have been a choir member from the tribe of Levi. Habakkuk 3:1 identifies it as a prayer of Habakkuk and says "according to Shigionoth," and verse 19 says, "For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments."
(Habakkuk 3:19) GOD the Lord is my strength; He makes my feet like those of a deer; He makes me walk upon the heights! For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments.
Date of Writing
The time of writing of the book of Habakkuk can be estimated from the prophecy in Habakkuk 1:6-10 of the invasion of Judah in the south by the Chaldeans (Babylon). The "Chaldea" spoken of here refers specifically to the "Neo-Babylonian" empire.
It was around 625-605 B.C., the period when Nabopolassar ruled, that the Neo-Babylonian empire began to grow in power. This almost overlaps the time when King Josiah of Judah in the south (640-609 B.C.) was ruling. But until the time of Josiah, the influence of Assyria was still relatively strong.
After that, when in 612 B.C. Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, fell to the invasion of the allied forces of Babylon and Media, the situation in the Near East came under the sphere of Babylonian power. In the end, in 605 B.C., when Assyria was completely destroyed, Judah in the south also suffered Babylon's first invasion.
Therefore, the prophecy of the Chaldean invasion of Judah in the south in Habakkuk 1:6 appears to have this event in mind. From this, the time of writing of the book of Habakkuk is estimated to be between 612 B.C., when Babylon conquered Nineveh and seized supremacy in the Near East, and 605 B.C., when it invaded Judah in the south. Habakkuk was a prophet who was active in the same period as Jeremiah.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
The ancient Near East around 612-605 B.C., when the prophet Habakkuk was active, was undergoing great change because of the rapid rise of the new empire of Babylon. Assyria, the dominant power in the northern region, was in effect in a state of destruction after its capital Nineveh fell to Babylon in 612 B.C. Egypt, the strong power of the southern region, also saw its power greatly weakened by its defeat in the battle of Carchemish (Carchemish) against Babylon in 605 B.C.
Amid this confusion of great powers contending for power, Judah in the south was placed in an uneasy situation, not knowing when it would be invaded. In particular, the death of King Josiah (640-609 B.C.) in 609 B.C. shocked Judah in the south greatly. He had been killed at Megiddo when he tried to block the advance of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, who was marching toward Carchemish to help Assyria. Afterward the people set up his son Jehoahaz (609 B.C.) as king, but Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, took Jehoahaz to Egypt and killed him, and set up another son, Jehoiakim (609-598 B.C.), as king in his place (2 Kings 23:30, 34).
Meanwhile, the new empire of Babylon, in order to extend its power southward, had to take control of the Palestinian region first, so the conquest of Judah in the south was essential. In the end, in 605 B.C., Babylon invaded Judah in the south for the first time and carried the nobles away as captives, among whom were Daniel and his three friends (2 Chronicles 36:6-8, Daniel 1:1-2).
During this period Judah in the south had fallen into serious corruption, religiously and morally as well as in political confusion. The rulers exploited and oppressed the people in order to pay tribute to the great powers (2 Kings 23:35-37, 24:4, Jeremiah 22:13-19), and even persecuted and killed the prophets who proclaimed the word of God (Jeremiah 36:20-32). As a result, the good people were groaning in suffering because of the tyranny of those in power.
Motive of the Writing
In such a hard and unjust reality, righteous people like Habakkuk could not but earnestly long and pray for God's righteous judgment to be carried out quickly. So the prophet Habakkuk wrote this prophetic book in order to comfort the suffering righteous and to encourage them to stand firm in faith even in a confused age.
Habakkuk puts questions to God on behalf of the hearts of the righteous remnant.
He asks, as though in protest, why God lets the unrighteous prosper and why He leaves the world as it is while justice has collapsed. But in the end he comes to realize through God's answer. He proclaims that God governs the whole world with justice and is One who surely judges the unrighteous.
Thus the book of Habakkuk emphasizes that one must not lose heart in any circumstances but must live by faith.
The word "the righteous will live by faith" is a great declaration given by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, and it still comes as living truth, not only in Habakkuk's time but to all faithful saints today who keep their faith amid persecution and suffering.
4. Structure of Habakkuk
In a situation where violence and rebellion were rampant, this book was written, in response to the religious question, "Why does God not quickly judge the unrighteous and save the righteous?", in the form of two questions from the prophet Habakkuk and two answers of God to them.
Through this it clearly testifies to the inevitability of judgment on the wicked and the certainty of salvation for the righteous who live by faith.
This book consists of a preface (Habakkuk 1:1) and the main body (Habakkuk 1:2-3:19).
The main body is further divided into two parts:
	•	First part (1:2-2:20): God's answers to the prophet Habakkuk's questions, asked on two occasions,
	•	Latter part (chapter 3): a song of praise, the prophet's confession of faith, in which he realized, through God's answers, God's sovereignty, power, and justice as Judge and Savior.
(1) Preface (1:1) _ The author of the book and its divine origin
(2) Main Body (1:2-3:19)
1) Questions and Answers between Habakkuk and God (Chapters 1-2)
2) Habakkuk's Song of Praise, a Confession of Faith in God (Chapter 3)
5. The Theme of Habakkuk
The book of Habakkuk is a book of dialogue of faith that begins with the question, "Why does God not carry out righteous judgment quickly, but keep silent?", in a reality where the unrighteous gain power and the righteous suffer unjustly. Through this it shows the certain truth that God will in the end judge the wicked and save the righteous. It also clearly reveals the sovereignty and righteousness of God, who presides over all things.
1) God's rule is righteous.
God, as the eternal King, sits on His heavenly throne and rules the whole world (Jeremiah 10:10, Psalms 103:19). God's rule is carried out especially within human history as well, and its foundation lies in justice (Psalms 89:14).
Habakkuk fell into religious doubt when he saw a reality in which God's justice seemed to be realized slowly. But God's answer shows that His rule is still righteous and good. Though for now it may seem that the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer, it is only for a moment. When the time that God has set comes, the wicked will be judged and the righteous will receive salvation and eternal blessing (Daniel 12:1-3). Therefore the people of God must believe in God's sovereignty and providence, and live looking to His righteous rule.
(Daniel 12:1-3) “At that time Michael, the great prince who stands watch over your people, will rise up. There will be a time of distress, the likes of which will not have occurred from the beginning of nations until that time. But at that time your people—everyone whose name is found written in the book—will be delivered. And many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt. Then the wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens, and those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever.
2) The purpose of God's discipline of His own people is repentance and salvation.
When the people He has chosen sin, God sometimes uses the unrighteous as instruments of discipline. But this discipline is not for destruction; it is for accomplishing salvation through repentance.
God disciplines His people when they sin, but if they repent and turn back, He restores them again. Therefore, when the people of God undergo tribulation, they should realize that it is God's will to refine them, rather than lose heart. And they should examine themselves and repent, and overcome that hardship with gratitude and patience (2 Corinthians 4:16, James 1:2-4).
3) The end of the wicked is destruction.
In the course of redemptive history, good and evil exist together, and there are times when the wicked seem to flourish. But that is only for a moment, and it can never last in the kingdom of God. The righteous God will on the last day separate the righteous from the wicked and judge them according to what they have done (Revelation 20:11-15, Matthew 25:31-46).
For the moment it seems that the judgment is delayed, but that is because God does not want anyone to perish but wants everyone to repent (2 Peter 3:9). But when the time that God has set comes, no more opportunity for repentance will remain.
4) God also uses the wicked as instruments to discipline His own people who have sinned.
God does not always use only righteous people; sometimes He uses even wicked people who do not know God or who rebel against Him to accomplish His will. The wicked can become instruments of discipline that cause the people of God to realize their sin and turn back. But at the same time God, in that process, wants the wicked too to realize His omnipotence and sovereignty and to return to God.
5) The righteous will live by faith.
The righteous live by faith even amid suffering and hardship. Since human beings fell after Adam's disobedience, they cannot achieve moral righteousness by themselves. Therefore the "righteous" spoken of here means a person whom God has declared righteous by faith.
God calls the one who repents and believes righteous, and saves him by faith.
Being saved through faith in this way is called "being saved by faith," "being made righteous by faith," and "being declared righteous by faith."
6. Characteristics of the Revelation of Habakkuk
The book of Habakkuk has a unique form unlike other prophetic books. Whereas most prophetic books take the form of proclaiming the word of God, the book of Habakkuk begins with "questions and answers" between God and the prophet, and ends with the prophet's confession of faith and praise.
Also, although this book does not often use the words "faith" and "salvation," deep truths of faith are contained within it. In particular, the verse "the righteous will live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4)" is frequently quoted in the New Testament (Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, Hebrews 10:38), and clearly shows the New Testament principle of faith.
(Galatians 3:11) Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.”
(Romans 1:17) For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.”
(Hebrews 10:38) But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.”
Unlike the other minor prophets, the book of Habakkuk does not specify a concrete audience, but judging from its content, it can be seen that its main audience was the people of Judah in the south.
7. The Book of Habakkuk and Christ
The central theme that the whole Bible conveys is only one: the salvation of humanity through the redemptive work of Jesus Christ. That is, the Bible is a book that shows the history of that redemption and its various aspects, centering on one unified theme: the salvation of the saints accomplished by the redemptive work of Jesus Christ.
The truths related to Christ that the book of Habakkuk shows are as follows.
1) Salvation through the First Coming of Jesus Christ
"The righteous will live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4)," the key verse of the book of Habakkuk, proclaims the core truth of the gospel that salvation is obtained through faith. This principle of "being saved by faith" appears throughout the whole Old Testament, and it is the fundamental idea of salvation fully revealed in the New Testament. But in the Old Testament there is no book that testifies to this principle as clearly and with as forceful a tone as this one.
Salvation obtained by faith is given only by the grace of God and the substitutionary atonement of the cross of Jesus Christ (John 3:16). Therefore the "faith" that Habakkuk spoke of is not mere faithfulness, but faith in the Messiah who would come in the future and save sinners.
2) The Final Judgment through the Second Coming of Jesus Christ
The event in which God judged Babylon and restored Israel becomes a type of the last judgment, in which Jesus Christ will come again, judge all evil, and save the saints forever.
The book of Habakkuk is, in the end, a book that prefigures the truth of the gospel that those who live by faith will in the end be victorious.

1. Title
The book of Zephaniah is named after the prophet "Zephaniah." It is a direct translation of the Hebrew original "Tsefanyah," and, as with the other prophetic books, the name of the author became the title of the book.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
Zephaniah was a prophet who ministered in the time of Josiah (640-609 B.C.), the sixteenth king of Judah in the south. He was a fourth-generation descendant of King Hezekiah and a relative of King Josiah. This is because Josiah is recorded as a third-generation descendant of Hezekiah and Zephaniah as a fourth-generation descendant.
Therefore Zephaniah, being of royal descent, lived in Jerusalem and had free access to the royal palace, and he seems to have had a direct influence on Josiah's religious reform. When Josiah sought God at the age of 16, removed the idols at 20, and at 26 discovered the book of the Law and carried out a sweeping reform (2 Kings 22-23, 2 Chronicles 34-35), Zephaniah's spiritual influence is presumed to have been great.
Zephaniah was a contemporary of Jeremiah. His name means "the one whom the LORD has hidden," and some scholars think that he was given this name because he was born during the persecution under King Manasseh.
Date of Writing
The book of Zephaniah was written in the time of King Josiah (640-609 B.C.). Judging from the fact that it influenced Josiah's reform movement, it is presumed to have been written around 630 B.C., before the religious reform got fully under way.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
The period when Zephaniah was active was just before King Josiah began the religious reform, before 622 B.C. At that time Judah in the south was a vassal state of the Assyrian Empire, and from the time of King Manasseh (697-642 B.C.) it had been influenced by Assyria politically and religiously.
Through Manasseh and his son Amon (642-640 B.C.), and until the early years of Josiah, Judah in the south accepted and served the gods of Assyria and went through a bleak period in which it even had to pay tribute. But after Josiah became king, Assyria suffered great turmoil from rebellions of various nations and the invasion of the Scythians (Scythians) from the north, and its control over Judah in the south weakened. At this time Josiah declared complete political independence from Assyria.
In order to restore faith in God, Josiah carried out a large-scale religious reform centered on Jerusalem, covering all of Judah in the south and even the territory of the northern kingdom of Israel, which had already been destroyed. Josiah became king at the age of 8, began to seek the LORD at 16, removed the idols at 20, and completed the reform at 26 by discovering the book of the Law.
Josiah is a very important figure in the history of Israel, and his name and work had already been prophesied by God about 300 years earlier, in the time of Jeroboam. God raised up and used Zephaniah to accomplish this religious reform.
Motive of the Writing
The purpose for which Zephaniah wrote this prophetic book was first of all to further promote King Josiah's religious reform.
He sharply rebuked the sin of idolatry in Judah in the south and of serving the sun, moon, and stars (the gods of the sun and moon), and criticized the corruption and injustice of the leaders.
He also proclaimed that "the day of the LORD," that is, the day of God's judgment, would come, and urged the people to repent. Through the judgment called "the day of the LORD," he says that the LORD is not merely a god who rules only Israel, the chosen people, but the Absolute One who has absolute sovereignty over the whole world and the universe.
Therefore, on that day when God intervenes in human history and judges good and evil alike, He will judge not only the chosen people who sinned but all the nations of the world that oppressed Israel and tormented it with evil deeds.
And just as "the prophetess Huldah" prophesied to King Josiah the destruction of Judah, this prophet too prophesies that Judah will surely come to destruction because of its wickedness.
At the same time he conveyed a message of hope that even in the midst of judgment the "remnant" who return to God will be saved. Through this he led the people to take an active part in Josiah's reform. Furthermore, Zephaniah prophesied a future in which even the Gentiles would fear the LORD, and looked ahead to the age of universal salvation through Jesus Christ.
4. Structure of Zephaniah
This book consists of a preface (Zephaniah 1:1) and the main body (Zephaniah 1:2-3:20).
The main body is further divided into two parts:
	•	First part (1:2-3:8): concerning God's judgment that comes on the day of the LORD
	•	Latter part (3:9-20): concerning the salvation of the remnant
(1) Preface (1:1) - The author of the book, its divine origin, and the historical background
(2) Main Body (1:2-3:20)
1) Prophecy of God's Judgment to Come on the Day of the LORD (1:2-3:8)
① Declaration of God's universal judgment to come on the day of the LORD (1:2-3)
② Declaration of judgment on Judah in the south (1:4-18)
③ Call to repentance for all peoples (2:1-3)
④ Declaration of judgment on the nations (2:4-15)
⑤ Declaration of judgment on Jerusalem (3:1-8)
2) Prophecy of the Salvation of the Remnant Before the Day of the LORD Comes (3:9-20)
① Salvation of the remnant (3:9-13)
② Restoration of Israel, the chosen people, and a song of praise for the joy of salvation (3:14-20)
5. The Theme of Zephaniah
The main themes of this book are God's judgment on the wicked who will face "the day of the LORD" and God's salvation of "the remnant."
(1) God's judgment on sin will surely be carried out.
God is One who patiently waits for a long time, but when the limit that the Lord sees is full, He judges thoroughly.
History up to now proves this truth.
	•	At the time of the flood, God waited 120 years, but because they did not turn back, the judgment was carried out.
	•	After delivering the people of Israel from Egypt, He waited for 1,500 years, but in the end, because they rejected Christ, God's judgment has come upon them in their history for 1,900 years.
	•	Now, in the history of the church, He is bearing with the world for 2,000 years.
There is a saying, "The mills of God grind slowly." That is, though they turn slowly, He will surely judge.
(2) The Objects of God's Judgment
God is the Creator of the whole universe and all things, and the Sovereign who presides over history. Therefore God is the true Ruler of all peoples and nations. For this reason God's judgment does not fall only on a particular people, nation, or individual in a particular age, but on all people of the past, present, and future who are defiled by sin.
The book of Zephaniah specifies concretely what kinds of people will be judged.
(3) The Two Sides of God's Judgment and Salvation
In God's judgment, judgment on sin and salvation are accomplished at the same time. Zephaniah begins with a terrifying judgment, but it ends with the most beautiful and comforting verses in the Old Testament.
(Zephaniah 1:2) “I will completely sweep away everything from the face of the earth,” declares the LORD.
(Zephaniah 3:9) For then I will restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD and serve Him shoulder to shoulder.
(Zephaniah 3:17) The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.”
(Zephaniah 3:20) At that time I will bring you in; yes, at that time I will gather you. For I will give you fame and praise among all the peoples of the earth when I restore your captives before your very eyes,” says the LORD.
The two sides of judgment and salvation can be seen in several cases in the Bible.
	•	In the flood judgment of Noah's time, Noah's family was saved; in the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah with sulfur and fire, Lot and his daughters were delivered; and in the judgment of the city of Jericho, the family of the prostitute Rahab was delivered.
	•	In the coming seven-year great tribulation as well, 144,000 of the people of Israel will be saved.
Even in the midst of judgment, God shows compassion.
(4) The Duty of Leaders
Political and religious leaders must realize God's justice within the sphere to which they belong.
God Himself established the institutions that human beings need, such as the church and the government, set up leaders, and gave them office and authority to establish order and to realize justice.
Therefore leaders must look squarely at the fact that above them is God, the true Leader of human life, and acknowledge that His authority is greater and higher than their own, act humbly, and do their utmost to realize God's justice on this earth.
If leaders forget their duty and, led by humanistic greed, take the lead in fostering corruption and decay and make the sphere to which they belong corrupt, God's wrath against them will be greater and more terrible in proportion to the weightiness of the mission they have received.
6. Characteristics of Zephaniah
	•	Unlike other prophetic books, the prophet's genealogy is recorded concretely up to his great-great-grandfather.
	•	It sharply contrasts the two sides of God's judgment on the wicked and the salvation of the righteous on the day of the LORD.
	•	Rather than the Gentile nations, it deals mainly with warning and encouragement for Judah in the south.
	•	It speaks much of the return of not only Israel but also the Gentiles to God.
7. The Book of Zephaniah and Christ
The central theme that the whole Bible conveys is only one: the salvation of humanity through the redemptive work of Jesus Christ. That is, the Bible is a book that shows the history of that redemption and its various aspects, centering on one unified theme: the salvation of the saints accomplished by the redemptive work of Jesus Christ.
The truths related to Christ that the book of Zephaniah shows are as follows.
(1) Jesus Christ Who Will Come as Immanuel
This book introduces a God who calls His people by unconditional grace, who makes them repent even when they sin and are disciplined, who dwells among them, loves them, and rejoices over them.
This shows the figure of "Immanuel," who came among us for us sinners, died for us and rose again, washes away our sins, and is among the saints.
(Zephaniah 3:17) The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing.”
(Matthew 1:23) “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and they will call Him Immanuel” (which means, “God with us”).
(2) Christ Who Will Be Worshiped as the Head of the Church
Zephaniah says that, even amid judgment, all the people of the coastlands of the Gentiles will worship God, each in his own place.
This prophesies the appearance of the New Testament church, in which the saints saved through the redemptive work of Jesus Christ will worship Christ in every part of the world.
(Zephaniah 2:11) The LORD will be terrifying to them when He starves all the gods of the earth. Then the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him, each in its own place.
(Colossians 1:18) And He is the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence.
(3) Christ Who Sanctifies (Atones)
Zephaniah mentions that in the last times God will purify the lips of the nations so that they may serve the LORD with one accord, and he said that the name of the LORD will be called upon among them. This prophesies that, through the event of redemption accomplished by Christ, our sins will be washed clean and we will come to serve the Lord.
(Zephaniah 3:9) For then I will restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD and serve Him shoulder to shoulder.
(Titus 3:5) He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
(Hebrews 13:15) Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.
(4) Christ Who Will Come Again as Judge
God's prophecy of judgment about the universal judgment to come on "the day of the LORD" and its horror is a prophecy of Jesus Christ, who will return as Judge. Christ, who will return in the last times, will utterly destroy all the forces of evil.

1. Title
It is called "Haggai" after the name of its author. The Hebrew original of "Haggai," "Haggay," means "festal," and it is a shortened form of "Haggiah," which means "festival of the LORD."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
From the internal evidence (1:1) (2:1,10,20) and the mention in the book of Ezra (Ezra 5:1, 6:14), the author of this book is clearly Haggai.
"Haggai" has the meaning "man of the festival, of the appointed feasts." It seems that he was born at a certain feast and so was given this name.
Haggai was born in Babylon during the captivity, and returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel at the time of the first return of the exiles by the decree of Cyrus (Cyrus, 539-529 B.C.), king of Persia (2 Chronicles 36:23)(Ezra 1:1). Haggai's ministry was a short period of four months, from the first day of the sixth month to the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (1:1, 2:10), but he carried out a more successful ministry than any other prophet.
Date of Writing
As is clearly stated at the beginning of each of the four prophecies contained in this book, it was written in a short period between the ninth and twelfth months of the second year of Darius I (Darius Hystaspes, 521-486 B.C.), the third king of Persia, that is, in 520 B.C.

3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
"Haggai" and "Zechariah," together with "Malachi," are prophets of the period after the return from the Babylonian captivity.
Historically, there was Babylon's first invasion of Israel in 606 BC, and in the third invasion in 586 BC Israel was destroyed. With the destruction of the nation, the people of Israel were taken to Babylon as captives. Afterward Babylon was destroyed by the allied forces of Media and Persia.
By the decree of Cyrus, king of Persia at that time, the people of Israel returned from Babylon to their own land in 536 BC. The people of Israel who had returned to their own land laid the foundation of the temple in Jerusalem. But this work of rebuilding the temple was halted by the persistent obstruction of Samaria and the neighboring nations, and the rebuilding of the temple remained suspended for as long as 16 years (until 520 BC). After that the temple was left desolate for about 16 years, and the people gradually became spiritually indifferent and lazy.
They regarded their own houses and the comfort of their lives as more important than the house of God, and pursued only physical ease.
Motive of the Writing
The message given to the generation that returned from the Babylonian captivity was an urging to resume the suspended work of rebuilding the new temple in Jerusalem.
They obeyed the word of God and resumed the construction, but they felt deep disappointment because the new temple looked shabby compared with the former temple. Because of this the construction was even in danger of being halted again. But God comforted and encouraged the discouraged people and gave them strength and courage to see the rebuilding of the temple through to the end.
God also showed them a greater and more glorious promise to be fulfilled in the future, and assured them that their labor was not in vain.
4. Structure of Haggai
Its content centers on the rebuilding of the temple, and four messages in all are delivered in chapters 1-2 of Haggai.
First message: Urging the resumption of the rebuilding of the temple (Chapter 1)

Third message: Urging obedience and purity, and the promise of blessing (2:10-19)
Looking back on past disobedience and God's discipline (2:10-19)
The promise of blessing for obedience (2:19)
Fourth message: The promise of future blessing for Zerubbabel (2:20-23)
Prophecy of judgment on the nations (2:20-22)
The glory that Zerubbabel will obtain (2:23)

1. Title
The title of this book is "Zechariah," after the name of the prophet Zechariah, who beheld the various visions that God showed him and received prophecies.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The meaning of "Zechariah" carries the confession of faith, "the LORD remembers," and it is in harmony with the content of this book, which urges the people of Israel to devote themselves to rebuilding the temple and, by giving them hope in the first and second comings of Christ, not to depart from the remembrance of the LORD God.
Zechariah was the son of Berechiah, the grandson of Iddo, and was born into a priestly family.
Zechariah returned to his homeland following the governor Zerubbabel, by the decree of King Cyrus of Persia for the first return of the exiles (536 B.C.), and his full-scale prophetic activity began in the second year of King Darius (520 B.C.), sixteen years after the return. Zechariah, who was called "young man," seems to have been young in age (Zechariah 2:4).
Zechariah was called to be both a priest and a prophet, and from his youth became one who proclaimed the word of God.
Date of Writing
Chapters 1-6 are set respectively in the eighth and eleventh months of the second year of Darius, king of Persia, 520 B.C.,
chapters 7-8 in the ninth month of the fourth year of King Darius, 518 B.C.,
and chapters 9-14 in 480-470 B.C.
Therefore the date of writing of this book can be regarded as between 520 and 470 B.C.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Haggai and Zechariah, together with Malachi, are prophets of the period after the return from the Babylonian captivity.
Historically, there was Babylon's first invasion of Israel in 606 B.C., Israel was destroyed in the third invasion in 586 B.C., and the people of Israel were taken captive to Babylon.
Afterward Babylon was destroyed by the allied forces of Media and Persia, and by the decree of Cyrus, king of Persia at that time (538 B.C.), the people of Israel returned from Babylon to their own land. The people of Israel who returned to their own land (42,360 people) laid the foundation of the temple in Jerusalem. But this work of rebuilding the temple was halted by the persistent obstruction (opposition) of Samaria and the neighboring nations, and the rebuilding of the temple remained suspended for as long as 16 years.
At this time the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who received the word of God, appeared and urged the rebuilding of the temple.
The people of Israel, moved by this, all rose up together and began the rebuilding of the temple again. This was on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month of the second year of King Darius (June 24, 520 B.C.). Then, four years later, on the third day of the month Adar in the sixth year of King Darius (December 3, 516 B.C.), the temple was finished.

5. Characteristics of Zechariah
Haggai and Zechariah were prophets who were active in the same period.
The message of the prophet Haggai centers on the rebuilding of the temple, and the message of the prophet Zechariah, together with the rebuilding of the temple, also proclaims the Messiah who is to come and the destruction of the nations that tormented the Lord's people.
The book of Zechariah is written centering on visions that give the Lord's people hope and expectation for the future.
6. The Theme of Zechariah
God's jealous love for Israel, His chosen people, appears in the completion of the temple and the restoration of Israel, that is, in the judgment of the nations. Also, by showing the first and second comings of Jesus and the arrival of the millennial kingdom, it gives motivation to hold hope even in present suffering and to prepare to enter that kingdom with a holy life.
The center of the faith of the people of Israel was the "temple." Therefore, through the message that God will surely accomplish the rebuilding of the temple and that "God is with Israel," it gives the word of [peace and comfort] to the people of Israel.
1. God first demands faith toward God. (He demands a "holy life.")
God tells the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian captivity to return to God first. To return to God means to put away the sinful life of the past and live a "holy life," that is, to establish faith toward God rightly.
(Zechariah 1:3) So tell the people that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you, says the LORD of Hosts.’
2. God desires not formality but true faith that obeys the word in daily life.
3. All who rejected Jesus will receive righteous judgment.
God's strict judgment is recorded on the sins committed by individuals (Zechariah 5:1-4) and national sins (Zechariah 5:5-11), and on the kingdoms of the world that oppose God (Zechariah 9:1-8) and the false shepherds who lead the people astray (Zechariah 10:1-5).
4. It tells us that the Messiah, who will give eternal-punishment judgment to the wicked and the blessing of eternal victory and glory to the people of God, and His kingdom will surely come.
5. Since the second coming of Christ, like the prophecy of the first coming in the book of Zechariah, will surely be fulfilled, we must look back on our lives and live more faithful lives so that we can stand without shame as those who await the Lord who will come again.

1. Title
This book is called "Malachi" after the name of its author. "Malachi" means "my messenger," and it is a shortened form of "Malakhiah," which means "messenger of the LORD." It also fits the theme of this book, which prophesies the coming of "the messenger of the covenant."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
Nothing is known about the prophet Malachi, but as internal evidence (Malachi 1:1) testifies that Malachi is the author of this book.
According to Jewish tradition, the prophet Malachi was from the tribe of Levi and a member of the Great Synagogue, which collected and preserved the canonical writings; and in light of the content of this book, it is quite possible that he was a prophet of priestly descent.
Date of Writing
The background of this book is very similar to that of the book of Nehemiah. From this it appears that this book was written in the same period as Ezra or Nehemiah, that is, after all three returns of the exiles from Babylon had been completed. That was a time when various rebuilding projects, such as the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem and the restoration of the walls, had been completed, so that outwardly it had taken on, to some degree, the appearance of a theocratic state.
Therefore this book is estimated to have been written around 432 B.C.
3. Motive and Background of the Writing
Background
At the time the book of Malachi was written, that is, in the middle of the 5th century BC, Israelite society was in an extremely bleak state politically, religiously, and economically.
The descendants of the first generation of exiles who returned from Babylon in three waves, with a calling and pride to rebuild the history of Israel, labored much: they completed Zerubbabel's second temple in 516 B.C. and rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. And although there were ups and downs, even while being checked by the native forces of Palestine, they built up to some extent an economic and social foundation centered on Jerusalem and the surrounding region. They believed that the glorious Messianic kingdom prophesied by the prophets Isaiah, Haggai, Malachi, and others would come visibly and immediately.
However, although the people turned back through Nehemiah's movement to rebuild faith, it was only temporary, and as the years went on their faith gradually grew dull and their sins increased. Although about 100 years had passed since the return from Babylon, the Messianic kingdom was not being realized, and the people came to harbor many religious doubts.
Politically, this was an age governed by governors of Persia. Although Israel, as a colony of the Persian Empire, was permitted a certain degree of self-rule and was not under severe oppression, as a colonial people without sovereignty they had to pay various taxes to the Persian Empire and live wretched lives.
Economically, continuing drought and plant disease, and especially attacks by swarms of locusts, left the fields and vineyards severely devastated.
In a situation where there was not even the slightest sign that the glorious Messianic kingdom of the Israelite people, which the generation of the returned exiles had eagerly awaited and expected, would come, the community of the returned exiles had come up against the limits of its faith and frustration.
Now those who committed all kinds of injustice for the sake of immediate comfort and satisfaction ran rampant rather than those who served God devoutly, and accordingly religious doubts about God's justice also grew.
Even the priests, who should have guided faith rightly, committed sins such as filling their own bellies with the good offerings the people brought and defiling the holy altar by offering blemished and sick offerings to God, so the temple was not the center of the chosen people's life of faith but rather a hotbed of sin.
Motive of the Writing
As God's chosen people, the people of Israel were to keep a holy life and prepare for the new age that would come with the first coming of Christ.
But when the Messianic kingdom and the day of the LORD that they expected were slow to come, the people felt doubt about their faith and became spiritually numb.
The book of Malachi points out this fallen reality, proclaims that the day of the LORD and the Messianic kingdom will surely be realized, and urges the people to repent and awaken spiritually.
4. Structure of Malachi
(1) Preface: The author and the divine origin (1:1)
(2) Main Body: Rebuke and warning concerning the corruption of the people of Israel (1:2 ~ 4:3)
1) God's unconditional love for Israel, the chosen people, and the privilege of the Israelite people (1:2-5)
2) The sins of the priests (1:6-2:9)
	•	Sins related to the duties the priests should have performed (1:6-14)
	•	Proclamation of a curse on the sins of the priests (2:1-9)
 3) The sins of the people (2:10-4:3)
	•	The sin of intermarriage with foreign women and of forced divorce from wives to whom they had pledged themselves (2:10-16)
	•	The sin of the people who scoff at God's justice (2:17-3:6)
	•	The sin of violating the regulations concerning tithes and offerings (3:7-12)
	•	The sin of the people who doubt a devout life, committed with their words (3:13-15)
4) The promise to the Israelite people: the book of remembrance and the reward that the coming Messiah will give (3:16-4:3)
(3) Conclusion: The promise to send the prophet Elijah (4:4-6)
5. Characteristics of Malachi
The time gap between Malachi and the Gospel of Matthew is about 400 years. During these 400 years of the intermediate period not a single prophet or inspired writer of Scripture appeared, so this period has been called the Dark Ages.
This gap between the Old Testament and the New Testament is called the intermediate period, and the study of this period is a great help in clearly understanding the beginning of the New Testament.
6. The Theme of Malachi
It awakens and leads to repentance the chosen people who have fallen into spiritual numbness and religious doubt, and instills hope and assurance regarding the coming Messianic kingdom. Written to exhort and teach the saints of every generation to live without shame as citizens of heaven, this book shows the following detailed themes.
(1) The Love of God
Before rebuking Israel's sins, Malachi first proclaims God's love.
The basis of God's love for Israel lies in the historical fact that He chose Israel, the descendants of Jacob. This is not due to human deeds or ability, but solely to the grace of God.
(2) The Sins of the Priests and Their Grave Responsibility
Malachi rebuked the sin and corruption of the priests, who not only offered formal and insincere sacrifices that despised God, but also led the people astray with narrow instruction in the Law.
Leaders are those who have the responsibility to teach the word of God to the people, make them turn away from sin, and lead them rightly. Therefore, if the people do not fear God and walk in sin, it is primarily because the leaders did not fear God and neglected their responsibility to convey the word of God correctly.
(3) The Sins of the People
The people of Israel had fallen from the family, which is the foundation of society.
Men committed the sin of divorcing their faithful wives and remarrying foreign women who served idols. Such conduct was an extremely wicked act that broke the commandment on marriage, neglected the faith education of their children, and in the end defied the Law of God.
(4) True Worship
Because God is Spirit and is not One who is to be treated lightly, He seeks those who worship in spirit and truth.
God delights in gifts offered with understanding and sincerity, and blesses those who honor the name of God. Formal offerings made with no fear of God at all, far from pleasing God, become unbearably loathsome.
(5) The God Faithful to the Covenant and the Coming of the Lord
The God who is faithful to the covenant surely fulfills His promise of glory to the righteous and His judgment on the wicked. Here lies the basis on which those who are the Lord's people can look to the glory of the promised day of the Lord and have hope and courage even amid tribulation.
Malachi prophesies about the first and second comings of Christ. Concerning the first coming, he speaks of the messenger who will prepare the way of the Lord, that is, John the Baptist, and concerning the second coming, he stresses that Christ will come on the last day as a mighty Judge.
The coming of Christ is the theme of the Old Testament, prophesied throughout the whole Old Testament. In particular, by prophesying the appearance of Elijah, that is, John the Baptist, who would carry out the ministry of repentance before the coming of Christ, this book not only prophesies concretely about the advent of the Messiah but also shows that the time was near.
This prophecy was fulfilled by the first coming of Christ about 400 years after the prophecy of this book, and likewise the second coming of Christ, repeatedly prophesied in the New Testament, will surely be fulfilled.

1. The Intertestamental Period (the 400 Years of Silence)
Between Malachi and Matthew there is a period of silence of about 400 years. Knowing this period is a great help in understanding God's administration, the background of the New Testament and the four Gospels, the words of the Lord, and the kinds of people who met Jesus at that time.
Just before Malachi, Israel was invaded by Babylon, Jerusalem was destroyed, and the people were taken captive to Babylon. As Daniel had prophesied (Daniel 2, 7), Babylon was destroyed by the allied forces of the Medes and Persians, and Cyrus issued a decree for the Jews to return to their homeland and build the temple. Thereupon, under the leadership of Zerubbabel, more than forty thousand people returned, and the temple was completed in 21 years (515 BC). Ezra also came with a small company and restored worship in the temple, and twelve years after that Nehemiah rebuilt the walls.
But politically this period was under the rule of Persia (538 BC), Greece (333 BC), Egypt (323 BC), Syria (204 BC), the Maccabees (165 BC), and Rome (63 BC). In particular, Rome in 40 BC set up Herod as king of Judea, and he is "Herod the Great," who was king at the time of Jesus' birth.
During this period, just as Judah went through many political changes, there were also many religious changes. New groups such as the scribes, Pharisees, and Sadducees, and institutions such as the synagogue and the Sanhedrin arose.
2. The Name "Gospel"
The first four books of the New Testament are called the Gospels. That is, they are books that record the gospel.
"Gospel" in Greek is "euangelion (εὐαγγέλιον)." "Euangelion (εὐαγγέλιον)" means "good news, glad tidings." But it does not mean simply trivial good news of everyday life; it means good news that has a profound effect on the whole life of a nation's people. Accordingly, this word means pan-national glad news, such as the news that victory in war over the enemy has been won and an age of peace has now arrived, the glad news of the birth and enthronement of a king, the pardon of criminals, and the establishment of a great festival.
Moreover, "euangelion (εὐαγγέλιον)" is a religious term that also implies the establishment of justice and peace, and salvation and pardon. It is very natural that this term was connected to the saving work of our Lord Jesus Christ, in which the Son of God comes to this earth, conquers the forces of Satan, saves sinners, and brings in the kingdom of God of justice and peace.
Therefore, to call the books that report the saving work of Jesus Christ the Gospels means in the end that the four Gospels are books that record the news about the work of Jesus. That is, they are books that record the glad news that must be made known to all the nations of the world: that through the completion of the redemptive work of Jesus Christ, anyone who repents and believes in Him can obtain salvation.
3. Why There Are Four Gospels
(1) From the time of the Old Testament, Christ was portrayed in four aspects.
Among the structures of the tabernacle that Moses set up in the wilderness, and of the temple built in its place afterward, the Most Holy Place, the place of God's presence, had a veil hung so as to be distinguished from the other places. This veil was a type of Jesus Christ, who came to this earth in the flesh.
That veil hung on gold hooks from four acacia wood pillars overlaid with gold, and the veil was woven of threads of four kinds of color: blue, scarlet, purple, and fine twisted linen. And cherubim were embroidered on it.
The cherubim are recorded in other places in the Bible as well, and they are always connected with the appearing of the glory of God. In the book of Ezekiel and in the book of Revelation, the cherubim appear as four living creatures. John saw them "in the midst of the throne and around the throne." The first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like a calf, the third living creature like a man, and the fourth living creature like a flying eagle.
Here we obtain a clear answer to why there are four Gospels rather than one. The key is the interpretation of the number "4." Just as the four living creatures are a type of our Lord Jesus Christ, who reveals the glory of God, the four Gospels show four aspects of Christ, who lived as a man while revealing the glory of the Father.
(2) Because the life of Jesus Christ cannot be told completely by only one Gospel.
Each of the writers of the four Gospels presents the Lord's life in a distinctive way. Only by combining all four Gospels can we see the complete picture.
At first glance there seem to be superficial discrepancies, but there is no contradiction between the historical facts and the truth that is to be conveyed; only the emphases differ. Each Gospel is complete in itself and forms a perfect harmony.
(3) Within the four Gospels there is only one gospel.
That there are four "Gospels" in the New Testament by no means means that there are four gospels. Christ, our Lord, is only one, and the good news for us is also only one. The four Gospels do not mean that there are four gospels. They mean the one gospel written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Therefore within the four Gospels only one gospel exists. Four Gospels were needed in order to tell that one gospel.
4. Why They Are Called the "Synoptic Gospels"
In 1774 the German scholar J. J. Griesbach called the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) "synoptic." The reason is that when the three parallel accounts in these three Gospels are arranged, there is much common material that can be easily viewed at a glance. The word "synoptic" has the meaning of "to survey or to observe together."
The Gospel of Mark consists of 660 verses. Of these, 606 verses are recorded wholly or partly in the Gospel of Matthew, and about 380 verses are also recorded in the Gospel of Luke. And almost all of what Matthew and Luke have in common with Mark is about "the life of Jesus." And a considerable part of the remaining portions of Matthew and Luke is "the teaching of Jesus." That is, "what Jesus said" is recorded in more detail than "what Jesus did."
So from the time of J. J. Griesbach these three Gospels have been called the "Synoptic Gospels." The four Gospels reflect the distinctive personalities of the Gospel writers, and each book has its own plan and purpose. When we look at anything three-dimensionally, we can understand more clearly what we want to know. It is the same with Christ. Through the Gospels, written by different writers from different perspectives, we can understand Christ more clearly and deeply.
5. The Order of the Four Gospels
No one would think that the order of the books of the Bible is inspired. Nevertheless, it is a historical fact that the order of the books of the Old and New Testaments was established under the leadership of devout people. The New Testament is not arranged chronologically like the Old Testament.
Then why are the New Testament, and especially the four Gospels, arranged in the present order? The Jews were "a people entrusted with the word of God (Romans 3:2)," and the coming of the Messiah was their theme. The Gospel of Matthew is a book full of quotations from the Old Testament. Therefore it would be fitting to begin the New Testament with a book that emphasizes the Old Testament so much. It is like opening the door of the New Testament with the key of the Old Testament.
Readers of the Old Testament will feel at home in Matthew. The genealogy in Matthew 1 introduces Christ as a descendant of the two persons most familiar to the Jews, namely Abraham and David. Also, the Gospel of Matthew devotes more space to the teaching of Christ than the other Gospel writers do. Therefore the Gospel of Matthew will make it easier for readers to become familiar with what Christ said about His own ministry.
The Gospels have 89 chapters in all. Of these, 4 chapters deal with the first thirty years of Christ's life, and 85 chapters deal with the last three and a half years. Readers can easily perceive that the last days of Christ's life are more important than the first thirty years. Of course the emphasis is on His death, burial, and resurrection. These three events provided the basis for the main theme of the apostles in the book of Acts and for the teaching to the various churches in the Epistles.
6. The Characteristics and Emphases of the Four Gospels
In fact, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John quite naturally portray four distinctive aspects of Jesus Christ. These four Gospels, each with a different emphasis, all portray the perfect Jesus, who is both God and man. There is an important connection between the four Gospels and the four living creatures of Ezekiel. Ezekiel says, "The form of their faces was that of a man, and each of the four had the face of a lion on the right side, the face of an ox on the left side, and also the face of an eagle." (Ezekiel 1:10) The lion, as the representative of the wild beasts, speaks of Christ's kingship; the man, as the representative of all visible creatures, speaks of Christ as the Son of Man; the ox, as the representative of domestic animals, speaks of Christ as servant; and the eagle, as the representative of the birds that fly in the sky, speaks of Christ's deity. The Gospel of Matthew shows Christ as King (the lion), the Gospel of Mark shows Christ as Servant (the ox), the Gospel of Luke shows Christ as the Son of Man (the man), and the Gospel of John shows Christ as the Son of God (the eagle).
Christ came to rule and reign as King. He came as a Servant to serve and to save others by sacrificing Himself in their place. He came as the Son of Man to be with human beings and to sympathize with them. He came as the Son of God to give eternal life. Therefore in the four Gospels we can see authority, humility, humanity, and deity.
If we follow the harmony of Ezekiel's four symbols and the four Gospels, we come to know that the four Gospels bear witness to one wonderful Jesus Christ. In other words, the four Gospels are closely related to the covenants concerning the Messiah in the Old Testament. The prophets prophesied about the Messiah's office and mission, birth and suffering, death, resurrection, and glory (1 Peter 1:11, Luke 24:24-25). The prophets presented Christ by four titles or offices. The four Gospels explain that Jesus is the Messiah prophesied in the Old Testament and that the prophecies of the prophets were accurately fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
(1) The Four Titles or Offices of Christ
1) Christ was called "King."
2) Christ was called "the Servant of the LORD."
3) Christ was called "Man or Son of Man."
4) Christ was called "God."
Thus Christ was King and at the same time a thoroughgoing servant. And He was clearly a man, but at the same time He is the wondrous Son of God.
(2) Characteristics of the Endings of the Four Gospels
1) The Gospel of Matthew ends with the Lord's resurrection. It announces that He has become our Messiah (Christ) and King (Lord).
2) The Gospel of Mark ends with the Lord's ascension. It announces that He who humbled Himself as a servant ascends to the position of glory and honor.
3) The Gospel of Luke ends with the promise of sending the Holy Spirit. It shows the promise of the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, Advocate, and Counselor, to people who are lost before God.
4) The Gospel of John ends with the promise of His own second coming by Christ, the Son of God.
