Part 2: The Main Content of Matthew
1. Title
The title of the Gospel of Matthew derives from the title of the Greek Bible, "According to Matthew." This uses the name of Matthew, the author of this book, as the title of the book. And because this book is one of the four Gospels, the word "gospel" is added, so that English Bibles use "The Gospel According To MATTHEW" and the Korean Revised Version uses "Matthew" as the title of this book.
2. The Author, Matthew
(1) Evidence That the Author Is "Matthew"
Unlike the epistles of the New Testament, the four Gospels do not state the author's own name within their content. In this respect the Gospel of Matthew is the same. Therefore the question of who the author is arises naturally. But from the early days of church history it was widely known that the Gospel of Matthew was the work of Matthew the tax collector, and it was acknowledged without dispute before the end of the second century. Writers of the time quoted the Gospel of Matthew more often than the other Gospels.
When Matthew was called by Jesus, Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 call him "Levi," whereas in Matthew 9:9 he is called "Matthew." At the same time, in the lists of the disciples in all the Gospels, Matthew is used, not Levi.
In conclusion, Matthew was not an especially prominent figure among the twelve disciples. Nor was there any rule that the author of a Synoptic Gospel had to be an apostle. Therefore, if Matthew did not actually write this Gospel, there is no necessary reason at all to attribute it to him.
Rather, the orderly arrangement and detail of the Gospel of Matthew are consistent with the characteristics of Matthew, who had the occupation of tax collector. His characteristic familiarity with calculating numbers also shows clearly in his frequent mention of money, his interest in large sums (Matthew 18:24, 25:15), and his statistics (Matthew 1:17). It should also be noted that in the dispute about taxes, which all the Synoptic Gospels record, Matthew alone used the more precise "nomisma (the provincial government coin)" instead of the usual "denarius." Therefore it is natural to think that this Gospel was written at least by a former tax collector.
(2) The Name of Matthew
The name "Matthew" means "gift of God." The places in the Bible where Matthew is mentioned are only the scene where he is called by Jesus (Matthew 9:9-, Mark 2:14-, Luke 5:27-) and the lists of the twelve disciples (Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, Acts 1:13).
Comparing the accounts of the three Gospels about his name, he is recorded as Matthew in the Gospel of Matthew and as "Levi" in the Gospels of Mark and Luke. He is also recorded as "the son of Alphaeus." This can be thought of in two ways. First, he may have had two names from the beginning. This is commonly seen among the Jews. Second, just as Simon came to be called "Peter," he may have come to be called "Matthew" as he followed the Lord. If the second case is right, then, considering the tradition of the Israelites of naming after their ancestors, Matthew is highly likely to have been from the tribe of Levi. His parents would have given him the name "Levi" hoping that Matthew would restore the former glory of the Levite clan and become a fine priest.
(3) Matthew, Who Left Everything
At the Lord's call, "Follow me," Matthew "left everything, rose, and followed" (Matthew 9:9, Mark 2:14, Luke 5:27-28). Like Abraham, who immediately obeyed God's command to offer his only son Isaac as a burnt offering, he followed the Lord immediately, without hesitation. Moreover, Matthew left everything before the Lord's call. What Matthew left was not "a part" but "everything." Although Matthew left everything, joy and deep emotion rather filled his heart. That was because he had met his Savior and had met One worthy to be served with all that he had.
3. Date of Writing
The expression "to this day" in Matthew 27:8 and 28:15 of the text means that considerable time had passed after each of the recorded events took place.
But at the same time these expressions also imply that the time of writing was before the city of Jerusalem fell to the Roman general Titus. Moreover, the fact that the so-called Olivet Discourse recorded in Matthew 24 and 25, that is, the words the Lord gave on the Mount of Olives, first about the destruction of Jerusalem and ultimately about the end times, is still recorded in the form of simple prophecy implies that this book was clearly before the fall of Jerusalem. Since the date of the fall of Jerusalem was AD 70, the date of writing of the Gospel of Matthew can be narrowed down roughly to between AD 60 and 70, shortly after the apostles began to write Gospels and epistles.
4. The Two Great Organizing Principles of Matthew
The Gospel of Matthew is a Gospel written under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. In the Gospel of Matthew there are the following two principles that are clearly distinguished from the other Gospels.
First, the "principle of thematic organization."
In recording the life of the Lord, Matthew did not write in chronological order. In the Gospel of Matthew he organized the work and sermons of Jesus by sub-themes related to the truth that is the theme he wished to emphasize, namely that "the Lord is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, and the Lord's gospel is the fulfillment of the Old Testament and a new teaching." This feature is found in part in the other Gospel writers as well, but it is a feature of editorial principle that stands out especially in Matthew.
Second, the "principle of five-part composition," in which the Gospel of Matthew is organized into five parts like the Pentateuch of Moses or the Psalms. To put it in more detail, Matthew first grouped the accounts and teachings of Jesus by theme according to the thematic principle mentioned above, and then organized them so that, apart from the introduction and conclusion, the body text as a whole forms five parts in total. And each part of the body text, made up of five parts, was made so that a narrative (Narrative) showing the work of Jesus and a discourse (Discourse) showing the teaching of Jesus are combined to form one part.
As with the other Gospels, Matthew did not arrange the deeds of Jesus in chronological order. Rather, he takes chronological arrangement as the basic framework but adopts a thematic method. Keeping this method of composition in mind, the development of its content may be summarized as follows.
(1) Introduction (The Birth of Jesus (the King) (Matthew 1:1-2:23)
Because it was said in the Old Testament that the Messiah would come as "the seed of Abraham (Genesis 12:3)" and as "a descendant of David," Matthew begins the Gospel of Matthew with a genealogy announcing that Jesus is the One who came as a descendant of Abraham and David. And he proceeds to prove that the miracle of the virgin birth of Jesus, and the events before and after His birth and the course of His upbringing, are the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy. That is, the whole process by which Jesus came to be born into this world testifies that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, that is, the King.
(2) Five-Part Composition (Matthew 3:1-26:5)
A. Part 1 _ The Self-Revelation of Jesus (the King) and the Beginning of His Proclamation (Matthew 3:1-7:29)
1) Narrative section (Matthew 3:1-4:25) _ The testimony of John the Baptist, baptism, the temptation by Satan, and the beginning of the public ministry.
2) Discourse section (Matthew 5:1-7:29) _ The Sermon on the Mount
B. Part 2 _ The Power of Jesus (the King) and the Appointment of the Disciples (Matthew 8:1-10:42)
1) Narrative section (Matthew 8:1-9:38) _ Various miracles
2) Discourse section (Matthew 10:1-42) _ The appointment of the twelve disciples and the words concerning the instructions for evangelism given to them
C. Part 3 _ The World's Rejection of Jesus (the King) (Matthew 11:1-13:53)
1) Narrative section (Matthew 11:1-12:50) _ The death of John the Baptist, the impenitence of the Jews, and the disputes with the Pharisees about the Sabbath and signs
2) Discourse section (Matthew 13:1-53) _ A collection of parables of the kingdom of heaven
D. Part 4 _ The Ministry of Jesus (the King) and Growing Rejection (Matthew 13:54-19:2)
1) Narrative section (Matthew 13:54-17:27) _ While Jesus carried on His ministry of the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, the Transfiguration, and the proclamation of the gospel, the rejection from His hometown people, the ruler Herod, and religious leaders such as the scribes and Pharisees, and the prophecy of the passion on the cross.
2) Discourse section (Matthew 18:1-19:2) _ Words in which He prescribes and proclaims those who will take part in His kingdom and the attitude of their lives.
E. Part 5 _ The Triumphal Entry and Passion of Jesus (the King) (Matthew 19:3-26:5)
1) Narrative section (Matthew 19:3-23:39) _ Events around the time of the entry into Jerusalem
2) Discourse section (Matthew 24:1-26:5) _ Prophecy of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and prophecy of the signs of the end of the world
(3) Conclusion _ The Redemptive Work of Jesus (the King) on the Cross, and His Resurrection and Ascension (Matthew 26:6-28:20)
This is the scene in which the Son, God the second Person of the Holy Trinity, the King of the whole universe, sheds the atoning blood for sin so that people may enter His kingdom, and suffers the passion of the cross at the hands of the powerful of this earth in order to become King of the new heavens and new earth in the future. But Jesus overcame death and rose again. Also, before ascending, the Lord gave the disciples the greatest command on earth: "Make disciples of all nations, baptize them, and teach them to keep the Lord's words."
5. Structure and Breakdown Table
The Gospel of Matthew is divided by precise geographical boundaries. Matthew 4:12 says that Jesus withdrew to Galilee. On the other hand, Matthew 19:1 says that Jesus left Galilee. So the Gospel of Matthew is divided broadly into three parts.
Matthew 1:1 through 4:11 corresponds to the introduction, and the place is the region of Judea. Matthew 4:12 through 18:35 corresponds to the main body, and the place is the region of Galilee. Finally, Matthew 19:1 through chapter 28 is the conclusion, again set in the region of Judea.
6. Characteristics of the Gospel of Matthew
(1) The Gospel of Matthew is a gospel for the Jews
1) The people Matthew had in mind first were Jews and Gentile converts influenced by Judaism.
Matthew sought to testify to those among them who did not believe in Jesus Christ as "the Messiah" that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, that is, the King of the Jews. Therefore the Gospel of Matthew testifies how all the prophecies of the Old Testament were fulfilled in Jesus Christ. There is a phrase that is repeated continually throughout: "All this took place to fulfill what the prophet said." Examples are the birth of Jesus and His flight to Egypt (Matthew 2:14-15), the slaughter of the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:16-18), Joseph's dwelling in Nazareth and Jesus' growing up there (Matthew 2:23), Jesus' speaking in parables (Matthew 13:34-35), the triumphal entry (Matthew 21:3-5), His being sold for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 27:9), and the casting of lots for His garments after Jesus was crucified (Matthew 27:35).
2) In history many Jews have come, by reading the Gospel of Matthew, to realize that the New Testament is not a heretical book (from the Jewish standpoint) but the fulfillment of the Old Testament. The Gospel of Matthew is a book written for the salvation and conversion of the Jews.
When the Canaanite woman (Syrophoenician) asked for Jesus' help, Jesus' first answer was, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 15:24)." When Jesus sent out the twelve for the mission of preaching the gospel, His command was, "Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter any town of the Samaritans, but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 10:5-6)."
3) Matthew wrote this Gospel to encourage those among the Jews who believed in Jesus Christ.
Although Jesus was the true Messiah, the terrible event occurred in which the Jews, the people of God, rejected Him and nailed Him to the cross. What would now happen to the Jews? In this respect Matthew had to give them words of encouragement. For even though the Jews are judged by rejecting Christ and disobeying God, God has not utterly cast them off. For the covenant and the kingdom of God promised in the Old Testament will surely be fulfilled when the time comes.
4) That Matthew had the Jews in mind also appears in his attitude toward the Law.
Jesus said that He had come not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, and said that not even the smallest part of the Law should be treated lightly. He says that no one should discard even the least of the Law or teach others so, and that unless the righteousness of believers surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, they will never enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:17-20). Jesus commands the fulfillment of the commandments (Matthew 23:23), and pays the Jewish temple tax (Matthew 17:24-27). The Jews' ordinary religious practices, fasting and bringing gifts to the altar, are recorded, and He also gives the admonition to pray that one's flight at the time of the final tribulation may not be on the Sabbath (Matthew 5:23, Matthew 6:16-18, Matthew 24:20). Jewish customs and terms are included without explanation (in the passage about washing hands in Matthew 15:2 the term "the tradition of the elders" is recorded, and in Matthew 23:5 phylacteries are recorded). The continuing theme of Jesus as the Son of David and the triumphal entry into Jerusalem focus attention on interest in Jesus as the One who fulfills the hope of the Jewish people.
5) There is no book like the Gospel of Matthew in which Jesus rebukes the formal and hypocritical life of the Jewish religious leaders.
From the very beginning the Gospel records the furious declaration of John the Baptist, who cried out to them, "You brood of vipers" (Matthew 3:7-12). Because special authority had been given to them, after saying, "The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat; therefore whatever they tell you, do and keep (Matthew 23:2)," He thoroughly and sternly rebukes and condemns the scribes and Pharisees, saying "Woe" to them. He warns the disciples to beware of the leaven, the evil teaching of the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 16:12). They are like the evil weeds destined to be uprooted (Matthew 15:13). They cannot discern the signs of the times (Matthew 16:3), and they are those who killed the prophets (Matthew 21:41). Among the 27 books of the New Testament, there is no chapter that condemns the scribes and Pharisees like Matthew 23. The condemnation of the scribes and Pharisees in Matthew is not a condemnation of their teaching but a condemnation of themselves. Jesus condemned them because they lived lives far removed from their own teaching and their faith and lives were thoroughly corrupt.
6) The greatest dispute within the church in the early days of the history of the gospel was the activity of the Jews in the church to build the church on their Law and traditions.
That is, they insisted on the Judaizing of the gospel (Acts 15:1-2, Galatians 2:14). But the Holy Spirit, working in the church, made all the clearer that the salvation of the Gentiles is obtained by believing in the grace of God, regardless of keeping the Law or circumcision, as the Jewish legalists claimed. Yet the Judaizers centered on Jerusalem, most of them, held to their claims until Jerusalem fell to Rome in AD 70 and they were scattered (Acts 21:20). Among them there were various groups that especially put forward Jewish nationalism and legalism and insisted on the Judaizing of Christianity, and a representative example was the Ebionites. The Ebionites made special account of the Gospel of Matthew and rejected or made light of the other Gospels, and this attitude of theirs also shows well that the character of the Gospel of Matthew is Jewish.
7) Another group Matthew had in mind were the Jewish Christians who had been living in strict observance of the Jewish Law that the Pharisees had taught, and who were confused by the gospel of Jesus Christ.
Although they had already accepted Jesus as the Messiah, they still had a legalistic tendency, being bound to the Law. Therefore they had conflict between legalism and the life principle of the gospel. Matthew wanted to show that the two are not contradictory, but that the gospel is the fulfillment of the Law.
8) Matthew also had in mind, at the opposite extreme, the antinomians, who thought that since they had believed in Christ and been freed from the Law, the Law was no longer necessary.
(2) Matthew by no means excluded the Gentiles.
Although the Gospel of Matthew is a Gospel written for the Jews, this Gospel does not exclude the Gentiles in any sense. When Jesus was born, the Gentile Magi came and worshiped Him (Matthew 2:1-12), and when Herod sent soldiers to Bethlehem to slaughter the infants, the place that became the refuge and shelter of Jesus was the Gentile land of Egypt (Matthew 2:13-18). Jesus healed the Canaanite woman's daughter in Tyre (Matthew 15:21-28), and, departing from His own way, preached the gospel to the Samaritan woman (John 4). Jesus said, "Many will come from the east and the west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 8:11)," and in the parable of the vineyard (Matthew 21:33-46) He said that another people would replace the original tenants, which clearly refers to the Gentiles. He also said that "this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations (Matthew 24:14)," and after His resurrection He said to the disciples, "Go and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18-20)."
(3) Another concern of Matthew is the church.
The Gospel of Matthew is in fact the only one of the Synoptic Gospels that uses the term "church." It is only the Gospel of Matthew that introduces the church after Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi (Matthew 16:13-23, Luke 8:27-33, Mark 9:18-22). In Matthew 16:18 it records the word about the rock that is the foundation of the church, and the giving of the keys of the kingdom of heaven together with the authority to bind and loose. In Matthew 18:17 as well it is recorded that similar authority is given to the church. But none of the other Gospel writers recorded Jesus speaking about the "church (ekklesia)." It is also only in the Gospel of Matthew that He said that when a brother sins against a brother, the matter is finally to be settled through the church. By the time Matthew wrote the Gospel, the church had already taken on a considerably developed form. That is, the church had in fact become a key element of Christian life. The Great Commission, to make disciples of all nations, baptize them, and teach them to keep what the Lord has commanded, is also, in the end, the future work of the church (Matthew 28:19).
(4) Matthew gave special weight to the events of the end of the world.
He has a particularly strong interest in the second coming of Jesus, the end of the world, and the last judgment. Matthew 24 has more words of Jesus about the end times than any of the other Gospels. Only the Gospel of Matthew has the parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14-30), the parable of the wise and foolish virgins (Matthew 25:1-13), and the parable of the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46). 1. Title
In the original Greek, the title of this book is "Kata Markon," that is, "According to Mark." The name of the writer was used for the title, and the word "gospel" (Greek, euangelion) was added later, so that the book came to be called "the Gospel of Mark."
2. The Writer, Mark
It is the unanimous opinion of the early church that the Gospel of Mark was written by John Mark. He was the son of Mary, who lived in Jerusalem, and since she had a house in Jerusalem, it was used as a meeting place for Christians. (Acts 1:13)
Mark had both a Jewish name, "John," and a Roman name, "Mark" (Latin). Like his uncle Barnabas, he was probably well-to-do. (Acts 4:37)
As external evidence, the apostle John is said to have stated that "Mark, the associate of Peter, wrote the Gospel of Mark," and Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and others also testify that it was written by Mark.
As internal evidence, the writer of the Gospel of Mark clearly knew Palestine, and especially the region of Jerusalem, well. The account of the upper room is more detailed than in the other Gospels, because the upper room was Mark's residence in his boyhood.
Parts of the Gospel of Mark have an Aramaic background (the language of Palestine at that time), and Jewish customs are presented as already understood; moreover, the vivid on-the-spot descriptions suggest close fellowship with an eyewitness. The outline of the Gospel of Mark closely resembles Peter's sermon in Acts 10. (Acts 10:34-43)
Mark is mentioned ten times in the New Testament by the Gentile (Latin) name "Mark," and three times by the compound name "John Mark" (Jewish plus Latin). Considering that Mark was first an attendant of Paul, then an attendant of his uncle Barnabas, and, according to reliable tradition, an attendant of Peter before Peter's death, he can be regarded as the most suitable person to write the Gospel of the perfect Servant.
Barnabas and Saul took Mark with them to Antioch. That they took Mark along on the first missionary journey seems to show that they trusted him. (Acts 13:5) But when they arrived at Perga, Mark lost courage and went back home. (Acts 13:13) On Paul's second missionary journey, Barnabas wanted to take Mark along, and in the end, because their opinions clashed, Barnabas parted from Paul and took Mark with him to Cyprus. (Acts 15:36-41)
Then, after nearly twenty years in which his name is not mentioned, Mark's name appears in the letter Paul sent from his Roman imprisonment to the church in Colossae.
"My fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you greetings, as does Mark the cousin of Barnabas. You have already received instructions about him: If he comes to you, welcome him. Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings. These are the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me." (Colossians 4:10-11)
Mark was still working for Christ and was recognized by Paul. In fact, Mark was about to make a journey to Asia Minor, where he had once turned back. So Paul tells the Colossians, to whom Mark's travel plans extended, to welcome him when he comes. And among the words Paul added, he declares that "these are the only ones who are working with me for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me."
"Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry." (2 Timothy 4:11)
Mark also appears in Paul's last letter, written shortly before his martyrdom. Even just before his final martyrdom, Paul wanted to keep Mark close. And Mark must have been loyal to Paul in Rome.
Peter also mentions Mark.
"And so does my son Mark." (1 Peter 5:13)
Mark was influenced by Peter. The beginning of the Gospel of Mark (Mark 1:1) starts from Peter's confession of faith (Matthew 16:16). And how is it that the Gospel of Mark is written in the order of the sermon Peter preached at the house of Cornelius (Acts 10:34-43)?
According to tradition, Mark carried out missionary work in Egypt, won many converts, and founded the first church in Alexandria. Mark failed at first. But from that place of failure he rose, looked to the Lord again, and was restored. And he became a martyr. That is, the former coward and failure rose into the ranks of the martyrs. There is a lesson here for us.
'Those whom God has used are not people who never failed once, but people who rose from the place of failure, looked to the Lord, and went forward. This reminds us that we need not ruin our present life because of past failures. And it reminds us that past failures are the thorn in my life that keeps me, who live in the present, humble....'
3. Date of Writing
The date of writing of the Gospel of Mark is not clear. Since Mark 13:2 foretells the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem, it seems certain that it was written before AD 70. However, the traditions of the early church are unclear as to whether this Gospel was written before Peter's martyrdom (about AD 68) or after it. Therefore, for the present we have no choice but to place the date of writing between AD 55 and 68. If, as most people now teach, the Gospel of Mark was the first of the four Gospels to be written, then Luke would have consulted the Gospel of Mark as well.
4. Outline
(1) The Servant's preparation (1:1-13)
(2) The Servant's early ministry in Galilee (1:14-3:12)
(3) The Servant's calling and training of disciples (3:13-8:38)
(4) The Servant's journey to Jerusalem (9:1-10:52)
(5) The Servant's ministry in Jerusalem (11:1-12:44)
(6) The Servant's Olivet Discourse (13:1-37)
(7) The Servant's suffering and death (14:1-15:47)
(8) The Servant's triumph (16:1-20)
5. Important Characteristics
(1) Purpose of the Writing
The Gospel of Mark is the shortest Gospel, and about 93 percent of its content appears in both Matthew and Luke, or at least in one of Matthew or Luke. In that case, in what respect does Mark make an independent contribution?
The purpose for which this book was written is to tell of "the deeds of Jesus." The deeds of Jesus prove what kind of person the Lord is, and the deeds of Jesus give authority to His teaching. That is, when we fix our eyes on Jesus' activity and supernatural ministry, assurance is given.
So Mark begins at once with the testimony of John the Baptist at the Jordan: "After me comes One more powerful than I." The Gospel of Mark is the Gospel of the deeds of Jesus.
(2) Omission of the Birth Narrative
The story of Jesus' birth is omitted. There is nothing at all corresponding to the introductions of the other three Gospels. Why are there no such records at all: the genealogy of David in Matthew, the visit of the wise men from the East, the announcement of the birth by the angels of heaven to the shepherds of Bethlehem and their worship in Luke, and the prologue on the preexistence of Jesus in John?
Mark's omitting these and entering abruptly into the ministry in Galilee is probably because that was the most suitable way to emphasize that Jesus is the "Servant."
(3) Omitted Teachings
Jesus' teachings too are thoroughly omitted and summarized. The Gospel of Mark has 16 chapters and the Gospel of Matthew has 28; in length, Matthew is twice the size of Mark. Yet if we exclude the genealogy, the infancy stories, and the chapters made up of teachings and parables, Mark's record of events is longer. This too is fitted to the fact that the "servant" puts action first.
(4) Omission of Rebukes of the Jewish Religious Leaders
The rebukes found in the other Gospels are absent. There is no rebuke of the unrepentant cities of Galilee (Matthew 11), no rebuke of the hypocritical scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 23; Luke 11), and no rebuke concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, which rejected Christ (Matthew 23; Luke 13). Likewise, it would have been fitting for a servant to leave out stern words such as "Woe to you" and accusations made in the manner of a king.
(5) The Characteristics of a Servant Are Emphasized
In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus' working with His hands is emphasized. When He healed Peter's mother-in-law, Jesus raised her up by "taking her by the hand" (Mark 1:31). At Bethsaida it is recorded that Jesus "took the blind man by the hand .... laid His hands on him .... and laid His hands on him again" (Mark 8:23-25). When He healed the one possessed by a demon, He "took him by the hand" (Mark 9:27) and raised him up, and when He healed a man who was deaf and mute, He "put His fingers into his ears" (Mark 7:33). And "many who heard were astonished, saying .... such mighty works done by His hands!" (Mark 6:2) they cried out. The Lord's hands are emphasized repeatedly in this way because the hand is the symbol of a servant.
In the Gospel of Mark the word "immediately" (Greek, euthys) is repeated often. This word occurs as many as 42 times. By comparison, it occurs 7 times in Matthew and once in Luke, so it is very frequent here. This is because a servant is characterized by being active and alert, never tiring, and getting work done quickly.

1. Title
The title in the original Greek is "Kata Loukan," that is, "According to Luke." This shows that the name of Luke, the writer of this book, was used as its title, and later the word "gospel" (Greek, euangelion) was added, so that it came to be called "the Gospel of Luke."
2. The Writer
Most of the records of the early church consistently state that the writer of this book, the third of the four Gospels, was Luke, "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14). There are four reasons.
First) The external evidence agrees with universally known Christian tradition.
Early figures of church history who support Luke as the author of the Gospel of Luke include Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, Hegesippus, Clement, and Tertullian.
Second) This book and the Acts of the Apostles were both writings of a single author sent to His Excellency Theophilus. (Luke 1:3, Acts 1:1)
Third) The expression "we" appears often in the Acts of the Apostles, which shows that the writer of Acts also took part in Paul's missionary journeys.
Luke joined Paul at Troas on Paul's second missionary journey and traveled with him (Acts 16:10-40), and on the third missionary journey too he went with Paul to Jerusalem (Acts 20:5-21). Also, when Paul wrote Colossians, Philemon, and 2 Timothy, he mentioned that Luke was with him (Colossians 4:14, 2 Timothy 4:11, Philemon 1:24).
Fourth) Medical terms appear abundantly in both this book and the Acts of the Apostles.
"and a woman there had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years. She was hunched over and could not stand up straight." (Luke 13:11) The word "healing" occurs more often in Luke than in Matthew and Mark combined.
He hid himself and made only Jesus stand out.
(1) A fellow worker of Paul
(Philemon 1:24) as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.
Luke was a precious fellow worker whom Paul could not do without. He was a fellow worker who stayed with Paul to the very moment of his martyrdom. (2 Timothy 4:9-11)
As his death in Rome drew near, many fellow workers who had supported him only with their lips left Paul. At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. (2 Timothy 4:16)
In times of disappointment and danger, the one who comforted Paul was his fellow worker Luke.
(2) A man who gave his talent to the Lord
Though as a physician he could have sought comfort in the world, he gave to the Lord the medical skill, the talent the Lord had given him, for the sake of the gospel.
(3) A man loved by believers

(4) A man faithful to the Lord and the gospel
(2 Timothy 4:10-11) because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.
3. Date of Writing
The date of writing of the Gospel of Luke, like that of the other Gospels, is not clear.
As seen in the statement in Acts 1:1, "In the first book, O Theophilus," this book was written before the Acts of the Apostles. And since the Acts of the Apostles is presumed to have been composed around the end of AD 63, the year Paul was imprisoned in Rome, the Gospel of Luke was clearly written at least before that.
Moreover, the Gospel of Mark, the first of the Gospels to be written, is dated between AD 58 and 68, and so Luke must be regarded as having been written after it. Therefore the date of writing is taken to be around AD 61-63, while the apostle Paul was staying in Rome.
4. Background and Motive for Writing
The Gospel of Luke is a Gospel that emphasizes Jesus' perfect humanity as the Son of Man and His being the Savior who redeems all peoples of the world from sin. This characteristic of Luke is closely related to the primary readers Luke had in mind. If Matthew had the Jews in mind as his primary readers and Mark the Romans, Luke has as his primary audience Gentile Christians with a Greek background within the Roman Empire. Theophilus, the recipient of this book, refers to a specific person, but at the same time he is also a figure who represents the situation of Christians of Gentile origin within the Roman Empire at that time.
When this book was written, it was an age in which Roman influence was absolute in politics and military affairs, and the influence of Hellenism was absolute in culture and thought. The people of the Greek world held a common ideal of the perfect human being in knowledge, appearance, morality, and so on. Luke, the author, who was himself a man of Greek background, discovered that Jesus fully realized this supreme Greek ideal, and he wished to present that to the people of the Greek world.
Presenting Jesus as the ideal human being starts from the fact that Jesus is God the Son. The reason Jesus came to this earth as the Son of Man was to pay in our place the price of the sin of human beings, who must die because of sin, and to save them. Jesus, as the only sinless and pure One, became the perfect Son of Man in the sense that He can make perfect and save human beings who must die because of sin. At the time Luke wrote this book, many false reports about the identity of Jesus, influenced by Greek culture in doctrine and thought, were circulating within Christianity. It was also a time when, as the gospel spread into the Gentile world, there was a need to give a clear answer as to what standing the Gentiles had in the kingdom of God. In this situation, Luke wrote this book to strengthen the faith of Gentile Christians in the Roman Empire who, like Theophilus, had encountered the gospel but needed to be assured once again of the certainty of Jesus as Savior.
Thus, in order to present effectively the certainty of Jesus as Savior to Gentile Christians within the Roman Empire as his primary audience, Luke displays the manner of a historian and closely ties the deeds of Jesus to the world history of that time, that is, the history of the Roman Empire. When describing the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, Luke makes clear that this event was related to the census decree issued by the Roman emperor Augustus (2:1-7), and in describing the appearance of John the Baptist, he names one by one the rulers of the Palestinian region of that time (3:1-2). By this Luke shows that the whole course of Jesus' birth and public ministry was a certain event that took place within the flow of actual history. By describing it in relation to actual history in this way and thereby bringing out the historicity of the gospel, he made what may be called the distinctive feature and contribution of the Gospel of Luke. In this context Luke is relatively faithful to chronological order, and he describes the deeds of Jesus most realistically and comprehensively among the four Gospels.
Meanwhile, compared with the other Gospels, the Gospel of Luke pays special attention to the concern Jesus showed for those who were socially marginalized at that time, such as women, children, the poor, and tax collectors and sinners. For this reason the Gospel of Luke is also called the gospel of the poor. This concern for the poor and marginalized seen in the Gospel of Luke, and the emphasis on His drawing near to them, rest on Luke's deep understanding of "the universality of God's salvation."
It shows that His work of salvation transcends all classes and statuses, and therefore even the boundaries of bloodline. In other words, it was Luke's intention to present the fact that He is the "Savior of all people," who grants salvation to anyone who receives Him, whether Jew or Samaritan or Gentile, man or woman, rich or poor.
Finally, we must not forget that this book is the first volume of a two-part work that continues into the Acts of the Apostles.
In the Gospel of Luke, along the line of continuity with the Acts of the Apostles, by first presenting who Jesus is and what He did, it shows how God's salvation came to have a basis for extending to all peoples, including the Gentiles.
5. Key Word
The key word of this book is "Son of Man." This is because Luke deals with the humanity of the Lord.
Gospel of Matthew (King): Jesus' words and sermons are well organized.
Gospel of Mark (Servant): It describes intensively and continuously what He did "again" and "immediately."
Gospel of Luke (Son of Man): It expresses Jesus' heart, thoughts, and state of feeling.
Jesus was indignant. He shed tears. He had pity. He had compassion. There are many descriptions of Jesus' heart, thoughts, and state of mind.

1. Title
The most important truth the Bible speaks of is the testimony to Jesus Christ. The Old Testament bore witness to the Christ who was to come, and the New Testament bore witness to the Christ who came to this earth as promised. In this way the whole Bible consistently bears witness to Jesus Christ, and among its books the Gospel of John bears witness to Jesus Christ and the gospel in the deepest and most detailed way. The title in the original Greek is "Kata Ioannen," that is, "According to John."
2. The Writer: The Apostle John
There is no direct statement that the apostle John is the writer, but the reasons for holding that the apostle John wrote it are these: the writer was a direct eyewitness of Jesus' deeds (John 1:14, John 19:35, John 21:24-25); whereas John's name appears often in the Synoptic Gospels, in the Gospel of John the names of other disciples appear often but John's name is missing; and it states that it is the record of the disciple whom Jesus loved (John 21:20, 24). Of the three disciples whom Jesus trusted, Peter appears distinct from the writer (John 1:41-42, John 13:6-8), and James was martyred early (Acts 12:2, around AD 44), so in the end John is the writer.
Among these three disciples John was the especially beloved disciple, who stayed close to Jesus and understood Him best.
John's father was Zebedee, a well-to-do fisherman, and his mother was Salome, who faithfully followed the Lord. John's occupation was fisherman, and his older brother was James (Matthew 4:21). The apostle John, the longest-lived of the twelve apostles, lived in Ephesus into old age and wrote the Revelation of John and the three letters of John (1, 2, 3 John). At first he was so hot-tempered that he was given the nickname Son of Thunder (Mark 3:17) (Luke 9:54-56). But as he walked with the Lord, John, who had been hasty and violent and full of ambition (Matthew 20:20-23), was changed through Christ into the apostle of love.
3. Date of Writing
It is thought to have been written between AD 70, when the writing of the Synoptic Gospels was completed, and AD 95, when John was exiled to the island of Patmos; but considering that there is no mention of Jerusalem's fall in AD 70 and that it was written before John's letters, which were written at the end of the first century, the date can be narrowed to between AD 80 and 90.
4. Background and Motive for Writing
Immediately after Pentecost, the church community and the Jewish community coexisted without any great problem, but as time passed the conflict between the two became sharply opposed. In particular, the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 became a decisive occasion that drove traditional Jews and the church community apart.
When Roman armed soldiers began to surround Jerusalem, the Jews gathered into Jerusalem, but the Christians, following the words of Jesus, left Jerusalem and fled. In the end, after Jerusalem fell to the Roman soldiers, feelings of accusation and hatred grew among the Jews that the Christians had fled cowardly, and the Sanhedrin, rebuilt with Rome's permission, took the extreme step in AD 90 of inserting into the synagogue prayers, to be recited, a curse reading: "May the Nazarene heretics perish in a moment. May they be erased from the book of life and not be mixed with the righteous."
In a situation of intensifying persecution, the apostle John had to assure Christians of Jewish origin, who were in a crisis of faith, that Jesus is the Son of God and that believing in Him is the same as believing in God, and to convince them that to accept the gospel of the New Testament, in which Jesus, the Son of God equal to the God who gave the Old Testament, fulfilled the contents of the Old Testament, is to believe in God. He also wrote this book so that the Gentiles of the Greek world too would believe that Jesus is the Son of God.
5. Purpose of Writing
"Who is Jesus?" is a truly important theme.
The apostle John directly refutes the Ebionites, who regarded Jesus merely as a prophet who had received power from God, and the teaching of Cerinthus, who taught that the divine Christ came upon Jesus, a splendid and wise man, at his baptism and left him on the night before the passion.
To the questions "Is Jesus only a man? Is the historical Jesus a being separate from the divine Christ? Or are they the same being? What is Jesus' relationship to God?" the apostle John gives a clear and concise explanation.
(John 20:30-31) Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.
Although there are countless facts that John knew about what Jesus did, he did not record them one by one; because he wrote this book to prove the fact that Jesus is the Son of God and to urge the decision to believe in Jesus Christ, he selectively recorded only the events suited to the purpose of the writing.
(John 21:25)There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.
Therefore the message keeps coming that if one believes there is salvation, but if one does not believe there is destruction. Therefore the Gospel of John is not only a record about the deity of Jesus but also urges a decision of faith.

The Structure of the Gospel of John
To explain a theme, the Gospel of John is structured in the form of first showing, as an introductory portion, an event and the miracles and signs within it, and then bearing witness to Jesus' teaching.
1. Introduction - The Word Became Flesh (John 1:1-18)
In John chapter 1 four titles for Jesus appear.
(John 1:1) In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
(John 1:4) In Him was life, and that life was the light of men.
(John 1:9) The true Light who gives light to every man was coming into the world.
(John 1:18) No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.
① In relation to God, Jesus is the Word and the only Son. He is the Word of God and the only Son of God.
② In relation to people, Jesus is the light and the life.
These expressions are needed because they are explained in words that are easy for humans to understand and take in. If "the Word" or "the only Son" is interpreted by itself, misunderstanding can arise.
If thought of only as a word, it is impersonal, and if only as an only son, it is like a created being. So "the Word" and "the only Son" work in a mutually complementary way. Since "the Word" alone seems impersonal, it is supplemented by "the only Son," and since "the only Son" alone seems like a created being, it is supplemented by the term "the Word." So if, in describing Jesus, one thinks deeply only about "the Word" or only about "the only Son," one falls into error. Therefore both must be understood. In the same way, life and light too must be used in a mutually complementary way.
The same is true of grace and truth. In relation to Jesus' ministry it is grace, and in relation to the word it is truth. Ministry and word complement each other and must be mutually complementary.
2. The Public Ministry to the Jews (John 1:19-12:50)
John records seven signs by which we can know that Jesus is the Son of God.
(John 3:2) He came to Jesus at night and said, “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.”
That is, John recorded the miracles repeatedly in order to awaken us to the fact that Jesus is the Son of God. These miracles also explain the change, as children of God, that comes to those who receive Jesus.
It was only through the first miracle that the disciples came to believe.
(John 2:11) Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.
The expression "believed in Jesus" is not repeated until the eighth sign appears (John 20:31). After the resurrection there is the miracle of the catch of 153 fish (John 21). This shows abundant success out of anxiety and frustration.

1. Title
The title of Acts is "Acts of the Apostles," named "Acts" following the title of the Greek original, "Praxeis Apostolon (Acts of the Apostles)."
2. The Writer: Luke
Like the Gospel of Luke, which was originally one book with this one, the fact that Luke the physician is the writer of this book has been widely known since the early church. In fact, this book uses technical terms reflecting Luke's profession as a physician, and distinctive stylistic features that can also be seen in the Gospel of Luke.
Meanwhile, in writing this book Luke generally uses the third-person pronoun "they" in the first half, and then uses the first-person pronoun "we" in the second half. This shows that many of the events recorded in this book were experienced by the writer Luke himself.
The Roman historian Eusebius left this record: "Luke was a native of Antioch, and his profession was physician. He mainly assisted Paul's ministry, and left two inspired books, the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles."
3. Date of Writing
The date of writing of this book cannot be known exactly. However, it seems it should be taken as around AD 61-63, the period of Paul's first imprisonment in Rome. This is because this book has no mention at all of the great fire of Rome, Nero's great persecution of Christians (AD 64), or the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70). And if this book had been written after AD 64, then since the attitude of the Romans toward Christians from about that time was very hostile, there would surely be some hint of it, yet no sign of such a thing is seen in this book.
4. Background and Motive for Writing
The direct purpose for which Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles was for Theophilus.
The purpose of writing the Gospel of Luke was to teach Theophilus more certainly about what he already knew concerning Jesus Christ (Luke 1:4). The reason Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles and sent it to Theophilus was the hope that, by Theophilus' coming to know through the apostles the birth of the church and the process by which the church spread, his faith would become still firmer. In particular, he wanted to make known that the apostles stood at the center of causing the church to be born and causing the church to spread.
In the Gospel of Luke he presented Jesus Christ's public ministry, His suffering on the cross, His resurrection, and all His deeds and ministry up to His ascension. And he emphasized that Jesus is the Savior of all classes, and especially of all peoples of the world, including the Gentiles. By this he intended to make Gentile Christians within the Roman Empire stand firm in faith and at the same time to bring unbelieving Gentiles to believe.
The Acts of the Apostles, the second volume of Luke's two-part work, in continuity with the Gospel of Luke, records the history of the early church over about thirty years from Jesus' ascension. Thus it shows the process by which the gospel of Jesus Christ's universal salvation, which was presented in the Gospel of Luke, was proclaimed to Jerusalem and Judea and Samaria and the ends of the earth (1:8).
The Acts of the Apostles records the founding and expansion of the church, which was accomplished through the remaining disciples of Jesus, especially the apostles, after the coming of the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the promise of the coming of the Holy Spirit and the great commission of world mission that Jesus gave when, having finished the redemption on the cross, He rose and ascended.
5. Theme
The most important significance of the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ is precisely the accomplishment of the work of redemption. In order for the work of redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ to be applied to human beings and take effect, the Holy Spirit had to come.
Of course the Holy Spirit was active in Old Testament times, and the Holy Spirit was also active during Jesus' earthly ministry. But it was only from the event of the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost onward that the Holy Spirit was given to all who believe, transcending race and region, without discrimination and without limit. The work of redeeming humanity is a cooperative work of the triune God, but if we distinguish more strictly, the planning of the work of redemption is by God the Father, its execution is by Jesus, God the Son, and applying the accomplished work of redemption to each saint is the leading work of God the Holy Spirit.
Viewing each era of redemptive history, in the Old Testament God the Father, and from Jesus' public ministry until His ascension God the Son, was the leader of the work of redemption; but in the New Testament era after the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, God the Holy Spirit becomes the leader of the work of redemption.
God's ultimate purpose is the completion of the kingdom of God. In accordance with this purpose Jesus came, brought the kingdom of God, and accomplished the work of redemption. That being so, what remains now is the work of "proclaiming" the gospel of accomplished salvation to the ends of the earth until the completion of the kingdom of God comes with Jesus' second coming.
The Acts of the Apostles shows that this work will be accomplished "by the Holy Spirit" and "through the Church." That is why the Acts of the Apostles is also called the "Acts of the Holy Spirit" or the "Acts of the Church." This is because, although the apostles proclaimed the gospel of the Lord, it is God the Holy Spirit who governed and ordered all this and established the church.
It is by no means a coincidence that the Acts of the Apostles begins and ends with accounts of the proclamation of the kingdom of God (1:3, 28:31). The transitional period between the ascension and the second coming of Jesus Christ is none other than the period of world mission, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God to the ends of the earth.

1. Title
The title in the Greek original is "Pros Romaious (To the Romans)." The English Bible too names it "Romans," reflecting the name of the recipients, but the Korean Revised Version names it "the Book of Romans," reflecting the name of the place of the recipients.
2. The Writer: The Apostle Paul
Around AD 57-60, as the apostle Paul was on his way to Jerusalem having nearly finished his third missionary journey, he probably wrote it in the region of Corinth or Philippi (Romans 15:24-29).
3. Background and Motive for Writing
The apostle Paul had wanted to go to Rome several times before writing Romans. He thought that if the gospel were brought to Rome, the center of the world at that time, it would spread across the world at a faster pace. But as circumstances did not allow it, he first wrote the letter to the Romans and sent it to the church in Rome by the hand of our sister Phoebe.
(Romans 1:13) I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, how often I planned to come to you (but have been prevented from visiting until now), in order that I might have a harvest among you, just as I have had among the other Gentiles.
(Romans 15:22) That is why I have often been hindered from coming to you.
(Romans 16:1) I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea.
The Christians of the early church did not have the 66 books of the Bible as we do today. The New Testament had not yet been written, and even the Old Testament was not common. Not only was the Bible not yet complete, but the apostles had not yet visited them, so the believers of the church in Rome were keeping their faith by fellowshipping with one another mainly on what they had each come to understand. Therefore the work of spreading the gospel could not help being weak. Also, false teachings could enter the church and harm it. So the apostle Paul wrote Romans to make firm what they believed, to make their faith complete, and to enable them to proclaim the gospel with power.
(Romans 1:11) For I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you,
4. Theme: The core principle of the gospel summed up as "justification by faith," and the practical application of the righteousness obtained by faith.
1) How can a sinner be justified before God?
Socrates is said to have told his disciple Plato, "Human beings have sinned, and the god would be able to forgive that sin, but I do not know how he can forgive it." The answer to this can be found in Romans. → It answers, "in the gospel the righteousness of God is revealed" (Romans 1:17).
The answer to Job's question, "How can a man be righteous before God?" (Job 9:2), is in Romans. → One is made righteous by believing the gospel that Christ accomplished.
After being saved, how can one overcome sin in daily life and live righteously? → It answers, "The righteous (united with the gospel) will live by faith" (Romans 1:17).
The theme of Romans is the gospel. By believing the gospel one is made righteous, by living for the gospel one is freed from sin, and by suffering for the gospel one obtains eternal glory.
2) The righteous will live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4) _ quoted three times in the New Testament
① Romans (Romans 1:17) - emphasizes "the righteous" → by emphasizing sinners thoroughly, it stresses that the only way to become righteous is the gospel alone.
② Galatians (Galatians 3:11) - emphasizes "will live" → of the law, "the one who does (the commandments) will live"; of grace, "the one who believes (the gospel) will live."
③ Hebrews (Hebrews 10:38) - emphasizes "by faith" → it stresses the power and nature of faith. It means that the righteous overcome suffering by faith.
The Structure of Romans
1. In two parts
Chapters 1-11 _ Evangelistic meetings (a seven-day Bible lecture series)
Chapters 12-16 _ Words for daily life (Wednesday and Sunday messages)
2. In three parts
Chapters 1-8 _ The doctrinal part (being made righteous by believing the gospel): salvation (salvation of the soul (justification), salvation of life (sanctification), salvation of the body (glorification))
Chapters 9-11 _ The dispensational part (God's plan for proclaiming the gospel to the whole world): Israel → the church → Israel
Chapters 12-16 _ The practical part (the actual life of a saved person, God - neighbor - church): labor for the gospel and the glory to be obtained afterward
3. In four parts
Chapters 1-5 _ Evangelistic meetings, days 1 to 6 (the gospel)
Chapters 6-8 _ Evangelistic meetings, day 7 (life after salvation)
Chapters 9-11 _ Division of the ages (Israel and the church)
Chapters 12-16 _ How should saved people live?
4. In five parts _ (From the viewpoint of the gospel → being made righteous by believing the gospel, being freed from sin by living for the gospel, and the labor done for the gospel being glory)
Part 1 (chapters 1-5) _ How is a sinner made righteous? → By believing the gospel (salvation of the soul)
Part 2 (chapters 6-8) _ How does a person who has been made righteous overcome sin in daily life? → By living for the gospel (salvation of life)
Part 3 (chapters 9-11) _ The failure and the future of the role of Israel, which was entrusted with the word (gospel) to be proclaimed to the whole world
Part 4 (chapters 12-15) _ How must the church (Christians), entrusted with the gospel, live in order to proclaim the gospel to the whole world?
Part 5 (chapter 16) _ Role models (co-workers) who labored for the gospel; these are heroes of faith who will shine forever.
Questions in Romans
1. The part of Romans 9-11 where Israel is inserted
In Romans it would seem natural to go straight from chapter 8 to chapter 12, so why was the content of "chapters 9 to 11 (Israel)" put in the middle? Two reasons can be considered: the viewpoint of the proclamation of the gospel, and preventing the error of replacement theology.
1) From the viewpoint of the proclamation of the gospel _ refer to the structure of Romans seen as five parts
① The most important of the reasons God chose the Jews is that He entrusted the word of God to them.
(Romans 3:1) What, then, is the advantage of being a Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?
Just as a farmer first prepares a seedbed before transplanting rice seedlings in a wide paddy, God first entrusted to the Jews the word that was to be proclaimed to the whole world. As promised in the Old Testament, Christ came and completed the work of salvation, and that word, planned so that the gospel would be proclaimed from Israel to the whole world, was first entrusted to the people of Israel. That was the greatest privilege entrusted to the Jews.
But the Jews did not make good use of this tremendous privilege. If the people of Israel had believed and obeyed the word of God, received Christ, and been saved, the gospel would have been proclaimed through them to the Gentiles all the more actively.
But the Jews disbelieved the word of God and rejected Jesus Christ and the gospel. When they, who had been entrusted with the word, rejected the word, God took the word (the gospel) that He had entrusted to the Jews and handed it over to the church. The apostles of the early church were all Jews, and the 120 who received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost were all Jews too. But the gospel was not entrusted only to the Jews. After the apostolic age many Gentiles were saved and came into the church. The church was formed of people who had been born again from among Jews and Gentiles, and the word was entrusted to the church.
Now the word is entrusted not to the Jews but to born-again saints. Saved Christians are those who have been entrusted with the word of God. They have the responsibility to deliver the word to people so that they may be saved. This is the command the Lord gave to all Christians, and it is the greatest mission and privilege on earth.

A priest solves the problem of sin that separates God and the people, and serves as a bridge that joins God and people in reconciliation. But Israel failed in that priestly role, and God entrusted that role to saved Christians (the church).
Christians are priests of the gospel who connect God and people by proclaiming the gospel. If there were no Christians in the world, the bridge to God would be cut off forever and hell would be opened. If the church is raptured, the Gentiles will no longer have a chance to be saved. The most needed and precious people in this world are the priests of the gospel. The most important mission of the church is proclaiming the gospel, and since the church exists for this, it must do its utmost in proclaiming the gospel.
2) It shows the error of replacement theology
① What is replacement theology? (substitution theology, displacement theology, Replacement Theology)
It is the claim that God has abandoned the Jews forever and that the blessings promised to Israel have been replaced by the church. It says that the Jews are no longer God's chosen people and that God has no specific plan for the people of Israel in the future. Because the church replaces Israel, it claims that many of the promises given to Israel in the Bible were fulfilled in the church, not in Israel.
Accordingly, prophecies concerning blessing and restoration for Israel are interpreted spiritually or as metaphors, and are replaced by promises of blessing that God made for the church. Because it does not take the Israel of the Bible literally, it does not acknowledge that Israel is restored as the word of the Bible says, does not know that the restoration of Israel is a sign of the end times, and does not know that during the seven-year tribulation all the Jews will return to their land and 144,000 will be saved. Naturally it does not acknowledge the millennial kingdom formed around Israel either. Therefore it cannot grasp the outline of the end times. Because it does not regard the church and Israel as completely different concepts, it cannot discern the times, and cannot make distinctions between ages.
② God has not abandoned Israel. (Romans 9-11)
(Romans 11:1) I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin.
After being driven out of their own land, they returned to their land after 1,900 years and re-established a nation. And as God promised, after the full number of the Gentiles has come in, He will surely grant Israel an opportunity for salvation. → 144,000
(Romans 11:25-27) I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob. And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.”

1. Title
The title of this book is "1 Corinthians," reflecting both its destination and the order of the letters. The Greek text too carries the title "Pros Korinthious A," that is, a letter sent to the church in Corinth, and, among them, the first letter.
2. The Writer and Date of Writing
That the writer of this book is Paul has been clearly proven by the internal evidence that the writer himself identifies himself as Paul in the contents of this book, as in 1:1 and 16:21, and by the external evidence that various documents of the early church period consistently state Paul as the writer of this book.
Meanwhile, the date of writing of this book can be narrowed down comparatively precisely to around the spring of AD 55. Paul began his third missionary journey in AD 53, toured regions such as Galatia and Macedonia, and stayed and ministered for a long time in Ephesus. It was during this very period that various problems arose within the church in Corinth. So Paul even sent Timothy hurriedly to the church in Corinth (1 Corinthians 4:17), and finally came to write this book. In 16:6-8 of this book Paul says that he will spend the Pentecost that was now not far off and then go to the church in Corinth and spend the winter together with them. Meanwhile, the period Paul stayed in Ephesus during the third missionary journey was roughly two and a half years or more. Therefore it can be concluded that the time when Paul wrote this book was the spring of AD 55.
