4. Motive and Background of Writing
Although the Corinthians readily accepted the Christian gospel, they did not fully rid themselves of the negative influences of Corinthian culture, such as religious syncretism, sexual immorality, lack of self-control, and frivolity. So when the apostle Paul left the church in Corinth to look for a new mission field, the saints in Corinth soon got caught up in a whirlpool of various errors and sins.
As a result, factions formed within the church and they kept engaging in division; even when a very serious sexual sin was committed they left it alone; they even brought lawsuits against one another; and there even arose the error of conducting the Lord's Supper without self-control. Moreover, the problem of how saints enveloped in the pervasive idol culture should respond appropriately to it came to the fore as a bigger problem than in other cities.
So Paul, who had been hearing directly and indirectly about the problems of the church in Corinth, around AD 55, roughly three to four years after leaving the church in Corinth, while sending workers such as Timothy hurriedly from Ephesus to the church in Corinth, also sent an apostolic letter, and wrote this book to urge the correction of the errors of the church in Corinth.
5. The Themes of 1 Corinthians
In short, 1 Corinthians can be called an epistle that, centering on the concrete problems that arose in the living situation of the church in Corinth and its saints at the time of the early church, shows several aspects of the right form that saints and the church should have in a corrupt secular society, and in the end presents the principles of life that saints should have: love, purity, humility, self-control, and an attitude of sacrifice.
① The church must maintain unity and oneness.
② The church must aim at absolute ethics.
③ The body of a Christian is a temple.
④ The value of marriage and the various matters related to it must be rightly understood.
⑤ There is diversity and unity in spiritual gifts.
⑥ The greatest gift is love, and Christians must do everything in love.
⑦ The church must conduct its public worship reverently so that it may be glory to God.
⑧ The resurrection is the core of the Christian's faith and the ground of hope.
⑨ Christians must maintain close fellowship centered on the church.
6. Special Features of 1 Corinthians
① This book is classified as a doctrinal epistle, but centering on each concrete current issue encountered in actual life of faith, it gathers and organizes the major principles of faith related to it. And by developing its arguments in the manner of presenting solutions to those problems, it has the characteristic of showing how the principles of faith are concretely applied in the setting of life.
② Whereas most epistles were written for warm comfort and encouragement to believers of the early churches in various places facing various crises, or for apostolic declarations of major doctrines, this book and 2 Corinthians were written on the whole from the motive of strictly rebuking the problems of the church in Corinth, which had committed errors, and urging its urgent renewal.
③ Among the doctrines of the New Testament, this book speaks the truth about church doctrines such as church organization, the role of spiritual gifts, and the resurrection, and at the same time gives detailed guidelines on marriage, food offered to idols, Christian freedom, and guidelines concerning the collection.
④ It deals with very many themes: division in the church, worldly wisdom and God's wisdom, the person of the flesh and the person belonging to God, sexual immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, the question of apostleship, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, and so on; but each is treated separately, so it is very easy to understand.
⑤ It has the richest indirect material about the situation at the time of the early church.
⑥ The most detailed and practical explanation of spiritual gifts in the whole Bible appears here.
⑦ It contains 1 Corinthians 13, in which the essence of love and exhortation are expressed in a beautiful poetic style, which is regarded as one of the most famous golden chapters in the Bible and is called the "love chapter."
⑧ This book can be called the most literary of Paul's epistles. Here Paul, using concise and logical yet strong and direct vocabulary on serious current issues of deep spiritual truth, and also through satire, appeal, and so on, conveys it persuasively with the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.
7. The City of Corinth and the Church in Corinth
Even before the time of Alexander the Great (356-323 BC), Corinth was one of the three great cities of Greece along with Athens and Sparta. Especially in the Roman period, for the geopolitical reason of being a key point of Mediterranean sea traffic, it prospered more than any other Greek city and became the fourth great city in the whole Roman Empire, after Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch.
In Corinth, so important in mission strategy, Paul stayed one year and six months during his second missionary journey (AD 49-52), preached the gospel in the region of Corinth, and established a church; and because of the various problems and questions within the church, around AD 55 he wrote and sent the two letters included in the Bible.
For a three-dimensional understanding of the accounts related to the church in Corinth, which form an important part of the New Testament and of the history of the early church period, the historical and cultural background of the city of Corinth and the church in Corinth is outlined as follows.
A. The City of Corinth
After the city of Corinth was rebuilt in 44 BC, as the city developed rapidly, many peoples from various regions around the Mediterranean, not only Romans but also Greek merchants, Jews, Egyptians, and Syrians, flocked here. So around the first century AD, Corinth developed into the fourth largest city of the Roman Empire, with a population of about 600,000.
At the time of the early church, the city of Corinth, a city hastily built by the Roman Empire after a break in history of about a century, was a newly risen metropolis chiefly in the economic sense. In short, Corinth was a newly risen port city, a multiethnic and multicultural society with abundance and diversity.
The cultural characteristics of this city of Corinth include a worship of money that prized material wealth above all else rather than political dignity and refined culture; an individualism that put one's own honor and disgrace before honor and tradition; a religious syncretism that accepted all the idol worship of the Mediterranean region; and an extremely corrupt sexual culture.
To give a short example, Corinth had at least twelve temples serving various Greek and Roman gods, and in the temple of Aphrodite located on the mountain of Corinth, about a thousand priestesses lived and engaged in prostitution as one of the religious rites. Although they readily accepted the Christian gospel, because Corinth was a city of such a cultural climate, the church established there was soon easily contaminated again by secular culture.
B. The Church in Corinth
① Origin
The gospel of Christ was first proclaimed in Corinth around AD 50, during Paul's second missionary journey of AD 49-52. Paul, who had left Athens and arrived at Corinth, resolved to preach the gospel in this city, which was very important in mission strategy yet morally corrupt and full of idol worship; he met Aquila and Priscilla, a couple among the Jews who had been unable to live in Rome by the edict of the emperor Claudius (AD 41-54) and had come to Corinth, and bore witness to the gospel while working together with them in the trade of making tents. Timothy and Silas, who had been sent to Macedonia, also joined the gospel ministry in Corinth (Acts 18:1-3).
Paul's early ministry in Corinth was carried out centered on Jews and Greeks who had converted to Judaism, with Sabbath discourses in the Jewish synagogue; but because of the opposition of the Jews, he later moved the venue to the house of the Gentile convert "Titus Justus," and preached the gospel and baptized many local Corinthians, including the synagogue ruler Crispus. This became the decisive occasion for the church in Corinth to be established, and Paul established the church in Corinth through a total of eighteen months of ministry in Corinth thereafter (Acts 18:4-11, 1 Corinthians 1:14-16).
② Characteristics and Related History
The members of the church in Corinth, like the other early churches established elsewhere in the Roman Empire, were a mixture of Gentiles and Jews. But since the whole city of Corinth had a cosmopolitan character, Gentiles were markedly more numerous than Jews. So they did not know the Old Testament well. And from the fact that in the letter Paul sent to the church in Corinth he reminded them of their status when they were called, it can be seen that the members of the church in Corinth were mainly people of the poor and despised classes (1 Corinthians 1:26-29).
Meanwhile, the culture of Corinth was so frivolous and decadent that the saying "to live like a Corinthian" became a proverb pointing to the life of a shallow person who knows only money and indulges in momentary pleasure. Since human beings cannot help being influenced by their environment, it was very hard for the saints of the church in Corinth to maintain complete ethics of faith even after being saved.
Moreover, unlike the apostle Paul, the so-called false apostles, who preached another gospel for personal gain, actually defended and encouraged such license and errors in the church in Corinth. The serious crisis that arose as a result became the very motive for sending strict apostolic letters like 1 and 2 Corinthians to the church in Corinth.

1. Title
The Greek text too has the title "Pros Korinthious B," reflecting that it is the second letter sent to the church in Corinth.
2. The Writer and Date of Writing
The writer of 2 Corinthians is Paul (2 Corinthians 1:1, 10:1). This book is presumed to have been written at Philippi in Macedonia at the end of AD 55 or the beginning of AD 56, about six months after 1 Corinthians was written.
3. Motive and Background of Writing
After the apostle Paul's painful visit and the sending of the tearful letter, most of the saints in Corinth repented, but there still remained some who misinterpreted and distrusted Paul's apostleship (qualification) and rejected Paul's exhortation.
So, first, Paul wrote this book for the purpose of rebuking and turning back those saints who denied and misinterpreted his apostleship, by making clear that his apostleship came from the Lord and by revealing the heart and attitude of a sincere and faithful minister.
(2 Corinthians 2:9) My purpose in writing you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything.
(2 Corinthians 13:9-10) In fact, we rejoice when we are weak but you are strong, and our prayer is for your perfection. This is why I write these things while absent, so that when I am present I will not need to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord gave me for building you up, not for tearing you down.
Second, it was to firmly establish a right faith in the saints of Corinth. He wrote with the hope that the church would be built up all the more firmly by obeying the exhortations added to the letter.
4. Christ as Seen in 2 Corinthians
(1) Christ who appoints workers (2 Corinthians 1:1)
(2) Christ who comforts suffering saints (2 Corinthians 1:5)
(3) Christ who is the source of victory (2 Corinthians 2:14)
(4) Christ who is the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4)
(5) Christ who is the guarantee of the saints' resurrection (2 Corinthians 4:14)
(6) Christ who is the final judge (2 Corinthians 5:10)
(7) Christ who reconciles sinners and God (2 Corinthians 5:18)
(8) Christ who is our substitute (2 Corinthians 5:21)
(9) Christ who is the Lord of the saints (2 Corinthians 10:7)
(10) Christ who is the reality of truth (2 Corinthians 11:10)
(11) Christ who dwells within the saints (2 Corinthians 13:5)
5. Development of the Contents
If the whole contents of this book, one of the epistles, are divided on the basis of the basic structure of an epistle, it can be divided into three parts: introduction, main body, and conclusion.
1) Introduction (the opening, 2 Corinthians 1:1-11)
First is the greeting that is officially found at the beginning of Paul's epistles, made up of naming the recipients and the sender and a wish for grace and peace through the apostleship received from God (2 Corinthians 1:1-2). And as a kind of opening part before beginning the main body, whose main content is the defense of his apostleship, he testifies about God's comfort and help, with which God helps with mighty power and boundless grace even amid the tribulations and adversities that came ceaselessly during his missionary journeys, and praises God. This clearly assures the church in Corinth, which was in various crises, that God's comfort will come to it too (2 Corinthians 1:3-11).
2) Main Body (2 Corinthians 1:12-13:10)
The main body, which occupies most of 2 Corinthians, can again be divided broadly into three parts. An inserted account containing teaching on the relief offering for the saints in Jerusalem, who were then suffering great hardship, is located in the middle of the main body. With that content in the middle, the first half is a passive defense of Paul's own ministry, and the second half is Paul's active defense of his apostleship.
① Passive defense of Paul's own ministry (2 Corinthians 1:12-7:16)
  - An explanation of the reason the plan to visit Corinth was changed, and the motive for sending the tearful letter   - A passive defense of Paul's apostleship and the carrying out of his duties
First, 2 Corinthians 1:15 - 2:13 is an explanation in response to the words slandering Paul as an untrustworthy man because he reversed his plan to visit Corinth several times. Next, 2:14 - 6:10 is an explanation addressed to those who fundamentally distrust Paul's apostleship, listing one by one, as evidence, the certainty of his apostleship and the facts that the saints of the church in Corinth had actually witnessed and knew about his unchanging manner of carrying it out. Finally, 6:11 - 7:16 points out that one of the essentials of apostleship is reconciling God and the saints and the saints with one another, and so refutes the claim that those who are now dividing him from the saints of the church in Corinth are true apostles, and shows his own true apostleship in that, though so misunderstood, he endures and seeks reconciliation. Through this Paul also strongly presents the need for the church in Corinth and himself to be reconciled again in the Lord.
② A request to raise a relief offering for the church in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8:1-9:15)
  - Exhorting them to prepare the relief offering in advance and complete it before Paul arrives in Corinth   - Presenting the model of the relief offering shown by the saints of Macedonia
This section, located in the middle of the main body whose main content is the explanation of Paul's own apostleship, is on the whole a kind of inserted account. Changing the subject for a moment, it speaks of the relief offering for the saints in Jerusalem, who were suffering the double burden of famine and persecution at that time. In particular, this section records in detail not only the fundamental teaching on the necessity and benefit of the relief offering but also concrete practical measures for carrying it out. This middle account confirms that in the early church period, when the gospel was spreading explosively to every part of the world but had not yet put down firm roots in each region, exchange among the churches of each place was all the more urgent and close, and it shows what the true form of the church is.
③ Paul's active defense of his apostleship (2 Corinthians 10:1-13:10)
  - An active assertion and defense of Paul's apostolic authority   - Announcing the plan for a third visit to the church in Corinth
The first half of the main body above, though likewise a defense of apostleship, first explained passively concerning the misunderstandings of the saints in Corinth and appealed, in the posture of making a request, for recognition of Paul's own apostleship. By contrast, this second half now actively asserts his apostleship, warns that those who in the end maliciously distrust his apostleship will be severely disciplined, and strongly urges them to repent quickly and to accept his admonition, which has the legitimacy of an apostle and gives good instruction.
Thus 2 Corinthians 10:1 - 12:13 concretely presents the evidence that proves the legitimacy of Paul's own apostleship. And 2 Corinthians 12:14 - 13:10, on the basis of the established apostleship, concludes by warning that punishment will at last be inflicted on those who to the very end maliciously reject Paul, and again urges repentance.
5) Conclusion (2 Corinthians 13:11-13)
Paul, who had written the epistle in a serious tone to solve the problems caused by those who distrusted his apostleship, now, as he ends the letter, reminds them that for a saint with whom the God of love and peace is present there will always be ultimate victory. And he closes the letter with a final greeting, a prayer of blessing to the triune God based on his apostleship.
6. Paul's Activities Related to the Church in Corinth
From the apostle Paul's first visit to Corinth, preaching the gospel and establishing the church, until his last ministry, he made "three visits and sent four letters." Looking at the background and schedule in a timeline...
(1) First Visit to Corinth (AD 51)
During his second missionary journey between AD 49 and 52, Paul visited Corinth for the first time, stayed one year and six months, preached the gospel, and established the church in Corinth. (Acts 18:1-18)
(2) First Letter: An Apostolic Letter (AD 54)
(1 Corinthians 5:9) I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people.
This first letter was a letter sent before 1 Corinthians was sent. It is presumed to have been written while Paul, during his third missionary journey of about five years from AD 53 to 58, was staying more than two years and six months in Ephesus, his central place of ministry...
(2 Corinthians 1:15-16)... "I planned to come to you first, and from you to pass through to Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and then to be sent on by you to Judea."
In this letter the apostle Paul stated his first plan for a missionary journey: Ephesus → Corinth → Macedonia → Corinth → Jerusalem (Judea).
(3) Second Letter: 1 Corinthians (AD 55)
Paul heard from Chloe's people the news of what the church in Corinth was facing, and in order to resolve the disputes (problems) of the church in Corinth, he first sent Timothy to Corinth in his place.
(Acts 19:22, 1 Corinthians 4:17, 16:10-11)
Immediately after sending Timothy, the apostle Paul wrote and sent "1 Corinthians" to resolve the various problems of the church in Corinth. In this letter Paul stated his changed plan for a missionary journey: Ephesus → Macedonia → Corinth → Jerusalem (Judea). (1 Corinthians 16:5-9)
(4) Second Visit to Corinth (AD 55)
(2 Corinthians 2:1) So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.
Having heard from Timothy, who had returned from Corinth to Ephesus, the sad news that the situation of the church in Corinth had deteriorated sharply, Paul changed his plan not to visit Corinth for the time being, and urgently visited Corinth in person from Ephesus, but for a reason that is not known had to return again to Ephesus. This became the so-called "painful visit" or "visit of sorrow."
(5) Third Letter: The Tearful Letter (AD 55)
(2 Corinthians 2:4) For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.
Paul, who had to return to Ephesus without seeing the result of the complete repentance and reform of the saints in Corinth... wrote a sorrowful letter, truly called the "tearful letter," which has not been handed down today, and sent it to the church in Corinth by Titus.
(2 Corinthians 7:8) Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it, I now see that my letter caused you sorrow, but only for a short time.
(6) Fourth Letter: 2 Corinthians (AD 56)
After Paul's "painful visit" and the sending of the "tearful letter," most of the saints in Corinth repented, but he wrote this book to explain the problem of the false apostles and some deluded saints who still misinterpreted (criticized) Paul's apostleship and apostolic office, and also in the hope that the saints in Corinth... would, taking this as an occasion, obey all the more and become a church being built up completely before God.
(7) Third Visit to Corinth (AD 57)
(2 Corinthians 13:1) This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.”
Paul, as he had promised in 2 Corinthians, visited Corinth a third time after the problems of the church in Corinth had been completely resolved. (Acts 20:2-3)
Having spent the winter in Corinth, Paul... wanted to go straight to Jerusalem according to the plan for the missionary journey stated in 1 Corinthians, but because there was a plot of the Jews who wanted to harm him, he changed his plan for the missionary journey once again... and passing through Corinth → Philippi → Troas and so on, and through several regions from Miletus, he finally "returned to Jerusalem." (Acts 20:3-21:16)

1. Title
In the Greek original, the title, reflecting the name of the recipients, was named "Pros Galatas (To the Galatians)," or it is given as "the letter sent to the Galatians."
2. The Writer and Date of Writing
The view that the writer of this book is the apostle Paul is accepted without objection. (Galatians 1:1)
On his first missionary journey Paul arrived in the region of southern Galatia and established churches. (presumed to be around AD 47) Around AD 49 he made his second missionary journey, and at this time Paul visited the region of Galatia once more. The saints of Galatia had heard the gospel through Paul. But when Paul visited the region of Galatia the second time, he discovered that during the two or three years after he first evangelized there and left, false teachers who taught not the gospel but a false truth had infiltrated the churches of Galatia, and a deception was occurring that was making the saints depart from the place of the right gospel.
So after returning to Antioch, Paul, thinking of the situation of the churches in Galatia that he had seen, began to write a letter to the saints of the Galatian region as the Holy Spirit moved him. The time when Galatians was written is not known exactly and is roughly presumed to be around AD 50.
3. Background and Motive for Writing
(1) The Problem of the Churches in Galatia
The reason Paul wrote the letter called Galatians to the churches in Galatia was to have the saints of Galatia live without losing their first devotion.
The apostle Paul wrote the letter after, two or three years after pioneering the churches in Galatia and leaving that region, he received the news that the churches and saints of Galatia, who had first received the gospel, had lost their first devotion and were wavering. This is Galatians.
(Galatians 1:6-8) I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— which is not even a gospel. Evidently some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ. But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be under a curse!
(2) It Is to Bring the Saints of the Galatian Region Back from a False Truth to the Place of the True Gospel.
(Galatians 3:1-2) O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified. I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?
☞ A typical wrong teaching that the false teachers taught
Believing in Jesus is important, but we cannot lightly cast away the Jewish traditions we have believed in since our ancestors' time. They spread among the saints of the churches of the Galatian region the teaching that the tradition of circumcision in particular must not be abandoned.
The false teachers did not appear as people who completely denied the gospel; they said that believing in Jesus is important but that one must also be circumcised to be saved, and began to make [circumcision], one of the traditional rites of Judaism, a condition for salvation. That is, the legalists began to add circumcision as a condition of salvation.
Being circumcised in itself is not bad. The problem is, "Can it become a condition of salvation?" If one begins to make being circumcised a condition of salvation, where is the place left for Jesus Christ to stand? Even if it is not a total denial of the gospel, once we begin to add something else in the place of Christ, Christ is naturally pushed out of our sight.
(3) It Is to Proclaim the Life of a True Christian.
(Galatians 5:13, 16) For you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love. So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.
We did not do what God commanded us to "do," and we did what God commanded us "not to do." Therefore we are breakers of the law and beings who cannot escape God's punishment and chastisement. But God sent Jesus Christ to solve the problem of human sin, which morality could not solve.
(Galatians 5:18) But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
(Galatians 5:22-24)But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
(Romans 8:1-2)Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For in Christ Jesus the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death.
The false teachers not only distorted the gospel but began to slander and plot against Paul, who taught the gospel. They said that Paul was not a man sent by God and denied Paul's apostolic authority. So Paul proclaims once again that his apostleship was not given to him by human beings but that God called him.
(4) It Is to Make Clear the Difference between Judaism and the Gospel.
If morality were the whole of Christianity, Christianity would be no different at all from Judaism. This is because even through the law of Moses, everything that human beings should do and should not do was taught.
Paul writes Galatians with the question, "How are Judaism and the gospel different?" Galatians is precisely what was written to proclaim the essence of the gospel and the true truth of God's grace.
4. Classification of the Contents of Galatians
(1) Chapters 1 and 2: Defense of Apostleship
(Galatians 1:1-3) Paul, an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead— and all the brothers with me, To the churches of Galatia: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,
Paul tells how he himself was called as an apostle and how he preaches the true gospel of God.
The false teachers (legalists) who had infiltrated the region of Galatia taught the keeping of the law, such as circumcision, as a condition of salvation in addition to the gospel of grace that Paul had delivered. In that process, the apostleship of Paul, the evangelist, was probably ignored and belittled. It is natural that when the evangelist cannot be trusted, the message he delivers cannot be trusted either. So Paul tells that his right and authority as an apostle were given by God.
(2) Chapters 3 and 4: The Doctrinal Part
(Galatians 3:10-11) All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.” Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.”
(Galatians 4:9) But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and worthless principles? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?
The apostle Paul writes Galatians in order to teach once again that very gospel which he had first taught to the people living in the region of Galatia when he established the churches there long ago. Telling that we were originally in a state of slavery to the law, he explains, "But now you are those who have obtained freedom in Christ."
(3) Chapters 5 and 6: The Part on Ethical Life
(Galatians 5:1) It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery.
(Galatians 5:22-26) But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit. Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another.
He speaks about the essence of the free life obtained in Christ and the proper ethical life of a Christian.
☞ In this way the three parts are being taught to us in a highly logical sequence.
a. After introducing that the one who delivers the word is a trustworthy man of God sent by God,
b. he says that the gospel he had been preaching is truly the genuine gospel that God has permitted.
c. Afterward he tells how a person who has accepted this gospel should live.
Thus, through the whole of Galatians, Paul deals with the true freedom we have obtained because of Jesus Christ and what that life should be like.

1. Title
In the original Greek text the title reflects the name of the recipients and is given as "Pros Ephesious" (To the Ephesians), or as "The Letter Sent to the Ephesians."
2. Author and Date of Writing
This is the word that Paul sent to the believers in Ephesus while he was in his first Roman imprisonment (A.D. 61-63). Ephesians is called a prison epistle. Of Paul's fourteen epistles, those called prison epistles are Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon.
3. Occasion and Background
Occasion of Writing
	1.	To teach the neighboring churches of Asia Minor, beginning with the church in Ephesus, a series of theological and doctrinal lessons for instilling a right understanding of the church, namely the origin of the church, God's purpose in establishing the church, and the essential nature of the church.
	2.	To set forth the inevitable reason why all believers in the church, whether Jews or Gentiles, must be united and live in harmony.
	3.	To present concretely a series of practical lessons on unity and harmony among believers, on the family life of believers, on a holy life as God's holy people, and on arming oneself with faith for spiritual maturity.
☞ The churches of Asia at that time, beginning with the church in Ephesus, were made up of both Gentiles and Jews, and so were always in danger of division. Well aware of this, the apostle Paul wrote this epistle in order to teach the mystery of God, that in Christ Gentiles and Jews have become one body.
Unlike the other epistles, this book does not have a specific situation in mind. For example, Colossians, which may be called its sister epistle, was sent to help its recipients deal with a particular situation that threatened the Christian faith, and so it may be called an epistle of an apologetic character.
This book, however, was written not so much to solve problems of the church as to make known what the "church" is, and therefore it came to have the strongest theological character among Paul's epistles.
 ☛ Ephesians is an epistle that emphasizes "ecclesiology" in the broad sense and, in the narrow sense, "the unity and oneness of the church in Jesus Christ."
Background
Ephesus, founded in the eleventh century B.C., was a hub of transportation in Asia Minor where politics, commerce, and culture were united, and idolatry flourished there because it had the great temple of the goddess Artemis (Diana).
The apostle Paul stopped by briefly on his second missionary journey and testified to the gospel (Acts 18:19-21), and on his third missionary journey he visited again and stayed about three years, ministering with tears and devotion (Acts 19:1-41).
For this reason the apostle Paul could not help having an unusual concern for the church in Ephesus. This is evident in the fact that, on his return from the third missionary journey, he summoned the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and exhorted them (Acts 20:17-35), and in the fact that he later sent Timothy, the pastor whom he called his son, to guide the believers there (2 Timothy 4:5).
4. Characteristics of Ephesians
Ephesians cannot be said to be long among Paul's epistles, yet it is a marvelous epistle filled with majesty and richness.
It is called "the essence of Paul's thought," "the queen of the epistles," "the most spiritual book," "the great epic of Christian salvation and the church," and "the refined essence of Christianity and the most authoritative and most complete summary of the Christian faith." Ephesians summarizes the main themes of Paul's theology and has the strongest theological character in the New Testament.
The theme of Ephesians is the "church," and it contains the mystery of the church. More than any other book of the Bible, Ephesians is filled with images of "riches" and "fullness," so that simply reading it will fill one with richness and fullness.
The phrase "in Christ" appears more than thirty times in Ephesians. This is the most important expression.
Ephesians also teaches who we, the saved, are, how we become rich and filled, and also the grace and glory that are in Christ. Perhaps for this reason, in Ephesians the word "riches" is used 6 times, "grace" 12 times, "glory" 9 times, "fullness" 5 times, and "in Christ" or "in Him" about 30 times.
Ephesians is a book that teaches "the grace, glory, fullness, and riches that are in Christ."
Ephesians is the book of the Bible that teaches best what the "church" is.
The life of faith after salvation is not accomplished by one's own will and effort but is lived out in the life of the community within the church. Even if one has been saved, if one does not remain attached to the church, one cannot receive the guidance and teaching of the Holy Spirit. Therefore we must know what the church is.
The church is an exceedingly precious place, and the first and most important reason is that Jesus died for the church (Ephesians 5:25).
Because the church is the one whom Christ loves most, it is only natural that everyone who belongs to Christ should cherish the church. In this world there is nothing more lovely to the heart of God than His church.
Paul describes the church as God's inheritance (1:11), the body of Christ (1:23), His fullness (1:23), God's workmanship (2:10), one new man (2:15), God's household (2:19), the dwelling place of God (2:21-22), the bride of Christ (5:23-32), the members of Christ (5:30), and God's warriors fighting against Satan (6:11-18).
5. Structure of Ephesians
The first half, chapters 1-3, is doctrinal, and the second half, chapters 4-6, is practical.
Chapter 1
☞ It teaches what each of the three Persons of God (the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit) did for the birth of the church, and that through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, Christ became the head of the church and the church became the body of the Lord.
① The origin of the birth of the church is recorded. (1:3-14)
② Paul's prayer for the church is recorded. (1:15-19)
③ It teaches that Christ is the head of the church and that the church is the body of the Lord. (1:20-23)
☛ The church is the body of Jesus.
Chapter 2
① (2:1-10) records the former state of the members of the church before they were saved, how they were saved, what blessings come through salvation, and what kind of life they live after being saved.
 - A change in conduct is recorded. (2:1-10)
② (2:11-22) records the status of the Gentile believers in Ephesus before they were saved, how they came to be saved, and how their status changes after being saved. The church is portrayed as a building under construction, and being saved means becoming a part of the building under construction.
 - A change in status is recorded. (2:11-22)
☛ The church is a building under construction.
Chapter 3
① The church is a mystery revealed to the apostle Paul. That mystery is that, as the Gentiles come to understand the gospel, they become fellow heirs with Christ, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise of hope. (3:1-13)
② Paul's prayer for the church is written. (3:14-21)
☛ The church is a mystery.
Chapter 4
☞ It teaches what kind of life is fitting for us, who have been saved by God's marvelous grace and have become members of the church.
① To live as one in the community. (4:1-6)
② That the church be made one through pastors who have received special gifts. (4:7-16)
③ The believers of the church are new men in Christ. (4:17-24)
④ It teaches the new conduct of the new man: to live in truth, good words, forgiveness, and kindness. (4:25-32)
☛ The church is the new man.
Chapter 5
☞ It teaches that the saved must live imitating God.
① To walk in love founded on sacrifice and devotion. (5:1-3)
② To walk in holiness in the light. (5:3-14)
③ To walk wisely, being filled with the Holy Spirit. (5:15-21)
④ It teaches the standard for a right family as the result of being filled with the Holy Spirit. (5:22-33)
☛ The church is the bride of the Lord.
Chapter 6
☞ It teaches that the church is a battlefield of spiritual warfare with Satan, and how to win in that battle.
☛ The church is a spiritual battlefield.

1. Title
"Philippians" is a prison epistle that the apostle Paul sent to the "church in Philippi" during his first imprisonment in Rome (A.D. 61-63). In the original Greek it is "Pros Philippesious," that is, "To the Philippians." Accordingly, English Bibles take "To the Philippians" as the title, and the Korean Revised Version takes "Philippians" as the title.
2. Author and Date of Writing
As the text itself states in chapter 1, verse 1, this is a letter that "the apostle Paul" sent to the church (the saints) in Philippi. Among the claims of those who deny the orthodoxy of the New Testament, doubts about the author are generally raised (for example, that the expression for the office of overseer and the tone of chapter 3 do not sound like Paul), but that Paul is the author of this book is the testimony of the church fathers of the early church (Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian), and Ignatius, Clement of Rome, Polycarp, Irenaeus, Origen, and others likewise unanimously acknowledged this book as Paul's writing and frequently quoted it in their own works.
Moreover, since Paul himself states in this book that he is "in chains" (Philippians 1:12-13), we can see that, like the other prison epistles, Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon, this book too was written by Paul in prison. In particular,
① the "whole palace guard" (Philippians 1:13) and "the household of Caesar" (Philippians 4:22) refer to the palace guard and the household of Caesar in Rome;
② Paul is seen waiting for the court's verdict with the expectation that he will soon be released (Philippians 1:19);
③ and many of the brothers have become more bold in preaching the gospel because of his imprisonment (Philippians 1:12-14).
From the above, this book too is considered to have been written during Paul's first Roman imprisonment (A.D. 61-63), like the other prison epistles.
However, whereas Ephesians, Colossians, and Philemon were written in the first half of the first Roman imprisonment, Philippians appears to have been written in the latter half of the first imprisonment, judging from Epaphroditus's service, his illness, and his recovery (around A.D. 62-63).
3. Occasion and Background
Background
The city of Philippi was founded in 350 B.C. by Philip II of Macedonia (Philip II, 359-336 B.C.). Its original name was "Krenides," meaning "Little Well," but Philip enlarged and built up the city and called it "Philippi" after his own name. Later it was conquered by Rome, and in Paul's time it was a colonial town in the Roman province of Macedonia.
Occasion of Writing
The "church in Philippi" was the first church in the territory of Macedonia, established as a result of the repentance of Lydia, a seller of purple cloth whom the apostle Paul evangelized on his second missionary journey (A.D. 49-52), of the "fortune-telling girl" (Acts 16:13-18), and of the jailer of the Philippian prison (Acts 16:23-34). This church developed relatively soundly, so Paul had great joy because of this church (Philippians 1:1-5).
Paul wrote this book to thank the Philippians for not holding back material support for his work of evangelism (Philippians 4:15) and for caring for him while he was imprisoned, and to reassure the Philippians who were distressed and anxious over his imprisonment.
In particular, when they heard the news that Paul had been imprisoned in Rome, they collected an offering and sent it by Epaphroditus to help Paul (Philippians 2:25). When Paul met Epaphroditus in prison, he discovered several problems in the church in Philippi: that there was a tendency toward division of hearts among the Philippian believers (Philippians 2:1-4, 4:1-3), and that Judaizing legalists and antinomians were threatening the church (Philippians 3:1-3, 18-19). Paul wrote this book of Philippians with the aim of correcting these circumstances, together with expressing thanks to the Philippian believers and exhorting them in faith.
4. Characteristics of Philippians
The New Testament can be divided broadly into the four Gospels and the church epistles, and the books that occupy an important position among the church epistles are Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians. For a person saved through the redemption that is in Christ to become mature as a Christian, the themes of faith that he must know and share are the church, fellowship, and Christ who works within them.
① Ephesians is the book that tells well what the church is,
② Philippians is the book that tells well what the fellowship that takes place within the church is. And
③ Colossians is the epistle that tells well what kind of person Christ is, who forms the church and leads the fellowship.
Looking closely at the portion of the main contents of Philippians concerning fellowship:
Chapter 1: It says that fellowship is fellowship in the gospel, and that cooperating for the faith of the gospel is fellowship (Philippians 1:5, 7, 27).
Chapter 2: It makes clear that the fitting attitude of heart in fellowship is the same mind and a humble heart (Philippians 2:1-5).
Chapter 3: It says that fellowship is sharing in the sufferings of the Lord (Philippians 3:10).
Chapter 4: It makes clear that fellowship is cooperating, materially and spiritually, in the preaching of the gospel.
Furthermore, the theme that runs through the whole of Philippians is the apostle Paul's joy and gratitude toward the Philippian believers, and this message of joy appears repeatedly in every chapter.
[Philippians 1:18] What then is the issue? Just this: that in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice. Yes, and I will continue to rejoice,
[Philippians 2:17-18] But even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you. So you too should be glad and rejoice with me.
[Philippians 3:1] Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. It is no trouble for me to write the same things to you again, and it is a safeguard for you.
[Philippians 4:4-7] Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice! Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near. Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
The Meaning of Christ as Applied to the Christian Life
In Philippians, four aspects of Christ as applied to the Christian life appear through the chapters.
Chapter 1: Christ who indwells me (Philippians 1:21)
Chapter 2: Christ who is the model for my life (Philippians 2:5-8)
Chapter 3: Christ who is the goal of my life (Philippians 3:7-14)
Chapter 4: Christ who is the power of my life (Philippians 4:13)
5. Structure of Philippians
If Philippians is regarded as an ordinary letter and its contents are divided, it can be broadly divided into the following three parts.
(1) Introduction (Philippians 1:1-11)
① Greeting (1:1-2)
② Paul's thanksgiving and prayer (1:3-11)
(2) Main body (Philippians 1:12-Philippians 4:9)
1) Paul's imprisonment and its significance (1:12-30)
① The significance of Paul's imprisonment (1:12-18)
② Paul's expression of his view of life and death (1:19-26)
③ The believers' attitude of faith and the significance of suffering (1:27-30)
2) Exhortation and warning (2:1-4:9)
① Exhortation concerning the communal life of the church (2:1-30)
- Abandon strife and vanity and imitate the Lord (2:1-11)

1. Title
The title in the original Greek is "Pros Kolossaeis" (To the Colossians). The English Bibles likewise reflect the name of the recipients and call it "Colossians," whereas the Korean Revised Version, reflecting the name of the destination, named it after the city of Colossae.
2. Author and Date of Writing
It was written by Paul (Colossians 1:1-2, 4:18), and the fact that Luke and Aristarchus, who are described in this book as being together with him at the place of writing (Colossians 4:10, 14), were among those who went to Rome with Paul (Acts 27:1-2) indicates that this book was written in the Roman prison during his first imprisonment in Rome (around A.D. 62-63).
3. Occasion and Background
Occasion of Writing
While Paul was in the Roman prison, Epaphras, a man of Colossae, came to Rome and brought news about the teachings of syncretistic heretics who were threatening the church in Colossae, and so Paul wrote in order to refute the heresy that had entered the church in Colossae. To accomplish this purpose, Paul speaks with emphasis on the truth about Christ. Colossians takes as its theme setting the perfection of Christ against the emptiness of the philosophies and ideas that human beings have invented. It also speaks about the desirable life of the believer who is united with Christ.
 At this time Paul wrote this letter and sent it by Tychicus and Onesimus (Colossians 4:7-9). They also delivered Ephesians and Philemon (Ephesians 6:21).
Background
The city of Colossae was located at a strategic point on the east-west trade route leading from Asia Minor to Syria. Naturally, therefore, Colossae became a place of exchange between East and West, with abundant goods, and it was frequented by merchants and many travelers, and from early on all kinds of philosophical and religious ideas were mixed there. Paul pointed out that false philosophy, Jewish legalism, the worship of angels, asceticism, and the like are contrary to the Christian faith, and by emphasizing the deity and supremacy of Christ he bore witness to Christ, who is the center of all things, and wrote about the desirable life of the believer who is united with Christ.
1. Jewish Ritualism
This refers to the things that God gave in the Old Testament as shadows of Christ and of what would be fulfilled in Christ. Since Christ, who is the reality, came and brought it to completion, the shadowy things have been done away with. Nevertheless, the teaching that the shadowy things must still be kept had entered the church in Colossae (Colossians 2:11, 16-17).
2. False Philosophy
This refers to a philosophy that worshiped a higher thought mixed together out of Greek, Jewish, and Eastern religions. The early Gnostics, basing themselves on their own experiences and on "human tradition," put forward spiritual "knowledge" (Greek gnosis) and tempted the believers to depart from the truth. They claimed to be those who had grasped spiritual secrets, and they denied the full deity and lordship of Christ (Colossians 2:8, 18).
3. Asceticism
The false teachers taught that the desires of the flesh must be suppressed by imposing extremely strict regulations on the body. They sought to worship God by methods of their own invention, such as afflicting their own bodies, and by doing so they behaved as though they were pious and humble people (Colossians 2:21).
4. Angel Worship: Angel Worship Related to Gnosticism
It can be understood to mean not so much "worshiping angels" as "the worship of angels." The false teachers tried to imitate the worship of the angels, in the sense that they themselves took part in the worship that the angels offer to God. Those who followed angel worship thought that they could communicate directly with angels and that a mediator between God and human beings was not necessarily required (Colossians 2:18-19).
4. Characteristics of Colossians
Christ as He Appears in Colossians
The key to not being stained by heretical doctrine, and to changing and growing the life of a Christian, is to know Christ accurately. Heresy does not necessarily deny Christ. It tries to pull Him down from the position that He rightfully holds. Therefore we must know Christ. This is because what we believe will determine how we act. Therefore, to make certain what we believe is the most important thing of all. That is why Paul prayed that they would grow in the knowledge of God (Colossians 1:10, 2:2).
1) Christ the Savior (Colossians 1:13-14)
All people are under the rulers of darkness (Ephesians 6:12). The Lord came to destroy the ruler of that darkness, the devil (1 John 3:8, Psalms 68:21, 74:13). There is no one other than the Lord who can deliver from the power of darkness. Redemption is a word that emphasizes liberation, the freedom obtained because the price of sin has been paid. The forgiveness of sins emphasizes that our sins are wiped away, just as a debtor's debt is canceled. Redemption and the forgiveness of sins cannot be accomplished by anything other than the Lord.
2) Christ Who Is God (Colossians 1:15)
The Lord who saved us is none other than God Himself, and therefore our salvation is complete. He is the beginning (Colossians 1:18). The word "beginning" means that He is the foundation of all things, the start, and the ground of existence. Because the Lord is the beginning and the end, He knows everything about us (Revelation 1:8). Therefore eternal forgiveness of sins is possible and His judgment is fair. He also knows the way I should go and commands it. Even if someone says that he has saved us, we cannot believe it. But the ground for our assurance of the salvation we have obtained is the fact that Christ is God.
3) Christ the Creator (Colossians 1:16-17)
Because Christ is the Creator, He is fully able to save us, and we can trust Him. When depositing money in a bank, one must confirm whether that bank is capable. If it is confirmed to be a safe bank, one can entrust it.
"He is before all things" means that Christ existed before the foundation of the world. "In Him all things were created" means that Christ is the Creator of all things. "All things were created ... for Him" means that the purpose of the existence of created things is for Christ. "In Him all things hold together" means that all things are sustained and preserved through Him.
4) Christ the Head of the Church (Colossians 1:18)
The Lord is the head, the church is His body, and each individual is a member. The body upholds the head. The body is under the control of the head. The body must remain attached to the head. The body grows through the head.
5) Christ the Mystery of God (Colossians 1:26-27, 2:2-3)
The whole Bible speaks of Christ, the mystery of God. Throughout the Old Testament, things concerning Christ are recorded. Yet the Jews did not know it and rejected Him. Many things are contained within a mystery, but people often do not know it and simply pass it by and throw it away. A mystery is revealed when there is a will to find it out. Unless someone who knows a mystery teaches it, one does not know it. The mystery concerning Christ cannot be known except by the Holy Spirit. Because Christ is the mystery, God can be known through Christ.
6) Christ the Life of the Believers (Colossians 3:1-4)
He gave eternal life to us who were dead in sins and trespasses. Through the church He continually supplies life. By that life He puts to death the members that are on the earth, has us take off the old practices, and has us put on the new man. Apart from the Lord, life can neither be obtained nor sustained. Because the Lord is life, as long as we maintain life we must live in Him and for Him.
Colossians and Ephesians
Colossians is very similar to Ephesians. The relationship between the two is the same as the relationship between Galatians and Romans. Romans speaks of the truth of being justified by faith in the gospel. Galatians was given to correct and rectify the error of seeking to be justified by works of the law, which departs from the truth of being justified by faith. Therefore the distinctive feature of Colossians and Galatians is the correction of doctrinal deviation.
Of the 95 verses of Colossians, 78 have a remarkable similarity to Ephesians.
Ephesians speaks of the fact that "the church is the body of Christ." Christ is the head (Ephesians 1:22, 4:15, 5:23), and the church is His body (Ephesians 1:23, 4:16). Each believer is a member of the body of Christ (Ephesians 5:30), and they are members one of another as an organism (Ephesians 4:25). The early fault in the church in Philippi was that the members, the parts of the body, were scattered and unable to cooperate (Philippians 1:27, 2:3-4, 4:2).
Colossians was written to correct the early Gnostic teaching, that is, the mistaken thought that prevented people from holding fast to the head, and to proclaim Christ fully.
5. Structure of Colossians
Colossians chapters 1-2 are the doctrinal section, and chapters 3-4 are the practical section. Colossians 1:9 prays "that you may be filled with the knowledge of God's will," and Colossians 1:10-11 prays that they may walk in a manner worthy.
Colossians chapters 1-2 bear witness to the things that are the foundation of Christ as the head of the church. They testify that believers are members of the body of Christ who can fully possess the life and power of Christ. Colossians chapters 3-4 are concerned first of all with the practical matters.

1. Title
In the original Greek text the title of this book is "Pros Thessalonikeis Alpha," that is, "To the Thessalonians, First," naming the recipients of the epistle. Also, as is mentioned in (1 Thessalonians 1:1) and (1 Thessalonians 2:18), the author of this book is the apostle Paul.
2. Author and Date of Writing
As mentioned in 1:1 and 2:18 of this epistle, it was written by the apostle Paul. Silas and Timothy are mentioned together with Paul, but judging from the frequent use of the first-person pronoun "I" in the contents, the author can clearly be regarded as Paul.
Taken broadly, the date of writing of this epistle falls between A.D. 49-52, the period of Paul's second missionary journey. However, Paul was accused over an incident that took place while he was in Corinth and was examined by Gallio, the proconsul of Achaia (Acts 18:12-17). The period of Gallio's tenure as proconsul of Achaia is estimated to be A.D. 51-52, and an inscription at Delphi carved in A.D. 52 records that the name of the proconsul of Achaia was Gallio.
Therefore the period Paul stayed in Corinth was between A.D. 50 and 52. Furthermore, judging from his evangelizing the region of Ephesus after his evangelism in Corinth (Acts 18:19-21), his fourth visit to Jerusalem and his return to Antioch in Syria (Acts 18:22), and so on, the time when Paul wrote this epistle can be regarded as about A.D. 51.
3. Occasion and Background
Background
The city of Thessalonica, known today as Thessaloniki, was the capital of the region of Macedonia and at the same time an important first-class city of the Roman Empire. As a port city it had well-developed sea transport, and on land the Via Egnatia, the main trunk road running from Rome to Asia, passed through the city, so that besides its importance as a trading port, it became a strategic, commercial, and political center of the Roman Empire as the hub that dominated Macedonia.
 When Rome fell into turmoil at the assassination of Julius Caesar in 42 B.C., the city became a free city from Rome for its merit in siding with Octavian, who later became emperor, and in the time of the apostle Paul this city had developed into the most densely populated large city among the cities of the region of Macedonia.
 Therefore the apostle Paul's preaching of the gospel here became a foothold for preaching the gospel throughout all of Macedonia, and this has important significance in the 2,000-year history of the church.
 This city was built in 315 B.C. by Cassander, the adopted son of Philip II, king of Macedonia, who built the fortress city of Philippi, as a hot-spring area located at the head of the Gulf of Salonica.
 The city was named Thessalonica after Thessalonike, the wife of Cassander and the half-sister of Alexander the Great.
At that time the church in Thessalonica was receiving much persecution from the Jews. The church in Thessalonica was enduring this outside pressure well, but internally there were problems.
 The believers in Thessalonica, because of a mistaken view of the end times, thought that the Lord's return was imminent and so did not work, lived in a disorderly manner, and neglected the many things they ought to have been doing in the world; they also worried and were anxious about what would happen to those who died before the return of Christ, which caused great confusion in their life of faith.
In the end, these things made the believers of the church in Thessalonica, who were at the beginner's stage of faith, forget their own mission to be carried out in the world and become indifferent to worldly affairs.
Occasion of Writing
Paul, who had stayed in Thessalonica three weeks and evangelized, fled to Berea because of a riot of the Jews, but because of the Jews who pursued him even there, he went as far as Athens. At that time Paul left Timothy in Thessalonica (Acts 17:10) and Silas in Berea, and afterward Silas and Timothy, who had rejoined him from Berea (Acts 17:14), came to Athens (Acts 17:15) and told Paul that the church in Thessalonica was receiving persecution and trials.
Upon hearing this news Paul wanted to go to Thessalonica himself but could not (1 Thessalonians 2:17-18), and sent Timothy there instead (1 Thessalonians 3:2).
Some time later, in Corinth, Paul received through Timothy a report about the church in Thessalonica. Contrary to what he had feared, he heard that the Thessalonian believers, even in the midst of tribulation, not only held firmly to their faith while eagerly awaiting the Lord's return but also abounded in faith and love, and he was greatly comforted. Through this epistle he sent a message of thanks, praise, and encouragement for the faith of the Thessalonian believers.
He also wished to establish the church in Thessalonica firmly by correcting their mistaken view of the end times (1 Thessalonians 3:6-10). Furthermore, Paul wished, on this occasion, to confront directly those who slandered and opposed him, and to say that the gospel he as an apostle of God had preached to the church in Thessalonica was true.
Considering the above facts, Paul wrote this epistle in order to comfort and encourage the weak church in Thessalonica and to correct their mistaken view of faith.
4. Characteristics of 1 Thessalonians
Main Contents
The true joy and comfort of a servant of the gospel are recorded.
 This epistle was written less than a year after Paul preached the gospel in Thessalonica and the church began. For this reason, the first half is permeated with the apostle Paul's anxious concern and worry for the newly born church. And it shows how great a joy and comfort Paul received when he heard the news that the church in Thessalonica, about which he had been worried, was standing firm in faith and growing even amid persecution.
 This heart of Paul would be the common heart of pastors toward new believers who have just received the gospel and begun the life of faith.
The importance of the exemplary life of a servant of the gospel is recorded.
 In this epistle Paul recalls the time of his evangelistic ministry in Thessalonica and reminds them in what manner he ministered as a preacher of the gospel.
 Paul preached the gospel with genuine concern and fervent love and continued to care for them. He reminds them that he loved the believers so much that he was willing to give even his own life, and that he conducted himself so holy and blamelessly that not only people but God Himself was witness.
 Sharing the gospel is not merely a matter of speaking words. That the gospel was proclaimed to the Thessalonian believers with power, with the Holy Spirit, and with full conviction, and that the Thessalonian believers were able to keep growing in the gospel to the point of giving Paul great joy and comfort, was because Paul himself directly set an example of what it is to live by faith.
And you became imitators of us and of the Lord when you welcomed the message with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering.
 This is a passage that cannot but make pastors who desire the spiritual growth of believers think seriously about what they should work at, along with the ministry of proclaiming the word. Life must make the message shine, not dim it.
Moral holiness of the Christian is emphasized.
 In the second half of this epistle Paul exhorts the believers to live a life that pleases God, and he especially emphasizes living a sexually pure life.
 The Bible teaches that the corruption of human nature leads to sexual immorality and depravity. Therefore, Paul's teaching of sexual purity in this epistle is not limited to the matter of sex alone, but teaches that believers who have become children of God must be holy in the moral sphere as well.
The spiritual awakening and sober life of Christians who await the Lord's return are emphasized.
 Without exception, the end of each chapter of this epistle refers to the Lord's return (1 Thessalonians 1:10. 2:19-20, 3:13, 4:13-18, 5:23.). Among these, 4:13-5:11 records teaching directly related to the return of Christ.
 This epistle presents the eschatological message most centrally, and exhorts the children of God to live with a fervent eschatological faith.
 Living a life with an eschatological faith is the practice of a spiritually awakened life. A believer who sincerely awaits the return of Christ should not meet that day in bewilderment, like being robbed by a thief, but should live an awakened life so that whenever the Lord comes, he can run out and meet Him joyfully without shame.
It records the faith in the Lord's return that must be applied in everyday life.
 Let us summarize the concrete teachings about the Lord's return.
① Be awake and sober, without falling into worldly ease and pleasure
② Pursue peace and good in relationships with others.
③ Live with the attitude of always rejoicing, praying, and giving thanks.
 In the end, it tells us that a right faith in the Lord's return can never be separated from everyday life. That is, living by faith in the Lord's return is not a life of idle living off others, looking forward only to that day and doing nothing in the world, but exhorts us that we must live keeping our souls and bodies holy in daily life so that we may be presented blameless at the Lord's return.
The Systematic Theology of 1 Thessalonians
 This epistle shows the doctrine of God, that God is the only true One (1:9) who guides all things (3:11), and
the Christology that Christ is essentially equal with God (1:1).
 In addition, this epistle records the pneumatology concerning the Holy Spirit (1:5), who gives joy even in the midst of tribulation, and
the soteriology that believers obtained salvation because Jesus died in their place (5:10).
 However, the most central thought in this epistle is eschatology, and this epistle in particular records the phenomena that will appear at Christ's return.
 1) When Christ returns, the dead will be the first to rise and welcome Christ.
 (1 Thessalonians 4:16) For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise.
 2) After that, the living who remain will also be caught up into the air to meet the Lord and will live together with Him forever.
 (1 Thessalonians 4:17) After that, we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord.
 3) No one knows the time and season of the return, and it will come suddenly when people say, "Peace and security."
 (1 Thessalonians 5:1-3) Now about the times and seasons, brothers, we do not need to write to you. For you are fully aware that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, “Peace and security,” destruction will come upon them suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.
 4) Finally, it records that on the last day, when the Lord descends, unbelievers will be destroyed but the saved believers will live forever with Jesus Christ.
 (1 Thessalonians 5:10) He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him.

5. Structure of 1 Thessalonians
In terms of content, 1 Thessalonians can be divided broadly into two parts, chapters 1-3 and chapters 4-5.
 In the first half of the main body, based on Paul's recollection of the past when he evangelized in Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 2:1-12), he deals mainly with thanksgiving for their present faith, so that the perspectives of the past and the present appear in combination,
whereas the second half of the main body (chapters 4-5) makes clear what a fitting life before God should be for believers who eagerly await the return of Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:1-12), and, based on the future event of Christ's return and the resurrection of believers (1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:11), deals with the holy life they should aim at in the present (1 Thessalonians 5:12-24).
First half: Praise and thanks for the church in Thessalonica (1:1-3:13) (faithfulness toward the Lord)
It contains praise and encouragement for the church in Thessalonica. Although the time that Paul, who had been driven out of this region by the riot of the Jews, actually stayed in Thessalonica and guided their faith was not long, Paul first gives thanks to God for the growth of their faith (1 Thessalonians 1:2-4) and praises and encourages them (1 Thessalonians 1:5-10).
Paul also recalls the attitude of love toward himself that the Thessalonian believers showed in the past (1 Thessalonians 2:1-12) and repeatedly praises the sincere attitude they showed in the past (1 Thessalonians 2:13-16).
 Meanwhile, Paul's desire to revisit them in order to share loving fellowship with them, out of concern that their faith might stagnate or go wrong, was not fulfilled (1 Thessalonians 2:17-20).   So Paul came to send Timothy in his place (1 Thessalonians 3:1-5), and Timothy's report on his return that their faith was firm enabled Paul to enjoy great joy as an evangelist (1 Thessalonians 3:6-10). Paul once again offers intercessory prayer for them (1 Thessalonians 3:11-13).
In this way it can be seen as the portion that records Paul's hope and prayer for looking back on the past and present state of the church in Thessalonica and leading them to a more mature faith.
1) Introduction (1:1-10)
2) Recollection of the evangelistic ministry in Thessalonica (2:1-16)
3) Timothy's dispatch and his report on his return (2:17-3:13)
Second half: Encouragement and teaching for the church in Thessalonica (4:1-5:28) (being watchful for the Lord's coming)
It records Paul's teaching and exhortation for eradicating the harm caused by the remnants of Gentile culture that they had as a Gentile church and by mistaken ideas about the Lord's return, despite their exemplary faith.
 First, in (1 Thessalonians 4:1-12), Paul gives teaching about the fitting life that a believer who follows Christ should aim at, having cast off the practices of the flesh from the past.
 And (1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:11) is teaching about the end, the most important part of this book. It taught about what will happen to believers who have already died at Christ's return, which was the most serious problem of the church in Thessalonica at that time. (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18)
 Furthermore, by making clear that the Lord's return takes place suddenly (1 Thessalonians 5:1-11), he taught that believers must always prepare for the return of Christ and live a sober life (1 Thessalonians 5:12-22). This is the portion that teaches concretely what the everyday life of believers awaiting the Lord's return should be like; that is, believers are to practice love toward the brothers they can see, and also to rejoice, to pray, and to give thanks to God, that is, to live a holy life in the Holy Spirit. Then, concluding the whole body of the epistle, Paul once more prays that the God of peace will keep the souls and bodies of the believers holy until the very moment when the historical end is accomplished (1 Thessalonians 5:23-24).
1) Exhortation to a life that pleases God (4:1-12)
2) The return of Christ and the right life of believers (4:13-5:24)
3) Conclusion (5:25-28)
It consists of a request for prayer for themselves as preachers of the gospel, an exhortation to greet the brothers, a request that the letter be circulated, and a benediction. Through this Paul makes even clearer that all his hopes are fulfilled solely by God's help.

1. Title
Because this book is the second letter that Paul sent to the church in Thessalonica, it is named "2 Thessalonians." In the original Greek text the title of this book is "Pros Thessalonikeis Beta" (Pros Thessalonikeis B), that is, "To the Thessalonians, Second."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Externally, that Paul is the author of 2 Thessalonians is even more certain than in the case of 1 Thessalonians. Internally, from the vocabulary, style, and doctrinal content, it can be known that Paul wrote this letter (2 Thessalonians 1:1, 3:17).
It was written in Corinth around A.D. 51, during Paul's second missionary journey (A.D. 49-52).
He wrote 1 Thessalonians in Corinth as a reply to the good news that Timothy brought. Several months later, hearing a report from a certain brother about the church in Thessalonica, he wrote 2 Thessalonians, also in Corinth.
3. Occasion and Background
Background
Paul came to write this letter as a result of the person who delivered 1 Thessalonians telling Paul about the recent events in Thessalonica.
Paul heard the welcome news that the believers in Thessalonica held a firm faith even in persecution and tribulation from outside and even showed progress in faith (2 Thessalonians 1:3-4). However, regarding the Day of the Lord, the church was in a more confused state than when he sent 1 Thessalonians. That is, some among the believers misinterpreted the sudden return that Paul had spoken of in 1 Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 5:1-5) and thought it to be an imminent return or a return that had already taken place, and as a result the harm arose of living in a disorderly manner, not working, and living idly (2 Thessalonians 3:11-12).
[2 Thessalonians 3:11] Yet we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies.
Not only that, some thoughtless people also threw the believers in Thessalonica into confusion by claiming that they had received a revelation of the Holy Spirit themselves or that they had received another letter from Paul (2 Thessalonians 2:1-2).
[2 Thessalonians 2:1-2] Now concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to Him, we ask you, brothers, not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed by any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us, alleging that the Day of the Lord has already come.
In response, Paul could not but write 2 Thessalonians in haste. Paul encouraged the persecuted believers and made clear that, although the return of Christ will surely take place, there will be signs before it, and he exhorted them to hold fast to the truth and live an orderly life so as not to be led astray by false teaching.
  In particular, the region of Thessalonica was a transportation hub that one had to pass through to go from Rome to Asia or to move to the province of Achaia, and the church in Thessalonica had the importance of being the second church established in the region of Europe. Therefore, since mistaken knowledge about the return could spread rapidly and cause serious problems for many churches, Paul hurried to write 2 Thessalonians.
4. Structure of 2 Thessalonians
■ Thanks and comfort for the church in Thessalonica (Chapter 1)
(1) Introduction (1:1-4)
(2) Encouragement and comfort for believers in tribulation (1:5-12)

1. Title
This book is the first of two letters that Paul sent to Timothy, his beloved fellow worker and son in the faith, who was at that time pastoring in the church in Ephesus. It is titled after Timothy, the recipient of this book, and in the original Greek the title is "Pros Timotheon Alpha," that is, "The First Book Sent to Timothy." The English Bibles take "1 Timothy" as the title of this book, and the Korean Revised Version takes "1 Timothy" as well.
2. Author and Date of Writing
The author of this book is the apostle Paul. Paul and Timothy probably met when Paul preached the gospel in Lystra during his first missionary journey.
they found out about it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region, where they continued to preach the gospel.
Timothy's maternal grandmother and mother had come to faith first, and Timothy was influenced by them.
(2 Timothy 1:5) I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.
Since they met in Lystra, Paul and Timothy kept up a close relationship, as precious brothers in Christ and as fellow workers in ministry. In fact, Paul's final message is 2 Timothy, the second epistle sent to Timothy.
The Pastoral Epistles, beginning with 1 Timothy, were all written against the background of the period after Acts chapter 28. It is certain that Paul was released two years after his first imprisonment in Rome and traveled through various regions preaching. During this evangelistic journey 1 Timothy was written.
This is estimated to be between Paul's first imprisonment in Rome (A.D. 61-63) and his second imprisonment in Rome (A.D. 67), that is, about A.D. 63-66.
	1)	After appealing to Caesar, Paul went as a prisoner to Rome. (Acts 25:11-28:16)
	2)	Paul was kept under house arrest for two years, and during that time he preached the gospel to a great many people in Rome. (Acts 28:23-30)
	3)	After being released from prison in about A.D. 63, Paul made evangelistic journeys for about four years.
    - He traveled to Crete and left his fellow worker Titus there. (Titus 1:5)
    - After traveling to Ephesus, he went to Macedonia. He left Timothy to oversee the church in Ephesus. (1 Timothy 1:4)
    - He stayed in Nicopolis during the winter. (Titus 3:12)
    - He visited Miletus, and the sick Trophimus stayed behind there. (2 Timothy 4:20)
    - He visited Troas. He left his cloak and the writings on parchment there. (2 Timothy 4:13)
	4)	During this period Paul wrote 1 Timothy and Titus. (around A.D. 63-66)
	5)	Paul was arrested again as a prisoner and transferred again to Rome. (2 Timothy 1:16-17)
	6)	During this final imprisonment Paul wrote 2 Timothy, his last epistle and farewell letter. (around A.D. 66-67)
	7)	Paul was executed in Rome. (around A.D. 67)
3. Occasion and Background
Background
After a riot broke out at the instigation of Demetrius, the silversmith (Acts 19), Paul gave the believers in Ephesus a final word of encouragement and set out for Macedonia.
(Acts 20:1) When the uproar had ended, Paul sent for the disciples. And after encouraging them, he said goodbye to them and left for Macedonia.
A few months later Paul invited the elders of Ephesus to Miletus and met them. At this meeting he warned the elders of Ephesus about false teachers who would tempt saved people away from the truth.
(Acts 20:28-31) Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood. I know that after my departure, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock. Even from your own number, men will rise up and distort the truth to draw away disciples after them. Therefore be alert and remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears.
Paul warned them that false teachers would arise, spent time in prayer, shared a deep parting of affection, and headed for Jerusalem. Paul loved the church in Ephesus very much, and he wrote from his Roman prison and delivered to them "Ephesians," one of the most important books of the Bible, which teaches what the church is.
After that, Paul was released from the Roman prison and visited Ephesus again.
During this visit he discovered that many spiritual problems had arisen in his absence. Paul and Timothy stayed in Ephesus for a short time, teaching the word and correcting what was wrong. But when, before long, Paul had no choice but to leave for Macedonia, Paul left Timothy there to guide and oversee the church.
(1 Timothy 1:3-4) As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith.
Occasion of Writing
After being released from his first Roman imprisonment, Paul, who was heading for Asia Minor, went to the island of Crete, and left Titus there to complete the work of organizing the church.
(Titus 1:5) The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you.
Then Paul went to Ephesus, and there he joined Timothy, who had returned from Philippi.
(Philippians 2:19-23) Now I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing. I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs. For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you know Timothy’s proven worth, that as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel. So I hope to send him as soon as I see what happens with me.
