As Paul had foreseen, he and Timothy saw that teachers who taught heretical doctrine were spreading false teaching, but Paul went to the region of Macedonia in order to keep his promise to visit the church in Philippi (Philippians 2:24), intending to finish his business there quickly and then return to Ephesus to see Timothy. But as circumstances did not permit and he was delayed, he wrote this book first, sending a letter to tell the young evangelist how to deal with the many problems of the church in Ephesus that were hard for him to bear, and also to give him strength and courage.
(1 Timothy 3:14-15) Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.
The central point of 1 Timothy lies in "the church of God." Here the church is described as "God's household, which is the church of the living God." How should Timothy, as a pastor, conduct himself in the church? The theme of 1 Timothy is directed to this.
	•	To encourage Timothy, the young pastor, and help him carry out a right pastoral ministry
	•	To provide the necessary guidelines to be applied in the actual church
	•	To help him deal with false doctrines
To this end Paul
	•	warns against false teachers (1:3-7, 4:1-5, 6:3-10),
	•	sets forth guidelines for church gatherings (2:1-15),
	•	explains the standards for choosing elders and deacons (3:1-13),
	•	explains in detail the pastoral attitude toward each group in the church (5:1-25),
	•	and gives commands about the pastor's own training in godliness (1 Timothy 4:6-16).
It is an epistle of encouragement to a young evangelist who must surely have been intimidated by believers older than himself, and it urges him to use boldly the gift God gave him.
4. The Message of 1 Timothy
To defend the truth of the gospel (1:3-11, 4:1-5, 6:3-5)
It was to fight against the false teachers who had infiltrated the church. In this letter Paul warns Timothy about the heretics three times. Each time, Paul adds an urging to Timothy to hold fast to the faith, to be strong, and to live a right life.
(1 Timothy 1:18-19) Timothy, my child, I entrust you with this command in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight,
(1 Timothy 4:9-16) Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity. Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching....
(1 Timothy 6:11-20) But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith.
And he mentions several characteristics of heresy.
	•	Preoccupation with myths and endless genealogies (1:4),
	•	legalism (4:3),
	•	not devoting oneself to the word of God (6:3),
	•	and teaching for selfish gain and financial profit (6:5).
Paul urges Timothy to fight against false teachings by opposing the false teachers (1:18, 6:12) and by having absolutely no association with them or their teachings (4:7).
And he exhorts Timothy to maintain love (1:5, 6:11), sincere and strong faith (1:5, 19, 6:12), a clean conscience (1:5, 19), and a godly life (4:7, 6:11).
The most powerful weapon against heresy is sound doctrine (6:3). That is, to hold fast to the truth and to put the truth into practice in life.
On church gatherings (2:1-15)
Paul next deals with the matter of gatherings within the church. He first emphasizes the necessity and importance of prayer. Because God desires all people to be saved, the Bible teaches that prayer must be made for all people, including "kings and all those in authority."
Next Paul discusses the attitude of women at church gatherings.
Paul explains that even though sisters enjoy a new freedom in Christ and study the Scriptures together with the brothers, they must not hastily claim a position of leadership or boast and show off their freedom. Rather, he teaches them to submit to the brothers within the order that God has established.
On the standards for choosing overseers and deacons (3:1-16)
Paul sets forth concrete guidelines on the qualifications of overseers and deacons of the church.
1) Those who are spiritually mature,
2) who have special spiritual gifts,
3) who possess sound faith,
4) who maintain a right family life, and
5) who have an excellent reputation were to become overseers and deacons of the church.
On the pastor's attitude toward each group of believers (5:1-25, 6:1-2, 17-19)
The most important proof that the believers in Ephesus are disciples of the Lord in the world is to be a church that loves one another. And the command to love must be put into concrete practice. So for Timothy's sake Paul provides guidelines on how the church should treat older men (5:1), younger men (5:2), older women (5:2), younger women (5:2), widows (5:3-6, 9-16), and church elders (5:17-20), and explains what attitude slaves should have toward their masters (6:1-2). And he exhorts Timothy to encourage the wealthy believers to use their wealth to help others (6:17-19).
On personal training (4:6-16, 6:11-12, 20-21)
Paul knew that training is necessary to become a capable leader of the church. Timothy must minister by faith and live a righteous life. Paul exhorted Timothy to carry out the work God had entrusted to him although he was young, that is, to set an example of a righteous life (4:11-12). And he urged him to diligently exercise his gift and to proclaim and teach the gospel (4:13-16). Timothy, as a pastor, had to keep himself pure, avoid worldly temptations, and especially not love money (1 Timothy 5:21-25, 1 Timothy 6:6-10). He urges him to be trained by not departing from the faith through endless, empty arguments (6:20-21).
5. Structure of 1 Timothy
1) First half (chapters 1-3): Exhortation to defend the truth of the gospel and to establish order and organization in the church
2) Second half (chapters 4-6): Teaching on the pastor's attitude

1. Title
2 Timothy is the second of the two letters that the apostle Paul sent to Timothy, his beloved fellow worker and son in the faith, who was at that time pastoring in the church in Ephesus. In the original Greek the title is "Pros Timotheon Beta," that is, "The Second Book Sent to Timothy." Following this, English Bibles take "2 Timothy" as the title of this book, and the Korean Revised Version takes "2 Timothy" as well.
2. Author and Date of Writing
That Paul is the author of this book is attested in 2 Timothy itself.
(2 Timothy 1:1-2) “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”
The date of writing of this book can be estimated almost exactly in the light of the circumstances Paul states in the text. That is, Paul states in this book that he was imprisoned in a Roman prison when he wrote it.
(2 Timothy 1:8) “So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God.”
(2 Timothy 2:9) “for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!”
Furthermore, in 4:16-17 Paul states that he had in the past defended himself before the Roman emperor and had also been released from prison. From this it is clear that the imprisonment of Paul stated in this book is his second imprisonment.
Most scholars hold that the time when Paul was imprisoned a second time in the Roman prison and suffered martyrdom was around A.D. 67 or 68. Meanwhile, in 4:6 Paul implicitly says that the day of his execution was not far off. And in 4:9-13 he asks Timothy to come to him quickly, bringing the cloak that he had left at the house of Carpus in Troas, before winter set in. From this it can be estimated that Paul wrote this at the latest in the autumn of A.D. 66 or 67.
3. Occasion and Background
This book is a letter that Paul, imprisoned for the second time in a Roman prison, wrote and sent, on the eve of his martyrdom, to Timothy, the young pastor of the church in Ephesus, with the character of a kind of last will and testament, and it is the second of the letters sent to Timothy. And it is the very last of Paul's epistles.
It was written with the following two purposes.
First, on the personal level, it was because he wanted to see Timothy, his son in the faith.
The condition of Paul during his second Roman imprisonment was that he was treated like an ordinary prisoner and bound in chains (1:16, 2:9), and was growing steadily weaker in a cold dungeon (4:13). Moreover, those who had attended him had all left his side for one reason or another, except for Luke the physician (4:10-11). So Paul wanted to see for the last time Timothy, who was so precious that he could say, "I have no one else like him" (Philippians 2:20). Through this epistle Paul expresses his hope of reuniting with Timothy and repeatedly urges him to come to him quickly (1:4, 4:9, 21).
Second, on the level of passing on the gospel ministry, it was to leave final teaching, exhortation, and commands to Timothy.
At the time when Paul wrote this book, the situation he had been concerned about when he wrote 1 Timothy had come very much into reality, and the circumstances were urgent. Externally, the great persecution of Christians by the Roman emperor Nero (A.D. 54-68), which began after the great fire of the city of Rome in A.D. 64, was at first carried out only in and around Rome but gradually began to be carried out sporadically throughout the Roman Empire. Apart from this heightening atmosphere of persecution from outside, internally in the church heretical doctrines such as early Gnosticism (Proto-Gnosticism) had infiltrated, were continually expanding their influence, and were threatening the truth of the gospel. Squarely facing this situation of the Lord's church, and foreseeing that his lifelong ministry was drawing to a close, Paul felt the need to leave a testamentary message to Timothy, the gospel minister of the next generation.
The second letter to Timothy was written in the Mamertine prison in Rome. 2 Timothy is a very personal letter. In this letter we learn more about Paul's thoughts and feelings. In this letter Paul speaks of the great apostasy that will all but wipe out "faith." This is in perfect harmony with what the Lord said.
(Luke 18:8) “However, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?”
4. Characteristics of 2 Timothy
2 Timothy is Paul's last writing. He is facing death. Paul had to say much in a short time. Great verses of Scripture are written in this book.
2 Timothy, together with 1 Timothy and Titus, is an epistle classified as one of the "Pastoral Epistles" among the New Testament epistles written by Paul, with contents consisting of teaching on the attitude of an evangelist and Paul's testamentary commands for defending and spreading the gospel.
Through this epistle, which is like Paul's last will and testament, Paul teaches and encourages Timothy to endure suffering and, further, to actively suffer for the gospel. And he leaves a final command to guard against the depravity of the last days and heretical ideas, and to defend and spread the gospel.
Through 2 Timothy we encounter the testament of a great servant of the gospel who looks back and says, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." (4:7). Although the times and circumstances differ, 2 Timothy is given in the same way not only to Timothy of that time but to believers of every age who must keep and spread the gospel.
5. Structure of 2 Timothy
The structure of the contents of 2 Timothy can be divided into three parts: the introduction at 1:1-5, the main body at 1:6-4:8, and the conclusion at 4:9-22.
Introduction 1:1-5 > Paul's greeting and prayer of thanksgiving
And it expresses Paul's earnest desire to see Timothy again, recalling Timothy's tears and sincere faith.
Main body 1:6-4:8 > divided into the first half of the main body 1:6-2:26 / the second half of the main body 3:1-4:8
First half of the main body
In 1:6-18, Paul reminds Timothy of the gift God gave him and encourages him to suffer for the gospel according to the power of God.
In 2:1-26, Paul teaches an attitude of enduring and being faithful even in suffering, through analogies such as the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer, and presents Christ and himself as models of such endurance. Paul goes on to present in order concrete teachings such as to be a workman who rightly handles the word of truth, to pursue a holy life, and to have a gentle attitude toward all people.
Second half of the main body
In 3:1-9, Paul prophesies that "terrible times in the last days" will come, and sets forth in detail the moral and spiritual depravity that will appear in people in the last days. And he also mentions the heretics who oppose the truth.
Having warned in this way about the depravity of the last days and the heretics, Paul in 3:10-17 exhorts Timothy to continue in "what you have learned and firmly believed," that is, in the truth of Scripture. And as the ground of that exhortation, he emphasizes that Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for equipping the man of God for every good work.
And in 4:1-8, by solemnly commanding him to preach the word in season and out of season, he reminds him that he must carry out the duty of guarding and spreading the gospel beyond all circumstances.
Conclusion 4:9-22 > It deals with Paul's personal news and requests.
Here Paul informs Timothy of his situation in the Roman prison and asks him to come to Rome quickly. He also mentions personal requests such as that Timothy bring Mark when he comes and bring the cloak and the parchment scrolls. And he conveys greetings to his fellow workers, and concludes 2 Timothy with a prayer for Timothy personally and for the believers of the church in Ephesus.
※ The Four Commands of 2 Timothy
Chapter 1: Guard the gospel.
Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. (1:14)
Chapter 2: Teach the gospel.
You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well. (2:1-2)
Chapter 3: Continue in the gospel.
while evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed... (3:13-14)
Chapter 4: Preach the gospel.
In the presence of God ... and of Christ Jesus ... I charge you: Preach the word. Be prepared in season and out of season. Reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction (4:1-2).
6. The Message of 2 Timothy
1. Endurance in suffering: the basic attitude of a faithful Christian.
The most frequent and central message of this epistle is "suffer for the gospel." Paul states several times that he himself suffered for the gospel (1:11-12, 2:9-10, 3:11), and he repeats his exhortation that Timothy, a younger evangelist, likewise bear suffering and actively accept it (1:8, 2:3, 4:5). Those who want to live godly lives cannot but be persecuted (3:12). If one truly wants to live for the gospel, suffering cannot be avoided. The attitude of enduring in suffering and, further, of actively accepting it is the basic attitude required of a Christian.
2. Rightly handling the word: the basic discipline of a Christian.
Paul presents concrete teachings on the attitude of a Christian and exhorts him to strive to present himself to God as a workman who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. To rightly handle the word of truth means to understand the word accurately and handle it correctly, that is, not to distort or corrupt the word with wrong motives or purposes. In context, Paul presents rightly handling the word as an important yardstick for distinguishing from false teachers (2:14-17).
3. A holy and gentle life.
In teaching about the attitude of a Christian, Paul does not fail to include teaching on a holy and gentle life. Holiness and gentleness are personal characteristics that come out through actual life. If these are lacking, serious hindrance results for the gospel ministry. Therefore a Christian must cleanse himself from defilements such as human passion and anger.
4. Guarding against the depravity of the last days.
In chapter 3, Paul prophesies that "terrible times in the last days" will come and sets forth in detail the moral and spiritual depravity that people of the last days will display. And it is said that this prophecy about the depravity of the last days has in mind not only unbelievers outside the church but also apostates inside the church. The reason Paul refers in this way to the depravity of apostates is to make us aware that the closer the last days come, the more human nature and religious tendencies will be hostile to the gospel, and so firmer arming is necessary.
5. Assurance regarding the truth of Scripture.
After warning about the depravity of the last days, Paul exhorts Timothy to continue in "what you have learned and firmly believed," that is, in the truth of Scripture. And he goes on to state that all Scripture is "God-breathed." That Scripture is God-breathed means that, although Scripture was written by human authors, God inspired them by the Holy Spirit and so caused it to become, as a result, Scripture without any mistake or error. The time of the last days is a time when truth is not accepted as truth. But Scripture, being God-breathed, is the word of absolute truth that Christians of all ages must be assured of and continue in.
6. The testamentary command to spread the gospel.
In this epistle Paul leaves to Timothy, the successor of the gospel ministry, the final testamentary command, "Preach the word in season and out of season." This command is in line with the Great Commission that the ascending Christ left to His disciples (Matthew 28:19-20), and Paul in fact makes him recognize this command as a divine command given in the presence of God and of Christ.
The mission of spreading the gospel was a mission Paul himself received from the Lord (Acts 20:24). Paul ran all his life to fulfill that mission, and now he is handing over the baton to Timothy. In 2 Timothy we encounter a solemn testamentary command to take up the baton, from a senior minister who ran his whole life without regret for the spreading of the gospel and has reached the finish line.

1. Title
The title of this book is the Greek "Pros Titon," which means "To Titus." Accordingly, English Bibles take "To Titus" as the title, and the Korean Revised Version takes "Titus" as the title.
2. Author and Date of Writing
 The author of this book is Paul. At the beginning of this book Paul makes clear that he himself wrote and sent it.
(Titus 1:1) Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness,
Titus was written and sent as follows: after he was released from his first Roman imprisonment (around A.D. 61-63), while visiting the churches where he had evangelized, he visited Crete, and, seeing the problems of the church in Crete, he left Titus behind to resolve the problems of the church, and later (around A.D. 64-66) he wrote and sent the Epistle to Titus so that Titus might carry out his mission well.
3. Occasion and Background
Background
Crete is the fourth largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily, Sardinia, and Cyprus. This island, consisting mostly of mountains, lies almost at the midpoint among Europe, Asia, and Africa, and was a strategic point connecting Asia Minor and Europe. It is about 250 km long and 11-54 km wide.
In Crete, the truth of the gospel of Christ had been considerably distorted by a Judaizing heresy, that is, legalism, influenced by Judaism, which put forward the observance of formal Old Testament law, such as the practice of circumcision, as a requirement for salvation.
Moreover, under the influence of an extremely morally corrupt Greek culture, not only the Cretans who were unbelievers but even a considerable number of the believers in the church in Crete had fallen into laziness and licentiousness, not only in faith but also in ethics.
After being released from his first imprisonment, Paul, while visiting the churches, visited Crete for a time, and, seeing the serious problems of the church in Crete, left his fellow worker Titus there to resolve the problems.
Occasion of Writing
At the time this book was written, the church in Crete was in a quite confused and disorderly situation, so it was urgent to establish order in the church and to set up a right view of faith. Therefore Paul wrote this book in order to encourage Titus, who was pastoring in such a poor environment, to root out the false teachers, and to present pastoral guidelines for setting the order of the church right.
(Titus 1:5) The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you.
4. About "Titus"
The meaning of the name Titus: "to honor"
A Greek (it is guessed that he may have been a brother or relative of Luke; the reason he does not appear in Acts is that Luke omitted his name)
(Galatians 2:3) Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek.
The relationship between Paul and Titus
Saved through Paul's evangelism
(Titus 1:4) To Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
For an evangelist, there is no greater joy anywhere in this world than to see the person he taught and trained being put to good use in the church
One recognized as a brother, from a son
(2 Corinthians 2:13) I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.
Through these words, it shows the brotherly affection between Paul and Titus, and Titus's preciousness and trustworthiness
A trustworthy man
A man who had won Paul's trust to the point of attending the Jerusalem council with Paul and Barnabas
(Galatians 2:1) Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas. I took Titus along also.
One who took part in the missionary journeys following Paul
Titus who labored in the church in Corinth
In particular, Titus shows a prominent role in his relationship with the church in Corinth
Paul's comforter
(2 Corinthians 7:6) But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,
(2 Corinthians 7:7) and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.
Through Titus, Paul learned that the letter he had sent to the believers in Corinth (a letter of rebuke and scolding) had brought the result he had hoped for. The reason Paul rejoiced was that the believers in Corinth not only repented but also gladly acknowledged his apostolic authority
Titus was a positive person who accomplished the difficult task of serving as a mediator and intercessor between Paul and the church in Corinth, which distrusted Paul
One who gives joy
(2 Corinthians 7:13) On account of this, we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus. For his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.
One of deep affection
(2 Corinthians 7:15) And his affection for you is even greater when he remembers that you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling.
The one who got the believers in Corinth to begin the collection
(2 Corinthians 8:6) So we urged Titus to help complete your act of grace, just as he had started it.
He handled well the matter of the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, encouraging the hearts of the believers in Corinth to prepare the collection well and to bring it to completion
A man of courage who volunteered for a difficult task
(2 Corinthians 8:17) For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition.
The apostle Paul sent Titus to the church in Corinth for the work of collecting the offering. A matter involving money is not entrusted to just anyone. It is entrusted only to someone who can be trusted. Titus showed that he was a man who could be trusted even in money matters.
To talk about money is a difficult thing. People avoid doing a difficult thing. One can talk about it only if one has boldness and assurance of faith and has become an example in giving offerings. Titus was a man with a talent for practical administration
One with earnestness (zeal, concern, seriousness)
(2 Corinthians 8:16) But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you.
One who did not take advantage (one free from material greed)
(2 Corinthians 12:18) I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?
Paul's companion and fellow worker
(2 Corinthians 8:23) As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker among you. As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ.
(2 Corinthians 12:18) I urged Titus to visit you, and I sent our brother with him. Did Titus exploit you in any way? Did we not walk in the same Spirit and follow in the same footsteps?
A companion is one who shares in the same circumstances. Titus thought the same as Paul. As Paul's helper, he held the same thoughts as Paul and showed the same actions. Paul valued Titus's partnership
Paul knew that Titus was handling matters in the same way he himself did. A person who has a deputy to whom he can entrust a task, someone who can surely carry out the task as intended, is happy.
After the ministry in Crete
(2 Timothy 4:10) because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia.
Dalmatia (present-day Yugoslavia) is the region south of Illyricum, located northwest of Macedonia. Since Paul had already preached the gospel in this region, it appears that Titus was sent to look after the church there
It is said that Titus returned to Crete, lived a long life there, died at the age of 94, and was buried there.
※ Titus's nickname = the fixer (problem solver, troubleshooter)
Titus was a fixer who went wherever there were difficulties, hardships, and many problems and solved the problems. Titus was a man who could bring order out of confusion and peace out of strife. Titus was trustworthy enough to be sent to a place with a difficult problem
5. Structure of Titus
1. Introduction (1:1~4): Greeting
2. Main body (1:5~3:11)
1) Guidelines for defending the truth of the gospel and establishing order in the church (1:5~16)
① Qualifications of elders (1:5~9)
② Warning against false teachers (1:10~16)
2) Guidelines for teaching believers to live a right life of faith (2:1~3:11)
① Guidelines for rightly nurturing believers (2:1~15)
② The believers' attitude toward civil authorities and unbelieving neighbors (3:1~8)
③ The believers' attitude toward neighbors who belong to heresy (3:9~11)
3. Conclusion (3:12~15)
1) Personal requests (3:12~14)
2) Final greetings (3:15)

1. Title
This book is a personal letter that Paul sent to Philemon, a believer in the church at Colossae, which was located in the valley of the Lycus River in Asia Minor. The title in the original Greek is "Pros Philemona," that is, "To Philemon." Accordingly, English Bibles use "To Philemon" as the title of this book, and the Korean Revised Version uses "Philemon."
2. Author and Date of Writing
That Paul is the author of this book is attested by the book itself. At the beginning of the book Paul identifies himself as the sender, and near the end he states that he wrote it with his own hand.
As for the time of writing, Paul mentions that he himself is in prison (1:1, 23), which agrees with the historical situation of Paul's first imprisonment in Rome (about A.D. 61-63). Therefore the date of writing of this book is estimated to be about A.D. 62.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
Background
Onesimus was a slave who had wronged his master Philemon and run away.
(Philemon 1:18) But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.
Under Roman law at that time, a slave who fled from his master could even be put to death. Yet Onesimus fled as far as Rome, and there, through Paul's ministry, he was converted and became a Christian.
(Philemon 1:10) I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains.
And he became one who served at Paul's side. Paul calls him "my very heart" (Philemon 1:12) in this letter, and in Colossians introduces him as "a faithful and beloved brother" (Colossians 4:8); so clearly had Onesimus been changed into a Christian.
For Paul it would have been useful to keep such an Onesimus by his side to attend to him, but so that the good deed might not be done under compulsion, he decided to send him back to his master Philemon. And along with Onesimus he sent this letter, appealing to Philemon to forgive Onesimus and receive him as a brother in Christ. Seeing that this letter was circulated among the believers and was even included in the New Testament, it is more than reasonable to suppose that Philemon, who received it, forgave Onesimus and accepted him as a brother of Christ.
Purpose of Writing
The purpose for which Paul, then in a Roman prison, sent such a personal letter to Philemon of the church at Colossae was to intercede so that a slave named Onesimus might be forgiven.
At the same time, in this letter we can see a dimension that goes beyond mere human kindness.
In the figure of Paul pleading for Onesimus, whom he gained through his gospel ministry, we can see the figure of Christ the Mediator, who pleads with God for us;
and in the figure of Onesimus, who is defended as one who has changed from being useless and harmful to being useful, faithful, and beloved, we can see ourselves, who are defended by Christ.
In the end, Philemon, Paul, and Onesimus, the main figures of this letter, all show how those who have experienced and tasted God's forgiving love in Christ apply that forgiving love in real life and in their relationships. Every believer is an Onesimus in Christ, but at times must also be a Philemon, and at other times a Paul.
4. About "Philemon"
Meaning of the name Philemon: "beloved one"
He is presumed to have been converted when Paul preached at the lecture hall of Tyrannus in Ephesus; he was kind to other believers and was wealthy enough that his house was used as a meeting place.
(Acts 19:9-10) But when some of them stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way, Paul took his disciples and left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.
He was the master of Onesimus, and he is presumed to have served as overseer of the church at Colossae and to have been stoned to death as a martyr during Nero's persecution (about A.D. 64).
5. Structure of Philemon
1-7 _ Introduction
It contains the typical opening of a letter, together with thanks and praise for the faith and love of the recipient, Philemon. Here Paul sincerely thanks and praises Philemon for his faith toward the Lord and his love for the saints. And by praying that through the fellowship of his faith Philemon might fully understand every good thing that believers enjoy in Christ and might advance even to Christ, Paul hints at his hope that Philemon's faith and love would proceed to the next step of forgiving and accepting Onesimus.
8-21 _ Main Body
This section deals with Paul's mediation and appeal on behalf of Onesimus, who had run away from Philemon. Here Paul does not command by his apostolic authority but appeals for the forgiveness of Onesimus on the basis of love. Telling of his own situation as an old man in prison, Paul earnestly defends the runaway slave Onesimus, declaring that he has been converted and changed into a useful person. Going further, he expresses his intention to repay on Onesimus' behalf any loss that Onesimus has caused. Then, as a final step, he adds an emotional appeal for the forgiveness of Onesimus by expressing his hope that Philemon will give him joy and comfort, together with his confidence in Philemon's obedience.
Verses 22-25 Conclusion
This section consists of Paul's personal requests to Philemon, together with the closing greetings and benediction. Anticipating his release and a visit to Colossae, Paul asks Philemon to prepare lodging for him and to intercede in prayer that his release and visit to Colossae might become a reality. Then, after conveying the greetings of the fellow workers who are with him, he closes the letter with a benediction.

1. Title
Most of the authoritative early manuscripts introduce it simply as "To the Hebrews." Most English Bibles likewise give it the title "Hebrews," and the Korean Revised Version takes the same common position and calls it "Hebrews."
2. Author and Date of Writing
An absolutely precise date of composition cannot be determined. But this letter was clearly written, as the glory of the church of Christ was increasing, in an age when the social institutions of the old Hebrews were gradually passing away. Some take the date of writing to be A.D. 60-70, on the grounds that this letter makes no mention at all of the destruction of the Jerusalem temple in A.D. 70, and that it stands on the verge of a time of suffering such as Nero's persecution.
Moreover, the recipients had experienced persecution in the past (10:32-34, 11:35-38, 12:1, 13:3) and were facing the crisis of a new persecution (12:3-7, 13:5-7, 13:13-); this relates to the period after Nero's persecution (64) and just before the persecution of the emperor Domitian (reigned 81-96), and so the date is estimated to be the late A.D. 60s.
Furthermore, the recipients were second-generation Christians (2:3), and among them were some who had lost the eschatological tension between faith and life and were about to fall away from the faith (3:12, 10:23, 12:15-16); for this is the period in which such a problematic situation appears.
Who wrote this letter is not known with certainty. Luther (Martin Luther, Nov. 10, 1483 - Feb. 18, 1546) thought that Apollos (1 Corinthians 1:12) wrote it. But the majority hold that the apostle Paul wrote it. The early church fathers likewise shared this opinion. In light of the character and content shown in this book, it is most likely that the author was the apostle Paul.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
Background
At first many Jews accepted Jesus as the Christ, but their faith wavered, or they fell into discouragement, because of the fierce opposition of the Jewish religious leaders. There were those who wanted to return to the Judaism that they had held since the time of their ancestors, and in Jerusalem there were still a great many Jewish Christians who were zealous for the law and the temple (Acts 21:20).
Motive for Writing
This word was written to testify to them that everything recorded in the Old Testament points to Jesus Christ; that the prophets, the sacrifices offered in the temple, the events that appeared in history, and the sacrificial rituals performed in the temple were all shadows of something better and truer; and that now all of these things have been wonderfully and certainly fulfilled through Jesus Christ. By conveying the essential truths about Christ and salvation concretely and in an orderly manner, it was meant to put their faith in order and to awaken the Jews who were still doubting so that they would hold a firm faith.
Probably a great many Jews believed in Christ and were saved through Hebrews, and when Jews come to believe in Christ in the future, they will gain still more understanding through Hebrews. As we study Hebrews, we come to feel all the more that we must know the Old Testament in order to understand the New Testament more deeply, and that the Old Testament is understood through the New Testament.
 The purpose for which Hebrews was written is to draw both Jews and Gentiles into the gloriously completed redemption of Christ, and to lead them to meet and have fellowship with God.
4. Characteristics of Hebrews
① It differs from the other letters in many respects
- It calls salvation "so great a salvation" (Hebrews 2:3).
- The author and the recipients are not mentioned.
- It explains the typological teachings of the Old Testament in more detail than any other letter.
- The priesthood of Christ is fully set forth only in this letter.
- Warnings against apostasy appear more often, and they are solemn.
- More than in any other book of the New Testament, it emphasizes "hold firm, be unshaken, and keep the faith."
② There are parts that cannot be understood without taking into account the physical and ethnic descent of the recipients and the situation in which they were placed.
It must be considered on the basis of the Old Testament.
③ It presents Christ as the One "who sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high."
The One to whom Christians are related is the Christ "in heaven."
④ The central purpose of Hebrews is the exhortation to "be steadfast."
The central content of Hebrews is that the new covenant is superior in contrast to the old covenant. This letter contains an exhortation to "be steadfast" that is to be applied to life.
In particular, chapter 11 explains the life of faith in detail and completely. By appealing to the course of life of the Old Testament saints, it describes clearly and in detail what it means to walk by faith. It keeps emphasizing: hold fast to Jesus the great high priest, and hold fast to real and true worship.
Hebrews exhorts us, in the presence of God, in the love and compassion of the Lord Jesus Christ, while having fellowship with the great cloud of witnesses surrounding us, to be steadfast and unshaken, to persevere, and to have hope.
⑤ It shows by contrast what the believing Hebrews had to give up and what they gain.
Note how many times the phrase "what we have" appears, in contrast to what the Hebrews had to give up, that is, what they gain.
We have a high priest (4:14, 8:1), an anchor of the soul (6:19), a better and lasting possession (10:34), and so on. The temple and the sacrificial system are nothing but a shadow, and we have Christ, who is the reality (2:17, 3:1, 4:14,15, 5:6,10, 6:20, 7:26, 8:1, 9:11, 10:21).
⑥ Through Hebrews it makes us look to what is in heaven.
	•	Christ in heaven (1:3,13,8:1,10:12).
	•	The heavenly calling (3:1).
	•	The heavenly gift (6:4).
	•	The things in heaven (8:5).
	•	The homeland in heaven (11:16).
	•	The heavenly Jerusalem (12:22).
	•	The assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven (12:23).
⑧ In Hebrews, words accompanied by exhortations and warnings appear.
Discouragement that could grow in the hearts of the Hebrew Christians, the persecutions they had to endure at that time, the destruction of Jerusalem (A.D. 70), and so on, made warnings against apostasy necessary. (Hebrews 1:6, 2:2, 4:1, 4:11, 4:14, 4:16, 6:1-2, 10:22, 12:1, 12:16) .
5. Structure of Hebrews
Hebrews is divided into two parts. The first is the doctrinal part, and the second is the practical part.
1:1-10:18
Doctrine teaching that Christianity is far superior to Judaism
	Chapter 1		Jesus Christ, greater than the prophets
      Chapters 1, 2 		Christ, greater than the angels
	Chapter 3 		Christ, greater than Moses
	4:1-13 		Christ, greater than Joshua
	4:14-5:14 	Christ, greater than Aaron
	Chapter 6		Warning
	Chapter 7		The high priest and Melchizedek
	Chapters 8, 9		The better tabernacle
	Chapter 10		The better sacrifice
10:19-13:25 
It reminds us that putting that faith into practice in life is both the privilege and the duty of the Christian.
	10:19-39	The absolute necessity of faith
	Chapter 11		The essence of faith and the heroes of faith
	Chapters 12, 13		Exhortations on faith and life, and their fruits
			       - discipline, warning, love, obedience, suffering  
6. Theme of Hebrews
The theme of Hebrews is that Christianity is supremely superior to Judaism. It lets us know that the essence and center of faith lie in "Christ." Accordingly, Hebrews shows that "Christ" is superior to anything that came before.
① It cites the various figures in whom the Jews took pride and shows that they are nothing before Christ.
	•	Christ is superior to the prophets. (Hebrews 1:1-3)
	•	He is superior to the angels. (Hebrews 1:4)
	•	He is superior to Moses. (Hebrews 3:5-6)
	•	He is superior to Joshua. (Hebrews 4:8, 10-11)
	•	It speaks of Christ, who came after the order of Melchizedek, who is superior to the high priest Aaron. (Hebrews 7:11)
	•	Christ is superior to the rituals of Judaism as a whole. (Hebrews 8:13)
	•	Christ is superior to each individual among the Old Testament saints. (Hebrews 12:1-2)
	•	In the end, it makes clear that if Judaism is a shadow and a type, Christ is the reality.
② By using many comparative words such as "better," it shows that what we enjoy in Christ is "superior" to what the Old Testament saints enjoyed within Judaism.
	•	Christ is better than the angels (1:4), 
	•	a better hope (7:19), 
	•	the guarantee of a better covenant (7:22), 
	•	a better covenant (8:6), 
	•	better sacrifices (9:23), 
	•	a better possession (10:34), 
	•	a better homeland (11:16), 
	•	a better resurrection (11:35), 
	•	something better (11:40).
③ Hebrews draws attention to six great things.
	•	A great salvation (2:3), 
	•	a great high priest (4:14), 
	•	a greater tabernacle (9:11), 
	•	a great struggle (10:32), 
	•	a great reward (10:35), 
	•	the great Shepherd of the sheep (13:20).
⑧ Through Hebrews we can know that Jesus Christ became the atonement "once for all," the final one. 
(Hebrews 6:4, 7:27, 9:12, 9:26, 9:28, 10:2, 10:10, 12:26)

1. Title
In the original Greek, the heading is recorded as "Of James" or "Letter of James."
On the other hand, most English translations, reflecting that this book is one of the general letters, not sent to a particular region or audience, added the word "General" and called it "The General Epistle of James." The Hebrew "Jacob" passed through Greek and Latin and became "James" in English.
 The Korean Revised Version took "James" as the title of this letter.
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The author of James clearly identifies himself in James 1:1 as "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ." However, several different people named James appear in the New Testament.
⓵ James the apostle, one of the twelve disciples (Mark 1:19)
⓶ James the son of Alphaeus (Mark 3:18)
⓷ James the father of the apostle Judas
⓸ James, the brother of Jesus, who later became overseer of the church in Jerusalem (Mark 6:3,1 Corinthians 15:7)
⓵ James the apostle was the first to be martyred. ⓶ and ⓷ lacked the influence to write this book and send it to many churches. Therefore the author of this book can be regarded as ⓸ James, the physical brother of Jesus.
There are several pieces of evidence that James, the physical brother of Jesus, is the author of this letter.
 First, in the early church James, together with Peter and John, was widely known as one of the "pillars of the church" (Acts 12:7, Galatians 2:12). Since the letter gives no particular introduction of James himself, we can see that its author was a person widely known to everyone.
 Second, the teaching and characteristics of what James said at the "Jerusalem Council (A.D. 49)" recorded in Acts and Galatians agree with this letter (Acts 15:13-21, 21:17-25, Galatians 1:19, 2:9-10).
Date of Writing
It is highly likely that James was written before A.D. 62. This is because there is the record of Josephus that James, the brother of Jesus, was martyred around A.D. 62 by the high priest Ananus.
There are two views on the date of writing.
1) The view that it was written before A.D. 49
2) The view that it was written in the early A.D. 60s
Most hold that it was written before A.D. 49, for the following reasons.
✅ There is no mention of the circumcision issue discussed at the Jerusalem Council (A.D. 49).
✅ The word "church" (James 5:14) appears once, and "synagogue" (James 2:2) is used.
✅ Only elders (James 5:14) and teachers (James 3:1) are mentioned, not overseers or deacons.
✅ There is no mention of the heresies that began to appear in earnest from the A.D. 60s.
The grounds for the view that it was written in the early A.D. 60s are as follows, but their validity is low.
❌ It is argued that it took a long time for Jewish believers to be scattered throughout the world, but they had already been scattered throughout the Roman world from the first century B.C.
❌ It is held that the letter was written to correct believers who misunderstood Paul's doctrine of "justification by faith," but this is only an inference.
❌ It is held that the tribulations and trials in this letter reflect a later situation, but this is not certain.
Therefore it is reasonable to regard James as having been written around A.D. 46-49, before the Jerusalem Council, and if so, we can see that it is the earliest letter written among the New Testament writings.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
James is a letter sent by James, the Lord's brother, who was one of the leaders of the Jerusalem church at that time, only a little less than twenty years after Jesus' resurrection and ascension, to Jewish-background believers scattered throughout the Roman Empire. They were people who had been scattered to escape persecution by Judaism after the martyrdom of Stephen (Acts 7:54-60) in the late A.D. 30s, and they were suffering great trials amid the rejection and persecution of their own countrymen.
Because they had not received sufficient instruction in the Christian faith, they still could not break free of Jewish habits, and they would proclaim godliness only in words while neglecting a practical faith (James 2:17-18). Moreover, some were more interested in accumulating wealth than in the kingdom of God and neglected their life of faith (James 4:13-17).
As a result, friction and quarrels arose within the church, and in particular the conflict between the rich and the poor became a serious problem (James 2:1-4, 4:1, 4:11-12).
Therefore James, a leader of the early church, sent this letter to the Diaspora Jewish believers, encouraging them to overcome trials by faith and exhorting them to grow in faith through a right life of faith that has works. Through this he sought to build up the early church firmly.
4. Characteristics of James
	(1)	Unlike Romans, which sets forth the principle of human salvation, this book records practical teachings that saved believers must keep in daily life, and it is called "the Proverbs of the New Testament" or "the Amos of the New Testament."
	(2)	It makes little direct mention of Jesus, but it contains more of the teachings that Jesus spoke than other books of the New Testament.
	(3)	It uses the most imperatives of any book in the New Testament. Of its 108 verses in total, 54 are in the imperative.
	(4)	Because it was written with Jewish-background believers as its primary audience, it has a strong Jewish coloring.
5. Main Themes of James
James is a letter sent in the late A.D. 40s to Jewish believers scattered throughout the Roman Empire, and it stresses practicing a mature life of faith with endurance even amid tribulation and trials. The main themes are as follows.
1) Trials and Temptation
The trials that believers undergo are of two kinds.
God's test (test): It appears as a trial (trial), and it produces refining and hope, leading to the crown of life.
Satan's temptation (temptation): It appears as an enticement, and in the end it leads to destruction.
Believers must overcome the trials of faith with endurance, and be on guard against Satan's temptation and cast off desires.
2) Faith and Works
Faith without works is dead faith (James 2:26). 
Saved believers must not stop at merely knowing the faith, but must put faith into practice in their lives.
3) Love Without Discrimination
Within the church, there must be no discrimination on the basis of wealth, poverty, or social status.
True believers must treat brothers and sisters with love and without prejudice, following the example of Christ rather than worldly values.
4) The Importance of Words
Wrong words within the church, the community of faith, do not end as an individual's problem but can destroy souls and throw the church into confusion.
Believers must grow in the character of faith, refrain from anger and rash words, and take care not to obscure the glory of God.
5) Avoiding Quarrels and Being Humble
Within the church community, believers must not stir up quarrels through desires, pride, and empty boasting.
Believers must humbly submit to God and hold a faith that makes peace.
6) Endurance and Prayer in Suffering
When persecution and trials come, it is important to endure and to pray.
God fills with good things even those who endure in suffering, and the prayer of faith becomes a power to overcome every difficulty.
Believers must also intercede for and help brothers who are suffering.
Thus James stresses the practice of faith and the right attitude within the community, and exhorts believers to advance toward a more mature faith.

1. Title
This book uses as it is the original title written in the Greek text, "Petrou Alpha (A)."
The titles of the New Testament books generally reflect the name of the writer (Matthew, James, Jude, etc.), the name of the recipient (1 and 2 Timothy, Philemon, etc.), the name of the place of the recipients (1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, etc.), or the subject (Acts); among these, this book reflects the name of the writer in its title. Moreover, the "Alpha (A)" after the name indicates that this letter is "Peter's first letter sent." The English version (KJV) also follows the Greek text and calls it "The First Epistle General of Peter."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
That Peter is the writer of this book has been accepted historically and traditionally.
In the early nineteenth century some critics doubted his authorship, pointing out that Peter, although a fisherman by background, freely quoted the Old Testament (the Septuagint). But this is an exaggerated claim that overemphasizes only his occupation.
- Peter was a devout believer (Luke 5:1-11),
- he met Jesus (about A.D. 27) and for some thirty years was active as a disciple and as an elder of the early church.
- By the time he wrote this book (about A.D. 64), he was already a leader with deep faith and rich experience.
- Moreover, considering that it was an age in which the illumination and power of the Holy Spirit were working strongly,
there is nothing strange at all in Peter's quoting the Scriptures (the Old Testament) (Acts 4:13-14). As concrete grounds,  
1) in 1:1 of this book the writer identifies himself as the apostle "Peter,"
2) the content of this book is the same as Peter's teaching that appears in Acts (1 Peter 1:7=Acts 10:24, 1 Peter 2:7-8=Acts 4:11),
3) and there is the testimony of the early church fathers (Polycarp, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, etc.).
Date of Writing
It is reported that Peter, as Jesus had prophesied (John 21:18-19), was martyred around A.D. 68, during Emperor Nero's persecution of Christians, by being crucified upside down in Rome.
Peter appears to have written this book around A.D. 62-64 while staying in Rome (referred to as "Babylon" in 1 Peter 5:13), and this coincides with the time when Emperor Nero's persecution of Christians began in A.D. 64.
Moreover, 2 Peter is presumed to have been written around A.D. 68, just before his martyrdom. This book was delivered throughout Asia Minor by Silvanus (Silas, 1 Peter 5:12), a fellow worker of Paul.
The letters that the apostles wrote at that time under the illumination of the Holy Spirit were read to one another in the local churches and became the standard for establishing order in the church, and the teaching of Christ, the prophetic promises, and the hope of the second coming became an important basis for strengthening the faith of the believers (Colossians 4:16).
[Colossians 4:16] After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
1 Peter is a letter that the apostle Peter sent to the believers in the regions of Asia Minor (Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia) (1 Peter 1:1-2). These churches had been connected with Peter from the beginning, and believers of Jewish and Gentile background lived the life of faith together, with people of various social classes mingled among them (1 Peter 2:1-25).
At the time Peter wrote this letter, under the reign of Emperor Nero (A.D. 54-68), the persecution of Christians that had begun in Rome in A.D. 64 was spreading throughout the empire, and the churches of Asia Minor were also already suffering considerable persecution from the Gentiles.
The reasons were:
1) Believers who had abandoned their former idols and turned away from the pleasures and sins of the world were slandered and persecuted (1 Peter 2:12, 3:9, 4:2-4, 4:14-16).
2) In the transitional situation of passing from Judaism of the Old Testament to the union of Gentiles in the New Testament age, the believers felt inner conflict in their attitude toward the Roman government in their locality, and they were experiencing confusion of faith about how to treat their Gentile masters (1 Peter 2:13-20).
Therefore Peter wrote this book to comfort believers who were suffering unjustly as Christians, to encourage them to strengthen their hope amid the coming persecution, and to establish the right attitude of faith toward Gentile authorities.
5. Characteristics of 1 Peter
1) It presents important subjects (doctrines) for Christians simply and clearly, and in variety.
 Although this book is a letter of short length, it contains in abundance the content of truth (the core doctrines) that the Holy Spirit reveals through Peter.
  - The work of each person of the Trinity (1 Peter 1:2)
  - The principle of the new birth (1 Peter 1:3, through the resurrection from the dead)
  - The principle of Jesus' substitutionary atonement (1 Peter 2:24, 1 Peter 3:18, =Romans 4:25)
  - Concerning the Creator (1 Peter 4:19)
  - Concerning Christ (1 Peter 1:20, 1 Peter 2:4-8, 21-25, 1 Peter 3:18-22, 1 Peter 5:1-4, 10)
  - Concerning salvation (1 Peter 1:8-9, 23-25, 1 Peter 2:9-10, 24, 1 Peter 3:18)
  - Concerning the church (1 Peter 2:5, 9, 1 Peter 5:1-9)
  - Concerning the end times and the second coming (1 Peter 1:13, 1 Peter 4:7, 13, 1 Peter 5:1, 10)
  - Concerning baptism (immersion) (1 Peter 3:21).. and so on
2) 1 & 2 Peter are letters of hope (Epistle of Hope).
 To the believers of Asia Minor who were being persecuted, this book gives comfort and hope by speaking of "the reward of the glory of heaven that is given when suffering is endured with faith."
3) Old Testament prophecy is mentioned more than in other letters.
 This seems to be a characteristic that arises because the writer of this book was Peter, the apostle to the Jews. By quoting Old Testament prophecy fittingly, Peter emphasizes that the Old Testament prophecies were fully fulfilled by Jesus Christ, and he clearly reveals the prophetic truths of the Old Testament in Christ.
4) It has many similarities with other letters, especially with the letters of Paul.
 This book has many similarities with the letters of the apostle Paul, Romans and Ephesians, and with James. Some even say that about half of the subjects dealt with in the New Testament letters are reflected in this book. (Holtzmann)
5) References to the words and teachings of Christ appear frequently.
 By directly quoting the words of Christ when presenting its core teachings, it suggests that Peter accompanied Jesus at His closest side during Jesus' public ministry. The more we understand this fact, the more the teachings and promises of the Lord, repeatedly stressed in this book through Peter, enable us who live in later generations to hope in faith for the promises of Christ's second coming and glory.
4. Structure of 1 Peter
 1) Introduction (1 Peter 1:1-12)
    ① Greeting (1:1-2)
    ② The reason believers can rejoice even in trials (1:3-12)
 2) Main Body (1 Peter 1:13-5:11)
    ① The holy life of the Christian (1:13-2:10)
- Personal exhortation / exhortation to love the brothers / the method and reason of sanctification
    ② The social duties of the Christian (2:11-3:7)
- Restraining fleshly desires / submitting to worldly institutions / the attitude of servants / the example of suffering / the duties of wife and husband
    ③ The Christian's attitude in overcoming suffering (3:8-5:11)
- Principal teaching / attitude toward persecutors / the benefit of suffering and exhortation to the life of a steward
- The joy of those who share in the sufferings of Christ / exhortation to the church in the midst of suffering
 3) Conclusion (1 Peter 5:12-14)
- Final charge and greetings (5:12-14)
★ Key word of 1 Peter: suffering (17 times in all: suffering of Christ: 7 times, suffering of Christians: 10)
6. Christ in 1 Peter
 The 66 books of the Bible differ in form and content, but their fundamental theme and purpose lie in "the salvation of us sinners through the redemptive work of Jesus Christ." When we meditate on the content about Jesus Christ in each book of the Bible written under the illumination of the Holy Spirit, we gain many truths and teachings.
In particular, when we examine the content about Christ presented in 1 Peter, ① through the picture of the suffering (death) that Jesus underwent we learn the attitude to take toward the suffering that comes upon believers, and ② through the picture of Jesus' resurrection and glory we strengthen the sure hope of the resurrection and glory promised to believers.
1) The Suffering Christ (1 Peter 2:21-25)
 Jesus Christ was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born; He committed no sin at all and no deceit was in His mouth, yet He was reviled by men, was struck with whips, and in the end was hung on a cross and put to death. Jesus' suffering and death were not because He was powerless or because of anyone's coercion, but He underwent them willingly, within the will of God, in order to redeem us sinners. (Matthew 16:21-28, Matthew 17:22-23, Matthew 20:17-19, Matthew 26:1-5 → repeated also in Mark and Luke)
[John 10:18] No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from My Father.”
This fact is so that saved believers, after being saved, may see this world rightly in the truth, place their true hope of life in heaven, and, whatever suffering they may encounter in this world, live a holy life in endurance, following in the footsteps of the Lord. That is why Jesus solemnly said to His disciples, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (Matthew 16:24, Mark 8:34, Luke 9:23)."
[1 Peter 2:21] For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps:
2) Christ at the Right Hand of God's Throne (1 Peter 1:3, 21 → 1 Peter 3:22)
And Jesus' resurrection focuses on one place all our recognition of value and the standard of our hope. That is, Jesus, who rose to justify us (Romans 4:25), is now at the right hand of God's throne, both the advocate of our redemption (1 John 2:1) and the guarantee of our glory (Hebrews 7:22-25). Also, just as God placed Jesus, who suffered even to death on this earth, in the highest glory (Philippians 2:9-11), we who are in Christ also suffer on this earth, but when the Lord returns in glory He will change our lowly bodies into the form of glory (Philippians 3:21). Thinking of Christ, who even now is at the right hand of God's throne as the guarantee of all these promises, we too are able to live in this world with strength, in hope.
[Romans 6:5] For if we have been united with Him like this in His death, we will certainly also be united with Him in His resurrection.

1. Title
In the Greek text it is given the title "Petrou Beta," that is, "Peter's second," in order to distinguish it from his first letter, "Petrou Alpha." The English Authorized Version (KJV) uses the title "The Second Epistle General of Peter."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
The evidence within this book itself that 2 Peter was written by Peter
1) In 1:1 the writer gives his name as "Simon Peter."
2) The writer says that he heard directly from Jesus about his death.
(2 Peter 1:14) because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me./ (John 21:18-19) 
3) In this book the writer clearly states that he was a witness on the Mount of Transfiguration. There were only three witnesses who saw the Lord's transfiguration on the mountain: Peter, James, and John. (Matthew 17:1-8, Mark 9:2-8, Luke 9:28:36)
(2 Peter 1:16-18) For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.
4) The expression "second letter" presupposes that there was a first letter, and it is clear that the writer of this book is the same person as Peter, who is mentioned as the writer of the first letter.
(2 Peter 3:1) Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking
Date of Writing
It is known that Peter was martyred during the reign of Emperor Nero in Rome by being crucified upside down (A.D. 68). Judging from the expression "it is time for judgment to begin at the household of God" (1 Peter 4:17), 1 Peter was written before the great persecution in Rome (A.D. 64) began. Then 2 Peter appears to date between A.D. 64, when the first letter was written, and A.D. 68, when Peter died, that is, between A.D. 66 and 67.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
Historical Background
The time when 2 Peter was written was the end of Nero's reign, and the Roman Empire had fallen into extreme moral corruption and social disorder. In particular, after the Great Fire of Rome (A.D. 64), the emperor laid the blame for the fire on the Christians and inflicted a large-scale persecution.
The believers of the early church at that time had been taught to live in hope of Christ's second coming and glory. But as the second coming was delayed and the persecution grew severe, the faith of some believers began to waver. Taking advantage of this, false teachers spread the claim that "the second coming and the judgment are false."
In this situation, within the church
- people whose faith was not firm compromised with unbelievers and fell morally.
- false prophets and false teachers (heretics) appeared and spread wrong teachings that corrupted the believers still further.
The representative false teachings were
1) abusing the freedom obtained by faith as moral license (2 Peter 2:19),
2) denying the second coming of Christ (2 Peter 3:4).
(2 Peter 2:19) They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.
(2 Peter 3:4) “Where is the promise of His coming?” they will ask. “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.”
Motive for Writing
After writing 1 Peter to encourage believers suffering from outside persecution, Peter immediately wrote 2 Peter to warn of the danger posed by false teachers within, and to enable believers to live with assurance of Christ's second coming without falling into deception.
In particular he
1) tried to protect the believers from being deceived by apostasy and false teaching.
2) tried to encourage and exhort the suffering believers.
3) warned not only of outside persecution (1 Peter) but also of the problem of heresy within (2 Peter).
4) exhorted the believers to discern false teachers and to fight against immoral hedonism (2 Peter 2:1-3).
5) realizing that the activity of the apostles, who had been the focal point of the early church, was all drawing to a close and that his own martyrdom was near (2 Peter 1:13), he left this book so that all believers, even after the apostolic age, might live with assurance of Christ's second coming and the end times.
That is, 2 Peter is a message that exhorts believers to hold fast to the hope of the second coming and to keep the faith to the end.
4. Characteristics of 2 Peter
	(1)	This letter, which warns against false teachers and exhorts believers not to fall into heretical thought, notably speaks of the judgment of the false teachers, and in particular, citing the precedents of God's judgment that appear in the Old Testament (2:3-8), it stresses that judgment will surely come upon them.
	(2)	Knowledge in Christ, by which truth can be discerned, is especially emphasized. The words "know" and "knowledge" occur as many as sixteen times in this book, and six of them refer to "the knowledge of Christ"; the knowledge this book speaks of is true knowledge that comes from the Holy Spirit, as a concept opposed to the false knowledge of the heretics.
	(3)	This book, whose main content is a warning against heresy, together with 1 Peter, which records comfort and encouragement for persecuted believers, is valuable material for the study of persecution and heresy, the two great problems of the early church of that time.
	(4)	It has much in common with the book of Jude, which contains a warning against false teachers.
5. Structure of 2 Peter
1) The Spiritual Maturity of Believers and the Certainty of the Second Coming (1:1-21)
①Greeting (1:1-2)
②Exhortation to a godly life and spiritual maturity (1:3-11)
③The motive for writing this book (1:12-15)
④Defense of the certainty of Christ's second coming (1:16-21)
2) Warning Against the Deception of False Teachers, and Their Unrighteousness and Judgment (2:1-22)
①The identity and nature of the false teachers (2:1-3)
②Judgment on the unrighteous and Old Testament examples (2:4-10a)
③The doctrinal and moral unrighteousness of the false teachers (2:10b-19)
④The final state of the apostates (2:20-22)
3) The Certainty of Christ's Second Coming and Judgment (3:1-18)
①The certainty of the end times and the second coming (3:1-7)
②The reason for the delay of Christ's second coming (3:8-10)
③Exhortation to long for the second coming (3:11-13)
④Concluding exhortation (3:14-18)
5. Christ in 2 Peter
1) Christ, the Source of True Spiritual Knowledge
 This book says that in order for believers not to be deceived by heretical teachings and to attain right spiritual maturity, they must possess Christ, the source of true spiritual knowledge. Through Christ's redemptive work He is our Savior, who has caused us to be legally declared righteous before God.
(2 Peter 1:1) Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours:
He is also the One who, by setting an example in His life during the period of His public ministry, has made known the goal of sanctification that believers are to achieve.
Accordingly, this book exhorts, "But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (2 Peter 3:18).
2) Christ, Who Will Come Again as Judge
Christ's second coming at the end of the world is the event that fulfills the prophecies and promises of the Old Testament, and it is the event that proves the truthfulness of the New Testament. And it proves that the faith of the New Testament-era believers who believed the promises of Scripture was not in vain.
Therefore the day of the second coming will be a day of judgment for those who did wrong, but for the believing saints it is the day of obtaining the glory of heaven.
Accordingly, this book refutes the false teaching that denies the second coming and stresses that Christ will surely come again as Judge (1:16-21, 3:4-7). It also exhorts believers to live a holy life worthy of the Lord's calling and election, in the assurance and hope of the second coming (3:8-14).

1. Title
The Korean title of this book, "1 John," reflects the name of the writer and the order in which the letters were written, and it takes over as it is the title of Codex Sinaiticus, which is recorded as "Ioannou Epistole Alpha (John's first letter)."
2. Author and Date of Writing
The writer of this book is "the apostle John," the writer of the Gospel of John. As for the date of writing, taking the book of Revelation to have been written last, it was written while John was in Ephesus, before he was persecuted and exiled to the island of Patmos.
Taking the date of writing of the Gospel of John to be A.D. 85-90, the letters of John would have been written in the period between the Gospel of John and Revelation, and they are presumed to have been written around A.D. 90-95. And the place of writing of this book is Ephesus. The recipients of this book are presumed to be the regions of Asia Minor, including the church at Ephesus where the apostle John was, and it would have been circulated among the churches and read as a public document.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
This letter was written about fifty years after the church began, when it was suffering from outside persecution and from the problem of heresy within.
At that time the Roman emperor Domitian (A.D. 81-96) called himself a god and severely persecuted the believers who confessed Christ as Lord. Because of this, the apostle John too was exiled to the island of Patmos.
Internally, a heresy influenced by Greek philosophy had infiltrated. Asserting a dualism in which spirit is good and flesh is evil, they
1) denied the incarnation of Christ,
2) denied the merit of the cross by claiming that salvation is obtained by spiritual knowledge (gnosis, Gnosticism), and
3) showed a tendency to fall into asceticism or hedonism.
Therefore, in order to protect the believers and establish the right faith, this letter was written 
① to emphasize that Jesus is God who came in the flesh, 
② to affirm that salvation is accomplished solely by the merit of Christ, and 
③ to make clear that one must live a holy life for right fellowship with God.
4. Theme of 1 John
John is called "the apostle of love," and this book is called "the letter of love." The core theme of this letter is "fellowship," and for true fellowship with God it stresses abandoning heretical ideas and standing firm on the truth of the gospel, and putting love for the brothers into practice.
1) Fellowship with God
It is thanks to the merit of Christ the Mediator that we, who were sinners, can have fellowship with God. Therefore faith in Christ and the gospel is necessary for right fellowship with God.
2) Sin and Fellowship
Sin cuts off fellowship with God. Because God is holy, He does not tolerate sin. Believers must walk in the light and keep far from sin, and if they sin, they must restore fellowship by confessing and repenting immediately.
3) Love for the Brothers and Fellowship with God
True love for the brothers comes from fellowship with God. The power to love the brothers comes not from our own ability but from faith through Jesus Christ. Believers, as beings like a mirror that reflects the light of God, must play the role of brightening the darkness of the world.
4) Love for God and Love for the Brothers
One who loves God must love the brothers. Mere religious zeal cannot be called loving God. Love for God is proved by loving the brothers. (1 John 4:12, 20)
5) Spiritual Discernment
One must not accept every spirit and teaching indiscriminately. Believers must discern whether a teaching belongs to the Spirit of truth that is of God, or to a false spirit that is of the devil. They must believe only in the deity and humanity of Christ and in the salvation and eternal life through His death on the cross and resurrection, and reject other teachings.
6) The Guidance of the Holy Spirit
The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth who bears witness to Jesus, and He dwells in believers and guides them. Therefore believers must day by day receive the illumination of the Holy Spirit, meditate on Scripture, and put the will of God into practice. (John 15:26-27)
7) The World and Idolatry
To love the world is to serve idols. Believers cannot serve God and the world at the same time, and must live a life of serving God alone.
5. Seven Contrasts in 1 John
1) Light and darkness (1 John 1:5-11)
2) Christ and the antichrist (1 John 2:18-28)
3) God the Father and the world (1 John 2:12-17)
4) Righteousness and lawlessness (1 John 2:29-3:24)
5) The Holy Spirit and the false spirit (1 John 4:1-6)
6) Love and false love (1 John 4:7-21)
7) New life and this world (1 John 5:18-19)

1. Title
"Ioannou Epistole Beta" is the original Greek title and means the second letter of the apostle John; it reflects the name of the writer and the order in which it was sent.
2. Author and Date of Writing
2 John was written by the apostle John, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus. He was called a "son of thunder" (Mark 3:17) and was a disciple especially loved by Jesus (John 13:23). He was also a son of Zebedee (Mark 1:19) and a brother of the apostle James (Matthew 4:21).
After the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, John led the church at Ephesus in Asia Minor for about twenty-five years. Later, because of the persecution of the Roman emperor Domitian (A.D. 81-96), he was exiled to the island of Patmos, and there he wrote the book of Revelation.
He wrote five books of the New Testament in all: the Gospel of John, 1, 2, and 3 John, and Revelation. In particular, 2 John is so similar in content and character to 1 John that it could be called an abridged edition of 1 John, so it is clear that the same author wrote it.
The date of writing is about A.D. 90-95; it is presumed to have been written after the Gospel of John (A.D. 85-90) and immediately after 1 John. 2 John was written for the purpose of supplementing and emphasizing the content of 1 John.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
In the early church there were itinerant evangelists and teachers who visited believers' homes and taught the word. But false teachers and heretics abused this, going around among the churches, deceiving the believers and leading them away from the truth.
Therefore the apostle John wrote 2 John, stressing that believers should be on guard against the antichrist who distorts the truth and deceives believers with sophistry, and that, as those who have received the love of Christ, they should put the love of God into practice.
4. Theme of 2 John
Exhortation to keep the commandment "love one another" and warning against the deceiving antichrist.
Abiding only in the word of Christ, who is the truth, as mature believers who have been saved,
it exhorts them to practice love for one another and enjoy true joy,
and at the same time it records, briefly and clearly, the warning (the attitude toward false teachers) against the antichrist who deceives people into drifting away from abiding in the truth and from true faith, and into immoral conduct.

1. Title
The title of this book, "3 John," reflects the name of the author and the order in which the letters were written, and derives from the title written in the Greek text, "Ioannou Epistole Gamma," that is, "John's third letter." Here "Gamma," which corresponds to the third letter of the Greek alphabet, tells us that this book was written after 1 and 2 John. Also, the title of most English Bibles follows the tradition of the original text and is recorded as "The Third Epistle of John."
2. Author and Date of Writing
The author of this book is the apostle John, the author of the Gospel of John, 1 John, 2 John, and Revelation. As in 2 John, in the first verse of 3 John the writer identifies himself as the elder. That he gives only the church title "elder," without writing his name specifically, hints that he was a famous person whom the recipients could immediately recognize.
"Elder" (Greek "presbyteros"): the comparative of "old" (Greek "presbys"). It was used not only in connection with a church office but also as a title of respect for the maturity and character that come with age.
By the time he wrote this letter John was a white-haired old man, and as pastor of the church at Ephesus he was a person for whom the title "elder" was fitting. In this sense the Korean Common Translation rendered it with the word "senior" instead of "elder."
As for the time of writing, like 2 John it was written while he was in Ephesus, before he was persecuted and exiled to the island of Patmos. The date of writing is presumed to be about A.D. 90-95, immediately after 2 John.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
This letter is a private letter sent to Gaius, and it deals with the church's problem in dealing with itinerant teachers. Gaius welcomed them, but Diotrephes, the church's domineering leader, rejected them.
Diotrephes was a leader who in particular exalted his own position, mistreated the itinerant teachers, and even committed the evil of excommunicating believers who received the itinerant teachers. Therefore the apostle John rebukes Diotrephes and shows his apostolic authority (verse 10). This letter was probably delivered to Gaius by Demetrius.
3 John was written around A.D. 90-95 amid the persecution of the Roman emperor Domitian (A.D. 81-96). At that time the church was suffering from the infiltration of heresy, the martyrdom of the apostles, a shortage of leaders, and so on.
In this situation John stressed the believers' hospitality toward itinerant teachers and the role of a right leader.
Purpose of Writing
1) Hospitality toward itinerant teachers
In the early church, itinerant teachers who preached the gospel devoted themselves without payment and lived by the help of the believers. But as false teachers disguised themselves as itinerant teachers and deceived believers, the true itinerant teachers came to suffer harm.
Therefore John contrasted Gaius, who welcomed the itinerant teachers, with Diotrephes, who rejected them, and taught that believers ought to receive and welcome the Lord's workers.
2) Resolving the problem of church leaders
At that time, domineering behavior and division on the part of leaders were occurring in the church. John set forth the picture of a right leader by comparing Gaius, who humbly served the servants of the Lord, with Diotrephes, who abused power and excommunicated believers.
3) Emphasis on the unity and cooperation of the church
He stressed that through the itinerant teachers all the churches should follow the apostle's teaching, and that the believers should realize they are one body in Christ and cooperate with one another for the expansion of the kingdom of God.
4) Recommending Demetrius and announcing a plan to visit
