John wanted to recommend Demetrius, who appears to have delivered this letter, to Gaius, and to announce his own plan to visit.
4. Structure of 3 John
[Key point] Do not imitate what is evil but what is good (1:11)
[Theme] The value of walking in the truth and the danger of pride
Introduction (1:1-4)
1:1 Greeting
1:2-4 A prayer of blessing for Gaius, who walks in the truth, and the expression of apostolic joy
Main Body (1:5-12)
1:5-8 Praise and encouragement for Gaius, who welcomes itinerant teachers (1:5-8)
1:9-10 Rebuke and warning of the proud Diotrephes
1:11 Charge to Gaius to imitate what is good
1:12 Introduction and praise of Demetrius
Conclusion (1:13-15)
1:13-15 Closing words, blessing, and greetings
5. Characteristics of 3 John
1) It is a personal letter sent to a specific recipient. 
Among the letters of John, this book has the most complete letter form and is a letter consistent in its personal content. 
2) There is no direct mention of Christ. 
There is only an indirect depiction by the expressions "for the sake of the name" (verse 7) and "truth." 
3) It specifically mentions the false forces opposing the truth. 
By naming not only the name Diotrephes but also listing the evil deeds he committed one by one, it urges thorough vigilance against him. 
4) It is a letter of short content, of a length that could be written on a single sheet of papyrus of that day. 
Like 2 John, this hints that a visit by the apostle John to the recipients would soon take place.

1. Title
The Greek title is "Ioudas," that is, "Book of Jude," which uses the name of the writer as it is as the title. The Korean Revised Version likewise follows the title of the Greek text and takes "Jude" as its title.
2. Author and Date of Writing
 The author of this book is recorded as Jude, the younger brother of James, who was the physical brother of Jesus. 
(Jude 1:1) Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ:
The writer introduces himself as "Jude, the brother of James," and James was Jesus' physical younger brother and a leader of the early Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13, Galatians 2:9). Although Jude lived together with Jesus for a long time as His physical brother, he did not recognize Jesus as the Christ and did not believe in Him; but only after Jesus' death, resurrection, and ascension did he receive Him as the Christ, and he played a pivotal role in the early church in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14, 1 Corinthians 9:5).
This book is presumed to have been written after A.D. 70, judging from the fact that it mainly speaks of a warning against the heresy of Gnosticism, which arose in the latter half of the first century, and that it contains no prophecy of the fall of Jerusalem (A.D. 70). Moreover, since Jude is thought to have been martyred between A.D. 70 and 80, the date of writing is presumed to be between A.D. 70 and 80. And the place of writing of this book is presumed to be Jerusalem, where Jude mainly worked.
(Matthew 13:55) “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son? Isn’t His mother’s name Mary, and aren’t His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas?
(John 7:5) For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.
(Acts 1:14) together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus and with His brothers, they devoted themselves with one mind to prayer
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
The Gnostics, who appeared from the latter half of the first century, undermined the believers' faith in two ways.
First, doctrinally, they denied the incarnation of Jesus Christ.
Second, ethically, they advocated extreme asceticism or, on the contrary, encouraged license and pleasure.
Jude too points out their problems and warns against making the grace of God a pretext for sexual license and against denying the incarnation of Christ (Jude 1:4).
Jude had originally intended to write a letter about the gospel, but seeing that false teachers had infiltrated the church, he changed the content to the message "contend for the faith." He starkly exposes the depravity of the heretics and stresses that God's judgment will surely come.
Even today, heretics try to undermine the faith within the church. Jude teaches us that toward teachings that threaten the essence of the gospel, not tolerance but resolute action is needed.
4. Lessons of Jude
Jude reveals the identity and fate of heretics and teaches believers how to hold fast to the faith. This is an important lesson not only for the early church but also for us who live under the threat of heresy today.
1) Heretics hide their identity
Heretics appear to follow the gospel, but in fact they spread false teaching. Believers must stand firm on the word of God and discern true teaching from false teaching. Only then can they avoid falling into the temptation of heresy and protect other believers.
(Jude 1:4) For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
2) Be resolute in guarding against heresy
Heretics make the grace of God a pretext for license, and they deny the incarnation of Jesus Christ. They cannot escape God's judgment. Believers must deal with them resolutely, without sympathy or an ambiguous attitude.
(Jude 1:4) For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
3) The way to victory in the fight against heresy
Obeying the word of Scripture, praying in the Holy Spirit, and abiding in the love of God is the way to victory in the spiritual fight against heresy. Because the forces of Satan are behind heresy, our fight can be won not by human methods but when we go forward wearing the full armor of God.
(Jude 1:20-21) But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life.
4) Live in hope of heaven
Believers must live with heaven, not this earth, as their final destination. To thoroughly reject heresy and humanistic philosophy, which make people cling to fleshly desires and to the world, and to depend on and obey God alone, is the mark of a true Christian.
5) Help brothers and sisters who have fallen into heresy
We must not turn away from believers who have been deceived by heresy, but with love and concern help them return to the truth. Correcting their errors and leading them to the mercy of God is our duty.
(Jude 1:22-23) And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.
Jude teaches us not to compromise with heresy but to contend for the faith. It is the mission of the believer to trust God, stand firm on the word, and keep the faith to the end.
5. Structure of Jude
 Jude is a single chapter made up of 25 verses; it is a short letter, yet it has all the elements of the general letter form. Looking at the content structure of Jude according to the letter form, it can be divided into the introduction of verses 1-4, the main body of verses 5-23, and the conclusion of verses 24 and 25.
① Introduction (Jude 1:1-4)
After conveying greetings to the recipients, Jude states that the direction of his writing has changed. He explains that he had originally intended to write about "the salvation we share," but because of the appearance of false teachers he had to send a letter of exhortation to "contend for the faith."
② Main Body (Jude 1:5-23)
In the main body he warns of the wickedness of the false teachers and the certainty of God's judgment on them. Jude sets out their characteristics in detail and, reminding the believers of the apostles' prophecies, urges them to be on guard against the false teachers. He also exhorts the believers to stand on the right faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, and hope for the second coming of Jesus Christ. Going further, he charges them to have mercy on those who have fallen into heresy and to save them.
③ Conclusion (Jude 1:24 25)
Finally Jude closes the letter by praising God, who keeps believers from all evil. He stresses that God alone is the One on whom believers rely, and the One who gives strength to overcome all difficulties.
7. Christ in Jude
The Bible contains a variety of forms and content, but its center is the redemptive work of Jesus Christ. In Jude too we can see various aspects of Christ.
① The Judge of Justice
Jesus Christ will come again and judge all people. In particular, He will judge the false teachers and those who follow them with eternal punishment. This is the same as what was said, that there is no forgiveness for those who oppose the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:31).
(Jude 1:15) to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.” 
② The One Who Shows Mercy

1. Title
Named according to the writer's name and the character of the book. Because it is "the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1:1), its title is "Revelation of John."
In the Greek text too it carries the heading "Apokalypsis Ioannou" (Revelation of John). The Greek title "Apokalypsis" (Apocalypse) literally means the "revelation" (Revelation) of what is hidden or concealed.
"Revelation" (apokalypsis) = "uncovering, unveiling, revelation" - a noun derived from "apokalypto" (to remove a covering, to make visible). "Apo" ("from" or "away from") + "kalypto" ("to cover, to conceal, to hide")
It is a word that appears often in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, and in Paul's letters, but is hard to find in other biblical texts. In this book too the word is used only in the opening text. "Apokalypsis" can be translated as "revelation (Revelation)," meaning "the act of God showing his will to human beings and the whole of its content in the broadest sense," or as "apocalypse (Apocalypse)," meaning "among God's revelations, only the act and content of disclosing his providence concerning the end times in the apocalyptic literary form, in a limited sense."
2. Author and Date of Writing
Author
It was written by John, the disciple of Jesus who wrote the Gospel of John and the letters of John. In style, vocabulary, and composition, it is certain that there was a single writer. The author of Revelation is John, as the Bible itself testifies (1:1,2,4,9; 22:8).
Because John introduces himself only as "a servant of Jesus" (1:1), there is some controversy over who this John is. But because he was widely known in the early church, we can see that he was someone whose apostolic authority was recognized without any special explanation.
Several fathers of the early church - Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Hippolytus, and Origen - all acknowledged that the author of Revelation was the apostle John.
He states that he was exiled while preaching the gospel (1:9), which agrees with the fact that the apostle John was exiled to the island of Patmos in the reign of the emperor Domitian (A.D. 81-96). 
Date of Writing
The date of writing too is presumed to be the Domitian period (A.D. 81-96). Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon (A.D. 140-200?), also testified, "Revelation was written not long ago but in the reign of Domitian." 
The end of Domitian's reign (A.D. 81-96), A.D. 95-96, is the most likely.
3. Occasion and Background of Writing
Motive for Writing
This book was written against the background of a crisis situation in which, when the church had overcome all the jealousy and persecution of the Judaizers and the challenges of various Gentile religious ideas and by about A.D. 90 had spread throughout Rome, the Roman government began a great persecution on an empire-wide scale, while within the church too heretics were incessantly tempting the believers. That is, in this crisis situation, it was given and written, above all, to present to the church the end of history and the resulting different destinies of the church and the world, so that the church would not be swept away within the world but would keep the purity of its faith.
Background
The tenth Roman emperor, Domitian (A.D. 81-96), deified himself in order to strengthen imperial power and forced all the people to worship him. As a result, religions that conflicted with emperor worship were prohibited, and in particular Christianity, which believes in the triune God, became a target of persecution. In the end an imperial edict prohibiting the Christian faith was proclaimed, and the early church faced full-scale organized persecution.
The early church faced not only outside persecution but also challenges from within. As the apostles and the first generation of the faith disappeared and the second and third generations became the center of the church, the passion of faith cooled and love among the believers weakened. 
At the same time heresies opposed to the gospel appeared; the Nicolaitans, in particular, said, "Since we have been cleansed of sin by the blood of Jesus, it no longer matters if we sin," and encouraged idol worship and an immoral life. They also ridiculed as foolish the believers who were martyred in resistance to emperor worship.
Thus the early church faced two great threats: outwardly, the persecution of the Roman Empire, and inwardly, the decline of faith and the spread of heresy. Therefore the Lord gave the believers a revelation, informing them that the powers of this world and of Satan are maintained only temporarily but will in the end be destroyed, and that the believers will enjoy eternal life and joy in heaven.
Revelation was written to instill in the believers assurance of ultimate salvation and victory and to encourage them to keep the faith. Although the seven churches of Asia Minor were the formal recipients, this message was for the church of every age, not only of that time.
This revelation is given so that the believers may keep the faith amid persecution, overcome the temptations and oppression of the world, and live a life that hopes for heaven. Ultimately the authority of Satan will end with the second coming of Christ, and the people of God will enjoy eternal blessing. Therefore we must not be deceived by the world before our eyes, but must keep our faith firmly and live a life that looks to heaven.
4. Characteristics of Revelation
Set against the background of the apocalyptic literature of the Old Testament (Daniel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc.), it is the only Christ-centered eschatological prophetic book of the New Testament, and it is highly symbolic.

[Chapter 1] The Beginning of Creation
God created the heavens, the earth, and all things in six days, and rested on the seventh day
① First day: He created the material world.
God created the heavens and the earth, and also created light (1:1-5). Out of the nothingness and disorder of heaven and earth, He created the heavenly bodies, order, and light of heaven and earth.
② Second day: He made the expanse (the sky), and made the waters above the expanse and the waters below (1:6-8).
③ Third day: He separated land and sea (1:9-13), and caused the earth to bring forth grass, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees bearing fruit with seed in it.
Because of this, it is thought that the law of photosynthesis and nature's capacity for self-purification came into existence.
④ Fourth day: He completed the original function of the sun, moon, and stars, causing them to make day and night, seasons, days, and years (verses 14-19).
⑤ Fifth day: He created soulish beings. He created the birds of the air and the fish (1:20-23).
⑥ Sixth day: He created spiritual man. He made the livestock of the earth, the creeping things, and the beasts.

[Chapter 2] The Beginning of Humanity
The creation of Adam, the making of the garden of Eden, Eve as Adam's helper suitable for him, the first family, the beginning of the family
Together with redemptive-historical truth, this text shows God's principle of creation concerning the relationship between man and woman. Man and woman were created by God according to the same principle and from the same elements, and they are legally equal persons. Nevertheless, there is a difference of order according to the order of creation. Furthermore, man and woman were created to complement each other, and in order to realize this, it stresses that the family institution, in which one man and one woman are united, is from the beginning the best institution in accordance with God's principle of creation.

[Chapter 22] God's Test Commanding the Offering of Isaac
Abraham
God gave Abraham the test of offering Isaac as a burnt offering. That test is a test of faith, a test of obedience, and a test of love. Just as a teacher gives students a test from the good motive of improving and checking their ability, God gives it from a good motive, to improve faith and devotion and to confirm faith. 
Isaac
Isaac carried the wood for the burnt offering up to Mount Moriah and built an altar with his father Abraham. Afterward Abraham bound Isaac and laid him on the altar.
Isaac's exact age is not recorded, but since he carried by himself the large amount of wood needed for the burnt offering, he was very likely about 17-20 years old. Abraham was then 117-120 years old, and if Isaac had wished, he could easily have resisted or run away. But the Bible has no record that he resisted. This shows that Isaac obeyed and entrusted himself wholly to his father.
Even before death, Isaac was not afraid but trusted God and obeyed. His figure foreshadows Jesus, who bore the cross and went to Golgotha. Like Jesus, "like a lamb led to the slaughter, silent" (Isaiah 53:7), Isaac too obeyed without saying a word. He was a type of Jesus.

[Chapter 32] Jacob's Wrestling with God
In the past Jacob had deceived his brother Esau and taken his birthright and blessing, and now he came to the moment when he had to face his brother's anger. He had fled from Laban, but now he was about to face another crisis, the meeting with Esau.
1. Preparation to Meet Esau
Although Jacob had experienced God's protection many times, he still relied on his own wisdom. He sent messengers to his brother Esau, intending to inform him of his change in a respectful manner, but when he heard the news that Esau was coming with 400 men, he fell into fear.
2. Praying, Yet Still Relying on His Own Plan
Jacob believed God's promise and prayed, but at the same time he made and carried out his own plans. Even while praying, instead of waiting for God's answer he tried to solve the problem in his own way.
3. Preparing Gifts to Appease His Brother's Anger
Jacob could not trust God fully, and he divided his livestock into several herds and sent them as gifts, trying to calm his brother's anger. But the pattern of trying to solve the problem in his own way rather than believing God's promise continued.
4. Wrestling with God (the Incident at the Jabbok River)
After sending his family and possessions across first, Jacob remained alone and wrestled with God all night. 
The wrestling here is an expression that shows not only physical wrestling but also Jacob's desperate and urgent supplication, clinging and crying out in prayer all night. 
God struck the hip socket so that Jacob would no longer rely on his own wisdom. In his helpless state Jacob had no choice but to cling to God, and in the end he came to obey God. 
※Hip socket: the lower part of the waist, the upper part of the leg, that is, the thigh; or the pelvic bone that supports the waist from the hip
5. Being Given the New Name "Israel"
Jacob received the name "Israel," which symbolizes a new personality and character. 
The name "Israel" fits better with the idea of "one who fought together with God and prevailed" or "one who fought with God's help" than with the idea of "one who contended with God and won."
It meant that Jacob must now live a God-centered life, not a self-centered one.
6. Further Sanctification at Peniel
Peniel is a compound word made up of two words, face and God (El).
Jacob named the place where he wrestled with God face to face "Peniel" and came to realize God's grace. Afterward he walked away limping, and this symbolizes that his old self was broken and a new life of relying on God had begun.

We can learn from the faith of Moses' parents who hid Moses (Hebrews 11:23). Moses' parents were born in Egypt (Numbers 26:59). [Chapter 4] Moses Receives a New Mission
He thinks, "They will not believe me or listen to my voice" (Exodus 4:1). He considers himself one who is not eloquent, slow of speech and slow of tongue (Exodus 4:10). He refuses, saying, "Please, Lord, send someone else" (Exodus 4:13).
With a different heart from the Moses of forty who had earlier set out to deliver the people of Israel by himself in Egypt, the eighty-year-old Moses is called by God and goes to the people of Israel.
We can see that Moses, who has received a new mission, still has an unresolved matter of circumcision (Exodus 4:24).

[Chapter 5] Moses Before Pharaoh and the Heavier Labor
Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and deliver the word of the LORD: "Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness" (Exodus 5:1). But Pharaoh not only refuses (Exodus 5:2); he judges that the people of Israel want to go into the wilderness because they are lazy, and he commands them to make the same number of bricks as before without giving them straw for the bricks (Exodus 5:7-8).
Because of this the people of Israel resent Moses and Aaron, and Moses also cries out to God, "Why have you done evil to this people?" (Exodus 5:22). Though they obeyed God's word and went to Pharaoh, the situation only grew worse.

[Chapter 6] Reaffirmation of God's Covenant and Promise of Deliverance
God tells the discouraged Moses that Pharaoh will in the end send the people of Israel out (Exodus 6:1).
God reveals Himself as the LORD and declares that He remembered the covenant He made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 6:2-5). God also promises, "I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians," and "I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God" (Exodus 6:6-7).
But the people of Israel do not listen to Moses because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery (Exodus 6:9). Moses hesitates again, saying that if even the people will not listen to him, how will Pharaoh listen (Exodus 6:12). Nevertheless God again commands Moses and Aaron with the mission to lead Israel out of Egypt. It shows that the accomplishment of deliverance depends not on people's circumstances or response but on God's covenant and power.

[Chapter 7] Moses and Aaron Display God's Power Before Pharaoh
God makes Moses like God to Pharaoh and makes Aaron his prophet (Exodus 7:1). Moses and Aaron deliver God's word to Pharaoh, but God says He will harden Pharaoh's heart so that signs and wonders will multiply in the land of Egypt (Exodus 7:3-4).
The miracle of Aaron's staff becoming a serpent is performed. The magicians of Egypt do something similar, but Aaron's staff swallows up their staffs (Exodus 7:10-12). Even so, Pharaoh does not listen to Moses and Aaron.
Then the first plague comes, in which the water of the Nile turns to blood (Exodus 7:20-21). When the magicians of Egypt do something similar, Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he does not accept God's word. The greatness of the LORD's power over the gods of Egypt begins to be revealed in earnest.

[Chapter 8] The Plagues of Frogs, Lice, and Flies, and Pharaoh's Repeated Change of Heart
When Pharaoh does not let the people of Israel go, the plague of frogs comes upon the whole land of Egypt. As the plague grows severe, Pharaoh promises Moses and Aaron that he will let the people go if they entreat the LORD to take the frogs away (Exodus 8:8). But when the plague stops, he hardens his heart again (Exodus 8:15).
Next comes the plague in which the dust of the earth becomes lice. The magicians of Egypt, who could not imitate this, say to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God," but Pharaoh does not listen (Exodus 8:19).
In the plague of flies, God sets apart the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel live, so that the plague does not come upon it (Exodus 8:22-23). Pharaoh again promises to let the people go, but after the plague is removed he hardens his heart once more.

[Chapter 9] The Plagues of the Death of Livestock, Boils, and Hail, and the Hardened Pharaoh
A severe plague on the livestock comes upon Pharaoh, who will not let Israel go. God sets apart the livestock so that the livestock of the Egyptians die but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel dies (Exodus 9:6). Even so, Pharaoh's heart is hardened.
Then the plague of boils comes upon man and beast, and even the magicians of Egypt cannot stand before Moses because of the boils (Exodus 9:10-11). After that, God warns of the plague of hail and gives those who fear the word of God a chance to bring their servants and livestock to shelter (Exodus 9:18-21).
Because of the plague of hail, Pharaoh says, "I have sinned this time; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong" (Exodus 9:27), and he asks Moses and Aaron to plead with God to stop the plague. But when the plague stops, he sins again and hardens his heart.

[Chapter 10] Pharaoh's Disobedience Revealed in the Plagues of Locusts and Darkness
When Pharaoh refuses, locusts cover all of Egypt and eat up every plant that remained after the hail. Pharaoh again admits his sin and asks that the plague be removed, but even after the locusts are gone he does not let Israel go.
Next a thick darkness, so dark that people cannot see one another, falls on the land of Egypt for three days, but there is light where the children of Israel live (Exodus 10:22-23). Pharaoh allows even the women and little ones to go, but proposes a compromise that the livestock be left behind.
But Moses refuses, saying, "Our livestock also shall go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind" (Exodus 10:26).

[Chapter 11] The Final Plague: The Declaration of the Death of the Firstborn
God tells Moses that after one more plague on Pharaoh and Egypt, Pharaoh will let Israel go completely (Exodus 11:1). The people of Israel are to ask the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and God causes the Egyptians to favor the people of Israel (Exodus 11:2-3).
Moses declares that at midnight God will go out into the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the maidservant, and even the firstborn of the livestock (Exodus 11:4-5). But no such plague will come upon the children of Israel, and through this they will know that God makes a distinction between the Egyptians and Israel (Exodus 11:7).
Despite the repeated plagues up to now, Pharaoh refuses God's word to the end. Through the final plague that will fall on the firstborn of Egypt, God's judgment reaches its climax, and the event of the exodus, in which Israel is freed from Egypt, draws near.

[Chapter 12] The Passover of the LORD
Being protected from the plague by the blood of the lamb, and what they eat while staying in the house, are a shadow of the life of being saved, having fellowship with the Lord, and living a life of faith.
1) The unblemished, year-old male lamb and its blood (Exodus 12:5, 13, 1 Peter 1:19, 1 Corinthians 5:7, Hebrews 11:28)
2) Roasting the lamb (head, legs, and entrails, all of it) with fire and eating it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs means a life of following all of the Lord. It is a life of suffering, of holiness, and of not forgetting having been slaves. We must achieve a life of experientially becoming like Christ in heart and in daily life.
3) For seven days they eat unleavened bread and must remove the leaven (sin) (Exodus 12:15, 18-20). We must achieve a holy and sanctified life.

(Romans 1:6) And you also are among those who are called to belong to Jesus Christ.
For seven days eat unleavened bread, and remove leavened bread and leaven (Exodus 13:6, 7). We must be set apart from doctrinal sin and moral wickedness.

[Chapter 21] Regulations on Servants, Life, and Injury
	1.	Regulations concerning Hebrew servants. If you buy a Hebrew servant, he is to serve six years, and in the seventh he is to go out free, without paying anything (Exodus 21:2). If the servant declares, "I love my master and my wife and children; I will not go out free," his master is to bring him before the judges, and at the door or the doorpost pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him permanently (Exodus 21:5-6). The mark left on the ear shows that he loved his master and voluntarily decided to continue serving. In the Bible a servant is described as one under the possession and authority of his master. This image of the servant also appears in Christ, who was prophesied as the servant of God (Isaiah 42:1; Matthew 12:18), and the apostle Paul also regarded himself as a servant of Christ and confessed that he bore on his body the marks of Jesus (Galatians 6:17).
	2.	Crimes punishable by death. It is prescribed that whoever strikes a man and kills him intentionally must surely be put to death (Exodus 21:12, 14). Whoever strikes or curses his father or mother, and whoever kidnaps a man and sells him or is found holding him, are also subject to death (Exodus 21:15-17). These are regulations established so that human life and the authority of parents would be regarded as weighty.
	3.	Laws of compensation for injury. When people quarrel and one injures the other, the offender must pay for the medical care and for the loss of time from work (Exodus 21:18-19). Even when harm results from injuring a pregnant woman, responsibility is assigned according to its extent, and the principle "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" is set forth (Exodus 21:22-25). This stipulates not unlimited retaliation but fair compensation corresponding to the damage.
	4.	Regulations on harm caused by servants and livestock. If a master damages the eye or the tooth of his servant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the injury (Exodus 21:26-27). If an ox gores a person to death, the ox is to be stoned to death, and if the owner knew of its habit of goring and did not restrain it, the owner is also held responsible (Exodus 21:28-29). Through this it is taught that one is responsible also when failing to manage one's own property and livestock causes harm to others.

[Chapter 22] Regulations on Property, Social Life, and Holiness
	1.	Laws of compensation for loss. When someone steals an ox or a sheep and kills it or sells it, he must repay with more than he stole. An ox is to be repaid with five oxen, and a sheep with four sheep (Exodus 22:1). When livestock graze in another's field or vineyard and cause damage, or a fire is started that burns up the grain, the person who caused the damage must make restitution (Exodus 22:5-6). Even when something entrusted to another person's keeping is lost or damaged, the question of responsibility is to be made clear and handled justly (Exodus 22:7-15).
	2.	Regulations on moral and religious immorality. A man who seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her must take her as his wife and bear the proper responsibility (Exodus 22:16-17). A sorceress is not to be allowed to live, and those who lie with an animal and those who sacrifice to any god other than the LORD are to be severely punished (Exodus 22:18-20). These are regulations so that the people of Israel would not be corrupted sexually and spiritually but would live according to the holiness of God.
	3.	Regulations on social life. It is commanded not to oppress or mistreat a sojourner and not to afflict a widow or an orphan (Exodus 22:21-24). Israel too must remember that they were sojourners in Egypt. When lending money to a poor person, one must not charge interest, and if a neighbor's garment is taken in pledge, it must be returned before the sun goes down (Exodus 22:25-27). Since God is the One who hears the cry of the socially weak, the people of Israel too must practice compassion and justice.
	4.	Regulations on religious duties. It is commanded not to revile God or curse a leader of the people, and not to delay giving to God the harvest and the firstborn (Exodus 22:28-30). Because Israel must be a holy people to God, it is prescribed that they not eat meat torn by beasts in the field (Exodus 22:31).

[Chapter 23] Regulations on a Just Society, the Feasts, and the Conquest of Canaan
	1.	Regulations on social life and fair judgment. It is commanded not to spread a false report and not to join hands with the wicked to be a malicious witness (Exodus 23:1). One must not follow a majority to do evil or pervert justice in a lawsuit (Exodus 23:2). If you come upon your enemy's ox or donkey wandering, you must bring it back, and if your enemy's donkey is fallen down under its load, you are to help with it (Exodus 23:4-5). Do not deprive a poor person of justice in his lawsuit, keep far from a false matter, and do not take a bribe (Exodus 23:6-8). The command not to oppress a sojourner is emphasized again (Exodus 23:9).
	2.	Regulations on the sabbatical year and the Sabbath. For six years the land is to be sown and its produce gathered, but in the seventh year it is to be let rest, so that the poor may eat, and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat (Exodus 23:10-11). Six days one is to work, and on the seventh day rest, so that not only the ox and the donkey but also the servant and the sojourner may be refreshed (Exodus 23:12). Through the regulations of rest it is taught that the land, people, and even livestock are all under the sovereignty of God.
	3.	Regulations on the feasts of the LORD. All the males of Israel are to appear before the LORD three times a year and keep the feasts (Exodus 23:14, 17). The Feast of Unleavened Bread is a feast in which, at the appointed time in the month of Abib, they eat unleavened bread for seven days and remember the deliverance of the exodus (Exodus 23:15). The Feast of Harvest is kept when the firstfruits of what is sown in the field are gathered, and the Feast of Ingathering is kept when the produce gained from the year's labor is gathered in from the field and stored (Exodus 23:16). These feasts cause them to remember that all produce and deliverance came from God.
	4.	Regulations concerning the conquest of Canaan. God promises to send an angel before Israel to protect them and bring them to the place God has prepared (Exodus 23:20). Israel must obey that angel's voice and not rebel against him. They must not bow down to the gods of the Canaanite peoples or follow their practices, and must utterly destroy the idols (Exodus 23:24). He promises that if they serve God alone, He will bless their bread and water and take sickness away from among them (Exodus 23:25). God says He will not drive out the Canaanite peoples all at once but little by little, until the people of Israel have increased and taken possession of the land (Exodus 23:29-30). He also commands them not to make a covenant with them or serve their gods (Exodus 23:32-33). This shows that the purpose of the conquest of Canaan is not mere territorial expansion but that the people of God, set apart from idolatry, serve God alone.

[Chapter 1] The Burnt Offering
(Leviticus 1:6) Next, he is to skin the burnt offering and cut it into pieces.
The five offerings of Leviticus point to Jesus Christ. The burnt offering points to His devotion on the cross. The grain offering points to His perfect public ministry.
How it is offered
It is killed and its blood is shed. The hide of the burnt offering is removed. It is cut into pieces. Fire is put on the altar, wood is arranged on the fire, and the cut pieces, the head, and the fat are arranged on the wood that is on the fire of the altar. The entrails and the legs are washed with water. All of it is burned on the altar as a burnt offering.
The hide had to be removed - Jeremiah 4:4 'Circumcise yourselves to the LORD; remove the foreskin of your hearts'
Uncleanness clings to the hide. Just as the hide is removed, after being saved we must take off our old self and put on the new self. Just as pain accompanies removing the hide, labor pains accompany the process of taking off the old self and putting on the new self (Ephesians 4:21-24, Colossians 3:5-11, Romans 13:11-14).
It had to be cut into pieces with a knife, the inner parts and all
When an animal is cut into pieces, it is divided piece by piece and fully laid open. In the same way, by the sword of the word we need to have our heart, thoughts, mind, soul, and body all laid bare. Before the word we must lay open our soul, heart, and thoughts and expose them just as they are, completely (Hebrews 4:12-13).
The entrails and legs are washed with water
When something wrong in us is exposed, we must wash it with the word, as one washes with water.
The offering had to be placed on the altar
The altar is a shadow of Jesus Christ. All our life is accepted through Jesus Christ. If the offering were not placed on the altar but on the altar of an idol, it could not be a pleasing aroma to God. (John 14:6)
It is all burned
First, God requires my all. Our life must be wholly devoted in being set aflame with love for the Lord. We must be wholly offered in the flame of the Lord's love. We need to devote ourselves wholly to the Lord in the flame of love that comes from the Holy Spirit.

[Chapter 2] The Grain Offering
How it is offered
Fine flour
For a grain of wheat to become fine flour, the grain must be crushed. Jesus submitted completely before the Father's will (Isaiah 50:5-7). The Lord crushed Himself completely and became the bread of life for us.
Oil - a type of the Holy Spirit
 Jesus' birth, life, death, and resurrection were all accomplished by the Holy Spirit.
Frankincense
 The incense of the altar of incense is based on "frankincense" (Exodus 30:34). The rising of the incense teaches prayer that ascends to God (Psalms 141:1-2, Revelation 5:8, Revelation 8:3). Jesus' public ministry began with prayer and ended with prayer. Jesus lived a life consistent with prayer.
Salt
Salt does not change. We too must be the same, unchanging, whether at the beginning or at the end. The fearful heart we have at the beginning we must carry to the end. The humble heart we have at the beginning we must carry to the end. Salt must dissolve. A Christian gives flavor by dissolving.
 Salt is what prevents decay. When we rely on the written word, we can prevent decay in our lives. Jesus' life was a life in which the Word became flesh, and there was nothing corrupt in it. He walked only the way within the Word. Just as when something is filled within, nothing else can enter, Jesus was filled with the Word and the Spirit. Let us too be filled with the Word and the Spirit. A life of service must begin with the Word and end with the Word.
What must not be put in - honey
The Lord's public ministry has nothing to do with human sentiment. Jesus did not seek His own glory.
What must not be put in - leaven
Jesus' life was without sin. In Jesus there was neither the old leaven (moral sin) nor the leaven of malice and evil (sin of faith). We too must follow after the Lord (2 Timothy 2:21, 1 Corinthians 5:7-8).

[Chapter 3] The Peace Offering

A characteristic of the peace offering is that "leavened bread is offered along with the thanksgiving sacrifice of the peace offering."
This shows that a Christian, though he has obtained forgiveness of sin and justification by faith, is in a relationship of peace with God while still having the nature and disposition of sin inherited from Adam. Because there is sin in the saint's character, "leaven" is permitted in the offering, and because there must be no sin in the saint's conscience, the "unclean person" was forbidden (Leviticus 7:13, Leviticus 7:20).
Even if a nature of sin is in us, no problem arises in our fellowship with God. This is because God knows there is sin in us and has dealt with it and handled it by the blood of redemption. But when a saint sinned by making use of the nature of sin, he had to first confess his sin and be cleansed before eating the meat of the peace offering.
"Being cut off from his people" means that if there is unconfessed sin, fellowship with God is broken. Trying to have fellowship with God while remaining in sin is wrong (1 John 1:6). Fellowship exists only "in the light."

[Chapter 4] The Sin Offering
If the priest sins so as to bring guilt on the people, he offers a young bull.
If the whole congregation of Israel commits any one of the LORD's prohibitions, they offer a young bull.
If a leader sins, he offers a male goat,
and if a common person sins, he offers a female goat.
At that time a young bull was worth more than a male goat, and a male goat was worth more than a female goat. From this we can see that even for the same transgression, God regards a priest's sin as more serious than the sin of a leader or a common person.

[Chapter 5] The Guilt Offering
The guilt offering is the sacrifice offered when one has done wrong concerning the holy things of God or a neighbor's property (Leviticus 5:15, 6:2-5). In particular, the guilt offering did not end merely with asking God's forgiveness; when loss had been caused by the wrong, the person was to make restitution for it and add a fifth to it (Leviticus 5:16, 6:5).
That is, it deals together with sin against God and the harm done to people. Being forgiven by God includes acknowledging the wrong and, as far as possible, setting the relationship right.

[Chapter 6] The Duties of the Priests
Chapter 6 speaks concretely of how the sacrifices are to be offered and also how the priests are to serve in the sacrifices.
The fire of the burnt offering was to be kept burning on the altar continually and never go out (Leviticus 6:12-13). Every morning the priest had to lay wood on it and arrange the burnt offering.
It also speaks of the regulations the priests must keep in the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering. In particular, that He prescribed in detail the priests' garments, the fire of the altar, the way of disposing of the offerings, and so on shows that service offered to God must be done not in a human way but in the way God has appointed.

[Chapter 7] Offerings
Chapter 7 concludes the regulations of the various sacrifices while continuing to explain the regulations for the guilt offering and the peace offering. In particular, the peace offering is characterized as a sacrifice in which the offering presented to God is shared and eaten together by God, the priest, and the worshiper (Leviticus 7:11-21).
However, those who took part in the sacrifice had to be clean, and eating blood and fat was forbidden (Leviticus 7:22-27).
Viewed as a whole, chapters 5–7 are a section that teaches how to deal with sin, how to worship God, and how the priests are to carry out those sacrifices.

As God commanded, Moses washed Aaron and his sons, clothed them, and set them apart as priests by pouring the anointing oil on them. It shows that before offering sacrifices for the people's sins, the priest himself was a sinner in need of atonement.

[Chapter 12] Regulations on Childbirth
Leviticus 12 contains the regulations on childbirth. It prescribed that a mother who bore a child was unclean. This hints that a person is born a sinner from birth, as Psalm 51 says (Job 25:4).

[Chapter 13] Diagnosis of Uncleanness
Leviticus 13 contains the regulations by which, when an abnormality arises on a person's skin, the priest examines it and distinguishes between what is clean and what is unclean (Leviticus 13:1-3).
The priest did not judge easily after a single look; he examined the spots and the condition of the skin and, if necessary, isolated the person for seven days and then examined again (Leviticus 13:4-8).
What mattered was not merely the fact that there was an abnormality of the skin but whether the disease was spreading. Therefore the priest did not judge by his own thinking but had to discern accurately according to the standard God had set.
In addition, spots appearing not only on a person's skin but also on clothing or leather were examined, and if they spread they were judged unclean and burned (Leviticus 13:47-59).
In particular, it was not the leprosy itself but "spreading" that was the problem. In the lives of the saints too, we must be on guard not so much against immature or lacking aspects in themselves as against sin being left alone and continuing to spread.

If leprosy points to a sinner who has not received atonement, a discharge probably points to the old habits that come from the saints' inherited nature. The high priest was set apart even more strictly (Leviticus 21:10-15).

Rest for the land (25:2). Rest from physical labor. Complete rest from debt (Deuteronomy 15:11).

It makes people realize that God is the owner of the land (25:23). The land, a fellow creature, must also be given the chance to build up its strength. Resting in the seventh year after six years of toil can be a type of the millennial kingdom that will be brought about by the second coming of Christ. At that time the land will enter complete rest under the rule of the Lord, the true King of Israel.
2. The Year of Jubilee
The Year of Jubilee begins with the joyful sound of the trumpet proclaiming the freedom of the land, together with the solemn Day of Atonement in which the nation makes atonement for its sins (Isaiah 61:1, Jeremiah 34:8). The eternal jubilee, true freedom and release, and liberation from the rule of sin and from death have come through Christ, whom the prophets longed for.
The key to understanding the Year of Jubilee is the word "liberty" (25:10). In this year three kinds of liberation are carried out: the liberation of slaves, the liberation of property, and the liberation of the land itself.
3. Spiritual lessons of the Jubilee (the Jubilee is a shadow of Jesus' first and second comings)
The Year of Jubilee is the year after the seventh sabbatical year, that is, the eighth year. If the seventh year signifies the millennial kingdom of Christ, the Year of Jubilee symbolizes the still more glorious state that follows the millennial kingdom. It is like the first day of the new week that begins after the Sabbath, the last day of the old week.
This first day is the day of Jesus' resurrection, the day the Holy Spirit came, and the day a new order began. That is, it is the day the new creation is accomplished in Jesus Christ. For this reason the Year of Jubilee can be seen as pointing to the future new heaven and new earth (Revelation 21–22). On that day all authority and rule will be placed under Christ's feet, and death, the last enemy, will be no more.
And we will hear the voice of God saying, "Behold, I am making all things new."
Just as slaves gain freedom in the Year of Jubilee, our souls were freed from sin by Jesus' first coming, and at His second coming our bodies too will be completely freed from corruption and futility. Also, just as inherited land returns to its original owner, the saints who have been freed from sin will finally receive the eternal inheritance God has prepared.
Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.
In this way the land too will be released from the curse and restored (cf. Romans 8:21).

  1) The leaders brought six carts and twelve oxen for transporting the tabernacle during the march through the wilderness (7:2-3)

The priests were in charge of the service of the sanctuary and the altar, and the Levites helped with the work of the tent of meeting but were not to encroach on the office of the priests. It also speaks of the regulations on the tithes and holy things that God gave to the priests and Levites.
If Korah's rebellion was an incident of coveting an office belonging to God, chapter 18 shows that the office God entrusts to each person carries not only privileges but also responsibilities and boundaries.

[Chapter 19] The Water of Purification
Chapter 19 speaks of the purification statute of the red heifer, for cleansing those who have become unclean through contact with the dead.
The red heifer was burned outside the camp, and its ashes were kept; for an unclean person, water for purification was prepared from them and sprinkled (Numbers 19:1-9). Because many people died through the rebellion and judgment of Korah's company, uncleanness from death arose among Israel. God provided a way for them to be made clean again from that uncleanness.
Even as death came through God's judgment, God provided a way for the unclean people to be made clean again.

[Chapter 20] The Waters of Meribah
At Meribah Moses and Aaron committed a decisive error. Considering the circumstances at the time, one can to some extent understand Moses' feelings from a human standpoint.
Moses was in an extremely difficult situation. Before the grief over the death of his sister Miriam, who had shared the journey of suffering with him for some forty years, had even faded, the people of Israel began once more their chronic complaints and protests (Numbers 20:1).
Although the people of Israel had received God's guidance and grace for 40 years, they repeated unbelief and disobedience, and although they had received discipline and punishment many times, they still had not changed. Moses was greatly worn out in body and mind by their persistent complaining and stubborn manner.
In the end, Moses made the mistake of momentarily forgetting God's word and giving precedence to anger and hot temper. Although it was only a single wrong, it came to be the decisive reason Moses could not enter the land of Canaan.
Edom's king refuses passage (Numbers 20:14-21)
To go from Kadesh-barnea to the land of Canaan, one had to pass through the land of the Edomites to reach the destination quickly, so Moses asked the king of Edom for passage, but the king of Edom firmly refused.
Israel obeyed God's word by avoiding conflict with the Edomites and turning back.
The death of Aaron (Numbers 20:22-29)
Because he rebelled against God's word at the waters of Meribah (Numbers 20:24), Aaron died on Mount Hor, located on the border of the land of Edom, and his son Eleazar put on Aaron's garments and succeeded to the office.

[Chapter 21] The Fiery Serpents and the Bronze Serpent
The people's sin (Numbers 21:4-5)
	(1)	The way was rough and their hearts were disheartened, and they complained against God and Moses.
	(2)	Looking back on life in Egypt, they disregarded the grace of God who had delivered them from Egypt.
	(3)	Unable to wait for God's provision, they complained about food.
▷ Even though 38 years had passed since they turned back from Kadesh, they were still not fully refined. Rather than being satisfied with the bread God gave, they longed for the pots of meat of Egypt. They did not remember God's power and deliverance, did not endure in faith, but rather tested God.
The LORD sends fiery serpents
The people's complaining and grumbling had already been a bite from Satan working in the serpent. In the end God sent fiery serpents, and many of the people died. Then the people realized their sin and repented.
Moses' intercession
Moses interceded with God for the people, and the LORD had a bronze serpent set on a pole. Anyone bitten by a serpent who looked at the bronze serpent lived at once. The bronze serpent symbolizes the serpent that has been judged. The place where Satan's power was broken is precisely the cross of Jesus Christ.
(Numbers 21:9) So Moses made a bronze snake and mounted it on a pole. If anyone who was bitten looked at the bronze snake, he would live.
(John 3:14-15) Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.

In the end Balaam says to Balak, "Whatever I say, that I must speak" (Numbers 22:38).
A person cannot curse, by his own will, one whom God has blessed.

Balak summoned Balaam to have him curse Israel, but as a result what came out of Balaam's mouth was not a curse but God's blessing and a prophecy of Israel's future.

[Chapter 25] Phinehas' Zeal
When the people of Israel committed sexual immorality with the Moabite women and fell into idolatry, God was angry. As a result a plague spread and the people died. While the whole congregation was weeping and repenting at the door of the tent of meeting, an appalling event occurred.
Zimri, a leader of the tribe of Simeon, brought a Midianite woman, Cozbi, and committed sexual immorality publicly before the congregation. Then Phinehas pierced the two of them through with a spear and killed them, and because of this the plague stopped.
Zimri's act was a wicked sin that disregarded God's wrath and even mocked the congregation of Israel who were trying to repent. He was one who deserved to be punished.
Phinehas' anger was not personal feeling but came from a desire to restore the holiness of Israel (Numbers 25:11).
Phinehas, discerning God's heart, acted swiftly, and because of that God's wrath toward Israel ceased (Numbers 25:11). God commended Phinehas by establishing the covenant of the priesthood with his descendants.

[Chapter 26] The Second Census on the Plains of Moab
Whereas the first census had as its purpose organizing the army for the march, the second census has as its purpose organizing the army for the distribution of the inheritance of the land of Canaan and for conquering the land distributed (Numbers 26:52-56).
Among the tribes, the number of the tribe of Simeon had decreased markedly compared with the first census (37,100). Considering that the Simeonite leader who committed sexual immorality with Cozbi in Numbers 25 appears to have been the ringleader of that immorality, it appears that many people of the tribe of Simeon took part and died in the plague.
Of those included in the first census, all but Joshua and Caleb died in the wilderness as God's word had said they would, so they were not included in the second census (Numbers 26:63-65).
Although many people died through God's punishments several times during the wilderness period, as a result the number counted from age 20 and over shows no great difference (Numbers 26:50).

[Chapter 27] The Request for Moses' Successor
When God spoke the words announcing Moses' death, Moses raised not the slightest objection to it, did not cling to the extension of his own life or to his position as leader of the people, and out of concern solely for the people asked God for someone to lead them. He was truly a man of obedience and a man who truly loved Israel.

[Chapter 28] The Continual Burnt Offering, the Sabbath, the New Moon, the Passover and Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Weeks
While the new generation on the plains of Moab was preparing to enter the land of Canaan, God first speaks again of the daily offerings and the offerings of the Sabbath, the new moon, and the feasts.
He set the offerings to be made at the Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Weeks, as well as on the Sabbath and the new moon, beginning with the continual burnt offering made morning and evening.
This teaches Israel, who were about to conquer Canaan, that worshiping God comes before preparing for war. Gaining the land of Canaan depended not on Israel's military strength but on God.

[Chapter 29] The Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths
Chapter 29 again speaks of the offerings to be made at the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Booths. In particular, at the Feast of Booths He had many offerings made over many days (Numbers 29:12-38).
Even after entering Canaan and settling, Israel had to remember God and offer sacrifices to Him at the appointed times. Therefore the core of chapters 28-29 is that keeping a right relationship with God is more important than entering Canaan itself.

[Chapter 30] Vows
It speaks of the regulation that what one has vowed or sworn to God must be done as the words came out of one's mouth (Numbers 30:2). However, concerning the vow of a young daughter or a married woman, it allowed the father or husband to hear the content and annul it.
One must be responsible for one's words before God and must not make vows rashly.

[Chapter 31] The War Against Midian
God commands Israel to strike Midian (Numbers 31:1-2). This was not a war for mere territorial expansion but God's judgment on Midian, which had caused Israel to sin through the incident of Baal-peor earlier (Numbers 25).
The soldiers who returned from the war went through a process of cleansing, and the spoils too were handled according to the method God had set. Part of the spoils was given to the LORD as a contribution (Numbers 31:25-30).
It shows that the victory in the war was not because of Israel's strength but because they carried out the war that God had commanded.

[Chapter 32] The Request of Reuben, Gad, and the Half-Tribe of Manasseh for an Inheritance
The request of the tribes of Reuben and Gad for the land east of the Jordan as their inheritance was certainly an improper act.
Because they did not yield even at Moses' rebuke, Moses accepted their request on the condition that they join in and help in the war west of the Jordan.

[Chapter 33] A Review of the Journey of the Exodus
From the exodus until encamping on the plains of Moab, they encamped some 42 times, which amounts to moving camp every 11 months over the course of 40 years. The itinerary that God had Moses record not only makes them recall the God who was with them during the 40 years of wilderness life after the exodus and who led them by grace and mercy despite the people's sin and rebellion, but also, recalling the events connected with the place names, makes them reflect once again on the lessons.
The command to conquer Canaan (Numbers 33:50-56)
God had the people of Israel sum up the 40 years in the wilderness as a review of the journey, and then gave them the command to conquer Canaan lying now before them, so that they would focus on the goal.

[Chapter 6] The Purpose of the Law and Instruction About the Promised Land
Deuteronomy 6 occupies a central position in Moses' second sermon (chapters 5-26), and its theme is love for the LORD God. Put more concretely, the central message of this chapter is to love God with the whole person, to obey the word of God with that love as the motive, and to transmit that word thoroughly to later generations.
In particular, the "Shema," the word beginning "Hear, O Israel," found in Deuteronomy 6:4-5, is the central confession of Jewish faith: God is one alone, and one is commanded to love God with all one's heart, mind, and strength. This word is the core and spirit of the whole law, and Jesus too referred to this word as the greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38).
Therefore Deuteronomy 6 is not merely an explanation of the law in a single chapter; it can be said to be the foundation of Israel's faith and the chapter that sets out the direction of life that must come first in one's relationship with God.

[Chapter 32] The Song of Moses
Deuteronomy 32 can be called a chapter that summarizes the flow of the whole Bible. Moses, moved by the Holy Spirit of God, composed the song recorded in this chapter, and the main content of this song carries the dark theme of Israel's corruption and God's resulting judgment.
The purpose of this song is to prevent the corruption of the people of Israel beforehand. Its intent was that, after the people had finished their training in the wilderness and before they entered the land of Canaan, they would remember this song amid the crises they would face later in Canaan. If the whole content is summed up in a word, it can be called the God of love. That is, it shows in contrast the lovingkindness of God, who goes on loving Israel unceasingly despite its repeated rebellion, and at the same time the figure of the righteous God, who surely judges sin.

[Chapter 33] The Blessing of Moses
Looking far off at the land of Canaan, as his death approached, Moses went up Mount Nebo for the last time and, in the form of a poem, proclaimed a testamentary blessing upon the twelve tribes of Israel. This blessing is structurally very similar to the blessing Jacob gave his twelve sons in Genesis 49, but it differs in that it appears in a more developed and supplemented form.
What is peculiar is that the tribe of Simeon is not mentioned in the blessing of Moses. The Bible does not state the reason explicitly, but several possible inferences exist. First, it may be because Simeon's portion was included within the portion of the tribe of Judah, so that it was not allotted a separate region (Joshua 19:1-9). Second, there is also the possibility that Moses omitted it deliberately because, after Jacob's curse recorded in Genesis 49:7, the tribe of Simeon continued to be implicated in sin, for example the incident of sexual immorality at Peor (Numbers 25:4).
This blessing of Moses was fulfilled entirely in the history of Israel.

[Chapter 34] The Death of Moses
Deuteronomy 34 is the last chapter of the Pentateuch of Moses, and can be called the conclusion of Deuteronomy and at the same time the conclusion of the whole Pentateuch. Yet this chapter is significant not as a mere ending but as a new starting point.
The work of God did not stop because Moses died; rather, a new era of the conquest of Canaan opens through Joshua. Therefore Deuteronomy 34 can be called a chapter that brings the life of Moses to a close and at the same time is a turning point that connects to a new chapter of redemptive history through Joshua.

[Chapter 6] The Oppression of Midian, and the Call and Reforms of the Judge Gideon
Judges 6, centering on the appearance of Gideon, unfolds around the background of how the people of Israel came to be oppressed by Midian and the scene in which God calls Gideon. The typical vicious cycle of the period of the judges [sin → discipline → supplication → deliverance → forgetting] is repeated in this chapter as well.

[Chapter 7] The Victory of Gideon and the Three Hundred Men
It unfolds around the incident in which Gideon, guided by God, crushed the great army of Midian with a small force. Gideon followed the word of God and obeyed to the end. Even among the enemy troops of Midian, God showed through a dream the sign that Gideon would defeat Midian, and so Gideon advanced all the more boldly.
God revealed His power not through a multitude of soldiers but through three hundred men, and God threw the enemy into confusion and made them collapse by themselves. As a result, people gathered from all over Israel and pursued Midian, and the tribe of Ephraim also joined in, seized the fords of the Jordan River, and killed Oreb and Zeeb, the princes of Midian.

[Chapter 8] Gideon's Punitive Campaign against Midian and a Summary of His Subsequent Deeds
Gideon pursued the remaining army of Midian and defeated it completely, and captured and executed the two kings, Zebah and Zalmunna.
After the war he wisely resolved the conflict with the tribe of Ephraim, and although the people of Israel tried to set Gideon up as king, he refused and declared that God alone is King. However, Gideon took gold earrings from the spoils and made an ephod, and the people came to serve it like an idol and fell into sin.
Gideon governed in peace until his death, and after his death Israel again served Baal and turned away.
The name of Gideon's son Jerubbaal (Gideon) continued to be remembered afterward, but the people did not remember his house and were also unfaithful to God.

[Chapter 9] The Rebellion of Abimelech and the Men of Shechem
It begins with the story of Abimelech, Gideon's son, setting himself up as king with the support of the men of Shechem.
He killed seventy half-brothers and became king, but Jotham warned of that wrong by means of a parable. Abimelech ruled over Shechem, but in the end he came into conflict with the men of Shechem and suppressed them. But he met his death when his head was struck by a piece of a millstone thrown by a woman, and God repaid his evil deeds.

[Chapter 10] The Deeds of Tola and Jair and the Sin of Israel
Tola and Jair are raised up in turn as judges, as deliverers of Israel.
But Israel again served Baal, Ashtaroth, and various other foreign gods, and turned away from God. God handed them over into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, and the people cried out to God in their suffering. God said, "Go and get help from other gods," but when Israel removed the idols and turned back sincerely to God, God again took compassion on them.

[Chapter 11] Jephthah's Exploits and His Vow
Jephthah had been driven out by his brothers because he was the son of a prostitute, but when Israel was oppressed by Ammon, they came looking for him and set him up as judge. Jephthah sent envoys to the king of Ammon and explained, on the basis of past history and God's guidance, how unjust the war was, but he was rebuffed and went to war. Before going out to war, Jephthah made a rash vow to God that if he were victorious he would offer as a burnt offering whoever came out of the door of his house. Jephthah won a great victory in the war, but a tragedy occurred in which his own daughter became the object of that vow. The daughter accepted her father's vow.

[Chapter 12] Civil War in Israel and Three Judges
Because of Ephraim's jealousy and envy, civil war breaks out in Israel. As a result, forty-two thousand men of the tribe of Ephraim were killed. Whether a fugitive was an Ephraimite or not was told by the pronunciation of "Shibboleth" and "Sibboleth." Jephthah died after judging Israel for six years.
After that, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon were raised up in turn as judges.

[Chapter 13] The Oppression of the Philistines and the Birth of Samson
When Israel again did evil, God gave them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years.
Manoah and his wife, of the tribe of Dan, had no children, but the angel of God appeared and foretold that they would have a son and that he would be set apart as a Nazirite. Following God's instructions, the two parents prepare for the child and hold him in reverence.

[Chapter 14] Samson's Wedding Incident with a Philistine Woman
Samson saw a Philistine woman of Timnah and told his parents that he wanted to marry her. His parents opposed marriage with a foreigner, but that was God preparing an opportunity to strike the Philistines.
Samson tore apart a young lion barehanded on the road, and later ate honey from the lion's carcass. Because of that, at his wedding feast Samson posed a riddle to the crowd of Philistines. When they had no way to find it out by their own strength, the Philistines used his wife to learn the answer. Samson was enraged, killed thirty Philistines, and began his revenge.

[Chapter 15] Samson Kills a Thousand Philistines in Revenge for the Wedding Incident
Samson went to see his wife and found out that she had been given to another man, and he was furious. Samson took his revenge by tying torches to the tails of three hundred foxes and burning the Philistines' grain. When the Philistines learned why Samson was angry and burned his wife and her father to death, Samson avenged himself with an even greater slaughter.

Or even after coming to Bethlehem, she could have gone after a younger and more capable man. He praises her lovingkindness, resolve, and purity, and promises to take on the redemption. But he makes known that there is a nearer relative than himself, and seeks to observe the proper order. [Chapter 4] [Conclusion] The Blessing and Reward That Came to Ruth
 (1) 4:1-12 The marriage of Boaz and Ruth in accordance with lawful procedure
Ruth chapter 4 corresponds to the conclusion (Conclusion) of the book of Ruth. The first of its three paragraphs, 4:1-12, depicts the process in which Boaz follows concrete lawful procedures in order to fulfill his responsibility as kinsman-redeemer.
 (2) 4:13-17 God who gives a son (Obed)
We have now reached the part of Ruth in which one of its happiest events is recorded. That event is that, because a son was born to Ruth, all the people of the town gave thanks to God for it.
 (3) 4:18-22 Becoming an ancestor of David and entering the genealogy of Christ
The book of Ruth concludes with a genealogy that begins with Perez and leads to David. This genealogy is the end of the book of Ruth and the starting point of a new history of redemption.
Perez was the son born to Judah and Tamar; though his birth appeared outwardly irregular, he became the ancestor of the covenant community through faith that believed God's promise.
Obed, the son born to Ruth the Moabitess, is a descendant of this Perez and becomes the grandfather of David, the great king of Israel. This connection shows that even a foreign woman can be included in the covenant genealogy through faith.
The purposes of recording this genealogy here are as follows.
First, it shows that the roots of the house of David were carried on through people who faithfully believed God's covenant.
Though they were people who met the storms of life, were wounded and despised by others, or were outsiders to the covenant as foreigners, the author who wrote the book of Ruth recorded the story of ancestors who, by faith, were blessed by God and came into the covenant people. This emphasizes that the essence of the covenant people is faithful trust in the LORD God. And it shows that God is the One who gives full reward (blessing) to those who have that faith.
Second, it shows that God's blessing is not cut off but is the consistent covenant history of God, continuing from Abraham to Jesus Christ and to the saints of today.
It means that God is faithful to His covenant and blesses the people of faith in that God.
David is the greatest king of Israel and an ancestor and type of Jesus Christ. Therefore, although the book of Ruth closes its genealogy with the name of David, it implies that this history of faith will continue. And in fact, in the New Testament it continues to Jesus Christ, the descendant of Abraham and David.
In the end, the purpose for which the book of Ruth was written is not merely to present the genealogy of King David, but it is a word that shows in depth the theme of the whole Bible: God's lovingkindness (hesed) and faithfulness to the covenant, and the blessing given to those who believe.

[Chapter 15] Saul, Who Failed by Disobeying the Word of God (the Destruction of Amalek)

The meaning of "God's regret"
(1 Samuel 15:11)“I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” And Samuel was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night.
Human regret and God's regret must be distinguished. Human regret carries the idea that when a person becomes aware of sin, he regrets it and can truly turn back to God. God's regret (Genesis 6:6, Exodus 32:14, Judges 2:18), on the other hand, refers to His having compassion on people or changing His attitude toward them according to His own sovereign will. God's regret does not presuppose any change in His character.
God's regret is an expression of the pain of God's holy love over human wickedness.
The expression "God regretted" is also used in verse 35. Yet in verse 29, Samuel uses this same word to describe God as the "God who does not change His mind," that is, the God who does not regret. If so, the description of "a God who regrets" in verses 29 and 35 seems contradictory.
Verse 29 does not mean that, however much Saul violated the LORD's command, the kingship of Saul, whom God had chosen and established, would never be revoked. This word can be rightly understood only when approached from the viewpoint of the covenant.
God is One who keeps His covenant faithfully. And a covenant once made with human beings He surely fulfills. But that covenant is not God's unilateral covenant; it is bilateral, in which human beings too have the duty to keep the conditions of the covenant. Therefore God's regret over Saul was not regret over having made Saul king in itself, but an expression of grief over the breaking, by Saul, of the covenant made with God.

The Holy Spirit in the Old Testament and the Holy Spirit in the New Testament
The Holy Spirit in the Old Testament
In the Old Testament period the Holy Spirit came only upon a very special few. In particular, the presence of the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament was generally connected with the work of God. That is, the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament came upon those who did the work of God so that they might carry out that work well. Therefore, if a person doing the work of God could not fully carry out the will of God, God would sometimes withdraw the Holy Spirit.
The Holy Spirit in the New Testament
If the purpose of the Holy Spirit's presence in the Old Testament was thoroughly related to the work of God, the Holy Spirit in the New Testament comes as the guarantee of the salvation of believers (Ephesians 1:13, 14). Once the Holy Spirit has come, He does not leave us until the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30, John 14:16).
When sins are forgiven the Holy Spirit comes and becomes the guarantee of salvation. And the Holy Spirit does not leave us forever. If we happen to sin, the Holy Spirit does not leave us but grieves within us.
Furthermore, the Holy Spirit Himself intercedes for our restoration with groanings too deep for words.
