This chapter shows how God's judgment on Solomon's sin was carried out. As a result, Israel is divided into Judah in the south and Israel in the north. The direct cause of the division was Rehoboam's oppressive rule.
The united kingdom had been maintained by faith that feared God and by just rule, but at the end of Solomon's reign faith weakened and the people's suffering grew severe. Rehoboam chose oppression rather than building up the people's faith, and this was the result of the fulfillment, within God's providence, of the word of judgment given to Solomon. At his accession he was asked to reduce the people's taxes and forced labor, but he ignored the counsel of the elders and followed the hardline counsel of the young men.
Because of this the people's discontent exploded, and the ten northern tribes separated under Jeroboam.
[1-15] Rehoboam's foolish decision and the people's backlash
[16-20] The revolt of northern Israel and Jeroboam's accession to the throne
[21-24] Rehoboam's attempt at war and God's intervention
[25-33] Jeroboam's policy of idolatry and the setting up of the golden calf altars

[Chapter 13] The Warning of the Man of God and Jeroboam Who Did Not Know How to Repent
God was angered at Jeroboam's idolatry and sent a prophet to warn him. But that prophet, on his way back, was deceived by a lie, disobeyed God's command, and was killed. From this we learn that we must discern the deception of liars and of Satan.
Jeroboam, though he saw God's signs and miracles, did not turn his heart back and in the end went the way of destruction. He considered kingship more important than God, and unlike David he did not confess his sin. David accepted rebuke and repented and so became a king after God's heart, but Jeroboam met a wretched end through pride and disobedience.
[1-10] The prophecy of the man of God and the warning of judgment on Jeroboam
[11-32] The lie of the old prophet, the disobedience of the man of God, and its consequences
[33-34] Jeroboam's endless sin and refusal to repent

[Chapter 14] God's Discipline of Jeroboam and Rehoboam
After Israel was divided into north and south from a theocratic nation, both Jeroboam of the northern kingdom and Rehoboam of the southern kingdom became religiously corrupt. Jeroboam, despite God's warning, did evil to the end, and as a result, along with the illness of his son Abijah, he received God's judgment in which his house would be destroyed.
Rehoboam of southern Judah also did evil before God with idolatry and the sin of sexual immorality. This seems to have been influenced by his mother, an Ammonite woman, and in the end, through the invasion of Shishak king of Egypt, the treasures of the temple and the royal palace were taken. He made bronze shields and kept up appearances, but he ended his life showing the end of a life that has turned from God, and his son Abijam succeeded to the throne.
[1-20] The illness of Jeroboam's son and the prophecy of the prophet Ahijah
[21-31] Rehoboam's evil deeds, the sins of Judah, and Rehoboam's death

[Chapter 15] The Continuing War between the Two Kingdoms and the Reigns of the Kings of the Two Kingdoms
Through the reigns of the second and third kings of the northern and southern kingdoms, it shows the harm of humanistic rule and God's discipline. Both north and south relied on man rather than on God, but in Judah the throne was maintained by God's grace according to the Davidic covenant. King Asa tried to restore a God-centered order through religious reform, but he also made the mistake of not relying on God during war.
By contrast, the northern kingdom of Israel kept doing evil, and its dynasties were repeatedly replaced through coups and assassinations, and this emphasizes the fact that God's redemptive history advances by grace.
[1-8] Abijam's reign over Judah and the war
[9-24] Asa's reform and the war with northern Israel
[25-32] Nadab's evil deeds and Baasha's rebellion
[33-34] The period and manner of Baasha's reign

[Chapter 16] The Succession of the Second and Third Dynasties in the Northern Kingdom and the Reigns of Five Kings
It records the frequent changes of dynasty and the political chaos that took place in the northern kingdom during the reign of King Asa. Five kings of three dynasties, from Baasha, Elah, and Zimri to Omri, replaced one another, and in particular Zimri left the throne after seven days. All the kings of the northern kingdom did evil in the sight of the LORD, and their iniquity grew worse and worse. Arbitrary kingship that disregarded the legitimacy of God led to assassinations, coups, and civil war, and this was the root cause of the unstable political situation.
[1-7] The prophecy of the judgment Baasha would receive
[8-14] Elah's reign and Zimri's rebellion
[15-20] Zimri's short reign and suicide
[21-28] Omri's rise to power and the building of Samaria
[29-34] The appearance of Ahab, Baal worship, and the deepening of evil deeds

[Chapter 17] Elijah's Proclamation of Drought and Elijah's Miracle for the Widow of Zarephath
This chapter is where the ministry of the prophet Elijah begins, who worked against Baal worship in the days of Ahab in the northern kingdom. Elijah challenged the belief that Baal governs rain and abundance and proclaimed a drought, and God led Elijah to the Brook of Cherith and fed him through ravens. Also, in the house of the widow of Zarephath in the land of Sidon, the center of Baal worship, He worked the miracle of flour and oil that did not run out, and He also showed the miracle of life in raising her dead son. This was an event that powerfully revealed that only God is the true God and that He rules nature and life.
[1-7] Elijah's prophecy of drought and the miracle at the Brook of Cherith
[8-16] The faith of the widow of Zarephath and the miraculous provision
[17-24] The death and resurrection of the son of the widow of Zarephath

[Chapter 18] The Showdown on Mount Carmel and the End of the Drought Judgment
1 Kings 18 records the incident in which, through the showdown on Mount Carmel between Elijah and the prophets of Baal, it was revealed that only the LORD is the true God. Elijah and Ahab clashed over the cause of the three-year drought, and this was a spiritual battle to decide which of the LORD and Baal is the true God. Elijah repaired the broken-down altar with stones symbolizing the twelve tribes and prayed that the people of Israel would return to God. Through the miracle of fire falling from heaven and consuming the sacrifice, it was proved that the LORD, not Baal, is the true God, and afterward the drought also ended.
[1-19] Elijah's meeting with Obadiah, and the confrontation with Ahab
[20-40] The showdown between Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel
[41-46] Elijah's prayer and the restoration of rain

[Chapter 19] Elijah's Despairing Plea and God's Revelation of Victory
This chapter contains the scene in which Elijah, seized by fear because of Jezebel's threat, flees in discouragement, and, in the midst of it, receives God's comfort and commission. Elijah asked to die under a broom tree, but after receiving food and comfort from the angel of God he heads for Mount Horeb. God came to Elijah not in a strong wind, an earthquake, or fire, but in a still, small voice, and commands him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha and so carry on God's plan of redemptive history. And by telling him that He had kept seven thousand who had not bowed the knee to Baal, He makes clear that even in despair God's redemptive history continues without rest.
[1-8] Elijah's flight and God's supernatural provision
[9-18] Elijah's plea and the revelation through the still, small voice
[19-21] The calling of Elisha and the disciple's response

[Chapter 20] The First and Second Wars between Aram and Northern Israel, and Ahab's Victory and Disobedience
This chapter records Ahab's disobedience to the LORD, centering on the first and second wars between Aram and northern Israel. It records that Ben-hadad king of Aram besieged Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and demanded enormous tribute and women from King Ahab; that a prophet prophesied victory over Aram in the name of the LORD, so that Ahab slaughtered them greatly in Ahab's first and second victories; that Ahab, in a treaty, spared Ben-hadad king of Aram, whom the LORD had determined to kill; and that, in this disobedience to God, Ahab was troubled and vexed but did not turn back.
[1-21] The first war with Aram and God's help
[22-34] The second war and Ahab's victory, sparing Ben-hadad
[35-43] The prophet's rebuke of Ahab's disobedience

[Chapter 21] The Seizure of Naboth's Vineyard, the Proclamation of Punishment, and Ahab's Repentance
1 Kings 21 records the incident of King Ahab seizing Naboth's vineyard and the activity of Elijah proclaiming God's judgment on it. Ahab coveted Naboth's vineyard, and Jezebel set up false witnesses, had Naboth killed, and seized the vineyard. This incident is a representative example of Ahab's humanistic rule, which disregarded God's sovereignty and law. Elijah prophesied the destruction of Ahab and Jezebel for this, and when Ahab repented for a time, the calamity was postponed until the time of his son.
This shows that God is still the true sovereign of Israel and shows the character of God, who shows compassion toward repentance.
[1-16] The murder of Naboth through the plot of Ahab and Jezebel
[17-24] Elijah's proclamation of judgment
[25-29] Ahab's repentance and God's postponement

[Chapter 22] The Third War with Aram and the End of King Ahab
1 Kings 22 deals with the process by which King Ahab meets his death, as prophesied, in the third war with Aram. Ahab allies with Jehoshaphat king of Judah, prepares for war, and asks the prophets about the LORD's will, but the four hundred false prophets all prophesy victory. But Micaiah, the only true prophet, prophesied Ahab's death and that Israel would be scattered, and for this he was thrown into prison. Ahab in the end ignores Micaiah's warning, goes out to battle, and is killed, and Elijah's prophecy is fulfilled.
Southern Judah too had faults, but because of God's redemptive-historical promise based on the Davidic covenant, the throne was preserved and the nation was maintained. This shows God's covenant love and the flow of His faithful redemptive history.
[1-28] The alliance of Ahab and Jehoshaphat, and the prophecy of Micaiah
[29-40] The death of Ahab in the war
[41-50] Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah
[51-53] Ahaziah's reign over northern Israel and his evil deeds

[Chapter 1] Ahaziah's Illness, Elijah's Prophecy of Judgment, and Ahaziah's Death
This chapter records the judgment on King Ahaziah (the eighth king), Ahab's son, and the history in which the prophecy of the prophet Elijah was fulfilled, recording the power and rule of God.
1. Ahaziah's illness and God's declaration of judgment (vv. 1-8)
2. God's judgment by fire (vv. 9-16)
3. The death of Ahaziah according to the word of God (vv. 17-18)

[Chapter 2] Elijah's Ascension and Elisha's Succession to the Prophetic Office
This chapter records the scene of the succession of Elijah's prophetic office to Elisha and the ascension of Elijah.
Here we can glimpse the earnestness of Elisha, who followed Elijah to the end. And Elisha, who had received the prophetic office, performed the miracle of crossing the Jordan River, which announced the beginning of his ministry, made known the succession of the prophetic office also to the sons of the prophets, and purified the water of the city, thereby showing to many people that he was a prophet of God who had inherited Elijah's power. But it records the history in which God judges with His justice those who do not acknowledge the prophet of God.
1. The ascension of Elijah (vv. 1-11)
2. Elisha's succession to the prophetic office (vv. 12-18)
3. Elisha begins his prophetic ministry (vv. 19-25)

[Chapter 3] The Period of Jehoram - Elisha's Miracle during the War of the Allied Forces of Southern Judah and Northern Israel against Moab
This chapter is a record of the reign of Jehoram (the ninth king) of northern Israel and of the war with Moab. Although he was a king evil before God, God by grace had Elisha proclaim that they would be victorious in the war with Moab, and made that word come true. Even so, it records that at the end they did not achieve complete victory in the war and gave up.
1. The reign of King Jehoram (vv. 1-3)
2. The betrayal of Mesha king of Moab and the campaign of the allied forces (vv. 4-12)
3. Elisha prophesying victory in the war (vv. 13-20)
4. The victory of the allied forces over Moab (vv. 21-27)

[Chapter 4] Elisha's Miracles toward the Wife of a Son of the Prophets and the Woman of Shunem
This chapter records the miracle of helping the widow of a son of the prophets and the miracle worked for the woman of Shunem, and it records the miracle of removing the poison of death at Gilgal and the miracle of feeding a great crowd with twenty barley loaves. Through these, God showed grace by looking after His people and abundantly bestowing His love.
1. Elisha's miracle of helping the widow of a son of the prophets (vv. 1-7)
2. The faith of the woman of Shunem and Elisha's miracle (vv. 8-37)
3. Elisha's two miracles at Gilgal (vv. 38-44)

[Chapter 5] Elisha's Miracle: The Healing of Naaman and the Sin of Gehazi
This chapter records the miracle in which Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Aram, who had leprosy, believed the words of the little girl, a servant in his house, went to the prophet of Israel, and was healed of his disease, and the incident in which, because of the greed of Elisha's servant Gehazi, he himself came to be struck with leprosy. Therefore, just as the commander of the army of the foreign nation of Aram was healed, it shows that anyone, even a foreigner, can believe if he seeks God, and through the figure of Gehazi we can learn the lesson that greed gives birth to sin.
1. Naaman, who accepted the counsel of the little girl (vv. 1-7)
2. Naaman healed of leprosy (vv. 8-14)
3. Naaman's act of thanksgiving (vv. 15-19)
4. Gehazi's sin (vv. 20-27)

[Chapter 6] Elisha's Miracle: The Horror in the City of Samaria
This chapter records Elisha's miracle of recovering an axe head that fell into the river, the miracle of victory over the Aramean army through Elisha's help, and the pitiful situation that arose, because of another Aramean invasion and the hunger in the city of Samaria, in which people ate their own children.
1. Elisha's miracle of making the axe head float (vv. 1-7)
2. The invasion of the Aramean army and Elisha who captured the Aramean army (vv. 8-23)
3. The invasion of Ben-hadad king of Aram and the horror in the city of Samaria (vv. 24-33)

[Chapter 7] Elisha's Miracle: The Deliverance of Samaria and the Fulfillment of Elisha's Prophecy
Because the city of Samaria was surrounded by the Aramean army, famine arose in the city and the horror of people eating their children was taking place, and when the messenger of the king of Israel came looking for Elisha, there was a work in which, as Elisha had prophesied, all the people in the city were delivered from hunger. Although He gives discipline for the wickedness of the people of Israel, the God of love once again shows the wonderful work of loving and saving His people.
1. Elisha's prophecy (vv. 1-2)
2. The good news brought by the lepers (vv. 3-10)
3. The fulfillment of Elisha's prophecy (vv. 11-20)

[Chapter 8] Elisha's Miracle: The Restoration of the Woman of Shunem, Elisha's Prophecy, and the Reigns of the Kings of Southern Judah
This chapter records the scene in which the woman of Shunem, who had obtained a son by God's grace in chapter 4, obeyed Elisha's counsel, left to escape the famine, and then came back to her hometown and recovered her property; Elisha's prophecy to Hazael, who would become the new king of Aram; and the reigns of the two kings of southern Judah, Jehoram and Ahaziah.
1. The restoration of the property of the woman of Shunem (vv. 1-6)
2. Elisha's prophecy about Hazael and its fulfillment (vv. 7-15)
3. The reigns of Jehoram and Ahaziah of southern Judah (vv. 16-29)

[Chapter 9] Jehu's Revolution and the Fulfillment of the Prophecy against the House of Ahab
Jehu's revolution is a history fulfilled several years after the prophecy of judgment against the house of Ahab was proclaimed through the prophet Elijah. The prophecy against the house of Ahab, which habitually did evil, was fulfilled as the word said.
That God's judgment was proclaimed and yet fulfilled only after a long time was due to God's patience. It shows that, although God is the God of love, He is also the God of justice, and therefore judgment will surely come.
1. Jehu, anointed as king of northern Israel (vv. 1-10)
2. Jehu's rebellion and the death of Joram (Jehoram) (vv. 11-26)
3. The death of Ahaziah, king of southern Judah (vv. 27-29)
4. The end of Jezebel (vv. 30-37)

[Chapter 10] Jehu's Religious Reform and His Incomplete Obedience
This chapter records Jehu, as an instrument of God's judgment, carrying out the judgment thoroughly, going as far as killing seventy sons of Ahab and forty-two brothers of Ahaziah king of southern Judah. Jehu, together with Jehonadab, carried out a religious reform in which he gathered the prophets of Baal in one place and destroyed all of them.
But he could not get free from the sin of Jeroboam and committed the sin of serving the golden calves. Though doing the work of God, he did not know the full will of God and his heart was captured only by human power. In the end it records that, as God's discipline, the fertile land east of the Jordan was taken by Aram through Hazael king of Aram.
1. The complete destruction of the house of Ahab (vv. 1-14)
2. The religious reform of Jehonadab of the Rechabite clan and Jehu (vv. 15-29)
3. Jehu's reign of incomplete obedience (vv. 30-36)

[Chapter 11] Athaliah's Rebellion, Jehoiada's Revolution, and Joash's Accession as King of Judah
When King Ahaziah died, his mother Athaliah killed Ahaziah's sons, that is, her grandsons, made herself queen, and ruled the kingdom of Judah. Athaliah, a daughter of Jezebel, spread idolatry widely among the people of Judah and made them even more corrupt.
God's plan is that by His promise the throne of David should continue and that Christ should appear as a descendant of David, but the devil tried to hinder God's work by cutting off the seed of David's descendants. But it records the history in which God let Joash live and so caused the throne of David to continue.
1. Athaliah's rebellion and the rescue of Joash (vv. 1-3)
2. Joash's accession as king of Judah (vv. 4-16)
3. Jehoiada's reform (vv. 17-21)

[Chapter 12] Joash, King of Southern Judah, Repairs the Temple
This chapter is a record of Joash, who became king at the age of seven and reigned for forty years, ruling the nation in his youth under the influence of Jehoiada. Through the instruction and counsel of Jehoiada he ruled the nation in a way pleasing in God's sight. And after he became an adult he had the temple repaired.
But because he could not completely remove the high places, he could not get free from the sin of idolatry, and after Jehoiada died he listened to the princes, abandoned the house of the LORD, and again served Asherah poles and idols, and afterward he did not listen to the words of the prophets of God but even went so far as to kill the priest Zechariah.
In the end it records that he received discipline from God, was killed through the invasion of Aram and the rebellion of his servants, and was not even buried in the tomb of the kings.
1. The reign of Joash, king of southern Judah (vv. 1-3)
2. Joash's instruction to repair the temple (vv. 4-16)
3. Hazael king of Aram's invasion of Judah and the death of Joash (vv. 17-21)

[Chapter 13] The Reigns of Jehoahaz and Joash and Elisha's Last Ministry
This chapter records the reigns of Jehoahaz and Joash, the son and grandson of King Jehu, who had been used as an instrument to judge the kings of northern Israel. It also records Elisha's last ministry and his death.
Elisha ministered until the very end on behalf of northern Israel, which did not serve God wholeheartedly, and so it records the history that shows God's love for Israel to the end.
1. The reign of Jehoahaz, king of northern Israel (vv. 1-9)
2. The reign of Joash, king of northern Israel (vv. 10-13)
3. The last ministry and death of the prophet Elisha (vv. 14-21)
4. The fulfillment of Elisha's last prophecy (vv. 22-25)

[Chapter 14] Amaziah King of Southern Judah and Jeroboam II King of Northern Israel
This chapter compares the reigns of Amaziah of southern Judah and Jeroboam II of northern Israel, and shows the foolish human response to God's favor.
Amaziah won the war with Edom by God's grace, but mistook it for his own merit, became proud, and challenged King Joash of northern Israel.
In the end God disciplined his pride and had Amaziah utterly defeated by Joash.
1. The reign of Amaziah, king of southern Judah (vv. 1-14)
2. The death of Amaziah (vv. 15-22)
3. The reign of Jeroboam II, king of northern Israel (vv. 23-29)

[Chapter 15] Two Kings of Southern Judah and Five Kings of Northern Israel
This content highlights the wickedness of the two kingdoms, north and south, which in the end cast aside and rebelled against God's patience and protecting love toward the kingdom of southern Judah and northern Israel.
1. The reign of Azariah, king of southern Judah (vv. 1-7)
2. The fall of the house of Jehu in northern Israel (vv. 8-12)
3. The chaos of northern Israel (vv. 13-31)
4. The reign of Jotham, king of southern Judah (vv. 32-38)

[Chapter 16] The Evil Rule of Ahaz King of Judah
Ahaz, the twelfth king of southern Judah, despite God's continued warnings, did not repent but instead served foreign gods and betrayed God. He committed idolatry and all kinds of evil, relied on the king of Assyria rather than on God, and even abolished the covenant and ordinances of the temple. Between his excellent father Jotham and his son Hezekiah, Ahaz is recorded as one of the most wicked of the kings of Judah.
He committed the same sin as the kings of the northern kingdom, that is, all kinds of evil including the religious sin of idolatry (v. 3)
He did not trust in God but submitted to the king of Assyria, who was nothing more than a man, and asked him for help (v. 7)
He broke the covenant and ordinances of the temple (v. 18)
1. The reign of Ahaz (vv. 1-4)
2. The invasion of southern Judah by the allied forces of Aram and northern Israel (vv. 5-9)
3. Ahaz's acts of apostasy (vv. 10-20)

[Chapter 17] The Fall of Northern Israel
Northern Israel, beginning with Jeroboam, lasted about 200 years but was destroyed by Assyria in the time of its nineteenth king, Hoshea. The reason northern Israel came to be destroyed was their sin of abandoning the word of God and worshiping idols.
As a result Samaria fell, and foreigners came to settle in that land.
1. The reign of Hoshea and the fall of northern Israel (vv. 1-6)
2. The causes of the fall of northern Israel (vv. 7-23)
3. Assyria's policy of forced resettlement and its results (vv. 24-41)

[Chapter 18] Hezekiah's Religious Reform and the Invasion of Assyria
This chapter records the reign of Hezekiah, the thirteenth king of southern Judah, who is regarded as the most outstanding king after the division of the kingdom of Israel, and the invasion of Sennacherib king of Assyria.
In the face of the powerful Assyrian invasion, Hezekiah at first escaped the crisis by offering tribute, but afterward he sought God's help by prostrating himself before God and praying earnestly. This was because he had keenly realized that only by relying on God alone, rather than on human means, could he overcome the crisis at hand.
His example shows that not human methods but only the power of God is the true way of salvation.
1. The good reign of King Hezekiah (vv. 1-8)
2. The invasion of Judah by Sennacherib king of Assyria (vv. 9-37)

[Chapter 19] Hezekiah's Prayer and the Deliverance of the LORD
This chapter tells how King Hezekiah, in crisis because of the invasion and demand for surrender by Sennacherib king of Assyria, himself prayed earnestly and also asked the prophet Isaiah to pray, and Isaiah comforted King Hezekiah with a prophecy of blessing.
Assyria was an instrument of God to discipline Judah, but Hezekiah, as a mediator for the people, becomes a type of Jesus Christ.
As it appears in verse 31, God saved Judah by the zeal of the LORD, that is, His faithfulness to the covenant with David.
1. Hezekiah, who asked the prophet Isaiah to pray (vv. 1-7)
2. Sennacherib's letter and Hezekiah's prayer (vv. 8-19)
3. Isaiah's prophecy and its fulfillment (vv. 20-37)

[Chapter 20] Hezekiah's Life Extended, and the Visit of the Babylonian Envoys
Hezekiah, who had repelled Assyria's attack by the power of prayer, when he fell ill with an incurable disease prayed earnestly to God once more, and the disease was healed.
Hezekiah, who had experienced the power of God, forgot his weak state before God, and with a heart lifted up again made the mistake of boasting of his wealth and glory to the delegation of the Babylonians who came to inquire after him, and of showing them everything in the royal palace.
Even King Hezekiah, who had been pleasing in God's sight, in his later years put himself ahead rather than putting God ahead, and so remains a king whose end was not good.
1. Hezekiah, who was given an extension of life (vv. 1-11)
2. King Hezekiah's pride and its result (vv. 12-21)

[Chapter 21] The Evil Rule of Manasseh and Amon, Kings of Judah
Even after the fall of northern Israel, God gave southern Judah mercy and a chance to repent, but Judah did even more evil and walked the road to destruction. It speaks of how southern Judah, already pronounced for destruction, far from repenting and having the judgment suspended or abolished, did even more evil and became more corrupt.
In particular, Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, brought on God's judgment by the extremely wicked sins of defiling the temple and Jerusalem, and his son Amon, continuing the evil, was killed by his servants.
Their sin was even worse than that of the Canaanite peoples, so that the covenant blessing of God was withdrawn and terrible judgment came.
1. The evil rule of Manasseh (vv. 1-18)
2. The wicked reign of Amon (vv. 19-26)

[Chapter 22] The Discovery of the Book of the Law and Josiah's Repentance
Through the book of the law, Josiah comes to realize the sin of Israel and the wrath of God. His realization was confirmed through the prophecy of the prophetess Huldah, and he also came to know that God's judgment on Israel had already been fixed.
Josiah went before God, tore his clothes, and was contrite, and because of that sincere contrition he experienced the mercy of having God's judgment postponed in his own time.
This shows the lesson that the favor of God that comes to the one who repents is greater than judgment.
1. King Josiah's repair of the temple and the discovery of the book of the law (vv. 1-11)
2. The prophecy of the prophetess Huldah (vv. 12-20)

[Chapter 23] Josiah's Religious Reform and the Reign of Jehoahaz
King Josiah came to the throne at a young age but was a king who followed the way of David and carried out faithful and good government; he read the book of the law, realized the sins of the people, and was so humble and obedient that he tore his clothes and was contrite.
In accordance with the word, he made a covenant together with the people, thoroughly removed idolatry, and carried out reforms to follow the will of God; with outstanding resolve and action, he burned and trampled all the vessels and images connected with idols, clearly revealing the futility of idols and that the LORD alone is the true God. This religious reform became an occasion to correct wrong faith and to remind the people that the source of blessing is God alone.
At the same time, by removing the social system that had formed around idols, especially those who enjoyed vested interests, he formed a just social order in which the poor and righteous were restored. He also tried to unify the idolatrous communities separated in each region into one community of faith, and, by removing the idol priests, to strengthen the kingship and restore the faith and identity of Israel as the chosen people.
Yet he also left a regrettable side in that, with regard to taking part in war, he did not ask God's will but decided by his own judgment.
1. King Josiah's renewal of the covenant (vv. 1-3)
2. King Josiah's great religious reform (vv. 4-25)
3. The death of King Josiah (vv. 26-30)

[Chapter 24] The Babylonian Invasion
It records the reigns of the last three kings of the kingdom of southern Judah (Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah), who came to the throne after Josiah and Jehoahaz. They were all evil and suffered at the hands of Babylon, the instrument of God's discipline.
As a result, the fact that in only twenty-two years after the death of King Josiah four kings changed and the kingdom was ceaselessly invaded and interfered with by foreign nations shows the fate of the kingdom of southern Judah, the chosen people of God, which was going to ruin as a result of forsaking God. Those who reject the light yoke that God has set and leave God end up bearing a heavier yoke.
1. The evil rule of King Jehoiakim (vv. 1-7)
2. The reign of King Jehoiachin (vv. 8-17)
3. The reign of King Zedekiah (vv. 18-20)

[Chapter 25] The Fall of Jerusalem and the Destruction of the Kingdom of Judah
Because of the destruction of the kingdom of Judah, everything that had symbolized the glory of Israel, the chosen people, disappeared.
The temple that God had chosen to put His name there, and the royal palace, which was the outward guarantee of the word in which God said He would make the throne of David firm forever, were burned and destroyed. Moreover, since the temple vessels were all plundered, they even lost the opportunity to go before God and offer sacrifices.
More serious still, the people of Israel were driven out even from Canaan, the Promised Land, which was their base for living as the chosen people and had been given as the fulfillment of the covenant repeated from the time of Abraham. In the end, every channel through which they could enter into a relationship with God was cut off.
The downfall of Judah was a judgment of discipline sent upon Judah, which had corrupted itself by rejecting God to the end. This was a just judgment.
Yet God did not forget the chosen people He had once chosen, nor the history of the Old Testament and the prophecy concerning David, through which He had decided to connect to the New Testament. Through the restoration of Jehoiachin, a descendant of the house of David, He finally brings it to realization in the return from the Babylonian captivity in 537 BC.
1. The fall of the city of Jerusalem and the destruction of the kingdom of Judah (vv. 1-21)
2. Those left in Judah and the governor Gedaliah (vv. 22-26)
3. The release of Jehoiachin (vv. 27-30)

[Chapter 1] The Genealogy from Adam to Esau (The Lineage of the People Chosen by God)
1 Chronicles 1 arranges the genealogy of the ancestors of Israel beginning with Adam, and so shows that this history is not merely the history of humanity but the history of a people chosen by God. This genealogy is based on the content of Genesis and emphasizes that the nation of Israel began and developed within God's plan.
1–4 _ The genealogy of ten persons from Adam to Noah. (Genesis 5)
5–23 _ The genealogy of each nation that branched off from the three sons of Noah (Shem, Ham, Japheth). (Genesis 10)
24–28 _ The genealogy from Shem to Abraham.
29–35 _ The lineage of Abraham's other descendants, that is, the descendants who came from Ishmael and Keturah
36–54 _ The lineage of the descendants of Esau (Edom)
While arranging the genealogies of the neighboring peoples related to Israel, this follows a structure that emphasizes that Israel is the central people chosen by God.

[Chapter 2] Introducing the ancestral line of David, centered on the genealogy of the tribe of Judah
1 Chronicles 2 concentrates on the genealogy of the tribe of Judah among the sons of Israel. This is not a mere record of bloodlines but is arranged along the genealogy of redemptive history, in which the Messiah was to come. The author who wrote this book looks at the genealogies of the people of Israel from a perspective of faith and the spirit, and at the center of it are David and Judah, and the Messiah who was to come.
1–17 _ The genealogy from the sons of Israel (Jacob), centered on the tribe of Judah, down to David
18–41 _ The descendants of Hezron, Judah's grandson
42–55 _ The descendants of Caleb, another descendant of Judah

[Chapter 3] The descendants of David and the descendants after the Babylonian exile (the course of the Davidic dynasty)
1 Chronicles 3 is recorded with the genealogy of the Davidic dynasty at its center. If the preceding chapter 2 foretold the appearance of David through the genealogy down to Jesse, this chapter introduces in earnest David's descendants and the course of the kingship. This is not merely a genealogy of kings; it carries important meaning as a genealogy of redemptive history connected with the coming of the Messiah. Because it includes the genealogy both before and after the fall of Jerusalem, it is a record of hope showing that the house of David was maintained even after the Babylonian exile.
1–9 _ The list of sons born to David by his wives and concubines
10–16 _ The royal genealogy from Solomon to Zedekiah, the last king of the kingdom of Judah
17–21 _ The genealogy after the fall of Jerusalem: the descendants of Jehoiachin, who was taken captive to Babylon, down to the grandsons of Zerubbabel
Zerubbabel was the leader who led the rebuilding of the temple after the return from exile, and this genealogy shows continuity rather than the severing of the dynasty.
22–24 _ The descendants of Shecaniah, a genealogy spanning four generations
This is a testimony of faith that the lineage of the Davidic dynasty continued unbroken even after the Babylonian exile.

[Chapter 4] The genealogies of the tribes of Judah and Simeon compared (the fulfillment of God's promise)
1 Chronicles 4 deals with the genealogies of the tribes of Judah and Simeon among the twelve tribes of Israel. Unlike chapters 1–3, which dealt with the genealogy from Adam to David, from this chapter on the genealogies of the tribes that make up the people of Israel are introduced in earnest. In particular, Judah is emphasized in its importance as the tribe that became the foundation of the united kingdom, while Simeon, by contrast, is shown gradually declining.
1–23 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Judah
24–43 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Simeon
Because the first half and the second half form a contrast between prosperity and decline, that is, between Judah and Simeon, they reveal how God's prophecy was fulfilled in history.

[Chapter 5] The genealogies of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan, and the result of their disobedience to God
1 Chronicles 5 deals with the genealogies and history of the three tribes [Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh] who lived east of the Jordan, and with God's judgment. They belonged not only to the same region geographically; they were also tribes that took part in war together and served God. In the end, however, because of the sin of turning away from God, they met the tragic end of being taken captive by Assyria.
What this chapter emphasizes is to show that the rise and fall of these three tribes was determined by whether they drew near to God or kept far from Him.
1–10 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Reuben and an introduction to their dwelling places
11–17 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Gad and the region where they settled
18–22 _ The victory of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and the reason for it
This emphasizes that this victory was possible because they relied on God.
23–26 _ The sin of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and its result
These tribes soon betrayed God and fell into idol worship, and in the end they were taken captive and scattered by Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria. This judgment was the result of keeping far from God, and it led to a ruin from which there was no recovery.
It contains a historical lesson: those who once won victories by relying on God came to destruction when they abandoned their faith. Chronicles makes clear that even the people of God cannot escape judgment if they neglect their relationship with God.

[Chapter 6] The genealogy of the tribe of Levi, their mission, and their cities (from a priestly perspective)
1 Chronicles 6 is recorded with the genealogy of the tribe of Levi, their roles, and their dwelling places at its center. It is a representative chapter showing that the author of this book has a priestly viewpoint. The placement of this chapter between the previous chapter (chapter 5), which presents the history and judgment of the tribes east of the Jordan, and the next chapter (chapter 7), which introduces the genealogies of the tribes west of the Jordan, is meant to emphasize the spiritual centrality of the tribe of Levi.
The Levites were the tribe responsible for the core of Israel's worship, namely sacrifice, praise, and temple service, and this chapter reveals not only their genealogy but also the permanence and importance of the duties entrusted to them by God.
1–15 _ The genealogy of the high priests from Aaron down to the period of exile
16–30 _ The genealogy of the descendants of Levi's three sons, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari
31–48 _ The genealogy of those in charge of singing praise in the temple [Heman (Kohathite line), Asaph (Gershonite line), and Ethan (Merarite line)]
49–53 _ The genealogy of the high priests
This is to emphasize the importance and the distinctive legitimacy of the priesthood.
54–81 _ An introduction to the dwelling places of the tribe of Levi and the cities allotted to them
This is a key chapter that clearly shows what position the tribe of Levi held within Israel.

[Chapter 7] The genealogies of the northern tribes west of the Jordan (the identity of the people of Israel who returned from exile)
1 Chronicles 7 deals with the genealogies of six tribes that belonged to the region west of the Jordan River, that is, northern Israel. Although these tribes came from northern Israel, which was later destroyed by Assyria, these genealogies show that even after the return from exile they were still remembered as the people of God. This record, written to restore the identity of the people of Israel in the time of Ezra, serves to reaffirm that the northern tribes too are the covenant people of God.
1–5 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Issachar
6–12 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin
13 _ The tribe of Naphtali
14–19 _ The genealogy of the western half-tribe of Manasseh
20–29 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim
30–40 _ The genealogy of the tribe of Asher

[Chapter 8] The genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin (the genealogy of the house of Saul)
1 Chronicles 8 is a chapter that deals intensively with the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. Unlike what was already briefly introduced in chapter 7, here it is described in more detail and centered on particular persons. It unfolds especially around the line leading to Ehud and the house of Saul, and its complicated genealogical structure can be seen as intended to emphasize their historical and spiritual importance.
This is because the tribe of Benjamin, though a small tribe, was the place of origin of the house of Saul, and it played the most important role, next to Judah, among the tribes that returned to Jerusalem after the exile.

[Chapter 9] The list of the people and priests who settled in Jerusalem after returning from exile
1 Chronicles 9 concludes the genealogies recorded earlier (chapters 1–8) and sets out the list of the people who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile and their roles. This is not a mere sorting out of bloodlines but a record showing how a new community was formed in Jerusalem, where the presence of God dwells. It also carries the intention of restoring the traditions and order of David's time, and it emphasizes the religious centrality of Jerusalem.
1–9 _ The list of those who returned to Jerusalem, centered on the tribes of Benjamin and Judah
10–16 _ The list of priests and singers of praise among those who returned
17–27 _ The gatekeepers who guarded the tabernacle in David's time
28–34 _ The various service duties in the sanctuary
35–44 _ The genealogy of the house of Saul
It is the conclusion of the whole genealogical section, and it also serves as a preface to the story of the Davidic kingdom that continues into 2 Chronicles.

[Chapter 10] The death of King Saul (foretelling the transition to David's reign)
1 Chronicles 10 is a chapter that, before opening in earnest the prelude to the Davidic dynasty, records the fall of the dynasty of Saul briefly yet instructively. Through the death of Saul before David's reign began, it reveals the justice of God and the principle of succession to the kingship, and it makes clear that Saul's failure was not merely a defeat in war but the judgment of God. Through this it assures the reader that David's appearance was a legitimate succession according to the will of God.
1–7 _ Saul and his house, who met a miserable end
8–12 _ The body of Saul put to shame by the Philistines, and the people of Jabesh-gilead who took it and buried it
13–14 _ The reason Saul died
Through the fall of Saul, it highlights that David's accession took place within the will of God, and it teaches that the kingship of Israel must be under obedience and a God-centered rule.

[Chapter 11] The accession of King David and the exploits of his mighty men
1 Chronicles 11 deals with the scene of David ascending to the throne with the support of all Israel, together with the conquest of Jerusalem and the exploits of the mighty men who founded the kingdom with him. It is an important chapter showing that the beginning of the Davidic kingdom was accomplished by the will of God, the unity of the tribes of Israel, and the devotion of loyal co-workers.
1–3 _ David ascending to the throne with the support of all Israel
This was an accession carried out according to the will of God, and it is the scene in which a covenant was made between David and the people.
4–9 _ King David's conquest of Jerusalem
10–14 _ The three most outstanding of King David's mighty men: Jashobeam and Eleazar
15–25 _ The second three
26–47 _ The list of David's thirty mighty men

[Chapter 12] The mighty men who supported David as king and the loyalty of the tribes of Israel
1 Chronicles 12 records the mighty men who followed David even before he took the throne, and how all Israel united after the death of Saul to set him on the throne as king. This chapter emphasizes the Israelite people made one around David, and the devotion of the mighty men who submitted to the king God had established. It shows that David's rule was not power given by chance but was established, under the providence of God, with the support of many tribes and mighty men.
1–22 _ The mighty men who came to David while he was suffering at the hands of King Saul
23–40 _ The numbers and tribal origins of the mighty men of each tribe who gathered at Hebron to make David king over Israel

[Chapter 13] Uzzah, who died trying to move the ark of the covenant
1 Chronicles 13 records David's attempt to move the ark of the covenant for the restoration of faith after he had achieved political unity. This was David's decision of faith to place the presence and rule of God at the center. However, the tragedy of Uzzah's death occurred as it was being moved in a way that did not follow the ordinances, and the ark came to stay in the house of Obed-edom. This chapter teaches that even zeal of faith must follow the will and the way of God.
1–5 _ David consulting in order to gather the concern of Israel
6–8 _ The ark of the covenant carried on a cart
9–11 _ The death of Uzzah and its reason: the wrong way of moving the ark of the covenant
12–14 _ The ark of the covenant left to stay with Obed-edom the Gittite
It shows that the presence of God is to be sought with joy, but that the way of doing so must also accord with the will of God. Through this experience David afterward grew into a leader who feared God all the more and served Him rightly.
Although it was halted by a mistake, David's attitude of placing God's rule at the center is clearly expressed in his longing for the ark of the covenant.

[Chapter 14] David, who strengthened his kingship in Jerusalem and won in the war against the Philistines
1 Chronicles 14 is a chapter recording the prosperity and victory that God permitted David in the early period of his reign, and it holds special meaning in that it is placed between the mistake of chapter 13 and the restoration of chapter 15. It emphasizes that God continued to bestow grace and blessing on David, and it is evidence that his reign was under the guidance of God.
Through the scene in which David gradually grew strong and defeated the enemy Philistines twice, it makes clear that the blessing and presence of God were with him.
1–7 _ The prospering Israel of David
8–12 _ Defeating the great army of the Philistines under God's guidance right after taking the throne
13–17 _ Israel annihilating, by a surprise attack, the great army of the Philistines that attacked again
It is a chapter that clearly reveals that God was with David, and it shows the principle of the blessing and victory that come to those who inquire of God and obey.
Moreover, by showing that God did not abandon David despite his failure but still worked through him, it speaks of the possibility of restoration and grace. This is connected with the decision in chapter 15 to bring the ark of the covenant in again rightly, and it makes more distinct the picture of a believer who obeys the will of God.

[Chapter 15] David, who moved the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem according to the ordinances of God
It records the scene in which David, remembering his past mistake, moves the ark of the covenant rightly according to the ordinances of God. After the incident of Uzzah's death in chapter 13, David realized how important it is to follow God's way, and this time he prepared thoroughly and moved the ark under the service of the Levites.
This chapter shows well the restoration of God's presence through repentance, obedience, and the restoration of worship.
1–15 _ King David thoroughly preparing to bring it to Jerusalem
16–24 _ The service of the Levites who attended the moving of the ark of the covenant
25–29 _ The praise of the whole throng of Israel as they successfully brought the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem
David learned through failure, and this time he succeeded in welcoming the presence of God by obeying the word thoroughly. Thereby Israel became one, centered on the word and on faith, and the blessing of God came all the more abundantly upon David's kingdom.

[Chapter 16] Praise and thanksgiving offered to God after the dedication of the ark of the covenant
1 Chronicles 16 is a chapter recording the sacrifices and devout institutions that David offered to God after he had moved the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem. With the ark of the covenant, which symbolizes the presence of God, settled in the City of David, David establishes Israel with faith at its center through peace offerings, the organization of a praise choir, the composition of a psalm of thanksgiving, and the arrangement of service duties.
1–3 _ David offers peace offerings before the ark of God.
4–6 _ He organizes a praise choir.
7–36 _ He composes a psalm of thanksgiving and has the choir sing praise before all the people.
37–43 _ The other institutions of service to God
This chapter shows well how the sacrifices and praise offered before the presence of God and the joy of the people are brought into harmony. David did not stop at merely moving the ark; through sacrifices and order fitting for it, he devoted himself to exalting God and setting the people of Israel apart as holy. This shows that all true restoration begins in a life centered on the word and on worship.

[Chapter 17] The covenant of an eternal dynasty given by God
1 Chronicles 17 is a turning point in redemptive history centered on the covenant God gave to David, and it is a chapter showing the culmination of David's religious work. David wanted to build a temple for the ark of God, but God prevented that plan and instead gave him the promise that He would make David's dynasty firm forever.
This chapter shows David's humble and grateful attitude toward the grace and promise of God.
1–6 _ God, who opposes David's intention to build the temple on his own
7–15 _ God, who promises that He will make David's dynasty firm forever
This promise leads to its fulfillment through the Messiah, Jesus Christ.
16–27 _ David, moved by God's promise, offering a prayer of thanksgiving
This chapter emphasizes the fact that the sovereignty of God and the covenant of grace precede human plans. David tried to do something for God, but God had instead prepared something greater and eternal for David. It also shows how important humble acceptance of and gratitude for the word of God, and a response of faith, are in a right relationship with God.
In the end, this chapter presents the central axis of redemptive history that leads, through the Davidic covenant, to the kingdom of Jesus Christ.

[Chapter 18] David expands the kingdom through military victories
This chapter records the beginning of David's military conquests, and shows the process by which, because God was with him, he defeated his enemies and expanded the territory of the kingdom.
Also, after the conquests David builds a stable administrative system and thereby lays the foundation of a strong kingdom. It emphasizes that this whole process was a faithful fulfillment of God's covenant and of His accompanying presence.
1–13 _ David, who, by being with God, conquers and rules all the enemies both within and outside Israel
14–17 _ The solid administrative system organized by King David
David was not merely a war hero but a leader of faith who believed God's promise, obeyed, and entrusted the war to God.
As a result, Israel was freed from its enemies and was able to grow into a strong nation, and David laid the foundation of a kingdom that became a model of the kingdom of God both internally and externally.

[Chapter 19] War begins from the provocation of Ammon and Aram, and David wins with the help of God
1 Chronicles 19 deals with the war against the Ammonites and records the incident in which David's righteous intention was misunderstood and spread into war.
This war began when David sent a condolence delegation to mourn the death of the king of Ammon, and through the process in which, as a result, Ammon and even their ally Aram were defeated by Israel, it shows the help of God and the rightful rule of David.
1–5 _ Hanun son of Nahash misunderstands David's pure intention and insults the condolence delegation
6–9 _ Hanun forms an alliance with Aram and starts a war, and David prepares for the war with Joab.
10–15 _ Aram fleeing at the sight of Israel's might
16–19 _ Aram being driven back by David and Joab

[Chapter 20] David continues to win in the wars against Ammon and the Philistines
1 Chronicles 20 deals with the final phase of David's military work, and records the ultimate victories Israel won in the wars against Ammon and the Philistines. With the help of God, David and his mighty men overwhelm the foreign nations, showing at the same time Israel's spiritual restoration and political stability.
1–3 _ David, who completely wiped out the Ammonites
4–8 _ Israel, victorious in the third war with the Philistines

[Chapter 21] David's census begun in pride, and David's repentance
Although this is the first chapter to deal in earnest with the work of David's reign, its beginning starts from David's pride and the sin resulting from it. In the stability and prosperity God had given, David became arrogant, and, falling into the temptation of Satan, he ordered a census and so committed a great sin before God. Yet David repented sincerely, and God graciously opened a way again.
1–6 _ David, who became proud after being tempted by Satan, orders a census
7–17 _ God's wrath and discipline against it
18–30 _ Building an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan and offering sacrifices
It shows how great an effect pride can have, and how true repentance and obedience call forth the compassion of God. It makes clear that God gives a new opportunity to the one who repents, and that He is the One who turns a place where calamity fell into a place of grace.
Ornan's threshing floor later becomes a holy place that serves as the site of the temple, and becomes a place where sin and judgment, repentance and restoration meet.

[Chapter 22] David entrusts the preparation for building the temple to Solomon and also urges all the people to take part
David, who in the previous chapter (chapter 21) went through the process of punishment for sin and repentance, shows in this chapter preparation and devotion for building the temple.
Although God did not permit him to build the temple, he prepares all the materials and manpower for his son Solomon, and thus succeeds to the kingship in faith.
1–5 _ David prepares building materials and workers for building the temple.
6–16 _ David calls his son Solomon and entrusts him with building the temple.
17–19 _ David also commands the leaders and officials of Israel to cooperate in building the temple.
This chapter shows that obedience and devotion follow in the life of one who has repented. Although David himself could not build the temple, he reveals the wisdom and humility of being faithful to his own role and preparing in advance.
Also, this chapter emphasizes that building the temple is not merely a human project but a holy work of serving God, and it stresses that the participation and devotion of all the people are needed.

[Chapter 23] Systematically organizing the duties of the Levites for temple service
David organizes the Levites in order to set in order the religious system for the time after the temple was built. In particular, at a time when he was approaching the end of his life, he systematically apportions the number and duties of the Levites who would serve in the temple, and thus prepares to support Solomon's kingship.
This is a scene that shows David's thorough preparedness in both faith and administration.
1–5 _ After making his son Solomon king, David assembles the Levites in Jerusalem
6–23 _ The Levites are subdivided according to the clans of the descendants of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari
24–32 _ Their duties in the temple
David completed the system of priests and Levites so that the next generation could serve God wholeheartedly. This was not a mere administrative measure but a spiritual foundation for maintaining Israel as a theocratic state. David's preparation came from a heart that desired a God-centered nation, and it reveals that he was not merely a military hero but a spiritual leader.

[Chapter 24] Organizing temple service by dividing the duties of the priests and Levites into 24 divisions
As part of the preparation for temple service, David systematically sets in order the duties of the priests and Levites. In particular, he divided the priests, who were descendants of Aaron, into 24 divisions and had them share the service in turns, and he also organized the descendants of Levi to take part in auxiliary duties according to their respective families. This was a measure for the order and continuity of temple service.
1–19 _ The divisions of the priests: the descendants of Aaron (the priests) divided into 24 divisions
20–31 _ The Levites are selected by casting lots and their divisions are determined.
David organized them so that all that service would be carried out faithfully within an established order. Serving God in such an orderly way is an example for all believers.

[Chapter 25] Organizing the temple choir
David organized a choir to take charge of praise in the temple. Following the arrangement of the duties of the priests and Levites, he sought to awaken the heart through praise. The choir was divided into 24 divisions in all and served at regular intervals.
1–7 _ The number and duties of the sons of Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, who formed the divisions of the choir
8–31 _ The order of service determined by lot
Whereas in the tabernacle of Moses there was no regulation concerning a choir, David organized a choir to serve in the temple. This became an important means of establishing the faith of the people in reverence.

[Chapter 26] Setting the order of the temple by dividing the duties of gatekeepers, treasurers, judges, and others
This chapter deals with the offices that support the work of the temple indirectly, not roles that offer sacrifices directly to God. The roles of gatekeepers, storehouse keepers, judges, and others are introduced, and the administrative ability of King David, who pursued order and thoroughness in everything, is revealed.
1–19 _ The 24 divisions of gatekeepers are organized by lot.
20–28 _ The division of work for the management of the temple storehouses
29–32 _ The officers and judges who carried out duties outside the temple
David regarded as holy not only the visible sacrifices in the service of God but also all the unseen work. He established each department, organized it in an orderly way, and prepared thoroughly for building the house of God completely.
This reminds us that in the church today, too, all service must be prepared honestly and thoroughly before God.

[Chapter 27] Setting in order the military organization and the system of regional administration
This chapter introduces King David's national defense system and administrative organization. He prepared thoroughly not only in religion but also in national administration and military matters, revealing his intention to hand down a complete kingdom to his son Solomon.
1–15 _ The army organized in 12 divisions
16–24 _ The administrative officers set over each tribe
25–31 _ The officials who managed the king's property
32–34 _ The royal staff, including the king's counselors, scribes, and the commander of the army
David was not merely a king of faith. According to the will of God, he was a king who set in order all spheres of the nation (military, economy, regional administration) in an organized way. His reign can be called a model in which God-centered theocratic government and practical administrative ability were in harmony.

[Chapter 28] David charges Solomon to build the temple, hands over the plans, and encourages him
This chapter records David's last testament together with the preparation and exhortation concerning the building of the temple. In his last years David brings his life to a close not with emptiness or regret but with an attitude of gratitude and obedience toward God.
In particular, by entrusting Solomon with the mission of building the temple and even handing over detailed plans, he shows himself setting in order his remaining work in accordance with the will of God.
1–10 _ Before the people of Israel, David establishes Solomon as his successor and asks him to build the temple diligently
11–19 _ David hands over to Solomon all the plans for building the temple and the list of the prepared materials
20–21 _ He encourages Solomon and urges him not to be afraid
David was a true believer who, to the very last moment of his life, kept the will of God at the center and passed on faith and mission to his successor. His obedience, preparation, encouragement, and humility show what a Christian ought to be.

[Chapter 29] David and the people devote themselves to the building of the temple, and David closes his life
This chapter is the concluding portion of the whole of 1 Chronicles and records the final scene of David's forty-year reign. David brings his life to a close as a God-centered life through his devotion to the building of the temple, the participation of the people, prayers of thanksgiving and sacrifices, and the transfer of the kingship and his death.
1–5 _ King David urges the people to take part willingly in the building of the temple
6–9 _ The people of Israel presenting their wealth to God in response to King David's moving exhortation
10–19 _ David and the people of Israel offering thanks and praise to God
20–22 _ All Israel offers sacrifices with joyful hearts, and the people make Solomon king.
23–25 _ Solomon, who ascends the throne after David
26–30 _ The death of David
The end of David's life is filled with thorough devotion to the kingdom and glory of God: longing for the temple, a community of faith with the people, voluntary devotion, prayers of thanksgiving, and the peaceful transfer of the kingship. This becomes a model showing what the end of a believer's life ought to be.

[Chapter 1] Solomon's thousand burnt offerings, his request for wisdom, and the prosperity of the united kingdom
This chapter announces the opening of the age of Solomon among the 21 kings who ruled the kingdom of Judah after David's time.
By mentioning that God was with Solomon on his throne, it seeks to show that his kingship has the legitimacy of inheriting the covenant of God.
1-6_King Solomon's thousand burnt offerings
7-13_Solomon's request for wisdom and God's answer
14-17_Prosperity through the blessing of God

[Chapter 2] Preparation for building the temple
Unlike the books of Kings, this book has no record of Solomon's reign (judgments, appointment of officials, glory, wisdom) and focuses on the building of the temple.
For the people of Israel who had returned from the Babylonian exile, one of the important things in restoring their faith in God was the building of the temple. This chapter records that Solomon, though young and weak at the age of 20, became king of Israel and undertook the building of the temple (922 B.C.).
1-2_The process of preparing to build the palace and the temple
3-10_The request for help to the king of Tyre
11-16_The king of Tyre's consent to Solomon's request for help
17-18_The foreigners who took part in building the temple

[Chapter 3] Completion of the main building of the temple
This chapter focuses on the building of the temple. The writer, as one who has returned from exile, feels the mission to establish once again the history of the chosen people. He reminds the people that the reason Israel was great in the past was that their faith in God was faithful, centered on the temple sacrifices.
Therefore, he stresses that the most urgent matter now is the restoration of faith, and that the blessing of God also depends precisely on this.
1-2_The beginning of the building of Solomon's temple
3-7_The dimensions of the temple foundation and the design of the porch (vestibule)
8-9_The design of the Most Holy Place
10-14_The design of the two cherubim in the Most Holy Place
15-17_The design of the two pillars before the sanctuary

[Chapter 4] The making of the temple furnishings
This chapter introduces in detail the making of the various furnishings to be used in the temple. Without the furnishings in the temple, the people of Israel could not fully carry out the sacrifices by which they had fellowship with God.
Because the sacrifices performed in the temple ultimately prefigured the redemptive work in which a sinner confesses his sin, offers a sacrificial victim, and in his place receives forgiveness of sin from God, the furnishings used in such sacrifices also each prefigure various aspects of Christ's redemptive work.
1-10_The making of the temple furnishings.
11-22_Huram makes all the furnishings.

[Chapter 5] Placing the ark of the covenant in the new temple
In chapters 3–4 the main building of the temple and the furnishings within it were completed. Chapter 5 records the placing of the ark of the covenant, the most important item of the temple, inside the temple, and afterward the appearance of the presence of God amid praise and thanksgiving before God.
1-10_Placing the ark of the covenant in the temple
11-14_The praise of the choir and the glory of God that came upon the temple

[Chapter 6] Solomon's address and prayer at the dedication of the temple
It records Solomon's congratulatory address on the completion of the temple, which was finally concluded with the placing of the ark of the covenant in the new temple, and his prayer of thanksgiving offered in the capacity of mediator for all the people.
1-11_Solomon's dedication of the temple
12-17_Solomon's prayer on the completion of the temple, and a prayer for the kingship of the house of David in accordance with the Davidic covenant
18-39_Intercessory prayer for Israel and for the foreigners, as king of the theocratic kingdom
40-42_The closing prayer

[Chapter 7] The dedication, the observance of the Feast of Tabernacles, God's warning of blessing and curse, and Solomon's accomplishments
It records the scene in which Solomon and the people of Israel, having completed the building of the temple with the placing of the ark of the covenant, keep the seven-day dedication and the Feast of Tabernacles, the great festival of the nation.

Asa's record also appears in Kings, but Asa's reign, introduced only briefly in 1 Kings 15:9-24, is explained in detail in this book, because Asa's deeds are very important for the purpose of writing 2 Chronicles.
This is because the content the Chronicler wants to emphasize, namely blessing when one fears God and curse when one apostatizes and disobeys, appears so well in the life story of King Asa.
Asa's reign began with changes close to a religious reformation, and especially the first ten years of his reign were a very dynamic period (14:1). He removed the foreign altars and high places, broke the sacred pillars and the Asherah poles, and commanded the people of Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to keep the law and the commandments (14:3–4).
This reform was a difficult task that went beyond a mere tidying up of religious ceremonies, fundamentally changing an idol-centered way of survival connected with Canaanite agricultural culture.
Just as God gave the nation peace when King Asa removed sin and idols, so too Christians today can enjoy true peace and prosperity when they cast away sin and idols in their hearts and seek God alone.

Azariah, who is mentioned only in this passage, conveys the word of God that came upon him and urges King Asa to carry out a religious reformation. Azariah first explains the principle of this reform.

[Chapter 16] King Asa, the third king of southern Judah: the last part of his reign
2 Chronicles 16 records the scene of a reversal in which the faith of King Asa, who had relied on God alone, collapses in the last part of his reign.
At that time northern Israel was ruled by King Baasha, and the background is the situation from the 36th year of Asa until the 41st year, when Baasha died (16:1, 13). To check southern Judah, King Baasha fortified Ramah and blocked Asa's access.
Asa was a man who had earlier won a great victory in the war with the Cushites by relying on God, and who had also carried out a sweeping religious reformation. But faced with the crisis that came at the end of his reign, he did not rely on God and instead tried to solve the problem by worldly means. The result led to a decline of faith and spiritual failure.

[Chapter 29] Hezekiah, the thirteenth king of southern Judah: the rededication of the temple and the sin offering in the first year of his reign
Hezekiah's religious reformation, recorded in 2 Kings, is expanded in 2 Chronicles to three chapters (chapters 29–31). This tells us that the Chronicler places more weight on recording the religious reformation than on the political side. In conclusion, Hezekiah's reform in 2 Chronicles is recorded as far more extensive and more positive than in Kings.
As soon as King Hezekiah came to the throne, he opened the doors of the temple and repaired them (2 Chronicles 29:3), convened the priests and Levites, and commanded them to realize the sin that he and the people had committed against God and to carry out consecration and the cleansing of the temple (vv. 4–5).
He pointed out specifically the sins of the ancestors, the heart of which was that they had shut the doors of the temple, put out the lamps, and not offered sacrifices (v. 7). This reflects the situation in which temple sacrifices had been completely suspended during the reign of King Ahaz (2 Chronicles 24:1~9).
Hezekiah recognized that the wrath of God had come because of the sins of the ancestors and that Judah had actually been punished by the attacks of various nations (29:8). He warned that even now Judah was under the wrath of God (v. 9), and sought to make a new covenant with God in order to turn it away (v. 10).
In particular, he reminded the Levites that God had chosen them, and commanded them to devote themselves to consecration and the cleansing of the temple (v. 11).

[Chapter 30] Hezekiah's observance of the Passover
When the temple was rededicated and the sacrifices restored, King Hezekiah sent letters inviting all Israel and Judah to keep the Passover together in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 30:1,5).
From the beginning he had a plan to keep the Passover also with the brothers who still remained in the land of northern Israel, which had been destroyed in the time of Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:8~15).
But because there were not enough consecrated priests and the people had not all gathered, the Passover could not be kept in the first month, as the law prescribes. In particular, the expression "did not come to Jerusalem" refers to the inhabitants of northern Israel. So Hezekiah consulted with the whole assembly and decided to postpone the Passover to the second month. This decision applied to the whole community, on the basis of the principle of the law (Numbers 9), the rule that an unclean person may keep the Passover a month later (30:12).
The king and the assembly rejoiced at this decision, and sent couriers to spread the king's message in the regions of northern Israel such as Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun. In his preaching Hezekiah announced that northern Israel too, like Judah, had sinned against God and received discipline, and was still under the wrath of God. By refusing the sacrifices offered at the temple in Jerusalem they had abandoned God, and he urged them now to repent and return to the temple (30:8).
But many of the people of northern Israel mocked and refused this invitation, and only a few responded to it (30:10). Even so, on the fourteenth day of the second month, a great crowd made up of people of Judah and of northern Israel gathered in Jerusalem and kept the Passover together (30:13).

[Chapter 31] Hezekiah's reform of the sacrificial system
King Hezekiah continued the reform even after the Passover and, together with the people, thoroughly removed the high places and idols in Judah and in some regions of northern Israel. He restored the sacrificial system so that the priests and Levites would fulfill their roles, and had temple worship carried out in the prescribed order.
Hezekiah commanded the people, according to the law, to bring tithes and firstfruits to God, and the people too gave abundantly and willingly. Because many offerings piled up as a result, storehouses were built, and officials were appointed to manage and distribute them in an orderly way.
The priests and Levites received their offerings fairly distributed to themselves and their families, and this was in accordance with the established ordinances.
Hezekiah acted faithfully and uprightly before God, and the reform of faith and administration led to the blessing of God.

[Chapter 33] The reigns of Manasseh, the fourteenth king, and Amon, the fifteenth king of southern Judah
This chapter records two kings of southern Judah, Manasseh and Amon.
First, Manasseh practiced all kinds of idolatry, such as the worship of the sun, moon, and stars, sorcery and witchcraft, and human sacrifice, and as a discipline from God he was taken captive by Assyria and led off to Babylon. But he repented in the land of his captivity, and God brought him back to Jerusalem and restored him to the throne. Afterward Manasseh removed the idols and rebuilt cities, putting into practice the restoration of faith and good government.
Whereas the books of Kings emphasize only Manasseh's evil deeds,
2 Chronicles records together with them also the positive results: his repentance and reform, and the resulting economic and military prosperity, building projects, and the welfare of the people.
This is because Kings emphasizes the rebelliousness of Israel from the viewpoint of a prophet, while 2 Chronicles seeks to show the importance of repentance and the mercy of God from the viewpoint of a priest.
Through the life of Manasseh, the Chronicler seeks to convey to the people a message of hope: "Even one who has left God, if he repents sincerely, will have restoration and blessing."
The second half records the reign of Manasseh's son Amon. Even in his short reign of only two years he engaged in evil deeds and idolatry, and in the end he met the miserable end of being assassinated by his servants.

[Chapter 34] Josiah, the sixteenth king of southern Judah: his religious reformation
This chapter records the 31-year reign of Josiah, the sixteenth king.
Beginning around the eighth year of his reign, King Josiah wiped out idols throughout southern Judah and northern Israel for more than ten years, and around the eighteenth year of his reign he carried out the work of cleansing the temple.
During the repair of the temple, the book of the law was found and read, and Josiah repented greatly, realizing his own sins and the sins of disobedience against God that his ancestors had committed up to that time.
Toward his humble attitude, God said that He would postpone, for the time of Josiah, the destruction of southern Judah that had already been determined, and this was confirmed through the prophecy of the prophetess Huldah.
Afterward Josiah read the book of the law found in the temple before all the people and carried out a covenant renewal ceremony in which they pledged to obey God.
This reform came from Josiah's passion for God since his childhood, but in the end it was by the help of God, who opened the hearts of the people so that they responded, that it could achieve great success. Also, the reform could succeed not only because of Josiah's personal resolve but because all the people together realized their sins, repented, and put into action their will to obey the word.

[Chapter 36] The fall of southern Judah, the history of the exile, and the proclamation of Cyrus's edict allowing the return from exile
This chapter is a record of the four kings from the seventeenth to the twentieth in Judea. It shows the stern judgment that came because of sin, and the mercy of God that appeared in the midst of it.
God had warned many times that blessing would follow obedience, and curse and destruction would follow disobedience, and that word became reality in the time of Zedekiah, the last king.
It was a punishment from God that had been foretold long before.
The fall of Judah was not a mere event; it was God's discipline on a people who, though given many opportunities to repent, did not turn back to the very end. Judah in the end was destroyed as the price of that sin. But if everything had ended with this, the covenant that God had given to Abraham, Moses, and David could not have been fulfilled.
God destroyed the kingdom of Judah, but He left the people, and later enabled them to rebuild the nation. This is God's preserving, by His sovereignty and grace, the covenant given to the house of David and the chosen people. Despite the disobedience of Judah, God in the end fulfilled that promise through Jesus Christ, the fulfiller of the Davidic covenant.
All the events in the history of Judah were not by chance but providence for the fulfillment of God's covenant. The history of God's salvation will surely be accomplished within His sovereignty and love, regardless of human failure.
Jesus Christ came as the fulfiller of the Davidic covenant, completed salvation by dying on the cross and rising again, and will come again and lead Christians to the eternal heaven. This promise too will surely be fulfilled within the providence of God.

But Tattenai, the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, came to them, yet God did not let them cease the work. Tattenai asked King Darius to confirm Cyrus's decree that had permitted the building, and waited for a reply.
