[Chapter 1] The news of the broken walls of Jerusalem and Nehemiah's intercessory prayer
Even after the first (536 B.C.) and second (458 B.C.) returns of the people of Judah, Nehemiah was still staying in the palace of Artaxerxes, king of Persia. One day he heard from men who had been to Jerusalem that the wall was broken down and the people were suffering, and he grieved deeply. This was because an earlier attempt to repair the wall had been stopped by hindrances and by the king's decree (Ezra 4:11-24).
Nehemiah, heartbroken at the dreadful state of Jerusalem, fasted and prayed, and then appealed directly to the king and went to Jerusalem to rebuild the wall (Nehemiah 2:1–7:4). His prayer is divided into four parts as follows:
➀ Praise of God's compassion (v. 5)
➁ Confession of the people's sin (vv. 6–7)
➂ Recollection of God's covenant (vv. 8–9)
➃ Petition for the people (vv. 10–11)
This prayer is an intercessory prayer that springs from assurance of the covenant and from faith that the help of God alone is the key to restoration.

[Chapter 2] King Artaxerxes' decree permitting the return, and preparations for rebuilding the wall
After hearing of the wretched state of Jerusalem and praying, Nehemiah asked Artaxerxes, king of Persia, for permission to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the wall. The king accepted Nehemiah's request, provided building materials and an escort of troops, and permitted him to return on the condition that he come back after a set period. This was an answer in accordance with the providence of God.
Having arrived in Jerusalem, Nehemiah first inspected the condition of the wall in secret, then announced the rebuilding plan to the people and urged them to join in. Thereupon the adversaries, such as Sanballat, threatened him with a charge of rebellion, but Nehemiah responded firmly on the basis of the king's permission and the help of God.
Sanballat, the center of the opposing forces, was the governor of Samaria, a powerful man with a mixed religion. He opposed to the end in order to prevent the restoration of the orthodox faith of Judea.

[Chapter 3] Those who deserve credit for the work of rebuilding the wall
This chapter introduces, section by section, the people who took part in the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem, and through them it emphasizes the blessedness of Israel's restoration and devotion.
First, from the Sheep Gate in the north to the Old Gate, the house of the high priest took charge and built it with consecration, because the sacrificial animals passed in and out through the Sheep Gate. The devotion of the men of Tekoa, who took part voluntarily even without leaders, is also noteworthy (v. 5).
In the western wall, people of various classes took part, goldsmiths, perfumers, and even women (v. 12).
For the southeastern wall, although it was the area farthest from the temple, the officials of the outlying districts, with a sense of unity as a covenant community, fulfilled their responsibility.
For the eastern wall, since its length and the degree of destruction were the greatest, many people were assigned, and even those who had already taken charge of other sections devoted themselves again.
Baruch, Meremoth, Hasshub, the men of Tekoa, Hananiah, Meshullam, and others showed double zeal.
Thus the rebuilding of the wall involved devotion that transcended status, region, and background, and it teaches that the kingdom of God gains strength and expands through those who fulfill their responsibility in this way.

[Chapter 4] Schemes to hinder the wall work, and the armed response of the laborers
As the plan to rebuild the wall got under way, Sanballat and Tobiah tried to crush the morale of the people of Judea with mockery and ridicule. They even slandered, saying that the wall would collapse if even a fox climbed up on it, and this was an obstructive scheme through psychological warfare. Nehemiah prayed to God, asking that their mockery be turned back upon themselves.
Even amid the mockery the wall was joined up to half its height, and in the end the adversaries planned an armed attack. Meanwhile, anxiety and pessimism about the work spread even among the Jews themselves, but Nehemiah prayed to God again, armed the people, and continued the work.
When Nehemiah armed the people in preparation for the armed attack of the adversaries, Sanballat had no choice but to give up, and Nehemiah led the work while never relaxing his vigilance and keeping the people armed. But what he relied on was not military force but the help of God. Like David, Nehemiah encouraged the people with the faith that "the battle is the LORD's" and kept pushing forward the rebuilding of the wall.

[Chapter 5] Internal difficulties in the wall work and their resolution
Because of food shortage due to famine and excessive taxes paid to the Persian empire, the rich actively took advantage of that situation to pursue their own interests. They took excessive interest from the poor, mortgaged fields, and made servants of the children of those who could not repay their debts. As a result, the cohesion of the internal community of faith fell, grumbling and complaints arose, and a serious problem arose that would destroy the community. Nehemiah clearly rebuked those wrongs and spoke of being set apart as the chosen people in the fear of God.
That is, he decided on the prohibition of taking interest and on returning the hundredth part that had been taken as interest, and put it into action. He was able to do so because of the upright life of Nehemiah, the leader. During the twelve years he served as governor he received no salary, did not buy land, and the servants belonging to the governor all joined in the work on the wall. In a word, he gave up of his own accord the rights granted to him.

[Chapter 6] The continued schemes of the opponents and the completion of the wall
As the completion of the wall drew near, Sanballat's party plotted to assassinate Nehemiah, but it failed because of his discernment. Next they spread a false rumor that Nehemiah was trying to become king and slandered him, but he prayed to God and was not shaken.
Also, the bribed priest Shemaiah gave a false prophecy telling Nehemiah to flee into the sanctuary, but Nehemiah immediately saw through the scheme and rejected it.
Thus Nehemiah, amid ceaseless obstruction, responded steadfastly and led the rebuilding of the wall by faith.
As a result, the thoroughly destroyed wall of Jerusalem was completed in only 52 days, and this struck great fear into the adversaries. This marvelous accomplishment was due to the working of God (v. 16).
But even after its completion, the obstruction of the Jewish leaders who were in league with Tobiah continued, and the threat did not disappear completely. This shows that the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem was not mere construction but a deep spiritual battle.

[Chapter 7] Appointment of those in charge of the defense of the city, and the plan to resettle the population
Although the wall of Jerusalem was completed, Nehemiah judged that the threat from the adversaries remained and did not relax his vigilance.
He set up an effective system of watch for the city and organized the administrative system while guarding against the influence of leading figures who were in league with Tobiah. This was a measure to preserve purity as the people of God.
Meanwhile, since the resident population inside Jerusalem was too small and this made it difficult to defend the city and maintain the community, Nehemiah re-examined the list of those who returned in the first return in the time of Zerubbabel (Ezra 2). This was preparation for resettling the people scattered in various regions inside the city, and it was part of a redemptive-historical plan to restore Jerusalem as the center of the national community.

[Chapter 8] Ezra's reading of the law and the observance of the Feast of Tabernacles
After the wall of Jerusalem was completed, Nehemiah did not stop at outward restoration but began a reformation of faith for the spiritual renewal of the people of Judea. As the first step, Ezra appeared and, on the first day of the seventh month, the Feast of Trumpets, read and interpreted the book of the law, and a great movement of repentance arose from it.
The people, whose longing for the law had grown, also discovered the ordinance of the Feast of Tabernacles and kept the most complete Feast of Tabernacles since the time of Joshua. The Feast of Tabernacles is a festival commemorating the life in the wilderness after the exodus, and through this festival the Jews who had returned from exile recalled the grace of God and resolved never to sin again.
This chapter is a turning point moving from outward rebuilding to inward restoration, and it shows the people of Judea seeking to be reborn as a law-centered community.

[Chapter 9] A review of Israel's past history and the people's contrition
After Ezra's reading of the law and the observance of the Feast of Tabernacles, a nationwide movement of repentance arose among the people of Judea. They fasted, confessed their own sins and those of their ancestors, and severed their unclean relations with foreigners. By reading the law for three hours a day and devoting three hours a day to repentance, they thoroughly examined their lives in the light of the word.
The prayer that the Levites, leading the people during this period, offered to God is divided into three parts.
➀ Praise and thanksgiving (vv. 6–15): They praise the grace by which God created heaven and earth, chose Abraham and made him the chosen people, and brought salvation through the exodus.
➁ Confession and recollection (vv. 16–31): They confess Israel's repeated disobedience and apostasy, and the lovingkindness of God, who did not give up and yet bestowed grace.
➂ Petition and covenant renewal (vv. 32–38): Seeking the help of God amid present suffering, they renew the covenant that from now on they will serve God alone.
This chapter shows the resolve of a people who, looking back on the history of Israel, remember the grace of God and seek to restore their faith through thorough repentance and devotion.

[Chapter 10] The renewal of the covenant and the people's oath to keep the law
The spiritual revival that had risen after the completion of the wall of Jerusalem reached its climax as the people of Judea renewed their covenant with God. The priests, the Levites, and the leaders of the people sealed the covenant document, thereby clearing away their past of disobedience before God and swearing to keep the law.
Next the ordinary people too joined in keeping the covenant and made the following pledges:
➀ To prohibit marriage with foreigners,
➁ To keep the Sabbath, the holy days, and the sabbatical year thoroughly,
➂ To pay the temple tax and supply the wood needed for the burnt offerings,
➃ To vow to give the firstfruits, the firstborn of the livestock, and the tithes.
This renewal of the covenant focused on the restoration of the temple and the sacrificial system, and it was an expression of a resolve of faith to revive Jerusalem and the temple that had been ruined by past disobedience.

[Chapter 11] Resettlement of the dwelling places of the people of Israel
Although the wall of Jerusalem was completed, few people lived inside the city, so Nehemiah carried out a redistribution of the population with reference to the list of those who returned in the first return. The method used at that time was "casting lots," which was an ancient Israelite way of faith of seeking the will of God. As a result one-tenth of the whole population came to live in Jerusalem, and the people willingly accepted this.
The text introduces the list of the residents of Jerusalem, recorded in this order:
➀ the ordinary people (vv. 3–9),
➁ the priests (vv. 10–14, the largest number),
➂ the Levites (vv. 15–18),
➃ the temple servants (vv. 19–24).
Next, the towns of the tribe of Judah (in the south, vv. 25–30) and of the tribe of Benjamin (in the north, vv. 31–36), who lived outside Jerusalem, are also mentioned together.
This chapter shows the orderly rebuilding of the national community centered on Jerusalem and a holy settlement as the people of God.

[Chapter 12] Confirmation of the genealogies of the priests and Levites, and the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem
After the completion of the wall of Jerusalem, Nehemiah organized the genealogies of the priests and Levites in order to set in order the temple sacrificial system. This list records in detail the roles and genealogies of the priests and Levites, from those who returned with Zerubbabel down to the time of Joiakim. This was so that, by restoring a God-centered sacrificial system, Israel could stand as the protagonist of redemptive history.
➀ The list of priests who returned with Zerubbabel at the first return (537 B.C.) (vv. 1-7),
➁ The list of priests in the time of Nehemiah (vv. 8-9),
➂ The genealogy of Jeshua, the high priest who returned with Zerubbabel and took the lead in rebuilding the temple (vv. 10-11),
➃ The list of priests in the time of Joiakim, Jeshua's son (vv. 12-21),
➄ The genealogy and roles of the heads of the Levites (vv. 22-26), and so on.
The reason Nehemiah recorded in such detail the list of those who served was that his concern lay in Israel's regaining, through the restoration of the temple sacrificial system, the qualification to be once again the protagonist of redemptive history.
The dedication of the wall was postponed because of the shortage of population in Jerusalem, but it was held with great splendor once conditions were prepared by the resettlement policy and spiritual revival. Nehemiah summoned the Levites and the choirs and had the priests prepare to purify the people and the wall. Afterward two groups led by Ezra and Nehemiah went around on top of the wall praising and offered sacrifices at the temple, thus concluding the dedication.
In particular it carried the meaning of a confession of faith that the safety of the wall depends on God, and the people actively restored the temple sacrificial system by bringing the full tithes in accordance with the covenant.

[Chapter 13] Israel's renewed sin and Nehemiah's second reform
While Nehemiah had returned to the Persian empire, the people of Judea broke the law and sinned again. Therefore, immediately after returning again, Nehemiah carried out reforms.
① Separation from foreigners: In accordance with the law he removed the Moabites and Ammonites from the community and restored the purity of the chosen people. Also, discovering that Tobiah the Ammonite, through collusion with the priest, had taken over a room of the temple, Nehemiah thoroughly removed him and purified the temple.
② Reinstatement of the Levites and restoration of the tithe: When the tithe ceased, the Levites abandoned their service in order to make a living, and Nehemiah rebuked the officials and restored the tithing system so that those who served could fulfill their roles.
③ Restoration of the Sabbath: When the people engaged in labor and trade on the Sabbath, Nehemiah closed the city gates to keep outside merchants from entering and had the Sabbath kept strictly.
④ Separation from intermarriage with foreigners: Learning that a priestly family had intermarried with the adversary Sanballat, Nehemiah removed the one involved from the priesthood and expelled him from the community.
Nehemiah firmly eliminated every compromise that went against the word, and concludes the book by praying that the reforms he had made might be remembered by God.

[Chapter 9] The victory and festival of the Jews
In the climactic section, verses 1–16, the scene of the Jews' enemies suffering fear and destruction and, conversely, of Israel, the chosen people of God, enjoying joy and victory appear in alternation, forming a dramatic contrast.
In the following concluding section, verses 17–32, it is recorded that Mordecai proclaimed the days of Purim and that the whole Jewish people resolved to keep, as a festival throughout the generations, this day on which they were delivered from the hand of their enemies.
The events of this chapter took place about nine months after Mordecai took power in chapter 8, that is, on "the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar," and the day after it.
In fact, this day was originally the day on which the extermination of the Jews was scheduled, when King Xerxes's decree had been promulgated because of Haman's wicked plot. But by the providence of God the situation was reversed: Haman was executed, and Mordecai took over all of Haman's authority, so that this day was instead turned into a day of destruction for the enemies who had tried to kill the Jews.
The events of this chapter did not remain merely a story of deliverance for one age; they became an event that sounded an alarm for the Jewish people, who, stained by the culture and customs of the Gentiles through long captivity, were losing their national purity and consciousness of being the chosen people. Furthermore, without this dramatic event of deliverance, the Jewish people would gradually have become Gentilized and would have been unable to bear their identity as the chosen people and the mission given to them as protagonists of redemptive history.
If that had happened, the restoration of the history of the chosen people through the later second and third returns from exile would also have been impossible, and it would have been a great obstacle to the spread of the gospel of Christ in the New Testament age centered on the synagogues of the Jews living in Gentile lands.

An active and direct rebuttal to Bildad's logic that Job is being punished as a result of having sinned
1-10 _ Human unrighteousness and the greatness of God
11-24 _ Protest to God, thinking that He treats him the same as the wicked or the righteous
25-35 _ Acknowledging the absoluteness of God, hoping for mercy and begging God for a fair judgment

[Chapter 10] Job's reply to Bildad's first speech: lament over suffering and longing for death
Job, setting aside for a moment his rebuttal of Bildad's words, expresses in the form of a plea to God his deep inner anguish over the unresolved problem between the suffering he is now undergoing and the almighty God.
1-7 _ An appeal against the unfairness of the suffering
8-17 _ A plea concerning the suffering
18-22 _ Longing for death and begging for peace during his lifetime

[Chapter 11] Zophar's first speech (rebuke of Job and urging repentance)
Zophar was convinced that Job was suffering because of the righteous providence of God, who judges the wicked. Yet when Job did not admit his own fault and instead tried to justify himself with long words, Zophar regarded Job's attitude as exceedingly detestable and wicked, and strongly rebuked and condemned him and urged repentance.
1-6 _ In accordance with the mistaken traditional view that the justice of God is strictly applied in reality, he rebukes Job as proud and irreverent.
7-12 _ He declares the profundity of the providence of the immeasurable Almighty God and His thorough watchfulness.
13-20 _ The blessing that follows when one repents, and the miserable outcome for one who does not repent.

[Chapter 12] A rebuttal of the three friends' limits of knowledge, and an acknowledgment of the sovereign providence and power of God
To the three friends, who condemn him with a this-worldly way of thinking about retribution, Job points out the essential limits of human beings and denounces their self-righteousness and folly. At the same time, he appeals and pleads his situation to God, who is the fundamental governor and solver of all problems.
1-12 _ A rebuttal of the three friends' limits of knowledge
13-25 _ The sovereign providence and power of God

[Chapter 13] A rebuke of the friends' self-righteousness and an appeal to God about suffering
This chapter is less a mere reply to Zophar's argument in chapter 11 than a comprehensive rebuttal of the arguments of the preceding three friends, in which he lays his anguish before God.
1-19 _ Denunciation of the three friends' vain arguments
20-28 _ An appeal about the suffering of body and soul

[Chapter 14] Lament over fleeting life and Job's plea longing for God's salvation
It records Job's lament over weak and fleeting life and his plea longing for God's salvation.
1-12 _ Lament over human weakness
13-22 _ Longing for God's salvation

[Chapter 15] Eliphaz's second speech (the miserable fate that will befall the wicked)
Eliphaz rebukes Job, who asserts his innocence, in a much stronger tone, and by explaining at length the end of the wicked he gives Job a strong warning and indirectly urges repentance.
1-16 _ A rebuke of Job
17-35 _ The miserable fate that will befall the wicked

[Chapter 16] Job's doubt about God's looking on, and his request for a defense of his innocence
Amid suffering so severe that he longed for death, Job suffered still greater disappointment and pain because of his friends, who pressed him as a sinner. Also, in a situation in which God seemed to be silent, he was tormented by doubt and anguish and experienced great confusion, yet even so he never lost, to the end, his hope for the vindication and restoration of God.
1-5 _ A rebuke of the friends
6-16 _ Doubt toward God
17-22 _ Assurance of innocence

[Chapter 17] Job's lament and his appeal for God's mediation
Although Job fell into great confusion in his suffering because he could not understand the providence of God and His will, he still retained a basic trust in the power and character of God. That is why, though disappointed by the fruitless debate with his friends and lamenting his own situation, he was able to plead with God for mediation.
1-9 _ An appeal for God's mediation
10-16 _ The lament of Job, who has lost hope

[Chapter 18] Bildad's second speech (a rebuke of Job's levity and an argument about the disaster that will befall the wicked)
When Job ignored Eliphaz's advice and instead criticized his friends at length, Bildad, saying that Job does not admit his own sin and only increases his anger, labels him a proud and wicked man and scolds him in a very strong tone. He also explains at length, on the basis of a this-worldly and simple doctrine of retribution, the destruction and death that the wicked will surely undergo.
1-4 _ He regards Job as proud and wicked and scolds him.
5-21 _ A long explanation, based on the doctrine of retribution, of the various forms of the destruction of the wicked and of their death.

[Chapter 19] Job's reply (a rebuke of his friends and assurance of the afterlife and the resurrection)
This chapter does not stop at mere complaint and protest. Even amid despair and lament, Job believes that a redeemer who will deliver him from suffering will appear in the future (v. 25), cherishes hope in the afterlife and the resurrection (v. 26), and trusts in God's ultimate intervention. In this respect Job's faith shows itself far more mature than in his earlier replies.
1-22 _ A rebuke of his friends and an appeal to God
23-29 _ Assurance of the afterlife and the resurrection

[Chapter 20] Zophar's second speech (the inevitable ruin of the wicked)
Zophar's speech is consistently a forceful assertion of the visible and inevitable ruin of the wicked, and in the end it indirectly stresses, in a threatening manner, that Job too is wicked and therefore cannot but be destroyed.
1-11 _ The temporary prosperity of the wicked
12-29 _ The inevitable ruin of the wicked

[Chapter 21] Job's reply to Zophar's second speech: an argument about the prosperity of the wicked and the postponed judgment
By showing that good and evil exist together and that life is vain in a world ruled by the righteous God, he explains, more objectively, logically, and gently, that the simple doctrine of retribution asserted by his friends is mistaken.
1-16 _ The prosperity of the wicked
17-26 _ The postponement of judgment
27-34 _ The futility of the friends

[Chapter 22] Eliphaz's third speech: applying the principle of God's retribution in a this-worldly way to condemn Job and urge repentance
By saying to Job, 'Your wickedness is great and your iniquity is extreme' (v. 5), Eliphaz bluntly brands Job a sinner, and then he condemns him by listing specifically even sins that Job had not actually committed (vv. 6-9).
1-11 _ Condemnation of Job
12-20 _ The principle of God's retribution
21-30 _ A call to Job to repent

[Chapter 23] Job's trust in the providence of God
Whereas in chapter 22 Eliphaz condemned Job as wicked and rebuked him, saying he would surely be destroyed, Job, rather than rebutting his friends' claims one by one, takes a non-argumentative attitude, appealing his own problem directly to God, the source of all things.
1-9 _ Longing to come to God
10-17 _ Trust in the providence of God

[Chapter 24] Conflict over an absurd reality and assurance of God's final judgment
Job has strong assurance of the righteous providence of God, but at the same time he experiences deep conflict and confusion over the problem of human existence, in which good and evil are often seen mixed together in reality.
1-17 _ Protest against an absurd reality
18-25 _ The final judgment that will come upon the wicked

[Chapter 25] Bildad's third speech (a comparison of the greatness of God and the lowliness of man)
Bildad rebukes Job, saying, on the basis of knowledge of God, what is there to say for a man who is like a maggot.
1-6 _ Bildad's speech

[Chapter 26] The power of God shown in the created world
Chapter 25 was Bildad's fictitious argument, which tried to stress Job's lowliness in the light of the greatness of God, and this chapter is the reply to it. In verse 14 Job points out, in the form of a counter-question, the flaw in Bildad's third speech, and in verses 5-14 he lists the majestic power of God shown in the created world in more detail than Bildad, emphasizing that he knows more deeply about the greatness of God. Whereas Bildad tried to highlight Job's lowliness through the majesty and might of God, Job shows that he hopes, taking the omnipotence of God as the ground of his own salvation. Job humbly acknowledges the power of God the Creator, and although human beings cannot fully know the providence of God, he was convinced of the righteous will of God, that God will surely lead for good the one who relies on Him.
1-4 _ The fictitiousness of Bildad's speech
5-14 _ The power of God shown in the created world

[Chapter 27] Job's last reply to his three friends: assurance of his own righteousness and of the ultimate judgment of the wicked
This section best shows the state of mind of Job, who was harassed by the narrow-minded and heartless rebukes of his friends amid unexpected suffering. Unlike his earlier replies, it is characterized by confidently rebutting only the vain claims of his friends, without lament or questioning toward God. This means that Job has moved away from the unbelieving state in which he used to complain to God about the unfairness of the suffering that had come upon him and to plead with Him, and has reached a mature stage of faith, though not yet complete, in which he is assured of the ultimate salvation of the righteous and the final destruction of the wicked.
Through Job's statements we can see that a person with mature faith holds a firm faith that is not shaken by the human evaluations of the world.
1-12 _ A statement about his own righteousness
13-23 _ The ultimate judgment of the wicked

[Chapter 28] Praise of wisdom
Job says that wisdom is more precious than the jewels of the world, and makes clear that the true value of life does not lie in material things. This hints that the suffering Job is undergoing is not simply due to material loss or health problems but is fundamentally related to God, the source of wisdom. It also shows Job's attitude of faith, which seeks to receive the wisdom God gives and to live rightly. Although his friends branded Job a sinner with a schematic and this-worldly doctrine of retribution, Job found no useful lesson or comfort in their claims, and acknowledges and praises that human life and death, blessing and woe depend on the will and providence of God, the source of true wisdom. Christians should not be disappointed or frustrated by trying to solve every problem by themselves, but by following the wisdom God teaches through His word and obeying His providence, they should live a life in which they finally solve every problem and win the victory.
1-22 _ The value of true wisdom
23-28 _ God, the root of wisdom

[Chapter 29] Job's soliloquy: recollection of past blessings
To his friends, who branded him a sinner, he strongly rebuts that their thinking is mistaken, stating that on the contrary he had been one who was protected by God and blessed, and who was respected by others for practicing justice.
1-6 _ Recollection of the past, when before suffering he enjoyed abundance under God's protection and presence
7-25 _ Recollection of the glorious past, when he was praised and respected by people and held a position of leadership

[Chapter 30] Job's soliloquy: an appeal about his present suffering
The pain Job is undergoing is a fundamental pain that comes from feeling that he is far from God and unable to have fellowship, and that God too is turning away from his pain. Because of this, Job experiences extreme anguish of heart and difficulty in faith.
1-15 _ The lament of Job in a wretched state, mocked even by worthless people.
16-23 _ The fundamental cause of the suffering: that he is suffering because he has been abandoned by God.
24-31 _ A lament over Job's desperate reality, in which he cries out earnestly but receives help from no one.

[Chapter 31] Job's soliloquy: his assertion of his own righteousness (Job who asserts his innocence)
Job strongly asserts his innocence using the ancient manner of oath, "If I have committed such-and-such a sin, may I suffer such-and-such a punishment." By explaining his innocence item by item with specific points, he shows that the rebukes and condemnation which his three friends have repeated so far are nothing but unrealistic, empty arguments.
1-15 _ Asserting item by item his moral purity, cleaner than anyone's
16-23 _ Asserting his social righteousness in treating the poor, widows, and orphans kindly
24-40 _ Insisting on his religious purity, in that he stayed away from idols and kept the commandments of God

[Chapter 32] The appearance of Elihu, and a declaration of the basis and necessity of his argument
Elihu makes clear that Job's suffering is not simply to be linked to some particular sin but may be part of discipline through pain, and so a shift to a new phase is achieved in the development of the content.
1-5 _ An introduction to Elihu
6-10 _ The legitimate basis of his argument, by making clear that his argument lies in wisdom that comes from God.
11-22 _ Seeing the truth distorted by the narrow logic of Job and the three friends, he declares the necessity of his having to step forward to argue, and his state of mind as he enters the argument.

[Chapter 33] A rebuke of Job's claim of innocence and a declaration of the righteous providence of God
Elihu criticized Job's assertion of his own righteousness. Job had few faults, to the point of being called righteous among men, but before God, who possesses absolute justice, no one can assert his own righteousness. Therefore Job's continued assertion of his own righteousness was not right. Yet Elihu, with deeper insight than the three preceding friends, does not see suffering merely as discipline for sin but explains it as a process of refining for a greater blessing (v. 30). Through this he shows that the deep providence and ultimate plan of God are based on mercy that leads human beings to salvation.
1-12 _ A rebuke of Job's self-righteousness
13-33 _ The righteous providence and works of God

[Chapter 34] A condemnation of Job on the basis of the justice of God
Elihu stresses that the all-knowing and almighty God watches over the ways of man and in the end renders righteous judgment. He says that God's scrutiny and judgment are more important than man's passing judgment, and shows that a person should rely on the mercy of God, fear Him, and live rightly.
1-9 _ An accusation against Job
10-30 _ Presenting a standard by which to judge Job, through the omnipotence and absolute justice of God, who rules heaven and earth.
31-37 _ A condemnation of Job

[Chapter 35] The futility of man before God, and the reason for unanswered prayer
He points out Job's problem by speaking of the finitude and futility of man to Job, who asserts his own righteousness.
1-8 _ The futility of man before God
9-16 _ Urging Job to humble repentance by citing the fact that God does not answer the prayer of the proud.

[Chapter 36] Praise of the providence and power of God
When Job, who has come to suffer because of the righteous sovereign providence of God, pours out doubts and complaints within it and asserts his innocence, Elihu demands that Job repent and obey Him.
1-23 _ The righteous providence and rule of God
24-33 _ Praise of the providence and power of God

[Chapter 37] The sovereign providence of God shown through natural phenomena
It speaks of the righteous God, the Creator who rules history, working with transcendent power behind all natural phenomena and human affairs. Even if there are things that human beings do not understand, it exhorts that one realize there is the deep and righteous providence of God behind them, and live a life of obeying the will of the infinitely good and wise God and fearing God.
1-13 _ The sovereign providence of God shown through natural phenomena
14-24 _ An exhortation to reverence toward God

[Chapter 38] Questions about the created world
God does not answer directly the reason for the suffering that Job and his friends have kept debating; instead, by speaking of His sovereignty and marvelous power, He makes Job, a limited and weak human being, realize his own deficiency and ignorance.
1-3 _ God appears and rebukes Job.
4-41 _ Questions about the created world

[Chapter 39] Questions about the habits of wild animals
If Genesis 1 shows that God's work of creation was accomplished by the power of the word, this passage shows that all creatures were created by infinite divine wisdom, that is, by righteous and perfect providence.
1-30 _ Questions about the habits of wild animals

[Chapter 40] A lesson through the hippopotamus
Taking as an example the hippopotamus, with its great strength and enormous bulk, it points out the omnipotence of God, who created and handles such an animal, and, in contrast to it, Job's powerlessness and his impatience, shaken even by small surrounding circumstances.
1-5 _ Job's answer
6-14 _ God's rebuke
15-24 _ A lesson through the ecology of the hippopotamus

[Chapter 41] A lesson about the limits of man through the crocodile
Through the difficulty of hunting a crocodile and the ecology of the crocodile, it repeatedly emphasizes man's powerlessness and, in contrast to it, the power of God.
1-11 _ A lesson through the difficulty of hunting a crocodile
12-34 _ A lesson through the structure of the crocodile's members and its might

[Chapter 42] The restoration of Job
The debates that Job, his three friends, and Elihu carried on over the cause of Job's unexpected suffering were all vain and futile and found no solution. But in the end it shows that the problem of Job's suffering is resolved through the appearance and word of God.
1-3 _ Confession of his own ignorance
4-6 _ Repentance for his own stubbornness
7-9 _ Job's intercession for his friends
10-17 _ The restoration of Job

[Psalms 40:5] Many, O LORD my God, are the wonders You have done, and the plans You have for us— none can compare to You— if I proclaim and declare them, they are more than I can count.

[Chapter 41] [Psalm of Supplication] “The blessing of the one who considers the weak”
A psalm of supplication in which a person who is suffering severely, despite having fulfilled his responsibility toward the poor, prays for God's help and vindication.
[Psalms 41:1] [For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David.] Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the LORD will deliver him in the day of trouble.

[Chapter 42] [Zion Psalm] [Psalm of Lament] “Looking to God again and restoring faith even in the despair of a broken heart.”
It is a psalm of lament that earnestly longs for the presence of God and the temple of Jerusalem, away from Zion and amid the persecution of enemies. It is regarded as one psalm together with Psalm 43.
[Psalms 42:5] Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence.

[Chapter 43] [Zion Psalm] [Psalm of Lament] “Lead me to Your holy hill and to Your dwelling”
A psalm of resolve, seeking the justice and guidance of God amid unjust enemies, and hoping in God again
[Psalms 43:4] Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God.

[Chapter 44] [Communal Psalm of Lament] “A national lament appealing for the deliverance of the chosen people, who are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered”
It is a national lament in which Israel, suffering innocently amid a national crisis caused by the Assyrian invasion, asks God for deliverance.
[Psalms 44:21] would not God have discovered, since He knows the secrets of the heart?

[Chapter 45] [Royal Psalm] “The people's congratulations on the marriage of the king whom the LORD has established”
A royal psalm singing of the king's wedding, which ultimately prophesies the glorious marriage and love of the Messiah, Jesus Christ, and the church.
[Psalms 45:10-11] Listen, O daughter! Consider and incline your ear: Forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty; bow to him, for he is your lord.

[Chapter 46] [Zion Psalm] [Psalm of Praise] “Praise of the LORD, who brings tribulation and war to an end”
It is a psalm praising the history of the almighty God delivering the community of the chosen people amid the crisis of the fall of Jerusalem, and the safety and peace enjoyed in Him.
[Psalms 46:1] [For the choirmaster. Of the sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A song.] God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble.

[Chapter 47] [Theocratic Psalm] “The reign of the LORD, who rules the whole earth for the sake of the chosen people”
It is a psalm that praises God as the universal King and proclaims prophetically the ascension of Jesus Christ and His being King of kings
[Psalms 47:2] How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth!

[Chapter 48] [Psalm of Praise] [Zion Psalm] “Praise of the authority and grace of the LORD who dwells in Zion”
It is a psalm set against the background of the event (2 Kings 19 or 2 Chronicles 20) in which Jerusalem, which had been on the verge of destruction through a foreign invasion in the time of Hezekiah's reign (c. 715-687 B.C.) or of Jehoshaphat's reign (c. 872-848 B.C.), was delivered by God's marvelous act of salvation.
[Psalms 48:14] For this God is our God forever and ever; He will be our guide even till death.

[Chapter 49] [Wisdom Psalm] “From an eschatological perspective, pointing out the folly of those who pursue wealth, and exhortation”
By speaking of the folly, and its result, of people who take worldly wealth as the standard for judging the value of life, it is a wisdom psalm that teaches a God-centered view of life that takes fearing God as the true happiness of life.
[Psalms 49:20] A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish.

[Chapter 50] [Wisdom Psalm] “The proclamation of the LORD the Judge, urging true sacrifices of thanksgiving and deeds”
It is a wisdom psalm that rebukes those who worship God with sacrifices that have only outward form and lack genuine thanksgiving and praise, that is, offerings without inner preparation, and teaches what true worship is.
[Psalms 50:22] Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you to pieces, with no one to rescue you:

[Chapter 51] [Penitential Psalm] “A plea for the blotting out of iniquity and the renewal of the heart, and three vows”
It is a model psalm of repentance in which David, after the Bathsheba incident, realized his corrupt sinful nature, repented deeply before God, and asked for the restoration of fellowship and for salvation. This psalm has the same background of composition as Psalm 6 and Psalm 32, which are likewise penitential psalms. Among these three, Psalm 51 is presumed to have been composed first, then Psalm 6, and last of all Psalm 32.
[Psalms 51:10] Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.

[Chapter 52] [Wisdom Psalm] “The ruin of the boastful and the confession of faith of the righteous who witnessed it”
It is a wisdom psalm that warns of the evil deeds of the wicked and of God's ultimate judgment, and teaches the victory of the righteous who trust in God even amid suffering.
[Psalms 52:8] But I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God; I trust in the loving devotion of God forever and ever.

[Chapter 53] [Wisdom Psalm] “The universal corruption of those who deny God, and the contrast between the fate of the wicked and that of the chosen people”
It is a wisdom psalm of David that warns the Gentiles about the atheism and folly of the wicked, and proclaims the salvation of those who fear God.
[Psalms 53:1] [For the choirmaster. According to Mahalath. A Maskil of David.] The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.” They are corrupt; their ways are vile. There is no one who does good.

[Chapter 54] [Psalm of Lament] “An appeal for deliverance and a vow, made while hunted by those seeking his life”
Based on the conviction that, in an utterly desperate limit situation in which nothing at all can be done by human strength, only God, who repays faithfully with justice, is his one and only deliverer, it is a psalm appealing for the destruction of enemies and for his own deliverance.
[Psalms 54:1] [For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Maskil of David. When the Ziphites went to Saul and said, “Is David not hiding among us?”] Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might!

[Chapter 55] [Individual Psalm of Lament] [Imprecatory Psalm] “The lament of one weeping under a companion's betrayal and oppression, and a declaration of assurance in the retribution of the LORD”
It is a prayer of lament in which David, in the sorrow of having been betrayed by his son Absalom and his friend Ahithophel, pleads with God and relies on Him.
[Psalms 55:12] For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. It is not a foe who rises against me; from him I could hide.

[Chapter 56] [Individual Psalm of Lament] “A duet of heart-wrenching appeal and confession of assurance of deliverance, amid oppression by men”
It is a prayer of lament in which David, in the desperate situation of being in danger at Gath of the Philistines to escape the persecution of Saul, sought trust and help from God.
[Psalms 56:11] in God I trust; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?

[Chapter 57] [Individual Lament Psalm] “Confident Praise That Wakes the Dawn, Sung by One Who Overcame the Threat of Men's Spears and Arrows”
A psalm in which David, hiding in the cave of En-gedi because of Saul's persecution, offers God the joy of salvation and praise even in the midst of desperate crisis, and confesses an unyielding faith.
[Psalms 57:7] My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music.

[Chapter 58] [Imprecatory Psalm] “A Curse on Unjust Judges and a Plea for God's Retribution”
An imprecatory psalm that accuses and curses judges who ought to administer justice but instead promote lawlessness and practice evil, and that pleads for the retribution of God's justice.
[Psalms 58:1] [For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Miktam of David.] Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?

[Chapter 59] [Individual Lament Psalm] [Imprecatory Psalm] “An Appeal for Judgment on the Wicked, from One Whose Life Is Threatened Without Cause”
A lament in which David, fleeing from King Saul's persecution, asserts his innocence and earnestly seeks God's righteous judgment and deliverance.
[Psalms 59:12] By the sins of their mouths and the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride, in the curses and lies they utter.

[Chapter 60] [Communal lament] "An Appeal for Victory, Based on the Covenant, Offered by the Chosen People in a Time of Defeat"
A national lament in which David, in a national crisis threatened by the allied forces of Edom and Aram, implores God for deliverance. (2 Samuel 8, 1 Chronicles 18)
[Psalms 60:11] Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless.

[Chapter 61] [Individual Lament Psalm] “David's Prayer, Pursued Because of Rebellion, for the Restoration of His Kingship”
A lament in which David, facing a crisis of kingship presumed to be Absalom's rebellion, earnestly seeks from God the restoration of his throne and deliverance.
[Psalms 61:4] Let me dwell in Your tent forever and take refuge in the shelter of Your wings. Selah

[Chapter 62] [Individual Lament Psalm] “A Troubled Soul That Waits for God Alone in Silence”
It emphasizes that the way for one in affliction to move toward salvation is to wait silently for God alone with absolute trust in Him.
[Psalms 62:1-2] [For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David.] In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken.

[Chapter 63] [Individual Lament Psalm] “Declaring the Joy of the Soul and Assurance of Salvation in a Time of Suffering”
A “song sung in the wilderness” in which David, who fled to the wilderness of Judah during Absalom's rebellion, longs for God and praises Him.
[Psalms 63:3] Because Your loving devotion is better than life, my lips will glorify You.

[Chapter 64] [Individual Lament Psalm] “The Arrows of the Wicked's Crafty Tongue and the Arrow of God's Judgment”
A psalm with a strong imprecatory character that asks for the retribution of God's justice against the wicked, who devise evil schemes to achieve their aims and do not hesitate to harm the righteous. The background is unclear. It is only presumed to have been composed during the time of Absalom's rebellion.
[Psalms 64:5] They hold fast to their evil purpose; they speak of hiding their snares. “Who will see them?” they say.

[Chapter 65] [Thanksgiving Psalm] “A Joyful Shout to God, Savior, Creator, and Benefactor”
A “song of bringing the harvest home,” offered at the Feast of Tabernacles, praising the absolute sovereignty and saving grace of God the Creator.
[Psalms 65:3] When iniquities prevail against me, You atone for our transgressions.

[Chapter 66] [Psalm of Praise] “Testimonial Praise for the Salvation Experienced by All the Chosen People and the Psalmist Personally”
A psalm of praise whose author and date are unknown. It praises God, who delivered from the Assyrian invasion, through the events of the exodus and the crossing of the Jordan, and proclaims that salvation to all peoples.
[Psalms 66:18] If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.

[Chapter 67] [Thanksgiving Psalm] “Prayer for the Spread of God's Salvation and Rule, and Leading All Nations in Praising God”
A missionary song, sung at the Feast of Tabernacles, in which all peoples praise God and pray that His salvation and righteousness may spread over all the earth.
[Psalms 67:1-2] [For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm. A song.] May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us, Selah that Your ways may be known on earth, Your salvation among all nations.

[Chapter 68] [Psalm of Praise] “Praise for the Power and Grace of God, Who Gives Victory to His Chosen People”
The background of composition is not clear. It is a psalm of praise offering thanks and praise for the power and grace of God, who enabled the chosen people Israel to gain victory over their enemies.
[Psalms 68:19] Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden, the God of our salvation. Selah

[Chapter 69] [Individual Lament Psalm] [Prophetic Psalm] [Imprecatory Psalm] “The Lament of an Aged King Sunk in the Deep Waters of Rebellion, and His Plea for Righteous Judgment and Deliverance”
Against a background presumed to be Adonijah's rebellion, it is a lament in which David pleads for God's deliverance amid unjust suffering, and at the same time a messianic prophetic psalm that foreshadows the passion of Christ through that suffering.
[Psalms 69:9] because zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me.
[Psalms 69:21] They poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst.

[Chapter 70] [Individual Lament Psalm] “Shame for the Enemies, Joy for Those Who Seek You”
A psalm of supplication that excerpts and revises part of Psalm 40 and earnestly asks God for swift deliverance amid a crisis caused by enemies.
[Psalms 70:4] May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, “Let God be magnified!”

[Chapter 71] [Individual Lament Psalm] “An Aged Person's Plea for Salvation, Looking Over Past and Future”
A lament of unknown author and date of composition. The background is also uncertain. The author, who is of royal status, pleads for God's deliverance amid rebellion and crisis and confesses lifelong trust. Some regard Psalm 70 as the introduction to this psalm.
[Psalms 71:17-18] O God, You have taught me from my youth, and to this day I proclaim Your marvelous deeds. Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation, Your might to all who are to come.

[Chapter 72] [Royal Psalm] [Prophetic Psalm] “A Prophetic Song About the One King of God Who Will Bring Peace According to Righteousness”
It is both a lesson on righteous rule given to the kings of the Davidic dynasty and, ultimately, a psalm that prophesies the perfect reign of the Messiah Jesus and the peace and blessing of His kingdom.
[Psalms 72:11] May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him.

[Chapter 73] [Wisdom Psalm] “Drawing Near to God Is My Blessing”
A psalm in which the writer realizes, even in the reality of the wicked prospering, that God alone is the source of true blessing and strength.
[Psalms 73:28] But as for me, it is good to draw near to God. I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may proclaim all Your works.

[Chapter 74] [Communal Lament Psalm] “An Earnest Appeal over the Destruction of Jerusalem 1”
A Maskil of Asaph, crying out with hope in God's salvation and covenant amid the despair of the temple's destruction.
[Psalms 74:16-17] The day is Yours, and also the night; You established the moon and the sun. You set all the boundaries of the earth; You made the summer and winter.

[Chapter 75] [Thanksgiving Psalm] [Psalm of Trust] “God Who Will Judge at the Appointed Time”
A hymn of assurance that God judges with righteousness at the time He has set and will never destroy the righteous.
[Psalms 75:2-3] “When I choose a time, I will judge fairly. When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars. Selah

[Chapter 76] [Thanksgiving Psalm] [Psalm of Trust] [Zion Psalm] “Praise for the Victory God Gave”
A psalm of thanksgiving praising God's judgment and salvation against the background of the defeat of Sennacherib of Assyria in the time of Hezekiah.
[Psalms 76:10] Even the wrath of man shall praise You; with the survivors of wrath You will clothe Yourself.

[Chapter 77] [Lament Psalm] “Comfort in the Day of Trouble, Deep Meditation on Salvation”
A lament of Asaph who, amid affliction, meditates on God's saving work in the exodus and gains comfort and strength.
[Psalms 77:7-9] “Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again? Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?” Selah

[Chapter 78] [Historical Psalm] “Lessons from Israel's History”
Psalm 78 is a historical sermon-psalm that gives lessons through the history of Israel and urges the people to establish a life of faith rightly.
[Psalms 78:37] Their hearts were disloyal to Him, and they were unfaithful to His covenant.

[Chapter 79] [Communal Lament Psalm] [Imprecatory Psalm] “An Earnest Appeal over the Destruction of Jerusalem 2”
Psalm 79 is a prayer of lamentation that mourns the destruction of the temple and the miserable condition of the nation caused by the Babylonian invasion, and earnestly seeks God's forgiveness and restoration.
[Psalms 79:9] Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of Your name; deliver us and atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name.

[Chapter 80] [Communal Lament Psalm] “God Who Saves from Destruction”
A prayer of lamentation and supplication that grieves over the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel and asks for restoration and salvation, taking God as shepherd.
[Psalms 80:19] Restore us, O LORD God of Hosts; cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved.

[Chapter 81] [Psalm of Praise] [Didactic Psalm] “An Invitation to the Feasts”
A psalm of praise and exhortation that reminds of the importance of the feasts and worship God gave and urges the people of Israel to pure worship and observance of the feasts.
[Psalms 81:11-12] But My people would not listen to Me, and Israel would not obey Me. So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices.

[Chapter 82] [Didactic Psalm] “God Who Judges the Judges”
A didactic psalm that solemnly urges judges to render just and fair verdicts according to God's justice.
[Psalms 82:8] Arise, O God, judge the earth, for all the nations are Your inheritance.

[Chapter 83] [Lament Psalm] “A Plea for the Ruin of the Enemies”
A psalm of Asaph that earnestly asks God for swift salvation and help amid the crisis when several foreign peoples allied together and invaded southern Judah.
[Psalms 83:18] May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth.

[Chapter 84] [Psalm of Praise] [Zion Psalm] “Song of One Who Longs for the Temple”
A psalm in which the sons of Korah, after leaving the temple, long with yearning for God's presence and praise the joy and peace of dwelling near the temple.
[Psalms 84:10] For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked.

[Chapter 85] [Lament Psalm] “Revive Us Again”
A psalm of restoration and supplication that earnestly seeks God's mercy and reconciliation, because Israel's spiritual and social recovery after returning from the Babylonian exile is slow.
[Psalms 85:6] Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?

[Chapter 86] [Lament Psalm] “David's Prayer in the Day of Trouble”
A psalm of supplication and trust in which David, amid extreme affliction, does not rely on himself but trusts in God alone and earnestly seeks salvation and guidance.
[Psalms 86:7] In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me.

[Chapter 87] [Zion psalm] [Psalm of praise] "The Importance of the Church"
A psalm of praise that extols Zion and proclaims that the church is the center of salvation and spiritual growth and the most important institution that God has established.
[Psalms 87:1-2] [A Psalm of the sons of Korah. A song.] He has founded His city on the holy mountains. The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.

[Chapter 88] [Lament] "Prayer in Deep and Dark Sorrow"
A lament written by Heman the Ezrahite, in which, even amid extreme physical, social, and spiritual suffering, he trusts God and begs for deliverance, offering a prayer of faith in the midst of dark and gloomy circumstances.
[Psalms 88:14] Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?

[Chapter 89] [Psalm of Praise] “The Faithfulness and Steadfast Love of God Seen in the Davidic Covenant”
A psalm written by Ethan the Ezrahite that praises God's covenant and faithfulness and recalls the promise concerning David and his kingship.
[Psalms 89:37] like the moon, established forever, a faithful witness in the sky.” Selah

[Chapter 90] [Communal Lament Psalm] “Life Like Dust”
A prayer-psalm in which Moses, on behalf of Israel wandering in the wilderness, confesses the transience and frailty of human life to God and asks for God's mercy and protection.
[Psalms 90:10] The length of our days is seventy years— or eighty if we are strong— yet their pride is but labor and sorrow, for they quickly pass, and we fly away.

[Chapter 91] [Wisdom Psalm] [Psalm of Trust] “One Who Dwells Under the Shadow of the Almighty”
A psalm of trust and protection praising the protection and peace God gives to those who trust in Him even in tribulation.
[Psalms 91:1] He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.

[Chapter 92] [Psalm of Praise] “The One Who Will Grow Rightly”
A Sabbath psalm of praise that praises God's righteous rule and expresses assurance of the judgment of the wicked and the prosperity of the righteous.
[Psalms 92:12-13] The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. Planted in the house of the LORD, they will flourish in the courts of our God.

[Chapter 93] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “The Sovereignty and Rule of the Eternal God”
A psalm of praise of unknown author and date. It is a psalm praising the kingship of God, Creator and Ruler of the world.
[Psalms 93:1] The LORD reigns! He is robed in majesty; the LORD has clothed and armed Himself with strength. The world indeed is firmly established; it cannot be moved.

[Chapter 94] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] [Psalm of Supplication] “The Lord Who Judges with Righteousness”
A praise psalm addressed to the Judge that accuses the injustice of the wicked and asks for God's righteous judgment.
[Psalms 94:19] When anxiety overwhelms me, Your consolation delights my soul.

[Chapter 95] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “Let Us Kneel Before the Creator”
A psalm of praise and exhortation that praises God as Creator and King and urges worship.
[Psalms 95:8] do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness,

[Chapter 96] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “The LORD Who Receives the Praise of All Things”
A psalm that sings of praising God among all peoples and proclaiming His righteous rule.
[Psalms 96:1] Sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth.

[Chapter 97] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “Praising God's Righteous Rule”
A psalm of praise and declaration of rule that praises God for ruling justly and perfectly, and sings that the saints will enjoy joy and peace under that rule.
[Psalms 97:1] The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad.

[Chapter 98] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “Praising the Lord Who Does Marvelous Things”
A psalm that exhorts praise for God's wonderful works.
[Psalms 98:1] [A Psalm.] Sing to the LORD a new song, for He has done wonders; His right hand and holy arm have gained Him the victory.

[Chapter 99] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “Praise of the Holy Kingship of the Lord”
A psalm of praise and worship that praises God's holy and righteous rule and proclaims the glory of the temple and the holiness of His kingship.
[Psalms 99:2-3] Great is the LORD in Zion; He is exalted above all the peoples. Let them praise Your great and awesome name— He is holy!

[Chapter 100] [Psalm of Praise] [Thanksgiving Psalm] [Psalm of God's Kingship] “Praise the Lord, All the Earth”
A psalm of thanksgiving and praise that urges all creatures to worship God with thanksgiving and joy and to offer voluntary praise and dedication.
[Psalms 100:3] Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture.

[Chapter 101] [Royal Psalm] “Rule of Lovingkindness and Justice”
A royal vow psalm in which David resolves to rule justly and uprightly before God, to keep far from evil, and to fulfill God's will together with faithful people.
[Psalms 101:2] I will ponder the way that is blameless— when will You come to me? I will walk in my house with integrity of heart.

[Chapter 102] [Psalm of Supplication] [Psalm of Trust] “Longing for Salvation, Praise for the Eternal One”
Psalm 102 is a prayer-psalm of supplication and trust in which an afflicted person, amid anxiety and despair, asks for God's help and praises God, trusting in His salvation and eternal unchangeableness.
[Psalms 102:26-27] They will perish, but You remain; they will all wear out like a garment. Like clothing You will change them, and they will be passed on. But You remain the same, and Your years will never end.

[Chapter 103] [Psalm of Praise] [Thanksgiving Psalm] “Bless the LORD, O My Soul”
A psalm of thanksgiving and praise in which the psalmist, aware of his weakness and sin, experiences new life and joy in God's grace and compassion and offers thanks and praise.
[Psalms 103:12] As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us.

[Chapter 104] [Psalm of Praise] “Praising God's Glory Revealed in the Created World”
A psalm of creation praise that praises God's creation and providence and shows the dependence of creatures and the purpose of human life in rejoicing in and relying on God. (The work of creation)
[Psalms 104:29] When You hide Your face, they are terrified; when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust.

[Chapter 105] [Psalm of Praise] [Historical Psalm] “God Faithful to the Covenant”
A psalm that proclaims God who is faithful to the covenant and, through the history of Israel, praises God's faithfulness and urges trust in Him. (Early history of Israel)
[Psalms 105:19] until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.

[Chapter 106] [Psalm of Praise] [Historical Psalm] “Repenting of a History of Disobedience and Praising Grace”
This psalm praises God, who shows grace despite the people's repeated rebellion, and through Israel's sin and God's judgment reveals the universal sinfulness of humanity and the justice of God. (History from the exodus to the Babylonian exile)
[Psalms 106:15] So He granted their request, but sent a wasting disease upon them.

[Chapter 107] [Psalm of Praise] “Thanksgiving Hymn Offered by Those Saved (Out of Suffering)”
This psalm praises God's compassion and lovingkindness, who saved the people of Israel who returned from the Babylonian exile and showed grace even in the wilderness and amid dangers, and urges the wise to understand this and praise. (God's mercy shown after the return)
[Psalms 107:9] For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.

[Chapter 108] [Psalm of Praise] [Psalm of Trust] “My Heart Is Steadfast”
A psalm in which David, remembering the protection and help of God he experienced in past suffering, offers praise and prayer to God and asks for salvation even before the crisis and war that are approaching.
[Psalms 108:1] [A song. A Psalm of David.] My heart is steadfast, O God; I will sing and make music with all my being.

[Chapter 109] [Imprecatory Psalm] [Psalm of Supplication] “The Prayer of the Righteous Against the Wicked”
A psalm in which David asks for God's righteous judgment on the wicked who harm and slander him, and proclaims God's justice through the destruction of evil and the victory of righteousness.
[Psalms 109:4] In return for my love they accuse me, but I am a man of prayer.

[Chapter 110] [Royal Psalm] [Prophetic Psalm] “Prophecy About the Messiah”
A psalm that prophetically proclaims the Messiah's eternal rule and priesthood.
[Psalms 110:3] Your people shall be willing on Your day of battle. Arrayed in holy splendor, from the womb of the dawn, to You belongs the dew of Your youth.

[Chapter 111] [Psalm of Praise] “Praising the Great Works of God”
An acrostic psalm that gives thanks for and praises God's great works and the salvation according to the covenant.
[Psalms 111:2] Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them.

[Chapter 112] [Wisdom Psalm] [Psalm of Praise] “The Blessing of Those Who Fear the LORD and Keep His Commandments”
An acrostic psalm that sings of the blessings and life of faith enjoyed by those who fear God and keep His commandments.
[Psalms 112:1] Hallelujah! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in His commandments.

[Chapter 113] [Psalm of Praise] “Praise the God Who, Though Most High, Humbled Himself”
A psalm praising God's faithfulness in exalting and saving the humble.
[Psalms 113:7-8] He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump to seat them with nobles, with the princes of His people.

[Chapter 114] [Psalm of Praise] “The Power of God Who Leads Israel”
