[Chapter 1] The Purpose of Solomon's Proverbs, and True Wisdom and Its Character
Chapter 1, which opens Proverbs, the finest work of Hebrew wisdom literature, serves as an introduction and speaks of the purpose of Proverbs and of what true wisdom is.
First it makes clear that the writer of Proverbs is King Solomon, and states that the purpose of writing it is to lead all people to understand true wisdom.
1-9 _ True wisdom comes from God.
10-19 _ It counsels us not to fall into the enticement of the wicked but to stay far from them.
20-33 _ It urges us to listen to the instruction of wisdom, because those who follow the instruction of wisdom enjoy safety and peace.
By contrasting the wicked with wise counsel, chapter 1 stresses that the instruction of Proverbs holds the path of true success and life.

[Chapter 2] The Moral Benefit of Wisdom
Following chapter 1, which spoke of the purpose of Proverbs and of what true wisdom is, chapter 2 speaks specifically of how to obtain wisdom and of the benefits wisdom gives.
1-6 _ True wisdom can be obtained when one keeps God's commandments in the heart and fears God.
7-12 _ Wisdom leads to the path of justice, fairness, and uprightness, and makes one turn away from the way of the wicked.
13-15 _ Wisdom delivers from the way of the wicked that leads to destruction.
16-19 _ Wisdom guards a person from the seduction of the immoral woman and saves him from lust and from the path of Sheol.
20-22 _ Those who follow wisdom obtain salvation and those who do not perish, so obey the word of wisdom.

[Chapter 3] The Blessings to Be Enjoyed by Obeying the Word of Wisdom
Following chapter 2, which dealt in general terms with the benefits wisdom gives, it speaks of the benefits wisdom gives in concrete daily life.
1-7 _ Because true wisdom is with God, do not depart from wisdom
This is because all instruction is meant to teach faith in God.
8-13 _ Wisdom brings material abundance and blessing into life.
14-26 _ Do not take God's discipline lightly. Wisdom guarantees long life and wealth, and is a precious gift from God, who created and rules all things.
27-35 _ The life of wisdom is not only for oneself.
God requires His people to do good and bestows blessing on those who do good.

[Chapter 4] Obey Your Father's Words and the Way of Wisdom Without Fail
It stresses once more the importance of wisdom, which leads a person on the path of glory, and teaches that one should strive to obtain wisdom.
1-9 _ The writer tells of his own experience of having been blessed with wisdom through his parents' teaching, and strongly urges us to obtain wisdom.
10-19 _ He contrasts the way of the wise with the way of the wicked. The evil way causes people to stumble and leads to destruction, so it must be avoided.
20-27 _ Keep his instruction in your heart and guard it. This is so that you may not be led astray by false teaching, and it says that those who keep the word in their heart become strong in soul and body.

[Chapter 5] Avoid Sexual Immorality by Stressing Its Cost
The writer records the instruction of wisdom about sexual immorality, which is the sin young people, whom he wishes to instruct, fall into most easily.
1-6 _ Sexual immorality seems sweet and pleasurable on the surface, but in the end it destroys life and brings unbearable suffering.
7-14 _ So as not to fall into sexual immorality from the start, one must remember the word of God and act according to it.
15-23 _ Unlike sexual immorality, love with the wife God has given is beautiful and beneficial.
Solomon's instruction comes from the experience of his own life, lived surrounded by political marriages to many foreign women and by concubines.

[Chapter 6] Avoid the Folly One Can Fall Into in Daily Life
Following chapter 5, which warned about sexual immorality, chapter 6 instructs about four wrong attitudes to guard against for a sound daily life.
1-5 _ Do not put up security for another. If you have, humbly ask to be released from the surety for the sake of your relationship with your neighbor.
6-11 _ A warning against laziness. Laziness is the greatest cause of poverty.
12-19 _ A warning against improper conduct and the evil way. Such a person is abandoned in time of urgency and is destroyed.
20-35 _ A warning against sexual immorality. An unrighteous sexual relationship is more fearful than any other crime and utterly ruins a person.
This is because sexual immorality is the sin to which young people are most easily tempted.

[Chapter 7] Guard Against Falling into Sexual Immorality
The writer, who continues to warn of the danger of sexual immorality, gives in chapter 7 a concrete example of a foolish person who fell into immorality, told in literary form, so as to give a firmer lesson.
1-5 _ Keep the commandments. He conveys a vivid lesson by likening wisdom to a sister and sexual immorality to the immoral woman.
6-12 _ The story of a foolish young man seduced late at night by a crafty woman.
13-22 _ The immoral woman offers the young man every pleasure and tempts him by saying there is no harm, and the young man listens and commits immorality.
23-27 _ The young man's conduct leads himself to destruction, and the immoral woman's house is described as the way to Sheol and the chambers of death.

[Chapter 8] Stressing That Obtaining Wisdom Is Better Than Obtaining Gold, Silver, and Treasure, So Strive to Obtain It
The writer, who until now has compared the wise way and the evil way through concrete examples and taught us to be those who long for wisdom, proclaims in chapter 8 the excellence of wisdom, which cannot be compared with anything. In this sense chapter 8 shows the central theme of the whole book of Proverbs.
1-21 _ Personifying wisdom, he urges people to listen to the voice by which wisdom calls and to follow it. The words of wisdom are the most valuable, and are the secret of all happiness and success.
22-31 _ The identity of wisdom is God, that is, the Lord who existed from the beginning and created heaven and earth. Therefore wisdom is more valuable and powerful than anything in the world.
32-36 _ He declares that whoever obtains wisdom gains life and receives God's favor, but whoever despises wisdom is one who hates God and will receive the judgment of death.

[Chapter 9] Wisdom Grows Wiser by Fearing the LORD, and Folly Avoids Such a Thing
As the conclusion of the instructions listed so far, it calls for a choice between wisdom and folly through the parable of an invitation to a feast.
1-6 _ Wisdom invites people with a house and with food to a feast of life.
7-12 _ Those who reject wisdom's invitation and are proud will suffer harm, but those who fear the LORD and obtain wisdom will gain benefit.
13-18 _ Folly is likened to a foolish woman who, on a high place in the city, holds a feast of stolen water and bread eaten in secret and invites people. That place is like Sheol, which the dead attend.
Through such an extreme parable the writer appeals for the choice of wisdom.

[Chapter 10] The Fundamental Difference Between the Righteous and the Wicked, by Solomon
From chapter 10 begins the second part of Proverbs, which consists of six parts in all.
From here on, unlike the earlier part that stressed wisdom itself, it shows the concrete form of the wise life by contrasting the lives of the righteous and the wicked.
1-6 _ God makes the righteous abundant, but He does not hear the desire of the wicked.
7-21 _ The righteous are recognized by others, benefit others, and gain life, but the wicked harm others, gain no profit, and head toward destruction.
22-32 _ The righteous, who take delight in wisdom, are blessed by God and enjoy long life and hope, but the wicked live a vain life, their years are short, and their hope vanishes.

[Chapter 11] Stressing Entry into a Righteous Community by Speaking of the Difference Between the Righteous and the Wicked Within the Community
It teaches about the attitude of life of the righteous and the wicked.
In particular, here it compares the form of life shown through relationships with others within the community.
1-8 _ Those who accumulate wealth by unjust means perish, but the upright prosper.
9-16 _ The righteous benefit others, but the wicked bring ruin on everyone, including themselves.
17-23 _ Those who hold firmly to righteousness gain a reward, those who do evil come to death, and even if the wicked join forces they cannot withstand judgment.
24-31 _ The righteous use their wealth to help the poor and become prosperous, but the wicked use it only for themselves and in the end even lose what they have.

[Chapter 12] The Characteristics of the Righteous and the Wicked and the Outcome of Each
It continues to contrast the characteristics of the wicked and the righteous. But unlike the previous chapter, which mainly compared outward forms of life, here it compares inner states.
1-8 _ The righteous value the word of God, are praised by people, and prosper, but the wicked treat it lightly and perish as the price of shedding others' blood.
9-14 _ The wicked covet unjust gain but in the end are ruined, while the righteous obtain abundant fruit as the reward of diligent work.
15-23 _ The foolish stir up strife with lies and words that harm others, but the righteous escape calamity by speaking the truth.
24-28 _ The diligent work faithfully and rule over others, but the foolish are ruled by others.

[Chapter 13] The Difference Between the Wise Who Listen Well to Instruction and the Foolish Who Disregard It, and Their Differing Outcomes
It continues to speak of the inner differences between the righteous and the wicked. But here, explaining in connection with the material blessings that result, it strongly urges the choice of the way of the righteous.
1-6 _ The righteous listen to their parents' instruction, guard their mouths, and enjoy blessing, but the wicked reach shame and ruin because of wrong words.
7-11 _ The righteous use wealth for a right purpose and grow increasingly rich, but the wicked use it only for themselves and lose everything.
12-20 _ The instruction of the wise and righteous is like a tonic; those who follow their words gain a reward, and those who follow foolish and wicked words receive calamity.
21-25 _ Because God is righteous, He gives ruin to the wicked and gives the righteous the prosperity of their inheritance for generations.

[Chapter 14] The Form of a Right Life Recognized by God and by Neighbors
It contrasts the wise and the foolish, the upright and the perverse, the scoffer and the discerning, the wicked and the upright, the wicked and the righteous, those slow to anger and those quick-tempered, and so on. Chapter 14, which compares the characteristics of the wicked and the righteous, shows the contrasting appearance of the two mainly from a social point of view.
1-9 _ The wise fear the LORD and live within their means, but the foolish scorn the LORD, tell lies, and are arrogant.
10-19 _ The righteous avoid the way of sin, but the wicked take the evil way for momentary pleasure and in the end fall down before the righteous.
20-25 _ Wealth is a blessing to the wise but a calamity to the foolish; truthful words save life, and lies kill people.
26-35 _ Those who fear God, help the poor according to His will, and live righteously receive blessing, and the wicked suffer wrath.

[Chapter 15] The Great Benefit That Can Be Bestowed Through Words
This chapter, which compares the characteristics of the righteous and the wicked, shows in particular in detail the difference in their attitude toward God.
This is to stress that all the differences between the wicked and the righteous mentioned earlier ultimately stem from faith in God. Therefore chapter 15 once again brings out “the theme of the whole book of Proverbs,” namely [the source of true wisdom is the fear of God].
1-7 _ Those who speak wisely bring peace, but harsh words stir up strife.
8-12 _ God does not accept the sacrifices of those who do not follow His word, but rather they receive judgment.
13-20 _ True joy lies not in material things but in peace of heart, and those who do not give way to anger and who hold love are blessed.
21-33 _ The righteous delight in wise words and keep far from unjust bribes, and their desires are fulfilled, but the wicked despise instruction and despise the LORD and go down to Sheol.

[Chapter 16] Commit All Your Works to the LORD
By means of God's sovereign response to the wicked and the righteous, it compares the characteristics of the two.
1-9 _ Because everything a person does depends on God, the wicked, however united and diligent, cannot succeed, and God leads the righteous in the way of success.
10-15 _ A ruler must rule with justice and fairness according to the word of God, and his authority to rule is assured when he follows the command.
16-24 _ Obtaining the wisdom of the word is better than gold and is the source of life. The wise bring blessing even to others.
25-33 _ The foolish bring division and ruin through their own knowledge, lies, and anger, so governing the heart and relying on God is the wise course of action.

[Chapter 17] It Is Good to Be at Peace Even in Poverty, and the Secret of a Wise Life Lies in Holding Back One's Words
It mainly shows the contrasting appearance of the righteous and the wicked in situations that arise in everyday life.
Through this the writer explains how wisdom is to be practiced in concrete life. Chapter 17, in which fragmentary lessons are listed rather than arranged by a set theme, can be divided in content into three.
1) Attitude toward wealth: obtaining material things by unjust means for the sake of immediate gain rather invites calamity (vv. 1, 8, 23).
2) Lessons on relationships with neighbors in the community: those who show love to their neighbors, help in times of urgency, and give material help to the poor receive God's blessing (vv. 2, 5, 9, 13, 17-19).
3) Lessons on right judgment: distinguish rightly between the wicked and the good, and do not pervert judgment because of favoritism or bribes (vv. 3-4, 6, 10-12, 20-22).

[Chapter 18] How to Live Wisely Within the Community
Compared with chapter 17, which dealt with lessons for individual life, chapter 18 teaches the form of wisdom to be practiced within the community. This is especially because Israel exists as a community as the covenant people.
1-9 _ Those in the community who disregard others or act only as they please are foolish, and those blinded by personal gain also perish.
10-15 _ One must cast off pride, walk humbly before people and God, and strive to obtain the wisdom of God.
16-24 _ Handle community matters fairly and resolve them by peaceable means. Be careful with words, and make true friends rather than many friends.

[Chapter 19] The Importance of Encouraging Generosity and Kindness, and of Discipline
Following chapter 18, which taught the concrete form of life to be realized within the community, chapter 19 again contrasts the characteristics of the righteous and the wicked as they appear in individual lives.
Even so, the writer wishes to stress through his instruction that only keeping the word of God guarantees the greatest blessing.
1-7 _ Those who act faithfully and treat friends with generosity and giving gain true friends, but those who habitually lie and are quick to anger lose trust.
8-17 _ Obtaining a diligent wife is a blessing from God, and those who help the poor are rewarded by God.
18-23 _ Those who listen to another's helpful counsel gain wisdom, and those who fear the LORD attain life.
24-29 _ The lazy and the arrogant become destitute and fall, and those who mistreat their parents suffer shame. True success is gained when one casts off the foolish teachings of the world and follows only the righteousness of God.

[Chapter 20] The Importance of Self-Control and of Obeying God
It continues to teach what a life of fearing God is concretely.
Chapter 20 does not deal with its lessons by theme but gives fragmentary lessons. This is due to the writer's intention to teach even the fine details of life, and through this he wishes to stress that the wisdom of God applies to all of human life and brings benefit.
1-19 _ Lessons on personal life. The wise must be careful with wine, must not stir up strife with people, and must work diligently according to the season. Also they must not take wealth by unjust means and must live a morally pure life.
20-30 _ It teaches us to strive to obtain wisdom. One must remember God's judgment before the benefit worldly goods give, strive to obtain wisdom, and rulers must rule with lovingkindness and truth.

[Chapter 21] Righteousness, Fairness, and Lovingkindness
It contrasts the attitudes of life of the wicked and the righteous. In particular, by stressing God's judgment and verdict on their conduct, it teaches us to live the life of the righteous.
1-12 _ God examines all of a person's deeds and even weighs the heart. Those who practice righteousness and fairness receive greater blessing than sacrifice, and those who gain wealth by deceiving others and those who practice violence perish. The arrogant and foolish despise wisdom and fall into tribulation.
13-31 _ The righteous delight in doing justice, and the righteous and the wicked are each repaid according to their deeds. The righteous gain glory by following righteousness and lovingkindness, avoid tribulation by being humble and prudent, and live a life of victory through diligence and the help of God.

[Chapter 22] Listen Attentively to the Wisdom of the LORD
As the conclusion of the second proverbs section begun at chapter 10 and the beginning of the third, it tells of the true values the wise must choose and at the same time gives concrete lessons of wisdom.
1-6 _ The wise do not pursue worldly goods, but by fearing the LORD gain glory and life.
7-16 _ The wicked sow evil and reap ruin, and through laziness and oppression of the poor they themselves in the end become poor.
17-21 _ The concrete lesson the wise must follow is only to seek the word of God and go forward in that way.
22-29 _ When in daily life they do not oppress the weak, do not give vent to anger, and live diligently, the wise gain glory.

[Chapter 23] A Self-Controlled Life That Guards Against Greed and Fleshly Pleasure
The writer, having taught the right choice the wise must make, tells in this chapter the concrete lessons the wise must practice in life.
1-9 _ The wise must not associate with the greedy and must not be enticed by the food and wealth they give. These give momentary pleasure but bring greater calamity.
10-21 _ Do not oppress the poor and weak, listen to instruction, pass on the word of God to your children and save their souls, and fear the LORD alone.
22-25 _ Do not neglect your parents, but serve them with devotion and make them glad.
26-35 _ Keep far from the prostitute who leads to adultery, and be careful not to fall into wine, which numbs a person's reason and makes him sin.

[Chapter 24] The Benefit of Wisdom
As the conclusion of the third proverbs section begun at chapter 22, it stresses that the instructions of wisdom listed so far are the very weapon by which one can overcome this world full of evil and obtain God's blessing.
1-12 _ Do not envy the prosperity of the wicked. Their end is destruction, and the righteous, if they long for the wisdom of God and endure patiently, will be repaid according to their deeds.
13-22 _ Wisdom is like honey from the comb and gives hope to life; the righteous do not fall, so do not rejoice at the tribulation of your enemy, but fear the ruler and live faithfully.
23-34 _ By rendering fair judgments in life, doing one's best in the work entrusted to him, and working faithfully without laziness, one enjoys abundant blessing.

[Chapter 25] Stressing Humility Before God and Superiors, and Speaking Carefully and in an Orderly Way When Dealing with People
It contains the introductory content of the fifth section of proverbs.
1-7 _ Before a king one must cast off pride and be humble, otherwise great calamity will come.
8-15 _ In relationships with neighbors one must be careful with words, not reveal another's secrets, speak words that suit the occasion, listen to the counsel of others, and speak gently so as not to hurt the other person's feelings.
16-28 _ Do not be greedy for food, speak and act truthfully, treat enemies with love, and do not accuse others. When one does not seek his own honor and governs his heart in all things, he escapes calamity and receives God's blessing.

[Chapter 26] Guard Against the Foolish, the Lazy, and Those Whose Words Run Ahead
It contains lessons about the foolish and the lazy.
1-12 _ The foolish gain no honor however hard they try, suffer because of useless words, cannot even make use of what is given to them, and repeat their folly.
13-19 _ The lazy dislike work and waste time only on useless things, deceive their neighbors, and cause strife within the community.
20-28 _ Those who are not careful with their words deceive others with cunning speech, plot evil, and lead others into evil, but because of this they themselves meet ruin.

[Chapter 27] The Need and Benefit of Reproof
It teaches about right conduct to be practiced in real life.
1-10 _ Since one cannot know about tomorrow, be faithful in the present, do not boast of yourself, be self-restrained, and do not take good counsel lightly.
11-16 _ Avoid calamity, and when choosing a woman, look for a well-rounded character rather than appearance.
17-27 _ Those faithful to their appointed duties gain glory; they hold their place amid hardship, are not dazzled by immediate gain, and can enjoy a happy life when they do their best in the work and family business entrusted to them.

[Chapter 28] Stressing That God's Judgment Will Fall on the Wicked, by Contrasting the End of the Righteous and the Wicked
By contrasting the characteristics of the wicked and the righteous, it shows the two results that follow from them, blessing and ruin. By this the writer wishes to strongly urge the choice of the way of wisdom.
1-12 _ The wise keep God's justice, but the wicked are forsaken by God for practicing injustice. Therefore those who hear the law and keep it will gain respect from people and receive God's blessing.
13-18 _ The wicked persecute the people and soon fall, but the righteous who act faithfully escape tribulation.
19-28 _ Those faithful in their work are greatly blessed, but those who covet unjust wealth and are unwilling to give to others will be cursed. Therefore those who deny themselves, rely on the LORD, and act justly according to His will shall obtain salvation.

[Chapter 29] Righteous Rule Is Required When Governing a Nation
As the concluding part of the fifth section of proverbs, it summarizes and compares the characteristics of the righteous and the wicked that have been mentioned so far.
1-15 _ In a nation ruled by the righteous the whole people are at ease, and those who do not repent of their sin perish. The king must rule with justice, officials must act uprightly, and they must take good care of the poor and marginalized.
16-22 _ Teach the people the law, and discipline the wicked.
23-27 _ The proud are brought low, and the humble gain honor. Those who humbly serve God are safe amid all tribulations.

[Chapter 30] Agur's Hope to Rely Only on the Word of God, and Its Importance
The proverbs of Solomon, the chief writer of Proverbs, end at chapter 29, and in chapter 30 the proverbs of Agur son of Jakeh are introduced.
Unlike the proverbs of Solomon, which introduce the way of wisdom, the content of chapter 30 centers on the frail nature of humanity. By this the writer wishes to stress the sovereignty and power of God.
First half) It is written in the form of Agur's self-confession, telling how foolish and wicked a being a human is, and confessing that therefore serving the LORD alone is the best way (vv. 1-9).
Second half) It lists in concrete terms various sins that people easily commit. These are the sins of holding a proud and stubborn heart, of greed and unfilial conduct, and of sexual immorality (vv. 10-20).
Last) The writer teaches what the life of the wise should be like by introducing four kinds of conduct despised in the world and four wise creatures (vv. 21-33).

[Chapter 31] Lemuel's Mother Stresses the Harmfulness of Wine and Defines the Virtuous Woman
The last chapter of the whole of Proverbs, it introduces the instruction that King Lemuel's mother gave her son.
For this reason the content of chapter 31 mainly deals with the right attitude a ruler should take and what kind of woman is a virtuous wife.
But the thought implied throughout chapter 31 is in agreement with the whole of Proverbs in that it is the fear of the LORD.
1-9 _ A king must not fall into lust and wine, must rule the people justly, and must take care of the poor and marginalized.
10-31 _ A virtuous wife is more precious than any wealth; she treats her husband well, diligently manages the household, builds up the family's livelihood, and is respected for showing love to the poor. She raises her children well and helps her husband succeed. The way to become a virtuous woman is to fear the LORD.

[Chapter 1] The Vanity of Life and the Limits of Humanity
Solomon declares that everything under the sun is vain and futile, and so reveals the limits of life. Since all toil in life is vain, he hints that true satisfaction is found in God.
1-11 _ All the toil of the world and human activity are vain and only repeat themselves.
12-18 _ Even wisdom and knowledge are vain and only add to vexation.

[Chapter 2] The Vanity of Pleasure and Toil
Solomon tried pleasure, building, the accumulation of wealth, and more, but in the end realized it was all vanity. All the achievements of life are fleeting, but the joy God gives is the only satisfaction.
1-11 _ Pleasure, great enterprises, and the accumulation of property are also vain.
12-17 _ Wisdom is better than folly, but in the end the wise and the foolish die alike.
18-26 _ The result of toil is also vain, because it passes to someone else.

[Chapter 3] A Time for Everything and the Sovereignty of God
It makes clear that all things in the world are under the times God has set, and reveals the limits of humanity. Humans are finite, but when they fear God, life becomes meaningful.
1-8 _ There is a set time for everything.
9-15 _ God has made everything beautiful in its time, and humans cannot know the beginning and the end of God's work.
16-22 _ Seeing that humans and animals die alike, one waits for God's judgment.

[Chapter 4] The Vanity of Oppression, Wealth, and Honor
It stresses the emptiness of the oppression and toil that fill the world, and of wealth and honor. Pointing out the emptiness of the fruit of power and toil, it stresses relying on God.
1-3 _ There is no one to comfort the sorrow of the oppressed.
4-7 _ All human toil springs from envy.
8-12 _ Two together are better than one alone.
13-16 _ Even the powerful in the end pass away in futility.

[Chapter 5] A Reverent Attitude Before God
It teaches about sacrifices and vows offered to God, and the vanity of wealth. True satisfaction lies in a life of fearing God.
1-7 _ Do not be rash before God, but go to Him with a reverent attitude.
8-9 _ The world is full of injustice and exploitation.
10-20 _ Wealth cannot give satisfaction, and it is a blessing to live in the enjoyment God gives.

[Chapter 6] The Fleetingness of Life and the Teaching of the Wise
While stressing again the vanity of life, it speaks of the light that the words of the wise give. Even in a vain life, the conclusion of wisdom is the fear of God.
1-6 _ Lamenting vain words and a life with no outcome.
7-9 _ The words of the wise are like goads and like guidelines that lead life.
10-12 _ Concluding everything with the fear of God.

[Chapter 7] The Benefit and Limits of Wisdom
While stressing the importance of wisdom, it makes clear that wisdom too has limits. Wisdom is beneficial, but because of human limits it shows that the fear of God is best.
1-14 _ A good name, the day of death, and sorrow are more beneficial than pleasure.
15-22 _ Seeing the prosperity of the righteous and the wicked, one experiences the contradictions of life.
23-29 _ He confesses that even if one seeks wisdom, perfect understanding cannot be obtained, and that humans are by nature beings who carry wickedness.

[Chapter 8] Authority and the Providence of God
It stresses the attitude to take before those in authority and the sovereignty of God. Even amid power and prosperity, one must trust in the providence of God.
1-8 _ The wise obey before the king and discern the time.
9-15 _ The prosperity of the wicked is brief, and God will surely judge.
16-17 _ God's work cannot be fully known by human wisdom.

[Chapter 9] The Uncertainty of Life and the Joy of the Present
Because life ends in death for everyone, it exhorts us to enjoy the life now given. We must remember death and live the present God has given with joy.
1-10 _ The righteous and the wicked are alike before death.
11-12 _ Life faces unexpected calamity and death.
13-18 _ Wisdom is better than power, but people often despise the wise.

[Chapter 10] The Attitude of Life of the Wise
It exhorts us to live wisely even amid the uncertainty of life. A wise life is revealed in words and actions.
1-11 _ Just as a few flies spoil the perfumer's ointment, a little folly damages honor.
12-15 _ The words of the wise are gracious and give life, but the words of the fool ruin himself.
16-20 _ Laziness and dissipation destroy a nation.

[Chapter 11] Not Knowing the Future and a Humble Life
It stresses the uncertainty of life and urges humility and wisdom. We must live acknowledging that everything in life is in God's hand.
1-6 _ Since you do not know what lies ahead, do good and do not miss opportunities.
7-8 _ Enjoy the joys of life, but remember the judgment.
9-10 _ In the time of youth live following your heart, yet you must remember God.

[Chapter 12] The Conclusion of Life: Fear God
In the last chapter the Teacher presents the conclusion of life. Ecclesiastes brings the conclusion of all vanity down to the fear of God and the keeping of His commandments.
1-8 _ Remember your Creator in your youth, because the frailty of old age and death are drawing near.
9-12 _ The words of the wise are like goads that guide the path of life.
13-14 _ The end of life is to fear God and keep His commandments.

[Chapter 1] The First Meeting of Bridegroom and Bride and the Joy of Love
The first chapter of the Song of Songs sings of the beginning of love; the bride rejoices in her love with the bridegroom, discovers her own inner self, and longs to know the bridegroom more. The bridegroom praises the bride, extols her beauty and worth, and the bride responds to this and worships the bridegroom. It is a chapter in which love and admiration for each other appear in harmony.
1-4 _ The bride's joy in the bridegroom.
5-8 _ The bride's self-discovery and her longing to know the bridegroom more.
9-17 _ The bridegroom's praise of the bride (the mare among Pharaoh's chariots, the dove), the bride's confession, praise, and worship of the bridegroom

The bridegroom and the bride sing of their love for each other. The bridegroom urges the bride to walk with him and stresses removing the small obstacles that hinder the relationship. The bridegroom and the bride belong to each other, and the bridegroom promises that he will surely return for the bride.
1-6 _ The bridegroom's praise of the bride (a lily among thorns), the grace that flows from the bridegroom
8-14 _ The swiftness of the grace given by the bridegroom and his concern for the bride, the bridegroom urging the bride to walk with him
15 _ A counsel to remove the small things that hinder the relationship between bride and bridegroom
16-17 _ The bridegroom and the bride belong to each other, and the bridegroom will return for the bride.

[Chapter 3] The Restoration of Love and the Joy of Marriage
The bride sings of the joy of fellowship restored after a brief interruption, and longs to meet the bridegroom. In the end she meets the bridegroom and rejoices, and the completion and joy of love are dramatically revealed in the solemn scene of the wedding.
1-5 _ Fellowship interrupted for a time and then restored
6-11 _ The wedding.

[Chapter 4] The Beauty of the Bride and the Praise of Love
The bridegroom praises the bride's beauty in detail and repeatedly expresses his love and admiration for her. The bride longs for intimate love with the bridegroom and conveys her heart in prayer.
1-7 _ The seven beauties of the bride
8-15 _ Repeated praise and love for the bride
16 _ The bride's longing and prayer

[Chapter 5] The Bride's Longing and the Majesty of the Bridegroom
The bridegroom answers the bride's longing and shows favor and then a brief withdrawal. Then, through the ten excellent and outstanding features of the bridegroom, his majesty and love are stressed.
1 _ The bridegroom's answer to the bride's longing
2-8 _ The bridegroom's favor and his withdrawal.
9-16 _ The ten features of the bridegroom, outstanding among ten thousand

[Chapter 6] The Bride Seeking the Bridegroom and the Praise of Beauty
The women of Jerusalem help the bride to seek the bridegroom, and the bride finds the bridegroom and confesses her love for him. Then the bridegroom repeatedly sings of the bride's beauty.
1 _ The women of Jerusalem offer to join in seeking the bridegroom
2-3 _ Finding where the bridegroom is, and her confession toward the bridegroom
4-10 _ The bridegroom's repeated song of the bride's beauty.
11-13 _ The bride's beauty and dance are described.

[Chapter 7] The Maturing of Love and Deep Intimacy
The bridegroom again praises the bride's beauty and sings that the delight of love has grown deeper still. It shows the maturing of love and intimate fellowship.
1-5 _ The women of Jerusalem sing of the bride's beauty in ten ways
6-9 _ The bridegroom sings of the bride's beauty
10-13 _ The bride's response to the bridegroom's love

[Chapter 8] The Completion and Eternity of Love
The bride longs all the more for the bridegroom's love, leans on the bridegroom, and passes through a rough path. Four characteristics of love are stressed, and the bride's privileges and duties are mentioned. Finally, through the glory of love and the second coming, it shows the eternity of true love.
1-4 _ The bride who longs all the more for the bridegroom's love
5 _ The bride who leans on the bridegroom and passes through the rough wilderness
6-7 _ The four characteristics of love
8-12 _ The bride's privileges and duties
13-14 _ Glory and the second coming

[Chapter 1] The Indictment of the People of God and the Call to Repentance
Isaiah accuses Judah and Jerusalem of their wickedness and rebukes their formal sacrifices and unjust conduct. But at the same time he promises God's forgiveness and restoration to those who repent.
1-9 _ A song of sorrow over the dreadful reality of Israel, which rebelled against God
10-20 _ A criticism of Israel's formal sacrifices and an invitation to restoration
21-31 _ Sorrow over fallen Israel, and the promise of restoration after judgment

[Chapter 2] The Mountain of the LORD and the Glory to Come
Isaiah proclaims that in the last days the mountain of the LORD will be established above all the mountains and the nations will stream to it. But at the same time he warns of God's judgment on human pride and idolatry.
1-5 _ The vision of a peaceful kingdom to be realized along with the temple in the last days
6-22 _ Presenting the cause of the judgment of southern Judah, and a warning of the judgment of the day of the LORD

[Chapter 3] The Judgment That Will Fall on Jerusalem and Judah
God warns that He will judge the leaders and the proud of Jerusalem and Judah and will bring down their social order.
1-12 _ A warning of the removal of those on whom southern Judah relies, and a rebuke of the profanation of the glory of the LORD
13-26 _ A warning of the LORD's judgment, appearing as the one who pursues sin and as judge, on the upper-class men and women of southern Judah
[Chapter 4] Prophecy of the Restoration of the Remnant of Zion

[Chapter 5] The Song of the Vineyard and Judgment
God tended the vineyard, but it bore no good fruit, so He judges it. He also pronounces six woes and speaks of the certainty of judgment.
1-7 _ The LORD's declaration of His will to judge southern Judah, likened to a good farmer and a worthless vineyard
8-17 _ Two of the six great evils of southern Judah, committed by the leading figures, and the declaration of judgment
18-25 _ Four of the six great evils of southern Judah, common to society as a whole, and the declaration of judgment
26-30 _ Prophecy of the judgment of southern Judah, the chosen people, through foreign nations

[Chapter 6] Recalling the Prophet's Call Through the Appearance of the LORD and the Vision of the Burning Coal from the Temple
In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the holiness of God in the temple and received his call.

Amid the threat of Aram and northern Israel, the sign of Immanuel is given to King Ahaz.
1-9 _ Prophecy of the preservation of southern Judah, which was attacked by the allied forces of northern Israel and Aram
10-16 _ The prophecy of Immanuel, a sign to confirm the prophecy of the preservation of southern Judah
17-25 _ Prophecy of the discipline of southern Judah through Assyria

God makes Assyria an instrument of judgment, but the people must hope for salvation through Immanuel.
1-4 _ The prophecy of Maher-shalal-hash-baz reconfirming the defeat of the allied forces of northern Israel and Aram
5-15 _ A twofold prophecy of punishment and protection for southern Judah, which relied on Assyria
16-22 _ The sealing of the documents testifying to the prophecy, and a warning against false prophecy

[Chapter 9] A Great Light and the Prince of Peace
A great light shines in the darkness, and it prophesies that the Prince of Peace will come.
1-7 _ The Messiah's birth, and the prophecy of light and joy through His rule
8-12 _ Fourfold prophecy 1 of the destruction of northern Israel, which rejected the LORD

[Chapter 10] Judgment on Assyria
God uses Assyria as an instrument of judgment, but He also judges proud Assyria and preserves the remnant.
1-4 _ Fourfold prophecy 2 of the destruction of northern Israel, which rejected the LORD
5-19 _ Prophecy of the judgment of Assyria, which forgot its standing as an instrument of the LORD's judgment
20-34 _ Prophecy of the repentance of the remnant of southern Judah and of deliverance from the Assyrian invasion

[Chapter 11] The Reign of the Messiah and Peace
A shoot comes forth from the stem of David and rules, filled with the Holy Spirit; all things are made peaceful, and the nations gather to Him.
1-9 _ Prophecy of the new kingdom of peace that comes through the Messiah's righteous rule
10-16 _ Prophecy of the future in which the nations submit through the Messiah, the remnant return, and the chosen people rule

[Chapter 12] The Praise and Joy of the Restored Remnant and the Proclamation of the Nations' Praise of the LORD
A song of thanksgiving praising that God has given salvation.

[Chapter 13] Judgment on Babylon
God proclaims the day of wrath against Babylon, and uses the Medes as His instrument.
1-8 _ God's army gathered for the judgment of Babylon, and a warning that the day of judgment is coming
9-22 _ The terrifying picture of the judgment to be poured out on Babylon, and a warning of that day

[Chapter 14] Mockery of the King of Babylon
God restores His people and humbles the proud king of Babylon.
1-2 _ The promise of the return and restoration of the captives of southern Judah after the fall of Babylon
3-20 _ A song of mockery against the king of Babylon on the day of Babylon's destruction
21-23 _ A restatement of the LORD's firm will concerning the judgment of Babylon
24-27 _ Prophecy of the destruction of Assyria, stressing the LORD's management of history
28-32 _ Prophecy of the destruction of the Philistines, the third in the continuous series of prophecies of the destruction of ten nations

[Chapter 15] The Sudden Fall of Moab, the Suffering of Its Subjects, and a Warning of Calamity (1)
Moab is laid waste by judgment, and its mournful weeping is depicted.

God rebukes Moab's pride and ultimately declares its destruction.
1-5 _ Presenting two ways by which Moab could escape ruin
6-14 _ The pitiful picture of the destruction of Moab, which in pride refused counsel, and a warning of its appointed time

Damascus and Ephraim receive judgment, but the remnant look to the LORD.
1-3 _ Prophecy of the destruction of northern Israel and Damascus, the capital of its ally Aram
4-11 _ Prophecy of the fall of northern Israel and of the small remnant left by grace
12-14 _ The miracle of the Assyrian army vanishing before southern Judah

It prophesies judgment on Cush (Ethiopia) and that in time to come the nations will worship at Zion.

God places Egypt in confusion and judgment, but in the end causes it to repent and serve the LORD.

16-25 _ An inserted prophecy of Egypt's conversion and restoration, and of the eschatological peace of Israel, Assyria, and Egypt

Isaiah gives a sign for three years, going about naked, and warns that Egypt and Cush will be taken captive by Assyria.

Judgment is proclaimed on Babylon, Dumah (Edom), and Arabia.
1-10 _ The second prophecy of Babylon's destruction, stressing God's sovereignty and work
11-17 _ Prophecy of the destruction of the inhabitants of Edom, south of the Dead Sea, and of northwest Arabia

He rebukes Jerusalem's dissipation and unbelief, deposes the leader Shebna, and sets up Eliakim.
1-14 _ A warning of the destruction of stubborn Jerusalem as though it were already settled
15-25 _ Prophecy of the judgment of the two officials who led the stubbornness of Jerusalem and southern Judah

Tyre, a commercial city, receives God's judgment and declines, and is restored after seventy years, but its profit is dedicated to the LORD.

15-18 _ Prophecy of Tyre, to be restored seventy years after its destruction, and of its role in helping the chosen people

God judges the whole world, but the remnant praise and look toward a new creation.
1-13 _ Prophecy of the devastation of the whole earth just before the great tribulation and great judgment of the last days
13-23 _ The glory of the LORD to be revealed after the great tribulation and great judgment of the last days

God's salvation and rule are proclaimed, death is destroyed, and eternal joy is given.
1-5 _ The prophet's praise of the LORD, who will bring about the great judgment and glory
6-12 _ The LORD's feast to be given at the end, and the judgment of Moab

It sings of God's salvation and peace, and the destinies of the righteous and the wicked are contrasted.
1-19 _ The song of praise and confession of faith of southern Judah entering the city of the LORD's salvation
20-21 _ An exhortation to take refuge at the time of the great tribulation to come

God punishes evil and gathers and restores Israel.
1 _ Renewed emphasis on the destruction of evil and the salvation of the chosen people
7-13 _ Renewed emphasis on the carrying out of discipline on the chosen people, unlike the judgment of the wicked, and on the resulting restoration of the chosen people

He rebukes the drunken leaders of Ephraim and Jerusalem and promises a foundation stone in Zion.

7-22 _ A warning of judgment against the corrupt and proud leaders of southern Judah

9-16 _ Pointing out the three great symptoms of the spiritual decline of southern Judah, the people of God
17-24 _ Prophecy of the restoration of the faith of the chosen people and of blessing for the lowly and the poor

Judah relies on Egypt, but it is nothing more than vain help, and it is proclaimed that God alone is the true Savior.

8-17 _ A warning of sudden and thorough judgment at the time southern Judah concluded the alliance with Egypt
18-26 _ The promise of waiting, answering, and restoring toward southern Judah, which is under discipline

All nations, beginning with Edom, receive God's judgment.

9-17 _ The final state of the land of the adversaries after the LORD's eschatological great judgment

1-10 _ Sennacherib's invasion and demands

[Chapter 13] [King Jehoiachin] The Sash Symbol, the Broken Covenant, and a Warning of Judgment
Using the symbolic object lessons of a rotted linen sash and a smashed wineskin, God declares through Jeremiah that the nation of Judah and the people of Jerusalem have become of no use at all.
▦ ㉠ The Parable of the Rotted Linen Sash
The parable of the rotted linen sash focuses mainly on pointing out the sin of Judah.
The “linen sash” refers to the sash the priests wore around the ephod (Exodus 28:30-42). Such a linen sash, together with the ephod, breastpiece, and turban, was a symbol of the holiness and glory of the priest. Here it is used to symbolize Israel, called by God to be a holy and glorious kingdom of priests. That is, “buying a linen sash and putting it around the waist” means that God set Israel apart as holy among the nations and made it a kingdom of priests toward the nations and glorified it.
But the sinning Judah is like a rotted linen sash and, being useless, is cast away.
▦ ㉡ The Parable of the Wine Jar
The “jar” symbolizes Judah, and the “wine” the wrath of God.
The parable of the wine jar centers on God's judgment, which is the result of sin. The parable of the wine jar means that, just as a jar is filled with wine, God's wrath will fill stubborn Judah, which does not listen despite the warning of imminent judgment from God.
‘Do we not know that every jar will be filled with wine?’ This is the people of Judah's mockery of the symbol of the “wine jar.” The words of the people of Judah carry contempt, in the manner of saying: Filling a wine jar with wine is perfectly natural, and you call this the word of God?
Though the sins of the people were many, the main reason for the judgment on the nation of Judah was their pride. Jeremiah declared that an enemy would come from the north and take Judah into captivity.

The Rechabite clan is the Midianite clan also called the Kenites. They were with the people of Israel from the time of Israel's life in the wilderness, and even after entering the land of Canaan they served God faithfully.
The Rechabite clan had several prohibitions. These were established by Jonadab, who was their spiritual pillar.
The first regulation was never to drink wine. The second was to maintain a nomadic life, and the third was not to live a settled life but to live in tents. These prohibitions are thought to have been measures to prevent the clan from being annihilated by enemy invasion and to prevent worldly corruption arising from settled life. How well they kept these prohibitions is evident in their confession.

[Chapter 39] [King Zedekiah] The Third and Final Invasion of Jerusalem
Jeremiah 39 records the fulfillment of the prophecy that had been warned of until now, that is, God's word of prophecy that Jerusalem would fall to Babylon.
Jerusalem was besieged by the Babylonian army in October of Zedekiah's ninth year, 588 B.C., and fell about eighteen months later, in Zedekiah's eleventh year, that is, on the ninth of April, 586 B.C. At this time Zedekiah's two sons were put to death, and Zedekiah himself, with his two eyes put out, was bound in chains and taken to Babylon with the people of Judah.
Thus Jeremiah's prophecy over forty years (627-586 B.C.) was fulfilled exactly. In the end the faithfulness of the word of God was confirmed. Jeremiah appealed with tears and pleaded with God that the people of Judah might repent so that such a day would not come.
Nevertheless, the people of Judah not only did not accept Jeremiah's warning but rather persecuted Jeremiah, and so in the end met the day of wretched destruction. By contrast, Jeremiah, who boldly cried out the word of God even amid suffering, and Ebed-melech, who saved his life (Jeremiah 38:7-13), survived.

[Chapter 50] The message of judgment against Babylon (1)
Jeremiah 50 is a prophecy of judgment against Babylon. The great coalition from the north refers to the Medo-Persian alliance led by Cyrus. As prophesied, Babylon was destroyed by Media and Persia in 539 B.C., and the Israelites who had lived in captivity in Babylon made their first return the following year, by the decree of Cyrus in 538 B.C.

Jeremiah 52 is the final conclusion of the Book of Jeremiah. It is an appendix added by Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, and compared with the account recorded in chapter 39, verses 1-10, it records in greater detail the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 B.C. and the events that followed.
In this last chapter of the Book of Jeremiah we come face to face with the fulfillment of Jeremiah's unceasing prophetic warnings: that the nation of Judah would fall, that the capital city Jerusalem and its walls would be destroyed, that the great temple of Solomon would be plundered and desecrated, that the kings of Judah would be imprisoned and executed, that the priests and the remaining national leaders would be put to death, and that the people would be scattered in foreign lands as captives. Yet at the very end, the king of Babylon releases Jehoiachin from prison and treats him with honor.
Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, added the historical appendix to make clear that the warnings of judgment against Judah that Jeremiah proclaimed were plainly fulfilled, thereby confirming that all of Jeremiah's prophecies, especially the prophecy of Judah's restoration, will surely be fulfilled as well, and further to stress that all of God's prophecies are certain to be fulfilled.

[Chapter 2] The wrath of God
Chapter 2 begins with "the day of his anger" (1) and ends with "the day of the LORD's anger" (22). Therefore the central point of chapter 2 lies in "the day of wrath." If sin was emphasized in chapter 1, then in chapter 2 the wrath against that sin, that is, judgment, is emphasized. The words "wrath" and "anger" appear intensively, as many as eight times.
If chapter 1 portrays a cry of shame and despair, then in chapter 2 an atmosphere of anger flows throughout. Moreover, the anger of the one who inflicted the suffering is expressed with its reasons enumerated point by point. The greatest sign of God's wrath is the "severing of fellowship (relationship)" with the chosen people.
What makes chapter 2 a warning to us is that God's wrath did not end merely as a judgment poured out on Jerusalem in the prophet's day, but was brought down on those who rejected Christ in the Lord's day, and is also warned of as being poured out on the unrepentant on the coming day of the final judgment.

[Chapter 3] A prayer seeking compassion
Chapter 3 is the central chapter of Lamentations in every respect: form, content, and structure.
Because the writer had this in mind, he made chapters 1, 2, 4, and 5 uniformly 22 verses long, and chapter 3 he set squarely in the very center with 66 verses, using an acrostic form in which each of the 22 letters of the alphabet is recited three times.
What was the writer trying to bring out by taking such pains? The answer appears in the first verse of chapter 3: "I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of the LORD's wrath." In the first section (1-18), the first-person pronoun "I" appears as many as 26 times.
Then who is the "I" who "has suffered under the rod of the LORD's wrath"? Primarily it is Jeremiah himself, who wrote Lamentations by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Overlapping with this is the plight of the people of Zion. The prophet binds himself and the people together as one, taking the people's suffering as his own. Moreover, the "affliction" that "I" suffer here can be seen as a shadow of the harm to be suffered by Christ, who comes as the suffering servant.

[Chapter 4] The siege of Jerusalem
Chapter 4 contrasts "Jerusalem past and present." Through this contrast, how wretched the reality under God's wrath is stands out in stark relief. It conveys vividly the painful reality of Judah, which was once regarded like a princess in the glory of God, but was cast down to the ground because of sinning against God.
Chapter 4 has something in common with chapter 2 in that its content is "the wrath of God." Yet when analyzed in detail, they carry different messages.
If chapter 2 emphasizes the "cause of mourning" resulting from God's wrath together with that wrath,
chapter 4 directly specifies the "cause for which wrath came upon them." In particular, it stresses that the main causes that brought on God's wrath were the corruption of the leaders, that is, the prophets and priests, and the unbelief of the people, who did not trust in God but relied on the surrounding nations.

In chapter 4, Jeremiah, who had looked to "God's covenant" in the words "O Zion, your punishment for iniquity is accomplished; he will keep you in exile no longer," goes one step further in chapter 5 before God's mercy and love.
In the first half, verses 1-18, he appeals for God's forgiveness and restoration, saying that the chosen people, with whom He once shared love, are now trembling in such a terrifying and wretched state of suffering. The mood is like that of a child who was loved by his parents, and who, after being severely beaten for a wrong he committed, nestles in his parents' embrace and murmurs, "It was so frightening and painful."
In the second half, verses 19-22, the earnest heart of the prophet (the writer), who wants to wipe out all the sinful relationship of the past and make his relationship with God completely new, is prayed out in fervent hope.
Thus the petition "restore the glory of old" is offered, relying on "God's greatness and faithfulness."

[Chapter 7] Revelation of the four beasts, the little horn, and the kingdom of the Son of Man (the first revelation)
Chapters 7-12, which make up the latter half, are revelations that Daniel himself received over his lifetime, and they show the unfolding of history from Daniel's time to the end of history through the rise and fall of the great empires connected with Israel.
Chapter 7 is the first of these revelations. It was given in the first year of Belshazzar, the last king of the Babylonian Empire (552 B.C.), and deals with Daniel receiving the vision of the four beasts and the little horn in a dream and with the angel's interpretation of that dream.
This is a revelation that outlines the entire course of history up to the end of history, from the soon-coming fall of the Babylonian Empire, through the Persian, Greek, and Roman empires, the rise of the antichrist at the end of the world, and further the final judgment and the beginning of the Messiah's kingdom.
We can see that the history of all the nations of this world unfolds just as decreed by the will of the eternal God. And we are repeatedly reassured that all sinners of this world will ultimately be judged, and that the people of God will enjoy the blessing of eternal life.

Chapter 8 is the second revelation. In the third year of Belshazzar, the last king of Babylon (550 B.C.), at the river "Ulai" by the city of Susa, Daniel received the vision of the ram and the male goat, the horns that came from the goat, and especially a little horn that newly came out of one of the four horns.
Then the angel Gabriel interprets Daniel's vision.
The vision of the ram: the rulers from the transitional Medo-Persian empire period to the time of the Persian Empire.
The vision of the male goat: it prophesies Alexander of the Greek Empire, who overthrew the Persian Empire, and that after his death the Greek Empire would be divided into four regions centered on Seleucus, Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus, the four generals of Alexander.
Especially the last vision, of one strange little horn: it prophesies the appearance and fate of Antiochus Epiphanes. He appeared as king of the Syrian region at the end of the Greek Empire and was a man who greatly persecuted the Jews.
This prophecy is a composite prophecy of the antichrist who will appear in the seven-year tribulation at the end of the age,
and the prophecy of persecution of the Jews in chapter 8 is also a prophecy of the later events in which the antichrist will oppose and persecute the saints.
This prophecy given to Daniel was actually fulfilled in the times of the Persian Empire, the Greek Empire, and Syria. By this, it gives repeated assurance that the other prophecies of the Bible, which is the same word of God, and even the prophecies of the end of history and the thousand-year kingdom, will surely be fulfilled.

[Chapter 9] Intercessory prayer in the first year of Darius and the revelation of the seventy weeks (the third revelation)
This chapter speaks of the revelation of the seventy weeks, which corresponds to the third revelation. As Babylon fell and great empires such as Media-Persia rose in succession, Daniel thought deeply about "the people of God and the holy city Jerusalem." And while studying the book written by the prophet Jeremiah, he came to understand the prophecy that "the people of Israel will return from captivity after seventy years," and the righteousness and love of God contained in it.
Daniel therefore offers a fervent prayer of intercession and repentance for the restoration of the holy city Jerusalem and of the people of Israel, the people of God.
To such a Daniel, God sends the angel Gabriel and makes known the revelation of the seventy weeks: that God will send "one anointed," that is, Jesus, who will redeem the city of Jerusalem and the people of God, and that through Him, ultimately, sin will be brought to an end and everlasting righteousness will be revealed, vision and prophecy will be fulfilled, and the kingdom of God will come.
Such a revelation of the seventy weeks reminds us that the age in which Daniel lived, and this age in which we live, are part of the process in which God's great plan of salvation is unfolding, and that through this process God's righteousness and love are finally realized.
Also, the fact that, as history proceeded after Daniel received this revelation, the prophecy up to the sixty-ninth week was fulfilled exactly gives assurance that the one remaining week will also be fulfilled exactly as God's word says, and at the same time makes us realize the solemn fact that the history of humankind, as decreed by God, now has only the last one week remaining.

Chapters 10 through 12 deal with the fourth revelation that Daniel received in 536 B.C., the third year of Cyrus, king of Persia, by the Hiddekel River during three weeks of fasting and prayer. This revelation centers on "what will befall the people of Israel in the latter days."
That is, it prophesies the rise and fall of the Persian Empire, the subsequent rise of the Greek Empire and its division into four regions, and the conquests of Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the eighth king of the Seleucid dynasty of Syria, one of the divided kingdoms, together with his profaning of the temple of God and his persecution of the Jews.
Epiphanes is a figure who serves as a type of the antichrist, and Epiphanes' activities mentioned in this chapter can be called a duplicate prophecy, as a foreshadowing of the antichrist's persecution of the Jews in the last age.
And it reveals the final great tribulation and the protection of the chosen people by the angel Michael, and the ultimate salvation of the chosen people, the resurrection of all the dead, and even the eternal punishment, eternal life, and glory of the righteous and the wicked.
This prophecy presents what the outcome of the great empires shown so far in the Book of Daniel will be, and it contains a vision of comfort and hope: although in the present age evil powers will temporarily gain the upper hand and persecute the people of God, in the end the Lord, the absolute sovereign of history, and His people will gain a glorious victory.

18-21 _ The second vision, of the four horns and the four craftsmen

[Chapter 2] God who protects us like a wall of fire
Though the people of Israel, worn out in body and mind from their long captivity, returned to Jerusalem with a thread of hope, through Zechariah's vision we come to see that the blessing God wants to give the people of Israel is not a mere thread of hope but a hope and blessing that changes the very foundation of life.
Through the prophet Zechariah, God conveys the message of heart-stirring hope that God is with the people of Judah and that the nations will be saved through Jesus Christ, who comes at His first coming.
It is a vision showing God, who restores not only the temple in Jerusalem but even the city of Jerusalem, and, as Jesus at His first coming completes the gospel, many nations will belong to the LORD, and the millennial kingdom in which rule is carried out centered on Jerusalem.

If the three preceding visions focused on the restoration of Jerusalem, this chapter, the fourth vision, focuses on the high priest Joshua, the spiritual and political leader who would lead the new age.
At that time the people must have wondered how a descendant of King David, that is, the Messiah, could come and reign when the temple was not yet completed. At first they had expected a revival of faith and the glory of Israel, but as time passed that enthusiasm gradually cooled.
Then God spoke through the prophets Haggai and Zechariah: "Build the temple. The Messiah will surely come to that temple." Through these words and visions He gave the people hope and assurance again.

[Chapter 4] The pure gold lampstand and the two olive trees
This passage is the fifth vision the prophet Zechariah saw. If the first through fifth visions conveyed a hopeful message about the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem and a message of judgment on the Gentiles, then from the sixth vision on it warns the people never again to repeat the failure of the past, when God's people, after returning to the promised land, enjoyed God's grace and yet practiced idolatry and various sins, so that the nation perished and they were carried off to Babylon.
That is, it urges the people of God who are rebuilding the temple to [live "a life worthy of the people of God"], unlike in the past.

[Chapter 6] The four chariots
The prophet Zechariah sees four chariots coming out from between two mountains made of bronze. Horses of different colors from those in the first vision come out, and this vision recalls the four horsemen in Revelation chapter 6 (Revelation 6:3-8). They ride horses of colors similar to those in this vision.
The red can be said to mean slaughter, war, and massacre; the black, sorrow and death; the white, victory; and the dappled, things like various plagues.
That is, the vision of the four chariots tells us that "God's judgment" has begun.
The last vision, the eighth, is similar to the first in several respects.
Just as in the first vision God makes clear that He governs the whole world through the horses going to and fro throughout all directions, in the last, the eighth vision too, it says the horses and chariots go to and fro throughout the whole world.
"The four chariots" symbolize "the angels who carry out God's providence." The number "4" refers to "four directions" and may be said to symbolize that authority extends over the whole earth. "The bronze mountains" signify God's immutable yet complete judgment appearing in God's majesty, and their coming out from between two bronze mountains shows God's providence, unchanging like mountains and firm like bronze.
God sends the four chariots in all directions to proclaim God's rule "over all the earth" and to judge those who do not submit to it (verses 4-8).

[Chapter 7] A question and answer about fasting - a rebuke of hypocrisy and disobedience
Zechariah chapters 7 and 8 record events that took place about two years before the completion of the temple. At that time the people of Bethel had one question.
Until then they had fasted, remembering the judgment of the past and hoping that the temple in Jerusalem would be rebuilt, but now that completion was in sight, they wondered, "Should we continue to fast?"
They seem to have thought that the rebuilding and completion of the temple was the result of their fasting. So they sent a delegation to Jerusalem to ask whether they should keep on fasting.
This is the historical background of Zechariah chapters 7 and 8.
To this question of the people of Bethel, God taught the people of Israel in four instances.
Israel had become corrupt through a merely formal religious life and received punishment for it. But now God will return and dwell among Israel and restore them again. Therefore He is telling the people of Israel that they must never again fall into a formal way of life like their forefathers of old, but must live obeying the word of God in practice.

But to the chosen people Israel He promises victory, God's protection, and the Messiah who is to come. Not a king of the world like Alexander, but the King of peace will come riding on a donkey's colt, and when He comes He will be a hope for the people trapped in a waterless pit.

Among these, chapters 9-11, the first part of the second half, are a word about how the people of God, who were to enjoy blessing when the Messiah came, would reject the Messiah, and chapter 11 shows in contrast the true shepherd whom God approves and the false shepherd whom God rejects.

[Chapter 1] The genealogy and birth of Jesus
1. The genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:1-17)
(1) Descendant of Abraham and David _ salvation and glory
The genealogy running from Abraham through the royal house of David to Jesus clearly seems intended to testify that Jesus is, in legal standing, the heir of the kingship. Although that kingship had been a name only for nearly six centuries since Israel was taken captive to Babylon, unless Jesus' descent from the royal line of David is proven, none of the Jews will acknowledge Him as the Messiah.
① As God made a covenant with Abraham and David and promised that the Messiah would come from their descendants, Jesus Christ came as a descendant of Abraham and David.
② Just as Abraham was justified by faith and became the source of blessing, so in Jesus Christ, the descendant of Abraham, we too are justified and receive every spiritual blessing belonging to heaven.
③ Just as David defeated Goliath by faith, became king by faith, conquered all the surrounding nations, and built the united kingdom of Israel, so we too, by faith in Christ, the descendant of David, have conquered the power of sin and Satan and come to share in the glory of Christ. Christ justifies those who believe in Him and causes them to triumph.
(2) The recording of the names of four women _ Jesus, who came to redeem sinners
For women's names to be entered in a Jewish genealogy is no ordinary matter. The genealogy of Matthew chapter 1 comes down through men in each case, yet four women appear in it. Two of them are Gentiles (Ruth the Moabite woman, and Rahab the prostitute of the city of Jericho), and the other two are women of illicit relationships (Tamar, the daughter-in-law of Judah, and Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah). These names were recorded not because they are glorious and worth displaying, but, paradoxically, because they are people who by all rights should never have been recorded. What God wishes to make known through such a genealogy is that human beings have fallen thoroughly in Adam, and that Jesus came to resolve and redeem the sin of thoroughly fallen humanity.
(3) Why the genealogies of Matthew and Luke differ
To state the conclusion first, the two genealogies are different genealogies. Matthew recorded the genealogy according to Joseph's family line, and Luke recorded the genealogy on the basis of Mary's family line (Luke 3). As Matthew 1:16 records, "Jacob was the father of Joseph the husband of Mary, and by her Jesus who is called Christ was born," Scripture does not say that Joseph fathered Jesus. Joseph is referred to only as "the husband of Mary, by whom Jesus who is called Christ was born."
On the other hand, Luke 3:23-38 records Mary's lineage, which can be known from the words in Luke 3:23, "Jesus ... being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph." Here the phrase "as was supposed" testifies that, although the public generally believes Jesus to be Joseph's son, in fact Jesus is not Joseph's son in the biological sense.
Furthermore, this verse turns attention to the mother, Mary, who in the end necessarily becomes the one human parent through whom Jesus had to pass in order to be born from some line of ancestors. So her genealogy is listed there, and its starting point, in contrast to Joseph's father Jacob (Matthew 1:16), is actually Heli, Joseph's father-in-law. Mary's line comes down through Nathan, the son of David's wife Bathsheba (the mother of Solomon). Therefore, by birth, Jesus is a descendant of David through Nathan, and legally, He is a descendant of David through Solomon.
(4) Comparison with the genealogy in Luke
1) The first fourteen names in Matthew (from Abraham to David) agree with the record in Luke.
2) Most of the names recorded in the genealogies differ from each other.
3) Matthew's genealogy, which records from Abraham to Jesus, is shorter than Luke's genealogy, which records from Jesus back to Adam and beyond that to God.
4) Matthew omitted far more people than Luke. In Matthew, sixteen names are recorded from David to Shealtiel, whereas in Luke twenty-two names are recorded.
5) Matthew was written in descending order (from father to son), and Luke's genealogy was written in ascending order (from son to father).
6) Because Matthew was written for the Jews, the genealogy begins with Abraham, and because Luke was written to explain Christ who became man, it is connected back to Adam and God. This is because Christ came for all humankind, and humankind originated from God.
(5) Characteristics of the genealogy recorded in Matthew
1) The division into fourteen generations
① For convenience, Matthew arranged the genealogy in his own distinctive structure, dividing it into three periods of fourteen generations each (Matthew 1:17). Luke listed the names without such a division.
② Matthew's reckoning records only forty-one names in all, which raises a question. To be divided into three periods of fourteen generations each, forty-two names should normally appear. Yet Matthew records only forty-one names.
③ In one view, "David" is counted twice, that is, once at the end of the first period and once at the beginning of the second, and in another view, "Jeconiah" is counted twice. That is, because "Jeconiah" lived both before and after the Babylonian exile, he belongs both to the second period, "from David to before the Babylonian exile," and to the third period, "from the deportation to Babylon to Christ."
④ However, in chapter 1, verse 17, Matthew explains his own division of the genealogy and mentions David twice. That is, he makes clear that he counts him once at the end of the first period and once at the beginning of the second.
2) The people omitted
① After Joram, the names Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah were omitted.
② After Josiah, Jehoiakim was omitted.
③ These omissions appear to have been made intentionally, because Matthew wished to divide the genealogy into three parts of fourteen generations each.
④ "Son" and "begot" are words that refer to direct descendants, but they need not necessarily be taken as the immediately following son. In Scripture the word "son" or "child (son)" can also mean "grandson." Likewise, the word "begot" can be used of a father or a grandfather. In other words, the word "begot" means "became the ancestor of," and therefore "begotten" means "descendant of."
⑤ Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), the son of Jehoiakim and grandson of Josiah, was regarded as the last king even though, in the exile of Judah, his uncle Zedekiah succeeded to the throne.
⑥ Therefore Matthew presents not a complete genealogy of the ancestors of Jesus Christ but an "abridged genealogy."
(6) Jeremiah's prophecy concerning Jeconiah (Jehoiachin)
Shealtiel is named as the son of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) (Matthew 1:12, 1 Chronicles 3:17). This seems to contradict the word of Jeremiah 22:28-30, "Record this man as childless ... for none of his offspring shall succeed in sitting on the throne of David and ruling again in Judah." But this word is by no means contradictory. This is because that prophecy is not a prophecy that he would "simply have no children," but says "childless" in the sense of "a son to succeed to the throne."
2. The birth of Jesus (Matthew 1:18-25)
(1) Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and was born in the flesh
In this passage it is stated twice, repeatedly, that He was "conceived by the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:18, 20). Jesus did not receive the seed of Adam but was conceived by the Holy Spirit, took on flesh, and was born into the world (John 1:14). As promised, Jesus came not receiving the seed of Adam but as "the offspring of the woman" (Genesis 3:15, Isaiah 7:14).
The reason is that if Jesus had received the seed of Adam, a sinner, He could not have become the sacrifice to die in our place. Jesus, conceived by the Holy Spirit, came in the flesh, and by offering Himself as a sacrifice on the cross to save us, He completed the gospel that saves us. Now, although we came into the world in the flesh, when we are born again of the Holy Spirit we become children of God and can enter the kingdom of God (John 3:3-7).
(2) The name "Jesus (salvation)" revealed to Joseph through an angel
God revealed beforehand, through the angel Gabriel, to Joseph and Mary that the name of the One to be born was "Jesus" (Matthew 1:21, Luke 1:31). "Jesus" means "salvation." That is, He said it is because He is the One who "will save his people from their sins."
When we speak of saving from sin, the meanings "salvation from the penalty of sin, salvation from the power of sin, and salvation from the nature of sin" are all included. First, the Lord has dealt with our sins legally by His blood. He also helps us overcome sin in our lives. When the Lord returns, He will remove the nature of sin from our bodies, change us into spiritual bodies, and take us with Him. That is, the word that He saves from sin includes all of this.
(3) Jesus and Immanuel
The name of Jesus is revealed in two ways. First, the name "Jesus" was revealed through the angel, and also, 700 years before Jesus came, the name "Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14) was revealed through the prophet Isaiah.
The two names of Jesus are for us.
The name "Jesus" means "the One who saves us from sin," and the name "Immanuel" is the promise that He "will be with" those who have been saved from sin. In fact, He is with them as the Holy Spirit comes and dwells within the person who is saved (Acts 2:38).

[Chapter 2] The Worship of the Magi, the Flight to and Return from Egypt, and Herod's Massacre of the Infants
Matthew 2 records the event in which Magi came from the East, guided by a star, to Bethlehem and worshiped the child Jesus and presented Him with gifts; and the event in which, when Herod sought to find and kill the child Jesus in Bethlehem, Joseph received a revelation, fled to Egypt, and then returned.
1. The Worship of the Magi (Matthew 2:1-12)
From the East (Babylon), 'Magi who studied the stars (astronomers)' saw the star and came a long way of more than 1,000 km on foot to the land of Israel to worship the One born as King. Guided by the star, they came to Bethlehem, worshiped the child Jesus, and opened their treasure chests and presented gold, frankincense, and myrrh as gifts.
(1) Those who worshiped at the birth of the Messiah were the Magi and the 'shepherds of humble status (Luke 2:8-20)'.
The Magi were Gentiles, and the shepherds were Jews. The Magi came from far away, and the shepherds were within the region of Bethlehem. The Magi were highly educated scholars, and the shepherds were people of humble status. Yet both the Magi and the shepherds of Bethlehem were people who waited for and longed for Christ.
First, this shows what kind of people will be saved through Jesus. It shows that, whether Jew or Gentile, whether from far or near, whether learned or unlearned, those who truly long to be saved through Christ, who are spiritually awake, can be saved.
It also teaches that, just as at Jesus' first coming, at His second coming only the saved, those who are awake and wait longingly for the Lord's return, will be able to welcome Him with joy.
(2) The news of Jesus' birth threw all of Jerusalem into turmoil.
But the Magi and the shepherds of Bethlehem worshiped Jesus. Jesus Christ is an object of fear and rejection to the forces of evil, but to those who long for Christ and are awake, He was an object of joy and worship. Those who love darkness more than light do not come to the Lord, but those who long for the truth come to the Lord (John 3:19-21).
(3) Gold, frankincense, and myrrh _ kingship, priesthood, and the Savior (death)
Gold is a gift given to a king; frankincense is used when offering sacrifices and is an incense; and myrrh is applied to a corpse. That is, it teaches that Jesus is King, is Priest, and will die in our place for our sins.
(4) The Magi were warned in a dream not to return to Herod, and they returned to their own country by another route.
The Magi did not return to Herod, who had asked them to let him know where Jesus was. This shows that those who are truly saved through Jesus are people who obey only the will and the word of God.
2. The Flight to and Return from Egypt, and Herod's Massacre of the Infants (Matthew 2:13-23)
This section records the fulfillment of three Old Testament prophecies about Jesus.
(1) The word 'Out of Egypt I called My Son (Hosea 11:1)' was fulfilled.
God called Israel His son, and called Jesus His son. This speaks of the exodus, in which He made Israel His son, and at the same time prophesies that Jesus would go into Egypt and come out. The reason God delivers the people of Israel who are in Egypt, and the reason He does not let go of them even though they have sinned, is that God is not a man and is faithful to His covenant (Hosea 11:9). This fact is shown through the birth and ministry of Jesus (Hosea 11:1).
(2) The word concerning the massacre of the infants was fulfilled.
(Matthew 2:17-18) Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more.”
This is a quotation of Jeremiah 31:15. Because Jeremiah 31 contains a prophecy about Jesus' first coming, this verse is quoted accurately. 'Ramah' was a place of sorrow, used as the assembly point for the Jewish captives taken to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1), and in fact the sorrowful wailing of mothers who had lost their children was heard because of the massacre of infants that took place in Bethlehem. What words could comfort a mother who has lost her children? 'Rachel' is the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and Ephraim, the representative of northern Israel, also came from Joseph. Since the representative tribe of northern Israel is the tribe of Ephraim, 'Rachel', who is its source, symbolically represents Israel.
(3) The word 'He shall be called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23)' was fulfilled.
There is no specific passage or prophet in the Old Testament that records this saying. The Korean Revised Version (Gaeyeok Hangul) renders it 'the prophet', but the original Greek text uses the plural 'the prophets'. Bibles in other languages also render it 'the prophets'. Why did Matthew say, 'that it might be fulfilled that He shall be called a Nazarene', which is not recorded in the Old Testament?
