There are various views, but as Nathanael said to Philip, 'Can anything good come out of Nazareth? (John 1:46)', at that time the expression 'a Nazarene' was widely used among the Jews as a term by which people were held in low esteem, despised, and mocked. It is recorded that the Messiah foretold by the Old Testament prophets would be despised and rejected by people; in fact Jesus lived in Nazareth and was called 'a Nazarene', which shows that the prophecy was fulfilled. That Jesus would be despised and rejected by people appears in many places in Scripture (Psalm 22, Isaiah 53).

[Chapter 3] The ministry of John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism
Matthew chapter 3 records the ministry of John the Baptist and the event of Jesus' being baptized. John the Baptist was the last prophet of the Old Testament era, sent to bear witness to Jesus. As prophesied in the Old Testament, John the Baptist administered a baptism of repentance at the Jordan River so that the Jews might receive Jesus. When He began His public ministry, Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan River and was baptized.
1. The ministry of John the Baptist (Matthew 3:1-12)
(1) John the Baptist is the prophet promised in the Old Testament to prepare the way for Jesus (Isaiah 40:3, Malachi 3:1, 4:5-6)
(2) The word of God did not come to the Jewish religious leaders but came to John the Baptist in the wilderness (Luke 3:1-2)
It shows that still today the word of God does not come to false and hypocritical religious people, but comes to those who have been saved and are set apart from those false things.
(3) John the Baptist administered a baptism of repentance.
John the Baptist's task was to come before Jesus and prepare the people of Israel to receive Jesus. So the baptism John administered was a baptism of repentance, that people might repent (Acts 19:4). It is the same today. Those who truly know God, who know that because of their sins they cannot but receive God's judgment and punishment, and who return to God, that is, those who repent, understand the gospel and receive Christ.
(4) The message of John the Baptist
1) "Repent" (Matthew 3:2, 11).
2) "Bear fruit in keeping with repentance" (Matthew 3:8-10)!
Repentance without fitting fruit is false repentance, and through it one cannot escape the wrath of God.
3) He bore witness, "Exalt Jesus, who comes after me, and believe in Jesus."
He bore witness that the One who comes after him will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11). The baptism of the Holy Spirit refers to a saved person's receiving the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:5), and the baptism of fire refers to the fire of hell into which those who are not saved will enter.
4) He bore witness that Jesus will separate the wheat from the chaff, and "gather the wheat into the granary (heaven) and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire (the lake of fire)."
2. Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:13-17)
(1) Baptism is received by sinners, so why did Jesus, who had no sin, receive baptism?
He received it as our representative, in our place, we who are sinners. Jesus' true baptism is dying on the cross, entering the tomb, and rising again. That is why Jesus, during His public ministry, said, "I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:50), making clear that Jesus' true baptism is the event of the cross. Therefore, Jesus' receiving baptism through John the Baptist was a proclamation to the whole world that Jesus is the Savior who would save us by dying on the cross and rising again. Jesus was baptized with water, died on the cross, and rose again. We are saved through Jesus, who died on the cross and rose again, and we receive baptism as a rite of proclaiming to God and to people what has been accomplished in our hearts (Matthew 28:19-20).
(2) What is the meaning of the three events that took place when Jesus was baptized?
When Jesus was baptized in the Jordan River and came up out of the water, there were three events. The heavens were opened, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." This was a proclamation to the whole world that Jesus Himself is our Savior, and it showed beforehand what will happen to us who are saved.
First, the heavens' being opened says that the gospel of salvation was completed by Jesus' dying on the cross and rising again, and that now a door has been opened by which we can come to God by repenting and believing the gospel (Hebrews 10:19-20). Second, the event of the Holy Spirit's descending like a dove showed that the Holy Spirit, who at the time of salvation makes us understand the fact of atonement, will come upon the saved person and dwell within him (Acts 2:38, John 14:16). Third, that a voice was heard saying "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" showed that when we are saved we become beloved sons of God and will live a life that pleases God.
(3) What is the meaning of Jesus' words, "for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness" (Matthew 3:15)?
This was not said merely about the event of baptism. "All righteousness" means all of God's holy will. Jesus came to do the Father's will, and He was saying that through Jesus' death on the cross and His resurrection all of God's righteousness would be fulfilled. Being baptized by John the Baptist was one part of that process.

[Chapter 4] Jesus' temptation in the wilderness and His ministry in Galilee
Matthew chapter 4 records the event in which Jesus, led by the Holy Spirit, went into the wilderness to be tempted, and after fasting forty days and nights was tempted by the devil and triumphed. It also records Jesus' public ministry in Galilee.
1. The event of Jesus' being tempted in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11)
After Jesus was baptized in the Jordan River and received the testimony "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," He immediately went to the wilderness and was tempted. This foretold and showed beforehand, through the example of Jesus, that when a believer too is saved and receives the testimony of being a "son of God," there will be temptation.
(1) Jesus was "led by the Spirit ... to be tempted by the devil" (Matthew 4:1).
He was not led by the devil; He was led by the Spirit to be tempted by the devil. From this we can see that the temptation given to Jesus was a temptation God permitted. The temptations that a saved believer receives from the devil also take place within God's permission (Job 1:12, 2:6).
(2) Jesus was subjected to three temptations: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (Genesis 3:6, 1 John 2:16).
Adam in the garden of Eden was tempted amid plenty, where he had everything, and fell, but Jesus triumphed over the devil's temptation in the extreme circumstance of being hungry for forty days. Jesus came to restore what Adam failed, and He actually triumphed over the devil's temptation. By triumphing in the temptation He proved Himself to be the One qualified to save us.
(3) The devil's temptation
First, the devil tempts people by obscuring a clear fact. Jesus is certainly the Son of God. Yet the devil repeated twice, "If you are the Son of God."
Second, the devil tempts in three ways: bread (the lust of the flesh), throw yourself down (the lust of the eyes), and "all the kingdoms of the world I will give you" (the pride of life). Even now the devil comes to tempt believers with greed for possessions, sexual desire, and desire for honor.
Third, just as he left Jesus for a time after tempting Him, then came back and followed Jesus to the end tempting Him, so even now he keeps on tempting believers so that they cannot live a life of faith (Matthew 4:11, Luke 4:13).
(4) The one weapon with which Jesus overcame the devil's temptation was the weapon of the word "It is written."
Jesus could have used various weapons. But He used only one weapon, the word. Even now the way for believers to overcome the devil is that the word "It is written" is the supreme weapon (Ephesians 6:17).
2. Jesus' ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:12-25)
(1) Jesus' ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:12-16)
Jesus ministered in regions neglected by the people of that time, beginning with the region of Galilee. This was the fulfillment of an Old Testament prophecy (Isaiah 9:1-2). Before the Galilean ministry, Jesus had already ministered briefly in the region of Judea (John 1:29-4:42). This content, which precedes the Galilean ministry, is omitted in Matthew.
(2) "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matthew 4:17)
The opening words are "From that time." This provides an important turning point in Jesus' public ministry. If Matthew is divided into three parts, Matthew 1:1-4:16 records the person of Jesus, Matthew 4:17-16:20 records Jesus' proclamation, and Matthew 16:21-28:20 records the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
What Jesus Christ cried out before the crowds was, like the cry of John the Baptist, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Mark 1:15, Matthew 3:12). This makes us realize what is important for us. He bore clear witness that every person must repent, receive Jesus as Savior, and go to heaven.
(3) The event of calling four disciples (Matthew 4:18-22)
It records Jesus' calling four of the twelve disciples. From the way Jesus called the four disciples, we can consider what kind of people He calls as workers even now.
(4) The early ministry in Galilee (Matthew 4:23-25)
It says, "teaching ... and proclaiming the gospel ... and healing ... healed." We can see that the core of Jesus' early ministry in Galilee was the ministry of teaching, the ministry of proclaiming, and the ministry of healing. Of these, the healing ministry is especially emphasized, which in the end shows that Jesus is the Messiah who saves those bound by the power of sin and death and makes them new creations.

[Chapter 5] The Sermon on the Mount 1
Matthew chapters 5 through 7 contain the Sermon on the Mount, which is so famous that it needs no further explanation.
1. The Blessed (the Beatitudes: Matthew 5:3-12)
This is the section known as the Beatitudes. It records what kind of person can enter the kingdom of heaven, that is, the qualifications of those who will enter it, the character that those who enter must have, and the suffering that those who have such character will receive. From chapters 3 and 4 we learn that once a person obtains the status of a son of God, temptation comes. Here we learn that once a person has acquired fitting character, suffering comes.
(1) The first two statements, "Blessed are the poor in spirit" and "Blessed are those who mourn," tell us what kind of person can be saved and enter the kingdom of heaven.
God saves the poor in spirit. Who are the poor in spirit? They are those who are not satisfied with the fleshly things of this world and therefore seek what is spiritual and eternal; these are the poor in heart. God lets such people understand the gospel and gives them citizenship in the kingdom of heaven. Who are those who mourn? Those who mourn are those who grieve over sin, over judgment and punishment because of sin. Such people will receive the comfort of the forgiveness of sins. Who can be saved and enter the kingdom of heaven? Those who are poor in spirit and mourn over their sin receive the comfort of forgiveness of sins and enter the kingdom of heaven, and so they are blessed.
(2) The next five statements, "Blessed are the meek, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers," describe the character of the saved Christian.
A saved person must have a character that fits one who is saved. That is, he must be made complete as a man of God (2 Timothy 3:16-17). He must take the yoke of the meek Lord upon himself and follow the Lord (Matthew 11:29-30). He must thirst for the accomplishment of God's righteousness. Because he himself has received mercy from God, he must have mercy on others. Because he is one who has fellowship with the Lord, his heart must be clean. One who has been reconciled with God must by all means be a peacemaker.
(3) The last statement, "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake," says that suffering follows when one has the character of a Christian.
For as long as a saved person lives in this world, there is persecution and suffering that he endures because he believes. When he stands before God, his reward will be great for having endured it. Therefore he is blessed.
2. Christians as the Light and Salt of the World (Matthew 5:13-16)
A saved person is the salt of the earth and the light of the world. If a saved person loses his taste like salt that has lost its flavor, and does not shine his light, he is of no use at all. Just as salt must dissolve in order to give flavor, a saved believer can become a Christian who gives flavor when he sacrifices himself. Just as a light must be put on a lampstand to shine on everyone in the house, a saved person can shine his light on those around him through good deeds.
Then why do saved believers fail to give light?
Three reasons may be considered. If a lamp is put under a bushel (Matthew 5:15), under a bed (Mark 4:21), or in a cellar (Luke 11:33), it cannot shine. That is, if a person is caught up in the matter of making a living, in laziness and idleness, or in sin, he will not be able to shine his light.
3. Jesus, Who Came to Fulfill the Law (Matthew 5:17-20)
(1) Jesus, who came to fulfill the law (Matthew 5:17-18)
If we say, "Because Jesus has forgiven all our sins of breaking the law, we have been set free from the condemnation of the law," some people may misunderstand Jesus as one who abolishes the law. Therefore Jesus says that He did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it. Jesus came in the flesh under the law and kept the whole law through His own life. Furthermore, He bore on the cross the punishment for all the sins by which people had broken the law, and by bearing the curse of the law He fulfilled the law. Thus the righteousness of the law was accomplished through the life of Jesus, the curse of the law was borne on the cross, and the requirement of the law, which is love, is to be fulfilled through the lives of Christians (John 13:34-35, Romans 8:4, Romans 13:10).
(2) Being called great or called least in the kingdom of heaven, once one has entered it, is related to one's life (works) (Matthew 5:19).
Whether, after being saved, one lived a life obedient to the Lord's word or not is related to glory.
(3) The matter of entering the kingdom of heaven is related to righteousness (Matthew 5:20).
In order to enter the kingdom of heaven, one must have a righteousness that exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees. That righteousness can be nothing other than "the righteousness of Jesus Christ." A person goes to the kingdom of heaven by believing in the righteousness of Jesus Christ. That is the only way to enter the kingdom of heaven (Romans 3:21-24).
4. Jesus' Reinterpretation of the Law (Matthew 5:21-48)
Those who sat before Jesus and listened to His words were Israelites. They were people familiar with the law of the Old Testament. But there were many things they had understood wrongly. Jesus explained in detail what the true meaning of that law was. He spoke on many matters: the sin of murder, the sin of adultery, oaths, a life of giving rather than retaliation, loving one's enemies, and so on.
(1) He said these things so that the people of Israel might realize what "sin" is in God's sight and thereby accept Christ.
As we can see from the words, "Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are on the way with him ... lest you be put in prison ... you will never get out till you have paid the last penny (Matthew 5:25-26)," the purpose is that they realize sin and find the way to be reconciled with God. The accuser on the way of life is the law. The prison is hell. If a person goes to hell without having settled even a small sin, there is no further opportunity.
(2) He showed what the life of those who have been saved and received the Lord's life should be like.
The words, "so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:45)," do not mean that one obtains the status of a son of God by doing such things. A person who has not been saved can never live as the Lord said. When a person is saved, he receives the Lord's life and lives with God's help, so that such a life appears, and as a result he will be called a son of God by those around him; this is what the Lord was saying. He also said, "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48)." These are words that only a saved person can receive.

[Chapter 5] The Sermon on the Mount 2
1. The True Attitude of the Believer (Matthew 6:1-18)
(1) Do not do it to be seen by people, but do it to God the Father!
In the passage Matthew 6:1-18 there are statements that repeat. One is "beware of ... [doing it] before men in order to be seen by them" (Matthew 6:1, 2, 5, 16); the other is "your Father who sees in secret will reward you" (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18).
This means that whatever a believer does, he must not do it to be seen by people, that is, to make himself known before people, to be praised, to exalt himself, or to gain glory for the sake of his own honor. Whatever it is, whether righteous deeds, almsgiving, prayer, or fasting, he must not do it to be seen by people, but must do it to God who is in secret, for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).
(2) The prayer the Lord taught (the Lord's Prayer: Matthew 6:9-13)
1) It is a private prayer, not a congregational prayer.
This is because, before teaching the content of the prayer, He said, "they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners, that they may be seen by others ... But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you (Matthew 6:5-6)," and then taught the content of the prayer. The fact that many churches now recite the Lord's Prayer at the end of the Sunday worship service has a strong sense of mere recitation.
2) One must first have the qualification.
From the words "Our Father in heaven (Matthew 6:9)," we can see that this is a prayer that only one who has first been saved and has obtained the status of a son of God can pray.
3) The prayer the Lord taught is a teaching of prayer topics.
What should we pray about when we pray to God? We should pray "that God's name be hallowed, for the work of establishing God's kingdom (evangelism), that the plan God has set up be accomplished on earth, that He give us our daily bread, that we be delivered from sin, that we not enter into temptation, and that we be delivered from the evil one, the devil."
4) What does "forgive us our sins" mean?
The Lord died in our place on the cross and rose again, and so He paid the penalty for all our sins and forgave all our sins. Why, then, did He tell us to pray, "forgive us our sins"? Because of this, some people misunderstand that, since we are told here to pray "forgive us our sins," our sins have not been forgiven forever but only the past sins have been forgiven. But we must look carefully at the text. In this passage He said, "forgive us our sins, as we also have forgiven our debtors." We forgive others when they sin against us. To forgive does not mean to pay the penalty for that person's sin on his behalf; it means to forgive for the sake of fellowship. If we do not forgive, we cannot have fellowship with that person. It is the same here. Although we have been forgiven all our sins, the sins that arise in our daily life hinder our fellowship with God. Therefore, the prayer asks for forgiveness for the sake of fellowship with God.
2. The Believer and Wealth (Matthew 6:19-24)
He said, "You cannot serve God and money (Matthew 6:24)." This section speaks of the attitude a believer ought to have toward wealth.
A believer must not store up wealth on earth. This is because moth and rust destroy there, and thieves break in and steal. Even if it is not stolen, its value returns to nothing when this world passes away. A believer must store up wealth in heaven for himself. He said "for yourselves," not "for God." This is because its value is preserved forever there.
Then what must we do in order to store up in heaven?
First, the eye must become clear to see treasure as treasure (Matthew 6:22-23). This is because people give up what has no value for the sake of what has more value. We must have eyes that can see that the Lord and the Lord's gospel are the treasure. When we have eyes that can see treasure as treasure, our heart goes where the treasure is (Matthew 6:24).
Next, we must invest the wealth we have for the Lord and the Lord's gospel. That is, when the wealth of this world is used to spread the gospel, it is stored up in heaven as something spiritual.
3. What the Believer Should Truly Seek (Matthew 6:25-34)
The people of this world seek only what is visible: "What shall we eat? What shall we drink? What shall we wear?" But for the saved person there is attached the promise, "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matthew 6:33)." He tells us what the saved person should pursue.
Why should we seek first His kingdom and His righteousness?
First, a person cannot add a cubit to his stature by being anxious, nor does he have the power to prolong his life.
Second, God also provides what the body needs. If God clothes the lilies of the field and feeds the birds of the air, how much more will He give what the body needs to a saved person.
Third, it is not too late to worry about tomorrow's matters tomorrow. Each day has enough trouble of its own. Tomorrow's matters belong to God.
Fourth, it is God's promise that if we seek first His kingdom and His righteousness, He will give what the body needs.

[Chapter 5] The Sermon on the Mount 3
1. Do Not Judge (Matthew 7:1-5)
How can we be freed from the sin of judging recklessly?
This issue is a very familiar topic for Christians. There is probably no Christian who wants to judge and criticize. Many people probably feel that they want to be free from the sin of criticizing, but that it does not come as easily as they would like.
The reason the Lord forbade criticism so strongly is that this problem has an especially serious effect on our life of faith. Recklessly criticizing and judging others can affect not only one's own life but also the many relationships one has, and even the whole church.
(1) Discernment is different from judgment and criticism that condemn others.
We must discern what could become leaven in the church. Sexual sins and doctrinal sins must be discerned so that they do not contaminate other people. That is, sins that become a problem for the church must be discerned and set apart (1 Corinthians 5, Galatians 5, Matthew 18:15-17).
But we must not make judgments that condemn others recklessly. The Lord forbade this and spoke strongly about it.
(2) Reasons we should not judge
      1) The Bible teaches, "As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions (Romans 14:1)."
In the church there are those who are strong in faith, and there are also those who are weak. Within the church, Christians must acknowledge the differences of faith and of measure.
      2) Because none of us is omniscient.
      3) Because the Lord forbade it, and because it will be a problem when we stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
      4) It is a great obstacle to evangelism.
(3) A person who enjoys criticizing may do so because he has not been saved.
(4) We must abandon our own standards. If we hold our own standards, we criticize easily.
(5) Instead of looking at the speck in a brother's eye, we must look to Christ.
(6) As in the saying to take the log out of your own eye, there must be self-reflection.
(7) Everything must be done in love.
2. What Is Holy and Pearls (Matthew 7:6)
In the Bible dogs and pigs are not used in a good sense (Matthew 15:26-27, Philippians 3:2, 2 Peter 2:22, Revelation 2:15). Dogs are used to refer to false prophets, and pigs are said to be unclean. What is holy belongs to God, and pearls are valuable. No one would throw what he treasures to dogs or pigs.
God, His grace, and His truth are the most valuable and precious things in this world. If the gospel of God is the most precious and valuable thing, it must be given to those who earnestly want to obtain it, who seek it and look for it. People who do not know the value of grace and truth will trample it underfoot and, instead, will obstruct and try to kill the one who preaches the gospel. Legalists, people who are morally thoroughly corrupt and enjoy sin, and those deeply immersed in heretical doctrines rather oppose the gospel. We should avoid unnecessary disputes and arguments with those who oppose the gospel, and preach the gospel all the more actively to those who are somewhere seeking the truth. Toward outsiders we must walk in wisdom, making the best use of the time (Colossians 4:5).
3. The Attitude of the One Who Asks the Lord, and What He Should Ask For (Matthew 7:7-11)
(1) The words, "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened (Matthew 7:7-8)," mean that He will surely answer the one who asks.
And the words, "If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him (Matthew 7:11)," also mean that if even people give good things to their children, God the Father will give good things to those who ask.
Then why do people not receive? It is because they do not ask, or because even when they ask, they ask wrongly, to spend it on their passions (James 4:2-3). It is because they do not ask to the end (James 1:5-8).
(2) Then what should believers ask for?
"Is there anyone among you who, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent?"
"Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? (Luke 11:12)"
     1) Bread refers to Jesus, who is the bread of life. Jesus said, "I am the bread of life."
The "stone" refers to the law. The Ten Commandments were written on two tablets of stone. A saved person must ask for Jesus, who is the bread of life. A saved believer should desire to gain the Lord (Philippians 3:8). He should ask for the life and grace that come from the Lord. When a believer asks to gain more of the Lord, God is not One who gives a "stone," that is, the curse and punishment of the law.
     2) The "fish" refers to the believer's dedication. In the Bible believers are described as fish.
The risen Jesus asked for broiled fish and ate it. This refers to His receiving the believer's dedication. The "serpent" is a symbol of the devil. A believer should ask that his life be dedicated to the Lord. When a believer asks God for the dedication of himself to God, God does not give him the devil.
     3) The "egg" refers to life.
That is, it refers to the work of life. The "scorpion" has "poison." A saved person should ask for the work of life, the work of salvation. He should ask for the work of evangelizing other souls. When he asks for the work of life that seeks to rescue and save other souls, God does not give him its opposite, poison.
Jesus says, "how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! (Luke 11:13)" A believer should ask for the Lord (life and grace), ask for dedication, and ask that the work of life (salvation) may appear. All of these are works that appear through the Holy Spirit.
4. The Golden Rule: "Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them" (Matthew 7:12)
"The Law and the Prophets" refers to the entire Old Testament. If we were to sum up the teaching of the entire Old Testament, it could be summed up in the words, "Whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them."
Jesus first treated us well and served us (Mark 10:45). As a result, those who have received the Lord's kindness and service treat the Lord well. They serve the Lord, exalt Him, and follow Him. They desire to repay the Lord's grace.
This verse is called the "Golden Rule." Because we have first received the Lord's service, we can live the rest of our lives an unselfish life of treating others well. And it is right to live that way.
5. The Two Destinies, Life and Death (Matthew 7:13-29)
This section gives several examples related to "the two destinies, life and death."
(1) There are people who pass through the narrow gate and walk the narrow way, and there are people who pass through the wide gate and walk the wide way (Matthew 7:13-14).
He said that the gate that leads to life is narrow and the way is hard, and those who find it are few. He said that the gate that leads to destruction is wide and the way is broad, and those who enter by it are many. The "narrow gate" refers to being saved through Jesus. When a person receives forgiveness of sins through Jesus, he passes through the narrow gate, and the one who has passed through the narrow gate walks the narrow way. Having passed through the narrow gate is the basis for entering the kingdom of heaven, and having walked the narrow way is related to the reward when one enters the kingdom of heaven. Therefore the narrow gate is related to life, and the wide gate is related to destruction, that is, death.
(2) A good tree bears good fruit, and a bad tree bears bad fruit (Matthew 7:15-20).
Everyone was born in Adam as a bad tree, a sinner. Therefore he bears bad fruit. When he is saved, he becomes a good tree. If he has become a good tree, good fruit will be borne. Therefore, by looking at the fruit one can know what the tree is. That is, by looking at the fruit of a person's life and conduct, one can know whether that person is a bad tree or a good tree who has been saved.
(3) Before the judgment seat there are those whom the Lord acknowledges and those whom the Lord says He never knew (Matthew 7:21-24).
Even if a person has done many things for the Lord, if he has not obtained the Lord's life, the Lord says He never knew him. Therefore, entering the kingdom of heaven is not by doing many things, but one must receive the Lord's life. The one who does the will of the Lord enters the kingdom of heaven. The Lord's will is that people see the Son of God and obtain eternal life (John 6:40).
(4) There is the one who built his house on the rock and the one who built his house on the sand (Matthew 7:24-26).
The rock refers to Christ. A person who is saved through Christ and lives the life of faith is the one who built his house on the rock. A person who claims to live the life of faith without having been saved is the same as one who builds his house on the sand. They seem the same, so when does the difference appear? In the case of a house built on the sand, it collapses when a great flood comes. In the same way, a person who has not been saved will be exposed and will have trouble when he goes before the Lord's judgment seat.

[Chapters 8-9] Miracles Performed by the Power of Jesus 1
Matthew chapters 8 and 9 record various miracles that Jesus performed in the early part of His public ministry, without regard to chronological order.
They record the miracle of healing a leper; the miracle of healing by a word the paralysis of the servant of the centurion of Capernaum; the miracle of healing Peter's mother-in-law of her fever; the miracle of calming the wind and the storm on the sea; the miracle of healing two demon-possessed men among the tombs in the region of the Gadarenes; the healing of a paralytic; the miracle of healing a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years; the miracle of raising the dead daughter of a synagogue ruler; the miracle of healing two blind men; and the miracle of healing a mute man possessed by a demon.
The miracles Jesus performed testify to the fact that Jesus is the Christ sent by God (John 5:36, 14:10-11), and they also show in advance what will be accomplished within our souls (John 14:12).
1. Cleansing a Leper (Matthew 8:1-4)
(1) Cleansing the leprosy shows that He will cleanse sin.
(2) Through the words "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean," we can see the leper's firm faith in the Lord.
Because he had faith, he was cleansed. Who can receive forgiveness of sins? When a person repents and believes in what the Lord accomplished on the cross, he receives forgiveness of sins and is saved.
2. Healing the Centurion's Servant of Paralysis by a Word (Matthew 8:5-13)
(1) The centurion said that he was not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof, and said, "But only say the word, and my servant will be healed (Matthew 8:8)."
The Lord did not go into the centurion's house, but healed the centurion's servant by a word alone. This shows that He will save souls by the word (Romans 10:17, 1 Peter 1:23, John 6:63).
(2) The centurion had firm faith in the Lord.
Just as soldiers under his authority obey when he commands them, he believed that the servant's illness would be healed if Jesus merely commanded it by a word.
(3) The centurion was a Gentile and had a remarkable faith that not even any Israelite had.
It was a shadow of the fact that many Gentiles would come into the kingdom of heaven. But He grieved over the fact that the natural sons of the kingdom would not enter the kingdom of heaven but would go to hell.
(4) During Jesus' public ministry, what amazed Jesus was faith (Matthew 8:10).
3. Healing Peter's Mother-in-Law of Her Fever (Matthew 8:14-17)
(1) It shows that He will heal souls made sick by sin.
Because Jesus took up our infirmities and bore the sickness called sin, sin was dealt with and the sickness of the soul was healed.
(2) Through the words "the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him," we can see that a person who has experienced the Lord's grace comes to obey the Lord and serve Him.
4. The Lord's Words to a Scribe and a Disciple (Matthew 8:18-22)
(1) A scribe said that he would follow Jesus wherever He went.
But Jesus did not permit him to follow (Matthew 8:19-20). This is because there was no place in the scribe for the Lord to lay His head. In order to follow the Lord, one must first be saved through the Lord's death and resurrection and have the Lord as master within. Such a person is qualified to follow the Lord.
(2) The place where Jesus lays His head is the church, which is His body. For the church, His body, where He is to lay His head, to be established, Jesus must first die on the cross and rise again.
The "fox" refers to Herod the tetrarch of that time (Luke 13:31-32). The "birds of the air" refer to the devil, the ruler of the world (John 12:31). Herod had his palace and the devil had his dwelling place. But before He died and rose again, Jesus had no place to lay His head.
(3) If one is a disciple of Jesus, he should leave to the dead what the dead can do, and first follow Jesus and devote himself to the work of giving life.
Jesus rejected the scribe's following Him, but when a disciple said he would bury his father and then follow, He said, "Leave the dead to bury their own dead, and you follow me." The "dead" in the first instance refers to those dead even in body, while the "dead" who bury are those who are alive in body but dead in soul. There is work for those whose souls are dead to do, and there is work for those whose souls have been made alive to do. The Lord was saying that the living have their own work to do, and He was telling us where to put our priorities. He made clear that even the closest family cannot be put before the Lord's work.
5. Calming the Wind and the Storm on the Sea (Matthew 8:23-27)
(1) Jesus showed that He is "the One who rules and governs nature by calming the wind and the storm on the sea."
This shows that He will give true peace to the soul (John 20:19, 21).
(2) Seeing the miracle of the calming of the wind and the storm, the disciples said of Jesus, "What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him? (Matthew 8:27)"
Through this event the disciples realized how weak their faith was, and they also came to know better who the Lord is. When one knows the Lord rightly, right faith arises and the storm of the heart is calmed.
6. Making Whole the Demon-Possessed Men Among the Tombs (Matthew 8:28-34)
(1) Jesus cast out the demons from the men who were possessed and lived among the tombs, and healed them completely.
This shows that "He will save those held captive under the power of the devil and transform them into new people" (Hebrews 2:14-15). Only when a person is saved does he come to his right mind and become a new person.
(2) The demons asked Jesus to send them into a herd of pigs.
From this we can learn that even demons are under the authority of Jesus, and that demons like what is unclean.
(3) The whole town begged Jesus to leave their region.
They had no interest in who Jesus was or what He had done. Their interest was only in fleshly things. Because the herd of pigs perished, they suffered great loss in material terms. Because of that loss, they pleaded with the Lord to leave their region.

[Chapter 9] Miracles Performed by the Power of Jesus 2
1. Healing a Paralytic (Matthew 9:1-8)
(1) Jesus healed the paralytic when He saw "the faith of the people (when he saw their faith)" who brought him lying on a bed (Matthew 9:1-2).
We can see that when a person is saved, that person's faith is important, but the faith of those who lead him is also important.
(2) Jesus said to the paralytic, "Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven (Matthew 9:2)."
He said this to make known that Jesus is One who has authority to forgive sins. Because Jesus is God, He has the authority to forgive our sins (Luke 1:77, Acts 10:43, 13:38, Ephesians 1:7, Colossians 1:14).
Of the two sayings, "Your sins are forgiven" and "Rise and walk," the more difficult is "forgiving sins." When Jesus healed the sick, He healed them by a word. But to forgive sins, He had to die, receiving the punishment for sin in their place. Therefore forgiving sins is a far more difficult saying than healing paralysis. Jesus healed the paralytic to testify that He has authority to forgive sins.
(3) He forgave the paralytic's sins and then healed his paralysis.
It is true that the paralytic suffered from paralysis, but even so, what he needed most was first to receive forgiveness of sins. By doing first what was most needed and important, Jesus taught what a sinner needs most urgently. Even now, for everyone who is in Adam, the most important and first thing to be resolved is to receive forgiveness of sins through Jesus and obtain eternal life.
2. The Calling of Matthew the Tax Collector, and Jesus, Who Came to Call and Save Sinners (Matthew 9:9-13)
(1) Jesus called Matthew, who had the most condemned occupation of his day, that of "tax collector," and sat and ate at Matthew's house, thereby showing in person that He is the One who came to call and save sinners, not the righteous.
(2) People must learn what Jesus meant when He said, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice."
Before a person does anything for God, he must first receive God's mercy and be saved. Jesus came to call sinners and save them.
3. Jesus, Who Brought Something New (Matthew 9:14-17)
The disciples of John came to Jesus and asked why, while they and the Pharisees fast, His disciples do not fast. Jesus heard this and answered with three examples. First, He said that the wedding guests need not mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them, but when the bridegroom is taken away from them, they will fast. This means that one should not fast at just any time, but that there is a time to fast. That is, He was telling when one should fast. Second, no one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. Third, no one puts new wine into old wineskins; new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. Through the first example Jesus made clear the purpose for which He came into the world. Jesus came into the world as the bridegroom to seek the bride (2 Corinthians 11:2). Through the second and third examples He makes clear that Jesus is One who brought something new. Jesus came to give us what concerns "the new covenant and new life."
4. Healing the Woman with a Flow of Blood and Raising the Dead Daughter of the Synagogue Ruler (Matthew 9:18-26)
(1) The woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years, believing that she would be healed if she only touched Jesus' garment, was healed the moment she touched His garment. This shows that the moment one repents and believes in the gospel Jesus completed, he is saved.
(2) He entered the house of the synagogue ruler and raised the ruler's dead daughter. This shows that He will make dead souls alive (Isaiah 55:3, Ephesians 2:1).
5. Healing the Blind and the Mute (Matthew 9:27-34)
(1) Two blind men cried out to Jesus, "Have mercy on us, Son of David."
Jesus confirmed the faith of the two blind men and healed them. This shows that when a person is saved, the eyes of the soul are opened and he will see spiritual things.
(2) The healing of the demon-possessed mute man shows that when a person is saved, his mouth is opened and he will speak rightly in faith.
6. Jesus' Evangelistic Ministry and the Request to Send Out Laborers for the Harvest (Matthew 9:35-38)
(1) Jesus went about all the cities and villages, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing the sick.
Through this the Lord showed an example of faithfulness. All who are saved must be faithful, imitating the Lord. We must evangelize everyone around us whom we know.
(2) Jesus ministered faithfully because He had compassion on the people who were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
The reason we must evangelize faithfully is that hell exists. We must have compassion on those who are going to hell.
(3) He tells us to urgently ask God, the Lord of the harvest of souls, for laborers for the harvest.
We must ask God that more laborers may be raised up. We must pray, "Send out laborers into the harvest!"

[Chapter 10] The Appointment and Sending Out of the Twelve Disciples
Matthew chapter 10 records how Jesus set the twelve disciples apart, and, sending them out two by two, gave them the instructions that workers need in the course of evangelism.
1. "He called ... gave them authority to heal ... He sent them out (Matthew 10:1, 5)."
Here we can see the order. Jesus called the workers, gave them the power to deal with problems, and sent them out. Even now the Lord calls workers, gives them power, and sends them out.
2. A Guide to Evangelism
(1) "Go, and as you go (Matthew 10:6-7)"
We can see that He commanded active evangelism (Matthew 28:19).
(2) Go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matthew 10:5-6)
When He sent out the disciples, Jesus had not yet died on the cross, so the message could not yet be carried to the Gentiles. But the Jews had been promised the Messiah through the Old Testament and bore the responsibility to receive the Messiah.
Even now, when a person is saved, it is fitting to evangelize first his close family and relatives.
(3) You received without paying; give without pay (Matthew 10:8)
We received the Lord's grace freely. Therefore we too must share it freely with others.
(4) A worker must believe that the Lord will supply what he needs (Matthew 10:9-10).
(5) Find out who is worthy in it and stay there (Matthew 10:11)
The Lord's work is accomplished and expanded centered on households. For the gospel to be carried to any region, a dedicated household is needed first.
(6) Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16)
This calls to mind the wisdom of the serpent in Genesis 3, and the dove that Noah sent out of the ark in Genesis 8 to see whether the waters had subsided, which found no place to rest and returned to the ark. Wisdom and purity are absolutely necessary for evangelism.
(7) Beware of men (Matthew 10:17)
We must be careful about people. Unexpected difficulties can arise because of people. The apostle Paul also told us to pray, "that we may be delivered from wicked and evil men (2 Thessalonians 3:2)."
(8) Because the Lord was persecuted, one must be prepared for persecution (Matthew 10:24-25).
(9) In evangelism, one must act boldly without fear (Matthew 10:26-28).
(10) By drawing near to the Lord, one proclaims what one has received from the Lord (Matthew 10:27).
(11) One must have faith that acknowledges the sovereignty of God (Matthew 10:29-31).
(12) One must not deny the Lord because of difficulties (Matthew 10:32-33).
(13) Although it is the gospel of peace, one must be prepared for discord in the household because of the gospel (Matthew 10:34-36).
(14) Put the Lord first in the order of priority of everything (Matthew 10:37-38)
(15) In following the Lord, one must even count one's life in the budget (Matthew 10:39).
(16) The Lord's worker is an envoy in the Lord's place (Matthew 10:40-41).
(17) The Lord's worker will surely have a reward (Matthew 10:42).

[Chapter 11] Rejection of Jesus 1
Matthew chapters 11 and 12 record the Lord's ministry and teaching during the so-called second Galilean ministry, at a point about a year and a half after Jesus began His public ministry. The record of these two chapters shows that from this time the rejection of Jesus by the Jewish leaders gradually began and intensified.
1. John the Baptist's Question to Jesus and Jesus' Answer (Matthew 11:1-6)
(1) In prison John heard of the works of Christ and sent his disciples to Jesus to ask, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?"
This was probably for two reasons. First, it was for John's own salvation. Although he had baptized Jesus and had testified that He is "the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," as for the matter of his own salvation, he too had to believe in Jesus as the Messiah (Christ) of the Old Testament. So he wanted to hear the answer directly from Jesus. Second, it was probably for the sake of his disciples who followed him. After John the Baptist had testified to Jesus, they were no longer to follow John the Baptist but to follow Jesus. So his sending his disciples to Jesus was probably so that they would believe in Jesus by hearing from Jesus Himself.
(2) Jesus said to John's disciples, "Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them."
At that time the Jews thought that the Messiah would come as a strong king who would conquer Rome. But Jesus told them to make clear to John that He had come not as a judge but as a Savior (John 3:17).
(3) Jesus said, "And blessed is the one who is not offended by me."
Jesus came in an utterly humble form and died hanging on a cross. Therefore, not one of the rulers of that time recognized that Jesus was the Savior who had come to save souls (1 Corinthians 2:8).
2. Jesus' Words About John the Baptist (Matthew 11:7-15)
(1) Jesus said, "Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist" (Matthew 10:9-11). "Woman" refers to Israel.
He was saying that John was the greatest among the many prophets who arose in Israel's history. The task of the prophets of the Old Testament era was to testify of the Messiah. Many prophets testified of Jesus, but John the Baptist testified of Jesus from the closest vantage point. Just as the moon does not look large because it is large but because it is nearest to the earth, John the Baptist enjoyed the joy of testifying to Jesus from the closest vantage point (John 10:41).
(2) What does the saying, "Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he," mean?
Because of this saying, some people say that John did not enter the kingdom of heaven. But that is not what it means. When John administered the baptism of repentance in the land of Israel, a tremendous number of people were baptized, as in the words, "Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him (Matthew 3:5-6)." John the Baptist's popularity at that time was tremendous. The words above mean that the glory John the Baptist received in this world is less than the glory of the very least person who enters the kingdom of heaven.
(3) The statement that the kingdom of heaven suffers violence is because it is given to those who are unqualified.
It is because it is given only by faith. If one repents and believes, it becomes his own. If one takes it, it becomes his own.
(4) John the Baptist is the last prophet among the many prophets of the Old Testament era who testified of Christ.
(5) John the Baptist is the Elijah who was prophesied in the Old Testament book of Malachi to come (Malachi 4:5-6).
3. Rebuke for Not Repenting Even at the Ministry of John the Baptist and of Jesus (Matthew 11:16-19)
Seeing that people did not repent even at the ministry of John the Baptist and at His own ministry, Jesus spoke of "this generation" in a parable. He said that people are like children sitting in the marketplace: when they play the flute for them, they do not dance, and when they wail, they do not beat their breasts.
John the Baptist cried out for repentance, but people did not grieve over their sins or repent. Even though Jesus came bringing the good news of the gospel, people did not know how to rejoice. Instead, when John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking, they said, "He has a demon," and when Jesus came eating and drinking, they accused Him, saying, "a friend of tax collectors and sinners."
He said, "Wisdom is justified by her deeds." Wisdom refers to Jesus Himself. The "deeds" are translated "children" in the marginal note. That is, Jesus was saying that through the lives of the children saved through His gospel, it will be clearly testified that Jesus is the Messiah, the Christ.
4. Rebuke for the Towns Where Most of His Mighty Works Were Done Not Repenting (Matthew 11:20-24)
(1) Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum were the towns where Jesus had done the most mighty works.
Yet they did not repent. So He said that at the judgment they would receive a greater judgment than Sodom and Gomorrah, Tyre and Sidon.
(2) From this we can learn that the more opportunities one is given to receive the gospel, the greater the judgment if one does not accept it.
5. Jesus' Invitation to Give True Rest (Matthew 11:25-30)
(1) It is God's will that the grace of salvation given through Jesus be hidden from those who consider themselves wise and understanding and be revealed to little children.
(2) A person who does not know Jesus does not know the Father either.
(3) The words, "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest," are an invitation to people burdened with sin to the place of salvation.
True rest of the soul is given to the person who has been relieved of the burden of sin and saved. These words speak of "rest of the soul."
(4) The words, "and you will find rest for your souls," speak of the "rest of the heart" given to a saved person.
For rest of the heart, one must take the yoke of the gentle and lowly Lord and follow the Lord. The Lord's yoke is easy and light because the Lord bears it together with us.
(5) The Lord takes off the burden of sin that we cannot bear, and has us take up the Lord's gentle and lowly yoke that we can bear. That is, He takes off the heavy burden and has us follow bearing the light burden.

[Chapter 12] Rejection of Jesus 2
1. Two Disputes About the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1-13)
Recorded are the dispute over the incident in which, as they were going through the grainfields on the Sabbath, the disciples were hungry and plucked heads of grain and ate them, and the dispute over the incident in which He healed a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath.
(1) The Pharisees, seeing them pluck and eat heads of grain on the Sabbath, condemned them as having sinned, but Jesus says that the disciples are guiltless.
"And if you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the guiltless (Matthew 12:7)."
When David was hungry, he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which no one but the priests could eat (1 Samuel 21:1-6). The priest at that time gave the bread of the Presence to David and those with him because he had mercy. God did not treat it as sin either. Why did the Pharisees condemn Jesus' disciples, who were without sin? Because they had no heart of mercy.
(2) In the Old Testament, the priests in the temple could break the Sabbath and be guiltless (Numbers 28:9).
The temple is a shadow of Jesus. Jesus is One greater than the temple. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath. Now a person who has been saved and has come into Jesus is a person in whom the rest of the soul has been accomplished, and he never breaks the Sabbath. But a person who has not been saved may say that he keeps the Sabbath, yet he is breaking God's rest. True rest is accomplished when one comes into Jesus.
(3) We see the hypocrisy of the Jews, who know that if a sheep falls into a pit on the Sabbath it is natural to lift it out, yet say that healing a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath is not permitted.
They had no heart of mercy at all to have compassion on a man with a withered hand. Jesus said to them, "Of how much more value is a man than a sheep!" and healed that man.
(4) Luke 6:6 says it was a man whose right hand was withered.
The right hand is the side of righteousness, the side of God. A person in Adam was like one whose right hand is withered: his left hand is sound and he does all the work of the world, but toward God he was of no use at all. By healing the right hand, Jesus made it a hand that is useful toward God. When a person is saved, his hand becomes a hand of service for the glory of God. It becomes a useful hand.
2. The Pharisees' Plot to Kill Jesus, and Jesus' Avoiding Extreme Conflict with Them (Matthew 12:14-21)
We see that the tension between Jesus, who proclaims the gospel of the kingdom of God, and the Pharisees, who were steeped in religious formality, was steadily mounting. But Jesus, knowing that the time had not yet come, withdrew from that place rather than provoke a state of extreme conflict and confrontation. This conduct of Jesus was the fulfillment of what had already been prophesied in the Old Testament. Jesus was never shaken by the persecution of His adversaries, but humbly carried out His ministry. It had been prophesied that in the end, by completing the gospel, He would cause the gospel to be carried to the Gentiles also, and those prophecies were being fulfilled one by one.
3. The Accusation That Jesus Is Beelzebul, and the Sin of Blaspheming the Holy Spirit (Matthew 12:22-37)
Because Jesus healed a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute, the Pharisees accused Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul. Jesus, knowing their thoughts, answered in several ways.
(1) Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste; if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself, so how will his kingdom stand?
(2) The sons of the Pharisees also cast out demons; if Jesus casts out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? He said that they would be their judges.
(3) Jesus' casting out of demons is done by the Spirit of God, and if it is by the Spirit, the kingdom of God has come to be within it.
This is because, in order to enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, one must first bind the strong man, and only then can he plunder his house. Here the strong man is the devil, and the stronger One who bound the strong man is the Lord.
(4) The Pharisees who accused Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul were those who opposed Jesus and scattered.
(5) The Pharisees' act was the sin of blaspheming the Holy Spirit.
Because Jesus cast out demons by the Holy Spirit, it was the work of the Holy Spirit. Yet to attribute the work of the Holy Spirit to the work of the devil is the sin of blaspheming the Holy Spirit. Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, but the sin of blaspheming the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven. Then what is the sin of blaspheming the Holy Spirit? Not accepting the gospel is the sin of blaspheming the Holy Spirit. Attributing the work of the Holy Spirit to the work of the devil is also the sin of blaspheming the Holy Spirit.
(6) That the Pharisees, seeing the work of the Holy Spirit, attributed it to the work of the devil is because they were a bad tree, and so bad fruit came out.
That is, because they had never received the life of God within them, they spoke evil words out of the evil stored up in their hearts. He is saying that the result will surely be condemnation.
4. The Religious Leaders Who Seek a Sign from Heaven, and Jesus, Who Offers the Sign of the Prophet Jonah (Matthew 12:38-45)
(1) The Jewish religious leaders asked Jesus for a sign.
Jesus called those who seek a sign evil and adulterous. Why is seeking a sign an evil and adulterous thing? In fact, in the history of Israel, God had already made known that He lives through signs; to those who knew that He lives He gave His word through the prophets and promised the Christ, and, as promised, the Christ has come. Yet to seek a sign again is to propose starting that whole process over again, and it is evil. And it is adulterous in that it means being ready to follow unconditionally anything that shows a sign.
(2) The most certain proof that Jesus is the Christ is the sign of Jonah.
Just as the people of Nineveh were able to believe because Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights, the death and resurrection of Jesus is the most certain proof that can be believed (Acts 17:30-31).
(3) He said that at the judgment the people of Nineveh and the queen of the South will be witnesses.
This is because the people of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and the queen of the South came to hear the wisdom of Solomon; to hear the words of Jesus, who is greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon, and yet not repent, deserves condemnation.
(4) Jesus likened this evil generation to the case in which an unclean spirit goes out and the house is left empty, swept, and put in order, but the spirit returns with seven other spirits more evil than itself, and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.
An empty house is not a case of being saved. A house in which the Lord has come in as master is a house that is saved.
5. New Family Relationships in Jesus (Matthew 12:46-50)
As the conflict of rejecting Jesus was mounting, Jesus' mother and brothers were standing outside, wishing to speak to Him. One person said to Jesus, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside." Jesus heard this and said, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" and "Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother." This is saying that a new spiritual family relationship will be formed in Jesus Christ. When a person is saved, he becomes a brother or sister who has God as one Father.

[Chapter 13] Seven Parables About the Kingdom of Heaven
Matthew chapter 13 records seven parables: "the parable of the sower, the parable of the wheat and the weeds, the parable of the mustard seed, the parable of the leaven, the parable of the treasure hidden in the field, the parable of the merchant seeking fine pearls, and the parable of the net that gathers fish of every kind."
1. The Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13:1-23)
The seed is the word of God and the field is the human heart, and four kinds of soil appear: the wayside, the rocky ground, the thorny ground, and the good soil. Of these, only the good soil is the case of being saved. Matthew 13:14-15 says that the people of Israel had become hard of heart and did not understand. Matthew 13:23 says, "the one who hears the word and understands it." Only the good soil is the case of having understood. One who understands bears fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. The minimum is thirtyfold. If a person has heard the gospel and understood it, there is surely a life that bears fruit.
2. The Parable of the Wheat and the Weeds (Matthew 13:24-30)
He sowed good seed in his field, but an enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. The good seed are the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, that is, unbelievers. Among the sons of the kingdom, sons of the evil one are also mixed in. But at the end of the age, the saved are gathered into the barn of the kingdom of heaven, and the sons of the evil one are gathered and thrown into the fire of hell.
3. The Parable of the Mustard Seed and the Parable of the Leaven (Matthew 13:31-33)
The parable of the mustard seed speaks of the work of life. No matter how small a mustard seed is, it has life. When a mustard seed is planted, it grows until the birds of the air can nest in it. The parable of the leaven speaks of the work of a false gospel. There is no life; there is only the work of a false gospel that puffs everything up.
4. The Parable of the Treasure Hidden in the Field (Matthew 13:44)
The field is the world. The treasure hidden in the field is the souls of people. As in the words that he sold all that he had and bought that field, God gave His only Son, His all, on the cross in order to buy our souls in the world at a price. And with that price He bought us.
5. The Parable of the Merchant Seeking Fine Pearls (Matthew 13:45-46)
The church is the merchant seeking fine pearls. A saved person sells all that he has and works to save the souls of others.
6. The Parable of the Net That Gathers Fish of Every Kind (Matthew 13:47-49)
Just as when a net is cast, good fish and bad fish are caught, we cast the net of the gospel into the world. When the gospel is preached, there are those who are saved, and there are also those who say they are saved but are not. At the end of the age the Lord will separate the evil from among the righteous. There may be people who were thought to be saved but are not.
7. The Scribe Who Has Become a Disciple of the Kingdom of Heaven (Matthew 13:51-53)
A scribe who has become a disciple of the kingdom of heaven is, unlike the scribes who are hypocritical religious leaders, a scribe who has become a disciple who will enter the kingdom of heaven. He understands the word, and when needed he will bring out of Scripture what is needed in due measure, and do the work of rescuing and building up souls.
8. What does it mean that Jesus spoke in parables and said nothing to them without a parable?
The answer is in Matthew 13:1. It does not mean that every word in the Bible is a parable; it means that everything He spoke "on that day" was spoken in parables. Therefore we must not be deceived by the falsehood that, because everything Jesus said is a parable, it must be interpreted as a parable.
9. The Rejection by the People of His Hometown, Nazareth (Matthew 13:54-58)
Jesus returned to His hometown, Nazareth, and taught in the synagogue. The people of Nazareth remembered only His fleshly appearance from the time He lived among them before He began His public ministry; they did not believe the fact that He had already revealed Himself as the Messiah through His public ministry, and they rejected Him. Therefore Jesus did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief. Where there is no faith, the work of God cannot appear either.

[Chapter 14] Continued Rejection and Jesus' Continuing Ministry 1
From Matthew 13:54 onward is recorded the content of the continued rejection of Jesus. Recorded in order are His rejection in His hometown of Nazareth, Herod's fear, the rejection by the scribes and Pharisees, and the rejection by the Pharisees and Sadducees.
Even amid such rejection, Jesus quietly carries out His ministry. Recorded are the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, the miracle of walking on water, the healing of the Canaanite woman's daughter, the miracle of the seven loaves and a few small fish, and so on.
Chapters 14 through 17 are events that took place when about two years had passed since Jesus began His public ministry and about one year remained until He suffered on the cross.

2. Herod's Fear of Jesus and the Martyrdom of John the Baptist (Matthew 14:1-12)
(1) Hearing the reports about Jesus, Herod said that John the Baptist, who had been killed, had risen, and was afraid.
Herod had fear in his heart, but he did not want to believe the fact that Jesus is the Messiah of the Old Testament.
(2) Herod knew John the Baptist to be a righteous and holy man and was inclined to protect him, and although he was greatly perplexed, he heard John gladly (Mark 6:20).
His heart changed after John rebuked Herod for taking his brother Philip's wife. He wanted to kill John for that rebuke, but because the people regarded John as a prophet, he feared the people and did not kill him. But on his birthday, when the daughter of Herodias danced and asked for the head of John the Baptist, he had him beheaded. In the end, Herod could not accept the rebuke of his wrongdoing, and he killed John the Baptist for the sake of his prestige and face.
3. The Miracle of the Five Loaves and Two Fish (Matthew 14:13-21)
(1) It shows that Jesus is the bread of life.
(2) With five loaves and two fish He fed five thousand and gathered twelve baskets. A child's lunch was a small thing that was offered up, and with it He displayed great power.
Through this He showed that through the small things we offer to the Lord, the Lord accomplishes great works.
(3) "He blessed and broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds." The disciples distributed to the crowds what they had received from the Lord.
Even now, we distribute what we have received from the Lord. If we have received nothing from the Lord, we have nothing to share.
(4) "They need not go away; you give them something to eat." The Lord has everything.
There is no need to send away those who come to the Lord to some other place. The Lord is One who is abundant. Everything a believer's faith needs is in the Lord.
4. Jesus and Peter Walking on the Water (Matthew 14:33)
(1) Jesus came walking on the water at night.
The water refers to the world. Jesus trod on the world. Although He came into the world, He is not one who belongs to the world but one who is set apart from the world. Peter also walked on the water. It shows that just as the Lord does not belong to the world, believers do not belong to the world (John 17:14).
(2) "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water."
When Peter saw Jesus coming on the water, he had a longing to be like the Lord. That is why he said this. A believer must have a longing to be like the Lord.
(3) "Seeing the wind, he began to sink."
When Peter looked at the Lord, he walked on the water, but when he looked at the wind, he began to sink into the water. If we, too, do not look at the Lord but look at the visible circumstances, we can sink into the world. Firm faith that looks to the Lord enables us to overcome the world (1 John 5:4).
(4) As the disciples went on in obedience to the Lord's word, they realized more that their faith was lacking and what kind of person the Lord is.

[Chapter 15] Continued Rejection and Jesus' Continuing Ministry 2
1. The Tradition of the Elders and the Commandment of God (Matthew 15:1-20)
(1) The Pharisees and scribes came from Jerusalem and made an issue of the fact that Jesus' disciples did not keep the tradition of the elders.
But Jesus rebuked the Jewish religious leaders who broke the commandment of God by the tradition of the elders.
The tradition of the elders was something added to and subtracted from the word of God. Because they learned the tradition of the elders rather than the commandment of God, their hearts drifted far from God, and they offered God vain worship rather than true worship. Vain worship means worship that God does not accept.
(2) Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.
(3) True cleanness is that when the heart (the inside) becomes clean, the outside, that is, one's conduct, also becomes clean.
2. The Healing of the Canaanite Woman's Daughter (Matthew 15:21-28)
(1) Jesus went to the Gentile region of Tyre and Sidon.
At that time a Canaanite woman came to Jesus. Jesus saw that the Canaanite woman asked humbly and earnestly, and also saw her faith, and healed her daughter.
(2) The Canaanite woman was commended, "Great is your faith."
3. The Miracle of the Seven Loaves and a Few Small Fish (Matthew 15:29-39)
(1) Jesus fed 4,000 with seven loaves and two fish, and gathered seven baskets.
(2) It shows that Jesus is the bread of life.

[Chapter 16] Continued Rejection and Jesus' Continuing Ministry 3
1. The Pharisees' Demand for a Sign from Heaven, and the Sign of the Prophet Jonah Offered by Jesus (Matthew 16:1-4)
(1) To the Pharisees and Sadducees who sought a sign from heaven, He rebuked them for being able to discern the appearance of earth and sky but not discerning the signs of the times.
That is, He rebuked them for not knowing what time it now was.
(2) The certain proof by which one can believe that Jesus is the Savior is the sign of the prophet Jonah, that is, the events of Jesus' death and resurrection.
The death and resurrection of Jesus are certain proof that Jesus is the Messiah.
2. Teaching to Beware of the Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 16:5-12)
(1) The disciples forgot the miracle of the five loaves and two fish and the miracle of the seven loaves and a few small fish, and worried because they had no bread.
Jesus rebuked the disciples for their little faith.
(2) The Sadducees believed only the Pentateuch of Moses. They did not believe in spirit, resurrection, or the world to come.
Believing in God, they sought only blessings of this present world. Believing Scripture only in part is leaven. Desiring only the blessings of the present world is leaven.
(3) The leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy, and the thinking that one can approach God by works.
Because they tried to approach God not by receiving the Lord's life but by keeping the law, it is leaven.
3. Peter's Confession of Faith and the Church (Matthew 16:13-20)
(1) When Jesus went to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He asked the disciples, "Who do people say that I am?"
Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets. Jesus asked, "But who do you say that I am?" What is most important is not other people's opinions, but how I know and believe.
(2) Simon Peter answered, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
Peter's answer was something God had made him understand through the Holy Spirit. Jesus is our Savior and Lord. Moreover, His identity is the Son of God, that is, God who has divinity.
(3) Jesus said, "On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it."
It does not mean that Peter is the rock. Jesus is the rock. The confession of faith that Peter made is the rock. Jesus died on the cross and rose again in order to become the rock foundation of the church. And the church built on that rock will not be overcome by the gates of Hades.
(4) The keys of the kingdom of heaven are entrusted to the church.
A lock has been placed on the words of Scripture. Unless one who has understood first unlocks it, others cannot understand.
4. Jesus' First Prediction of the Cross (Matthew 16:21-28)
(1) "From that time ... He began to teach"
Jesus began to teach the disciples about His death on the cross and His resurrection. This was the first prediction of the suffering.
(2) Peter, rebuking Jesus out of human feeling, received the rebuke, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me."
The devil who worked in Eve worked for a moment in Peter. Because Peter set his mind not on the things of God but on the things of man, the devil worked in him for a moment.
(3) On the way of following the Lord, one must follow after drawing up a full budget.
One must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow, counting even his life in the budget.

[Chapter 17] Continued Rejection and Jesus' Continuing Ministry 4
1. The Event on the Mount of Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13)
(1) Just as Jesus had foretold, "there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28)," six days later Jesus showed, as a preview, the scene of His return on the Mount of Transfiguration.
(2) Jesus appeared accompanied by Moses and Elijah.
Moses is the representative of the law and Elijah is the representative of the prophets. Moses is the representative of those who died and met the Lord, and Elijah is the representative of those who were taken up alive. When the Lord returns, those who died and met the Lord and those who were raptured alive will meet together.
(3) A voice came from heaven and said, "Listen to him."
We must listen only to the words of Jesus. Moses and Elijah were only people who testified of the Lord. We must listen to the words of Jesus.
2. Healing a Boy with Epilepsy Caused by a Demon (Matthew 17:14-21)
(1) Jesus rebuked "this faithless and twisted generation."
This statement includes the disciples, the people of the world, and the boy's father.
(2) He said that it could be healed by "prayer and fasting."
3. Jesus' Second Prediction of His Suffering (Matthew 17:22-23)
Jesus predicted for the second time that the Son of Man would be delivered into the hands of men and killed, and on the third day be raised. The disciples heard it and were grieved.
4. Paying the Temple Tax with the Shekel from the Fish's Mouth (Matthew 17:24-27)
(1) The kings of the earth collect customs and taxes not from their own sons but from others.
Sons do not pay the tax. Since Jesus, as the Son of God, is the Lord of the temple, there was no need for Him to pay the temple tax, but He paid it so that people would not misunderstand. He did so in order that it might not become a hindrance to His ministry.
We too, in preaching the gospel, must strive that our dealings in worldly matters not become a hindrance to the gospel.
(2) With the shekel from the fish's mouth, the temple tax was paid for Jesus and Peter.
Jesus is One who can command even the fish.
(3) The fish is a shadow of believers.
He is saying that dedication will come out of saved believers. Is the church's finance hard? Just evangelize more people.

[Chapter 18] Humility, and Sins Committed by Believers
Matthew chapter 18 records what results are obtained when one takes an attitude of humility, and what to do about sins that believers commit against the church and sins committed against an individual.
1. Teaching About Humility (Matthew 18:1-14)
(1) A person who humbles himself like a little child is saved and enters the kingdom of heaven.
(2) A person who humbles himself like a little child becomes great in the kingdom of heaven.
(3) Receiving a little child is receiving the Lord, and who can receive a little child? One who humbles himself can receive a little child.
(4) Woe to those who cause to stumble.
Then how can one avoid causing others to stumble? One who humbles others will not cause others to stumble.
(5) Who can avoid entering the eternal fiery lake? The humble.
(6) In order not to despise one of these little ones, one must humble himself.
A person who exalts himself comes to despise others.
(7) It is not God's will that one of these little ones should be lost.
We see the great love of God, which He shows even to the little ones.
2. Sins Believers Commit Against the Church (Matthew 18:15-20)
(1) "If your brother sins": here it speaks of sins that become a problem for the church.
An individual exhorts him, then two or three persons exhort him, and finally he is exhorted in the name of the church, and if he refuses to listen even to the church, he said to regard him as a Gentile and a tax collector.
(2) The Lord's authority has been given to the church.
This means that if the church decides according to God's will, God also will accept it.
3. Sins Believers Commit Against an Individual Believer (Matthew 18:21-35)
(1) Regarding sins that a believer commits against a believer, He said to forgive even seventy times seven.
It does not mean to forgive only 490 times, but to forgive without limit. This is because God is forgiving us without limit.
(2) If one who has been forgiven ten thousand talents cannot forgive one who owes a hundred denarii, it is not fitting.
We are those who have been forgiven ten thousand talents by the Lord. What fellow believers do wrong to us as individuals would amount to a hundred denarii.

[Chapter 19] Divorce and Celibacy, the Rich Young Man, Salvation and Glory
Matthew chapters 19 and 20 record the ministry and teaching that the Lord carried out in Judea and Perea and other places for about six months, after He had finished the Galilean ministry entirely and before He finally entered Jerusalem to suffer on the cross.
1. Jesus' Ministry in Judea (Matthew 19:1-2)
2. Divorce and Celibacy (Matthew 19:3-12)
(1) Hearing the Pharisees' testing question about divorce, Jesus quoted Genesis 1 and 2 and said that what God has joined together, man must not separate.
Jesus believed the events of Genesis 1 and 2 literally.
(2) That a certificate of divorce was given through Moses, making divorce lawful, was permitted because people are evil.
Even if told not to divorce, people would divorce anyway, so by giving a certificate of divorce and making it lawful, He established social order rightly.
(3) To live without marrying, one must be born so.
3. Jesus Lays Hands on the Little Children (Matthew 19:13-15)
Jesus warmly welcomed the little children who came to Him and laid His hands on them. He rebuked the disciples who scolded the children for coming.
4. The Rich Young Man Who Came to Jesus to Obtain Eternal Life (Matthew 19:16-22)
(1) The rich young man misunderstood that he could obtain eternal life by doing some good deed.
(2) To the rich young man who thought himself good, Jesus said that no one is good except God alone, so that he could know himself to be a sinner before God.
He also presented the law so that he could see himself as a sinner before the law. To make known to the rich young man, who said he had kept the whole law, that he had "covetousness," He told him to give his wealth to the poor and follow Him. But the rich young man, never knowing himself to the end, left Jesus' presence.
(3) The rich young man wanted to obtain eternal life, but he valued wealth more than eternal life. In the end, he gave up the way to obtain eternal life because of wealth.
5. Salvation (the Kingdom of Heaven) and Glory (Matthew 19:23-30)
(1) It is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. Those who are poor in heart are saved, and it is hard to become poor in heart.
(2) Being saved is a work that God accomplishes.
(3) Those who, having been saved, have left everything and followed the Lord will surely have a reward.

[Chapter 20] The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
Matthew chapter 20 records the parable of the laborers in the vineyard and the third prediction of the suffering. It also records the disciples' quarrel over places, and the healing of the two blind men at Jericho.
1. The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16)
