The owner of the vineyard agreed with the laborers to work in the vineyard for one denarius a day and sent them in. He also told those he found standing idle at the third hour to go into the vineyard, and at the sixth hour, the ninth hour, and even the eleventh hour, he sent laborers into the vineyard. When evening came and the laborers' wages were being settled, he had the steward pay the wages beginning with those who came last and ending with those who came first. Seeing those who came last receive one denarius, those who came first expected to receive more, but when they were each given only one denarius, they grumbled. The owner said, "Did you not agree with me for a denarius? It is my will to give to the last the same as to you. Do you begrudge my generosity? Take what belongs to you and go."
What those who came first received was a fair wage. But what those who came last received, one denarius, was clearly grace. Through Jesus Christ, God bestowed the grace of salvation on us, who had done no work. It is not the wage for our work. It is grace alone.
2. Jesus' Third Prediction of the Suffering (Matthew 20:17-19)
As Jesus was about to go up to Jerusalem, He took the twelve disciples aside and predicted for the third time that He Himself would die on the cross and rise on the third day.
3. The Twelve Disciples' Struggle to Take the High Places (Matthew 20:20-28)
(1) James and John, through their mother, lobbied Jesus to let them sit at His right and left when He went up to Jerusalem and became king.
The other ten disciples heard and were indignant, but their hearts were probably not very different.
(2) When James and John asked to sit at His right and left, Jesus asked whether they could drink the cup that He drinks.
The two said they could. Jesus said that they would indeed drink it. As a result of what they asked, James was the first to be martyred, and John lived the longest and preached the gospel. They drank the cup of suffering as a result of what they asked.
(3) He said that in the world the great are those who rule, but in the Lord the great are those who serve.
The person who lives a life of service on this earth will be great above. This is because Jesus came to serve and lived a life of service.
4. Healing the Two Blind Men at Jericho (Matthew 20:29-34)
(1) The two blind men heard that Jesus was passing by and cried out, "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us!"
Though those around them told them to be quiet, they cried out all the more loudly. From this we can see how earnest their hearts and how certain their faith were.
(2) After being healed, they followed the Lord. A person who has received grace from the Lord follows the Lord.

[Chapter 21] Jesus' Entry into Jerusalem
Matthew chapters 21 through 27 record the events of Passion Week, from Jesus' entry into Jerusalem on the colt of a donkey as the King of humility and the King of peace, for the final accomplishment of the work of redemption, until His suffering on the cross.
1. Jesus' Entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:1-11)
(1) Jesus' entry into Jerusalem was the event in which He proclaimed that He is King.
(2) Entering on the colt of a donkey was entering as the King of humility and the King of peace.
(3) Jesus' entry into Jerusalem was the fulfillment of prophecy in the Old Testament.
2. The Cleansing of the Temple (Matthew 21:12-17)
(1) Jesus cleansed the Jerusalem temple, the house of prayer for all peoples.
Our body is the temple in which the Holy Spirit dwells. We must keep it clean and set apart. The church is the temple in which the Holy Spirit works. We must not defile the church.
(2) Because Jesus is the King of humility, when He entered, the children came out and cried, "Hosanna! Blessed is he."
Jesus made provision so that the children could come near. But the Jewish religious leaders, being proud in heart, disliked the sound of the children's praise.
3. The Cursing of the Fruitless Fig Tree, Which Withered (Matthew 21:18-22)
By cursing the fruitless fig tree so that it withered, Jesus showed in advance that the Jews of that time, who seemed outwardly to serve God well but had no heart of love for God and rejected Christ, would be cursed.
As for His mentioning faith as the reason the fig tree withered, this was not in answer to a question about the lesson of the fig tree's withering; because they asked how it had withered when He cursed it, He answered that it was faith.
4. The Question About Jesus' Authority (Matthew 21:23-32)
(1) While Jesus was teaching in the temple, the chief priests and elders asked by what authority He taught.
Jesus said that if they answered the question He asked, He would answer too, and asked whether the authority of John the Baptist came from heaven or from man. The Jewish religious leaders reasoned that if they said "from heaven," He would ask why they did not believe him, and if they said "from man," the people regarded John as a prophet, so, fearing the people, they said they did not know. Jesus also said, "Neither will I tell you." This was not Jesus' evading an answer. It is because if one does not accept John the Baptist, one cannot accept Jesus either.
(2) The saying that tax collectors and prostitutes enter the kingdom of God before the religious leaders means that it is easy for tax collectors and prostitutes to realize that they are sinners. He told them to repent and believe the gospel.
5. The Parable of the Landowner and the Tenants (Matthew 21:33-46)
(1) The owner of the vineyard leased the vineyard to tenants and went to a far country; when the season of fruit drew near, he sent servants to receive the fruit, and they killed one and stoned another.
He sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them the same as the first. "They will respect my son." He even sent his son, but they said, "This is the heir; let us kill him and have his inheritance." Then, when the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants? He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.
He said, "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you (Israel) and given to a people (the Gentiles) producing its fruits." That is, He was saying that the gospel would pass to the Gentiles.
(2) Jesus is the cornerstone; the Jews did not recognize Him and rejected Him, but Jesus became the cornerstone of the church.

Matthew chapter 22 records the parable of a king who gave a wedding feast; the question of the Pharisees and Herodians to Jesus about whether it is right to pay taxes to Caesar; the Sadducees' question about the resurrection; the question of an expert in the law about which commandment is great; and Jesus' question to the Pharisees, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?"

[Chapter 23] Woes Pronounced on the Pharisees and Scribes
Matthew chapter 23 records the proclamation of "woe" to the Pharisees and scribes, repeated as many as seven times.

[Chapter 24] The Olivet Discourse 1
Matthew chapters 24 and 25 are the discourse that Jesus gave on the Mount of Olives. He spoke of the signs of the end times, of His second coming, and of what will happen at His second coming. The parable of the ten virgins, the parable of the talents, and the parable of the sheep and the goats are recorded.

Matthew chapters 26 and 27 record Jesus' sharing the Passover meal with His disciples, the prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, His arrest, His suffering at the house of the high priest Caiaphas and in Pilate's court, and finally His death on the cross and burial in the tomb.

[Chapter 28] Jesus' Resurrection and the Great Commission
Matthew chapter 28 records Jesus' resurrection on the first day of the week and the Great Commission that the risen Jesus gave to His disciples on earth.

[Chapter 1] Preparation of the Servant and the Beginning of the Galilean Ministry
The Gospel of Mark begins as the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. It testifies that Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ through the Old Testament, the testimony of John the Baptist, God's direct testimony, and the works Jesus performs. After being baptized by John and tempted by Satan, Jesus began to preach the gospel in Galilee. And He called Peter and Andrew, James and John, to be the people who would preach the gospel.
(Mark 1:15) “The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!”

While healing a paralytic, Jesus showed that He has authority to forgive sins. He called Levi, ate with tax collectors and sinners, and said that He came to call not the righteous but sinners. Through the disputes about fasting and the Sabbath, Jesus revealed not a formal religion but a new age centered on Himself. In particular, He made clear that Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath.
(Mark 2:17) On hearing this, Jesus told them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

2:1-12 _ Healing a paralytic - salvation from sin that makes one powerless
2:13-17 _ Calling Levi and eating with sinners in his house
2:18-22 _ The dispute about fasting, and new wine and new wineskins
2:23-28 _ The disciples pluck heads of grain on the Sabbath, and Jesus, the Lord of the Sabbath

[Chapter 3] The Servant's Authority and the Appointing of the Disciples
By healing a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, Jesus showed that giving life to people is the meaning of the Sabbath. Afterward, He publicly appointed the twelve disciples, had them be with Him, and prepared them to preach the gospel. The work of the kingdom of God and the work of Satan, who hinders it, appear in contrast. Jesus said that those who do the will of God, rather than blood relations, are His family.
(Mark 3:14-15) He appointed twelve of them, whom He designated as apostles, to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons.

[Chapter 4] Disciples Who Receive the Word and Grow
Through the parable of the sower, Jesus taught the different responses of those who hear the word. Through the parable of the growing seed, He showed how the work of God grows. As He crossed the sea with the disciples, by calming the fierce storm He gave comfort to the disciples who were in suffering. Jesus, who rules the storm of nature, is the One who also rules the storm of human life and the soul.
(Mark 4:40) “Why are you so afraid?” He asked. “Do you still have no faith?”

4:1-20 _ The parable of the sower - various hearts that receive the word

By healing the man possessed by a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes, Jesus showed the helplessness of human beings under the power of Satan, the Lord's power, and His compassion for people. Through His dispute with the Pharisees and scribes, Jesus contrasted the commandment of God with the tradition, which is the commandment of men. By healing a man who was deaf and spoke with difficulty, He displayed His salvation from the helpless sin of being unable to hear and unable to speak.

[Chapter 1] Jesus, Who Became Flesh as the Word
The most important truth spoken in the whole Bible, Old Testament and New Testament alike, is that it aims to bear witness to one person, Jesus Christ. The Old Testament bore witness to the Christ who was to come, and the New Testament bore witness to the Christ who came to this earth just as the Old Testament had promised. In this way the purpose of the whole Bible is to bear witness consistently to Jesus Christ, and among its books the Gospel of John is the word that explains Jesus Christ most deeply and in the most detail.

[Chapter 2] Jesus, Who Changes
John 2 records the event in which Jesus made wine for a feast that had run out of wine. This first sign can be said to show what kind of work Jesus would do during the period of His public ministry. The miracle of the Lord making wine from water bears witness that the Lord is the one who changes our hearts and our lives.
When the wine ran out at the feast, that is, when the pleasures that people seek in this world have ended and people have realized for themselves how frustrating an existence they are, from that time the Lord begins to do something. The Lord said, "Fill the jars with water," and we can take this word to mean, "Fill our hearts with the word of God." When the Lord shows His power in the word that fills our hearts, that word changes our lives and becomes true joy and life for us (2 Timothy 3:15).

[Chapter 3] Jesus, Who Causes Us to Be Born Again
In John 3, when a man named Nicodemus, one of the Pharisees, came to Jesus and greeted Him, Jesus told him how one can enter the kingdom of God and how one can be saved, saying, "Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." And He said that being born again comes by believing in Jesus Christ.

[Chapter 4] Jesus, the Source of Living Water
Chapter 4 tells how Jesus brought the gospel to a dissolute, sinful, immoral woman of Samaria. Whether privately or publicly, Jesus always spoke the word to everyone He met and earnestly desired to save their souls. For those who have been saved as well, the most important thing to do while living on this earth is to pass on to others this truth, life, and hope that has been given to us. The gospel must be proclaimed to all people without distinction: the learned and the unlearned, the morally upright and the fallen, those who have a religion and those who have none.

[Chapter 5] Jesus, Who Gives True Rest
The sick people of every kind lying in the colonnades beside the Pool of Bethesda, whose name means "house of grace," show before God the condition of all the sinners in the world. Death came because humanity sinned against God, and at the same time bodily pain and disease came. Humans are born, live in suffering amid sin, die someday, are judged after that, and go to hell, where they suffer forever. The healing of the sick that Jesus performed when He came was a foreshadowing of how He would heal sinners.
The sick people of every kind beside the pool waiting for the water to be stirred represent sinners of every kind watching the word so that their souls may be healed. The human soul is healed by the word of Scripture. Just as the first one to plunge in when the water was stirred, after waiting beside the pool, was healed, so any sinner who plunges in when the work of the Holy Spirit appears and the grace of the Lord is testified to while studying the word of Scripture will obtain salvation. But when the water is not stirred, one cannot be healed even by plunging into the water. This shows that no matter how much one studies the word of Scripture, one cannot be saved unless the Holy Spirit works.

[Chapter 6] Jesus, the Bread of Life
Jesus went up on the mountain and sat down with His disciples, and He saw a great crowd coming to Him. In Matthew 9:36 we read that Jesus saw the crowds and had compassion on them because they were suffering and wandering like sheep without a shepherd. Jesus saw not only the people of Israel of that time but also all the crowds of the generations to come, and He saw us now. He saw the crowd suffering and wandering without a shepherd, the crowd that wants its eternal problem solved, the crowd that wants to be set free from its wretched condition, that pitiful crowd.

[Chapter 7] Jesus, the Water of Life
People have a thirst of the soul that cannot be resolved by anything physical. That thirst of the soul arises from the fact that people stand in the status of a condemned prisoner awaiting death, having received a spiritual death sentence from God. For a condemned prisoner in this world, being pardoned and walking out alive would be the greatest joy and satisfaction. In the same way, when humans who lie under sin, death, and judgment receive forgiveness of sins and obtain salvation, they are freed from all conflict of the soul, and true satisfaction and peace are established within the soul.
The true rest and joy given to humans through Jesus come into being only when a person understands the gospel through the work of the Holy Spirit. Jesus said that from the heart of the one who believes in Him rivers of living water would flow. This refers to the true satisfaction and peace that come when salvation is accomplished in a person's heart, and at the same time it means the power of abundant life (referring to the Holy Spirit) that the Lord continues to give afterward.

[Chapter 8] Jesus, Who Set Us Free from the Curse of the Law
Jesus spoke mostly in Jerusalem, but there is no record that He ever slept in Jerusalem. Within Jerusalem, with the palace of Herod and the swarms of false religious people, He could not rest in peace even for a moment. So Jesus did not rest in Jerusalem; when night came He went to the Mount of Olives, where He prayed in the cold dew and slept. And in the morning He came into the temple and taught the people. Then suddenly an incident occurred.

[Chapter 9] Jesus, the Light of Life
That the disciples asked specifically about the cause of the man's blindness in connection with sin reflected the common belief of the Jews of that time that when a person falls ill or meets with misfortune, it is because of sin. When Jews suffered some misfortune, they thought the cause was sin.
The purpose for which Jesus came into the world was to save human beings who are spiritually blind from birth in this way. Jesus came to rescue from the power of death and darkness those who are spiritually dead in Adam, sinners who will be destroyed forever, and people wandering in pitch darkness. God wished to reveal the works of God through Jesus to all people who are spiritually blind from birth. Therefore, Jesus' healing of this blind man's eyes and letting him see the light was a preview of how He would rescue people from the power of sin and death and lead them into the light of God.

[Chapter 10] Jesus, the Good Shepherd
"I am the gate for the sheep." (John 10:7)
I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture. (John 10:9)
Because Jesus is the gate for the sheep, a person can obtain salvation only by entering the fold through Jesus.
Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. But small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it. (Matthew 7:13-14)
The narrow gate refers to Jesus Himself. The Passover doorway marked with the blood of the lamb (Exodus 12:7) also symbolizes Jesus, and the door of the tabernacle and the gate of the temple are likewise shadows of Jesus becoming the gate.
"I am the good shepherd."
Just as a shepherd calls his sheep and leads them out, this shows that Jesus will call people's souls out, lead them, protect them, and feed them.
He led out His people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness. (Psalms 78:52)
After leading the people of Israel out of Egypt like sheep, God protected and guided them in the wilderness and brought them all the way into the land of Canaan.
This shows that in the distant future Jesus would become the shepherd and rescue us from the power of death and darkness and lead us. The thief comes only to steal and kill, but Jesus came so that the sheep might have life and have it more abundantly (John 10:10). The life of true faith is not a stereotyped religious life but a life lived in abundant life and power after receiving life.

[Chapter 11] Jesus, the Resurrection and the Life
The raising of Lazarus is an important event directly connected with the arrest and death of Jesus. With the raising of Lazarus, the miracles that Jesus performed during His public ministry came to an end.
Because of the miracle of raising Lazarus, a great uproar arose in Israel. The Jews who had seen with their own eyes Jesus raising the dead Lazarus spread the news, so people flocked to see Lazarus, the central figure of the event; and many who met him and confirmed the facts came to believe in Jesus.
As matters grew, the chief priests and the Pharisees were greatly alarmed, convened the Sanhedrin, and discussed how to deal with it. That the Sadducees, who were concerned only with politics, did so is one thing, but that even the Pharisees, who took a godly life as their goal in life, showed the same behavior proves how corrupt the Jewish religious leaders of that time were.
With the exception of a few, they had no regard for the will or glory of God; they showed such corruption that they went so far as to commit the greatest sin in human history, killing the Son of God; and they judged that if they left Jesus alive, even more people would follow Him, and in the end the Romans might mistake it for an independence movement and the nation might be destroyed, so they agreed that getting rid of Jesus was the best course.
The Roman government basically followed a tolerant policy toward the nations under its rule but never tolerated riots, so the Jewish leadership put forward precisely this point on the surface and made it a pretext for removing Jesus. Since they could find no injustice or lawbreaking in Jesus, they tried to replace it with the pretext of "for the sake of the nation."

[Chapter 12] Jesus, the King of Peace
Just before the Passover, Jesus entered Jerusalem, where His public ministry would reach its final journey. Far from riding a splendid horse such as a white horse, He entered Jerusalem riding a colt of a donkey, which no one would give a second look.
In ancient times the horse was used mainly for war, whereas the donkey is an animal that symbolizes peace and humility, and Jesus' entering on a donkey means that He entered Jerusalem as the "King of peace and tranquility." In connection with this event the prophet Zechariah prophesied,
"Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion... See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey." (Zechariah 9:9)
In this way Jesus came as the King of peace at His first coming. But at His second coming He will come as the Lord of judgment. At His first coming the Lord rode a donkey, but at His second coming He will come riding a white horse.
Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war. (Revelation 19:11).

[Chapter 13] Jesus, Who Cleanses Us
Among the twelve disciples whom Jesus loved to the end was Judas Iscariot, who was looking for an opportunity to sell Jesus. Jesus knew from the beginning that Judas was the one who would betray Him, yet He kept him among the twelve disciples. He even entrusted the money bag to him. In Judas' heart there was nothing but money, but Jesus loved such a Judas just as He loved the other disciples. When He distributed bread and wine to the disciples, He gave them to him also, and He explained to him also that before long, by dying on the cross, He would become the life of salvation for each person. So at the last supper Judas received and drank the wine that Jesus gave. Also, when Jesus washed the disciples' feet with His own hands, He washed the feet of Judas too, and later He even dipped the bread Himself and gave it to him.
Everything Jesus did for Judas was a sign of love for Judas. The love of the Lord is of a different dimension from human love. The Lord's love is perfect, holy, and unconditional, one-sided, and never changing.

[Chapter 14] Jesus, the Way, the Truth, and the Life
"I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me."
It meant, 'I will open the way to God, and after I go ahead on that way, you will follow after Me and come to the Father.' The way for people to go to God had been completely blocked because of sin. But by dying on the cross, Jesus opened that way that had been blocked before all people.
Before every person there are "two ways." There is the way of the righteous, the way that saved people take, the way to God; but there is also the way of the wicked, the way that people who do not know God take, the way to destruction.
"I set before you the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8).
There is a way of life and a way of death. The way of life is the way Jesus went, the way Jesus has prepared for us. Those who believe in Jesus have become able to go to God through "the way that is Jesus."
① The way of receiving forgiveness of sins
② The way of being declared righteous
③ The way of being set free from wrath and judgment
④ The way from destruction to eternal life
⑤ The way from the earth to eternity
⑥ The way of fellowship with God
⑦ The way for sinners to go to the glorious God
⑧ The way for sinners to become children of God
⑨ The way from hell to heaven
⑩ The way to go freely, without any merit

[Chapter 15] Jesus, the True Vine
John 15 is the passage that best explains the relationship between the Lord and Christians. Here the Lord said that He is the true vine, that Christians are the branches attached to the Lord, connected to that life, and that God the Father is the farmer who tends the vineyard.
In that day: “Sing about a fruitful vineyard. I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it; (Isaiah 27:2-3).
The vineyard that God Himself tends is the people of Israel, the chosen people selected by God.
"For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight" (Isaiah 5:1-2, 7).
God planted Jesus, the true vine, as the vine and made born-again believers its branches, thereby cultivating a new vine in which Christ and the saved believers are united as one. The one and only vineyard that God tends is the Lord's church, in which the saved believers are united.
A branch of the vine bears fruit by itself if it stays attached to the vine. Even without any special effort of its own, even without anyone helping from the side, a branch bears fruit on its own simply by staying attached to the vine. For that reason a branch of the vine has value for existence only while it is attached to the vine.
Just as no fruit can form on a branch that has withered for lack of nourishment, a person whose heart has dried up apart from the Lord can do nothing at all for God. The fruit of the vine forms when the sap rises from the roots of the tree and is supplied sufficiently to the branches, and the fruit forms on the branches as a result.
When we too are sufficiently supplied with grace and life from the Lord, and spiritual grace overflows within us, that fullness of the Lord's life is borne as the fruit of faith. A saved person, being guided by the Holy Spirit in the Lord, must bear fruit for God and fitting for God even while living in this world. That is possible only when one is in the Lord. The vine and the branches are inseparable and stand in a relationship of absolute mutual dependence. For a branch to be attached to the vine means to depend entirely on the Lord.

[Chapter 16] Jesus, Who Gives Victory
Jesus said many things to the disciples in advance in order to set them free from doubt, anxiety, worry, and fear, and to give them the Lord's true peace.
“Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well. (John 14:1).
The Lord knew the disciples' hearts, filled with anxiety and worry, and comforted them by telling them in advance what would happen to them so that they could enjoy the Lord's peace, but the Lord's peace had not yet been established in the disciples' hearts. This was because until then they did not yet have firm faith in Jesus.
Only after Jesus died and rose again and the Holy Spirit came into the hearts of the disciples would the true peace of which Jesus spoke be established within them. When we realize the grace of God and are saved by faith, and at the same time the Holy Spirit comes into us, the Lord's peace is established in our hearts.
While He lived in the world Jesus suffered a great deal. The sufferings, hardships, and pains that Jesus bore in the world were all tribulation. Jesus Himself endured tribulation in the world in that way, but He overcame all that tribulation Himself. To people He may have seemed to have failed in this way, but on the cross He said, "It is finished." The saying "It is finished" means that He had fully accomplished the purpose for which He came into the world, that is, the plan and will of God. It was a song of triumph that Jesus Himself had won the supreme victory. Jesus was the true victor.
"In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!" As this word says, the outcome of the war has already been decided. The Lord has won, and the devil has been defeated. Therefore the life of faith is taking part in the complete victory that the Lord has already won.

[Chapter 17] Jesus, Who Offers the Prayer of Intercession
The "hour" here refers to the time that God had appointed, and it means that the time for Jesus to die on the cross had come. Jesus, knowing that the time was near for the many words written in Scripture about Himself to be fulfilled, prayed for the last time to God the Father for that purpose. On the night before His death Jesus prayed about many things, and if their content is summarized briefly, it can be condensed into the words, "Glorify Your Son, that the Son may glorify You."
From His birth to His death, all the time and every course of Jesus' life consistently exalted the name of God and glorified God.

[Chapter 18] Jesus, Who Suffered
The garden on the other side of the Kidron Valley refers to the Garden of Gethsemane. The Garden of Gethsemane is a small garden on the west side of the Mount of Olives, and the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke record the scene of Jesus praying in the Garden of Gethsemane on the night before His death.
By day Jesus mostly taught people the word of God in and around the temple in Jerusalem, and at night He went into the Mount of Olives, where He rested and slept. As the saying goes, "Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head" (Matthew 8:20), while Jesus was in the world He had no house or dwelling where He could rest in comfort. The Mount of Olives was Jesus' only place of rest.

[Chapter 19] Jesus, Who Was Humiliated
The disgrace, pain, and punishment that Jesus received were exactly what each one of us should have received. They were the shame and punishment that we should have received before God because of the sins we committed with our mouths, hands, feet, hearts, and heads. But Jesus came to this earth to bear in our place the punishment that we ought to have borne, and because only by doing so could we be set free from the power of sin, death, and judgment, He accepted all that shame and pain with His whole body.
Jesus' wearing the crown of thorns on His head means that He wore on His head the curse of God that came because of human sin. Thorns and thistles came into being when humans sinned and were cursed by God.
Putting the "scarlet robe" on Jesus means that He bore our sins in our place. As the word says, "Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool" (Isaiah 1:18), sin is "like scarlet, like crimson."

[Chapter 20] The Risen Jesus
The resurrection of Jesus is the surest proof that makes us believe that, as God promised in the Old Testament, Jesus came to this earth as the Messiah and saved us. Jesus rose on the first day of the week. The first day of the week on which the Lord rose can be said to signify the starting point of the new life that Christians enter after being saved. Just as the Lord rested after accomplishing everything and then rose on the first day of the week, so a person is saved by the Lord's cross, first rests in the Lord, and then begins a new life of following the Lord according to the Holy Spirit.

[Chapter 21] Jesus, Who Brings Us into Fellowship
For three and a half years Peter learned from Jesus and followed Him with zeal in his own way, but he could not follow Jesus to the end. Yet after He rose, Jesus spoke to Peter with special love. Peter certainly had weaknesses and made many mistakes, but Jesus loved such a Peter and had compassion on him. The Lord regards our good points as even more precious, and He has compassion on our weaknesses and loves us.
Peter had seen the risen Jesus, but without yet having the qualifications of a fisher of men, he took up again the nets he had put down three years earlier in order to catch fish, and went out to sea. But just as on that day three and a half years before, this time too Peter caught not a single fish. This was so that the Lord might make Peter realize that he could do nothing by his own effort and strength alone. He made him understand that the work of God is accomplished only by the word and power of the Lord, not by human will and strength.

[Chapter 1] The Promise of the Coming of the Holy Spirit and the Ascension of Jesus
In this first chapter of Acts, the author Luke, rather than writing a full-scale introduction as in other completely independent books, briefly states only that the author of Acts is Luke himself, just as in the case of the Gospel of Luke.
After that, he describes in greater detail, centering on the Lord's promise of the coming of the Holy Spirit, the account of the Lord's resurrection and ascension that was briefly outlined at the end of the Gospel of Luke (verses 3-11). Then he briefly reports the transitional situation of roughly ten days from the Lord's ascension until the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, and the greatest event of that period, the election of a new apostle, Matthias, to fill the place among the twelve apostles left vacant by the death of Judas Iscariot (verses 12-26).

[Chapter 2] The Coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, the Birth and Growth of the Early Church, and the Election of the New Apostle Matthias
To the crowds who mocked the event of the coming of the Holy Spirit and the speaking in the languages of all nations that appeared as an outward phenomenon of that coming, Peter, through a sermon, expounds the work of the Holy Spirit and the redemption of Jesus Christ.
Through the work of the Holy Spirit's coming at Pentecost and the apostles' proclamation of the gospel, the number of believers increases and forms a kind of community, which can be called the prototype of the church today. This text introduces the life of this early Jerusalem church community and teaches the typical life of faith of an exemplary church.

[Chapter 3] The Healing of the Lame Man and Peter's Sermon at Solomon's Colonnade
This chapter shows concretely how, after the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, the work of the Holy Spirit began to take place in earnest through the disciples of Jesus. In particular, Peter and John, empowered by the Holy Spirit, raise up the lame man who was begging at the Beautiful Gate of the temple.
It is the sermon that Peter gave to the crowd astonished at the miracle of healing the lame man, and it is the scene of his second sermon, following the sermon he gave immediately after the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. This second sermon of Peter is similar in content and structure to the first sermon he gave after the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. That is, citing the Old Testament, he proclaims that Jesus Christ is the Savior and urges the people to receive Him through repentance.

[Chapter 4] The Arrest of Peter and John and Peter's Defense Before the Sanhedrin
Peter's first sermon led to the repentance of as many as three thousand people. But the sermon at Solomon's Colonnade, given after healing the lame man, was followed by persecution from Judaism. Just as the Jewish religious leaders had persecuted Jesus, they persecuted the apostles' proclamation of the gospel and put Peter and John in prison.
The apostles are interrogated before the Sanhedrin, and the Sanhedrin, having heard Peter's bold defense in this interrogation, can do nothing to the apostles and releases them.

[Chapter 5] The Sin of Ananias, the Apostles' Miraculous Release from Prison, and Gamaliel's Intervention
Ananias and Sapphira, out of greed for wealth, deceive God and the church and meet death. This event contrasts with Barnabas' donation of his property recorded in the last paragraph of the previous chapter, and by showing the negative side that lay behind the positive picture of the early church community, it teaches believers what the true form of a devoted life should be.
When the Sanhedrin leaders put the apostles in prison again to stop the spread of the gospel, the Lord miraculously rescues them and has them preach the gospel again, and when the members of the Sanhedrin, enraged at hearing such proclamation by Peter, try to kill the apostles, Gamaliel, a Pharisee and teacher of the law, intervenes.
The reason Gamaliel defended the apostles was his character and moral standing, which led him to handle this matter fairly and on the level of common sense, since the apostles had not seriously broken the law (verses 38, 39). But the most decisive reason Gamaliel came to defend the apostles is that the grace of God, who works all things together for good (Romans 8:28), was at work.

[Chapter 6] The Appointment of the First Seven Deacons and the Arrest of Stephen
Through the process by which church organization is formed for the first time, it shows that the duties of church office-bearers lie in evangelism and the life of service; and in order to carry out the spread of the gospel and service effectively in parallel in the early church community, seven deacons are appointed. Stephen preached the gospel in the synagogue whose members were mainly Diaspora Jews, but because he spoke with the wisdom of the Holy Spirit, they realized they could not overcome Stephen, so they plotted and accused Stephen before the Sanhedrin.

[Chapter 7] The Sermon and Martyrdom of Stephen the Deacon
Stephen's sermon is the only content among the sermons recorded in this book that was not preached by an apostle. Stephen conveyed the orthodoxy of the gospel of Jesus Christ, like the sermons of Peter and Paul. In particular, more than in the other sermons, he narrates the history of Israel in terms of redemptive history and presents the lessons it contains, thereby urging the Jews of that time to reflect and repent.

[Chapter 8] Saul's Persecution of the Early Church, Mission in the Region of Samaria, and the Evangelization of the Ethiopian Eunuch
Prompted by the martyrdom of Stephen the deacon, Judaism intensified its persecution of the Jerusalem church. As a result the church was scattered to various places to escape the persecution of Judaism, but it continued to preach the gospel even there, and so the Jerusalem church came to a turning point in which it broke out of the regional and ethnic frame of Jerusalem and Judea and spread the gospel to Samaria and even to the Gentile world.
As one example of the success of Philip's evangelistic ministry in Samaria, it introduces the salvation of the people of Samaria and the repentance of Simon the magician.
The news of the success of the Samaria mission reached the ears of the apostles who had remained in Jerusalem, and this must have been very encouraging to the apostles. For although Jerusalem was being persecuted at that time, news that the gospel was being widely spread in other places must surely have brought them great joy. Upon arriving at the city of Samaria, the mission field of Philip, Peter and John immediately prayed that the Holy Spirit would come upon the men and women who had been baptized.
The Holy Spirit guided Philip and sent him to the eunuch of the queen of Ethiopia, and also moved the eunuch's heart so that he accepted the gospel of Jesus Christ without doubt, and continued to guide Philip to preach the gospel in many cities.

[Chapter 9] The Conversion of Saul, Peter's Healing of Aeneas, and the Miracle of Raising Tabitha
While going to Damascus to arrest the disciples of the Lord, Saul experienced the appearing of Jesus Christ and was personally appointed by Jesus as the apostle to the Gentiles. The reason Jesus appeared to Saul in person was that, just as the apostles had directly seen Jesus and taken part in His ministry, Saul too was to be appointed as the apostle to the Gentiles through such an experience.
The scene is introduced in which Peter evangelizes the western region of Palestine along the Mediterranean coast; Peter went around preaching the gospel, passing through Lydda (verses 32-35), then Joppa (verses 36-43) and Caesarea (Acts 10).

[Chapter 10] The Coming of the Holy Spirit upon the House of Cornelius
Through the evangelization of the household of Cornelius, a Gentile, the gospel of Jesus Christ at last moves beyond Judea and Samaria and spreads to the Gentile world. Cornelius was a Roman centurion who did not know the gospel of Jesus Christ but was a devout Gentile who feared God and helped people in need. This piety and charity of his ascended before God, and Cornelius received the grace of being able to welcome the gospel.

[Chapter 11] Peter's Defense Concerning the Salvation of Cornelius, and the Founding of the Church in Antioch
Peter's visit to the household of Cornelius was raised as a problem by the believing Jews (verses 1-3), and Peter, by explaining the vision he had seen and the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the household of Cornelius, defends that the salvation of the Gentiles is the will of God (verses 4-17), and the Jerusalem church is shown acknowledging the mission to the Gentiles (verse 18).
The process of the founding of the Antioch church, which became the forward base of the Gentile mission, and the beautiful scene of the Antioch church helping the mother church, the Jerusalem church, which was in difficulty because of famine, appear.

[Chapter 12] The Great Persecution by Herod Agrippa I and the Angel's Rescue of Peter
Just when the Antioch church was greatly flourishing, the Jerusalem church once again faced persecution. That is, Herod began to harm the main leaders of the church. Whereas the persecution of the Jerusalem church up to that point had been religious persecution by the Jewish religious leaders to protect their vested interests, this time Herod's suppression of the church was political persecution by state power, more blatant and harsh, and the Jerusalem church was placed in great crisis.
Through the death of Herod who persecuted the church, it shows how miserable is the end of those who reject the work of the Holy Spirit and the power of the gospel and oppose the church and God.

[Chapter 13] The Apostle Paul's First Missionary Journey
From this chapter on, the first half of the record of Acts ends and a new history of mission begins.
When the apostles Paul and Barnabas were in Antioch of Syria, God the Holy Spirit had them set apart and commanded them to proclaim the gospel of the grace of God. In accordance with that command, the church sends these two apostles to the Gentiles.
The two apostles returned after successfully completing the work of preaching the gospel in Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, and Iconium, and in Lystra and Derbe, the two cities of Lycaonia. God the Holy Spirit brought about a great work in which Jews and Gentiles living in the various regions of Asia Minor heard the gospel and turned to the Lord.

[Chapter 14] The Ministry in Iconium and Lystra and the Return to Antioch
When the apostles Paul and Barnabas preached the gospel in Lystra in the region of Lycaonia, they met a man who had been lame from birth and had never walked, and made him stand up.
The apostles Peter and John had healed a lame man who sat begging in front of the Beautiful Gate of the temple. That man too was lame from birth. That the apostles Paul and Barnabas did the same thing as the apostles Peter and John did in healing a man lame from birth means that the Lord recognized Paul and Barnabas as apostles in the same way as Peter and John.
Peter and John made a Jewish lame man walk, and Paul and Barnabas made a Gentile lame man walk.

[Chapter 15] The Jerusalem Council and the Beginning of Paul's Second Missionary Journey
This chapter records the scene of the first Jerusalem Council, which holds important significance in the history of Christianity. This first Jerusalem Council was originally convened because of the question of Gentile believers' observance of the law and circumcision, but its importance is heightened by the fact that its result officially recognized the Gentile mission and the authority of Paul's apostleship.
When Paul and Barnabas had returned to Antioch after finishing their first missionary journey to the Gentiles, Jewish believers who held to the tradition of legalism came from Judea to the Antioch church and insisted that Gentiles too must be circumcised according to the law of Moses in order to be saved, and so a dispute arose between Paul and Barnabas and them.
It introduces the scene in which the Jerusalem Council, having completed its final decision, conveys it to the Antioch church in writing. The Jerusalem Council chose Judas and Silas, together with Paul and Barnabas, as those to be sent to the Antioch church (verse 22), and, on the grounds that there is no salvation apart from the grace of Jesus Christ and that the yoke of the law should not be laid on the Gentiles, resolved to abolish the obligation of circumcision for Gentile believers and have them keep only four prohibitions, and decided to have an official document recording this delivered (verses 23-29); when Paul's party arrived in Antioch and conveyed the resolution to the church, the Antioch church is shown rejoicing with very great joy (verses 30-35).
Before setting out on the second missionary journey, Paul and Barnabas differed over whether John Mark should accompany them, and in the end the two quarreled sharply and parted ways, and Barnabas took John Mark and Paul took Silas, and each set out on a missionary journey by a different road.

[Chapter 16] The Apostle Paul's Ministry in Philippi
Going to Derbe and Lystra, the first places of ministry on the second missionary journey, he meets Timothy there. Timothy was a person familiar with the Scriptures from childhood, who accepted the gospel on Paul's first missionary journey and made a significant contribution to gospel ministry. Because Timothy was also commended in faith by the believers of that region, Paul must have thought him a suitable coworker for himself.
Paul, who began the second missionary journey by taking Timothy as a coworker in Lystra and Derbe (verses 1-5), continued to wish to bear witness to the gospel centered on the region of Asia Minor. But, in some way unknown to us, Paul was prevented by the Holy Spirit and could not go to Asia Minor. So Paul changed direction and tried to go north through the regions of Phrygia and Galatia into the region of Bithynia. But the Holy Spirit prevented even that way (verses 6, 7).
When this happened, Paul had no choice but to give up his plan and wait for the will of God in Troas. At this time God turns Paul's steps toward Europe through a vision.
Silas, Timothy, Luke, and others accompanied him, and they came to Philippi, the first city of Macedonia, as the first region. Paul and Silas were beaten by the magistrates of Philippi and put in prison, and this suffering is the first record of Paul suffering directly at the hands of Gentiles, not Jews, while preaching the gospel. Paul and Silas pointed out the injustice of the punishment by asserting their Roman citizenship, and were released with honor.

[Chapter 17] Ministry in Thessalonica, Berea, and Athens
Paul and Silas come to preach the gospel in Thessalonica, about 160 km southwest of Philippi. When Paul preached the gospel in the synagogue, a great crowd of devout Greeks and not a few prominent women welcomed the gospel, whereas the Jews were instead jealous of Paul and were bent on harming him.
Jason and his brothers, who had hidden Paul and Silas, were dragged before the city officials and, after being greatly ill-treated, were released upon paying bail. Even amid such persecution, the seed of the gospel spread in Thessalonica grew greatly and bore fruit and became the foundation for the spread of the gospel throughout Europe. (1 Thessalonians 1:1-10).
Berea was a small town about 80 km south of Thessalonica and not a very important city. But when the Jews of Thessalonica heard that the gospel was being preached in Berea, even though this was about 80 km from Thessalonica, they chased after them all the way there, stirring up the people and obstructing the evangelistic work.
Paul engaged in philosophical and speculative debate in order to make the gospel understood by the people of Athens. Because of the exclusive attitude of the Greeks, who did not accept the resurrection out of intellectual pride, Paul's evangelism moved only a few people to accept the gospel and could not produce a great effect (verses 32-34). In the end, Paul keenly felt the limits of evangelistic ministry because of the pride and ignorance of the people of Athens, concluded his ministry in Athens, and changed his destination to Corinth.

[Chapter 18] The Ministry in Corinth, the End of the Second Missionary Journey, and the Beginning of the Third Missionary Journey
It introduces the evangelistic ministry in Corinth, which can be called the last stop of the second missionary journey. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, an important center of commerce and trade located at the southern tip of the Balkan Peninsula, and a prosperous city that controlled the trade sphere of the Mediterranean.
Paul, who arrived in Corinth from Athens, meets the couple Aquila and Priscilla, who had moved to Corinth in accordance with the expulsion of the Jews from Rome (A.D. 49-50) decreed by Emperor Claudius (A.D. 41-54) (verse 2). But the Jews, who opposed Paul wherever he went and obstructed the witness to the gospel, opposed Paul here too and obstructed the witness to the gospel. So Paul stopped witnessing to the gospel to the Jews in the synagogue and came to witness to the gospel to the Gentiles in the house of Titus Justus.
With the ministry in Corinth, Paul ends his second missionary journey and returns to Antioch, and immediately sets out again on the third missionary journey, in which he carries out a so-called pastoral-level evangelistic activity of visiting again and strengthening the faith.

[Chapter 19] Events During the Ministry in Ephesus
At first, in Ephesus too, as in other regions, Paul bore witness to the gospel in the synagogue (verse 8). But because of the rejection by the stubborn Jews, he had to stop after about three months.
Paul moves to a different place and bears witness to the gospel in the hall of Tyrannus, and since the evangelism in the hall of Tyrannus was undisturbed for two years or so until the uproar of the silversmiths (verses 23-41), the witness to the gospel in Ephesus achieved very great success, and the fruit was that the gospel spread not only to Ephesus but even to the surrounding regions.

[Chapter 20] Ministry in Macedonia and Greece, the Return from Corinth to Troas, and the Farewell Sermon at Miletus
Paul, who left Ephesus, had two problems to resolve during his journey. One was to resolve the problems being heard from the Corinthian church, and the other was to raise a relief offering to send to the Jerusalem church.
During his third missionary journey the apostle Paul preached the gospel in Ephesus for nearly three years. Then he went again to Macedonia and Achaia, and on the way to Jerusalem by ship he passed along various coastal regions of Asia Minor. In the course of this, when he arrived at Miletus near Ephesus, he sent for the elders of the Ephesian church to come. The apostle Paul confesses to them his state of mind about going to Jerusalem and conveys his charge to them with tears. The apostle Paul knew what would happen to him if he went to Jerusalem.

[Chapter 21] Paul's Return to Jerusalem and His Arrest Because of the Clash with the Judaizers
With the schedule of the third missionary journey completed, the apostle Paul, before going up to Jerusalem, reached Caesarea, a port city where the residence of the governor of Judea was located at that time. There the prophet Agabus, conveying the word of the Holy Spirit, prophesied that in Jerusalem the Jews would bind the apostle Paul and hand him over to the Gentiles. Upon this, his companions and the people there, with one voice and in tears, urged the apostle Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
But the apostle Paul declared that he was 'ready even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus' and did not accept their urging. He had no choice but to entrust himself to the Lord's leading, saying, 'The Lord's will be done.'

[Chapter 22] Paul's Defense Before the Jewish Crowd and the Uproar of the Jewish Crowd
After finishing the third missionary journey and returning to Jerusalem, the apostle Paul, following the advice of James, entered the temple and performed the prescribed rite of purification. Just as he was about to finish the rite of purification, Jews from Asia found Paul in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd, seized him, and lynched him. Hearing the news, the commander came with soldiers and rescued him.
The apostle Paul asks the commander and gives a sermon defending himself before the Jews. But before he could finish the sermon, the Jews raised an uproar, shouting, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! He is not fit to live.'

[Chapter 23] Paul's Defense Before the Sanhedrin, the Plot to Kill Paul, and Paul's Transfer to Caesarea
Because of the uproar in the Jerusalem temple, the apostle Paul came to be interrogated before the Sanhedrin, including the high priest. During the interrogation there was a great dispute between the Sadducees and the Pharisees. The cause of the dispute was their difference of opinion about the resurrection and angels. The Sadducees claimed that there is no resurrection, no angel, and no spirit, whereas the Pharisees believed in all of them.

[Chapter 24] Tertullus' Accusation and Paul's Defense Before the Governor Felix
The plot to kill the apostle Paul was exposed, and the commander quickly and safely transferred him to Caesarea, where the residence of the governor of Judea was located. Some time later the apostle Paul was tried before Felix, the governor. The high priest Ananias, who accused the apostle Paul, accusing him through a lawyer, poured out words of cursing, saying, 'We have found this man to be a plague, one who stirs up all the Jews throughout the world and a ringleader of the heresy of the Nazarenes.'

[Chapter 25] The Jews' Accusation and Paul's Defense Before the Governor Festus
While the apostle Paul was in prison in Caesarea, the governor Felix finished his term and Festus took office as governor in his place. Some time later, as the apostle Paul was being tried before the governor Festus, he appeals to Caesar, the emperor, for trial. At that time a Roman citizen had the right to appeal directly to the emperor if he was treated unjustly. The first reason the apostle Paul wanted to be tried by the emperor was that the Jews were trying to kill him. But the true reason the apostle Paul appealed to Caesar was to fulfill the will of God. It was the will of God that the apostle Paul go to Rome.
At that time the capital of the Roman Empire was Rome. The role of the apostle Paul, as the apostle to the Gentiles, was to preach the gospel to all the Gentiles. For this he could travel to every region within the Roman Empire and preach the gospel, but this has many difficulties, both physical and in terms of time.
But if the gospel is preached in Rome, the capital of the empire, it has the advantage that the gospel can easily be conveyed from Rome to the various regions within the Roman Empire. Therefore the reason the apostle Paul appealed to Caesar was that the purpose of spreading the gospel of God to the ends of the earth took priority over his own safety.

[Chapter 26] Paul's Defense Before Agrippa
It was settled that the apostle Paul would go to Rome. However, in order to gather the material for the appeal to be reported to the emperor, the governor finally had Paul examined before King Agrippa. The apostle Paul boldly proclaimed before the governor and King Agrippa why he preaches the gospel and what the content of the gospel he preaches is. And he pleads that the governor, King Agrippa, and all the people around would become believers like himself. At this, when the governor Festus said, 'You are out of your mind,' Paul cried out in a loud voice and answered, 'I am not speaking madness, but true and sober words.'

[Chapter 27] The Beginning of Paul's Voyage to Rome and the Events Before and After the Storm of the Northeaster
It was decided that the apostle Paul would go to Rome, and he boarded a ship bound for Rome under the charge of the centurion Julius and set sail. Passing the island of Cyprus, they arrived at a place called Fair Havens in Crete. The apostle Paul advised wintering there, but the centurion, relying on the words of the experienced pilot and the ship's owner, decided to winter at Phoenix and set out.
But suddenly they met a violent storm called 'the Northeaster' and had no choice but to be driven helplessly across the open sea. For many days the great storm did not subside, and in a condition where black clouds were so thick that neither sun nor stars could be seen day or night, they were being driven this way and that on the Mediterranean like a leaf floating on water.
But, thankfully, God preserved the lives of all 276 people intact except for the ship and the cargo. The only thing God regards as most precious is 'life.' God would not trade one person's life for the whole universe. The ship and the cargo cannot be compared with life. But the regrettable thing is that this world values the 'ship' and the 'cargo' more than life.

[Chapter 28] The Journey from Malta to Rome and a Summary of Paul's Ministry in Rome
Until the apostle Paul came to Rome, difficulties large and small did not cease. In particular, the opposition of the Jews and even threats to his life continued. Besides that, hardships and sufferings hard to put into words lay before the apostle Paul. But even though such difficulties were ever present, he finally arrived in Rome.
The book of Acts ends with the apostle Paul entering Rome, living in a rented house, and preaching the gospel of God for two years. Acts, recorded centering on the deeds of the apostles, stopped here at chapter 28, but the Acts of the Holy Spirit continued afterward. The Acts of the church did not stop. Although most of the apostles were martyred and died, God the Holy Spirit, unbound, has worked until now together with countless forefathers of faith.

[Chapter 1] The Reason for Writing Romans, the Evidence of God's Existence, and the Sin of People Who Do Not Believe in God (Gentiles)
1:1-7 _ The Apostle Paul, a Servant of Christ
Paul says that the gospel was already promised by the prophets and that this promise was fulfilled through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. He also makes known to the believers in Rome that he received the office of apostle in order to preach the gospel to the Gentiles so that they might be saved and to make those who were saved obedient to God.
1:8-15 _ The Apostle Paul, Longing to Preach the Gospel in Rome
Paul's reason for wanting to go to Rome was to preach the gospel, to impart spiritual gifts to the brothers of the church in Rome, and to strengthen their faith. They had been saved but did not clearly know what a normal life of faith is, and they were in the midst of persecution and hardship.
1:16-17 _ The Righteousness of God Revealed in the Gospel
The gospel becomes the power of God that gives salvation to all who believe, and through that gospel it leads those who believe the gospel and are saved to obey God and live in faith.
1:18-32 _ The Sin of the Gentiles
All people have utterly fallen before the holy God. Not knowing that the judgment of God's wrath comes upon those who have fallen, people live in sin. The Gentiles may excuse themselves by saying that they did not believe because they did not know God. But that is not a valid reason. People have a soul created in the image of God and so can seek God, and by seeing the power of God displayed in all things they can believe in God.

[Chapter 2] The Sin of Those Who Claim to Believe in God (the Jews)
2:1-16 _ A Warning to the Jews
The Jews condemned the Gentiles for not knowing God and for being immersed in idolatry. But they did not realize their own sins and condemned only the Gentiles. The passage says that, on the contrary, the Jews will incur the wrath of God by despising the kindness of God, who is patient and gives them an opportunity to repent.
2:17-29 _ The Sin of the Jews
The Jews lived with the thought that, even though they did not keep the law perfectly, they would not be judged because they were the chosen people. They relied on the law, boasted in God, approved what is good, and believed themselves to be teachers, but they lived in transgression of the law. Rather, by breaking the law in front of the Gentiles, they caused the name of God to be dishonored. If they had done the law, there would be benefit as the chosen people, but if they do not keep it, they are no different from the Gentiles. Therefore the Jews, too, receive the same judgment of God as the Gentiles.

[Chapter 3] All People Are Sinners, the Purpose of Giving the Law, and Salvation by Faith in the Redeeming Grace of Jesus
3:1-8 _ The Objections of the Jews
Concerning the fact that the Jews receive the same judgment as the Gentiles, this passage speaks of the justice of God's judgment in answer to the objections that the Jews might raise.
'If even the Jews, without the benefit of circumcision, receive the same judgment as the Gentiles, what is the privilege they have as the chosen people?'
The Jews were entrusted with the word of God. They had the word through which they could obtain the grace of God. God promised to send the Christ to save humanity, and they received that word of promise from God. Compared with other peoples, this is a wonderful privilege.
'Can the unbelief of the Jews nullify the faithfulness of God who chose them?'
= 'Isn't the reason the Jews came not to believe, in the end, God's fault?'
That cannot be. Even if the Jews fall and are disobedient, there is no change in the faithfulness of God. Rather, the fault lies with the Jews. When David committed the sins of adultery and murder and then repented, God forgave him and so revealed the righteousness of God.
'If sin results in displaying the righteousness of God all the more, should we sin more?'
Absolutely not. If God were one who encourages sin, how could He judge the world? Sin cannot glorify the holy God.
3:9-20 _ All People Under Sin
God declared that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin. The expression 'under sin' means that all people are sinners subject to judgment and therefore need to be saved. Every part of human beings has utterly fallen. Because they are sinners, people live committing sins. Our status is not that of the righteous but that of sinners.
3:21-31 _ Justified by Faith
How can people who have now become aware that they are sinners be saved? God revealed the righteousness of God that comes not through the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.

[Chapter 4] The Truth of Being Made Righteous by Faith, Spoken of Through Examples from the Old Testament, for Example Abraham and David
4:1-25 _ David and Abraham, Who Were Justified by Faith
The Jews, who insist that one is made righteous by doing the law, thought that Abraham, their ancestor, was declared righteous by relying on works. They also claimed that the reason he was chosen as the ancestor of the people of Israel was his righteousness. But what God counted as righteousness in Abraham was not his works but his faith.

[Chapter 5] Just as We Became Sinners Through One Man, Adam, So We Become Righteous Through One Man, Jesus
5:1-4 _ The Blessing of Those Who Have Been Justified
Those who are saved receive the blessing of God throughout their whole lives. We who were enemies of God now enjoy peace with God. The relationship between God and us has changed from the relationship of judge and sinner to the relationship of father and son.
5:5-11 _ The Ground of Assurance of Glory
Can the glory that God has decided to give us be revoked? Could someone like me enter into the glory of God? We have no need to be ashamed of our hope of glory. Our hope will never disappoint us.
5:12-21 _ Adam and Jesus, the Representatives of Humanity
Someone who has been saved might have this question: How can the sins of all people be forgiven through the sacrifice of one man, Jesus, and how can it be possible for so many blessings to be given to us? But once we learn the reason all people came to be condemned, we can be certain that all of this is possible.

[Chapter 6] The Reason God Saved Us: So That We Would Live Not for Ourselves but for the Lord
6:1-14 _ I Have Died (Reason 1 Why We Cannot Remain in Sin)
Those who do not know the gospel and have not been saved slander in this way: 'If a person sins and sin is forgiven by the grace of God, wouldn't it be all right to sin more in order to obtain more grace?' That cannot be. They slander in that way because they do not know who a Christian is. A Christian is not merely one who is acknowledged as righteous but one who is 'justified in Christ.' This means that he is one united with Christ.
6:15-23 _ I Am a Servant of God (Reason 2 Why We Cannot Remain in Sin)
Another reason we cannot remain in sin is that I have become a servant of God. A servant is one who absolutely obeys his master's commands. Before we were saved, we were servants of sin. We took sin as our master and lived as the master ordered.
But now, by obeying the word of the gospel, we have been set free from sin and have become servants of righteousness. Our status has changed from servants of sin to servants of God. We who have become servants of God cannot again be enslaved to sin. Therefore we cannot remain in sin so that grace may increase. We must know the fact that I have already become a servant of God.

[Chapter 7] The Two Laws in the Saved Person (the Law of Sin That Wants to Live for Oneself and the Law of the Mind That Wants to Live According to the Will of God)
7:1-6 _ Jesus, Who Became Our Husband
Before we were saved, the law as our husband bound us and condemned us. We were condemned by the law and received a death sentence. The relationship between husband and wife is severed only by death. So God prepared a way for us to die in order to give us freedom from the law. That is precisely Jesus' death on the cross. We who are united with Jesus died together with Him in His death.
7:7-13 _ The Law, Which Makes Us Aware of Sin
Because the law condemned and bound us, can we say that the law is wrong and that it is sin? No. We cannot condemn the law. What is wrong is the sinful nature of people who cannot keep the law; the law itself is not sin.
7:14-25 _ The Inner Self Fighting Against Sin
It records the contents of the distress and failure of the apostle Paul as he sought to be freed from the power of sin and to serve the law of God. It does not record the state of mind of an unsaved person who, watching himself being dragged to hell, earnestly wants to be saved.

[Chapter 8] By Abiding in Christ Jesus (the Church), We Overcome Sin Through the Supply of the Holy Spirit
8:1-4 _ The Power of the Holy Spirit in the Church
It is by no means that I have within myself the power to overcome my sinful nature and to rescue me from this body of death. I have no power to overcome sin. We must know that only the power of the Holy Spirit, who works within the church, can rescue me from the body of death. When I follow the Holy Spirit within it, the requirement of the law, which could not be fulfilled because the flesh is weak, is fulfilled through my life.
8:5-14 _ The Holy Spirit, Who Leads Us
Depending on what a person sets his mind on, he can follow the Holy Spirit or follow the flesh. In order to follow the Holy Spirit, we must set our minds on the things of the Spirit. The mind of the flesh becomes an enemy of God and cannot please God.
8:15-17 _ The Holy Spirit, Who Bears Witness to Our Adoption
The Holy Spirit works among us and leads us, and also bears witness that we are sons of God. Whereas before we were in the status of servants who feared God, now we have become sons of God. The faith by which we can truly call God Father is the witness that the Holy Spirit bears.
8:18-25 _ The Holy Spirit, Who Guarantees the Redemption of the Body
We must know that suffering comes before receiving glory. Of course, the glory that will be revealed to us cannot be compared with the present suffering. Even if every kind of figure of speech is mobilized, suffering and glory cannot be compared.
8:26-27 _ The Holy Spirit, Who Helps Us in Our Weakness
The Holy Spirit makes us know what we do not know and prays for us. When, because of our weakness, we do not know the will of God and cannot pray, the Holy Spirit prays in our place. The reason the Lord hears our groaning even while we groan is that the Holy Spirit knows our hearts and prays.
8:28-30 _ God, Who Prepared Our Glory
It is not all that God sent Jesus Christ for us only to forgive sins. God saved us in order to give us glory.
8:31-39 _ The Love of God That Cannot Be Severed
If the one who planned everything in order to give us glorification is the Lord, who can raise an objection to this, and who can stop it? Who can oppose us, accuse us, or condemn us? Who can separate us from the love of Christ? We are certain that nothing in this world can separate us from within the love of God.

[Chapter 9] Israel's Past: Emphasizing That in the Past God Specially Chose Israel
9:1-5 _ The Apostle Paul, Who Longs for the Salvation of the Jews
Before the people of Israel, a people chosen by God of whom only a few accepted the gospel and who were far from the blessing of God, Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, earnestly wishes as one of the same people that they might be saved. All the promises of God had been given, and Christ came through them, but they rejected Christ.
9:6-13 _ The Children of Promise Whom God Sees
9:14-18 _ The Sovereign Grace of God
The Gentiles received the blessing of God by obeying, and Israel did not receive the blessing of God because it rejected Christ; can it be said that God did wrong in this? No.
9:19-29 _ The Justice of the Sovereign Grace of God
Even if God takes away the blessing of the people of Israel who rejected grace and bestows that blessing on the Gentiles who obeyed, can the people of Israel raise an objection against God? They did not receive the blessing because they rejected the grace of Jesus.
9:30-33 _ Israel, Who Relied on Works
Paul concluded that Israel did not attain salvation because it relied on works. The Gentiles lived without knowing God but were justified before God by faith, while the people of Israel lived relying on the law but did not reach the standard of the law.

[Chapter 10] Israel's Present: Emphasizing That at Present Israel Is Rejecting the Gospel of God
10:1-4 _ Israel, Who Did Not Know the Righteousness of God
Why did Israel rely only on its own works? It was because they did not know how evil a person is and had no knowledge of God.
Because they did not know the righteousness of God, Israel put forward its own righteousness. They had zeal for God. But this rather produced the result of disobedience to God. The reason Israel was far from the grace of God was that they had no knowledge of God. Israel did not know that the righteousness of God is based on the redemption of Christ.
10:5-15 _ The Righteousness of God That Comes by Faith
Israel, who did not know that one is made righteous by faith alone, lived relying only on the law of Moses. The righteousness that comes from the law says that a person can live if he does the law perfectly. But there is no one who can keep the law.
10:16-21 Israel, Which Did Not Obey the Gospel
The reason Israel was not saved is that they did not obey the gospel. It is not because they did not hear the gospel. Even in the Old Testament times the gospel was conveyed to them through the prophets. Also, Jesus preached the word, and the apostles also preached the gospel. But they never obeyed in the end.

[Chapter 11] Israel's Future: Emphasizing That the Opportunity for Israel to Be Saved Will Come
11:1-6 _ God, Who Did Not Reject Israel
From the standpoint of the people of Israel, they may think that God has rejected them. But just as Paul himself was an Israelite and yet was saved, there are saved people among the Israelites. There are saved people in our age, too, and there will be people to be saved in the future. But it is accomplished only by the grace of God, not by human works.
11:7-12 _ Israel, Which Was Hardened
The people of Israel did not obtain what they sought from God. Only a few obtained what they sought, and the rest, through pride and hardness, became distant from the blessing of God. By rejecting Christ, the blessing they should have received became instead a curse, and they were scattered over the whole world. Nevertheless, they have not stumbled completely.
11:13-24 _ A Warning to the Gentiles
Because the Gentiles came to receive the blessing promised to Israel as a result of Israel's refusal, the Gentiles must not be arrogant toward Israel. If the Gentiles do not accept the kindness of God, the Gentiles too will be cut off. It is God's warning that the age of grace given to the Gentiles will come to an end.
11:25-32 _ The Promise of Israel's Salvation
When the number of Gentiles being saved is full, the opportunity to be saved as a nation will be given to Israel. Israel rejected Christ and was scattered over the whole world. But, as He promised through the prophet Isaiah, God will bring the scattered Israel back, forgive their sins, and save them.
11:33-36 _ Praise for the Wisdom of God

[Chapter 12] Offer Yourselves to God as Living Sacrifices! Christians Are Priests of the Gospel; Know Your Measure in the Church and Be Faithful to the Role Given You! What About Relations with Those Outside?
12:1-2 _ Spiritual Worship
If we have come to know the wonderful love God has shown to save me, we must now offer everything of ourselves to God. We once offered this body to sin, but since we have become servants of God, we must offer this body to God, our master, as a living sacrifice. A servant must discern what his master's will is and obey his master's commands.
12:3-8 _ Roles in the Church
The church is called the body of Christ. We are the members who make up the body of Christ. Just as each member has a different role, God has given us gifts according to the measure of faith. Also, the gifts were given to us so that we might offer living sacrifices to God, and this takes place within the church.
12:9-13 _ Attitude Toward Believers
Christians who have been saved by the love of the Lord and live as one body must love one another and put the love of Christ into practice. Fellowship without love cannot move anyone, and service without love cannot please God. If one hates one's brother and does not love him, one cannot love God. The one who sincerely loves his brother is the one who loves the Lord and serves the Lord.
12:14-21 _ Attitude Toward Society
Those who do not know Christ persecute Christians. But we should not curse them but bless them. We should leave vengeance to God, and rather do good, not being overcome by evil but overcoming evil with good. God's permitting us such persecution is providing us with an opportunity to do good.

[Chapter 13] To Preach the Gospel, the Church Should Obey the Authority of the State and Do Good to Neighbors!
13:1-7 _ Attitude Toward the State
When we are born physically, we belong to a family and at the same time to a nation. In the age when Rome ruled Israel, the apostle Paul says to submit to Rome. This is because worldly authority too comes from God.
13:8-10 _ Attitude Toward Neighbors
We must show love also to the people of the world. We should not stop at not doing evil to people but should put love into practice and bear witness to the love of Christ. Putting love into practice fulfills the requirement of the law, and this is accomplished when we live following the Holy Spirit.
13:11-14 _ Attitude Toward the End Times
As citizens of heaven, it is all the more important to have the right attitude toward the Lord's return. We who wait for the redemption of the body with hope must live a watchful life. Duties toward the world are not everything. We should not plan for the works of the flesh, but, as befits citizens of heaven, think of the spiritual things of heaven and live for them.

[Chapter 14] To Preach the Gospel, the Church Must Be One. Do Not Judge One Another, but Pursue What Makes for Peace and for Building Up One Another
14:1-12 _ Do Not Judge
In the church, believers whose faith differs from one another form one body. Conflict can arise in the church because of cultural differences or differences in circumstances. Even so, we must not judge and slander one another.
14:13-23 _ Build One Another Up

[Chapter 15] To Preach the Gospel, the Church Must Be One. Do Not Please Yourselves, but Accept One Another
15:1-7 _ Consideration for the Weak in Faith
For believers to be of one heart and one mind and to live a life that gives glory to God is the right attitude that believers should have.
15:8-13 _ Praise Toward God
For the sake of God's promise to save all people, Jesus kept the law and took upon Himself the curse of the law in our place, and so saved us. He did this in order to fulfill God's promise to the people of Israel and to make the Gentiles glorify God for His mercy.
15:14-21 _ The Apostle Paul, Priest of the Gospel
15:22-33 _ The Apostle Paul, Who Wishes to Go to Rome
Paul's plan was to have fellowship with them, strengthen their faith, and preach the gospel to the whole world with Rome as the center.

[Chapter 16] Coworkers in the Church Who Labored for the Gospel (Heroes of Faith Who Will Shine Forever)
Romans 16:1-27 _ Coworkers in the Gospel, Greetings, and a Warning Against False Teachers
Paul greets the fruit of salvation through his preaching of the gospel and the coworkers who gave up everything and helped him in order to preach the gospel with him. On the other hand, he also warns against those who for their own gain go against the teaching and do not serve Christ, and speaks of turning away from them. Because the work of Satan always appears wherever the gospel is preached, every believer in the church must obey the church with one mind and one purpose and strive for the gospel.

[Chapter 1] The Impropriety of Division in the Church and the Cross as the Standard of Unity
1:1-9 Introduction and Paul's Thanksgiving
1:10-17 A Rebuke of the Division in the Corinthian Church
The Corinthian church was divided into many factions and given to quarreling, and the cause was excessive attachment to particular leaders from a human point of view. Against the factional tendency of the Corinthian church, Paul reminds them of his own ministry in Corinth, points out the impropriety of their division, and rebukes them
1:18-25 The Cross as the Standard of Church Unity
At that time the Corinthians were divided because they valued human wisdom more than the wisdom of God.
