For this reason it was necessary to make clear the absolute superiority of the wisdom of God and the limitations of worldly wisdom. The aim was to point out the impropriety of church division based on worldly wisdom and to make the Corinthians realize that only the gospel that preaches the message of the cross of Jesus Christ is the one truth of salvation and the power and wisdom of God, and so to unite the Corinthians as one in the gospel.
1:26-31 Jesus, the True Boast

[Chapter 2] Paul's Preaching of the Cross and the Wisdom of God Understood Through the Holy Spirit
2:1-5 Paul's Ministry of Preaching Only the Cross
Paul reminds the believers of the Corinthian church that he had the wisdom and knowledge to match the outstanding philosophical knowledge and eloquence of the Greeks of that time, yet he had determined to testify only to the cross of Christ. This was because Paul regarded the knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ as the most noble thing, and also because he knew well that the salvation of souls is accomplished only by the power of the Holy Spirit.
2:6-16 The Wisdom of God Understood Through the Holy Spirit
Paul says that the gospel he has preached up to now is the wisdom of God, which cannot be compared with limited and fragmentary human wisdom; that it was predestined and hidden before the creation of the world; and that it is God's providence of salvation, who gave Christ as a ransom to save sinful humanity.
Saying that because the rulers of this age did not know this wisdom they committed the folly of crucifying Christ, he emphasizes that this secret wisdom of God, that is, the gospel, can be understood only by the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

[Chapter 3] The Impropriety of Factions and Christ, the Only Foundation of the Church
3:1-9 The Impropriety of Division Along Fleshly Connections
The Corinthians were divided from one another because of the problem of not understanding the role of God's servants. Because they were 'people of the flesh,' saved but still unable to cast off the things of the flesh, having an elementary faith like spiritual infants, it diagnoses their spiritual immaturity of being more concerned with the affairs of people than with the work of God
3:10-17 Christ, Who Became the Only Foundation of the Church, and Believers, Who Are the Temple of God
The meaning of 'gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw':
1) A lesson concerning how evangelists taught and built up believers within the church
'Gold, silver, precious stones' can be seen as the reward for the labor of evangelists who toiled only with the wisdom of God and right biblical teaching in order to build up each believer in the Lord, whereas 'wood, hay, straw' can be seen as worldly wisdom and human teaching, which will be burned up.
2) A lesson concerning how each saved believer lived the life of faith in the Lord.
'Gold, silver, precious stones' are all the rewards for each believer who lived by faith while obeying the word of God in the church, whereas 'wood, hay, straw' are the things of those who lived only for the flesh and that will be burned up at the judgment seat of Christ.
3:18-23 The Folly of Worldly Wisdom

[Chapter 4] The Prohibition of Judging Gospel Ministers, and an Exhortation to End Division Through Paul's Example
4:1-5 The Prohibition of Judging Gospel Ministers
Believers must exclude every worldly judgment by regarding gospel ministers as 'servants of Christ' and 'stewards of the mysteries of God,' and since God, the Judge, will judge everything righteously, they must entrust everything solely to Him. In return, gospel ministers should not indulge in complacency just because they are not judged by believers; rather, they should have an attitude of being faithful to their calling.
4:6-13 The Humility of the Apostles and the Pride of the Corinthians
4:14-21 Paul's Fatherly Exhortation for Resolving the Disputes
Through an exhortation overflowing with love, he urges them, as a father would exhort his sons, to imitate his faith. Of course, this exhortation does not mean that the Corinthians should belong to the party of Paul. It is an exhortation to imitate his sufferings for the gospel and his practice of humility and love, and ultimately a word to imitate Christ.

[Chapter 5] A Rebuke of Sexual Immorality in the Church and a Command to Carry Out Discipline
5:1-8 Paul's Condemnation of the Incest in the Corinthian Church
5:9-13 A Command to Expel the Sexually Immoral
He instructs them to expel the sexually immoral. Paul had earlier taught the Corinthians not to associate with those who commit sexual immorality, but the Corinthians misunderstood this as meaning to cut off fellowship with worldly people entirely, and were feeling considerable confusion in their social life. Paul makes clear that such an exhortation did not mean to cut off fellowship with worldly people and live in complete isolation, but meant to keep away from fellowship with insincere Christians who bring disgrace on the holy image of Christ and the church.

[Chapter 6] An Exhortation Against Lawsuits Among Believers, and the Nature of Sexual Immorality
6:1-11 A Rebuke of the Problem of Lawsuits Among Believers and a Warning Against Unrighteousness
6:12-20 The Problem of the Misuse of Freedom and the Nature of Sexual Immorality
In the Greek cultural sphere of that time, especially in Corinth, it was common for priestesses who worked in the temples of idols to engage in prostitution with men. Some of the Corinthians, still unable to cast off their old habits, committed the sin of sexual immorality with prostitutes just as worldly people did.

[Chapter 7] Teachings on Various Aspects of Believers' Marriage and Married Life
7:1-7 General Exhortation Concerning Marriage and Married Life
Paul's exhortation to remain single is not a denial of the institution of marriage itself, which is a basic truth of Scripture. His exhortation must be understood as having been spoken with his passion for spreading the gospel and the tribulation that would come before the return of Christ in mind.
This is also proven by the fact that Paul advised that if a person cannot control the passions of the flesh, it is good to marry because of sexual immorality. Of course, Paul's advice does not present marriage as a refuge from sexual immorality; it is only saying that human sexual instinct must be resolved within the normal relationship of marriage.
7:8-16 Teachings on Singleness and Divorce
He gives exhortations about the problem of divorce among married people, which is broadly divided into the divorce of those both of whom are believers and the divorce of a believer married to an unbeliever. First, Paul in principle forbids the divorce of those who have become husband and wife in Christ. In particular, he reminds them that the command forbidding divorce for couples who are both believers is not a mere opinion but 'the Lord's command,' and demands absolute obedience.
7:17-24 An Attitude of Life Not Bound by Status
Paul extends the principle that he applied in exhorting about married life up to this point and applies it to the whole life of Christians. That is, just as whether one is married or not is itself not important, believers too, whatever their worldly status and circumstances, should not be bound by them but should discern what the will of God is in the given situation and live a life worthy of it.
7:25-40 Concrete Teaching on Whether to Marry and the Problem of Widows' Remarriage

[Chapter 8] The Problem of Christian Freedom Concerning Food Sacrificed to Idols
8:1-13 The Problem of Eating Food Sacrificed to Idols
At that time there was a sharp conflict within the Corinthian church over whether, in connection with idol worship, it was permissible or not to eat food sacrificed to idols. Those who insisted that it was permissible thought that they themselves were spiritually superior.
Christian freedom is not that one may do whatever one thinks right or whatever one wants to do, but must always presuppose a sense of responsibility as a community.

[Chapter 9] Paul's Example and Exhortation in Giving Up Freedom and Rights
9:1-14 Paul's Example of Voluntarily Limiting the Rights of an Apostle
Paul sets forth that he has the right as an apostle to be supported by the church, and that his not using that right is based on the following principle of restraining one's freedom. He makes clear that the reason was to ensure that there would be no hindrance at all in spreading the gospel of Jesus Christ.
9:15-23 The Ultimate Purpose of Restraining One's Rights and Freedom as an Apostle
Although he was an orthodox Jew, when Paul preached the gospel to the Gentiles who did not know the law, he conducted himself as one without regard to the law, and when he preached the gospel to the Jews who were still under the law, he showed himself striving to keep the law, and to the weak he behaved as one who is weak.
This attitude was not double-dealing or opportunistic; he took it because he wanted to be faithful to the great principle of spreading the gospel and saving souls. So he had no great difficulty in restraining his rights and freedom as an apostle.
9:24-27 The Parable of the Athletes and an Exhortation to Self-Control Through His Own Example
In Corinth the Isthmian Games were held every three years. He teaches that, like athletes running toward the finish line, believers should take Christ as their goal and live limiting and controlling their freedom in order to obtain the eternal crown of the kingdom of God. Paul emphasizes that, in order not to lose this reward, he has a clear goal and also thoroughly strikes his own body and brings it into subjection, urging believers to imitate his life of self-control.

[Chapter 10] The Prohibition of Idolatry Through the Example of Israel's History, and an Exhortation Concerning Food Sacrificed to Idols
10:1-13 The Danger of Abusing Freedom as Seen Through the History of Israel
He reminds them that although the people of Israel at the time of the Exodus personally experienced the tremendous power of God, because of idol worship and absurd grumbling and complaining against God, most of them did not enter the promised land of Canaan and were punished.
10:14-22 A Warning Against the Danger of Falling into Idol Worship
Paul first commands them to avoid eating food sacrificed to idols knowingly, because doing so is idol worship. To explain the reason, he takes as an example the Lord's Supper that Christians observe, and, illustrating the meaning and lesson that the cup of blessing we drink is a participation in the blood of Christ and the bread we break is a participation in the body of Christ, he warns that because what the Gentiles sacrifice is fundamentally the worship of demons, eating food sacrificed to idols is having fellowship with those demons and participating in the cup of demons and the table of demons.
10:23-11:1 Concluding Exhortation Concerning Food Sacrificed to Idols

[Chapter 11] The Position and Order of Sisters in the Church, and the Right Attitude Toward the Lord's Supper
11:2-16 The Position and Order of Sisters in the Church
Interpreting Scripture as supporting male superiority is not appropriate at all. Paul emphasizes that both men and women belong to God and fulfill indispensable roles toward each other. That is, men and women are by no means in a competitive relationship but rather in a relationship of mutual dependence and complementarity. That the positions and roles of brothers and sisters in the church differ from one another is not to determine who is higher or lower in rank but only for order and harmony so that glory may be given to God.
11:17-34 Teaching on the Lord's Supper
The Lord's Supper of the early church took the form of a communal meal combined with fellowship. They first had the love feast (communal meal) to promote the fellowship of believers, and near the end of the love feast they held the Lord's Supper. Paul sternly rebuked the Corinthian church for using the communal meal to divide along class lines, and taught the right observance of the Lord's Supper by explaining its origin and fundamental meaning.

[Chapter 12] The Diversity and Unity of Gifts, and Gifts Related to Public Duties in the Church
12:1-11 The Diversity and Unity of Gifts
The Corinthian church was a church rich in gifts and lacking in nothing. But the various gifted people were each eager to boast, regarding only the gift they had received as the highest. So through this text Paul, while making known the origin of spiritual gifts, also speaks of the diversity of spiritual gifts, urging the church to become one through a right understanding of gifts.
12:12-27 The Analogy of the Members of the Body
The church is the body of Christ, formed by believers who have different gifts and offices united as one. Therefore believers should respect one another and abandon the attitude of boasting of their gifts or despising others. Also, within the church they should use the gifts God has given them by taking on not the service they want but the service the church needs. In the end, when all believers love and devote themselves to the church, the church will become firmer and the gospel will be actively spread.
12:28-31 Gifts Related to Public Duties in the Church

[Chapter 13] The Nature and Eternity of Love, the Greatest Gift
13:1-3 Love, an Essential Element in the Use of Gifts
He speaks of 'the necessity of love,' that every act without love as its premise is of no benefit. To explain this, Paul presents as concrete examples the ability to speak in tongues and prophesy, the faith to perform miracles, and the acts of giving to the poor and being martyred for the kingdom of God.
13:4-13 The Nature and Eternity of Love
Paul emphasizes that the essence of love is agape love, which is an attribute of God, and that this is the absolute love revealed in the sacrifice of Jesus Christ. Love is practice, not theory, and is accompanied by self-sacrifice. Also, love is eternal: other gifts will pass away, but love, which is the essence of God, lasts forever. Therefore believers should imitate the love of God and sacrifice and serve for their brothers and for lost souls.

[Chapter 14] Exhortations Concerning Prophecy and Tongues, and Concluding Exhortations for Establishing Order in Public Gatherings
14:1-19 The Relative Benefit of Prophecy over Tongues
Concerning the Corinthian church's regarding the outwardly mysterious-seeming tongues as the highest gift and using them indiscriminately, thereby increasing the confusion of the church, Paul points out the limits of tongues in comparison with prophecy, which uses the same language, and exhorts them to eagerly desire gifts that can benefit the whole church.
14:20-25 The Purpose of Tongues and Prophecy
He describes the fundamental purpose of tongues and prophecy and encourages prophesying. Paul first urges the Corinthians to become mature in wisdom. This is Paul's judgment that the reason the Corinthians, more than the other gifts, desire and insist only on the gift of tongues is that they are still spiritually immature, and it means that the Corinthians should become spiritually wise, realize what is truly beneficial to the church and practice it, and show the maturity of faith.
14:26-40 Concluding Exhortation on Order in Public Gatherings
For the order of the church, Paul teaches the right use of tongues and prophecy and exhorts women to keep silent in the church. He rebukes the spiritual pride of the Corinthians and emphasizes that all gifts must be used in love to build up the church. He also states that his teaching was received from God and urges that it must be kept.

[Chapter 15] Teaching on the Certainty of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ and the Believers' Final Victory in the Resurrection
15:1-11 The Historical Certainty of the Resurrection of Jesus Christ
He mentioned the resurrection of Jesus Christ. This is because, had there been no resurrection of Jesus, we too could not have hope of resurrection. Therefore Paul first emphasizes that the resurrection of Jesus Christ is a clear historical fact.
The meaning of the resurrection of Jesus Christ is: ① it is the result of the fulfillment of the prophecies of Scripture; ② there are many witnesses who saw it, and a considerable number of them are still alive; ③ it is also proven by Paul's own salvation.
The reason Paul was changed into the greatest and most devoted evangelist of the gospel is that he met the risen Lord on the road to Damascus.
15:12-19 The Resurrection of Christ, the Absolute Ground of the Christian Faith
15:20-28 The Resurrection of Christ, the Guarantee of the Restoration of All Things
Paul emphasizes that the resurrection of Christ is the firstfruits that guarantees the resurrection of believers, and explains it by 'the principle of representation and union.' He states that the resurrection of believers will take place at the return of Christ, and that afterward, with the end of the world, Christ, having conquered all evil and death, will hand all things back to God.
15:29-34 The Believers' Faith in the Resurrection
Paul confesses that his assurance about the resurrection had a great influence on his evangelistic ministry and that he was able to preach the gospel boldly even amid danger. He emphasizes that faith in the resurrection is not mere theory but the power of true faith that overcomes despair and conquers fear. He also strengthens the Corinthian believers in their faith in the resurrection and exhorts them to avoid fellowship with those who hinder faith and to live a right life of faith.
15:35-49 An Answer Concerning the State of the Resurrected Body
15:50-58 The Believers' Ultimate Victory Through the Resurrection
Paul declares that when the Lord returns, the believers who have already died will rise first and live with new bodies, and the believers who are alive until then will also be changed into spiritual bodies. And he declared that, as the power of death no longer exerts any force, believers will in the end enjoy complete victory. Therefore believers should never be discouraged but stand firm in faith and hope, and, looking forward to certainly receiving a fitting reward for their labor, live with even greater zeal for the Lord's work.

[Chapter 16] An Exhortation to Give, Notice of Visiting Plans, and Greetings
16:1-4 Encouragement to Give for the Jerusalem Church and Guidelines for the Method of Delivery
Paul exhorted all believers to take part in the collection regularly every week to help the Jerusalem church, which was suffering from famine. He also said that the collection should not be made on impulse but prepared in advance, and that a church representative should manage it to maintain transparency, and Paul's attitude in actually doing so showed an exemplary stance of avoiding suspicion in the matter of church finances and carrying out good works carefully.
16:5-12 Notice of Plans to Visit Corinth and Mention of Timothy and Apollos
Paul states that he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, then pass through Macedonia and stop at Corinth to spend the winter, and afterward, with the help of the Corinthians, return to Jerusalem. Meanwhile, because Paul was not in a position to go to Corinth given the circumstances in Ephesus, he states that he is sending Timothy and asks that he be well cared for. From Paul's mention of Apollos, it appears that Apollos too refused to return so as not to be caught up in the factional disputes and so as to benefit the church.
16:13-18 Paul's Final Exhortation
Paul exhorted the Corinthians to be strong and courageous in the faith and to do everything in love. He also asked them to obey those who serve the church and to acknowledge and respect their labor. He emphasized that this is the fundamental solution and the best way to resolve division in the church and to extend the kingdom of God.
16:19-24 Final Greetings

[Chapter 1] God Who Comforts in Tribulation
1:1-2 _ Greeting
1:3-11 _ Comfort and Help in Tribulation
This is a message of thanksgiving and praise to God who rescues and comforts believers in the tribulations they suffer. God is the Father of mercies, and 'the God of all comfort' (verse 3). That God allows Christians to endure severe hardship is so that they would 'rely not on themselves but on God, who raises the dead' (verses 8-9). God is 'the God who delivers us' (verse 10).
1:12-14 _ Paul's Sincerity Toward the Corinthian Believers
This is a defense of the sincerity of Paul and his coworkers in dealing with the Corinthian believers. The apostle Paul did not act with fleshly wisdom when dealing with the believers of the Corinthian church. He acted only in the holiness and sincerity of God and by the grace of God. And he was able to testify to this by his conscience.
1:15-24 _ An Explanation for the Change in Plans to Visit the Corinthian Church
'So that you might receive a double blessing (2 Corinthians 1:15)' - this simply means that he hoped to meet and fellowship with them face to face twice. Paul planned to visit Corinth first, go from there to Macedonia, and then come again from Macedonia to Corinth. In this way he could meet the Corinthian believers face to face and fellowship with them twice. Therefore the saying that he would let them receive grace twice means that by meeting face to face and fellowshipping twice they would come to share grace.
Because of the change in his plan to visit Corinth, Paul was accused of being unfaithful and rash. As a result, there was a danger that the gospel Paul preached would come under criticism. So in this section he actively defends that the gospel he preached is trustworthy. Despite the weakness of the evangelist who preaches the word, the truth of the gospel is sure truth. This is because that gospel did not come from the evangelist but is founded on the faithful God.

[Chapter 2] The Fragrance of Christ
2:1-4 _ The Reason for Postponing the Third Visit to Corinth
The apostle Paul did not want to go to Corinth in sorrow. What would be a case in which Paul would go in sorrow? It would probably be a case where, because some of the Corinthian believers did not turn from their wrongdoing, he would have to discipline them using the apostolic authority given to Paul. Because Paul had overflowing love toward the Corinthian believers, he truly wished to go to them with joy.
2:5-11 _ Church Discipline and Forgiveness of the One Who Sinned
'Such a person' spoken of in this text seems to refer to the one who committed the sin of incest recorded in 1 Corinthians 5. That the person was punished by the majority seems to refer to his having received public discipline. Here we should think about the fact that the authority of church discipline has been entrusted to the church of God.
The reason Paul told them to forgive and comfort him is that the one who had sinned had already turned back. Although he had sinned, the one who repented should be forgiven and comforted. The apostle Paul was concerned that the offender, discouraged and in despair because of the discipline, might even give up his faith in God.
2:12-13 _ The Reason Paul Left Troas and Went to Macedonia
After 'the uproar in the theater of Ephesus over the goddess Artemis (Acts 19),' Paul left Ephesus and crossed over to Troas. Although a door was opened in Troas to preach the gospel, he did not meet Titus, whom he had sent to find out the situation of the Corinthian church, and his spirit was not at rest, so he went to Macedonia.
2:14-17 _ Believers Are the Fragrance of Christ Before God
In this section Paul speaks of two reasons for giving thanks to God. First, because He always leads us in triumph in Christ. Second, because through Paul's party He reveals the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ in every place.
Through the proclamation of the gospel by saved people, God makes the knowledge of Christ spread. Paul makes clear that in revealing the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ in every place he himself is no more than an instrument, and that the one who accomplishes all this is entirely God.

[Chapter 3] The Glory of the Ministry of the New Covenant
3:1-5 _ Letters of Recommendation from People and the Letter of Christ
Certain people went around carrying 'letters of recommendation written in ink by people,' boasting of themselves, denying Paul's apostleship and criticizing him. In response to such criticism, Paul testifies to his apostleship by making clear that the Corinthian believers, who were saved through his preaching of the gospel, are the letter of Christ, sealed by God through the Holy Spirit. Letters of recommendation written in ink by people are merely temporary things of paper, but he testifies that the Corinthian believers, as the letter of Christ, are eternal life written by the Spirit of God on the tablets of the human heart, and are therefore eternal.
3:6-11 _ The Glory of the Ministry of the New Covenant Compared with the Ministry of the Old Covenant
He is saying that the gospel, the new covenant, is superior in every respect to the law, the old covenant.
 1) The law is the old covenant, but the gospel is the new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6, Jeremiah 31:31-33, Hebrews 12:24).
 2) The law is the letter, that is, something written in letters, but the gospel is of the Spirit alone (2 Corinthians 3:6, Exodus 31:18, 1 Corinthians 2:4-5).
 3) The law kills, but the gospel gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6).
 4) The law was engraved on tablets of stone, but the gospel is engraved on the heart (2 Corinthians 3:7).
 5) The position of Moses, who delivered the law, was the ministry of the letter, but the one who preaches the gospel has the ministry of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:7-8).
The ministry of the letter also had glory, though a temporary glory. But the ministry of the Spirit is even more glorious.
 6) Moses, who delivered the law, had 'the ministry of condemnation (the ministry of death),' but the one who preaches the gospel has 'the ministry of righteousness (the ministry of life)' (2 Corinthians 3:9).
 7) The law too was glorious, but the gospel is even more glorious (2 Corinthians 3:9-10).
'What was glorious' is said of the ministry of condemnation, and it declares that this ministry of condemnation is no longer glorious because of the ministry of righteousness, which is greater.
 8) The ministry of condemnation will pass away, but the ministry of the Spirit will remain (2 Corinthians 3:11).
 9) Under the law one cannot see the glory of Christ, but the gospel lets one see the glory of Christ clearly (2 Corinthians 3:15-16).
 10) The law binds, but the gospel sets free (2 Corinthians 3:17).
 11) The law does not do so, but the gospel transforms a person to be like the image of Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18).
3:12-18 _ The Work That Appears Through the Spirit of the Lord
It speaks of the work that appears through the Spirit of the Lord, the Holy Spirit. The Jewish legalists were hard of heart, and their hearts were still covered by the veil called the law. But when they turn to Christ, that veil will be taken away. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is the work that sets free, the work of gradually seeing the glory of the Lord clearly.
[Chapter 4] God Who Works Through Weak People
4:1-6 _ The Attitude in Life of Those Who Have Received the Ministry of the New Covenant
It makes clear the attitude in gospel preaching of the apostle Paul, who received the ministry of the new covenant from God.
1) A worker must not lose heart under any circumstances (2 Corinthians 4:1).

[Chapter 12] The Revelation Shown to the Apostle Paul
12:1-10 _ The Visions and Revelations of the Lord Shown to Paul
Fourteen years earlier, Paul had the experience of being caught up to the third heaven (paradise). By the word "caught up," Paul makes clear that he was taken up to the third heaven entirely by the sovereignty and power of God, quite apart from his own will. The reasons he speaks of his own experience as though it were that of a third person are:
1) He was probably aware that what he wanted to say, for whatever reason, belonged to the category of boasting.
2) He did not make himself prominent because the subject of this event was Christ. Even in telling of this experience, Paul had a humble heart, holding that only Christ should be seen.
3) He wanted to build up the church rather than seek personal benefit.
4) He may have said "a man in Christ" because all Christians will have the same experience later by the power of God.
"Whether in the body or out of the body" - He does not know whether it was an experience in which the soul left the body or whether the body too was taken along.
Paul was a man who had received many revelations from God. Therefore there was a danger that he might exalt himself, that is, become proud. Not because he was proud but to prevent that pride, a thorn in the flesh, that is, a messenger of Satan, was given to Paul.
"A messenger of Satan" - Because it could become a channel through which Satan could work. Paul boasted of it. In keeping with the word that God's power is made perfect in weakness, it was because he was willing to accept the thorn in his flesh as much as necessary if God's power could rest upon him.
12:11-13 _ All the Patience, Signs, Wonders, and Miracles Shown in the Corinthian Church
"Though I am nothing" - This means that Paul himself is nothing when compared with the Lord. That is, the Lord alone is everything. It means that Paul has nothing at all to boast of in himself.
"I am not at all inferior to the super-apostles" - These words come from his confidence in the calling and office entrusted to him by God.
12:14-18 _ The Plan for the Third Visit to Corinth
This passage reveals Paul's plan for his third visit to the church in Corinth. It also announces his policy that even when he visits, he will keep to self-supporting ministry as he has done until now. Next, he declares his innocence regarding the slander against him. What Paul truly desired from the Corinthian believers was the Corinthian believers themselves. Because Paul valued souls highly, he was prepared to spend even his possessions and his life.
12:19-21 _ Various Cases Expected When Facing the Corinthian Believers
When Paul visited Corinth, he feared that four situations might occur. First, he feared that they would meet in a way neither of them wanted. Second, he feared that there might be quarreling, jealousy, anger, factions, slander, gossip, arrogance, and disorder. Third, he feared that God might humble Paul before the Corinthian believers. To be humbled means to be looked down upon. Fourth, he feared that he would be grieved over the many who had sinned and had not repented. He says this in order to urge their repentance indirectly.

[Chapter 1] Defending the Gospel of Grace 1
1:1 ~ 5 _ The Office of Apostle Was Received from God
"Paul, an apostle through Jesus Christ and God the Father"
False teachers attacked Paul's apostleship. In response, Paul first states to the Galatian believers that his apostleship is not from men but came about through God.
"The gospel of grace according to the will of God"
These are words that condense the gospel. The gospel of grace was accomplished by Jesus according to the will of God the Father. By becoming the sacrifice of atonement for sinners, Jesus showed grace so that sinners might receive salvation.
1:6 ~ 10 _ An Explanation of the Other Gospel
"Another gospel"
The representative false teaching that the false teachers taught. It is the teaching of legalists who claim that salvation cannot be received by the grace of Christ alone (the grace of Christ + keeping the law, such as circumcision).
The false teachers were not completely denying the gospel. They claimed that one must believe in Jesus too, but must also be circumcised to be saved. "Another gospel" seems similar to the gospel, but it differs in a decisive point. They speak of the Lord's death and also of the resurrection, but they say that being saved by these is not enough, so one must also be circumcised and keep the law. Since Jesus Christ alone is not enough, doing something more - that is another gospel.
1:11 ~ 24 _ Receiving the Gospel of Grace by the Revelation of God
The apostle Paul felt the need to defend the authority of his apostleship. He testifies how he met Christ and how his life was changed through Christ.
"But through a revelation of Jesus Christ"
'Revelation' - "to lift the lid," "to open the stage and show"
Revelation is not meant to hide but to make known. Therefore the gospel is something God has made known to us. The gospel was not made through human speculation or study but was revealed by God to man.
"Not according to man"
The apostle Paul stresses that the message he proclaims is not a conveying of his own thoughts, was not received from men, and was not learned, but is the gospel that God alone revealed. Paul did not learn directly from Jesus as the twelve disciples did.
But God showed the apostle Paul a wondrous mystery and made him know it. He did not consult with flesh and blood. The revelation of Jesus that he received on the road to Damascus was so clear that Paul, having received the revelation, had no need at all to consult with others.

[Chapter 2] Defending the Gospel of Grace 2
2:1 ~ 10 _ The Leaders in Jerusalem Approve the Gospel of Grace
To refute the claim of the legalists that circumcision and keeping the law are conditions for salvation, Paul mentions what was discussed and decided in the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15).
"The apostle Paul's visit to Jerusalem"
He first states that going up to Jerusalem was by the revelation of God. The apostle Paul reported to the church in Jerusalem the wondrous result of the mission by which God had saved the Gentiles. The reason for giving a mission report to the church in Jerusalem was that he needed to be recognized by the church in Jerusalem, which was the center of the early church.
The influential ones: Peter, John, James, and the leaders of the church who had an important influence on the believers of the Jerusalem church at that time.
After formally giving the mission report before the church in Jerusalem, Paul conveyed it privately to a few of the influential ones.
Paul stresses that he met the influential ones separately and reported the results of the Gentile mission, not for any personal benefit or to strengthen his personal standing as an apostle, but out of a desire that his labor for the gospel up to that time not be in vain.
2:11 ~ 21 _ The Gospel of Grace Is Revealed by Rebuking Peter's Error
Even one regarded as a pillar of the church in Jerusalem, if he did not walk according to the truth of the gospel, could not but become a proper object of rebuke.
The cause of Peter's wrong conduct was fear. Because he feared men, he acted in a way unworthy before God.
Peter's conduct was not merely a private act but a public matter that affected the rest of the Jews and even Barnabas, so Paul could not but rebuke him openly so that everyone would take warning. Through this incident, Paul taught that no one may be allowed to act outside the truth of the gospel, and by being able to rebuke even the apostle Peter, he dismissed the claim that his own apostleship was inferior to that of the other apostles.
The gospel of grace given by God makes Jews and Gentiles one. Peter's hypocrisy was to divide Gentiles and Jews. Peter's conduct was contrary to the gospel of grace, and by rebuking Peter's hypocrisy, the gospel of grace given by God came to be revealed all the more.
"To be justified" - It means 'to declare righteous'
A person cannot be justified by works of the law. All people have sinned and so cannot attain the righteousness of God. But God, the sovereign of righteousness, has opened the way for Him to recognize as righteous those who believe in Him through Jesus Christ. That God recognizes someone as righteous is not according to human ethics but is a legal declaration of God.
"We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners"
"Jews by birth" = it means that they were Jews from the time they were born, not Gentiles who had converted. "Gentile sinners" = from the Jewish viewpoint, it refers to 'people outside the covenant.' Because they are not God's chosen people, they are sinners.
Paul explains that one does not obtain salvation merely by being a Jew from birth, nor are Gentiles judged because they do not keep the law. Being justified means that both Jews and Gentiles must believe in Christ.
"But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were found to be sinners"
"If being justified by faith in Christ is wrong before God, like the Gentile sinners who break the law"
If [eating with Gentiles] is wrong and a sin before God as the Jews thought, then the teaching of Christ, who saved Jews and Gentiles and made them one, would be wrong, and Christ would be one who promotes sin.
But since Christ is by no means one who causes sin, Peter's hypocrisy was wrong, and no one can ever be justified by works of the law but only in Christ.
"For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor"
Even if following the example of Jesus were to cause one to sin by breaking the law, Paul says there is no reason to rebuild and follow the sphere called the law, which has been torn down.
To follow again the law that he himself had torn down would make him self-contradictory and a sinner who opposes God. Paul says that if he were to follow again the law he had rejected, that would be enough to bring ridicule on him as the most foolish of all sinners.

[Chapter 3] Explaining the Gospel of Grace 1
3:1 ~ 5 _ The Holy Spirit Is Received by Believing the Gospel of Grace, Not by Works
Rebuking the foolishness of the Galatian believers, he makes clear that receiving the Holy Spirit is possible only by believing the gospel.
"You foolish Galatians"
① Because, though they know the meaning of Christ's being crucified, they turn back to works of the law. (verse 1)
② Because, though they know that being saved is the work of the Holy Spirit and that the Holy Spirit is received when one believes, they turn back to the law. (verse 2)
③ Because, though they suffered much from the legalists after receiving the gospel, they accept the law. (verse 4)
④ Because they turn back to the weak and worthless elementary principles and become slaves.
"Did you suffer so much in vain?"
'Did you suffer so much in vain? Is it truly in vain?'
Although they suffered much because of believing the gospel of grace, if they now follow the conduct of the legalists, he is saying that the labor of faith they have built up until now and the persecution they have received all amount to nothing but wasted effort.
3:6 ~ 14 _ Abraham Was Justified by Believing the Gospel of Grace
Taking Abraham, the ancestor of the Jews, as an example, he shows the validity of justification by faith and explains the blessing of salvation that everyone who believes the gospel of grace will enjoy.
"Abraham believed God": quoted from Genesis 15:6
When Abraham obeyed the word of God and came to the land of Canaan, God promised to give him a son. Since there was no news of a child even though he waited, Abraham's heart wavered. To such an Abraham, God confirmed the promise again that He would give him a son.
Abraham believed the word that God would give him descendants, the word of promise. God counted it as righteousness. In terms of time, the righteousness of Abraham shown in Genesis 15 was recognized before he received circumcision, which is spoken of in Genesis 17. And in Genesis 22, Abraham was "justified by works" by obeying the word to offer Isaac to God. This is Abraham's proving by works the righteousness he had received by faith.
The reason the apostle Paul makes Abraham the center of the argument in front of the legalists of Galatia is precisely the fact that Abraham was justified while uncircumcised.
The reasons the apostle Paul cites Abraham whenever he stresses justification by faith: - Most of the legalists were Jews, and Jews were always boasting of being descendants of Abraham. - It was because he wanted to teach that salvation by faith is also found in the Old Testament.
3:15 ~ 24 _ The Purpose of the Law Is to Lead to Christ, Who Fulfilled the Gospel of Grace
The law is like a mirror. For a person to be saved, he must repent, and to repent he must realize how wretched a sinner he is before God. Therefore the law is needed in order to make clear that one is a sinner.
One of the important functions of the law is "to make one aware of sin." The law only shows sin. When one stands before the law, one discovers what is dirty and wants to wash it with water. It leads one to come to Jesus to solve the problem of sin.
The law plays the role of awakening sinners to the fact that they need the grace of God. The law only exposes the wounds of sinners; it does not heal their wounds. The law was given to make people realize the need for a Savior. It was so that sinners would realize that the law is not sufficient for them to be justified, and so be led to believe in Christ and obtain the grace of the promise.
"The law was our guardian"
Guardian: "a teacher who awakens," "a home tutor who teaches young children"; it means a teacher who was temporarily in charge of education in order to impart some important teaching
In wealthy homes in Rome at that time, a home tutor was kept to teach the children, and the tutor was even given the authority to strike the child. This tutor was chosen from among the household's slaves. The slave tutor took charge of the master's child and taught him well, and when the child had grown to a certain degree, he left the post of tutor.
This shows that the law has the limitation of serving as a tutor who leads people to Christ until Christ comes. God made them aware of sin through the law and used it in the role of leading them to Christ.
When the law, concretely put into written form, was given through Moses, it had the special purpose of making us aware of our sin and leading us to Christ. In that sense the law is temporary.
"It was added because of transgressions"
He teaches that the law was given not only to make people aware of sin but because of human transgression.
God promised grace through Abraham, and the people of Israel, though under grace, did not know how to be thankful for that grace. Because the people of Israel did not know their own weakness and thought they could obtain righteousness before God by themselves, He gave it to awaken that thinking. He gave it to make them aware of their sin and to keep them from sinning.
"Ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator"
The law was given through Moses. The law was given through a human mediator called Moses.
The gospel was given to us directly by Christ. This reveals a marked difference in their value and weight.
3:25 ~ 4:7 _ The Privileges of Those Who Have Become Children of God by the Gospel of Grace
"We are no longer under a guardian"
After Christ came into this world and fulfilled the gospel of grace, the law could no longer continue to rule over people. This is because after Christ came, people are not bound by the law but accept the gospel of Christ, which leads to salvation by faith. Therefore one who is saved by faith is no longer under the rule of the law.
"You are all sons of God"
All who believe in Christ have become sons of God. A sinner who could not escape the wrath and curse of God has now become a child of God. Even by moral resolve and works of the law one could not become a son, but through Christ one has become a son of God.
At the moment one accepts and believes in Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of the Son, dwells in our hearts, so we have come to be able to call God "Father." It is a beautiful title that only children of God can use.
"You have put on Christ"
When one becomes a person who belongs to Christ, next one puts on Christ. That is, it means entering into Christ as one puts on clothing. One becomes a person united with Christ. Here 'clothing' originally refers to a kind of adult garment worn by Romans after they came of age, which wrapped around the whole body. It carries the meaning of maintaining habits of life that become like Christ.
"You are all one in Christ"
The law clearly distinguishes between Jew and Gentile, male and female, master and slave. But those who have become children of God by believing in Christ are now all one. The fact that, knowing the truth of the glorious gospel and being saved, we have become one family in Christ lets us know that a Christian can be reconciled with anyone. Even someone like an enemy can enjoy peace by becoming a child of God.
"You have become heirs of God"
He said that if one belongs to Christ, he is Abraham's offspring.
"Those who belong to Christ" - those who have accepted the gospel of Christ by faith. "Abraham's offspring" - the same meaning as "sons of God."
Only believers in Christ can obtain the inheritance God promised. Physically we are not descendants of Abraham, but by coming to believe, through Jesus Christ, in the God whom Abraham believed, we have become Abraham's descendants spiritually. So, as promised, we have come to obtain the inheritance of God.
"Freed from guardians (protectors) and managers (administrators)"
"Elementary principles" - it means all the elementary learning of the world.
What the text especially speaks of through its background is the 'law,' which refers to the rules and norms that set down the conduct of life. When the gospel of grace of Jesus Christ was being spread, the law, after the new covenant had come, was nothing more than elementary principles.
Those who are under the law are called "still children, or slaves." Those who live under the grace of God are called sons who have come of age and enjoy the rightful standing of being able to inherit all the father's property. Jesus Christ redeemed those under the law. Jesus died on the cross and shed His precious blood. He paid the price and set them free from the law of sin and death. He lets us know that we are no longer under guardians and managers.
Redemption: releasing a slave from his status by receiving a ransom and setting him free. Paying a costly price to set a slave free.

[Chapter 4] Explaining the Gospel of Grace 2
4:8  ~ 20 _ The Galatian Believers Drifting Away from the Gospel of Grace
"You were slaves to those who by nature are not gods"
"Those who are not God" - "those who are not gods"
The apostle Paul speaks of the state the Galatian believers were in when they did not know God. Serving images made by man is idolatry, and God clearly forbade it. Even so, man who has left God by nature becomes a slave of idols. If one does not know God, one comes to serve idols.
"Turning back to the weak and worthless elementary principles"
"Worthless": it means a 'state of deprivation' in which people can do nothing but beg because of absolute poverty
The poverty that the law has is a concept in contrast to 'the riches of Christ,' and at the same time it describes the poverty and shabbiness of those who have left Christ. The law is weak, powerless, and poor, and so has no ability to redeem or ransom man.
Yet there were foolish believers who were turning back to the law. Their faith ought to be advancing, but it was going backward.
"Do you want to be enslaved to them all over again?"
He rebukes the conduct of the Galatian believers, who were leaving the redemption through the cross of Christ, that is, the gospel of grace, and returning to a legalistic way of life, as a life of abandoning the freedom of having been released from sin and going back to being slaves.
"You observe days and months and seasons and years"
'Days' - it means the fast days and the Sabbath that the Jews traditionally observed. 'Months' - it points to the new moon observed on the first day of each month, the month of Abib when the harvest begins, and so on.  'Seasons' - it refers to the Passover, Pentecost, the Feast of Tabernacles, and the Feast of Trumpets, the Feast of Dedication, the Feast of Purim, and so on, which were added by Jewish tradition.  'Years' - it means the sabbatical year that comes every seven years and the jubilee that comes every fifty years.
The apostle Paul rebukes them because, failing to realize the true purpose of the law and holding a distorted faith that makes the law a means of salvation, they have fallen into a greater yoke and bondage and have a vain zeal.
"To change my tone"
"Your faith seems somehow to be mistaken. I somehow have to change my tone. I cannot remain as I am. My heart aches so that I cannot bear it."
It means that Paul changes to a gentle attitude from the strong attitude with which he had rebuked the legalistic life of the Galatian believers until now. If Paul could go to Galatia right now and meet the believers, he would ask them directly about the points he doubted and confirm them, and so change his strong tone and treat them softly and gently.
4:21 ~ 31 _ Those Who Believe the Gospel of Grace Are Children of Promise
Using as an example the status and fate of the children born of Sarah and Hagar, it shows the difference between the gospel and the law, and teaches that those who believe the gospel are children of promise and can enjoy true freedom.
The Jews thought Ishmael was a Gentile. But the apostle Paul said that the Jews who held to legalism are Ishmael. The apostle Paul called true Christians 'children of promise.'
He says that just as the slave woman and her son were driven out, the Jews too, if they are not saved, will be driven out and will not obtain the inheritance. The only way for Jews to become like Isaac, the child of promise, is to be in Christ. The apostle Paul stresses that since the Galatian believers were not born of legalism but were born free, they must live freely, enjoying freedom in Christ.

Covenant of grace|Covenant of law|
Sarah represents the covenant of grace|Hagar represents the covenant of law|
Isaac symbolizes all who come to God by faith|Ishmael symbolizes people who put their hope in their own works and are bound to the law|
Isaac symbolizes the covenant of grace, in which one is saved by faith based on the word of God|The act of obtaining Ishmael through Hagar symbolizes the human act of trying to obtain salvation by one's own works by keeping the law|
A promise that came from God|A promise made at Mount Sinai through the law with Moses (the nation of Israel)|
It sets us free|It enslaves us|
Belonging to the Spirit|Belonging to the flesh|
Given in the land of Canaan, the Promised Land|Given at Mount Sinai|
Dwells in the Jerusalem above (the church)|Dwells in the present Jerusalem.|
A son of promise was given|A slave was given|
"For the children of the desolate woman will be more than those of the one who has a husband" - quoted from Isaiah 54:1
A prophecy that makes known God's providence that the people of Israel taken captive to Babylon would be restored and reach a glorious state
Expressing the relationship between God and Israel as that between husband and wife, He describes Israel as a wife forsaken by her husband and grieved in heart, one who had been a wife and then was cast off. Because of the wife's iniquity He forsook her for a moment, but He promises to show great compassion and, with everlasting kindness, to have compassion on her whose face He had hidden for a moment in wrath.
It is a promise that He does not abandon a soul that has sinned before God but will atone for it forever through Jesus Christ and have compassion on it.
"The children of the desolate woman" - the children of Hagar. The descendants of Ishmael. (the one born according to the flesh, the one under the law, the child of the slave woman) "The children of the one who has a husband" - the children of Sarah. The nation of Israel. (the one born according to the Spirit, the child of promise, the child of the free woman)
By saying that the children of the desolate woman are more than the children of the one who has a husband, it says that there are more people who try to become children of God by observing the law than children who appear through the promise of God.

[Chapters 5-6] Applying the Gospel of Grace 1
Christians who have received the gospel of grace through faith have obtained freedom from the bondage of the law. While actively exhorting believers to be free in Christ, the apostle Paul speaks about how to apply that freedom to life.
5:1  ~ 12 _ Stand Firm
To the believers who have obtained freedom from the bondage of the law because of Christ, he urges them no longer to be bound to their past legalistic way of life and to be on guard against the conduct of the legalists who lead believers astray.
5:13 ~ 15 _ Love One Another
He says that the freedom obtained through the gospel of grace should not be used for the flesh but only for serving the believers.
"Serve one another"
'Freedom' and 'serving as a slave' are completely opposite concepts, yet there is no contradiction at all. Such service is an act done voluntarily, from the heart, by a truly free person, and is service that follows the example of service shown by Jesus. A believer who possesses eternal freedom through the gospel serves as a slave by imitating the life of Christ.
"Serve as a slave" - it means "to do a slave's work," and this speaks of the attitude of service that believers should have toward one another.
"Do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh"
"Do not turn your freedom into an opportunity for the flesh"
It is a warning that believers should not make the freedom they obtained through the gospel an occasion for license.
It teaches that one must not fall into the temptation of legalism, and also must not take release from the law as an opportunity to fall into fleshly pleasure. A believer who possesses eternal freedom through the gospel must live a self-controlled life.
"Love your neighbor as yourself"
The whole law is summed up in the word 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' It is also a word that Jesus often stressed. The reason Paul urges love on the Galatian believers in this way is that he perceived a dispute that could well arise among them, as they, through a wrong idea of the freedom the gospel brings, would fail to show consideration for their neighbors and insist only on their own freedom.
5:16 ~ 26 _ Walk by the Spirit
The life of a believer must be a life guided by the Holy Spirit and one that welcomes the Holy Spirit. For a Christian to avoid a corrupt life and the path of destruction, above all he must live obediently, following the guidance of the Holy Spirit.
"You will not carry out the desire of the flesh"
The desire of the flesh is a concept completely opposite to the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and in the end it only adds sin to man. The desire of the flesh cannot be overcome by the law. Only by receiving the Holy Spirit can one avoid carrying out the desire of the flesh, serve as a slave in love, and enjoy true freedom.
"Walk" - continuous present tense. One must continue to walk by the Spirit.
One should not pray that the desires of the flesh be taken away but should pray to live by the Spirit. The desires of the flesh keep rising up. But the person who walks by the Spirit overcomes the desires of the flesh.
"You are not under the law"
The law cannot stop the flesh. The law only stirs up the flesh and brings sin to light. The only way to conquer the flesh is to walk by the Spirit. Because a believer saved by the gospel has come to be led by the Holy Spirit, he no longer remains under the bondage of the law, that is, under sin and death.
"Bear the fruit of the Spirit"
The fruit of the Spirit refers to the nine characteristics shown in the character of Jesus. When the Holy Spirit dwells in me and the Spirit of the Lord comes to rule over me, the fruit of the Spirit is borne in me. That is, the character of Jesus is being formed in me.
The fruit of the Spirit refers to the character that the Holy Spirit produces in a Christian when the Christian obeys the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

[Chapters 5-6] Applying the Gospel of Grace 2
6:1  ~ 10 _ Do Good to All People
To those who have received the gospel of grace, the apostle Paul says to do good. He says to do good to all people, and especially to do good to the household of faith.
"If a brother sins, restore him"
The spiritual (those advanced in faith) may have a sense of superiority over those who belong to the flesh (those of weak faith). The spiritual may lord it over those who belong to the flesh. Paul is warning against that. The spiritual must not lord it over a brother, must not arrogantly look down on a fallen brother, but must bend down and help them to rise. They must restore him with a gentle spirit.
"Sin" - "to stumble and fall," "a misstep," "to fall away"           It speaks of a sin closer to a fault or a mistake. It indicates taking part in an unlawful act because of weakness of the flesh. "Be caught" - 'to be discovered,' 'to be startled'           It means the embarrassment and surprise felt when a person who has sinned unknowingly comes to know the sin one day.           It is the fact of the sin becoming known by other people.
It means not to condemn or judge, with a sense of superiority, a weak brother who has committed such a sin, but to build him up.
"Restore" - "to return to the former state, or to be restored"
It presupposes that the one who has fallen was once a spiritual Christian who lived by the Spirit and had the mind of Christ but has now fallen into a fleshly state. Believers must exhort and set upright the one who has sinned. And they must be careful, since they too may be tempted in the same way.
"Bear one another's burdens"
"Burden" - a task or load that is harsh and hard to bear alone.             That is, an exhortation to strive to share the toil and pain suffered because of sin.
When a brother nearby commits a fault, they must bear one another's burdens. Even after raising up a brother who has sinned, they must hold him up and help him bear his own load. Merely raising someone up is not enough. There are cases where one must keep holding him up.
"Share all good things"
"Share" - it means to have or hold in the same way. It means common fellowship.  "Good things" - it has the meaning of 'good' and 'right.'
The one who is taught must have common fellowship with the one who teaches. Through that fellowship they must share all good things.
It includes not only material things but also spiritual things. It can be understood to mean that the one who is taught should not only supply the teacher with material support but also take part in the teacher's good ministry and share spiritual things together with one another. The apostle Paul is exhorting true oneness, in which all good things are shared together.
"Let us not grow weary of doing good"
"While we do good, we must not keep yielding to evil"
A Christian can grow weary in many ways. He may want to live the life of faith earnestly but grow weary because of the weakness of the flesh. He may grow weary when evangelism does not go as he wished. He may grow weary because of unexpected tribulation and long-lasting pain. He must remember the promise that if he does not lose heart but perseveres and endures, he will reap in due time.
"As we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone"
"As we have opportunity" - "making time."
He is not saying to do good when an opportunity comes, but to seek out opportunities and do good. He especially requires that it be done to the family of God. When a Christian sows to the Holy Spirit, he reaps an abundant blessing. Therefore one must do good to everyone without ceasing.
He sets a priority: do good to all people, but first to "the household of faith." One must live a life of sharing, with thanksgiving, the blessings God has given. He stresses concrete almsgiving and good works: sharing good things with those who teach and bear witness to the Word, and helping materially the many people around who are in need. This is a life of sharing blessings.
6:11 ~ 18 _ The Marks of Jesus
In the course of spreading the gospel, the apostle Paul suffered much, and because of persecution he came to have many wounds on his body.
"Wounds from persecution"
"Marks" - leaving a 'mark' or 'brand' on cattle or sheep, or on a person's slave, by branding, to show the owner
The marks of Jesus that Paul spoke of mean the many marks of suffering he received because of the name of Jesus in the course of spreading the gospel. They mean the wounds of persecution actually left by many physical sufferings. The marks of Jesus show Paul's life united with Christ and show that he followed Jesus to the end even amid many sufferings and persecutions.
"Let no one cause me trouble"
"Trouble" - it means 'inner pain or sorrow.' (Matthew 26:10, Luke 11:7)
The trouble Paul suffered was not violence or abusive words from the legalists. It was following another gospel, doubting his apostleship, and the dispute over circumcision. It is the grief of having to watch the Galatian believers being led astray by the legalists. The words 'let no one cause me trouble' have a strong character of an appeal earnestly hoping that there will be no more people in the Galatian church led astray by false teaching.
And there is probably also an appeal contained in it: 'let no one question my authority.'
"See with what large letters I am writing to you"
When the apostle Paul wrote letters, he did not write much of it himself but had others write for him. Perhaps one of the reasons Paul did not write many letters himself is not that the apostle Paul disliked work, but that because of an impairment of his eyesight he could not write in ordinary script.
The reason he himself wrote the end in large letters is to make certain that it was a letter sent by Paul himself. That is, it was probably to prevent forged letters.
"Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ"
"In my flesh, in my résumé, I have nothing to boast of. If it were not for Christ, who gave me forgiveness of sins, gave me eternal life, and changed my life, I would have nothing at all to boast of."
Through his final appeal to the Galatians, Paul says there are only two choices. He tells them to choose one of the two: either boast of the flesh or boast of the cross.
"By which the world has been crucified to me"
'Because of the cross of Jesus Christ, I and the world have drawn a line that can never be crossed. I have come out of the world and live looking only to Christ, who saved me.'
It means that through the cross, I and the world were cut off from each other. When Paul met Christ, he nailed the world to the cross. He says that the world's desires and ambitions were extinguished beneath the cross. It also shows that, as a result, Paul and the world are in a state of complete separation from each other. This change came about because of the cross of Christ. The personal change of a Christian does not come from willful resolve or moral pursuit. It occurs through the joy of regeneration, of having become a new creation through Christ.

[Chapter 1] The Church Is the Body of the Lord, Prepared Before the Foundation of the World.
The church was born through the wondrous work of the triune God; Jesus, by dying and rising, became the head of the church, and the church became the body of the Lord.
Structure
1) Praise for the saving work of the triune God for the church : 1:3-14
- The saving work of God the Father : He planned to send Christ and save us.
- The saving work of God the Son : God the Son came to this earth and completed salvation by shedding His blood.
- The saving work of God the Holy Spirit : He applies to each individual the work of salvation that the Father planned and the Son completed.
2) Paul's intercessory prayer for the believers in Ephesus : 1:15-19
- He desires that God give the spirit of wisdom and revelation so that they may know God.
- He desires that God enlighten the eyes of their hearts so that they may know what is the hope of His calling, what are the riches of the glory of His inheritance, and how great is the power He has bestowed on us.
3) The authority given to Christ, who died and rose again : 1:20-23
- Christ was raised from the dead.
- Christ sat at the right hand of God in heaven.
— He became the name above every name
— All things were put in subjection under the Lord
— He became the head of the church
— The Lord's power that fills all things is within the church.
☛ The church, born within God's wondrous plan, is not left on this earth like an orphan but is under the protection and nurture of Jesus Christ, the head of the church.

This is the chapter that gives the answer to the question of who the members of the church are.
Structure
1) The believer's past, present, and future (change of state) : 2:1-10
- The state before being saved : 2:1-3
- Salvation through grace : 2:4-9
- The future of the one who is saved : Ephesians 2:10
☞ It is one of the chapters of the Bible that best sets out the fundamental doctrine of salvation, and it records six basic doctrines about salvation.
Salvation is
① From sin
② By the love of God
③ Into life
④ Through faith
⑤ To display grace
⑥ For good works
☛ We who were by nature children of wrath were saved, by the love of God, through believing the gospel, and became people who do good works.
2) The believer's past, present, and future (change of status) : 2:11-22
- Our status before being saved (at that time) : 2:11-12  : the status of being outside God and Christ
① Gentiles,
② the uncircumcised,
③ people outside Christ,
④ people outside the nation of Israel,
⑤ strangers to the covenants of promise,
⑥ people without hope,
⑦ those without God.
- The wondrous grace of salvation (but now) : 2:13-18 : in Christ, through the blood of Christ, salvation was obtained, and Jew and Gentile became one.
- After being saved (from now on) : 2:19-22 : the church, a building in which Jew and Gentile are being built together
① Citizens of the kingdom of heaven and members of God's household.
② Built upon the foundation of Jesus Christ.
③ Becoming a member of the church, which is being completed like a building under construction.

[Chapter 3] The Church (in Connection with the Salvation of the Gentiles) Is a Mystery Revealed to Paul.
Paul became a minister for the sake of the gospel.
Structure
1) The mystery of the church revealed to Paul : 3:1~13
- The Gentiles become members of the church through the gospel : 3:5-6
2) Paul's intercessory prayer for the spiritual maturity of the church : 3:14-21
- That He may strengthen your inner man with power through the Holy Spirit
- That through faith Christ may dwell in your hearts
- He prays that, knowing the love of Christ, the fullness of God may dwell
☛ In the Old Testament one can find many verses saying that the Gentiles will be blessed, but there is no verse saying that the church, a third community in which Gentiles and Jews have become one, would be born. God revealed the mystery of the church to Paul, and Paul writes that the church is a mystery revealed to him.

[Chapter 4] We Must Be One Within the Church and Must Also Act in New Ways as a New Person.
This speaks of what must be done in a manner worthy of the calling.
Structure
1) On the unity and growth of the church : 4:1-16
- The command to the unity of the church : 4:1-3 (becoming one through humility, gentleness, patience, and forbearance)
