[Chapter 1] Opening Greeting and Paul's Explanation of His Imprisonment
The first half [verses 1-11] corresponds to the introduction of the whole book, and is the part in which Paul gives his greeting and offers thanksgiving and prayer for the believers in Philippi.
The second half [verses 12-30] corresponds to the first half of the main body of the whole book of Philippians [Philippians 1:12 - Philippians 4:9], and is the part in which, in the form of a testimony, Paul explains his imprisonment in order to reassure and encourage the Philippian believers, who were worried about it.
While Paul was imprisoned, he was able to preach the gospel to the guards who watched over him, to the Roman praetorian guard, and to the many people he met in prison (verse 13). As we look at the apostle Paul's imprisonment and the process of the spread of the gospel resulting from it, we are taught what a life worthy of the gospel is, and are taught to live a life that deeply recognizes and prepares for the significance of the suffering that is inevitably experienced in that process.
[Philippians 1:1-2] Greeting
The letters of Paul all begin in common with "grace and peace" to the believers of each church. We can learn that this is a greeting that reminds us that, for the Christian, this world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19) and is an environment in which suffering cannot be avoided, but that 'the grace and peace of God' are with us in the midst of it, enabling us to bear it abundantly.
Also, when the greetings of the letters are compared, the way Paul introduces himself differs slightly: in 1 and 2 Thessalonians and Philippians he does not refer to himself as an 'apostle,' but in the other letters he mentions 'his apostleship.' We can see that the reason is that where the church receiving the letter doubted the 'apostleship' of the apostle Paul, he wanted to make known that he holds the office of apostle according to the will of God, whereas for churches that already recognized Paul's apostleship there was no need to use such an expression.
[Philippians 1:3-11] Paul's Thanksgiving and Prayer
The apostle Paul gave thanks to God and rejoiced whenever he thought of the Philippian believers, and the reason is that the Philippian believers had been in fellowship in the gospel from the first day. What we must not forget as we live a life of fellowship within the church is that all our fellowship must proceed within the gospel.
We are taught that fellowship that departs from the gospel, fellowship that is not of people who live for the gospel, falls outside the work and power of the Holy Spirit who works in it, and cannot attain the goodness of God.
Christian fellowship is fellowship that accomplishes the Lord's will (preaching the gospel outwardly and perfecting the believers inwardly). Through fellowship, Christians preach the gospel together, do the Lord's work together, pray together, sing praises together, share life together, and share joys, angers, sorrows, and pleasures together. A life that is not active but passive in fellowship, a life in which fellowship does not take priority over life but one decides whether to attend fellowship according to one's own circumstances, is a very dangerous life in terms of faith.
Just as an electronic product is useless if it is not in contact with electricity, a Christian who should receive power through fellowship has a life of faith that cannot but be useless if he is not first connected to fellowship. The theme of faith to which a born-again Christian must be connected first is fellowship, that is, connection with the church. A Christian has fellowship within the church, which is the body of the Lord, and, following the power of the Holy Spirit, comes to acquire the character and qualities of a complete Christian.
[Philippians 1:12-26] Paul's Circumstances and the Spread of the Gospel
The apostle Paul testifies that his being imprisoned had rather served to advance the gospel. Paul was imprisoned, but because of this he had the opportunity to preach the gospel to the whole praetorian guard and to many people.
Even in prison, Paul testified of Christ and the gospel, and this became an opportunity for evangelism to people who did not know Christ. We can also see that even while imprisoned he set an example of a Christian through a right way of life as a Christian. As a result, the apostle Paul came to spread the gospel even to those of Caesar's household.
[Philippians 1:27-30] A Life Worthy of the Gospel and the Significance of Suffering
'Guidelines for living a life worthy of the gospel'
1) Cooperate with one mind for the gospel : Spreading the gospel is not done by doing it half-heartedly. Spreading the gospel is a spiritual battle with the devil, and a disadvantageous battle against the power of sin and the circumstances of this world. Therefore it is a hard battle that cannot be won unless all believers cooperate with one heart and one mind.
2) Do not fear your opponents and do not waver : Just as the stronger the light, the sharper the shadow appears, so when the gospel appears strongly, those who oppose it also appear strongly. The more opponents there are, believe that the light of the gospel is working strongly through me, and do not waver, relying all the more on the power of the light that is with me behind me.
The important exhortation that the apostle Paul commands us, as he exhorts Christians to a life worthy of the gospel, is that we suffer for Christ and for the gospel. This is an important guideline of exhortation that all Christians who believe in the suffering of Christ's cross and the grace of salvation through it must necessarily recognize and put into practice throughout their whole lives.

[Chapter 2] Urging Church Unity and Sanctification, and Commending Fellow Workers
The appearance of a complete Christian is formed through fellowship, and the chapter teaches the important elements that must be possessed within that fellowship.
[Verses 1-11] is the part that exhorts the Philippian believers, who had the problem of internal division, to be one with Christ at the center, and teaches that this is achieved only when they hold and practice 'humility,' the mind of Christ.
[Verses 12-18] is the part that urges them to strive for 'sanctification,' the more mature life of a Christian.
[Verses 19-30] informs them of the fact that Paul is sending back to the church in Philippi Timothy, his own fellow worker, and Epaphroditus, who had come to help him.
In chapter 2 we must especially remember 'the principle of church unity' and the mind and life of Christ that we must hold within it, that is, 'a mind of humility and a life of serving.'
[Philippians 2:1-4] The Principle of Church Unity
1) Christian fellowship has exhortation.
(Exhortation : to admonish so that one understands, and to make one strive for good works)
Through many exhortations, such as exhortation for spreading the gospel (2 Timothy 4:1-2), exhortation not to be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Hebrews 3:13), for an orderly life (1 Thessalonians 5:14), to practice love diligently (1 Thessalonians 4:9-10), to be sober-minded (Titus 2:6-8), to strive to assemble together (Hebrews 10:25), to strengthen the heart (Acts 14:22), and exhortation not to be led astray by another gospel and heresies (Jude 1:3-4), one is trained in faith within fellowship.
2) Christian fellowship has the comfort of love.
God permits Christians to suffer tribulation (the significance of suffering). But in the midst of that tribulation He gives overflowing comfort. Within the church, He has God's workers who first experienced tribulation and experienced God's comfort in it comfort many other Christians, so that they can endure other sufferings and tribulations.
3) Christian fellowship has compassion and mercy.
Compassion and mercy are to have pity and to show forgiveness and grace. We were saved by the great love and mercy of God, who is rich in compassion. Now the Christian who is saved must show that compassion and mercy within fellowship. In such fellowship of compassion and mercy we realize all the more what is the breadth and length and height and depth of God's love, and I too grow more complete in that love.
4) The necessary elements that believers must have for such fellowship
(1) Be of the same mind : Being of the same mind speaks of the unity of the believers. To be of the same mind, one must think the same thing. This is something Paul repeatedly stressed to the churches, and it is mentioned ten times in the book of Philippians.
(2) Have the same love : What is essential for the unity of the believers is to have the same love. The same love is possible only for Christians who have experienced salvation by the one Spirit of God. This is the love of the cross. Truly saved people can be united because they have the same love.
(3) Be united in spirit : When some goal is decided in the Holy Spirit within fellowship, they must go forward as one toward that goal.
'Being united in spirit' (Greek, σύμψυχοι) means 'of one breath, of one mind, spiritually one.'
(4) Think one purpose : This is a repetition of the earlier expression 'being of the same mind,' and the repetition of this exhortation lets us see how important oneness within fellowship is.
5) Things that must not be done within fellowship
(1) Strife : Strife is a work of the flesh planted by Satan, and because of it the fellowship of the Holy Spirit is cut off and the Christian's life of faith is destroyed. Strife comes from the desires of the flesh, that is, the fallen old nature.
(2) Vain conceit : Vain conceit is seeking one's own glory rather than the glory of God, and it means pretension and the perishable ambitions of the world. It becomes a cause of conflict that divides the church.
(3) Pride : Strife and vain conceit within fellowship come from pride, and we must not forget that this is a great sin before God. A person with a proud heart despises the other side, tramples on them, tries to stand above them, and recklessly says things that damage others' character.
The reason 'Lucifer' went from a powerful angel to the devil was 'pride.' (Pride is the cause of all ruin)
[Philippians 2:5-11] Christ as the Model of Humility
Christ Himself showed what this mind of humility is during the period of His public ministry and proved its result.
Jesus, who came to this earth, took 'the yoke of gentleness and humility,' was thoroughly humbled, came to serve all people (sinners), and died on the cross by obeying even to death. It was precisely this 'mind of humility' of the Lord that enabled Him to fully carry out the will of God the Father.
And at the resurrection He also clearly showed what the result of that humility is. That is, the risen Christ, as the result of humility, received the name above every name, and by being acknowledged by every tongue as Lord, entered into eternal glory. This is something we should meditate on deeply and be instructed by.
[Philippians 2:12-18] Exhortation for the Sanctification of Believers
The process by which a person is saved is this: from the fate of being born in sin and doomed to destruction, he receives 'salvation' freely by believing in the grace of the redemption of the cross of Jesus Christ, which God alone accomplished.
Receiving salvation is receiving 'justification' before God solely through faith. This is called 'salvation obtained by being justified through faith' (Justification), that is, 'the salvation of the soul.'
A person who has been justified by faith (= received the salvation of the soul) must now be changed as a complete Christian. This is called sanctification (Sanctification) and is called 'the salvation of life.'
The New Testament consists of the Gospels and the church epistles, which shows that the 'salvation of the soul' is achieved through the Gospels, and that the person who has achieved the salvation of the soul must go on to achieve the 'salvation of life' through the teaching of the church epistles. That is, the person who has obtained the salvation of the soul through the gospel must now necessarily grow into a man of God by accomplishing the salvation of life.
This salvation of life becomes an important factor that will determine the glory of eternal resurrection (the salvation of the body, glorification, Glorification) before Christ, who will judge us in the future.
[Philippians 2:19-30] The Plan to Send Timothy to Philippi and the Commendation of Epaphroditus
The apostle Paul commends (recommends) two men, Timothy and Epaphroditus, who devoted themselves for Jesus as true servants of Christ. The reason a certain person and his life are described concretely in the Bible is that they become a model and a lesson for our lives living today (Romans 15:4). We should deeply understand the life of the apostle Paul and the fellow workers of faith who walked with him, and imitate his life.
Those who can labor for the gospel are people of 'humility,' 'obedience,' and 'sacrifice' before God.
1) A person who humbles himself before God,
2) a person who obeys the will of God,
3) a person who knows how to sacrifice himself.
Also, as fellow workers, they...
1) shared the same mind with the worker (Paul) for the gospel. (Philippians 2:20) → (Matthew 10:41_In the name of a prophet..)
2) genuinely cared about the circumstances of the church. (Philippians 2:20)
3) put the work of Christ Jesus before their own. (Philippians 2:21)

5) had a heart not to cause the church worry. (Philippians 2:26)
6) risked their own lives for the work of the gospel ministry. (Philippians 2:30)

[Chapter 3] Warning Against Legalists and Antinomians
The 'warning against Judaizing legalists' and the 'warning against antinomians,' which were the most conspicuous sources of conflict among the believers of the early church, appear here.
The Jews, who had lived under the law by custom from childhood, tended to find the truth of salvation, 'one is saved only by believing in the grace of God,' too simple; on the other hand, among those who came into the church saying they had been saved after living in sin until yesterday, there were some who could not abandon their past sinful life and rather tried to settle into the world and a sinful life. So he awakens them to their mistaken points and teaches that the Christian must look toward heaven and strive all the more to know Christ.
Paul announces the standard by which he has lived with the goal throughout his life, and exhorts the Philippian believers to take that goal as a lesson and imitate it. Above all, this chapter presents the goal of faith that all Christians must look to, and presents a clear standard on which believers who desire a genuine life of faith can be united.
[Philippians 3:1-9] Warning Against Judaizing Legalists
Paul tells the believers to beware of the dogs, beware of the evildoers, and beware of the mutilators. These all refer to the Judaizers. The Judaizers at that time claimed that even if one believed the gospel of Jesus, one had to be circumcised in order to be saved. This was a subtle heresy that denied that the redemption of Jesus' cross is the complete and eternal gospel.
There is the work of the devil that persecutes the work of the gospel, but let us deeply recognize that the thought that subtly distorts the work of the gospel and claims that the gospel of redemption of Jesus Christ is insufficient is also the work of a high-ranking devil.
The true circumcision
1) Serving by the Spirit of God : serving not by one's own zeal but by the strength God helps with (1 Peter 4:11)
2) Boasting in Christ Jesus : boasting not of one's own works and righteousness but only of Christ's merit and grace
3) Putting no confidence in the flesh : the Judaizers prided themselves on being of the bloodline of Abraham and the people of God
[Philippians 3:10-16] The Goal of the Apostle Paul
The three values the apostle Paul pursued throughout his life
1) Jesus Christ : the apostle who recognized most clearly that Christ is the mystery of God. (Colossians 2:2)
2) The power of the resurrection : he knew that the eternal value of man will in the end be revealed in the power of the resurrection
3) Sharing in the sufferings : knowing that suffering is the value connected with eternal glory, he wanted to share in that suffering
[Philippians 3:17-21] Warning Against Antinomians
Gentiles who had lived until now not knowing God and never having learned God's law come into fellowship after being saved from sinning until yesterday, yet there are antinomians who cannot truly hate or repent of the sins they committed before being saved and the sinful nature of the flesh, and who even after having faith secretly keep their sinful life as it was and rather live settled in it. But Paul teaches with tears that the end of such a life is certainly destruction.
People who walk as enemies of the cross of Christ (the three great enemies of the Christian : the devil, the world, and the desires of the flesh)
The apostle Paul defines the life of the antinomians as a life lived as enemies of the cross of Christ. The enemies that drove Jesus Christ to death were 'the devil,' 'this world,' and 'the sin of my flesh.' Christians must clearly recognize these things,
① must resist the schemes of the devil,
② must not set their hope on the things of the world,
③ and must not be absorbed in the affairs of their own flesh.
Our citizenship is only in heaven
Here it is necessary to pay attention to the word 'only.' This world is not our true home. Our true home is 'only the kingdom of heaven,' where we serve the Lord forever and share love with the Lord. These 70-80 years in this world are a place where we learn for a while and pass through, and we are living the life of sojourners.

[Chapter 4] Paul's Comprehensive Exhortation to the Church in Philippi and Closing Greeting
Paul gives a comprehensive exhortation to the church in Philippi. Specifically,
① he urges the unity of the church that was stressed in chapter 2,
② he declares the thanks and joy that Paul holds toward the church in Philippi and asks them to share in it,
③ and he teaches once more about the right attitude of life of believers.
[Verses 10-23] is the concluding part of the book, and from it we can be taught the faith outlook of the apostle Paul, who testified, 'I can do all things through Him who gives me power' even though he was in suffering and humble circumstances, and we can glimpse Paul's heart as he conveys sincere joy and thanks for the help and material support the church in Philippi had given him.
[Philippians 4:1-3] Exhortation to Unity Among Believers
The meaning of 'stand' denotes the figure of a soldier on the battlefield standing firmly at his post even before the enemy.
Paul commands the Philippian believers that, although there are tribulations of the world and difficult situations within the church at present, they must not waver but must stand firm in the Lord. This brings to mind the command of the Lord, who commands us who are now 'soldiers of Christ' led by the Holy Spirit.
[Philippians 4:4-7] A Life of Rejoicing in the Lord
Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice! Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near.
A person who cannot forgive others and hates them can never rejoice.
Be anxious for nothing
It stresses being bold through faith. Because believers always believe that God is with them, whatever happens they have nothing to be anxious or afraid about.
But in everything, by prayer and supplication, let your requests be made known to God with thanksgiving
Because believers have a powerful weapon called 'prayer and supplication.' Therefore, it says always to ask God with thanksgiving. Then it says that the peace of God will guard our hearts and minds.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
The greatest grace granted to a Christian is not freedom from suffering and tribulation but the grace called 'peace,' by which one can overcome and bear them even in the midst of suffering and tribulation. Let us not forget that this peace guards and guides us until the day of Christ.
[Philippians 4:8-9] The Virtues Believers Should Strive For
The apostle Paul tells the Philippian believers to practice what they have learned, received, heard, and seen in him. This is the teaching of the gospel of Christ. The gospel is the gospel in itself, but for that gospel to be a true blessing to those who have learned, received, heard, and seen it, that person must practice the teaching of the gospel. This is faith that acts, and the Bible says that faith that acts is true faith. (James 2:17, 26)
- True : a heart and attitude that is not false
- Honorable (godly) : a state without fault in faith
- Right : a state recognized as right by God
- Pure : moral modesty
- Lovely : a state worthy of being loved
- Commendable : a state worthy of being praised
- If there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise : being morally outstanding and recognized and praised
[Philippians 4:10-20] Paul's Thanks to the Philippian Believers
A Christian must not avoid or resent the circumstances of life given to him but must learn to be content in those circumstances. It says that this is the secret of how a Christian lives in this world.
All the Christians who went before, including the Lord and the apostles, learned to be content in poverty and suffering, and they believed and hoped in the principle that that 'poverty' and 'suffering' would later be repaid as 'eternal wealth' and 'eternal glory.'
Paul rejoices greatly and gives thanks that the Philippian believers sent what he needed. Paul had already experienced the Lord's comfort and God's power amid his many sufferings (Philippians 4:11-13).
Apart from the Lord's comfort and power, he is commending the Philippian believers' sacrifice in worrying about his need and sharing in it, for which he is very glad and thankful. What we should consider from this is that, although there is the power of God working through us and our churches in this age, all the toil and cooperation by which we ourselves worry about and take part in our own church is something that truly pleases the Lord.

2:8-23 _ Warning Against the Heretical Thought That Entered the Colossian Church
This passage is a warning against the heretical thought that had entered the Colossian church.  It speaks of the things to be guarded against: philosophy and empty deceit, human tradition, and the elementary principles of the world (Colossians 2:8-10); Jewish ritualism (Colossians 2:11-17); exaggerated humility, the worship of angels, and boasting by relying on what one has seen (Colossians 2:18-19); and asceticism (Colossians 2:20-23).

[Chapter 3]
If chapters 1-2 of Colossians were the doctrinal explanation, chapters 3-4 are the part of practical exhortation about the Christian life. 'How do I live?' is determined by 'What do I believe?' This is because doctrine is the foundation of practice.
3:1-4 _  Principles of the Christian Life (Purpose and Direction)
It presents the goal and direction of life that a saved believer should pursue. As in the words 'Seek the things that are above!', the great principle, goal, and direction of the Christian life is 'a life that pursues the things above.' It also tells why one should live that way.
'Seek the things that are above'
First, because we have been raised with Christ.
Second, because Christ is seated there at the right hand of God.
Third, because the life given to us is hidden with Christ in God.
Fourth, because when the Lord returns, we will appear with Christ in glory.
3:5-11 _ The Character and Conduct of the Old Man That the Christian, Now a New Man, Must Put Off
A person who has been saved is one who has died and been raised with the Lord, one who has died as the old man and put on the new man (Colossians 3:10). Therefore he must put off the character and conduct he had when he lived as the old man before being saved. It says, ‘Put to death what is earthly in you (Colossians 3:5), but now you must put them all away (Colossians 3:8), you have put off the old self with its practices (Colossians 3:10).’
3:12-17 _ The Virtues of Faith That the Christian, a New Man, Must Practice, and a Christ-Centered Life
It speaks of the virtues of faith that the Christian, as a new man, must practice, and of a Christ-centered life. Because one has become a new man, there are things to put off and, at the same time, things to put on.
(Colossians 3:12-14) Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity.
One must clothe oneself with the character of Christ and practice forgiveness and love (Colossians 3:12-14). It tells us to let the peace of Christ rule in our hearts and to be thankful (Colossians 3:15). The word of Christ must dwell richly, and one must live a life of admonishing one another and praising God (Colossians 3:16). One must live a Christ-centered life (Colossians 3:17).
 ‘God's chosen ones, holy and beloved’ refers to Jesus Christ. It means to clothe oneself with the character of Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:27, Romans 13:12-14). It means to become more and more like the image of Jesus Christ. In particular, it tells us to practice a life of forgiveness and love. These two are the most important elements by which believers can become one.
3:18-21 _ The Family Life of the Christian, a New Man
It speaks of the family life of the Christian as a new man. It speaks of living a life of submission and love between wife and husband (Colossians 3:18-19), and a life of obedience and respect between children and parents (Colossians 3:20-21).
3:22-4:1 _ The Work Life of the Christian, a New Man
It speaks of the work life of the Christian as a new man. It urges Christian slaves and masters to live lives of sincerity and fairness. It says that slaves must act toward their masters with obedience and sincerity. And it tells the reason they must do so. The saved slave must act as to the Lord, with sincerity of heart and fearing the Lord, because he is one who serves the Lord and the Lord gives the reward (Colossians 3:22-25).

[Chapter 4]
4:2-4 _ The Prayer Life of the Christian, a New Man
A saved person must be devoted to prayer always and be watchful in prayer with thanksgiving. And what to pray for the evangelists is that God would open a door for the word, so that they may boldly speak the mystery of Christ. When prayed for, workers can, by the strength of prayer, make known in the words they ought to speak the mystery of the gospel, the mystery of Christ.
That it says to be devoted to prayer always means that prayer is not easy. A life of prayer does not come about by itself; one must strive in order to pray. And when one prays, one can receive answers and give thanks. And one can live a watchful life. In particular, it says to pray for evangelism.
4:5-6 _ The Social Life of the Christian, a New Man
It speaks of two things in the social life of the Christian as a new man.
First, it says not to waste too much time in relationships with outsiders (unbelievers) but to make the best use of it.
Second, it speaks of the life of speech. A saved person's speech must be restrained and controlled.
When words are spoken in grace and thanksgiving, they will be able to function like salt. If words are spoken in grace and thanksgiving, one will know how to answer each person.
4:7-9 _ Commendation of Tychicus and Onesimus
In commending Tychicus, Paul did not praise Tychicus's talents or knowledge. He merely stated that he is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord. Tychicus was a man born in Asia and raised in Ephesus, and was a fellow worker of Paul. On the missionary journey he was one of those who went ahead of Paul from Macedonia to Troas and waited for Paul's party (Acts 20:4).
Paul had Tychicus deliver Paul's letters to the churches in Ephesus and Colossae (Ephesians 6:21, 2 Timothy 4:12, Titus 3:12).
4:10-14 _ Introduction of Paul's Fellow Workers and Their Greetings
Aristarchus was a man of Thessalonica. He went to Ephesus with Paul, and there he was seized in the Demetrius riot and suffered (Acts 19:29). At the end of Paul's third missionary journey he became his companion again at Troas (Acts 20:4-6). He also accompanied Paul when he went to Rome as a prisoner awaiting trial (Acts 27:1-2), and in Rome he lived in prison with Paul and helped him (Philemon 1:23).
Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, during Paul's first missionary journey could not endure the hardships of the mission, left the mission team, and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). He was also the cause of the parting of Paul and Barnabas when they were preparing for the second missionary journey. But later his faith was restored, and he helped Paul and also helped Peter (1 Peter 5:13). He is also the writer of the Gospel of Mark in the New Testament.
Jesus who is called Justus is a fellow worker of Paul. He was one of those who worked for the kingdom of God.
Epaphras was a minister who preached the gospel. He seems to have gone back and forth among the church in Colossae, the church in Hierapolis, and Laodicea, preaching the gospel (Colossians 1:7-8). Epaphras prayed that the believers might stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.
Luke the beloved physician was a fellow worker who joined Paul at Troas during Paul's second missionary journey in Acts 16 and helped Paul at his side. By caring for Paul in his illness, he was a great strength to Paul. And he became the writer of the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts.
Demas was still at Paul's side up to this time. But later he left Paul's side and went off to Thessalonica (2 Timothy 4:10-11).
4:15-17 _ Instruction Concerning the Church in Laodicea and the Minister Archippus
Nympha's house was used as a place where Christians gathered.
Archippus appears to have been one who taught the word to the church in Colossae. That is why Paul urges them to tell him to take heed to fulfill the ministry he had received in the Lord (Philemon 1:1-2).
4:18 _ Closing Greeting
‘Remember my chains’ - this is the final concluding word of the whole letter, probably so that the Colossian believers, remembering Paul imprisoned and suffering for the gospel, would not be led astray by heretical thought but would stand firm in the gospel and work for the kingdom of God.
‘Grace be with you.’ The grace of God is the greatest gift that believers have received, and when that grace is present, believers live in peace and joy.

[Chapter 1] Thanks and Praise for the Church in Thessalonica, Which Rejoices Even in Tribulation
In this chapter, although the weak church in Thessalonica, having had only a short time of contact with the gospel, was at a beginner's stage in terms of faith, Paul expresses thanks and joy, and sends praise and encouragement, at the news that in the midst of tribulation they practiced the work of faith, the labor of love, and the endurance of hope, rejoicing and bearing up well under suffering, so that they became an example to all the believers in the surrounding regions of Achaia and Macedonia, and moreover that they had abandoned idols and served only God and held the eschatological faith of awaiting the return of Christ.
1:1 _ Greeting
1:2-10 _ Paul's Thanks and Praise for the Church

[Chapter 2] Paul's Recollection of His Evangelistic Ministry in Thessalonica, Thanks for the Church, and the Expression of His Hope to Visit Again.
As a series of passages in the first half of the main body of this letter (1 Thessalonians 1:2-3:13), which contains praise and encouragement toward the church in Thessalonica, it makes known the reasons for the praise and encouragement concerning the believers' attitude when Paul preached in this region in the past, and together with this it contains Paul's earnest hope to share a deeper fellowship with the Thessalonian believers.
 Accordingly, this chapter can be said to be the part that, by once again repeating the content of the previous chapter (1:2-10), in which thanks and praise for the faith of the Thessalonian believers are recorded, encourages the believers and also makes known the reason for sending Timothy that appears in 1 Thessalonians 3:1-10.
 Paul, who in the previous chapter greeted the church in Thessalonica, now in the main body of this chapter recalls his own zeal that he had shown to the Thessalonian believers all that time. That is, Paul makes clear that he undertook evangelism amid all persecution (1 Thessalonians 2:1-2), with the sole purpose of pleasing God (1 Thessalonians 2:3-6), with deep affection, resolved to sacrifice even his own life (1 Thessalonians 2:7-12).
 This recollection of Paul is meant to make the Thessalonian believers look at themselves once more and use it as an occasion to examine and reflect whether they have strayed from the gospel Paul preached in the past.
2:1-12 _ Paul's Recollection of His Evangelism in Thessalonica
2:13-16 _ Paul's Thanks for the Church in Thessalonica
2:17-20 _ Hope to Visit the Church in Thessalonica Again

[Chapter 3] The Sending of Timothy, and Paul's Joy and Intercessory Prayer After Receiving Timothy's Report
In the first part, verses 1-5, Paul, concerned about the persecuted church in Thessalonica, wished to visit but could not fulfill his wish because of Satan's hindrance, and so, in his place, he sends his fellow worker Timothy in order to strengthen the faith of the believers in the church in Thessalonica so that the work of evangelism would not be in vain.
In the middle part, verses 6-10, Paul, who heard through Timothy in Corinth the news of the church in Thessalonica, hears that the Thessalonian believers are standing firm in faith and love and overcoming well with joy amid all want and tribulation, and he is relieved and rejoices and gives thanks to God.
In the same way, God too is concerned about weak believers who easily stumble in daily life because of tribulation, persecution, or temptation, and in order to strengthen them He sends the Holy Spirit to comfort them, and always watches over and helps them.
The latter part, verses 11-13, records Paul's intercessory prayer for the church. Paul was deeply aware that, even if the plans are in man, the one who accomplishes them is God (Proverbs 16:9), and he teaches the believers by showing the faith that it is entirely possible only by the protection of God to keep right faith even while Satan, like a roaring lion, tempts believers, and to go boldly before the returning Christ.
3:1-5 _ The Motive and Purpose of Sending Timothy
3:6-10 _ Timothy's Report and Paul's Joy
3:11-13 _ Paul's Intercessory Prayer

[Chapter 4] Teaching on the Worthy Life of Believers and Teaching on the Return of Christ
The first half of this chapter (1 Thessalonians 4:1-12) keeps in mind that the church in Thessalonica, as a Gentile church, though it held faith in Christ, had not completely escaped the sexual corruption that was common in the Greek cultural sphere, and teaches the life of an exemplary believer by giving instruction on holiness in actual life and exhortation on brotherly love and diligence, which are Christian virtues.
The second half of this chapter (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18), together with the first half of the next chapter (1 Thessalonians 5:1-11), deals with the problem of the end times, which is the central theme of this letter; while the latter (1 Thessalonians 5:1-11) speaks centering on the timing of the return, the former (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18) gives teaching on the return of Christ and the resurrection of the believers that follows it.
In particular, in this chapter Paul corrects the Thessalonian believers' mistaken view of the return.
Because of a mistaken view of the return, the Thessalonian believers, judging that the end would come soon, did not work and only waited for the return of Christ; and when believers who had been longing for the return died without seeing it, they came to have doubts about the return.
So Paul says that when Christ returns, the dead will receive Christ before the living, so that the living are by no means better off than the dead, and he exhorts them to faithfully carry out the work entrusted to them until Christ returns and not to lose hope in the return.
In this way, it teaches that today's believers who await the return of Christ, holding a right view of the return, should be all the more alert and watchful, examine what they will be shown to be in the future, and faithfully carry out the things entrusted to them until Christ comes again.
4:1-12 _ Teaching on a Life of Holiness and Diligence.
4:13-18 _ Teaching on the Return and the Resurrection of Believers

[Chapter 5] Paul's Teaching on the Return of Christ
Paul, who in the previous chapter taught the right view of the return to the Thessalonian believers who lived disorderly lives with a mistaken view of the return, in this chapter teaches about the timing of the return and the duty of believers who await the return.
 It says that for unbelievers the Lord's return will come like a thief, but for saved believers who are awake it will not be a day that comes like a thief. This is because, although one cannot know the day exactly, one can prepare by watching the signs that will appear in the last times as recorded in the Word. (Matthew 24:3-31)
Therefore Paul urges all believers, in order to prepare for the return, to be always awake and sober, and to exhort one another with the hope of the return.
5:1-11 _ The Timing of the Lord's Return
5:12-22 _ Teaching on the Daily Life of Believers Awaiting the Return
5:23-28 _ Paul's Final Prayer and Greeting

[Chapter 1] Paul's Thanks and Encouragement to the Persecuted Church
Before correcting the misunderstanding about eschatology that arose from misunderstanding 1 Thessalonians (chapter 2) and correcting the idle, disorderly life (chapter 3), in chapter 1 Paul gives thanks for the growth of the Thessalonian believers' faith even amid persecution and tribulation (2 Thessalonians 1:3-4). And he encourages the believers by assuring them that when the Lord Jesus is revealed "from heaven with His mighty angels in flaming fire" (2 Thessalonians 1:7), He will repay those who persecute with the righteousness of God (2 Thessalonians 1:5-10).
In this way, unlike the content of chapters 2-3, which point out the errors of the church in Thessalonica and try to correct them, in chapter 1 Paul's love for the church in Thessalonica is well displayed even on the surface.
This record in chapter 1 shows well that Paul's rebuke and exhortation toward the church in Thessalonica that follow arise from Paul's love and concern to lead them to the right path. In this way we learn Paul's love and wisdom: rather than first reproaching believers when we see their shortcomings, he praises what they have done well and corrects what is lacking.

[Chapter 2] The Working of Satan and the Comfort of God
This chapter 2 corrects the present error concerning mistaken eschatology. Some of the believers in Thessalonica were swept away in an instant by the false teaching that the day of the Lord had already come. In response, Paul first makes clear the source of the false teaching about the day of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 2:2), and also makes clear the events that must take place before the return of Christ (2 Thessalonians 2:3-12). By explaining in detail the things that will happen before and after the Lord's coming, he had them hold a right eschatology.
Paul assures them that the day of the Lord has not yet come and that the day of the Lord will not come without warning. In particular, he explains that the apostasy must come first in the spiritual realm, and that the man of lawlessness (the son of destruction), who borrows the power of Satan, must appear (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4, 8-9). This man of lawlessness is the antichrist (Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:11, Matthew 24:15, 1 John 2:18, Revelation 11:7, Revelation 13:1-10).
At present there is one who restrains this, and it is until the one who restrains is taken out of the way (2:7). After that, the son of destruction will appear openly (2:8) and will work with power, signs, lying wonders, and deception (2:8-10), but in the end he cannot help being destroyed together with those who were deceived by him (2 Thessalonians 2:5-12).
But since those who hope for the return of Christ will obtain the glory of Christ (2:14), he exhorts and entreats them to stand firm on faith and hold to right faith (2 Thessalonians 2:13-17).

[Chapter 3] Exhortation Concerning the Disorderly Life
Paul asked the Thessalonian believers to pray for him (2 Thessalonians 3:1-2). He also prayed that they would hold to right faith (2 Thessalonians 3:3-5). After praising, correcting, and comforting those who read this letter, he ends the letter by admonishing in a resolute tone the group who lived disorderly lives using the truth about the coming of Christ as a pretext (2 Thessalonians 3:6-15). The doctrine of the Lord's return means that believers live diligently and wait with patience. This does not mean idleness but a faithful life.
