[Chapter 1] Greeting, Warning Against Heresy, and the Pastor's Attitude in Eradicating Heresy
Leaving his junior pastor Timothy as pastor of the church in Ephesus,
- he asks him to deal resolutely with heretical doctrine,
- he offers Paul's personal praise of the wondrous God,
- and he asks Timothy to fight boldly for the truth of the gospel.
It lies in "wage the good warfare, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you" (18). Paul, on his way to Macedonia, had Timothy remain in Ephesus. This was because there were those who taught "a different doctrine" (1:3), and it was to stop them. The teaching of the false teachers, "like gangrene," overthrew the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17-18).
Therefore a conflict between "sound doctrine and different doctrine" was unavoidable. This conflict will continue from the Garden of Eden until the day Jesus returns. The apostle who in the first chapter commands, "Timothy, my son, I entrust this charge to you ... wage the good warfare" (18), in the last chapter too urges again, "But you, O man of God ... fight the good fight of the faith" (6:11-12).
Paul himself, who gives this command, also writes, "I have fought the good fight" (2 Timothy 4:7). Here lie the tension and the prayer topics of pastoral ministry.
1:1-2 Greeting
1:3-11 Warning Against Those Who Teach a Different Doctrine
He urges him to block the influence of the different (false) doctrine and to strive to establish pure doctrine based on right doctrine.
1:12-17 God's Mercy Shown to Paul
It is a passage in which Paul recalls his own salvation and praises with fervent thanks God, who saved him, the foremost of sinners, and entrusted to him a precious office. This was to remind Timothy that just as Paul himself became a preacher of the gospel by the grace of God, so Timothy's becoming a preacher of the gospel was by the grace of God, and so to have him faithfully carry out his duty as a pastor.
1:18-20 Charge to Timothy
He urges him to have faith and a good conscience, which are the most important attitudes a pastor must have, and he refers to those who, by rejecting conscience, have suffered shipwreck in their faith. This is at once an urging for Timothy to guard his own faith and an urging to deal strongly with the heretics.

[Chapter 2] Teaching on Intercessory Prayer at Church Gatherings and on Keeping Order Among Brothers and Sisters
It records the command to Timothy, the evangelist, regarding intercessory prayer at church gatherings, and guidelines for keeping order among brothers and sisters.
The prayer in "make petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving for all people" does not refer to individual prayer but to prayer at church gatherings.
Why must we pray "for all people"? In the Old Testament era, the duty of the priest was not for himself but for the people. In the same way, Timothy, the evangelist, may be said to carry out the duty of a "priest" for the believers. By praying for all people, we may be said to fight the good fight for the kingdom of God and His righteousness.
2:1-7 The Command of Intercessory Prayer
It gives teaching on the command of intercessory prayer in prayer at church gatherings for all people, especially for those in authority in the nation, and on the necessity of it.
2:8~15 Teaching on Unity and Keeping Order Among Believers in the Church
It teaches that at church gatherings brothers must have unity without quarreling, and teaches about the attire and the sense of order that sisters must have at gatherings.

[Chapter 3] Qualifications of Overseers and Deacons, and the Purpose of Writing This Letter
It records the qualifications of the overseer, who holds the most important leadership position in the church, and of the deacon, who in practice takes charge of much administration and financial accounting, as well as the purpose for which this letter was written.
These are the qualifications of overseers and deacons. They may be called the commanders of God's army fighting the spiritual battle. For the church to carry out its mission of spreading the gospel, leaders are needed, and they must be those well furnished with qualifications. Therefore the church must look strictly at the standard. The reason many modern churches have declined in quality and the work of the gospel has ceased stems in many cases from the problem of the salvation and the caliber of their leaders.
3:1-13 The Kinds and Qualifications of Important Offices in the Church
Overseer and elder are used interchangeably, but "overseer" emphasized the responsibility of the office, while "elder" emphasized spiritual maturity more. A pastor is an elder in terms of spiritual maturity, and an overseer in terms of ministry.
The Greek word translated "overseer" (bishop) is [episkopos], and it refers to one who manages and controls. The other name in the New Testament that denotes the same position is "elder." Overseer and elder are often used interchangeably.
He was mainly in charge of teaching the word and looking after and guiding the whole life of the believers.
A deacon is one who in practice takes up various church tasks, takes charge of church administration and financial accounting, and assists the elder.
3:15-16 The Purpose of Writing 1 Timothy
The purpose for which 1 Timothy was written is that it is a book that teaches exactly how Timothy, the pastor, should carry out his pastoral ministry within the house of God, that is, the church.

[Chapter 4] Prophecy of Apostasy in the Last Days, Warning Against Heretical Doctrine, and the Pastor's Attitude in Training in Godliness
As the opening of the second half (chapters 4-6), which presents more concrete and practical solutions to pressing pastoral matters, it points out the prophecy about apostasy and the error of ascetic teaching. It also gives exhortation and teaching about self-discipline as a pastor.
"Deceiving spirits and the Holy Spirit" (1) appear. Spiritual warfare is the battle between the Holy Spirit and evil spirits. Paul urges Timothy: "Command and teach these things (11), devote yourself to teaching (13), persevere in this by watching your teaching (16)." Spiritual warfare is the battle between the Holy Spirit and evil spirits, the battle of the Word, and the battle of teaching.
4:1-5 Prophecy of Apostasy and Warning Against False Doctrine
While foretelling the phenomenon of apostasy, it warns against the mistaken teaching of those who had been tainted by heretical thought.
4:6-16 The Pastor's Attitude in Training in Godliness
It urges the pastor not only to strive himself to reach godliness but also to be an example to others in everything, to strive in the study of the Word, and to strive in exhorting and teaching the Word.

[Chapter 5] Pastoral Care for the Various Groups Within the Church
It teaches the instruction to treat all believers, men and women, old and young, as one's own flesh and blood, and guidelines for honoring widows. It also records the honor due to elders and how to handle accusations against elders, and records the attitude of the pastor who carries out church discipline.
This is teaching on how to care for the various groups within the church. The key lies in "treat them as you would a father, as brothers, as mothers, as sisters" (1-2). It means treating people of every group within the church like family. By serving like family, they become one. Thus the church is healthy and can exert strength.
5:1-2 Honoring Various Kinds of Believers
It exhorts that when dealing with the various people of the church, we must treat them like family. Even when giving an admonition or rebuke to older men, it must be done with an encouraging attitude. Younger men too must be treated as one would treat one's own brothers. When dealing with the older or the young, one must always treat them with a gentle and tender attitude.
Older women must be treated as mothers. Younger women must be treated with a truly pure heart.
5:3-17 Honoring Widows
It speaks of the matter of the treatment of widows, for which a solution was urgently required at the time and which required the greatest care. It says to care for widows who have difficulty making a living by themselves, and to guide well the younger widows who go about idly spreading gossip or meddling in others' affairs, so that they do not have a bad influence on the church.
5:17-20 Honoring Elders and the Attitude in Discipline
It exhorts them not only to respect the spiritual authority of the elders but also to support them well economically. This is because, if the authority of the elders is not respected, church order will not be properly established. It is also because, if spiritual leaders are troubled about making a living, the care of the believers will be neglected to that extent.

[Chapter 6] Teaching on the Slave's Attitude Toward Masters, on Godliness and Restraint of Greed, and Personal Exhortation to Timothy and Closing Words
It urges that those who are slaves socially have a right attitude toward their masters, that they devote themselves to the word of God and strive for godliness, and that they give up the desire for wealth so as not to fall into sin through covetousness.
It records the exhortation to fight the good fight of faith and the charge to tell the rich to strive for good works.
Warning once more against "a different doctrine," one of the most important purposes of writing this letter, it encourages, "Fight the good fight of the faith."
6:1-2 The Slave's Attitude Toward Masters
It is said that at the time this Scripture was written there were as many as 60 million slaves within the Roman Empire. This was about four times the number of free people, so one can guess how many slaves there were. Because of these slaves, the Roman Empire sank into luxury and pleasure.
But the Bible neither points out the mistaken contradiction of the system of slavery nor makes any claim about realizing a just society, such as rising up and starting a revolution.
It only speaks of the unseemly matters that arose within the church because of slaves. It seems that it frequently happened that a person who had been a slave until yesterday, after being saved, treated his master disrespectfully on the grounds that they had received the same salvation, or neglected work and so caused his master loss, or disobeyed his master's orders.
In response, Paul commands that as slaves they treat their masters with even more humility, and desires that they do their best in their position. This was the will of God.
6:3-10 Teaching on Godliness and Restraint of Greed
We must not be led astray by false teaching but strive to spread right faith, and we must strive to obtain the eternal reward of heaven rather than desire for the wealth of this earth.
6:11-21 Personal Exhortation to Timothy and Closing Words
Paul urges Timothy to fight the good fight of faith in order to take hold of eternal life. And he urges him to guide well those who are rich and capable in worldly terms so that they can strive for good works, and finally, once more warning against heretical thought and false teaching, he gives a closing greeting while urging him to hold fast to the faith.

[Chapter 1] Guard the Gospel
2 Timothy is a pastoral letter written by the apostle Paul, imprisoned in a Roman jail for the second time and facing his martyrdom, to Timothy, his son in the faith and fellow worker, the young pastor of the church in Ephesus, to warn him of the persecution of the church by worldly people and the attack of heresies that will rise fiercely in the last days, to teach and encourage him to deal with these with boldness and endurance, and to carry out all the better his mission as a pastor even in such circumstances.
1:1-5 _ Greeting and an Introduction Made Up of Thanks for Timothy and Hope of Meeting Him
The passage speaks of the notation of sender and recipient, the benediction, thanks for Timothy, and the hope of meeting Timothy.
1:6-14 _ Acceptance of Suffering for the Gospel and the Charge to Defend the Truth of the Gospel
The passage mainly deals with teaching and encouragement related to the attitude of a pastor. Here it reports the exhortation to accept suffering for the gospel and the charge to defend the truth of the gospel.
1:6-8 _ He commands him to suffer for the gospel by the power God gave.
1:9-12 _ He explains the reason one must suffer for the gospel in that way.
Because the grace of God's salvation has been clearly revealed in the gospel, and Paul himself says that he was appointed for this gospel, and he said he is confident that God, who gave the gospel, will guard that gospel until the last day. Therefore he exhorts Timothy too not to be ashamed of the gospel and to accept suffering for that gospel.
1:13-14 _ He repeatedly charges him to guard the truth of the gospel.
1:15-18 _ The Contrasting Conduct of Acquaintances Toward Paul, Imprisoned in a Roman Jail
This passage mainly deals with teaching and encouragement related to the attitude of a pastor, and here it is a word concerning the contrasting conduct of acquaintances toward Paul, who was imprisoned for the second time in Rome.
1:15 _ He states that all his acquaintances in Asia had abandoned him, and that among them Phygelus and Hermogenes were two of such people.
1:16-18 _ He states that even while everyone was leaving him, only Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Paul but diligently searched for Paul and comforted him, and he petitions the Lord to show mercy to the household of Onesiphorus.

[Chapter 2] Teach the Gospel
2 Timothy is a book written for all believers of the New Testament era who have the responsibility to endure all things with patience and strive for the expansion of the kingdom of God even though, as the last days draw near, there will be countless persecutions from the world, and in particular for pastors who have the responsibility to protect the church and the believers amid tribulation.
Accordingly, chapter 2, which teaches about the attitude and reward of the Lord's servant through the three illustrations of the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer and through the testimony about the attitude of his own life, which he had devoted for a lifetime as the Lord's servant, and which also teaches about the things pastors should strive for in order to have a successful ministry, can be called the key chapter of 2 Timothy.
2:1-7 The Command to Carry On the Gospel Ministry by Training Ministers, and Teaching on the Attitude of a Faithful Minister of the Gospel
The passage is a command to carry on the gospel ministry by training ministers and a teaching on the attitude of a faithful minister of the gospel.
2:1-2 _ He commands Timothy to train ministers and carry on the gospel ministry.
2:3-6 _ As guidelines for training ministers and also guidelines for Timothy himself, a pastor, he teaches the attitude of the Lord's servant through the illustrations of the good soldier, the athlete, and the hardworking farmer.
Here the illustration of the good soldier was introduced to teach that the Lord's worker must not be entangled in the life of this world but must live a life of absolute obedience to the Lord's command for the sake of the kingdom of God; the illustration of the athlete, that he must live according to the word of truth the Lord taught; and the illustration of the hardworking farmer, that he must carry out the ministry with faithfulness until the fruit of the ministry is borne.
2:7 _ He urges him to ponder deeply these teachings of Paul himself.
2:8-13 The Model of Endurance That Ministers Should Imitate, and the Presentation of Certain Future Glory
The passage presents the model of endurance that ministers should imitate and the certain future glory. That is, Paul makes clear that endurance is essential in order to be a faithful minister and that the result of such endurance is to reach glory, thereby stressing endurance for the gospel ministry, and instilling comfort and assurance in ministers who cannot but suffer for the gospel ministry.
Verses 8-10 The model of endurance that Paul presents is Jesus Christ, who endured all sufferings, even the suffering of death, in order to save sinners and finally rose again, and Paul himself, who was even bound like a criminal for the gospel.
Verses 11-13 The glory that those who endure will enjoy in the future is to share in the Lord's resurrection and to reign over the world with the Lord. Paul stresses this with assurance, based on the faithfulness of the Lord.
2:14-19 The Charge of Devotion as a Right Minister of the Word, and a Warning Against Heretical Talk
2:14~15 _ Paul is charging Timothy to devote himself as a right minister of the Word.
That is, he charges him to sternly command those who will teach the Word, bringing to their remembrance Paul's own teaching about endurance, not to quarrel, and to devote himself before God as one who rightly divides the word of truth and is approved as a worker who has no need to be ashamed.
2:16~18 _ He urges him to warn against heretical talk that has an evil influence on the whole church, in particular the profane and empty words of such people as Hymenaeus and Philetus, who claim that the resurrection has already taken place.
2:19 _ He makes a declaration full of confidence that, despite the rise of heresy, the firm foundation of God, that is, the church, will never be overthrown.

[Chapter 3] Continue in the Gospel
Chapter 3 especially teaches how pastors and Christians should deal with the moral corruption and persecution of worldly people in the last days, when they will appear more severely than at any other time.
3:1-5 _ By foretelling the moral and religious corruption that will appear in the last days, it urges attention to the last days.
3:6-9 _ Foretelling the phenomenon of apostasy as one representative phenomenon of the last days, it teaches to be on guard against the false teachers who oppose the truth.
3:10-17 _ It teaches that in such times godly believers are bound to be persecuted, and that all the more they should hold fast to the Bible, the word of God, and remain in what they have learned and become convinced of, without wavering.
3:1-9 Foretelling the Corruption of the Last Days, and the Reality of the False Teachers and the Final Warning
The passage prophesies that the time of distress in the last days, that is, the period of tribulation, will come, foretells in detail the moral and spiritual corruption that people of the last days will display, and exposes the reality and the end of the false teachers who will appear at that time. The passage warns that the nearer the end of the world, the more hostile human nature and religious tendencies will become toward the gospel, suggests that it will be that much harder for a minister of the gospel to be faithful to his duty, and teaches that in order to be faithful to his duty the minister of the gospel must firm up his resolve and determination all the more.
3:10-17 Exhortation to a Life Abiding in the Truth of the Word, and the Inspiration and Usefulness of Scripture
The passage reports the exhortation to a life abiding in the truth of the Word and the usefulness of Scripture. First, in verses 10-11, Paul recalls the persecution he suffered and testifies to the Lord's salvation.
3:12-15a _ He says that everyone who desires to live a godly life in Christ will be persecuted, and teaches that in order to cope with such persecution and live a life of victory, all believers should hold fast to the Scriptures and remain in what they have learned and become convinced of.
3:15b-17 _ He presents the inspiration and usefulness of Scripture as the reason believers should remain in the truth of Scripture.
All Scripture is inspired by God and is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, making believers complete for every good work, and so believers must remain in the truth of Scripture no matter what persecution comes.

[Chapter 4] Preach the Gospel
This chapter contains the last words the apostle Paul spoke or wrote. At the solemn moment when he was imprisoned in Rome a second time and facing death, he urges Timothy, in a charge like a last will and testament, to fulfill his ministry as a pastor.
1-5 _ Paul charges Timothy to diligently carry out the pastor's duty of preaching the word, and the duty of giving believers sound instruction in the faith so that they do not fall into the deception of heresy,
6-8 _ Paul, who had carried out the mission of spreading the gospel, now senses his own death and expresses a hope filled with assurance that after his death he will receive the crown of righteousness the Lord has prepared; by this he reminds Timothy of the proper attitude of a pastor and of what the reward to come will be like,
9-22 _ after making personal requests of Timothy, Paul mentions Alexander the coppersmith, a heretic who had done him harm, urging once again that Timothy be on guard against heresy, and the chapter records that Paul gave his final greetings.
Paul is writing this when his martyrdom is only a few weeks, or even a few days, away. According to tradition, Paul was beheaded on the Ostian Way. For about thirty years Paul labored without rest as an apostle and itinerant evangelist. He fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith. Therefore 2 Timothy is Paul's legacy to the church. This letter conveys an exceedingly solemn atmosphere. One cannot read it without being deeply moved.
4:1-8 The absolute command to preach the word, and the declaration of victory of Paul as he faces death
4:1-2 _ He solemnly commands Timothy to devote himself to preaching the word regardless of circumstances.
4:3-5 _ He exhorts Timothy that, even though many people in the world will turn away from the truth of the gospel because of the rampant heresy that will stand out in the last days, he must not be discouraged but fulfill the duty of an evangelist with sobriety and endurance.
4:6-8 _ Looking back on his own life as one who fought the good fight as an evangelist throughout his life, Paul makes a confession of faith filled with assurance that the crown of righteousness will surely be given by the Lord to all who devote themselves to the Lord's work as Paul did, himself included.
4:9-18 A request for Timothy to come to Rome, and Paul's personal circumstances and feelings
This passage reports Paul's request that Timothy visit Rome, together with his personal circumstances and feelings.
4:9-13 _ He asks Timothy to come quickly, explains his lonely situation, and urges him, when he comes, to bring Mark along with the cloak and the books written on parchment that were left at the house of Carpus in Troas.
4:14-15 _ He mentions that Alexander the coppersmith did him much harm and warns Timothy to be on guard against him.
4:16-18 _ Although no one is at Paul's side at present, he praises God, who has protected him from all harm until now and will lead him to salvation in the heavenly kingdom.
4:19-22 Final greetings

[Chapter 1] The Church Life of Saved Believers
Verses 1-4 identify the sender and the recipient according to the standard greeting form of the epistles and record a greeting based on apostolic authority. Here Paul declares his apostleship and, at the same time, makes known the mission of an evangelist that he received from the Lord, reminding Titus that he too has received the same mission of an evangelist as Paul.
Verses 5-16 provide instruction for resolving the various pressing issues facing the church in Crete, where Titus was ministering. That is, they teach the two matters that are most important for establishing order within the church and guiding believers in right living: the qualifications of an elder or overseer, and a warning against the Judaizing heresy.
1:1-4 _ Greeting
This is the introductory part of Titus, in which the greeting is given, and Paul asserts his apostleship.
1:5-9 _ Qualifications of an elder
This passage is the opening of the main body of this book, which runs from 1:5 to 3:11. Of this, 1:5-9 mentions the qualifications required of an elder (overseer), who is responsible for establishing order in the church and for defending orthodox Christian doctrine.
At that time the church in Crete, like the early churches in other regions, had many false teachers who were greatly influenced by heretics, especially by Judaizers who made keeping the law of Moses a condition of salvation. Because of them, orthodox Christian doctrine was seriously threatened, and the order of the church was also gravely threatened. Paul's purpose in writing this book was to call on Titus, the pastor, to take the lead in protecting the church in Crete from such confusion and establishing right faith.
The reason Paul speaks first in this book about the qualifications of elders is that, in such a situation, choosing right leaders is the key to establishing order in the church, protecting the church from the deception of false teachers, and defending the right truth of the gospel.
① Church leaders bear the responsibility of protecting believers and the church from the wrong thoughts and teachings of heretics.
② To carry out this responsibility, church leaders must hold fast to the word of God and live a right life of faith.
③ Their words and conduct must be exemplary, and they must take care not to become a cause of hurt, stumbling, or slander for others.
④ They must not do anything that damages the glory of God, the unity of the church, or harmony among believers.
⑤ They must have a thorough sense of responsibility, determined to complete the work and mission entrusted by the Lord even to the point of death.
When leaders are like this, believers can give them the due treatment of regarding them as worthy of double honor (1 Timothy 5:17). When this happens, the church becomes truly the church and a beautiful community that fulfills its function fully. Meanwhile, the qualifications of an elder mentioned in this passage are similar to the qualifications of an overseer in 1 Timothy 3:1-7.
1:10-16 _ A warning against false teachers
After speaking about the true leaders of God's church, the passage speaks about the character of false teachers, who stand in contrast to them.

[Chapter 2] The Personal Life and Family Life of Saved Believers
This chapter is part of the main body of Titus (Titus 1:5-3:11) and records practical teachings such as pastoral guidelines for resolving the various pressing issues facing the church in Crete, where Titus was ministering, guidelines for guiding believers in right living in the faith, and the right attitude of believers toward the authorities of the state and toward unbelieving neighbors.
2:1-10 _ Guidelines for the personal life and family life of believers
This chapter is part of the main body of the book, which runs from 1:5 to 3:11.
Besides the role of defending the truth, the passage speaks of another important role required of a pastor, namely, guiding and teaching believers with sound doctrine. For this purpose, Paul, keeping in mind the various kinds of believers in the church, teaches older men, older women, younger women, and younger men (verses 1-8).
And, in connection with the situation at that time, in which slavery still existed, he also teaches slaves (verses 9-10).
2:11-14 _ The course and content of faith
Verses 11-14 state the basis and reason why believers must live a good life.
2:15 _ Pastoral guidelines for Titus
This verse states the attitude required of a pastor when guiding believers. Paul requires Titus to exhort believers with the teachings presented in verses 11-14 above and, in addition, to rebuke with all authority.

[Chapter 3] The Social Life of Saved Believers
First, the first half, 3:1-11, is the concluding part of the main body of this book (1:5-3:11). This section records practical teachings on the right attitude believers should have in dealing with the authorities of the state and with unbelievers of the world.
3:1-8 _ Guidelines for the social life of believers (verse 1 - attitude toward state authority; verses 2-8 - attitude toward neighbors)
Paul teaches the attitude believers ought to have toward those who hold the authority to govern the state. (verse 1)
Because the state is a social institution that God has permitted since the fall of humankind, believers ought to submit to the demands of the state with a heart of obedience to the will of God, as long as what the state demands does not conflict with faith in God.
Paul teaches the basic virtues believers should have when dealing with unbelieving neighbors. (verses 2-8)
Reminding them that before they were saved and became believers they too were the same kind of unbelievers and evil people, Paul exhorts believers to have a heart of compassion for the souls of unbelievers and to do good to them with care.
3:9-11 _ Attitude toward heretics
Paul teaches that one should treat neighbors who belong to a heresy kindly, just as one treats other unbelieving neighbors, but that any debate with them is futile, so one must never debate with them, and after admonishing them once or twice one should keep away from the relationship. This is because, unlike relationships with other neighbors, fellowship with neighbors who belong to a heresy can have a very serious bad influence on one's faith, and so he told believers to keep away from them.
3:12-14 _ Paul's request
3:15 _ Final greeting

[Chapter 1]
1:1-7 _ Introduction: the address and greeting, and thanksgiving, prayer, and praise on account of Philemon
 Apphia, a woman whose name means "most beloved sister," was Philemon's wife. She is probably mentioned as a recipient because Paul thought the person who could have the greatest influence on Philemon was his wife.
 Archippus, whose name means "master of horses," was Philemon's son.
(Colossians 4:17) Tell Archippus: “See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.”
1:8-21 _ Main body: Paul's mediation and appeal on behalf of Onesimus
(Philemon 1:8) So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper,
At that time Paul was recognized in the early church as having apostolic authority, so he could have commanded it by his own order, as in "order you to do what is proper," but Paul chose to make his plea, hoping for Philemon's voluntary forgiveness and love toward Onesimus.
(Philemon 1:9) I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well.
Paul pleads with Philemon rather than commanding him with his apostolic authority.
1. "For love's sake" is a plea that Philemon forgive Onesimus, just as Philemon himself, who would have had to go to hell as a sinner in a wretched position, was forgiven the debt of his sin by the blood of Jesus.
2. "Aged" (old) was used to bring forward the image of the old apostle so that Philemon could not refuse his request.
3. "A prisoner for Jesus Christ" means that he was imprisoned and suffering for proclaiming Jesus; by telling Philemon this, he makes Philemon understand his situation. It also implies that for Philemon to answer his plea for Onesimus is to help his ministry.
Philemon, reading a letter containing such a pitiable story, could hardly have failed to accept the affectionate appeal of the old apostle, which was more earnest than a command.
(Philemon 1:11) Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.
By contrasting the time-indicating words "formerly" and "now," Paul emphasizes how Onesimus has changed.
"Onesimus" is a name meaning "useful," and it was a name that masters of that time commonly gave to slaves, meaning that they should become servants useful to them. In this verse Paul makes clear that, although Onesimus had formerly been a useless servant to Philemon, contrary to his name, after believing in Christ and becoming a believer he has become useful, as his name says, both to Paul and to Philemon.
(Philemon 1:13) I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel.
Paul had cherished a desire to keep Onesimus, a servant useful to him, with himself. The reason Paul wanted to keep Onesimus at his side was the utmost sincerity and devotion that he had shown. Onesimus, who had already changed from "useless" to "useful," was a person very much needed by Paul for the advance of the ministry.
Because Paul was bound and could not move about freely, he greatly needed Onesimus, who served him wholeheartedly.
That Paul uses the expression "in your behalf" here shows that he had no doubt at all, and was fully confident, about Philemon's desire to serve him.
And the expression "in your behalf" was probably used because, as a practical matter at that time, Onesimus's practical help was more needed than Philemon's loyal heart. Nevertheless, Paul thought it was not right to keep Onesimus at his side without Philemon's permission, and so he sent Onesimus back to Philemon for the time being.
(Philemon 1:14) But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will.
In "I did not want to do anything without your consent," the reason is stated why Paul did not keep Onesimus with him but sent him back to Philemon for the time being. It was because he wanted Philemon to do the good deed not by compulsion or necessity but voluntarily. It means that he did not want to keep Onesimus at his side without the permission of Philemon, Onesimus's master.
(Philemon 1:15) For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good—
   ➾  (Korean Common Translation) "Perhaps the reason he was separated from you for a little while was God's providence, to make him your own forever."
"For a while" (for a little while) refers to the time that Onesimus was away from Philemon, and "forever" refers to the time of the new relationship that he would form again with Philemon.
"Separated," when translated, means "to divide," and indicates the separation of oneself from another; that this word is used when dealing with divorce occurring between husband and wife shows that Onesimus left Philemon intending never to see him again.
"Have him back" (receive him back) is a technical commercial term meaning to receive money and give a receipt, and it was used in the sense of "to receive back."
This expression implies that God secretly arranged in his providence for Philemon to receive back Onesimus, who had run away from him. Onesimus's flight was a deliberate act of an individual, yet within it lay hidden the marvelous providence of God; without knowing it himself, Onesimus met Paul under God's sovereign intervention and became a faithful worker for the gospel.
(Philemon 1:16) no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord.
In "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother," the phrase "better than" is a preposition with the idea of transcendence, indicating that he must be regarded as a "brother," transcending the status of "servant."
Paul now asks Philemon to receive Onesimus not merely as a slave but as a brother beloved in the Lord.
"He is especially beloved to me" - Paul asks that, just as he and Onesimus had formed a spiritual relationship as brothers,
"but even more so to you" - Philemon too should receive him as a brother. When Onesimus had only the relationship of the flesh as Philemon's slave, he was no more than one among Philemon's many slaves; but now that he has been saved through Jesus, he has become a beloved brother in the faith who helps Paul's ministry. So Paul asks Philemon also to show generous magnanimity, no longer reckoning him a slave merely on the basis of the past relationship of the flesh, but regarding him as a fellow member and brother who, in the Lord, spiritually forms one body.
(Philemon 1:17) So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.
"Partner" means "companion" or "fellow worker," and refers to a person who does something together with another; this word is derived from a word meaning "fellowship." That is, it refers to a close person who is truly a companion, sharing purposes and sharing deep inward fellowship.
If Philemon regards Paul as a fellow worker for the gospel, Paul is asking him to identify the runaway slave Onesimus with Paul himself.
(Philemon 1:18) But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.
"has wronged you" - "to become a wrongdoer," "to commit some fault"; "owes you anything" - "to be in debt for money."
From these expressions it can be seen that when Onesimus ran away in the past he stole his master's money and fled. In any case, the statement that Onesimus had wronged Philemon and owed him something hints that he had stolen money and fled.
"charge it to my account" - "to reckon."
Even so, it means that Paul himself will repay the money Onesimus owed. Paul did not think that sin is resolved by forgiveness alone, but that responsibility for restitution and compensation for the wrong must follow. He did not take up the mediation with words only, but carried out the role of mediator with an attitude of love and devotion that did not hesitate at self-sacrifice. Paul's conduct here calls to mind the love of the sinless Jesus, who paid the price of sin in place of sinners. Furthermore, that Paul, who was in prison and not well off financially, undertook to be responsible for compensation that was probably not small shows how great his love for Onesimus was.
(Philemon 1:19) I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self.
   ➾  (Korean Common Translation) "I, Paul, guarantee in my own handwriting that I will repay it all. It is true that you owe your present standing to me, but I do not mean to demand payment of that from you."
In "I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it," among Paul's letters there are some that, following the custom of the time, were written by a scribe, with only the final greetings written in his own hand. But here Paul says he wrote with his own hand even though the main body of this letter to Philemon was not yet finished; this is to state his intention to make restitution in place of Onesimus and to emphasize that his promise of restitution will never be reversed.
In "you owe me your very self," Philemon came to God and obtained salvation through Paul. Although it is not certain whether he came to Ephesus himself and heard the gospel from Paul or heard it indirectly through Epaphras, it is a fact that he owes Paul a debt for eternal life. The debt of salvation is a debt of love that cannot be reckoned in money. Having obtained eternal life, more precious than physical life, is a debt that cannot be repaid with anything in this world.
(Philemon 1:21) Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask.
By stating that he is confident that Philemon will gladly grant the request to mediate for Onesimus, Paul conveys his state of mind more clearly.
"Confident" means "to be confident about some person or thing," and indicates that he had been confident in the past and is still confident now. Paul wrote the letter already confident of Philemon's good decision. Also, "obedience" is not merely obedience to Paul's request but obedience to the will of God, that is, gladly receiving Onesimus in the Lord.
Because Philemon was a person who knew the will of God and obeyed it, he could do even more good than Paul was asking. This is truly a level of mature faith that goes beyond the level of Paul's request and plea and voluntarily puts God's love into practice.
In the letters of Ignatius, the church father of Antioch in the period of the early church, it is recorded that Onesimus became bishop of the church in Ephesus. If these two persons are the same, then the apostle Paul's affectionate letter and Philemon's loving forgiveness resulted in making the former runaway slave a bishop of the church in Ephesus in later years.
1:22-25 _ Conclusion: the closing section consisting of a personal request and final greetings
(Philemon 1:22) In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.
  Paul now changes the subject; expecting, if he is released, to visit Philemon's house church, he asks Philemon to prepare a lodging and to intercede for him in prayer. Paul's words "prepare a guest room" mean that once he is soon released from prison he will go to Colossae, and in asking that the necessary arrangements for lodging be made, they carry Paul's earnest desire to go from Rome to Colossae. So he asks for intercessory prayer that these things may actually be accomplished in Christ, hoping that God will cause Paul to be released from prison and go to the church in Colossae.
The meaning of the phrase translated "to you" is "for you"; Paul asks for intercessory prayer on behalf of the church in Colossae and Philemon, showing that his purpose in wishing, by God's grace, to be released from prison and go to Colossae is not for his own benefit. This is a passage that clearly shows Paul's God-centered attitude, firmly believing that humans make plans but it is God who brings them to pass.

[Chapter 1] Christ, the Superior One
1:1-3 _ Christ, superior to the prophets of the Old Testament
This is both the preface to the whole book of Hebrews and a doctrinal summary. It is a brief yet conclusive statement that Christianity is superior to Judaism. It speaks of Christ as superior to the prophets of the Old Testament and also as the one who brings revelation to completion.
1:4-14 _ Christ, superior to the angels
Because the Jews regarded angels as exalted beings, the passage shows that Christ is superior to the angels. Angels are ministers, but Jesus, the Son, is God and King.

[Chapter 2] Jesus, the Restorer of All Things
2:1-4 _ So great a salvation
By reminding readers that those who transgressed the law given through angels also received due retribution, the passage warns how great the punishment will be for those who neglect the gospel of salvation that was first spoken by the Lord.
2:5-13 _ Jesus, the Restorer of All Things
It explains the reason and purpose for which Christ was made a little lower than the angels for a while (becoming a man and dying on the cross). He redeemed us from sin, was crowned with glory and honor, and is able to help those who are tempted.
2:14-18 _ Jesus, who took on flesh and blood
It makes clear the meaning and purpose of the incarnation of Jesus.

[Chapter 3] If We Hold Firm to the End, We Are His House
3:1-6 _ Christ, superior to Moses
Moses was a servant, a faithful attendant, in all God's house. Jesus Christ, on the other hand, is the master who rules over God's house and is the Son, and is therefore superior to Moses.
3:7-19 _ If we hold firm to the end, we are his house
Just as the people of Israel could not enter the promised land in the wilderness because of unbelief, this is an exhortation to hold firm to the end so as not to fall into the same unbelief.

[Chapter 4] Eternal Rest
4:1-11 _ Rest of the soul and eternal rest
The seventh-day Sabbath and the Canaan rest through Joshua are types of the eternal rest.
Just as the people of Israel who came out of Egypt could not enter the rest (the land of Canaan) because of unbelief, fear that any of you might fall short of the promise of rest. Those who are saved by faith have entered the rest of the soul. Those in whom the rest of the soul has been accomplished will enter eternal rest.
4:12-13 _ The sword of the word
Those who disobey Christ and the gospel will surely be exposed before the word of God and come under judgment.
4:14-16 _ Jesus, our great high priest
Because we have a great high priest, Jesus Christ, it urges us to hold fast the confession of faith. It also urges us to approach the throne of grace with boldness so that we may obtain grace to help in time of need.

[Chapter 5] Christ Who Became High Priest
5:1-4 _ A weak human high priest
A high priest is chosen from among men and offers sacrifices to God, but because he is weak he must make atonement for himself as well.
5:5-11 _ Christ who became High Priest
Christ was not appointed by men but was called by God and became an eternal high priest after the order of Melchizedek. He learned obedience through suffering and became the source of perfect salvation.
"Order" means "line, lineage, rank, position," and so on. It testifies that the high priesthood of Jesus Christ is not of the Levitical line but of the line of Melchizedek. Melchizedek, when translated, means "the king of righteousness."
5:12-14 _ The elementary teachings of the word, by which they failed to become teachers as they ought
It rebukes the Jewish believers because, although they have had faith for a long time, they still remain at elementary teaching, and instructs them that they must have discernment like the mature.

[Chapter 6] Christ's Oath and Exhortation
6:1-8 _ Those who return again to the elementary teachings about Christ
We must not remain in elementary teachings of the faith but go on to mature faith. Those who have fallen away after having once been enlightened are hard to bring back to repentance again.
First there is something that must be made clear. It is the fact that a person who has been saved once can never be lost. When a person is saved, the Holy Spirit comes in at the time of salvation. And that Holy Spirit does not leave but indwells forever. The Holy Spirit is in the saved person as a guarantee. He is there as a guarantee of being children [2 Corinthians 1:21-22], as a guarantee of the inheritance [Ephesians 1:14], and as a guarantee of the resurrection body [2 Corinthians 5:5].
Therefore the persons spoken of in this passage are meant to be Hebrews who came into contact with the gospel but, without having the experience of being saved, returned again to Judaism.
6:4 _ Once enlightened, having tasted the heavenly gift
  Jesus came as the light of life and appeared first to the Hebrews, and the light of the completed gospel was also delivered to them first. In that sense the Hebrews were "once enlightened." But although they received clear teaching about the light of the gospel, that light was not planted in their souls by the help of the Holy Spirit so as to become fully their own.
6:4 _ Having shared in the Holy Spirit
The Hebrews are people who have shared in the Holy Spirit. By the power of that Holy Spirit Jesus went about healing all who were oppressed by the devil [Acts 10:38]. Therefore the Hebrews are people who shared in it by witnessing the work of the Holy Spirit through the public ministry of Jesus.
What we should note here is that the "sharing" used here differs in meaning from the "sharing" used in [2 Peter 1:4] and [Philippians 3:10]. The persons mentioned in this verse are by no means people who have been born again of the Holy Spirit. It also says that their bodies never became the temple of God, and that the Holy Spirit never worked within them.
6:5 _ Having tasted the powers of the coming age
 "Those who have fallen away" means "those who have fallen."
They were once enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, and shared in the Holy Spirit. Even so, they finally rejected the gospel that Christ had completed, and chose to return to Judaism. This is a spiritual sin of crucifying the Son of God again, that is, a sin that cannot be brought to repentance again because it is the final rejection of Christ. All sins are forgiven through the cross of Christ, but the sin of rejecting the cross cannot be forgiven.
6:9-12 _ The church's exhortation to the beloved
For this reason, those who are saved must trust the justice of God and hold fast to hope with faith and perseverance to the end.
6:13-20 _ God's oath and the hope of the promise
There is a promise that does not change, like the oath God made to Abraham, and this hope is as firm as an anchor for our souls.

[Chapter 7] Christ, After the Order of Melchizedek
7:1-3 _ Melchizedek
Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God, a mysterious person who blessed Abraham and received a tithe from him, and his priesthood has the quality of eternity.
7:4-10 _ Melchizedek and the Levitical priests
Because Abraham gave a tithe to Melchizedek, the Levitical priests, who are descendants of Abraham, stand in a lower position than Melchizedek, and this foreshadows a priesthood better than the Levitical priesthood, represented by Melchizedek.
7:11-25 _ The abolishing of the order of Levi and the establishing of the order of Melchizedek
Because perfection could not be achieved through the Levitical priesthood, a better priestly office was needed.
Jesus is the eternal high priest established after the order of Melchizedek, appointed not by human lineage but by the oath of God. The priests under the law were weak and could not escape death, but because Jesus lives forever, his priestly office is also eternal. Therefore Jesus is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God.
7:26-28 _ A high priest who meets our need
Jesus, holy and blameless, the eternal high priest in heaven, offered himself once for all as a sacrifice and accomplished perfect atonement.

[Chapter 8] The Mediator of a Better Covenant
8:1-5 _ Jesus, the high priest seated in heaven
Jesus is the true high priest seated at the right hand of the throne in heaven, and he serves in the sanctuary set up not by man but by God.
The earthly tabernacle and sacrifices are nothing more than a shadow copying the heavenly reality. Just as Moses had to follow the pattern God showed him when he built the tabernacle, the ministry of Jesus fulfills a higher reality.
8:6-13 _ The mediation of a better new covenant
Jesus is the mediator of a new covenant established on better promises, and because the old covenant was not perfect, a new covenant was needed.
In the new covenant God puts the law in the heart and establishes an intimate relationship, and said that he will remember sins no more. Therefore the old covenant is becoming obsolete and disappearing.

[Chapter 9] Christ, the Source of Eternal Atonement
9:1-5 _ The sanctuary and the Most Holy Place of the first covenant
Under the first covenant the earthly tabernacle was set up, and it was divided into the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place. In the Holy Place were the lampstand and the bread of the Presence, and in the Most Holy Place were the ark of the covenant and the mercy seat. All of these were provided according to the regulations for meeting with God.
9:6-10 _ The first tent brought to completion by the second tent
The priests served daily in the Holy Place, but only the high priest entered the Most Holy Place, once a year. This shows that the sacrifices of the first covenant did not achieve complete salvation. Therefore these sacrifices were nothing more than external rituals and applied only temporarily until the new age came.
9:6 _ The priests entered regularly into the first room to perform their sacred duties
The tasks the priests had to do daily in the Holy Place were tending the lamps of the lampstand and burning incense on the altar of incense there. They filled the lamps with "pure oil of crushed olives" and cleaned them by removing the snuffings and the residue. When the priests trimmed the lamps in the morning, they burned incense on the altar of incense [Exodus 30:7-8], and when they lit the lamps in the evening, they burned incense. Burning incense typologically represents praising and praying to God morning and evening. They also replaced the bread of the Presence on the table once a week [Leviticus 24:8].
9:7 _ But only the high priest entered the second room, once a year
Here it refers to the sacrifice of the Great Day of Atonement, performed once every year as the ritual of service in the second tent, the Most Holy Place. On the 10th day of the 7th month [Leviticus 16:29-34] the high priest of Israel enters the Most Holy Place alone, without his attendants, and offers an atoning sacrifice before the LORD. The smoke of the incense offered at that time covers the mercy seat. This shows that when Christ offered himself as an atoning sacrifice, he was accepted by God as a fragrant offering.
9:8 _ As long as the first tabernacle was still standing
"The first tabernacle" includes the tabernacle, the sacrificial laws, and all the Old Testament elements established on the foundation of the old covenant.
In the words "as long as it was standing" there is a hint that the first tabernacle is not eternal and that all the systems of worship belonging to the old covenant of the Old Testament are imperfect.
9:9 _ It is an illustration for the present time
The writer of Hebrews makes known that the tabernacle included in the old covenant and all its rituals are imperfect, and that because of the defects of the Jewish system of law, the Jews are unable to accept the complete gospel. At the same time he intends to show how foolish and evil it is for believing Hebrew Christians to return to that system. They were merely illustrations for the present time, and no more than institutions that God had appointed until the time of reformation.
9:11-14 _ Christ, who accomplished eternal atonement
Christ entered not a sanctuary made by hands but the greater and more perfect sanctuary in heaven. He accomplished eternal atonement not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood. The blood of Christ cleanses our conscience so that we may serve God.
9:15-22 _ The result of the shedding of Christ's blood
Jesus, as the mediator of a new covenant, accomplished redemption from sin by his death. Just as a will takes effect only when the one who made it has died, God's covenant given to people was not ratified without the sacrifice of the shedding of blood. Christ, as the "mediator of the covenant" and the "mediator of the will," confirmed his promise to all humankind through his death.
9:23-28 _ The true heavenly sacrifice offered once for all
To cleanse the heavenly sanctuary a better sacrifice was needed. Jesus entered not the earthly sanctuary but the true heavenly sanctuary, and by offering himself once for all he put away sin. Christ will not come again as a sin offering, but will appear to those who are waiting for him for salvation.
9:23 _ The heavenly things
This refers to the "church" that will enter the heavenly sanctuary with all the spiritual blessings Christ accomplished by fulfilling the role of mediator [Ephesians 1:3], and it can be seen to include also heaven, the dwelling place of Christ and the redeemed people [John 14:2].
The cleansing of "the heavenly things" means, together with the inner cleansing of the conscience of the members of the church, the complete renewal of the whole universe with respect to sin.
9:24 _ But into heaven itself
Christ entered heaven as the high priest of his church, as the mediator of the new covenant, and as their advocate. This confirms full satisfaction with the work of salvation accomplished by Christ and the perfect disposal of all the sins imputed to him.

[Chapter 10] The Eternity of Christ's Sacrifice and the Boldness of Believers
10:1-4 _ The imperfection of the typological sacrifices in the Old Testament
The sacrifices of the law were only a shadow of the good things to come and did not completely remove sin. The yearly sacrifices could not make sin completely clean, and if they could, there would have been no need for the sacrifices to be repeated. Rather, these sacrifices served to remind people of sin. The blood of animals can never remove sin.
10:5-10 _ The incarnation of Christ and the sacrifice offered once for all
God took no pleasure in animal sacrifices, but sent his Son into the world and fulfilled the will of God. Jesus offered his own body once for all in place of the sacrifices of the law. By this we have been sanctified, and repeated sacrifices are no longer needed.
10:9 _ He takes away the first to establish the second
The Levitical sacrifices could not fully accomplish the will of God. When the incarnate Son was offered, that work was at last completed. The word "take away" has a stronger meaning than "obsolete" and "disappearing" [Hebrews 8:13]. The sacrifice of Christ's cross is a proclamation of the permanent abolition of the first. It also shows clearly that what is needed for human salvation is not the law of the Old Testament but the grace of Christ in the New Testament.
10:11-18 _ The perfection and eternity of Christ's sacrifice
The priests of the Old Testament offered the same sacrifices every day but could not completely remove sin. But Jesus accomplished eternal atonement by a single sacrifice and sat down at the right hand of God. Since the Holy Spirit also testified that He will remember our sins no more, sacrifices are no longer needed.
10:19-25 _ The boldness of believers by the blood of Jesus
By the blood of Jesus we have obtained a new and living way to approach God boldly. Our hearts have been cleansed, and we must draw near to God with the assurance of faith. We must encourage one another to love and good works, strive to meet together, and keep the faith to the end.
10:25 _ Neglecting to meet together
The original word for "neglect" means "to leave behind, to give up, to abandon." Therefore "neglecting to meet together" refers to "abandoning Christ and the gospel and leaving."
It refers to people among the Hebrews who, having had Christ and the gospel presented to them and remaining among the crowd, in the end do not accept Christ and leave the church. The reason they abandon the gathering is probably, in the end, that they did not have a sure faith.
10:26-31 _ Judgment and punishment for deliberately rejecting the gospel
For those who deliberately go on sinning after knowing the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. There remains only a fearful expectation of God's judgment and a fury of fire. One who violated the law was put to death, so those who have trampled the Son of God underfoot and insulted the Spirit of grace will receive an even more severe judgment. God is the living Judge.
10:26 _ If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth
The word "deliberately" means "of one's own accord, intentionally." The Korean edition of the NKJV translates "if we sin willfully" as "if we sin intentionally."
This refers to one's own voluntary action, not something done under outside pressure or compulsion. That is, it refers to an individual deliberately and intentionally rejecting Christ and the gospel.
The "deliberate sin" spoken of in this verse is different from "willful sins." The "willful sins" of Psalms 19:13 are "sins committed knowingly" and do not refer to the sin of rejecting the gospel. But the "deliberate sin" of this verse refers to the sin of rejecting Christ and the gospel. So "deliberate sin" can be called the sin of deliberately blaspheming God and despising and destroying the word.
The warning about "deliberate sin" is directed at those who, having seemed at the time to have converted to Christianity, return again to Judaism. They are those who abandon Christ and return to the law not through ignorance or error but deliberately. In the end, the reason they return to Judaism is that they had no sure understanding of the gospel.
This does not mean that "salvation can be lost." Among the people to whom the gospel was presented at that time, there were those who seemed to believe but in whose souls it was never firmly established, and they deliberately rejected the gospel and returned to Judaism. They did not receive salvation and then lose it; they had not been saved from the beginning.
10:32-39 _ The suffering and endurance needed to receive the promise
The Jewish believers kept the faith and fought boldly even amid the trials of the early faith. Because they knew they possessed a better and lasting inheritance, they rejoiced even when their property was seized. Therefore they must not lose heart but persevere and keep the faith to the end. God is pleased with those who live by faith, and those who shrink back will come to destruction.

[Chapter 11] The Essence of Faith
11:1-3 _ The definition and effect of faith
Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the certainty of things not seen. Through faith the people of old received God's approval. Also, because we have faith, we know that the unseen God created the world by his word.
11:4-7 _ The aspect of faith before Abraham
Abel, by faith, offered a better sacrifice and was commended as righteous, and though he died, his faith still speaks. Enoch walked with God by faith and was taken up without seeing death. Whoever draws near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards. Noah, believing the warning about things not yet seen, built an ark and became an heir of righteousness.
11:8-22 _ The aspect of faith in the age of the patriarchs
When God called, Abraham obeyed by faith and went out to the land of promise. Sarah believed in God's faithfulness and bore Isaac even in old age. The forefathers of faith received the promises, but died before they were fully fulfilled, and they longed for a better, heavenly homeland. Abraham believed in God's power even when he offered Isaac. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph also looked toward the future by faith and blessed their descendants.
11:23-31 _ The aspect of faith from Moses to the entry into Canaan
Moses' parents, by faith, hid him, not fearing the king's edict. Moses chose to suffer with the people of God rather than enjoy the wealth of Egypt. The people of Israel crossed the Red Sea by faith, and the walls of Jericho fell by faith. Rahab welcomed the spies in peace and escaped destruction.
11:32-40 _ The aspect of faith after the age of the judges and the new promise prepared for believers
Many forerunners in the faith, such as Gideon, Barak, Samson, and David, conquered kingdoms by faith, did what is righteous, and obtained promises. Some kept the faith amid suffering and persecution and did not fear even death. But they did not receive what was promised, because God had prepared something better for us. It is so that they might be made perfect together with us.

[Chapter 12] Exhortation to Faith and a Warning Against Apostasy
12:1-3 _ The race of faith, run with perseverance, looking to the Lord Jesus
To run the race of faith we must throw off every weight and sin. Jesus, as the founder and perfecter of our faith, endured the suffering of the cross and sat down at the right hand of God. We too must look to Jesus, not lose heart, and persevere to the end.
12:4-13 _ The meaning and benefit of discipline (refining)
Suffering is discipline that God gives because he loves us as his children. God refines us so that we may share in his holiness. Discipline seems painful for the present, but later it yields the fruit of righteousness and peace. Therefore we must not lose heart, but strengthen our weak hands and knees and walk the right path.
12:14-17 _ Exhortation to a life of peace and holiness
We must pursue peace with everyone and holiness. In particular we must look back with fear. First, we must see whether anyone falls short of the grace of God; second, whether there is a root of bitterness, that is, a teaching or a false worker that threatens the peace and holiness of the church; third, whether there is anyone who, like Esau, lets go of what is eternal because of worldly pleasure.
12:18-29 _ Exhortation to a life of grace and godliness
We have come not to the fearful Mount Sinai but to the heavenly Mount Zion and the city of God. We must not refuse the God who speaks from heaven, but obey his voice. On the last day God will shake the earth and the heavens once more. Since we have received a kingdom that cannot be shaken, we must serve God with reverence and thankfulness.
12:28 _ A kingdom that cannot be shaken
A kingdom that cannot be shaken refers to the eternal kingdom that will not pass away. Saved believers are people who have received a kingdom that cannot be shaken. To enter heaven, the kingdom of God, the kingdom of God must first be established in one's soul. When we receive forgiveness of sins, the Holy Spirit comes into our soul as its master. Then the kingdom of God is established in the soul. Our soul comes under the rule of Christ, the master of the kingdom of God.

[Chapter 13] The Final Exhortation to Obey Sound Teaching and to Love
13:1-6 _ Exhortation to brotherly love and purity
Keep on loving one another as brothers, open your heart to hospitality, honor marriage, and keep the family pure. Rid yourselves of greed and live with a heart of contentment. The reason is that God is with us. God is the one who helps us and who protects our lives.
13:7-9 _ Exhortation on the principles of contentment and loyalty
Do not be swayed by worldly teachings, but be loyal to the unchanging truth of Jesus Christ. The sight of a heart strengthened in grace is a beautiful sight.
13:9 _ Not by foods
This refers to those who insist on Judaism and strive to add the ceremonial law to the gospel, and it refers to their attitude of doing what is altogether useless and worthless (Mark 7:3-13).
13:10-17 _ Exhortation on the principles of worship and on serving church leaders
Just as Jesus suffered for us, we too must meet suffering as Jesus did. Looking forward to the eternal heaven that is to come, we must offer a sacrifice of praise in a way that bears witness to Jesus. And we must offer sacrifices pleasing to God by doing good and sharing. For our own benefit as well, we must cooperate in step with those who work ahead of us.
13:10 _ We have an altar
"We" refers to saved Christians. For saved Christians, Jesus is the altar. The Lord first sanctified himself in order to sanctify us (John 17:19). As a result he became the atoning sacrifice for us. Jesus Christ is at once the altar and the sacrifice offered on it. The altar on which the gift is offered and the gift laid upon it meet in Christ. It is as though the priest who offers the sacrifice and the sacrifice he offered were accepted as perfect.
13:18-25 _ Closing words, with a request for intercessory prayer and greetings
He asks for prayer and wishes for the peace of God. He hopes that grace in Christ Jesus will come upon all people, and conveys greetings.

[Chapter 1] Be Persevering amid Trials and Temptations, and Be a Doer Who Hears the Word and Acts on It
1:1 _ Greeting
1:2-12 _ The attitude of believers when they face trials of many kinds, and its result
2-11 _ The attitude of believers when they face trials of many kinds (Jas.)
2 _ Consider it pure joy
4 _ Let perseverance finish its work
5 _ Ask God, but by faith alone
9-11 _ Think of what is spiritual and eternal rather than what is of the flesh and lasts only a short while and then disappears
12 _ The final result given to the one who endures trials (Jas.)
1:13-18 _ A warning against temptation and the desire that causes it; God's gifts and presents
13-16 _ A warning against temptation and the desire that causes it (Jas.)
The "trial" spoken of in this section is a different kind of trial from the "trial" spoken of in the previous section (James 1:2, 3, 12). The trial spoken of in the previous section is a kind of trial (test, trial) in which the agent is God, to make the faith of believers grow and to give them glory. But the trial spoken of here is one in which the agent is the devil, and its purpose is to tempt (temptation) and to destroy.
17-18 _ God's gifts and presents (Jas.)
It makes clear that God is the one who gives every good gift and every perfect present. It speaks by contrasting the devil and God. That is, the devil leads people astray with bad things and brings them to destruction, but God is the Father of lights, who sends down good things.
Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow … (James 1:17).
"Gift" means "something given," and "present" means "grace"; in the end the two have the same meaning, and the KJV translates both as "gift."
First, God is the "Father of lights." God himself is light (Psalms 84:11, 1 John 1:5) and is also the one who made the lights (Genesis 1:14-18, Psalms 136:7).
Second, God is the one who "sends down every good gift and every perfect present."
Third, God is the one who "does not change" (Malachi 3:6, Hebrews 13:8).
Fourth, God is the one who is a Spirit, with "no shifting shadow" (John 4:24).
Fifth, God is the one who "gave us new birth by the word of truth, made us his children, and made us heirs."
1:19-27 _ A life of hearing the word and putting it into practice
It speaks of "faith and works," the core of this whole epistle. This passage, the first section, speaks of "true godliness of hearing the word and acting on it."
19-21 _ The attitude of hearing the word carefully (Jas.)
It exhorts believers to listen carefully when they hear the word from others or from God.
22-25 _ Blessing received when the word heard is put into practice (Jas.)
Be doers of the word (22); if one hears the word and does not do it (23); not a forgetful hearer (25); but a doer who acts (25)
Four times in all it urges that the word heard must be put into practice.
26-27 _ True godliness is proved only by putting the word into practice (Jas.)
To emphasize that true godliness is proved only by putting the word into practice, it gives examples of worthless godliness and true godliness.

[Chapter 2] Practice Love Without Partiality, and Prove Your Faith
2:1 -13 _ Do not show favoritism, but practice the royal law of love for neighbor
It says that believers who hold faith in Christ must not show favoritism but must practice the royal law of love for neighbor.
1-4 _ A rebuke of discriminating between the poor and the rich in the church according to appearance (Jas.)
5-7 _ God's calling the poor to be rich in faith, and a warning about the conduct of the rich (Jas.)
Continuing from the previous section, it further states why believers must not discriminate against or despise the poor.
8-13 _ An urging to practice the law of love recorded in the word, and a warning against the sin of showing favoritism (Jas.)
 'Mercy triumphs over judgment (James 2:13)'
'Mercy triumphs over judgment' = it means that it triumphs over 'judgment without mercy.' The mercy that a saved person practices in life is sure outward evidence that he has escaped the judgment without mercy that unbelievers will receive. 'Triumphs' = it means not only that he has escaped judgment without mercy but also that he will even receive a reward before God.
2:14-19 _ Dead faith without works, and true faith proved by works
It speaks of 'dead faith without works and true faith proved by works.' And as examples of true faith proved by works it cites 'Abraham and Rahab the prostitute.' This section contains the core message of this epistle.
14-19 _ Dead faith without works (Jas.)
First, it cannot save one's own soul.
Second, it cannot give any benefit to brothers and sisters.
Third, it is in itself dead faith.
Fourth, it is faith that cannot be shown to others, that is, faith that cannot be proved.
Fifth, it is the same faith as that of demons.
2:20-25 _ Examples of true faith proved by works (Jas.)
It cites Abraham and Rahab the prostitute as examples of 'true faith accompanied by works, faith proved by works.'
21 _ Abraham, an example of true faith whose faith was proved by works
 Faith is inward and therefore unseen. But when that unseen inward faith is revealed in concrete deeds in life, it comes to be recognized as true faith.
 ‘As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.’ (James 2:24),
Faith and works cannot be separated; they are connected.
25 _ Rahab the prostitute, an example of true faith whose faith was proved by works
Abraham was a person honored as the father of faith, but 'Rahab the prostitute' was a Gentile by origin and had the lowly status of a prostitute. Yet she too had her faith in her God proved by works, and she and her family were saved from the destruction of the city of Jericho.
26 _ In conclusion, faith without works is dead faith

[Chapter 3] Guard Your Tongue. True Wisdom Shows Itself in Gentleness and Peace
3:1-12 _ The untamed tongue
1-2 _ The heavy responsibility of those who become teachers, and a warning about slips of speech (Jas.)
'Not many of you should become teachers!' Although the office of teaching is certainly necessary in the church, no one should rashly try to take up that office. The office of teaching in the church is an office God gives to build up the faith of believers and the church, which is the body of Christ, the head.
'We who teach will be judged more strictly (James 3:1),'
This is the reason for 'Not many of you should become teachers!' Responsibility necessarily goes with the office of teacher, because teaching as a teacher exerts great influence on other people. Therefore if a teacher fails to carry out that responsibility faithfully, he will receive a stricter judgment from God.
3-5 _ The characteristics of the tongue, which is small yet exerts great influence (Jas.)
It speaks using as examples the 'bit of a horse,' the 'rudder of a ship,' and 'a small fire that sets ablaze a great forest.'
The 'bit' refers to the piece of iron placed crosswise in a horse's mouth, to which the reins are fastened and the bridle put on. Even a fierce wild horse is controlled in the direction a person wishes to move by using the bit and bridle.
The ship refers to a very large sailing ship in ancient times, driven by the wind. Compared with the ship, which is a large sailing vessel, the rudder that determines its direction is very small. Even so, the helmsman steers as he wills with that small rudder.
The tongue too is a small member, but its influence is very great, just like the rudder. Sadly, however, among the many members of the human body the tongue is very small yet cannot be controlled so easily. If the rudder of a ship is well steered, the ship arrives safely at its destination, but if it is steered wrongly, it runs aground. In the same way, how one uses the tongue determines victory or failure in that person's life.
6-8 _ The serious harm when the tongue is misused (Jas.)
'The tongue ... pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire (James 3:6)'
'The tongue among our members pollutes the whole body' - this says that the words we speak corrupt and defile our entire character.
'Sets the course of life on fire' - it means 'sets the course of our life on fire.' This means that, just as fire burns up everything, misusing the tongue can ruin our whole life.
'And is itself set on fire by hell' - as the final result of the harm from misusing the tongue, one goes into the fire of hell.
9-12 _ The duplicity of the tongue, and that it is not fitting for believers to use the tongue as an instrument of evil (Jas.)
3:13-18 _ Evil wisdom and true wisdom from God
13 _ Wisdom and understanding that must be proved by good deeds that come from gentleness (Jas.)
'Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.'
Probably James asked this because there were people in the church at that time who claimed to have 'wisdom and understanding' and tried to become teachers themselves (James 3:1).
'Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom (James 3:13)'
'In gentleness' means 'in the gentleness.'
It says that good deeds can come from gentleness.
14-16 _ Evil wisdom marked by envy and strife (Jas.)
17-18 _ The characteristics of good wisdom from God (Jas.)

[Chapter 4] Do Not Love the World, but Humbly Submit to God
4:1-10 _ Be separate from passions and the world; resist the devil
1-3 _ You cannot get what you want by following your passions, but only by asking (Jas.)
'You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight (James 4:2)'
A literal translation of this verse from the original is:
'You crave but do not possess; you kill and covet but cannot get it in your hands. You fight and wage war.'
It means that believers crave, kill, covet, quarrel, and wage war in order to possess and get into their hands what they each want according to the passions of their flesh. It even says that believers 'kill,' but this is presumed to be not actual murder but a way of speaking about being angry and furious at a brother.
4-5 _ For believers to be friends of the world is spiritual adultery that makes them enemies of God, and a sin that provokes the indwelling Holy Spirit to jealousy (Jas.)
'You adulteresses! (James 4:4)'
Just as it is adultery when a wife who has made the marriage covenant with her husband abandons her fidelity to her husband and goes to another man, so if believers who have entered a covenant relationship with God abandon their fidelity of faith toward God and love the world, it is spiritual adultery.
6-7a _ God, who gives greater grace to those who humbly submit (Jas.)
7b-8a _ Believers must resist the devil and draw near to God (Jas.)
8b-10 _ Sinners and the double-minded must repent, be saved, and be purified (Jas.)
'Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded (James 4:8)'
