[Chapter 1] Greeting, Living Hope, and the Exhortation to Sanctification
This epistle is an official letter that the apostle Peter sent to the believers of the churches in Asia Minor in AD 64, when the persecution of Christians by the emperor Nero (AD 54-68), which began in Rome, was spreading throughout the empire.
At that time the age was shifting from the Old Testament to the New Testament, and even Gentiles were in the process of sharing in the promises of God within the gospel (Galatians 3:26-29). Because of this there were various tasks of establishing the faith, and in particular how to understand suffering, and how believers should treat the authorities of the world and people, were important questions.
In these circumstances Peter wrote this epistle to make firm the hope that believers should look to even amid tribulation and suffering, and to teach the right attitude for living as believers.
1) The first half (1:1-12): Together with the greeting, it explains the reason believers can rejoice even in suffering.
2) The second half (1:13-25): It teaches the holy life of believers, and it is the beginning of 'the holy life of Christians,' the first theme of the main body (1:13-5:11).
Through chapter 1 we realize the following.
- Christians suffer on this earth, but they share in the glory promised on the day of the return.
- We who have this hope must live a holy life.
1:1-2 _ Greeting
Although the definition of a Christian can be given in various parts, through [1 Peter 1:1-2] Peter defines them as 'those who are chosen' (according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by his blood), and describes them as 'sojourners' scattered in the various regions (churches) who quietly carry on their lives.
1:3-12 _ The reason believers can rejoice even in suffering
1:13-21 _ Exhortation to a holy life
Holiness is the most central element of the divine nature of God and is the first thing required of believers.
If a believer does not understand 'holiness,' the most central divine nature of God, and neither experiences it nor possesses it in his own heart, this means that he lacks the most basic qualification. The Lord's command, 'Be holy, because I am holy,' is the most basic element of life that believers who will enjoy eternal life with the Lord must possess.
Holiness refers to the state of being set apart from the filthy sins of the world and offered to God.
1:22-25 _ Exhortation to love the brothers in the truth

1) [Verses 1-11]: Concluding the third theme of the main body, 'the attitude for overcoming suffering,' it exhorts elders and young men about the attitude of faith believers should have within the church.

First Peter teaches us to accept in faith the suffering that accompanies the Christian life and to hold fast to the will and promise of God contained in it. Through this we can be assured that, just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so God's comfort will also be all the more abundant (2 Corinthians 1:3-5).
5:1-6 _ Exhortation to elders and young men
Up to the previous chapter, the apostle Peter had been exhorting individuals about the attitude of faith in a situation where they would face great suffering, but now, concerned for the church, he exhorts the elders within the church and the young men who follow their example.
Recognizing that elders are leaders of the church who must care for and shepherd Christians, he presents in contrast what they especially must not do and what they must do.
He reminds them of three areas in which one may easily go wrong, saying they must not do these things, and conversely he qualifies the things they must do with the word 'rather,' clearly reminding church leaders of the attitude they should hold fast to.
1) Not under compulsion, but rather willingly, according to the will of God
Under compulsion means doing something not gladly of one's own accord but out of a sense of duty, or in a state where the heart is pressed down by some external factor.
2) Not for shameful gain, but rather eagerly
Avoiding the temptation of money applies to all Christians, but it is a subject that those in the position of leader of an organization especially must be alert to.
3) Not domineering over those in your charge, but rather being examples to the flock
When fellowshipping from the position of leader, one may sometimes, without realizing it, take a domineering attitude toward other believers. Moreover, until one realizes this about oneself, the suffering of the believer being dominated is bound to increase.

Seeing that the common testimony of believers who have run the whole course of the life of faith is the confession that [all my life was the grace of God], the final word of promise through Peter truly offers us, above all else, great comfort and a ground of sure hope.

[Chapter 1] True Fellowship with God
1:1-4 _ The motive for writing this book
The purpose of writing 1 John lies in 'the fullness of joy through fellowship' of saved believers.
Saved believers have joy (1 Peter 1:8-9), and for that joy to become fuller they need right fellowship with God and Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:9). Salvation is not an event of a single moment but a life to be enjoyed in a continuing relationship with God. Just as a married couple must continually cultivate their relationship with each other even after marriage, believers too must have fellowship with God daily. The deeper this fellowship becomes, the fuller the joy.
1) The basis of fellowship is Christ, who is the mediator.
2) A person who has become an eyewitness of the word is a witness of Christ.
1:5-2:11 _ The attitude of true fellowship with God
1:5-7 _ Walking in the light
God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all. God is called the 'Father of the heavenly lights' (James 1:17), and everything that belongs to the light comes from God. Darkness, on the other hand, has nothing to do with God. Therefore if a person is in darkness and yet says he has fellowship with God, that is a lie. True fellowship is accomplished when one walks in the light. This is because for fellowship to be harmonious, there must be an equal footing.
Then what does it mean to dwell in the light? This does not mean not sinning at all. It means that when God points out a fault, one immediately admits it and turns back. A clean room is not a room with no dust at all, but a room that is cleaned each time it gets dirty.
... the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).
'Us' = it means saved believers, and it means that he cleanses not only from the punishment of sin but even from sins committed in daily life. That is, he purifies us daily for complete fellowship with God.
1:8-10 _ Confession of sin and forgiveness
"If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves" (1 John 1:8)
If a saved person says that there is no inclination to sin or fallen nature in his flesh, he is deceiving himself, and it is like making God out to be a liar.
Then a saved person must admit that there is a sinful nature within him, and when he has sinned he must confess honestly to God.
Confess (Greek homologeo) = 'to say the same thing, as it is.' That is, when God calls it sin, to admit it and agree with it as it is is confession. When God points out our fault by his word, an attitude of not denying it but admitting, "Yes, that is right," is needed.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins" (1 John 1:9)
That is, it is a promise that he forgives and cleanses the sin that has been confessed. Also, "cleanses us from all unrighteousness" means that God thoroughly purifies even the sins of which we are not aware.
Confession takes place in the relationship of father and son. Before we were saved, our relationship with God was that of judge and prisoner. The judge demands the price of sin, and if the price of sin is not paid, he judges. But after being saved, we became children of God.
God, who is our Father, deals with us in love, and when we have done wrong he wants us to confess. This is not for judgment but for loving discipline and restoration. Therefore believers must admit and confess their sins honestly every day for the sake of fellowship with God. (Matthew 6:9-13)

Before being saved, even if there is a will to obey, one cannot follow the word because the Holy Spirit does not dwell within. But because the Holy Spirit is with a saved person, when he has a heart to obey, the strength to obey is also given.

When we obey the word, we can know that the love of God is perfected in us.

A person has no ability to love his neighbor as he loves his own body. But to us who are saved he gave a new commandment. He spoke of love for the brothers: 'Love one another.' But what differs from the old commandment is that we are to love 'as I have loved you.'
In the past we had no ability to love, but now we do. This is because Jesus showed love in person and put that love into us. So because love has come to be in us, he gave the command to love, and it is natural.
But one who does not love his brother and hates him is evidence that he does not dwell in the light (fellowship). That person is one who has not been saved. A person who has not been saved is in the end one who does not know where he is going, that is, one who has not prepared a place to go. Why? Because his eyes are shut. (John 9:41, Psalms 82:5)

If faith stands still, it regresses. Just as a bicycle falls over when it stops, faith too must keep growing. That is, we must advance into deeper fellowship with God.
1. The word given to the children: ① They are sure that their sins are forgiven ② They know God as Father
The young faith that has been saved clearly knows that sins have been forgiven through the Lord's merit. It realizes that God is the Father and provider of the saved. (Romans 8:15-16, Galatians 4:6)

3. The word given to the fathers: They come to know God deeply
As in the words 'you know him who is from the beginning,' beyond God as provider, they come to realize God himself more deeply.
15-17 _ We must be on guard against loving the world
First. If you love the world, the love of the Father is gone.
Second. Everything in this world, the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, has come from the devil.
Third. This world is passing away. 'Passing away' means that it will be here for a short time and then disappear. Whatever is in time and space will someday vanish. Only the eternal remains. When this world is judged by God and burned, everything in this world will also burn up and disappear. When this world burns, what one has set his hope on in this world will also burn, and his hope will become vain. (2 Corinthians 4:18, 1 Corinthians 7:31, Habakkuk 2:13)

18-26 _ A warning against the antichrist and his deceptive teaching
The antichrist is one who opposes Christ and will appear during the seven-year tribulation at the end time. Also, there are many who resemble the antichrist, and Scripture tells us to be on guard against such false teaching.
We will not see the antichrist who will appear in the tribulation, but we must be careful about false teaching. The nearer the last time draws, the more antichrists will appear, and already in the early church there were many antichrists (Matthew 24:4-5, 11, 24, 2 Corinthians 2:17).
The teaching of the antichrist causes people to deny that Jesus is the Christ. In particular, it typically denies the truth that sins are forgiven through the blood of Jesus and claims that one can be saved by spiritual knowledge (gnosis) (2 Peter 2:1).
Those who accept such false teaching and depart from the truth lose fellowship with God. If someone says at first that he received forgiveness of sins through the blood of Jesus but then falls into false doctrine and denies this, it finally reveals that he was not saved.
Therefore we must hold fast to the truth we heard from the beginning (1 Corinthians 15:1-2, 1 Corinthians 2:2, 2 Peter 1:12-13). Only then can we dwell in fellowship with God.
27-29 _ An exhortation to abide in the teaching of the Holy Spirit
The Holy Spirit is the author of Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16, 2 Peter 1:21), and because the Holy Spirit is in the church, no other teaching is needed. There is no need to add anything of the world. The Holy Spirit teaches us everything needed through Scripture, and abiding in that teaching is itself abiding in the church.
If we abide in the teaching of the Holy Spirit, we will not be ashamed when the Lord returns. Conversely, even if one has been saved, leaving that teaching results in a shameful salvation (1 Corinthians 3:10-15, Proverbs 18:1, John 15:3).

[Chapter 3] The Life of Believers in Fellowship with God 1

1-2 _ The status of believers (saved persons)
① 'Children of God' are those who have experienced the love of the cross.
② The reason the world does not recognize the children of God is that it does not know God and Christ.

[Chapter 4] The Life of Believers in Fellowship with God 2
4:1-6 _ Discerning false truth and true truth
This passage speaks of the Spirit of God (the Holy Spirit) and the spirit of the antichrist (the spirit of deception). The Holy Spirit dwells in a saved person, and the spirit of the antichrist is in a person who is not saved. Therefore the way their lives look cannot but differ, and we must by all means discern this.
1) Does he acknowledge the incarnation of Jesus Christ?
Jesus came to this earth to deal with our sins and to save us. To confess Jesus is not simply to believe in the incarnation, but to believe and follow him as the Savior who has resolved one's own sins. One who confesses Jesus lives by welcoming and exalting him as the master of his life.
2) Does he live a life set apart from the world? (Romans 12:2)
A saved person is one called out of the world and lives overcoming the world. A person who is not saved is assimilated to the world, lives together with the world, and is approved by the people of the world (John 15:19, John 17:14).
3) Does he hear and obey the word of God? (Ezekiel 33:30-32, 2 Timothy 4:3-4)
A saved person belongs to God, and so hears and obeys the word of God. A person who is not saved has no interest in the word of God and ignores and rejects it.
4) Does he love the truth?
The Holy Spirit is 'the Spirit of truth,' and a saved person comes to love and follow the truth. On the other hand, those who dislike and reject the truth belong to the spirit of deception.
4:7-10 _ The source of love
The source of love lies in God. 'God is love.' That love of God was shown to people. He sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. So it makes clear that love certainly did not start from us.
4:11-18 _ The effect of love
In this passage the word 'love' is used 14 times as a noun and 15 times as a verb. Together with 1 Corinthians 13, this chapter is the part of the Bible that emphasizes love most. But there are differences.
	•	1 John 4 emphasizes the origin of love.
	•	1 Corinthians 13 emphasizes the practice of love and describes love in verb form.
The source of love is God, and we who have received God's love must imitate that love and put it into practice (2 Samuel 1:26, Matthew 5:46-48).
1) When we believe in the love of the cross, the fear of judgment disappears.
2) When we love one another, the Lord abides in us and we abide in the Lord. This is evidence that we are in fellowship with the Lord.
3) A person in whom love has been made perfect can have boldness on the day of judgment. This is because he has been changed into the likeness of the Lord (Romans 13:8-10, 2 Peter 1:5-7).
4:19-21 _ An urging to practice love
A saved person loves God and loves his brother. It says that the claim of one who does not love the brother he can see to love the God he cannot see is a lie. Just as one who loves a parent loves those born of that parent, one who loves God likewise loves those who are equally saved children of God, that is, brothers.

[Chapter 5] Faith as the Basis of True Fellowship
5:1-5 _ Faith as the basis of true fellowship
In 1 John 5:1, 'everyone who believes' is used in the present tense, and 'born' in the past perfect.
	⁃	'Born' (past perfect) → it means that one has already become a child of God. Our salvation is a fact already accomplished in the past.
	⁃	'Everyone who believes' (present tense) → it means not simply that one believed in the past, but that one continues to believe now.
If one believed in the past but does not believe now, that faith was false (Matthew 13:20-21).
Faith is the basis of everything
	⁃	The relationship with God and love for the brothers begin with believing that Jesus is the Son of God and the Christ.
	⁃	Through this faith we can love God, love the brothers, and overcome the world.
	⁃	The 'one who overcomes' in Revelation means one who overcomes by faith.
	⁃	In the Old Testament, Samson had great power when he had faith, but became powerless when he abandoned faith.
Why keeping the commandments is not burdensome
1) The Holy Spirit helps: the Holy Spirit gives a heart and ability to obey (Deuteronomy 30:14, Ezekiel 36:26, Jeremiah 31:32, Hebrews 10:16, Philippians 2:13).
2) One comes to obey with joy: before being saved, the world was attractive, but after being saved, doing the will of God becomes more joyful and valuable. The believers of the early church shared what they had without holding back, and this was possible because they had obtained what is eternal.
5:6-12 _ Christ, the object of faith
The object of our faith is Jesus Christ. Scripture speaks of three things that testify to Christ. It says they are the Spirit, the water, and the blood.
Jesus died on the cross and shed blood. The blood of Christ testifies. And that fact is recorded in the word. The word testifies. And the Holy Spirit opens our hearts and makes us realize what Christ has done. Therefore there are three who testify.
We accept human testimony too. How much more certain is the testimony of God. God has testified to Jesus Christ as the object of our faith. Not to believe is to make God out to be a liar.
Also, the one who believes has the testimony within himself. It is believing the word that the blood of Jesus has resolved sin. That is, believing the testimony of Scripture, accepting the enlightenment of the Holy Spirit, and being assured of redemption through the blood of Jesus. This itself is the testimony.
5:13-15 _ The result of faith
① One who believes has eternal life.
② As children, we know that when we ask the Father for anything, he hears. (Psalms 5:2-3, Psalms 55:17, Song of Solomon 2:14)
③ The faith that he hears gives us assurance of an answer. (John 16:23-24)
5:16-21 _ The command to intercede, and the preservation of believers
5:16-17 _ The command to intercede
This word was given to saved persons. This is because it begins with the words 'If anyone sees his brother.' And the death spoken of here is not hell but physical death. It means that if a brother sins and does not turn back, and God has decided to put him to death, there is no longer any need to pray. (Jeremiah 7:16, 11:14)
5:18-20 _ The preservation of believers
5:21 _ A warning against idolatry

1) Abiding in truth and love - 2 John 1:1-3
Abiding in the truth is repeated three times.
Because Jesus is the truth, living by following the Lord's teaching is an essential part of the Christian life. And the Lord's true disciples hold fast to his word of truth and obey it. For us to be people who are faithful to the Lord's teaching, we must above all strive to know Scripture accurately. We must not distort the message of Scripture to fit our own needs or purposes, but must live by the pure word as it is, taught by the Holy Spirit alone.
2) Let us love one another - 2 John 1:4-6
The command of Jesus given to Christians is to 'love one another.' This is the basic element of the true church. To show our love for the Lord, we must live by following the Lord's command to love other people. That is, there must be the practice of love that helps, gives, and shares.
A Christian's love is not a love that likes anything or anyone without thought. The love taught in Scripture is a matter of choice. This is because indiscriminate love is dangerous and foolish. The false teachers deny that Christ came into this world in the flesh. Therefore the act of opening the door to false teaching is false compassion. We must have fellowship with God, and we must have fellowship with and love believers who hold the truth within the truth.
3) A warning against heresy - 2 John 1:7-10
Christians must be on guard against religious leaders who are not faithful to the word of truth. They must not associate or fellowship with them and their followers, and must discern truth from falsehood and be on guard so that the false religionists who teach falsehood have no place to gain a foothold.
4) Closing greeting in the hope of a face-to-face visit - 2 John 1:12-13
Because he has much to say, he expresses the wish to visit in person and speak face to face rather than by letter, and makes clear that this is to make complete the joy of the believers chosen by God.

[Introduction]
1:1 Greeting
1:2-4 A prayer of blessing for Gaius, who walks in the truth, and an expression of the apostle's joy
2 _ Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers.
The apostle John earnestly prayed for health and prosperity for Gaius, who had devoted himself to the itinerant teachers. This shows that physical blessing must be based on the spiritual, and it also carries the meaning of refuting the Gnostic thought of that time, which separated body and spirit.
'As' (Greek kathos) = it means 'in the same way,' emphasizing that body and soul cannot be separated.
John also warned against dualistic Gnosticism in 2 John, and in this book too he teaches that since both soul and body are creations of God, neither should be neglected.
'To prosper' = prosperity in all things continues / 'I pray that you may enjoy good health' = it means physical health
John continued to pray that Gaius would receive God's blessing in every respect, in soul, body, and daily life. What is important is that this intercessory prayer is not for everyone but applies to those who obey and walk in the truth. For those who have not been born again, those who slander the church, and the proud, the priority is not blessing but praying that they will repent and return to the Lord.
In the end, if one lives a life devoted to God and the church and loved by believers, like Gaius, Jesus too will intercede at the right hand of God for the health and prosperity of our soul and body.
3 _ For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk.
The people who brought news about Gaius to the apostle John were the itinerant teachers, called 'strangers' (verse 5) and 'brothers' (verse 10). In the early church they were appointed to help the apostles by preaching the gospel and caring for the churches, and they visited local churches and reported to the apostles.
'Came' (Greek erchomenon) = it means they visited several times. It shows that the itinerant teachers repeatedly gave good testimony about Gaius.
Gaius put into practice in his life the truth of the gospel he had received, and he warmly welcomed and supported the itinerant teachers, helping them to carry out faithfully their mission of evangelism. In the early church, caring for and showing hospitality to traveling evangelists was the due duty of believers.
'Walk' (peripateo) = a verb meaning everyday life; the use of the present tense shows that Gaius's faith was continuous and unchanging.
John rejoiced greatly at this. Also, the reason John described Gaius's good deeds as 'walking in the truth' is to contrast them with the evil deeds of Diotrephes (verses 9-11). That is, he emphasizes that conduct shown in actual life is the true truth, and truth separated from life is false.
John rejoiced that Gaius held to the truth and lived faithfully for the church, and even as he was writing the letter his emotion did not fade. To John, who had gone through many hardships, the faithfulness of Gaius was an exceedingly great joy.
[Main body]
1:5-8 Praise and encouragement for Gaius, who welcomes the itinerant teachers
Through praise and encouragement for Gaius (verses 5-8) and rebuke of Diotrephes (verses 9-10), this passage shows the attitude of one who walks rightly in the truth.
John first praises Gaius's good deeds (verse 5) and encourages him to keep doing good (verses 6-8). Gaius's good deed was to receive and treat generously the strangers, that is, the itinerant teachers. This was a practice faithful to the law (Leviticus 19:34, Deuteronomy 10:19) and to the teaching of Jesus (Matthew 10:40).
By contrast, Diotrephes and some others mistreated the itinerant teachers for various reasons, but Gaius took the lead in serving them with material help and a warm heart. Through this contrast John emphasizes how exemplary Gaius's conduct was.
5 _ Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you.
Gaius spared no effort and welcomed warmly the itinerant teachers (the brothers, the strangers) so that they could devote themselves to preaching the gospel and pastoral work. His continuing good deeds were reported even to the apostle John through the itinerant teachers.
'Brothers, and strangers' = refers to the itinerant teachers who travel to various places to preach the gospel. Reflecting the original, it means 'brothers, especially strangers.' That is, 'brothers' includes all Christians, and 'strangers' refers to a particular group who travel for the gospel. 'Faithful' (Greek piston) = a word derived from 'pistis,' which means 'faith' and 'belief'; it means not mere human faithfulness but a loyal manner that comes from right faith. That is, Gaius's love for the brothers was not done perfunctorily but was the practice of genuine love rooted in his faith.
6 _ You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God.
This verse implies that the itinerant teachers visited Gaius again, carrying the apostle John's letter. Also, John asks Gaius to treat them well and send them on to the region where they are going.
'In a manner worthy of God' = 'in a way worthy in God's sight, in keeping with God's viewpoint,' that is, it means 'treat the itinerant teachers as God's representatives.'
'Send them on their way' (Greek propempsas) = it means to send them off by providing supplies and travel expenses needed for the journey. That is, a request to support the itinerant teachers actively so that they can continue their ministry.
8 _ Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
The apostle John says that it is right to help the itinerant teachers and meet their needs. This is because they work 'for the sake of the name' and receiving them is the same as receiving Christ (Matthew 10:41-42).
'Support' = 'to receive under one roof'; it emphasizes that the church and believers should invite evangelists who preach the gospel into their homes and serve them with food and material help.
This contrasts with the teaching of 2 John (2 John 1:10-11), which said not even to greet false teachers, and means that love and hospitality should be shown to those who convey the truth.
'We ought' = 'what a debtor must do'; it emphasizes that it is a natural duty for believers who have received grace through the gospel to help those who spread the gospel.
'For the truth' => 'truth' = for the apostle John it means 'eternal life' or 'Christ,' the gospel of Christ's salvation, distinguished from the false teaching of the Gnostic heretics.
Another reason to receive itinerant teachers is that, even if one cannot take part directly in evangelism, by showing hospitality to evangelists one cooperates in mission work as a fellow worker in mission.
1:9-10 Rebuke and warning for the proud Diotrephes
It points out the evil conduct of Diotrephes, in contrast to the good deeds of Gaius, and emphasizes that one must be on guard against him.
Diotrephes, as a leader of the church to which Gaius belonged, should have been an example, but because of a heart that 'loves to be first' he instead rejected the itinerant teachers. Fearing that his authority and vested interests would be weakened, he
	•	did not receive the itinerant teachers and slandered them, and
	•	even excommunicated the believers who helped them, acting in a way unfit for a church leader.
John therefore states that he will visit the church in person and discipline Diotrephes, and exhorts Gaius to be on guard against his evil conduct.
9 _ I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction.
The apostle John had sent a letter to the church to which Gaius belonged before, but it is presumed that Diotrephes did not accept it and rejected it. That letter probably included an exhortation to welcome the itinerant teachers and a pointing out of Diotrephes's fault.
Because of his desire to become a leader, Diotrephes disregarded John's authority, and not only did not receive the itinerant teachers but also prevented the members from receiving them. This serves as a warning about the 'lust for power' into which leaders easily fall.
'Diotrephes' = 'nourished by Zeus'; in the end he became an unfortunate figure who departed from the teaching of God.
10 _ So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church. (1:10)
The apostle John points out Diotrephes's disobedience and says he will visit the church in person and expose his fault.
Diotrephes committed five faults:
	•	He loved to be first - he coveted the position of leader (verse 9)
	•	He rejected the apostle John - he disregarded his authority (verse 9)
	•	He slandered John with malicious words - he spread false accusations and gossip (verse 10)
	•	He did not receive the itinerant teachers - it seems he rejected them in order to be recognized as the teacher (verse 10)
	•	He drove out of the church even those who helped them - he hindered believers who wanted to do good (verse 10)
Diotrephes may have put forward the pretext of protecting the church from false teachers and persecutors. But John makes clear that his conduct was an evil deed that caused groundless slander and division in the church. In particular, he emphasizes that although it is a problem that one himself does not do good, it is a greater sin to hinder those who want to do good, and teaches that one must be on guard against groundless slander and division.
1:11 An exhortation to Gaius to imitate what is good
The apostle John, concerned that the evil conduct of Diotrephes might influence even Gaius, exhorts him to be on guard against him. He then presents Demetrius as a good example and stresses that Gaius must not imitate Diotrephes.
The original does not have the expression 'imitate'; the expression 'do not imitate' is what is emphasized. This means that keeping away from the conduct of Diotrephes is all the more important.
The reason the northern kingdom of Israel was destroyed was also that they imitated the evil of Jeroboam and followed the practices of the nations that God had forbidden (2 Kings 17:5-23). This shows how great the consequence of following what is evil is. In the end, only by turning away from evil can one begin to do good. Therefore it emphasizes that abandoning evil is a more urgent matter than doing good.
'One who does good' means, as said in verses 5-8 above, one who loves the brothers and welcomes strangers in accordance with the word of truth. This proves that they belong to God, that is, that they are saved children of God (1 John 3:10).
On the other hand, those who do evil show that they have never seen God. So the apostle John exhorts Gaius to imitate what is good and be one who belongs to God.
'Has not seen' = it means 'has never seen even once until now.' This is because the Gnostics of that time and Diotrephes, who was led astray by them, claimed that they alone had had a mystical experience of seeing God.
They said that they alone had seen God and had special spiritual knowledge, but John clearly points out that they have never seen God even once. This does not mean seeing God with the physical eye, but refers to genuine salvation of the soul.
1:12 Introduction to and praise of Demetrius
There are various views about Demetrius, but it is not possible to know exactly who he was.
'Demetrius' = 'belonging to Demeter,' the Greek god of grain, which indicates that he was a convert from paganism. The silversmith who caused the riot in Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41) also had the same name.
Demetrius was a faithful man who received testimony from everyone and from the truth (the gospel) itself, and he was a good example of a Christian. John says that Demetrius is a person whom Gaius also already knows.
The reason John mentions Demetrius is that he is one of the itinerant evangelists who had been with the church of Gaius and returned to John, and he is about to go again to Gaius carrying this letter. John wants to stress that he is a good person completely different from Diotrephes, whom he rebuked earlier.
The apostle John presents three testimonies about Demetrius:
1) The testimony of all people: he had a good reputation among everyone inside and outside the church.
2) The testimony of the truth: he put the word of God into practice in life and was approved by the truth itself.
3) The testimony of the apostle John and the church: John and his friends also testified to Demetrius's good deeds.
Demetrius was a blessed man whose faithfulness was recognized by both God and people, and his life gives a good lesson to Christian teachers.
[Conclusion]
1:13-15 Closing words, blessing, and greetings
13 _ I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink.
It shows the heart of the apostle John, who wants to fellowship with Gaius and tell him more but feels frustrated by the limits of the letter form. It means that he has much to say but will stop with the letter and say it by visiting in person.
By announcing his own visit to Gaius and the church to which he belongs, these words of John also comfort the believers who are suffering from the evil conduct of Diotrephes (verse 10).
14 _ Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face.
The apostle John intended to visit Gaius and his church and discuss the problems mentioned earlier (verses 9-10). It seems he intended to visit suddenly, either while traveling around the churches or so as not to be noticed by Diotrephes and his group.
'I hope' (Greek elpizo) = it means not merely 'expect' but 'trust'; this shows that John not only earnestly wished to see Gaius but was confident of the meeting. 'Face to face' = it means to talk 'mouth to mouth,' 'face to face' (NASB, NIV 'face to face'). This shows the apostle John's deep love and affection for believers.
John, though over ninety years old, had a burning passion for Christ and the church. He intended to act without delay, not only to share joy but also to resolve the difficulties of the church and to deal with the problem concerning the evil leader Diotrephes.
15 _ Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name.
Peace - Old Testament (Hebrew shalom): 1) mainly 'a peaceful state without war' 2) derived from 'make restitution' (Exodus 22:6), a state of being freed by paying a debt, meaning 'complete' and 'safe.' In Scripture it is used mainly in relation to God, and it expresses the peace of heart and spiritual safety that come when the relationship with God is restored. Peace - New Testament (Greek eirene): 1) 'the state in which reconciliation between God and people has been accomplished through Christ' 2) a quiet state of heart with no disturbance at all, like a wilderness. = a state achieved when the dividing wall with God is torn down and God's grace fills the heart
The apostle John blesses Gaius that he may enjoy this peace through a right relationship with God.
A person who has such peace is not shaken by outside temptation or confusion and can go forward firmly in the truth. John prayed that this peace would come upon Gaius.
'By name' = 'according to the name'
John urged Gaius to remember the names of all his fellow workers in the faith whom he could not mention one by one and to convey his greetings to each of them individually. In a church situation where people like Diotrephes, who follow heretical teachings and persecute the brothers, take the lead in exerting a bad influence, greetings that comfort one another and look after and encourage them so that they do not fall again into wrong teaching must have been all the more necessary.

1:3-4 _ The motive for writing
Jude states that he had originally intended to write to the believers about the gospel of salvation, but because of the false teachers who had infiltrated the church he had to change the purpose of the letter.
He urges the believers to "contend earnestly for the faith" and warns that the false teachers are distorting the faith within the church and promoting licentiousness.

Jude states that the false teachers have crept in secretly, abuse the grace of God, and deny Jesus Christ.
Outwardly they look like people of faith, but in reality they are corrupt and are those who will be judged by God.
“For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.” (Jude 1:4)
1:5-7 _ Historical precedents of God's judgment on the unrighteous
Jude cites historical examples of those who disobeyed God and were judged, and is confident of the destruction of the false teachers.
1) The people of Israel who perished through unbelief after the exodus (Jude 1:5)
2) The judgment of the fallen angels (Jude 1:6)
3) The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Jude 1:7)

Jude exposes that the false teachers sin by following visions, despise authority, and oppose God. Their sins are similar to those of the wicked in the Old Testament.
1) The way of Cain: greed and murder (Jude 1:11)
2) The way of Balaam: false teaching for money (Jude 1:11)
3) The way of Korah: rebellion against God (Jude 1:11)
“These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted.” (Jude 1:12)
1:14-16 _ The certainty of judgment on the heretics
Jude quotes the prophecy of Enoch and warns that the false teachers will surely be judged by God. They are those who grumble and complain, live by their passions, and speak arrogant words while flattering others for the sake of gain.
“Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.”” (Jude 1:14-15)
1:17-23 _ A warning against heresy and exhortation
Jude says that the apostles had already warned that false teachers would appear, and urges the believers to keep the faith.
1) Build yourselves up on your faith
2) Pray in the Holy Spirit
3) Keep yourselves in the love of God
4) Wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ
He also stresses having mercy on those who have been led astray and rescuing them from sin.
“save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.” (Jude 1:23)
1:24-25 _ Conclusion
Jude concludes the epistle by praising God, who keeps the believers and makes them stand holy and in joy.
“Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy—” (Jude 1:24)

[Chapter 7] [Interlude Chapter] The 144,000 Jews Who Are Sealed
The key to understanding Revelation 7 is the expression 'After this' (Revelation 7:1, 9). Depending on whether one takes it as a temporal sequence or as a change of scene, the interpretation of the whole of Revelation differs.
Some interpretations understand 'After this' as a temporal sequence and claim that during the seven-year tribulation 144,000 Jews are saved and become evangelists, and through them 'a great multitude that no one could count' is saved. But this interpretation is not correct. If 'After this' meant a temporal sequence, then after the plagues of the sixth seal (earthquakes, falling meteorites, and so on), world peace would suddenly come, 144,000 would be saved, and they would evangelize for a short time so that 'a great multitude that no one could count' would be saved. But such a claim is unrealistic.
Therefore 'After this' means a change of scene. After the plague of the sixth seal appears in Revelation 6, chapter 7 shows a different situation from a new perspective.

7:9-12 _ The Christians saved during the church age, seen in heaven by the apostle John
7:13-17 _ The future of the saved, seen in advance by the apostle John

[Chapter 20] The Millennial Kingdom and the Final Judgment
In church history many problems arose from misinterpreting Revelation 20. If Revelation 20 is understood correctly, one can be freed from many historical errors. In the latter part of Revelation 19 the scene of Jesus returning to the earth is recorded. And in chapter 20 appears the Lord, who has returned to the earth, establishing the millennial kingdom.
20:1-3 _ Satan is bound for a thousand years
'The Abyss' = 'a bottomless, endless pit'; it is used only for the devil and demons. God prepared it to confine the angels who sinned temporarily.
The demons know well that they will go into the Abyss in the future (Luke 8:30-31). The devil and the demons will go into the Abyss for a thousand years just before the millennial kingdom. But the Abyss is not the devil's final place. After the millennial kingdom ends, the devil will finally be thrown into the eternal lake of fire in hell.
20:4-6 _ The believers reign with Christ
'Those seated on thrones who were given authority to judge' = all the believers of the Old and New Testament ages who were raptured before the seven-year tribulation (Revelation 4:4, Ephesians 1:20, 2:4-6, Luke 22:28-30).
'The souls of those who had been beheaded for their testimony of Jesus and for the word of God' and 'those who had not worshiped the beast or its image and had not received its mark on their foreheads or hands' are the same persons. They refer to the 144,000 Jews saved during the seven-year tribulation (Revelation 6:9-11, 14:9-13, 15:2)
The first resurrection = the resurrection of saved believers (resurrected in glorious form before the millennial kingdom) => after reigning with Christ for a thousand years they live in the eternal new heaven and new earth. The second resurrection = the resurrection of judgment (resurrected after the millennial kingdom). 'The rest of the dead did not come to life until the thousand years were completed' => 'the rest of the dead' = all who were not saved. Between the resurrection of life and the resurrection of judgment there is a time gap of a thousand years (John 5:28-29, Acts 24:15)
20:7-10 _ The final rebellion of Satan, released, who is defeated
When the millennial kingdom begins, the devil is confined in the Abyss and disappears from the world. But after a thousand years the devil is released and deceives 'Gog and Magog,' that is, all the forces opposed to the Lord. At that time people are divided into two groups. Many who had seemed to serve the Lord will take the devil's side, and their number will be like the sand of the sea.
Therefore being born in the millennial kingdom is not necessarily a blessing. The people of the millennial kingdom also must pass the devil's test, and in the end each must choose. Finally God throws the devil and his followers into the eternal lake of fire. The antichrist and the false prophet go into the lake of fire first (Revelation 19:20), and John witnesses and explains that after a thousand years the devil meets the same fate.
20:11-15 _ The great white throne judgment, and the eternal judgment of death and Hades
